COMMODORE 'S NOTES

With the end of the Sailing Season, we have held the Laying Up Supper at the Heybridge which was an ex tremely pleasant evening. On behalf of us all I would like to thank Peter Bloomfield and the Social Committee for organising the event.

AMENDMENTS TO BYE LAWS

The Main Committee have approved the following Bye Law amendments and additions as indicated by the passages underlined. These amendments become effective from 15th October 1989

6. CAMPING

Camping shall be restricted to members and their Guests except that it shall be open to members of R.Y.A clubs attending open race meetings at the Club. Camping shall only be permitted at times decided by the Committee,

Before establishing camp, members shall report to the camping marshall or the 0.0.D., to pay the appropriate fee and receive any instructions on siting. No tent or caravan is to be on the site prior to 0830 hrs on the

first day of camping and all tents and caravans must be removed before 2100 hrs on the last day of camping.

9. Winter Storage.

Only those boats for which a Winter Storage fee has been paid may be left on the site between lst December and Ist March, All such boats are to be visibly marked with the Class of boat, Name and Telephone number of the Owner, The owner of any boat left on the site between the above dates for which a Storage Fee has not been paid will be subject to a fine not exceeding twice the Storage Fee which would have been payable.

OSEA ICICLE:

As OOD at this event, I would remind potential sailors that personal buoyancy will be required to be worn by helms and crews to qualify for the race. The Club also requires that wet or dry suits must be worn by competitors. The water will be extremely cold whatever the air temperature on the day, and these rules will be enforced,

It should also be said that the Club rules are the minimum requirements for personal safety, but as always it is the individual's own responsibility to decide if he/she is adequately experienced and kitted out for the conditions on the day.

Let's hope for a fine day and some good sailing.

Cruiser Fleet AGM: Wednesday 31st January 1990, 8pm, Conference Room, MASC, Beehive Lane,

Mooring Buoys It breaks my heart to see so many defunct and deflated Mooring Buoys coming up at the end of each season, (Especially as one of them was mine.) I have approached Hippo Marine who manufacture buoys for

most of the time,

10% discount. The cost for the S83 buoy will be in the region of £108 and the SB2 £139, less any discount I
can get.

Derek Hall, Billericay (0277) [redacted].

HANDICAP NEWS

Having been asked to represent the Handicap Fleet for next year, the first thing I must do is get to know its members, Being a relatively new member of the Club, there are many of you whose faces I cannot put a name to, although I may well have spoken to you during the course of 1989, So let's have a Handicap Fleet Meet ing/New Year's Drink/or even an AGM! We are going to hold this at the Crown Pub at Sandon, on Thursday llth January
1990 at 8pm.

Potentially the Handicap Fleet is the largest at the Club with some 70-odd craft in the Dinghy park. Unfortunately only a handful of these have participated in the Club's racing programme during the past season and those of us who do race regularly on Sundays share the disappointment of the small turnout from the Handicap Fleet. There is no doubt that racing will improve your sailing skills and help you to tune your boat for a better performance. The Club provided a full sailing programme from March through to November, together with a most efficient race organisation team and competent rescue cover for participants.

Last year Mike Duckmanton ran a race training day which was of tremendous help to those who attended. I think that Mike was a little disappointed that so few attended and I am hopeful that we can persuade him to repeat the programme at the beginning of next season (but hopefully to a larger class!)

For those taking part in Handicap racing it is important to have a large fleet to race against, so that both the faster and the slower boats have some similar handicaps to race against. So step forward all you dinghy sailors, we would like to meet you on the water on Sundays. The sailing committee has assured me that the Race Officers will not be setting such testing courses as seen recently in the Whitbread Round the World!

I would be delighted to hear from anyone who has any ideas or suggestions directed towards encouraging members to join in the Club's racing programme, I look forward to meeting you on Thursday 11 January in The Crown at
Sandon - please try to attend.

Meanwhile, Merry Christmas and Happy New Year

Ian Caruth, Handicap Fleet Captain, Chelmsford [redacted]

AN EXPERIENCE NOT TO BE MISSED 4,

The transition from one hull to two wasn't as smooth as I expected (or hoped!) All through the Summer and Autumn Series I had threatened to join the Cat Fleet with some late starts in my Enterprise and my chance arrived to try it officially in Autumn Points 11, On arriving at the Club I learned that the Boreham Dart was looking for a 'heavier crew'!, Well, “I'm game if you are,” making my first bad decision of the day. I eased myself into a borrowed trapeze harness and, walking on tiptoe, made my way to the hard,

Up with the mainsail, adjustment to the jib and into the water. A few beats up and down the Blackwater to find my sea legs so to speak, and into the race, “Don't hang on to the shroud, just lie back on the wire,"
Right. Away we went wondering where the two Mercurys were hidden, "Abandon Ship,” or was it "Oh Sh... I

heard, Anyway I was ahead of the game seeing the leeward hull dipping into the water and the windward hull rear high above me, I had somehow become detached from my wire as if the automatic ejector button had been pressed, "If I enter the water head first, the hull can only come down on my feet,” I thought. If I could only remember the technique and tidy up my entry, I think I'd stand a good chance in the World Springboard

Championship, Now with the capsized Dart being blown towards Bradwell, I found myself all alone in the Blackwater, Ship Ahoy! two Darts heading for me; are they coming to finish me off? No, one of them tacked away leaving me firmly in Dave Onyon's sights. Up I climbed, feeling relieved at last to be pulled from the
water,

While all this was going on Damian had managed to right the Dart and made ready to sail again. "Right,

there's your boat - jump." Back I was in the water, to be quickly hauled aboard and ordered to return to my
station, Unfortunately with three sail battens broken we couldn't join the race so it was back to the club and an ‘early bath',

The wind eased a little after lunch and I thought let's get back to sanity and take the Enterprise out, Tr proved to be my second bad decision of the day. The Hellewells joined us and we had a Handicap Fleet for the afternoon race, All rigged up, away from the hard and away we went in plenty of time to get a good start, I looked back and, yes, 'Paranoid' was in the water with the wind starting to blow up a bit, Did I say "back to
sanity?” Once again the cry of “Oh sh...” rang out as the boom and gooseneck fitting was torn away from the
mast, Nowhere to sail but the way I was pointing and beach the boat on Osea Island. What would we do without

that last straw to grasp? Lose half the fleet, no doubt,

Where did all that wind suddenly come from? and the waves! Still, at least we were upright and relatively

sate holding onto the Enterprise just off Osea beach, While I took down the sails, Baddow Star was launched to our rescue and we were towed back to the Club for another early bath, Thankfully, only minor damage, but ales the end of an enjoyable season for E 4021, After a few Eskimo Rolls 'Paranoid' came in under tow from Jack B end racing was abandoned. One by one the stricken Solos returned from No.2 buoy and some unusual sailing techniques were observed,

Well, I'm looking forward to next year and taking on the rest of the Handicap Fleet with my Enterprise 4021 after a winter lick of paint and varnish, Thanks, Damian for the brief taste of Catamaran sailing, tut I think I'll resist the temptation to change fleets. I prefer less contact with the water!

lan Caruth

IT'S A GREAT IDEA

(shame about the planning)

The MSC's Main Committee is always Willing to encourage new ideas and new approaches to the club's activities but, at the same time, the Main Committee has the duty to exercise a sensible
control over what is happening in the name of the club - that is why you, the MSC membership
as a whole, elect a main Committee to run the club on your behalf. There is no doubt that over recent years the club has become more adventurous and ‘high profile’ in its activities and public awareness. The revival of the Regatta, the introduction of the East Coast Piers Race and the embryo Osea Icicle, the various requests we receive to run special events for non-member groups
(eg. Gull nationals in 1989 and Dart Travellers Trophy races in 1990) and the gradual extention
of the club's own sailing season towards the 31 December each year all point towards a club which is changing, ever so gradually, in its basic character. These changes and new activities bring with them problems and implications which are not always appreciated by those who are suddenly blessed by a flash of brilliance . Things like insurance, safety, licencing laws, availability of equipment and services, the willingness of ‘people’ to do the less glamourous jobs that go with the ‘new idea’, even questions of tax, etc., have to be taken into account before embarking on a new venture. All these ‘problems’ are capped by the greatest ‘problem’
of al] - how much will it cost and who will pay ?

As a matter of policy, the main Committee wish to make it known that:-

(a) all proposals to extend the activities of the MSC should, in the first instance, be
put to the appropriate sub-committee. This does not only cover the obvious new ideas such as the introduction of new sailing events but also applies to ideas to extend the ‘official’ sailing programme outside the 'normal' period, introduce new social events, new equipments, new services, etc. The appropriate sub committees will usually be the following:-

- sailing sub-committee
- Social sub-Committee
- clubhouse sub-committee

(b) Since each sub-committee has one member serving on it who is a Flag Officer, the Main
Committee will automatically be made aware of the proposals being considered. Where the matter is purely ‘internal’ to the club, it will usually be considered sufficient for the sub-committee itself to make a final decision on the new proposals.

However, where the proposals involve matters ‘external' to the club, particularly matters which could affect its public relations/public awareness image, then the Main Committee might wish not only to be consulted but also to take the final decision on the acceptance or rejection of the proposals. Liaison between the main Committee and the sub-committees is always maintained by the appropriate Flag Officer or an appointed
deputy.

Similarly, where the proposals involve/imply non-budgeted expenditures or the collection of non-budgeted income in the name/on behalf of the MSC, the main Committee might exercise its prerogative to make the final decisions.

(c) No member of the MSC is permitted to issue press releases or make public statements in
the name of the club except with the prior approval of the appointed club Press Officer (in the case of established activities such as Regatta, ECPR, etc) or, in the absence of an appointed Press officer, with the prior approval of thé Main Committee or a Flag Officer.

If your reaction to this article is one of despair (ie. more ****** bureaucracy), just stop to think ‘who js responsible for the proper conduct of the club’ ? Nobody wants to unnecessarily curtail

activity at the club and past and current main Committees have invariably encouraged and supported

sensible new ideasy but some control has to be exercised otherwise you might find a keen member has
organised a camping convention for his/her favourite charity - right in the middle of Regatta,
E.C.P.R or the middle of winter when we ain't got no water supply !

FINAL COMMENT - NO MEMBER SHOULD ENTER DISCUSSIONS ON 'SPONSORSHIPS'
FOR THE CLUB
WITHOUT THE AGREEMENT OF THE MAIN COMMITTEE.

COMMODORE
'S ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING REPORT - NOV '89

The Club has this year seen a level of activity both on and off the water which exceeds that of the recent past and we must aim to nurture and carry forward this growth into the future, The weather this year has been exceptionally kind to us, The Regatta was extremely successful, and I must thank Malcolm Stuart and all the teams of helpers for the very smooth running of the event. Camping Fortnight was a success notwithstanding the problems of the water supply. The only really disastrous weekend for weather, coincided with the East Coast Piers Race,

Tasks Carried Out: During last Winter each Fleet undertook a specific task which resulted in a very much smarter appearance to the Clubhouse and Site, Early in the summer the Water Board carried out a4 major rebuilding of the seawall immediately in front of the Clubhouse and we took the opportunity to have the Hard resealed between the blocks, This was much cheaper than it would have been if carried out as a separate
exercise,

Social Events: The Barn Dance and Laying Up Supper of last Winter were both very well supported, But support for the Fitting Out and the Mid-Summer Parties was disappointing and I am sure that the Social Committee would welcome suggestions and help on ways of improving the popularity of these two events.

Future Tasks: This Winter we have a number of tasks to complete and the Fleet Captains have already agreed on the work to be carried out by each Fleet, Following changes in legislation relating to the use of Channel M2 by Clubs, we are having to replace all the Club radios over the winter, as those in both the Race Box an Clubhouse are illegal; and the radio on Jack B cannot be modified to use Channel M2, This will involve an expenditure of approximately £2,000, We should, however, end up with a communications system with many years of operational life, We also have the task of replacing the water main fraa the Gate to the Clubhouse, which will cost about £1500 and which the Main Club has agreed to fund.

Purchase of Field: We are currently negotiating with Cambridge University to buy the field beyond the Race Box which is an extension of the Cruiser Park, and again the Main Club has agreed to provide the money for this, Whilst this will allow us to utilise the existing space differently in the future, next Season the Cruiser trailers will be parked up there during the Summer so that a start can be made on improving the drainage of the Cruiser Park.

The Main Committee has accepted the recommendation of the Sailing Sub Committee that a second Rescue Boat
should be purchased, It is anticipated that the cost will be in the region of £6000 - £7000 and we have
approached the Main Club for their assistance and until a reply is received from them, no date can be given for its purchase,

As you are aware there have been problems with the Gate Lock this season, These have not been due to the lock mechanism itself but were caused by both pillars rising out of the ground and leaning apart. Our resident blacksmith/engineer Pete Clayton will be solving the problem for the future,

Clubhouse Extension: A further problem that the Main Committee has been examining is the size of the mar:
lounge area of the Clubhouse, because we are reaching the capacity of the Lounge on many occasions during the year, Also we have a permanent problem on Sundays after lunch with the state of the Lounge, which is normally wet underfoot and unpleasant for non-sailors to sit in. One solution would be to ban the wearing of wetsuits or wet clothes in the Lounge, which is impractical, Plans have been drawn up to extend the Lounge to the South, making it approximately twice the size, and providing a large workshop/storage area below, The first hurdle to overcome is that of planning permission which is now being pursued. However, the major problem will be the financing of the estimated cost of £60,000. We have approached the Main Club, but it is unlikely that this level of funding will be available, It will therefore be necessary for us to find a source of funds and to undertake to service the interest and repay the debt, Let's not back away because of the problems of funding, but tackle it, and provide the basis for the next twenty years of the continuing growth of the Club,

I would like to thank all who have helped me during this year. When so many are involved, it is hard to single out particular people, but Malcolm Stuart and George Robinson both retire from the Committee this year, Whilst Malcolm has been involved on the sailing side, the stature of the Club and its events have reached a peak due to his unflagging efforts, George has been involved with the Clubhouse and grounds and again has brought about some remarkable changes, In addition to them I would like to thank all those who have served on the Committees of the Club; those who have turned out at working parties; those who have had that marvellous idea, and when asked to carry it through have done so, and not left it "to the Committee"; those who have done the odd job for the Club of which none of us is aware, Without their support the Club would not function,

Lastly, I must thank a group without whom there would be no Club. I refer here to the wives and families of us all; they tolerate our absence whether we are sailing or serving on Committees, they support us by coming down to the site in all weathers and doing many tasks around the site which we take for granted, I believe that all of us who sail owe a major vote of thanks to them,

N.T. Pembleton, Commodore

THE BLACKWATER AND COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION = — BACSPA

Representing the yacht clubs of the Blackwater and Colne Rivers

Most of the boats have gone from our creeks and estuaries, leaving them to the Brent Geese, the ducks and the waders, A few hardy souls are still sailing, but I suspect that the majority are, like myself, sitting by the fire looking forward to the New Year and remembering a long sunny sailing season,

The year started quietly enough but, as often happens, some clouds have begun to gather. Most of the potential problems seem to relate to money-making schemes of one sort or another, usually at the expense of sailing man or woman, Light Dues, for example, have surfaced again as a proposal, and of course some well-known marks have disappeared in the name of economy. A new idea involves charges for laying racing marks, and I have no doubt that somewhere lurks a confidential file marked ‘Licensing of Yachtsmen' waiting to be dusted off at an appropriate timel

'Development' too gives us problems, The Colne Barrier Project bodes very badly for Wyvenhoe Sailing Club, that fine old Colne family club who have been put in a potentially difficult position by the loss of their traditional sailing water and moorings, On the Blackwater, the Saltcote Marina Scheme has reappeared as an outline plan, It is to be hoped that common sense will prevail here also since no regard seems to have been paid to the manifest disadvantages of a large (150-boat) marina in the crowded, shallow, upper Blackwater. Despite protests, six swinging moorings have been allowed in a favourite anchorage and stopping-place at Osea Island, to go with a development on the Island. The precedent established here is extremely worrying.

Above ell we cherish the freedom of our East Coast rivers, but, as ever, the price of freedom is vigilance. BACSPA frequently finds itself in the thick of things and our voice is heard. Please don't hesitate to contact John Chandler, Colin Lambert, Tony Williamson or myself if you hear of anything to the detriment of our river community.

Whatever, wherever or indeed however you sail (or motor) may I wish you all good luck for 1990,

R.N.L.1. SPONSORED ROW, MALDON, 30TH DECEMBER 1989

The Club was well represented in this year's event,

The MSC men's team entered the Fisherman, its crew of 4 dressed as Father Christmases. The Fisherman sported rather natty Christmas tree complete with coloured lights. Unfortunately, due to an earlier injury, Roger Smith, @ regular team member, was unable to reach the peak of fitness necessary for this gruelling race and John Salmon very kindly took his place et the oars at short notice, The other three Father Christmases were Malcolm Stuart, Mike Hellewell and Ray Ball, The men won second place in the Fancy Dress and would have had a first prize if there had been a category for the fastest clinker-built wooden boat with Christmas tree, lights, and 4 Father Christmases!

fearsome Foursome of Rosie Duckmanton, Lucy Boreham, Melanie Keeble and Jenny Ball entered the race dressed as pirates, Their boat was kindly loaned by Charles Anderson, The Ladies received several edible and

drinkable prizes for their fancy dress and rowing prowess, and it required a party at the Keebles' house the following week to consume the goodies,

The Cadet/Mirror Fleet was represented by Mirror Fleet Captain David Ball rowing a tender. David rowed a

brilliant and inspired tactical race. ("Thanks, Dad," = “That's OK, Son.")

Young Melanie and Mathew Booth from ‘Mare Lutra' in the Cruiser Fleet also took part and completed the course

in their tender, I apologise here to any other MSC entrant I've failed to mention,

Local press and TV cameras were present, and MSC entries featured on the photo page of the Maldon & Burnham
Standard - did anyone see whether the event was shown on TV?

Once again the weather was kind and there was a good turn-out of spectators, and the West Mersea Atlantic 21 Lifeboat came along to support the proceedings, Thanks to all who came along to lend moral support on the day
and many thanks to all of you who sponsored the competitors. This was a good event - it was fun for

competitors and spectators, provided useful cash for the Lifeboats and some positive publicity for Marconi ‘Sailing Club.

Ray Ball (Father Christmas No.4)

INFORMATION CIRCULATED BY MALDON DISTRICT COUNCIL

HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS - There have been a few incidents recently of containers of
HAZARDOUS CHEMICALS being washed up along the Essex Coast. Because of recent weather conditions, the shipping agents have been worried that more containers could be washed up over the next few weeks.

The canisters have come fran the M.V. Murree which sank off the South Coast a couple of months ago. Over the past two or three weeks a small number of the containers have arrived in our area. Same gave off cyanide fumes; the contents of a drum washed ashore at Foulness becomes inflammable on contact with the air; and yet another turns to sulphuric acid on contact with water.

The majority of the hazardous chemicals were in small brown bottles varying in size from 100ml (about 25 teaspoonfuls) to 2.5 litres. They could be loose or packed in
white polystyrene, possibly with marks giving chemical name and manufacturer - either
M & B (May and Baker) or BDH.

In addition to those already described, extreme care should be taken if any form of containers are discovered. Same of the chemicals involved are very nasty indeed and
NO ATTEMPT SHOULD BE MADE TO INVESTIGATE THEM,

T£ any suspicious containers are found, please contact Maldon Police, Tel. Maldon 852255, and they will alert the relevant response agency.

Dear Member,

I am writing to you as an Ordinary member of the Club regarding the future membership of the Executive and Main Committees.

As you are aware, the positions of Commodore, Hon Secretary, and Hon Treasurer have to be filled under the Constitution by Ordinary Members and not Family or Associates. In addition any person standing for these offices must have served for one year on the Main Committee.
Pat Black has indicated to me that he will not be seeking re-election at the end of this year, and the Club will therefore require a new Secretary. In addition I will also point out that should I stand and be re-elected as Commodore for next year, it is the last year that I can serve in the post under the
constitution.
I would therefore ask you to consider whether you could help your club by serving on the Main Committee and particularly if you would stand for Secretary at the A.G.M. in November. If you are able to do so, the Main Committee can co-opt you now so that you have time to become involved and understand its working. If you want any further information about the position please contact either Pat or myself.

I also consider it essential that the Club is adequately represented on the
M.A.S.C. Main Committee and would like to thank both John Weedon and Reg Floydd
who are currently on that committee. It would be nice if the section had three representatives on the Committee in the future. Again if anyone would like further information about the function of the committee, I am sure that either John or Reg would be happy to help them.

I appreciate that many of you already take an active role in supporting the Club in many varied ways but would request that you very seriously consider whether you could help in any of the roles above. It is only by ensuring continuity in the future that the Club will continue to flourish and provide the facilities that we all enjoy.
Yours,

THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE AND THE RYA_SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION

IN 1988 THE CLUB PUT ON THE FIRST EAST COAST PIERS RACE, A LONG DISTANCE EVENT FOR CATAMARANS UP TO
WALTON-ON-THE*NAZE AND BACK; THAT YEAR IT SUPPORTED CANCER RELIEF AND ESTABLISHED AN EXCITING RACE FOR THE

COMPETITIORS.

IN 1989 IT WAS DECIDED TO SUPPORT TWO CAUSES OF DIRECT INTEREST TO US AS SAILORS, THE RNLI AND SAILING FOR THE
DISABLED (ACTUALLY THE RYA SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION); IN 1990 ALL THE PROCEEDS WILL BE GIVEN TO THE RYA SF, THE
RYA SF IS A REGISTERED CHARITY FOUNDED BY THE RYA IN 1973 AND HAS THREE SPECIFIC AIMS.

TO PROVIDE OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUNG PEOPLE, PARTICULARLY FROM DEPRIVED BACKGROUNDS, TO TAKE PART IN
SAILING-RELATED ACTIVITIES,

TO ENABLE HANDICAPPED PEOPLE TO LEARN TO SAIL ON EQUAL TERMS WITH THE ABLE-BODIED,

TO IMPROVE THE LEVEL OF SEAMANSHIP IN THE PLEASURE=BOAT COMMUNITY.

TO THESE ENDS THE RYA SF HAS BEEN INVOLVED IN THE PROVISION OF NEARLY 200 BOATS OF MANY CLASSES, OVER ONE
HUNDRED OF WHICH ARE 15' CHALLENGER TRIMARANS DESIGNED FOR USE BY ABLE-BODIED OR DISABLED PEOPLE. IT IS THE
ASPECTS OF THE WORK OF THE RYA SF THAT INVOLVE HELPING HANDICAPPED PEOPLE TO HAVE THE OPPORTUNITY TO SAIL THAT
THE PIERS RACE IS SPECIFICALLY ADDRESSING, AND IT IS OUR HOPE THAT, GIVEN GOOD SUPPORT THIS YEAR, WE SHOULD BE
ABLE TO PURCHASE A CHALLENGER FOR PLACEMENT BY THE SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION WHERE IT CAN BEST BE USED. IF WE
FALL SHORT OF THIS TARGET THEN THE MONEY RAISED WILL SUPPORT SAILING FOR THE DISABLED IN A MORE GENERAL WAY BY
ASSISTING THE RYA SFWITH SOME OF THEIR MANY PROJECTS,

IN 1989 THE PIERS RACE RAISED A TOTAL OF £1,600 FOR THE RNLI AND THE RYA SF; THIS YEAR WE INTEND TO BEAT
THAT! WE WERE HELPED IMMENSELY IN 1989 BY ‘INDUSTRIAL AND COMMERCIAL ENGINEERING SERVICES' AND ‘BRAMHAM

BROTHERS', TWO ENGINEERING FIRMS WHO PROVIDED THE CASH NEEDED TO RUN THE EVENT, AND ALSO BY A NUMBER OF PEOPLE
AND ORGANISATIONS WHO PROVIDED HELP IN KIND. WE NOW FIND OURSELVES IN THE POSITION OF NEEDING SIMILAR
SPONSORSHIP FOR 1990, £2,000 IS NEEDED TO ENABLE US TO PUT THE RACE ON IN A FASHION THAT WILL BE SAFE,
ENJOYABLE AND PROFITABLE....FOR CHARITY

42,000 IS A LOT OF MONEY, BUT THE RACE HAS SHOWN OVER THE LAST TWO YEARS, EVEN WITH THE FOUL WEATHER
EXPERIENCED LAST YEAR, THAT MORE THAN THE TOTAL SPONSORSHIP WILL BE GIVEN TO CHARITY, WE HAVE TRIED VERY
HARD TO FIND SPONSORSHIP AT THIS LEVEL FOR 1990 BUT WITH NO SUCCESS SO FAR; IF ANYONE IN THE CLUB FEELS HE OR
SHE HAS ANY IDEAS THAT MAY BE OF HELP, OR FEELS THAT HE OR SHE IS ABLE TO APPROACH HIS OR HER OWN EMPLOYERS
FOR SUCH A GOOD CAUSE, THEN I'D BE VERY PLEASED TO HEAR FROM THEM.

AT SAILBOAT '90 WHILST NEIL WAS MEETING HIS CHUM (SEE COMMODORE'S NOTES) AND I WAS TAKING SNAPS, MIKE
DUCKMANTON WAS TO BE SEEN ORGANISING HIS BAND OF HELPERS WHO WERE SHAKING TINS FOR THE SEAMANSHIP FOUNDATION
AND, IN THE PROCESS, RAISING £231.51 FOR THE CAUSE, AS WELL AS FURTHER PUBLICISING THE PIERS RACE. THANKS ARE
DUE FROM ALL OF US TO EVERYONE WHO WORKED SO HARD AND RAISED SUCH A GRAND SUM, AND IN ADDITION TO MIKE FOR
MAKING US “BY APPOINTMENT"!

SAFETY NOTE

A recent incident highlighted the need for care and preparation when sailing from the Club, especially during the early part of the season when the water is cold.

Accidents can happen to anyone, and by definition are unexpected. We can, however, prepare ourselves for an unexpected event by considering what could go wrong and then planning to minimise the effects of such a misfortune. The following may be worth
considering

SITUATION 1: Gear failure resulting in the boat drifting at the mercy of wind and
tide.

Contingency Plan.
Is there an anchor on board?
Is the boat provided with a second means of propulsion e.g. oars/paddle?

SITUATION 2: Capsize or Swamping.

Contingency Plan.
Has the boat sufficient built-in buoyancy to support itself and crew?
Is there a means of bailing the boat dry?
Have you practised capsize drill and recovered the boat once it has
inverted?
Are you protected from the debilitating effects of immersion in cold water? Are you wearing a buoyancy aid and will it support you?

SITUATION 3: Boat Inverted and Cannot be Righted

Contingency Plan
Are you able to climb onto the upturmed hull?
Are there lines or handles rigged to prevent your being separated from the
boat?

Finally, in the event of an accident, stay with the boat. Sail in company, there is safety in numbers.

Remember, we are each responsible for our own safety, do not rely on being rescued by someone else.

Pat Black

Chapter 1 - Boater Beware

At the time of writing, the sunis shining through my office window (actually it is snowing but we'll pretend it never happened) and itis altogethera most pleasant day (well is was until the snow came). With not too much wind apparent, it doesn't take too much effort to day-dream of going for a sail (remember, we're still pretending it isn't snowing) and I make a mental note to look for a suite of offices in Steeple. Judging from the rapid growth of plants in our garden, we've quite genuinely had a number of ‘very pleasant days' recently and it is tempting to assume that summer is, indeed, ‘a'cumin in' and has virtually arrived. However, as you will read elsewhere in this Navigans, although it might be a ‘very pleasant day' in the warm sunshine above the water level, it is still a very cold regime below the surface of the river Blackwater. Our unfortunate member who found him/herself with a problem, and in drastic need of outside assistance, can be forgivenfdr doing what he/she did onthe grounds of inexperience. However, I am sometimes surprized at the apparent inclination of some members to ‘strip off' the wet or dry suits at the first hint of the sun's warm rays. Perhaps I've got it wrong, but I thought the purpose of a wet or dry suit was not so much to keep me warm above the water, but to give
me a fighting chance of survival when literally up to my neck in bee cold water - not to mention
being up the creek without a paddle. As one who tends to wear the 'full wet-suit gear' even at the height of summer, it might be that I subscribe to the ancient chinese proverb which states "better to be a boiled lobster than a cold fish’.

Chapter 2 - Remember, Remember, who's not a member.

At a recent Main Committee meeting, someone asked if a member invited visitors to the club (without the visitors using the clubhouse or club facilities) then is it necessary to sign them in? The answer is YES, all visitors should be signed in even if they do not enter the clubhouse; it is sufficient that they are on the club site that they be signed in.

The discussion then turned to consider ‘regular visitors' to the club i.e. those who are ‘regularly invited' to sail at the club. To be fair to those who pay both their MASC and Sailing Section subscriptions (and that is, of course, all fee-paying members) those who are ‘regular visitors' ought
to be 'regular' members - '‘regular' in this sense meaning proper or correct paid-up members of the
club in accordance with its rules. It is worth noting that one privilege of ordinary membership is that one's husband/wife and (their) children under the age of 18 are ‘permanent guests'. Presumably,
once the kids are over 18 - they're on their own.

Chapter 3. - SOSOTTI (is this a new kind of sausage ?)

To those members both bushy of beard and somewhat long in the tooth, the meaning of the word SOSOTTI should be clear enough. No, it's not sausage; it is the annual war cry of the Results Secretary or, to be more accurate, the annual impassioned plea to helms and crew to help get the race results reasonably near correct. Just to remind you :-

SO = SIGN ON ( forename and surname of both helm and crew - preferably
printed rather than the 'signature')

so = SIGN OFF (If you don't, you are automatically disqualified. Also please sign off in the right column. ie. If you are

The signs of the times Did you read the article ‘Answering a question of survival’ in The Times,
Thursday, 26 April ? It was a report of part of the ‘Safety at Sea' Conference held recently
in London. The most interesting things in the report for me were the suggestions that:-

(a) a dry suit was the best means of protection against ‘cold shock' on entering
the water when 'man overboard’, as well as against hypothermia

(b) 'man overboard’ can be more quickly recovered by adopting the ‘quick stop'
(ie. yacht going head-to-wind) method of controlling the yacht so as to
quickly locate and pick up the overboard crew - as opposed to the more
usually taught method of ‘'reach-tack-reach' operation.

It will be interesting to see what the yachting press has to say about these suggestions, and what will happen about the various ‘teaching methods' currently in voque. Admittedly, the discussion probably tended to be conducted within the context of offshore yacht racing, but nevertheless, it offers some food for thought for us creek dwellers.

Mike Boreham, Rear Commodore.

Ed's note:

Although the author of the next article would, no doubt, not mind being identified, I have deliberately amitted the name. The object of publishing this story and last month's warnings about the river being cold is not to embarrass any individual ('there, but for the grace of God, goes any of us') but to focus our minds at the beginning of the season to the potential hazards of our sport. We are at our most vulnerable when the water is so cold and we, and our gear, have perhaps not fully emerged from the winter's hibernation:

THAT INCIDENT

In the May Navigans there were same notes dealing with an incident in March. I was the 'principal character' involved and had intended to give an account in that issue but was too late to meet the deadline, hence its belated appearance now.

Having joined the Club in mid-summer last year it galls me somewhat to think I have gained same dubious prominence, if not notoriety! However, what's done is done. Let me say right away I fully subscribe to the constructive comments made, particularly about adequate and sensible preparation before setting sail. On the whole, I think my boat met those requirements and, certainly, the paddles were secure and at hand if I had decided to paddle up the creek! Nevertheless, I have learned that, particularly when sailing solo there are extra points to consider. The 'safety in numbers' suggestion is, I suppose, self-evident but I have a preference for solo sailing. In any case my present boat is a little cramped to accommodate a crew. There is also the difficulty of saneone willing to crew when you decide to sail, although I myself would welcome more opportunity to crew for experienced helmsmen. Undoubtedly I must give more thought to wearing clothing appropriate to the time and conditions of the season, but the wearing of the ‘full regalia’ in warm sunny weather I would find decidedly uncomfortable. There aught to be same concession to individual preference.

As to what happened. I had a leeward capsize because, in a sudden strong gust of wind, although releasing the mainsheet in time, I was unable to do likewise with the jib sheet as it had got out of reach. The taut jib alone caused a complete heel over, ejecting me headlong into the grey water. Emerging, I unwisely delayed giving priority to righting the boat, squandering time and energy trying to recover items which drifted out of the storage locker (I had not secured the cover properly). One of my boots also came off during my exertions and pranptly disappeared! Eventually, having righted the boat, I caused it to capsize again by trying to make a quick entry over the side instead of the stem. Attempting another righting became more difficult as the jib sheet had sanehow fouled up underneath the boat, preventing me
gaining enough purchase to throw it over the hull.....but before this account begins

6.
to sound like Gerard Hoffnung's sketch of the descending barrel of bricks, suffice it to say I became quite suddenly aware of an overall chilling with numbing in the hands and, at the cost of extreme annoyance in having to do so, decided to signal for outside help.

If I could just make my main point, I learned to sail last year on the adult course run by Mike Boreham and Malcolm Stuart. I found the relaxed nature, but steady tempo, of the course just right to enable me to fairly quickly venture out to sail solo which, apart from once or twice when I crewed, I did up to the end of October. What I didn't do was re-inforce the capsize and recovery drill using my own boat, and without assistance. I think my neglect to achieve a higher proficiency was the main cause of an otherwise manageable situation deteriorating into a much more serious one. I need hardly say, therefore, that a high priority for me is more practice as soon as is practicable.

Looking back, perhaps I can at least take same encouragement from the not-so-old
English proverb; "if you don't make mistakes, you don't make anything" - but I hasten
to add I acknowledge my mistakes also cost the efforts of other people. It follows that, although I have already done so, I would like here to record my appreciation for the efforts of Lee Tridini and Barry Marke in recovering my boat, and of Pat Black the OOD on 'that day'.

In spite of everything my enthusiasm remains undanpened..... and I look forward to
warmer days afloat. As Mike has said “Summer is a'cumin' in." Indeed, looking out of my window, I think it is a'cam!

I should think most of us who sail could think of a few Gerard Hoffnung-type tales of
our own activities over the years - and now for another

TROLLEY SAILING IN THE BLACKWATER

I firmly believe that it can only be healthy for any sport or acitivity to embrace new developments and innovations. It is therefore with same sense of pride, if not a little humility, that I introduce this latest offshoot of sailing to the Club, namely, Trolley Sailing.

The beauty of this activity is its simplicity. The objective is merely to sail a full blown Cruiser Trolley out into the river as far as you can. The Rules are extremely simple. The Trolley should be a substantial affair capable of carrying at least a medium-sized cruiser. Mickey Mouse affairs with pram wheels are not eligible, and the Trolley should not possess any additional buoyancy aids such as oversize tyres etc. Spinnakers are not allowed.

contd....

Ti.
As the only person, to my knowledge, to have engaged in this activity at Marconi to date, I can with some confidence claim to be the current Club Champion, with a sailing distance achieved of sane thirty feet (yet to be ratified). I can for those yet to be initiated in the sport, only attempt to convey the sheer excitement and intense adrenalin flow that the activity produces, especially if, like me, you inadvertently dismount the Trolley just before lift-off.

My only concern in introducing this sport is that in time it will, like so many others, lose sight of its homespun roots and became over-sophisticated and over tuned. Will we eventually see an array of Pete Clayton Specials in racing black and gold livery, complete with balloon tyres, high aspect uprights and low wetted surfaces, sporting hard racing antifoulings and go-faster stripes, their crews resplendent in multi-coloured wetsuits?

To get back to the present, however, the sport has the further attraction of opening up access to a number of spin-off activities such as Trapping the Stump (in which you aim to sink the trolley after its distance sailing attempt so that it straddles
strategically placed stumps in the river bed - only for the particularly skilful,
this one!) This leads naturally to Tractor Bouncing, in which you attempt to make a tractor airborne by pulling the trolley hard against the aforementioned stump. Then there is Trolley Jumping whereby the trolley has to be assisted in leaping the Stump. The attraction of this particular activity can be measured by the number of. people still involved at dusk on a Saturday night.

There must be endless variations of this sport just waiting to be discovered. A whole Regatta could surely be organised around these and other associated activities such as Mast Tossing.

On the other hand I might just go back to Sailing. It hasn't got anywhere like the same appeal as a spectator sport, but it's generally a lot more peaceful and I'm not sure that the limelight is all it's cracked up to be. I'll see you in Pyefleet
Creek.

Malcolm Shaft

AMBULANCE

Yet another water-skiing accident off Stansgate brought a bleeding and unconscious casualty to our hard at lunchtime on Bank Holiday Monday 7th May. The Club rose to the occasion and dealt very competently with the incident. It was particularly comforting to observe that we have a number of Club Members interested in First Aid and prepared to cane forward and do sanething constructive.

The incident was almost an exact rerun of last year's Rescue Boat Competition with the mangled eye and unconscious body, plus another member of the boat crew in deep
shock. The extra factors in our real case were that the skier had taken in a lot of water and that he was already blind on one eye. The drowning bit solved itself
simply by putting the casualty in the Recovery Position - he emptied himself although
remaining unconscious. All we could do with the eye problem was to ensure a note was taken to hospital.

The 999 call raised same interesting points. The ambulance cames from either Burmhan or Maldon and may take about 20 minutes to arrive. However, the G.P.s on the Dengie run a paramedic response which receives the same '999' call and invariably beat the
ambulance to the scene, as in our case with the G.P. fran Althorne. Mike Boreham who initiated the 999 call very wisely went down to the main road to direct both the Paramedic car and the Ambulance up the Stansgate road.
It is not unknown for new ambulance crews to get Stansgate confused with Stone and our G.P.from Althorme
hadn't
known there was a Sailing Club at Stansgate.

This incident will have focussed attention on the need for a high level of First Aid competence in the Club. For those interested, who don't receive training elsewhere, Our own St John Ambulance team of David & Ione will be giving First Aid talks and demonstrations during Cadet Week. One thing they will be explaining is the latest thinking on resuscitation and hopefully we will have a copy of the British Heart Foundation video "Don't Just Stand There" which, amongst other things, points aut that the old 4 rapid inflations can actually do more harm than good. They now recommend, after clearing the airway, if breathing cannot be detected, two slow inflations making sure that the chest rises in response.

Malcolm Stuart

A_STORM_IN AN EASTER EGG CUP (Through the Eye of the Hurricane)

EASTER SUNDAY DAWNED CLEAR AND BRIGHT AND EXTREMELY WINDY, DESPITE A FORECAST OF WESTERLY FORCE 3,
COMPETITORS TO THE EASTER SERIES WERE GREETED AT STANSGATE BY NORTH-WESTERLY FORCE 5 GUSTING 7! OUR VISITORS
WERE IMPRESSED. WITH PERMISSION OF THE MAIN COMMITTEE, A NUMBER OF HURRICANE 4,9s HAD COME TO THE CLUB TO
PARTICIPATE IN THE EASTER SERIES, THE HURRICANE 4,9 FLEET (FORMERLY THE CONDOR, BUT WITH AN UPDATED RIG) WILL

BE HOLDING THEIR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS DURING REGATTA, AND ASKED PERMISSION TO TRY THE WATERS IN ADVANCE,

ABOUT 5 HURRICANES ARRIVED, AND ALTHOUGH SMALLIN NUMBERS THEY PROCEEDED TO EAT THE GALLEY CLEAN. JEAN FLOOK
REPORTED THAT ONE INDIVIDUAL HAD 4 HAMBURGERS TO HIMSELF AT LUNCHTIME,

RACE ONE CONSISTED OF R2B3, NO, NOT A DROID FROM STAR WARS, BUT A COURSE CONSISTING OF 3 LAPS OF As,1p,Cs,Bs
& Ds, FOLLOWED BY 2 LAPS OF As,1s,Bs,Ds. THIS COURSE GAVE AN INTERESTING REACH BETWEEN C AND B AND WITH WIND
AGAINST TIDE THE INFAMOUS BLACKWATER CHOP WAS THE ORDER OF THE DAY. WITH THE WIND GUSTING UP TO FORCE 7, ONLY
5 BOATS TOOK TO THE WATER, THE FLEET CONSISTED OF JOHN NICKALLS & CAROLINE HOLLINGS IN THE TORNADO, TWO
VISITING HURRICANE 4,9s, ONE WINDSURFER AND A MIRROR, THE TORNADO LED, FOLLOWED BY THE HURRICANES AND THE
WINDSURFER, THE RACE OFFICER WISELY DECIDED TO SHORTEN COURSE AND PLANNED A MAXIMUM OF TWO LAPS OF COURSE R,
HOWEVER, THE COMPETITORS DECIDED DIFFERENTLY AND THEY ALL CHOSE TO RETIRE AFTER THE FIRST LAP. JOHN CLAIMS
THAT IF HE HAD SPENT MUCH MORE TIME UNDERWATER HE WOULD HAVE QUALIFIED FOR A COURSE AT HMS PERISHER (THE
SUBMARINE TRAINING SCHOOL.) ONE OF THE VISITORS PITCHPOLED, BUT INSTEAD OF GOING END OVER END, THEY
PIROUETTED NEATLY ON THE LEEWARD BOW AND ACTUALLY CAME DOWN ON THE SIDE OF THE HULL. BEFORE THE CREW COULD
BALE OUT, THE BOAT RETURNED TO THE UPRIGHT. HOWEVER, ALL WAS NOT WELL! THE FORCE OF THE "EVENT" SHEARED OFF
ONE OF THE BOLTS HOLDING THE REAR BEAM, AND THEY DESCRIBED THE BOAT AS BEING AS STIFF AS A BOWL OF JELLY!
THEY SAILED SLOWLY (7?) BACK TO THE CLUB.

AFTER DEPLETING THE GALLEY OF FOOD, AND REALISING THAT THE WIND HAD DROPPED TO A MER® FORCE 4, 12 CREWS
VENTURED ONTO THE WATER FOR THE SECOND RACE. THE RACE OFFICER AGAIN SET R2B3, AND AGAIN JOHN AND CAROLINE
SPED INTO THE LEAD, HOWEVER, DAVID BEECH SAILING A HURRICANE 4.9 CHARGED AROUND THE COURSE AFTER JOHN, NEVER
LETTING HIM GET TOO FAR IN FRONT, AND AT THE END DAVID TOOK HONOURS AND HANDICAP FROM JOHN, FURTHER DOWN THE
FLEET, THE OTHER TWO 4,9s WERE RACING AROUND TOGETHER, FOLLOWED BY A GAGGLE OF CLUB DART 18s, IT WAS
NOTICEABLE THAT THE 4,9s SEEMED TO POINT HIGHER THAN THE DARTS, WHICH GAVE THEM AN ADVANTAGE ON THE BEAT.

MONDAY AGAIN DAWNED CLEAR AND BRIGHT, BUT THE WIND WAS ONLY A MERE FORCE 5 GUSTING 6, SO A GOOD FLEET
ASSEMBLED TO START RACE 3, BECAUSE OF THE DIFFERENCE IN THE SPEED OF THE BOATS, THE RACE OFFICER SET A
COURSE OF R3, WHICH STILL FAVOURED THE FASTER BOATS, BUT DID ALLOW THE MIRROR FLEET A LONG SPINNAKER LEG, IF
THEY WERE BRAVE ENOUGH TO FLY ONE, ON SUNDAY THE STARTS HAD BEEN POSTPONED TO GIVE EVERYBODY SUFFICIENT TIME
TO GET ON THE WATER, BUT THE RACE OFFICER CORRECTLY STUCK TO THE PUBLISHED TIMES ON MONDAY AND, ACCORDINGLY,
BOATS WERE GOING IN ALL DIRECTIONS AT THE START OF RACE 3! IT DIDN'T HELP THAT THE RACE BOX CLOCK IS RUNNING
ABOUT 2 MINUTES FAST (FROM GMT), THUS THE COMPETITORS WERE ALL EXPECTING THE SIGNALS AT DIFFERENT TIMES! JOHN
AND CAROLINE MADE THEIR CUSTOMARY GOOD START AND SPED OFF IN FRONT. DAVID BEECH AND PETER GOLDING, 80TH IN
HURRICANE 4,9s LED THE CHASE, FOLLOWED BY YOURS TRULY WHO, AS USUAL WAS POINTING IN THE WRONG DIRECTION WHEN
THE GUN WENT, I MEAN IT WHEN I SAY GUN, AS THE CANNONS WERE IN USE AND THEY COULD BE HEARD ABOVE THE WIND,
WHEREAS THE HOOTER WAS A BIT PATCHY.

WITH A LOW-WATER SHORT-LINE START, THE BEAT TO 'A' MARK WAS FULL OF CRIES FOR WATER, AND WE ALMOST SHORTENED A
4.9 WHEN WE TRIED TO BEAR AWAY ACROSS HIS STERN (WE WERE ON PORT) JUST AS HE BORE AWAY (ON STARBOARD) TO AVOID
THE MOORING BARGE. DAVE WAS YELLING FOR ME TO BEAR AWAY AND AS I PULLED ON THE TILLER IT JUST DECIDED TO
EXTEND RATHER THAN OPERATE THE RUDDERS. THE 4.9, WHO HADN'T SEEN US TACK BY THE SHORE, COULD DO ABSOLUTELY
NOTHING AS HE WAS SANDWICHED BETWEEN US AND THE MOORING BARGE. HOW WE MISSED EACH OTHER I DO NOT KNOW, BUT WE
DID! HAD I TRIED TO TACK TO AVOID A COLLISION, WE WOULD HAVE UNDOUBTEDLY COLLIDED AS I WOULD HAVE ENDED UP
DIRECTLY IN FRONT OF THE 4,9, THIS WAS JUST A CASE OF OBSTRUCTIONS BLOCKING BOTH HELMS' VIEW AND THE WIND

BLOWING OUT CRIES FOR WATER,

MEANWHILE JOHN WAS WELL AWAY, FOLLOWED BY THE TWO 4.9s, JOHN LAID 'C' MARK IN ONE TACK, WHILST EVERYBODY ELSE

HAD TO TACK AT LEAST ONCE. ON THE LEG TO 'B' MARK WE PASSED THE SECOND 4,9 AND SET ABOUT OVERHAULING THE

LEADING 4.9, WE SEEMED TO BE MUCH FASTER DOWNWIND THAN EITHER OF THE BOATS IN FRONT, AND WERE ABLE TO SAIL
MUCH LOWER, THUS WHEN WE REACHED 'B' MARK WE WERE CLOSE TO THE LEADING 4.9 AND CLOSING ON JOHN. DAVID BEECH
SEEMED TO BE POINTING AT LEAST 10 DEGREES HIGHER THAN US, BUT OUR SUPERIOR SPEED ALLOWED US TO PASS HIM AS WE
CROSSED THE LINE FOR THE END OF THE FIRST LAP, MEANWHILE, JOHN AND CAROLINE WERE PULLING AWAY AGAIN. JOHN

Who's a lucky boy then ? - I was much amused to read in one of the daily papers a snippet about
Argentinian polo players being in great demand in this country; apparently they can get up to £10,000 per month for a 5-month season. It wasn't that which amused me (rather it made me lament my mis-spent youth not learning to ride a horse) but what followed in the article. I quote:-

"| ....-£10,000 a month for a five-month season paid on top of accommodation,
cars, expenses, ponies, equipment and a posse of female fans. One polo wife explained: "They eat with us, they train with us, they sleep with us. We own them for three months" ".

As I was saying, who's a lucky boy then ? Say chaps, anyone for polo ?

From little shrimps, mighty (h)elms will grow - I doubt that this saying will be familiar to many
of you, although you will probably recall its better known partner which links ‘acorns' to 'oaks'. Never mind, we can't all be familiar with the rather fishy literature of 17th century Mersea oystermen, but it does serve as a rather lengthy way of reminding all you parents that there is a Cadet Series of races. The Cadet Series (for the Payne Cup) is a handicap series in any measured dinghy for helms aged 18 years and under on lst January (of the year in question). It is a well-known fact that sailing parents tend to use their offspring as forced labour at the sharp end of the boat. The Cadet Series gives said offspring a chance to shine as helms (and get their own back on the parents). However, not many parents would be willing to allow their ‘pride and joy' (ie. their boat) to be sailed off into the
wild Blackwater river with little Jane or Johnnie at the helm - the risks would be too great (ie. risk of
scratching the paintwork) . Thus, it is widely accepted that provided the Cadet does the helming, an
adult can act as crew. My own children started helming in the Cadet races from the age of 8 and | can
honestly say that I never touched the tiller from the 5-minute gun to the end of the race - but I did
shout a lot. Now they teach me.

"No Rules' Rules OK ? - we'd all like to think others see us as ruggedly independent, vigorously championing
the rights of the individual against bureaucracy and standing aloof from the sheep-like obeisance of the rest of mankind. This image can be easily established by loudly proclaiming that rules are made to be broken, bad rules lead to bad government and rules should be applied with discretion. All very true but who judges when a rule is ‘bad', or should be broken ‘with discretion’ ? What carnage on the roads if someone wasn't prepared to apply the rules; what a worry if we really believed the majority would not, in
fact, ‘obey the rules'. Even worse is a rule which cannot be enforced - or which ‘the authorities’ are
unwilling to enforce. I heard the other day that a law (ie. rule) still exists which forbids Welshmen to be inside the walls of Chester upon pain of death ; now there's a case for discretion if ever there was one. A rule exists in the club's Sailing Instructions which is rarely (if ever) enforced and might just possibly be unenforceable. It is S.1.Rule 5. which says , amongst other things, that ‘for all sailing after October and sailing before the end of May, Wet or Dry suits must be worn by all competitors. Failure to do so in a race will result in disqualification’. A quite clear breach of this rule by several competitors in'a recent race (before end-May) resulted in neither automatic disqualification or subsequent protest. Let's be honest, who at our club level sailing would WISH to make such a protest; none I would think. The day in question was gloriously sunny and warm at surface level and there was little wind; there was little danger of someone falling into the still cold waters of the Blackwater. Anyway, who is to say what is a ‘wet suit' or ‘dry suit' or whether such aq item should be worn ‘complete’ or in part, done up or open, or even be adequate for its normal purpose ? S.1.Rule 5 is unenforceable if those concerned are not willing to accept it as being enforceable; therefore the Rule should be changed to be a recommendation and not an edict. A 'bad' rule might be annoying but an unenforceable rule is a waste of everybody's time.

Five Wise Men - a recent Sailing Sub-Committee meeting discussed at some length what was perceived to be
a 'Race Officering' problem, ie. the general standard of Race Officering was not as high as it should, or could, be and that some sailing members of the club might leave unless the standard was improved. I'm not sure that many would actually leave, or that we should be worried if they did, but nevertheless it is very annoying for those who race if too many R.O. mistakes are occurring week in and week out. Since those who race are also those who perform R.O. duties, it follows that most of us are guilty. Therefore, it has been decided to find 'Five Wise Men' who will take it in turns to be available each week to give advice to the R.0. if requested. They will not dictate to the Race Officer, but merely introduce themselves and offer their advice if the R.0. feels he/she needs it.

Another Five Wise Men - arising from the 'Five Wise Men' discussion, it was also suggested that each week,
the Race Officer, the Officer-of-the-day, the Duty Coxswain, the Wise Man (for that week) and at least one Fleet captain should meet at 09.30 on the sea wall to assess and discuss the conditions of wind, tide, sea state and support boat status before the Race Officer decides and sets the courses for the day's events.

TROLLEY SAILING IN THE BLACKWATER

To put the records straight, Malcolm Shaft cannot claim to be the only person to indulge in this sport at M.S.C. In October 1988 I successfully floated an all-metal trailer. I therefore claim to be the inventor of 'Trolley Sailing', unless (to quote Esther Rantzen) "You know better". I will not dispute Malcolm's claim for the distance record, I only sailed 29'11" before being winched ashore, together with a suitable weight (sailing cruiser).

On the same day I also invented (patent applied for) an automatic rudder dismounting process using the 'cruiser tipping' procedure. This involved positioning a 22' cruiser on a two-wheeled road trailer in such a manner that the centre of gravity of the unit is behind the axle, and then removing the support under the vessel's stem. The rudder is automatically lifted from its pintles when the star of the vessel strikes the ground. There are three disadvantages which I have yet to overcame - suggestions please:

1) Having to manhandle the boat back on the trailer.
2) Having to repair the stern of the boat where it struck the ground
3) Being reminded of the incident at frequent intervals by the rest of the family.

Any member of M.S.C. can feel free to use this invention and I shall be grateful for any comments for improvements and on its effectiveness as a labour-saving process.

SAILING & RUNNING RACE

Now that the 1990 sailing season is under way, I thought that the readers of Navigans might enjoy a description of an unusual sailing event that two club members, Mike Tumer and Jack Hardie, took part in last year.

"I know where we can get a yacht"

Memos fran the boss always induce something of a sinking feeling, and that's how I approached the one that landed on my desk in May 1989. Closer inspection proved that this one was at least different. It had the usual wad of typescript with the obligatory yellow-peril sticky note, but the note simply said "I know where we can get a yacht" and the typescript told of a new Five Hundred Mile, non stop sailing and running race. Start at Southampton; 100 miles sailing to Salcombe; 20 miles running to Dartmouth; sail to Exmouth; Royal Marines endurance course; 75 mile sail to Alderey, 10 miles run round the
island, 100 miles sail back to Fowey in Cornwall; 30 mile run; 120 miles to Yarmouth; ten
mile run to the Needles and sail back to finish in the Hamble. I thought he'd gone mad.

Well, we did it. We came sixth in our class out of fifteen boats, gained a special prize for entering into the spirit of the race, and raised £700 for charity.

The boat was a Dufour 39 donated by our sponsor, Lamerair Yacht Charter, who certainly did us proud. If you ever want to charter or buy a boat in the Solent area then I strongly
recommend you give David Square a ring at Lamerair (04895-83601), he deserves the advert.
We were a crew of six on the boat, of whom two were dedicated runners, with a backup tee
ashore. Four of the team worked for our other sponsor - Ashridge Management College, so
at least we had same theoretical expertise on teamworking! Apart from Mike Turmmer and ne, the rest of the team had fairly limited sailing experience so they had to learn as they went along.

We certainly learned a lot; particularly about our own endurance and capabilities under stress. The two runners covered the equivalent of three marathons, over rough hilly coastal paths, in six days. Between runs they slept on the yacht and ate whatever food we could manage to provide them with, ranging from chicken casserole and rice at best to cold cooked pasta and Mars bars at worst. The four sailors worked the boat almost continuously for six days, sleeping in four-hour watches when conditions and landfalls allowed any sleep at all. Despite the stress, there was also a lot of fun and humour and not a sign of anger or irritation. Perhaps we were all too tired to disagree!

Six days is too long to tell in full, and anyway it sticks in my mind as a series of snapshots, sane of them observed personally, same of them related by others.

The first night with a strong headwind and a rough confused sea. The skipper/cook couldn't understand why the crew attributed the subsequent malaise to his Commish Pasties but pleaded that he wasn't prepared to invest in any more expensive fo considering the element of risk.

The second night: winding the yacht up the muddy estuary of the River Exe in pitch darkness until we were finally stopped by shallow water, then the farce of dragging the rubber dinghy over partially covered mudbanks. We were trying to conserve the strength of our runner by sitting him in the dinghy while two sailors dragged him along. It worked well until, with the timing of a circus performer, he decided to stand up just when one of the sailors gave a mighty heave. Result: general collapse into the mud. The farce continued with the theft of our dinghy at one o'clock in the morning in a tiny Devon village. Sadly, I didn't witness the sight of two respectable citizens planning a temporary dinghy hi-jack to get them back to the yacht (how else do you acquire waterborne transport at one in the morning?), while a younger crew member looked on and pretended he wasn't with them. They returned at about 3 am, paddling a thing that looked like the smallest trawler in the world, and covered in mud from head to toe. One of our runners reporting to the Royal Marine Barracks after midnight, with balaclava helmet, track suit and two-day stubble, to be told at the gate to pop into the camp and find sameone to ask. I'm still not sure if they thought he was an honest citizen or such a pathetic terrorist that he deserved same help.

All the times after that (having safely returned our hi-jacked tender) we used the forty-foot yacht where we would normally use a dinghy, nosing it gingerly up to harbour walls, fishing boats, freighters and any other piece of terra firma where we could put our runners ashore with speed and safety.

7.

-..-The frustration of my tactical error which left us within yards of the harbour at Aldermey but unable to cheat the tide to make the entrance.

...Our shore support team, filling up rabbit holes on Alderney where the runners would
be in danger in twisting an ankle at night. Then the lights of the runners bobbing along in the dark while the runners themselves were invisible.

...-Becalmed in the shipping lanes off Alderney and poking my head up on deck, to see
Mike Turner waving cheerfully at a towering wall of floating steel which had just altered course to avoid us.

.«».The small town seen at night but not shown on the chart, and the subsequent confusion of the watch on deck until the 'town' detached itself from the shore and became an ocean
liner.

...The sail change which should have taken a few minutes and took three quarters of an
hour, because the crew were crippled by tiredness, seasickness, wave motion and an unlikely attack of the giggles.

.-..The conversation overheard on the VHF between a becalmed yachtsman and a motor vessel
skipper who was threatening to run him down if he didn't get out of the way - then the
calm intervention of the British Coastguard who sorted the whole thing out with a few well-chosen words.

...The wild run from Plymouth to Yarmouth under full sail at night in a _ phosphorescent
sea, with waves that needed bold and well-timed swings of the wheel to keep in control. After a four-hour watch in big waves, you really know the meaning of the phrase "shoulder to the wheel'. We averaged seven knots over 120 miles and missed the prize for the fastest passage by nine minutes.

There are lots of 1esagne for sailing and racing. The secret of winning was not occasional brilliance, by constant competence. Among the monohull boats, the differences in passage times were often less than an hour, and overall we beat our nearest rival by only forty minutes. When we lost time, we often lost it during the easy passages where we were too relaxed, and not so much when conditions were testing us to the limit. When we made mistakes there was often sameone who spotted it, but it wasn't always the person in nominal authority. We discovered that the cook was at least as important as the skipper and that sleep is more important than heroism.

Would I do it, or something like it, again? Funnily enough - yes! There was considerable
disconfort and maybe a small element of real danger, but the experience of working towards
a single clear objective, with a good team, over a significant period of time is - believe
it or not - a luxury.

JACK HARDIE

REGATTA 1990

Congratulations to Marconi Sailing Club members :-

Howard Knott and Stuart Knott

Gull National Champions 1990

Howard and Stuart won the Gull National Championship at our Regatta over the week-end 26-28 May and we are very proud of having a national championship team which we can truly claim as being ‘home grown’.

Howard was planning to sell his Gull and change to another boat, perhaps a 420. If he does sell, then he goes out on a ‘high’ but, if he doesn't sell, then he has set himself a high mountain to climb for the 1991 Gull Championships. Whatever he does, we are very pleased for Howard and his son Stuart.

Of the Regatta itself, more than 120 boats attended the event. Of the 13 classes competing, two classes (the Hurricane 4.9/Condor and the Gull) were using the Regatta for their national championships. Strictly, speaking there were 3 classes doing so because the Condor championship was also awarded but there were only two entries.

Saturday morning was devoted to the Rescue Boat Competition, an annual Marconi event designed to increase
the awareness of rescue boat drivers and crew to various aspects of ‘the role of rescue'. Although the event was open to any BJRC club, only three Marconi club teams took part and, to be honest, they were really scratch teams. Nevertheless, the competition was held and was judged by representatives from the Marine Division of the Essex Police, HM Coast Guard and St.John Ambulance and our thanks is extended to them for
their help. Perhaps next year........se00?

Saturday afternoon provided winds of around Force 3 for the practice race, enough to send the catamaran
fleets up to the baffle and back down to number 4 and 2 channel markers. The purpose of the Practice Race is to allow visitors to get to know where the buoys are, and it is perhaps unfortunate that the Hurricane 4.9
fleet decided to include it in their championship race series - unfortunate because some of them couldn't
find the marks. Presumably, none of the locals got lost and the Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup race was extracted from the result. The small fee charged for the Practice Race was donated to the Steeple Church Roof Appeal and about £30 was raised.

Both Sunday and Monday morning races (races 1 and 3) saw very little wind and competitors spent a long time on the water achieving very little. Some retired but some made it round the course and there was much moaning from some competitors. On Sunday, the sea breeze filled in during the middle afternoon and the race was started at 16.45 and at least gave the competitors a bit of a reasonable sail. On Monday, the

race organisers feared that the Regatta Race 4 would have to be cancelled if the wind conditions were a
repeat
of Monday but, fortunately, by 13.45 it had increased in strength sufficiently for a 15.00 start and
all fleets finished off Regatta with another reasonable sail, even if it was only a relatively short one.

Although the Regatta race 4 might have been cancelled due to fast running out of time, the race organisers promised the Hurricane 4.9 and Gull fleets a 4th race to complete their championships for as long as the
competitors were prepared to wait - even to running the race on Tuesday if necessary. Much to the relief
of the fleets, the wind came sooner rather than later.

At some time between Sunday 17th June and Tuesday 19th June, Number One garage was broken into and the green Hayter mower was stolen. This mower cost the Club approximately sg99 when purchased in 1985, and it is unlikely that we will receive this amount from the insurance.

It is essential that we all take more care of our, afid the Club's, property. A Sumber of members have

complained to me that they have found the gate left open when they arrived at the Club. Short of asking Pete to weld it shut, I cannot ensure that it is always kept closed. Only you can, by always shutting the gate even if you see someone else just about to enter or leave the site. When you arrive ALWAYS SHUT THE GATE BEHIND YOU. If there is another car immediately behind you, check that he is a club member, do not just assume that he is.

Remember that Club property is generally more securely locked away than your own; it may be your mast, tender, or dinghy that goes missing next time.

AN IMMEDIATE ADDITION TO THE SAILING INSTRUCTIONS.

At its meeting on 2nd July, the Main Committee unanimously agreed the following immediate additions to the Sailing Instructions:-

Any boat which, whilst sailing under the MSC Sailing Instructions and associated Racing Rules, touches any part of a craft which is attached to an MSC mooring shall be automatically disqualified. For the purposes of this additional Sailing Instruction, the term ‘any part of a craft' shall be deemed to include the mooring, equipment and tackle to which it is attached, together with any temporary extensions to the moored craft and any part of a dinghy, tender or craft which is secured to the mooredcraft or its associated mooring, equipment and tackle.

Any boat which, whilst sailing under the MSC Sailing Instructions and associated Racing Rules, touches an MSC mooring and associated equipment and tackle and to which no craft is attached, shall not be disqualified under the provisions of this additional Sailing Instruction.

The technical reasons for the additional Sailing Instruction.

There is no reason, other than lack of seamanship, why a boat (which is racing) should 'touch'sto a greater or lesser degree (eg. collide with; scrape past ),an obstruction such as a mooring, its equipment and tackle and/or any boat which is secured thereto. A boat which is racing should be sufficiently aware of the impending lack of room to clear the obstruction in a seamanlike manner. Where room to clear the obstruction is baulked by another boat which is sailing, then the boat which is impeded should ‘call for water' in order to pass to leeward, to windward, to tack or gybe in order to avoid the obstructing moored boat. Where 'water' is not given, the impeded boat should take seamanlike action to avoid or
minimise touching/colliding with the moored boat and its...etc.etc. If the boat failing to 'give water'
is racing, then a Protest can be raised but, if it is not racing, then a senior club member should be asked to ‘have a quiet word’ with the offending helm (who might not be aware of his/her obligations).

The human reasons for the additional Sailing Instruction

If you were to find scrape marks, dents or occassionally actual damage had occurred to your car whilst it was parked in the car park, you would naturally feel somewhat vexed.

If you were to be told it was all part of the risks of modern-day driving and such things must be
expected
to happen, you might politely express a wish that the person responsible would (a) learn to drive with a
little more care and consideration and (b) at least report the mishap.with an apology.

If you were to be told that you can ‘always get it repaired on your insurance so what are you worrying about', you might get very cross indeed.

So - why should your fellow boat-owners be expected to feel any different ?

An appeal for mutual co-operation.

Our club brings together a relatively few number of people who share a common interest in sailing but fulfill their interest in different ways. Thus we have sailboarders doing wonderful gyrations in wind conditions which keeps me firmly in the club-house. The satisfied joy of our cruiser members as they spend half the season painting, varnishing and anti-fouling their pride and joy, whilst our dinghy
racers spend week-in and week-out chasing each other around the same local buoys - usually well within
sight of the clubhouse (andequally usually with the same result) is another example of different people achieving the same degree of satisfaction in different ways. We implicitly trust our fellow members to act in a ‘reasonable way' both on and off the water and we are fortunate that the various interest groups within the club co-operate with considerable success.

The Regatta Format - what should it be ?

What should the club be aiming at in its promotion of Regatta - apart from promoting sailing ?

Theoretically, one could say it depends upon what the club membership as a whole wished to achieve; in
reality it depends upon what individual members are willing to do - or not to do - in order to run the
Regatta. Whether Regatta is a high profile event, attracting lots of top class sailors, and providing side shows of discos, BBQs, meals-on-wheels, cabaret and crowded bars 100' long depends solely upon the willingness of individual members to provide all these things, either via money or effort, rather than by any resolutions of a committee. Whether this is what the membership ‘as a whole’ wants is questionable, but certainly in the past there has been a sufficient number of very keen individual members willing to put in the effort to provide these things. The question is : as the very keen individuals ‘drop out' will there be others willing to take their place ? If not, will those same very keen individuals have to make a come-back to promote the type of regatta they feel is required ? There might also be occasions when trouble could arise simply by one circumstance leading to another - such as

am encounter with a roaming dog could lead to friction between dogs and owners alike.

year's cruise to the same area which quite took our fancy, for those of you who do not know her, Rodnigon is a fin keeled Varne 27, sloop rigged, with a LOA of 8,5 metres and powered by a Volvo MD6A twin cylinder diesel. In the five seasons of our ownership we have cruised her to Holland and Belgium, down to Normandy, the Channel Islands and North Brittanny, Boulogne and N. France, as well as local sailing on the East Coast and one foray to Dartmouth,
