M.S.C, - DOVER There are a number of routes which can be taken to cross the Thames Estuary, all of them
dependent on the tide time and state. My own particular favourite is to go cut via the Spitway on the ebb and

to cross the Sunk Sand just north of the Sunk beacon by the Black Deep No.5 buoy. Timed correctly, this allows you to take the new flood through Fisherman's Gat and down to Ramsgate or Dover, Not so good for the return trip unless you have an accurate fixing aid because Fisherman's Gat is not buoyed.

In this instance we chose to take the inside route, as the wind was N/E giving us a downwind leg to Barrow, a broad reach acrossthe Kentish Flats to Margate roads and a short beat along to the North Foreland,

Dover is more hospitable than one might think for a busy port, but contrary to advice in pilot books, the Port Control don't mind which entrance you use as long as you call them 2 or 3 minutes from the entrance to request entry permission, just stay well clear of the numerous ferries and hovercraft, You have the choice of

anchoring in the small craft area or of locking into the Wellington Dock, The anchorage can get quite rough in easterly winds but is handy if you do not wish to be tied down to dock opening times, (2 hours either side of Hw)

DOVER - NEWHAVEN There is no reel refuge for deep keel yachts between Dover and Newhaven - Rye and
Folkestone are both drying harbours, Eastbound this leg can be completed with the tide assuming that a yacht can make 44 = 5 knots and can reach the tidal gate at Dungeness as the tide turns, This tactic gives about 10 hours of favourable tide to cover the 50 miles, Westbound this is not possible so we anchored in Pevensey Bay to await the westbound tide to take us round Beachy Head and into Newhaven, past the Seven Sisters, Newhaven Marina is suffering badly from silting up so we found ourselves aground for an hour or so at low spring tide, this was so even in an outside berth and despite Rodnigon's modest 1.3m draught, The Yacht Club is very

hospitable and comfortable and provides very reasonably priced meals as well as good showers.

NEWHAVEN - CHERBOURG This is a long Channel transit of some 95 rm, There is nothing much to see excepting
the heavy traffic and ferries. The main trick is to avoid being downtide when approaching Cherbourg as the

tides are very strong on the approach, However, Cherbourg is a big target with its 2 entrances, a good ROF and the visual assistance given by the frequent exits and entrances of the cross channel ferries. Once inside the outer harbour you still have well over a mile to sail before reaching the yacht harbour. All facilities including showers, chandlers and duty free shops are available nearby,

9.

CHERBOURG - ALDERNEY Only a short leg of some 20 miles but one which has to be planned carefully so as to
cross the Alderney race before the southbound tide sets hard, We failed last year and arrived in Guernsey instead of Alderney after being set into the race, The approved ploy is to make use of the westbound inshore eddy toward Cap de la Hague, This allows you to arrive off Cap de la Hague at slack water ready to transit the eight miles to Braye, This transit must be made so as to position well north of the island and then to allow the tide to take you into Braye harbour, There are two main points to watch during the transit, firstly

the overfalls cause really rough seas, even in calm weather and the underwater noise which transmits through
the hull is definitely frightening - I was convinced that Rodnigon had sprung a leak! The second point is
that Alderney lies in a N/E - S/W direction, this has the visual effect of fooling oe into thinking that you
are further north of the island than is actually the case, The answer is to keep a really careful check on bearings from identified landmarks, On this occasion we positioned ourselves nicely for the harbour entrance,

got to within 2 miles, when Alderney disappeared in fog, a common trick I am told. We crept in on Decca and when we finally got frightened by the rocks which appeared out of the murk, dropped anchor to find that we

were actually in the harbour, We then motored very, very slowly in the general direction of the breakwater until some mooring buoys and a solitary yacht appeared with it's crew genially welcoming us to Guernsey! Alderney itself is a delightful little island although the harbour is subject to a lot of swell under certain

conditions, There are showers available near the harbour and a number of shops including the Braye Chippie. We pedalled round the island on our bikes before returning to Rodnigon to take the tide through the Swinge and

on to Beaucette Marina in Guernsey,

ALDERNEY - BEAUCETTE A really downhill leg this one, we had the spinnaker up until an enormous broach rolled

Sarah off the bunk, We went into Beaucette Marina for the night after a short wait on the buoy outside to allow sufficient water over the sill, Beaucette is formed from an old quarry which was allowed to flood and an entrance was then blasted through the cliff, It is really pretty although quite a long way from St Peter

Port and its shops. The Solent sailors who crowd St Peter Port Marina at weekends do not seem to like Beaucette, perhaps the rock strewn entry frightens them, although it is well marked for both day and night entry. Macmillans Almanac contains a table which allows calculation of the sill depth at any particular time

and there is a tide gauge at the entrance.

GUERNSEY BRITTANY (TREGUIER) Off again down the Little Russell channel with good views of Herm and Sark as we left the Channel Islands behind. Another long leg with very little commercial traffic but lots of fishing buoys to look out for, A glance at the tidal chart will show that careful tide planning can carry you most of the way on a favourable, or at worst, a cross tide, The huge lighthouse on Les Roches Couvres shows up from a

long way out as does Les Heaux lighthouse when approaching the Treguier River, Time now to hoist both the Tricoleur and the Breton Ensign and get out the French charts and the pilot for entrance to the Treguier River, There are three entrances of varying difficulty, all of them demanding careful attention to the marks and transits so as to avoid the many hazards, Once into the river proper, it's all straightforward although the Marina berths at Breguier are in the mainstream which flows very strongly through the pontoons, The

Treguier river is very wooded and there is a very comfortable sheltered anchorage half a mile downstream of the town for those who do not wish to utilise the marina facilities, The chandlery is worth a visit, it's quite large and very traditional with all sorts of nice goodies. It is situated just over the bridge upstream of the marina,

TREGUIER - PLOUMANAC'H While in Treguier we met a retired army RSM who was making a leisurely trip to the
Far East via the Med. He came with us for the ride to Ploumanac'h which turned out to be a beat all the way. We had a good view of Les Sept Iles as we approached Ploumanac'h. This port of Brittanny is the Pink Granite Coast and this is literally true when the sun shines on the rocks because they show a pink hue. Ploumanac'h is easily picked out by the Chateau Costolaeves which dominates the entrance and looks rather like something out of a fairy tale film set, The pilot books claim a difficult entrance, but we found it fairly straightforward, although we had to anchor in the entry channel to wait for water over the sill into the very sheltered harbour, It is a nice place to spend a few visits and perhaps to sail over to the nearby Sept Iles which are well worth a visit.

PLOUMANAC'H - PRIMEL Primel is another place with a dramatic rock strewn entrance so we kept very strictly

on the approved line and moored on the visitor's buoys. A touch bouncy in the harbour so we stayed only the one night.

PRIMEL - ROSCOFF The harbour at Roscoff dries out, although it is possible for keel boats to dry out against
the harbour wall, We went in to have a look at the harbour, but elected to go around the corner to the

Bloscon ferry port, where we found a nice little anchorage with some unoccupied buoys, Roscoff is literally surrounded by rocks and requires great navigational care when on the approach, The Chenal de Batz provides a good high water shortcut between the mainland and the Ile de Batz for yachts em route to L'Abervrach or further south, The weed in this area is very prolific and I had to don snorkel and wetsuit to clear

10,

Rodnigon's propeller which was well fouled. Roscoff itself is a pretty little place and well worth a visit, especially so for the restaurants which sell an enormous variety of different crepes,

ROSCOFF - MORLAIX Roscoff was the furthest west point of the holiday, an intention to go the L'abervrach
was frustrated by the wind and a lack of time, We sailed along the north side of the Ile de Batz before turning back and down towards the Morlaix estuary and its river. Initial perusal of the pilot book was somewhat twitch-inducing, but in fact the entry channels and transits are very clearly marked and give no problem in reasonable visibility, Again a dramatic rock strewn entrance to the wide Morlaix river which is navigable only on the tide. Morlaix is at the head of navigation and the marina is accessed by a lock which
opens at HW - 1% hours, HW and HW + 1 hour. The town is dominated by a tall viaduct across the valley and is
well worth a visit. We spent two days there making full use of our bikes to inspect the countryside,

OUR RETURN was by a very similar route via Ploumanac'h, Guernsey (St Peter Port this time,) Alderney, Dover, Ramsgate to MSC with no major occurences other than a chance encounter with a fishing buoy,

Hopefully this account will encourage more forays of the MSC Kamikaze Seagull into foreign parts. We certainly recommend North Brittanny as a cruising ground, but you do need three weeks' holiday, If you do intend a trip to this area it would be worth considering leaving your boat on the South Coast ready for the transit to Cherbourg or the Channel Islands.

SPEED BOAT INCIDENTS

Every class of water sports attracts its small minority of ‘idiots' - the sailboat category included.
However, the ‘mechanised sea-horses' (ie. speedboats, jet-skis, etc) are, by their nature, rather likely to be more lethal than the average dinghy sailor ‘idiot' and therefore a great deal of trust and responsibility is placed in the hands of those who drive them. The Sailing Sub-Committee have been alarmed by what is perceived to be an increase in ‘incidents’ involving the speed boats and jet-skis . Without wishing anyone to get neurotic or paranoid about it, the Sailing Sub feel that if anyone experiences a genuinely dangerous incident then they should report it to the 0.0.D. with a view to reporting the matter to the police. You

will need to note the number/name of the boats involved and, of course, have some independent witnesses.

That is not to say that you report every time a speed boat's wash rocks your sailboat when you're trying to get across to Goldhanger with little wind and an adverse tide; the speed boats have as much right to use the river as we sailors and, like us, are normally considerate and responsible but occassionally make
a mistake. Let's keep an eye on it - but not go overboard (literally).

COMMODORE

What a Camping Fortnight. Although I was unable to attend, I believe the sun shone, it was warm (even hot) and dry for the whole time. I would like to thank all concerned who helped throughout the fortnight during which I understand there were fifty five Cadets attending. I am sure that everyone would join me in thanking Mike Turner for his efforts in arranging the Cadet Week tuition.

Our next major event is the East Coast Piers Race which will be on Sunday 16th September and I am sure that John and his team will be hoping for similar conditions.

Some concern has been expressed to me regarding the new rule in the Sailing Instructions. The potential risks of the increased number, size and speed of dinghies racing in the moorings was first brought up at the April Main Committee Meeting and was referred to the Sailing Sub Committee with a request that they put forward sane proposal. The matter was left with them, but they could not agree a suitable formla. At the July Main Committee Meeting it was decided to adopt the rule which is similar to that used by most of the Burmham Clubs. The intention is not to prevent sailing in the moorings, but to try to ensure that we do not end up with damage to racing Dinghies or Cruisers. While I am not conversant with the racing rules, I presume that any 'innocent' party who was disqualified as a result of the rule, would be able to protest any 'guilty' party.
It is my intention that during the closed winter season, the whole question of the start line, the courses we sail and the support boat facilities is fully examined to formulate a way forward into the future.

I will close by expressing my thanks once again to all who helped during the Camping
Fortnight.

Neil Pembleton

While sailing on the Blackwater one sunny summer Sunday and passing north of the picturesque Bradwell Power Station, I noticed lots of yachts, same of them belonging to MSC alas, which appeared at first sight to be at anchor. Well they were all lying to the tide, sails neatly furled and with bits of rope or chain attaching bows to
water.

Then suddenly I realised my mistake, silly me, of course they were not at anchor. Quickly checking my 1937 Manual of Seamanship, I confirmed that ships at anchor in daylight must exhibit a round shape in the forward rigging. There was not a round shape to be seen on any of these yachts.

It must be a new game to replace the now passe launching trailer sailing. I was daft enough to ask the Cruiser Captain the rules, but he just muttered something about Dutch motor sailing triangle, hit me with his scrap bag and shambled off.

SUNDAY 24TH JUNE 1990 - A DAY'S RESCUE

What can be more pleasant than a day on rescue boat duty. No bruises, no getting wet, no trapeze belt cutting into you, or that's what I thought.

Take a camera, you never know, might get some shots for the photo competition. Take a snack, won't be a lot to do except:

- Bring back three sailboarders and two dinghies.
- Look for two lost racing marks.
- Put up with faulty radios.
- Try to assist two cats. in trouble on lee shores.
- Slip over on hard.

Let's go back to the start of the list: Two sailboarders taken fran the water, neither wearing buoyancy aids, one transferred from a yacht with a damaged board, again no buoyancy aid, and yet Flag B was being flown. One young lady sailboarder when asked where her buoyancy aid was replied "In the club locker roam", She was informed in no uncertain termns of my views. Sailboarders must be exempt from personal buoyancy, maybe they can't drown, only they know that perhaps they can walk on water. CATAMARANS AT MARCONI

During the course of the 1990 season a number of occurrences have led to the impression that the interests of the Catamaran Fleet are not being served as well as might be hoped. Recently letters to Navigans have indicated the level of dissatisfaction in same parts of the Fleet. I think it is important that all of us who sail Catamarans at the Club and who are not happy with recent events -
particularly the imposition of the new Sailing Instruction - should understand the
situation and take positive steps to ensure the Club continues to be (or becomes) the sort of Club to which we want to belong.

My own personal feelings are:

1. The Club offers an excellent site, with good facilities, for Catamaran sailing.
It would be hard to beat elsewhere for the variety it offers.

2. The Club caters for a wide variety of interests, and each group of members
benefits from the presence of the others: for instance a considerable number of Cruising members have very kindly offered their services in support of the Piers Race. The variety of interests necessarily implies a variety of facilities needed.

3. At any one time a large number of Cruisers are to be found unused on moorings. At
any one time an equally large number of Catamarans can be seen in the Cat Field.

4. By their nature Cruisers have to be kept on moorings, and as such will inevitably
became an obstacle to other river users.

5. Races imply a concentration of fast-moving craft, and as such will inevitably
became a risk to other river users.

6. The moorings used by the Club are allocated by Maldon District Council; their
positions may or may not be negotiable. The start line used for racing is in our own hands, but is limited by the strong tide.

7. The wish to avoid severe damage to a Cruiser on a mooring is obvious. The need to
take urgent steps to improve the present situation is debatable. The need to invoke

a new Sailing Instruction aimed at outlawing something which doesn't happen anyway (i.e. helms deliberately hitting and damaging Cruisers) is obscure to say the least. The method of introducing the new measure seems to have raised in same the emotions which might be associated with returning hame and finding the bailiffs have posted a notice re-possessing one's house.

8. Why do collisions occur?

- [he start area is congested and control can be lost by the inexperienced in a melee
of manoevering boats.
- Tactical actions by same boats may lead to those less tactically aware into
Situations where a collision ensues.
- Leaving the Hard under certain wind conditions can be difficult.

None of these will be affected by the new Sailing Instruction.

9. How can we reduce the risk of collisions?

- Start in an area free of moored boats.
- Clear the area in front of the Hard of moored Cruisers.

10. In light winds, collisions may occur but damage is unlikely. In strong enough
winds the tidal flow beyond the moorings does not preclude a sensible start on a long
line.

11. I propose:

We keep the start line clear of moorings (and, no, this isn't done already).
- In strong enough winds we start the Cats on a long line (i.e. beyond D mark and
inside the orange flagged outer distance mark, using a transit of the racebox and D mark, not the mete.)

miniscule flags which are often unidentifiable. This may involve lights or shapes, and certainly much more noise.

alternative first mark in westerly winds.

them.
- Anyone who camplains about grass-roots representation on Club committees_ should

M.S.C./M.A.S.C. FINANCIAL RELATIONSHIP (and its effect on Club policy.)
The Sailing Club operates as a section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Ci and as such is bound by its constitution. Under this the section is run by i committee(s) who have to discharge a responsibility to ensure the finacial wei being of the section; basically 'break even', not run at a loss. Whilst the section is not allowed to hold a bank account nor to enter into any loan agreement and it must have M.A.S.C. agreement for any major capital purchase, its finances are run in a separate account within the MASC (this is the same for all sections). Such profit as is made by the section is held in a Reserve Fund, which bears interest, and used for two purposes. Firstly it can be used to "smooth' out a small loss in any one year, however the Main Committee policy is to avoid a loss in the first place. Secondly it is used to help with the cost of major equipment replacement such as replacement rescue craft, tractors etc.. The section has over the years managed its affairs in a professional manner and by following this policy operates free of interference from the MASC, unlike some other sections.
Since the club moved to the Stansgate site, the MASC has invested £90,000.00 approx of their money by buying the site (i.e. it is owned by the M.A.S.C. not the Sailing Section, as are all the assets), building of the clubhouse, installation of the sewage plant and help with the Jack B purchase for example, in the site. For this and to offset the costs incurred by us at the MASC, accountant help etc., we pay an annual contribution; this year £7375.00. By this investment, they have demonstrated their willingness to help the section grow over the years.
Turning to the events of the last couple of years, at the time that I first approached them for assistance with the second rescue boat and extension, this coincided with a downturn in their own finacial situation. As those who attended the MASC Annual General Meeting on the 26th September will know, they
have operated with a loss of £23,000.00 in 1988/1989 and a loss of £30,000.00 in
1998/1990. This has obviously reduced their own reserves considerably. In part the situation has not been helped by the decrease in the Marconi working population as the level of Associate membership is limited to 12.5% by the
Magistrates.
Looking to the future the MASC has been involved in a cost reduction exercise which is starting to bear fruit this year. In addition it wants to amend its constitution to make all members 'Ordinary' not associate, this will remove the current restriction and allow a larger number of non GEC members. This resolution was put to a Special Meeting on the 26th September but had to be withdrawn because of some technical inaccuracies. These have now been resolved and a new meeting will be called on 17th October. Drawing some parallels with our own section, we found ourselves in the same situation in 1983/1985 when we had exhausted the Marconi companies for members. We wanted to improve and expand the facilities, costs were rising on the existing facilities, and there
was a 'market value' above which subscription increases would lead to reduced membership. We therefore set out to increase the level of associate membership with all the heartache of 'the club will not be the same'/'the passing of an era' that the MASC is now experiencing. It is true that the club has changed but I believe that the foresight at that time was right and the club is the better for it today. We may have a new set of problems but we still have a club we all can afford.
I am sure that the changes proposed by the MASC will have the same effect and would ask ALL Ordinary members to watch out for the notice of the meeting and come along to support the motion.

NAVIGANS PAST - How many members actually read Navigans I wonder ? I guess we will never know ‘cos
only those who read it could possibly reply to a questionnaire. Certainly in our household there's a fair old scramble to be first to read it. “What's your favourite feature?” I ask the rest of the family; "Through the eye of a hurricane" they reply . Thank's a lot family, nothing like loyalty to your nearest and dearest to cheer me up through the eye of the storm, let alone that hurricane.
Although we've been MSC members from about 1972/73, I can't actually remember reading or seeing Navigans from the '70s. The earliest Navigans we kept was December'79 and shows a youthful Dave Lawson in very
close proximity - and obvious enjoyment - to a belly-dancer at the Laying Up Supper. This might have
been the same Laying Up Supper that the then Mirror Fleet were ‘well into their cups' - and resulted in
a letter of complaint saying how dreadful it all was, speaking of which......seeceee

NAVIGANS PRESENT - My suspicions were aroused at the late-August Bank Holiday Camping Weekend when a stream
of gleeful members kept sidling up to the Fletcher's caravan for a peek at what was obviosly a pretty hot publication. Curiosity aroused, I casually wandered over to 'pass the time of day' and was met by Dave F with a grin well worthy of the cat (pussy-type) from Cheshire; “Collector's item this, Mike" he said “it's burnt brown and crisp around the edges". Well, I must say, it made good reading and, whether one agrees with

‘the letters' or no, it makes a change from the usual round of race reports and lists of winners, and even overshadows 'My trip up the Orinoco in Bathtub IV'. The September Navigans was somehow different.

Handing back the crisped publication, the thunder growled, the lighting flashed and - down came the rain
from the hosepipe in the sky. Val F. advanced upon me accusingly, waving said crisped publication menacingly.
"It's all your fault” she said quietly - but firmly. I nipped around the other side of the table, just to
be on the safe side; “But they're entitled to their opinion" I cried , "and in any case, I was merely reporting
the unanimous decision of the Main Committee - I was merely the winged messenger" (literally ready to take
flight). "In any case, there were other 'dinghy' people at the meeting to voice opposition if they wished
- it was a unanimous decision*®. I moved a chair nonchalantly seas toblock the nearest approach between
Val and me; perhaps it was time to leave. "No", says Val "I'm not talking about ‘the Rule', I'm talking about the traditional thunder storm during camping fortnight. If you hadn't mentioned it had not come on time, this storm wouldn't have happened; It's all your fault". "Oh", says I, mightily relieved 4I suppose it is:
Sorry" - and made off for the safety of my own caravan. At that moment the heavenly lights fused, the Thunder
God belched and all hosepipes were clearly aimed at the MSC.

SCHOOL MEALS UGH! - I'm not sure I agree with Robin Smith that Neil's comments in the August Navigans showed
any marked bad tempered traits, but, if they were a little tetchy, then I'm not surprised. With a ratio of almost 500 members : 1 Commodore, the steady rain of complaints, gripes and moans covering all things under the (MSC) sun must get a bit wearing, even for a fairly mild-mannered chap like Neil. Still, if one allows oneself to be put up for ‘high office’ I suppose one must expect to be shied at now and again. As the saying
goes:-

‘If you can't stand the heat, then get out of the kitchen'

But how's this for a matching maxim:-

‘If you don't like the meals we serve, come into the kitchen and cook them yourself’

SPEECH DAY - There is no truth in the rumour that the AGM is to be re-named Speech Day, nor that the Laying
Up Supper is to become known as the Master's Dinner Party. Mind you, the prospect of Neil appearing in mortar board and gown might bring in a bigger attendance at the AGM than usual, not that he need get up to such antics this year to attract an audience; I suspect this year it might have to be an open-air meeting and should provide lots of fun for all concerned. Let's hope the Thunder God has forgiven me and the Sunshine Girls look kindly upon me 'cos I'll be there.

BEANE SAUCE - I enjoyed Dave Beane's little snippets evenifl didn't understand all the words (I couldn't
find Sebacious in my dictionary but I think it's something to do with a border in the garden). The image of Derek Hall 'shambling off' scrap bag over his shoulder, muttering about Dutch elm disease, or something, was worth contemplating.

PS. What's a scrap bag?

THOUGHT FOR THE DAY - it's not what you read, it's the way that you read it.

** joking apart, I rather like to read the cruiser articles. At least it covers a different type of sailing than I am used to and I remember Derek Hall's article with particular pleasure.

Mike Boreham

THE EXPERIENCES OF THE THORNE FAMILY CAMPING

For years Chris and I have told ourselves that we would stay at the Club for the Camping Fortnight. Most

years we have only thought about it when reading the adventures of other people in Navigans. Every Blue Moon we have actually intended staying and once even hired a caravan only to be rained off almost as soon as we

arrived. This year was going to be different. Our children, Stephen aged 12, and Michael aged 8, were going to do the Cadet Course and we bought a new tent to make certain it would not rain again. Full of hope we set
off - I must admit I had already arranged an escape route of returning home during the fortnight for essential
supplies and a comfortable night's sleep,
—

As everyone knows the weather was superb and our first week passed gently by. We even got our Cruiser in the
water for the first time in two years, We still, as yet, haven't been anywhere in her - that highlight is

still to core,

Chris took our boys out in the Mirror and in true "Captain Bligh" spirit managed to upset them in a very short

time. The usual helming skills of shouting continuously at your Crew with instructions they don't understand, being hit with the boom because your head isn't low enough or moving quick enough, and the tiller being rammed into your side because you haven't moved sufficiently aut of the way. Anyway Cadet Week started with Michael announcing that he wasn't going to do the capsize drill, and if that meant not doing the course then he wasn't going to do it, After a bit of "you are going to do it" persuasion, he agreed to do it, Neither boy had any

real experience of sailing despite Stephen's assurance that sailing a Topper for half an hour at Center Parcs on a lake only 3ft deep throughout, was sailing single-handed,

The boys entered into the spirit of the week and thoroughly enjoyed everything. Once Michael had done sis capsize drill he enjoyed falling into the water at every opportunity, By the time the boys were able to helm

they too seemed to have caught the "Captain Bligh" spirit (is this something one catches sailing on the Blackwater???) Our funniest moment was listening to Stephen telling us about his first outing helming. there he was, helming and all his crew were interested in was looking at the other boats and not doing as he told
them - even shouting didn't produce the right responses.

I am sure other people will explain in greater detail the things the Cadets did in their week, but for us the

pleasure of seeing our children sailing on their own in our dinghy was something we won't ever forget. We would like to take this opportunity to thank the two Mikes for all their efforts and the hard work they put in

CONTD.....

to make the week so successful, The boys are already talking about next year and looking forward to the Winter Series, As to whether they will be so keen when normal sailing weather returns only remains to be
seen,

The only drawback to the fortnight was Chris and the boys sailing in the Cats, I can see this adventure might

prove very expensive, Stephen's comment was "If we had one of those, Dad, we could core sailing every weekend." I have my suspicions that as time goes on I shall be outnumbered by the Sailors in my family and

will pass some very contented weekends sitting on the sea wall, reading my book and getting sun tanned, or weather-beaten as the case may be, Still isn't that what family sailing is all about!

KNOW YOUR LOCAL AREA - BRIGHTLINGSEA & ST OSYTH

Most Cruiser folks go to Brightlingsea fairly regularly, moor up on the trots and wander over to the Yacht Club quay for a drink in the pub, to imbibe the odd fish and chip, or just to have a stroll round the town.

An alternative venture is to take a trip by dinghy in the opposite direction with a view to exploring St Osyth creek, the village and priory.

The creek is very twisty but deep enough for a dinghy at all states of the tide except for extreme low water. A row or motor of about two miles will bring you to the boatyard at the head of the creek, the site of a

long-extinct tide mill. Here you can disembark and quench your thirst at the nearby pub just a few yards

along the road to your left,

Having satisfied this priority you can then walk further along the road towards the east and pay a visit to

the remains of the 12th century priory before going back to your dinghy for tke return voyage,

St Osyth creek joins Brightlingsea creek to the east of Cindery Island so it is possible to return to the trots by a slightly different route round the north of Cindery Island,

Dave Beane

IT COULD ONLY HAPPEN AT SEA - (Through the Eye of the Hurricane)

As the newly-elected Chairman of the Hurricane Class Association I felt it to be my duty to accept as many free meals as was on offer at the recent Hurricane National Championships, Accordingly, Bank Holiday Monday morning found me filling my stomach with a generous helping of Eggs and Bacon thanks to the generosity of Chris and Trevor Milton, Duly satisfied, I left the two of them to proceed out onto the water for day 3 of the event, whilst I found myself a comfortable chair in the Race Box at Pentewan Sands Sailing Club to watch the 53 entrants chase the wind around the bay, My eyes felt like doorstops against which my brain was endlessly swinging, which will teach me to stay away from the booze which flowed after the Class AGM.

CONTDO.....

Suddenly I was awoken fror my doze by the urgent calling of my name! There before me stood Chris. "Help!" she cried, with e pleading look in mer eye, "I don't feel well, so will you crew for Trevor?" How could 1 refuse the woman who had filled my stomach that morning? My brain urgently sougkt an excuse!

"I haven't got any sailing gear!" I replied with relief. "No worry, we'll find you some," came the reply. So with mo more ado I trotted, in time to the pounding in my head, around to the camper to kit up. As well as providing the sailing gear, Chris also provided the headache pills to see me on my way.

Now you have to use your imagination! The wet suit belonged to Trevor, so it only fitted where it touched,

If it bad been in green I could have done a very good impersonation of a Mutant Ninja Turtle. On me, the suit had more spare tyres than the Michelin Man, the legs looked like Nora Batty's stockings, and I had the only double breasted buoyancy sid available in the country! The trapeze belt felt like a loose-fitting pammock

despite my attempts to pull it tighter as I waddled down the beach like a hippo, with Trevor only just managing to stifle bis laughter, "Whose gear ere you wearing?" asked Trevor, “Yours!" I replied, "No wonder

it's big," smiled Trevor, "That's my spare suit and it's six inches too big for me!" “Ak well, I was always the wrong skape to model wet suits anyway!"

We pushed the boat off and then came the difficult part. With all the spare tyres, and the double breasted buoyancy aid, I couldn't get on the boat, so I was dragged alongside for about tke first 50 yards, whilst Trevor made comments like "stop mucking about, and pull the jib in!" I finally struggled aboard and we headed for the start. "Hello Christine, where are your curls?" The comments care thick and fast from the rest of the fleet. Sore people kad difficulty getting their eyeballs back in their heads, after the shock of seeing me in all this gear,

Well, whilst Trevor had been collecting me there had been a general recall,end accordingly the start sequence was only 5 minutes, and wren the gun went, we were 100 yards behind the line, facing the wrong way, whilst waiting to check the signal. We hadn't seen the preparatory signal amongst the melee of boats, so we were

second from last across tke line, and with me clad in trainers we proceeded to bump together all the way around the course, To Trevor's credit he managed, despite my slippery antics, to get us back to the lower middle of the fleet by the end of the race, At this point we decided that a comfort break was in order before

the next race, so we headed for tke shore,

The wind was onshore so as we headed for the shallows, I decided to slide along tke bows to step smartly off

when Trevor rounded up to stop. Step off I certainly did! Unfortunately we were still 50 yards from tke

shore, The boat dipped on a wave, and I said goodbye, fell between the hulls, and the boat sailed over me, 1 kept my head down to avoid the dolphin striker, so the water poured down the neck of the wet suit, giving me a

good soaking inside. Meanwhile Trevor wko had been watching me to ensure that I was alright, proceeded to

sail straight up the beach without stopping! The boat ended up about 10 feet clear of the water, but because the beach is sand and very shallow, no damage occurred, Whilst Trevor was driving up the beach, I was

atterpting to swim for shore, Have you ever tried swimming in an oversize wetsuit, where with every stroke water pours in the front? After about ten strokes I stopped for a rest, and decided to let my legs dangle

below me, It was then that I discovered the water was only six inches deep! Was I embarrassed! I struggled to my feet, floundered my way ashore, and explained to an anxious Trevor tkat I was alright and what had

happened,

After a comfort break, althougrt why I bothered I do not know, we went afloat again for the second race, With @ falling wind (it never did get above Force 2 during the whole weekend,) our combined weight, plus the water

still resident in the suit meant that we gradually drifted slowly backwards through the fleet, to end up
second from last - but maybe next time!

Where was Christine when all this was happening? Sleeping her headache away and missing all the fun, My thanks go to Trevor and Christine for the breakfast and the loan of the gear, but next time I'll take my own boat and leave the falling off to Dave

Steeve Keeble

CADET SERIES 1990.

Once more, the Cadet Series turned out to be a cliff-hanger with any one of three competitors able to win the series as they went into the last race. The difference this year is that the winner of the Cadet Series was a young lady, so it is 'Congratulations' to:-

LUCY BOREHAM

on winning the 1990 Cadet Series and becoming the first young lady to do so since Alix Richards in 1972. Before that it was Susan Tillotson (1969) and Anne Palmer (1968); I wonder what they are doing now ? Did they keep up their sailing ? Are they still members of the MSC under a different name ? Perhaps someone who knows could drop a line to Navigans.

The winds this year were decidedly fickle, a typical pattern for the Cadet races being that the R.O. would set a course in a steady F2 (maybe F1+), the wind would die at the start, causing the fleet to stay bunched together for the first lap, and then come up for the last lap (the race inevitably being shortened). Very frustrating for the competitors to say the least. Only the first (F2) and last races (F2/3) presented anything like a steady wind throughout.

Debbie Yorston scored well in the fickle winds, scoring two 1sts and a 2nd - plus a retired in the 4th race when the wind died. Going into the last race, Debbie needed to finish within two places of Lucy in order to win the series; in the event she finished 6th to Lucy's 1st.

Lee Harrison had an outside chance of winning on going into the last race; if he won and both Lucy and Debbie finished well down the list, he might just have got the series. Alas, he decided to round two buoys the opposite way to everyone else (and to R.O. Colin Willsmore's course instructions) and so scored a retired, although it would be fair to say that it would have probably made no difference to the overall result as the course tended to favour the monos rather than the cats.

Another competitor to round the buoy the wrong way (in race 2, R.O.Phil May) was Chris Caruth in the Laser Fun. He decided to round F to port and chase off towards Breezy, instead of rounding to starboard and making for D mark. Claire Davies rounded the marks OK and always seems to enjoy her sailing.

Mel Keeble had a good series in her Topper and actually won the last race by 21 seconds over Lucy (420).

Ben Holroyd clearly enjoys his sailing in his Laser, which is not the easiest of boats to race in light winds. Stephen Caruth sailed well in the Enterprise and scored over his brother by ensuring he knew which way to go ! Paul Harrison sailed his Dart 15 consistently and it's nice to seem him out pretty regularly in the Cat races; keep going Paul, it's coming along nicely.

David Ball's pure love for sailing is well known, as is his seamanship and boat-handling ability. By his own admission, he doesn't take racing too seriously - he just likes to sail. Tom Ashley sailed both Mirror and Marauder (but not at the same time) and finished 5th overall. Stuart Golding helmed his Mirror in the 1st race but elected to crew for some of the remaining races. Mike Fletcher is always competitive, completed all the races and got some good results; next year...who knows?

Finally, Ian Chaplin (aged 9 or thereabouts) took part in his first race, crewed by sister Rachel. The difficult light-wind conditions precluded him from finishing the course, but it was a good try. Ian's Mum, Linda Chaplin, once won the Ladies Cup so it's obviously 'in the family' and, again, in a year or twos time... who knows ?

SOLO NATIONALS: ABERSOCH, AUGUST 1990

On Saturday 11th August SOLOs from all over the UK and 2 from Holland hitched up their personal transports to find their way to the remote fishing village of Abersoch in North Wales, The reason: The 1990 National Championships, In all 86 boats turned up to the event at South Caernarvonshire Yacht Club. Only Colin Willsmore and Roger Smith went from Marconi, With Malcolm Gandy and Alan Buwell from Halfway, The Essex Star was Malcolm Gandy who finished 13th overall having led one race for over a lap and finally finishing 5th,

The wind was too strong for racing on 2 days which meant that two races were sailed back to back on the last day, We were on the water in quite strong winds for 74 bours so there were some very tired legs plodding up the beach to pack their boats away in the rain,

Altogether @ good week in good surroundings for family, sightseers and sailors,

Who won? Geoff Carveth - who else?

Roger Smith

M.S.C./M.A.S.C. FINANCIAL RELATIONSHIP (and its effect on Club policy.)
The Sailing Club operates as a section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club and as such is bound by its constitution. Under this the section is run by its committee(s) who have to discharge a responsibility to ensure the finacial well being of the section; basically 'break even', not run at a loss. Whilst the section is not allowed to hold a bank account nor to enter into any loan agreement and it must have M.A.S.C. agreement for any major capital purchase, its finances are run in a separate account within the MASC (this is the same for all sections). Such profit as is made by the section is held in a Reserve Fund, which bears interest, and used for two purposes. Firstly it can be used to "smooth' out a small loss in any one year, however the Main Committee policy is to avoid a loss in the first place. Secondly it is used to help with the cost of major equipment replacement such as replacement rescue craft, tractors etc.. The section has over the years managed its affairs in a professional manner and by following this policy operates free of interference from the MASC, unlike some other sections.
Since the club moved to the Stansgate site, the MASC has invested £90,000.00 approx of their money by buying the site (i.e. it is owned by the M.A.S.C. not the Sailing Section, as are all the assets), building of the clubhouse, installation of the sewage plant and help with the Jack B purchase for example, in the site. For this and to offset the costs incurred by us at the MASC, accountant help etc., we pay an annual contribution; this year £7375.00. By this investment, they have demonstrated their willingness to help the section grow over the years.
Turning to the events of the last couple of years, at the time that I first approached them for assistance with the second rescue boat and extension, this coincided with a downturn in their own finacial situation. As those who attended the MASC Annual General Meeting on the 26th September will know, they
have operated with a loss of £23,000.00 in 1988/1989 and a loss of £30,000.00 in
1998/1990. This has obviously reduced their own reserves considerably. In part the situation has not been helped by the decrease in the Marconi working population as the level of Associate membership is limited to 12.52% by the
Magistrates.
Looking to the future the MASC has been involved in a cost reduction exercise which is starting to bear fruit this year. In addition it wants to amend its constitution to make all members 'Ordinary' not associate, this will remove the current restriction and allow a larger number of non GEC members. This resolution was put to a Special Meeting on the 26th September but had to be withdrawn because of some technical inaccuracies. These have now been resolved and a new meeting will be called on 17th October. Drawing some parallels with our own section, we found ourselves in the same situation in 1983/1985 when we had exhausted the Marconi companies for members. We wanted to improve and expand the facilities, costs were rising on the existing facilities, and there
was a 'market value' above which subscription increases would lead to reduced membership. We therefore set out to increase the level of associate membership with all the heartache of 'the club will not be the same'/'the passing of an era' that the MASC is now experiencing. It is true that the club has changed but I believe that the foresight at that time was right and the club is the better for it today. We may have a new set of problems but we still have a club we all can afford.
I am sure that the changes proposed by the MASC will have the same effect and would ask ALL Ordinary members to watch out for the notice of the meeting and come along to support the motion.
Obviously these problems and the restrictions on the section by the constitution have affected the Section's Main Committee's plans for the future. The cost of the second rescue boat is in the order of £10,000.00 and the extension

£60,000.00. These alone would represent an investment of £70.000.00. However
it does not stop here as the annual running costs would increase and to maximise 5. the return will probably need a full time steward, both being an annual cost to be funded. In addition it would probably be necessary to provide some accommodation; another capital investment. All of this at a time when our backers have a major financial problem themselves.
Under these changed circumstances the the planning of such large scale investment and ENSURING THE FUTURE WELLBEING (even survival) of the Sailing Club requires considerable research, time and effort. We all want to move forward into the future but the main committee does have to recognise the risks
involved.
I hope that this somewhat lengthy item will give you an indication of the background to, and the current situation. I would like to thank also all the members of all the committees who contribute freely their time and effort in running the club on the day to day AND planning its future.

RUN AND PLENTY OF GOOO LANDMARKS; ORFORDNESS LIGHT, SIZEWELL B, SOUTHWOLD HARBOUR, AND FINALLY, LOWESTOFT WITH
A LARGE GASHOLDER JUST BEHIND THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, IT WAS JUST A MATTER OF PICKING UP THE E. BARNARD BUO*
AND FOLLOWING THE BUOYED PASSAGE INSIDE THE NEWCOMBE SANDS, THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, WITH ITS TWIN WHITE PAINTED
CUPOLAS EITHER SIDE, IS EASY TO SEE. THE EBB TIDE HAS A STRONG SET ACROSS THE HARBOUR MOUTH SO IT PAYS TO
STAY CLOSE TO THE SOUTH SIDE ON ENTRY. ONCE INSIDE, THE YACHT HARBOUR AND THE ROYAL NORFOLK AND SUFFOLK YACHT
CLUB ARE AHEAD AND SLIGHTLY TO PORT, LOWESTOFT PORT CONTROL OPERATES ON CHANNEL 12 AND SHOULD BE CALLED PRIOR
TO ENTRY, IF YOU WISH TO VISIT THE LOWESTOFT CRUISING CLUB ON LAKE LOTHING, THEN YOU WILL NEED TO PASS
THROUGH THE ROAD BRIDGE. THE BRIDGE CONTROL IS ALSO ON CHANNEL 12 AND WILL ADVISE YOU OF THE NEXT OPENING AS
THEY PREFER TO CO-ORDINATE YACHT MOVEMENTS WITH COMMERCIAL TRAFFIC,

THE YACHT HARBOUR IS FAIRLY BASIC, THE RN & SYC LOOKS PRETENTIOUS BUT IS VERY FRIENDLY, SERVES A NICE MEAL AND
SELLS ADNAMS BITTER AT £1 A PINT, IT COST US £8 PER NIGHT STAY FOR RODNIGON'S 28 FEET, WE SPENT TwO NIGHTS
IN LOWESTOFT, THEN DEPARTED ON THE TIDE FOR THE SHORT HOP UP TO YARMOUTH, THIS IS AN INSHORE PASSAGE INSIDE
THE SANDS WHICH RUN PARALLEL TO THE COAST FROM LOWESTOFT TO YARMOUTH. IT WAS A FAST SMOOTH TRIP WITH JUST A
SLIGHT POBBLE OFF THE NESS POINT (THE MOST EASTERLY POINT OF ENGLAND.) IN FACT WE ARRIVED TOO EARLY. HAVING
OBTAINED ENTRY PERMISSION FROM YARMOUTH PORT CONTROL (CHANNEL 12) WE HAD QUITE A STRUGGLE AGAINST THE STRONG

EBB OUT OF THE RIVER AND TOOK NEARLY AN HOUR TO COVER THE 2 MILES TO THE HAVEN BRIDGE. WE THEN COMPLETELY
FAILED TO GET THROUGH THE BRIDGE, AS THE TIDE RUNNING THROUGH THE BRIDGE PIERS PROVED TOO STRONG FOR OUR 10 HP
DIESEL. WE THEREFORE SPENT THE NIGHT MOORED ALONGSIDE AN OLD DRIFTER WHICH IS A FLOATING FISHING MUSEUM, THE
RIVER WALL IS DEFINITELY NOT SUITABLE FOR YACHTS AS IT IS VERY ROUGH AND UNEVEN, DOWNRIVER FROM THE BRIDGE,
YARMOUTH IS DEFINITELY A COMMERCIAL PORT FOR THE OFFSHORE OIL AND GAS INDUSTRY, BEING PACKED WITH SUPPORT AND
SUPPLY VESSELS OF ALL KINDS OF NATIONALITIES. WE FELT VERY SMALL AND VULNERABLE IN SUCH COMPANY,

THE NEXT DAY WE TRANSITED THE HAVEN AND BREYDON BRIDGES ON THE FLOOD TIDE IN COMPANY WITH A 35 FOOT YACHT
WHICH HAD TRAVELLED UP FROM GIBRALTAR, WE WERE A LITTLE DISCONCERTED TO SEE HIM GOING THROUGH STERN FIRST,
BUT APPARENTLY THE ENGINE HAD FAILED, SO WE GAVE HIM A TOW TO THE NEAREST MARINA,

THERE HAD BEEN A SEVERE GALE DURING THE NIGHT AND WITH WIND AGAINST TIDE, THE WAVES ON BREYDON WATER WERE
SURPRISINGLY SHORT AND STEEP, ONCE IN THE RIVER WAVENEY IT ALL CALMED DOWN AND WE MOTORED AS FAR AS ST
OLAVES, WHERE FURTHER PROGRESS WAS BARRED BY A FIXED ROAD BRIDGE. IT AMUSED US TO NOTICE THAT THE BROADS HIRE
CRUISERS INVARIABLY MOTORED ALONG WITH ALL FENDERS HANGING, WE THOUGHT THAT PERHAPS THE BOAT HIRERS MADE THIS
A RULE TO MINIMISE DAMAGE! HAVING TURNED AT ST OLAVES, WE THEN SAILED UNDER JIB ALONE TO THE JUNCTION WITH
THE RIVER YARE AND POTTERED ALONG TO REEDHAM FOR LUNCH AT A PUB NEAR REEDHAM RAILWAY SWING BRIDGE. THIS
BRIDGE WILL OPEN ON REQUEST TO ALLOW ACCESS TO NORWICH, BUT WE HAD TO BE BACK AT YARMOUTH FOR OUR ARRANGED
15.30 OPENING OF THE TWO BRIDGES. THESE BRIDGES ONLY OPEN FOR COMMERCIAL TRAFFIC, OR BY PRIOR ARRANGEMENT
USING R/T ON CHANNEL 12, OR BY PHONE, HAVING SUCCESSFULLY TRANSITED THE BRIDGES WE TRAVELLED ALONG PAST
YARMOUTH AND GORLESTON AND OUT OF THE HARBOUR FOR OUR RETURN TO LOWESTOFT AND THENCE BACK DOWN TO MSC VIA PIN
MILL. WE WERE VERY GRATIFIED TO FIND THE CRUISER CAPTAIN LURKING ON THE MERSEA FLATS TO WELCOME US BACK, BUT

LESS PLEASED TO FIND OUR DINGHY MAKING LIKE A SUBMARINE.

NONETHELESS IT WAS QUITE AN INTERESTING LITTLE VOYAGE, PERHAPS NEXT TIME WE WILL GO RIGHT UP TO NORWICH AND
MAYBE SEE IF IT IS POSSIBLE TO GET UNDER THE NeW CUT BRIDGE FOR A VISIT TO OULTON BROAD OR BECCLES,

DAVE BEANE, RODNIGON

THE 1990 EAST COAST PIERS RACE - (Through the Eye of the Hurricane)

WHAT A WEEKEND! COLOURFUL, CROWDED, EXCITING AND,,.. WHO TOOK THE WIND? THE EAST COAST PIERS RACE WEEKEND
STARTED ON FRIDAY WITH MANY OF THE MEMBERS OF MARCONI CLUB ARRIVING ON SITE TO ENSURE THAT ANY LAST MINUTE
HITCHES WERE IRONED OUT BEFORE THAT GREAT MASS OF CAT SAILORS DESCENDED ON US LIKE A SWARM OF LOCUSTS,

SATURDAY DAWNED! I ROLLED OVER AND RAISED MY HEAD TO LOOK OUT OF THE WINDOW AND MADE OUT THE SHAPES OF MANY
COLOURFUL PRINDLE SAILS - THERE OUGHT TO BE A LAW AGAINST ASSAULTING PEOPLE'S EYEBALLS SO EARLY IN THE
MORNING! I LOOK AGAIN AND REALISE THAT I CAN SEE RIGHT THROUGH ONE SAIL TO THE BOATS BEYOND. NOW THAT IS A
NOVEL IDEA, HAVING A WINDOW FROM TOP TO BOTTOM, IS IT A PLOY TO SEE DOWN TO LEEWARD WHEN HEELED OVER, TO
WATCH OUT FOR LOW FLYING AIRCRAFT OR TO BE ABLE TO WATCH THE REST OF THE FLEET SAIL AWAY FROM YOU DOWNWIND?
(I WAS LATER TOLD THAT MAINSAILS LIKE THESE COST OVER £1,000, WHICH SEEMS A LITTLE ODD FOR A SAIL OBVIOUSLY
MADE FROM THE BITS LEFT ON THE CUTTING ROOM FLOOR AFTER THE NORMAL SAILS HAVE BEEN MADE - BUT I SUPPOSE THERE
IS A LOT OF SEWING INVOLVED!) GRADUALLY THE CAT FIELD WAS FILLING UP, AS NORMAL, CHAOS REIGNED, BUT IT WAS
AT LEAST PARTIALLY ORGANISED, IT IS A KNOWN FACT THAT CAT SAILORS ARE DEAF, IF YOU ASK THEM TO PARK IN A
CERTAIN PLACE THEY WILL TOTALLY IGNORE YOU AND PARK IN THE MOST INCONVENIENT PLACE POSSIBLE, IF THEY IGNORE
YOUR WORDS ON THE WATER, THEN YOU CANNOT EXPECT THEM TO LISTEN ON LAND,

AT LEAST THERE WAS SOME WIND, WITH A STEADY 3 - 4 BLOWING, THE RACE OFFICER HAD ORGANISED A RACE FOR 12.00
HRS, AND SO, ANTICIPATING THE ARRIVAL OF MY HELM, FOR THE WEEKEND, I PROCEEDED TO RIG THE BOAT. RACE ONE
STARTED WITHOUT US, AS HE HADN'T ARRIVED, THE COURSE FOR THE FIRST RACE WAS THE BAFFLE TO PORT, THE NASS TO
PORT, THE MARK OFF OSEA PIER TO PORT AND FINISH AT THE RACE BOX, A GOOD SELECTION OF CATS HEADED DOWN TO THE

PIER TO START, AND AFTER A SHORT DELAY, THE FLEET HEADED UP TOWARDS THE BAFFLE, WITH AN EASTERLY WIND IT WAS
A LONG BEAT, ALTHOUGH THE TIDE HELPED, THERE WAS LITTLE IN IT AS THE FLEET PASSED THE CLUB, WITH THE FASTER

BOATS AHEAD AND THE SLOWER (7) BOATS FOLLOWING CLOSE BEHIND, OFF THEY WENT INTO THE DISTANCE, WHILST THE
PEOPLE ON THE SHORE WANDERED OFF TO HAVE LUNCH,

IT WAS THEN THAT MY HELM CHOSE TO ARRIVE, IT MUST HAVE BEEN THE THOUGHT OF LUNCH, FOR THOSE OF YOU WHO HAVE
NEVER MET PAUL SMITH, HE IS BEST DESCRIBED AS BEING TOO TALL, TOO WIDE AND TOO HEAVY, PAUL IS ALSO THE GUY
WHO REALLY GOT THE HURRICANE 5.9 CLASS ASSOCIATION OFF THE GROUND, ALTHOUGH HE NOW SAILS A 2? TOPPER OUT OF

RAMSGATE. AS DAVE PAYNE WAS BUSY GETTING BURNT TO A FRAZZLE IN FLORIDA, I ASKED PAUL IF HE WOULD LIKE TO

REFRESH HIS EXPERIENCE OF SAILING A REAL BOAT, AFTER LUNCH WE STROLLED BACK TO THE HARD TO WATCH THE FINISH
OF THE RACE, COMING TOWARDS US FROM STONE WAS JOHN NICKALLS AND CAROLINE HOLLINGS SAILING THEIR NEW BOAT (EX
ROBIN SMITH), CLOSELY FOLLOWED BY KEITH AND NEIL SIMMONDS (WHO WON THE PIERS RACE IN 1989 SAILING A DART 18)
ALSO IN A HURRICANE 5.9, HOWEVER, ABSOLUTELY STEAMING UP BEHIND THEM WAS A PRINDLE 19 COMPLETE WITH MASTHEAD
GENNAKER (DID I GET IT RIGHT THIS TIME, MR FLOOK?) WHICH APART FROM "LOOKING THE BIZ" WAS RAPIDLY OVERHAULING

ALL THOSE AHEAD, THIS BOAT FINALLY TOOK THE LEAD AS THE FLEET PASSED THE CLUB, AND DESPITE A VALIANT EFFORT

BY JOHN AND CAROLINE HELD ON TO TAKE LINE HONOURS, PITY, BUT WITH A HANDICAP REDUCED FROM 76 TO 71 BECAUSE OF
THE GENNAKER, HE WAS BEATEN ON HANDICAP BY THE FOLLOWING BOATS, ALL THE PEOPLE STANDING ON THE HARD WERE
AMAZED BY THE MASTHEAD GENNAKER, FOR EVERY TIME THE WIND GUSTED, THE TOP OF THE MAST BOWED FORWARD, WHILST THE
MAST BELOW THE HOUNDS WAS BENT BACK BY THE PREBEND IN THE RIG, THUS THE MAST WAS TAKING UP AN "S" SHAPE,

WHICH CAUSED MANY TO COMMENT, "I'M GLAD IT'S NOT MY MAST!" THOSE BOATS WITH 2 RIGGED GENNAKERS DID NOT SEEM
TO EXPERIENCE THIS "S" SHAPE, ALTHOUGH IT MIGHT HAVE JUST BEEN LESS NOTICEABLE, WHILST ALL THIS EXCITEMENT
WAS GOING ON, ANOTHER PRINDLE 19, WITHOUT A GENNAKER, WAS SNEAKING IN TO WIN THE RACE ON HANDICAP,

RACE 2, IN THE LATE AFTERNOON, FEATURED A SIMILAR COURSE TO RACE 1 BUT WITHOUT INCLUDING THE NASS, PAUL AND I
ENTERED THIS ONE AND FOUND OURSELVES IN A SMALL GROUP OF PORT-TACK STARTERS BEING “CHARGED DOWN" BY A MASS OF

STARBOARD-TACK STARTERS ON WHAT WAS AN INCREDIBLY PORT BIASED LINE, THE STARBOARD-TACK BOATS COULD ONLY JUST
LAY THE LINE, AND THEREFORE COULD AFFORD TO HARDEN UP EARLY AND CHARGE DOWN THE LINE KNOWING THAT WHEN THE GUN
WENT THEY ONLY HAD TO POINT A LITTLE HIGHER TO CROSS THE LINE, THE PORT-TACK STARTERS WERE HOPING THAT THE
GUN WOULD GO BEFORE THE STARBOARD-TACK BOATS REACHED THE MIDDLE OF THE LINE, THUS PREVENTING THEM FROM
CROSSING AHEAD, THE PORT-TACK STARTERS LOST! THE GUN WENT AND WE, LIKE MOST OF THE PORT-TACK STARTERS, WERE
30 YARDS BACK FROM THE LINE REACHING TOWARDS THE COMMITTEE BOAT AND LOOKING FOR A GAP, THE STARBOARD-TACK

STARTERS WERE IN A TERRIBLE POSITION AS THE LEADERS COULD NOT TACK BECAUSE OF THE FOLLOWERS AND THEY WERE
GRADUALLY BEING PUSHED CLOSE INTO OSEA AND OUT OF THE WIND. SO THE BEST STARTS WERE MADE BY EITHER THE TAIL

ENO STARBOARD-TACK BOATS OR THOSE PORT-TACK BOATS THAT FOUND A GAP, TREVOR (SON OF HOBIE DEALER NORMAN)
ANNELS, CREWED BY EMMA (DAUGHTER OF PRINDLE IMPORTER DON) FINDLAY, SAILING A HURRICANE 5.9 (WHO SAID CAT

SAILORS DON'T MIX) SHOT STRAIGHT INTO THE LEAD, BEING THE ONLY PORT-TACK BOAT WHICH CROSSED THE FLEET, PAUL
STEERED US THROUGH A GAP INTO SECOND BUT TREVOR MILTON AND KEITH GURNEY, WHO USED THE SAME GAP SAILED OVER THE
TOP OF US, RELEGATING US TO THIRD, JOHN NICKALLS WAS CLOSE BEHIND, MEANWHILE, CALLS OF "STARBOARD", "WATER!"
AND "OH

contd....

10,

OFF WE WENT TOWARDS STONE. SUDDENLY, “BANG!” WHAT WAS THAT? 1 LOOKED AROUND AND DISCOVERED THE SHOCK CORD

FROM MY TRAPEZE HAD SNAPPED AND THE LEEWARD TRAPEZE WAS SWAYING ABOUT BY THE REAR OF THE BOAT. "GO AND SECURE
IT,” CRIED PAUL, SO I SWUNG IN, SLID DOWN THE TRAMPOLINE AND VAINLY TRIED TO CATCH THE WIRE WHILST PAUL TRIED
TO AT LEAST KEEP SOME POWER ON, THERE IS SOME ADVANTAGE TO A HEAVY CREW! AT LAST I CAUGHT THE ERRANT WIRE,
CLIMBED BACK TO WINDWARD, ONLY TO LOSE MY GRIP AND WATCH THE TRAPEZE GO SWINGING BACK OUT INTO THE BREEZE,
BACK I WENT TO RETRIEVE IT, MEANWHILE THE TWO TREVORS WERE PULLING AWAY SLIGHTLY AND JOHN AND CAROLINE WERE
SLOWLY PASSING US TO WINDWARD, RETRIEVING THE WIRE, I AGAIN RETURNED TO WINDWARD AND TIED THE SHOCK CORD BACK
TO THE TRAPEZE. “TACK,” SAID PAUL, AND ROUND WE WENT, "BANG," WHAT WAS THAT? I LOOKED AGAIN AND FOUND THE
SHOCK CORD HAD SNAPPED ON THIS SIDE. POOR MAINTENANCE, YOU MAY ASK? BUT THE SHOCK CORD HAD BEEN REPLACED
ONLY TwO WEEKS EARLIER, IN FACT THE CORD HAD NOT SNAPPED, BUT PULLED OUT OF THE FETAINING CLIPS! BACK TO THE
LEEWARD SIDE; RETRIEVE THE TRAPEZE; TIE OFF THE SHOCK CORD, THE TROUBLE NOW WAS THAT EVERY TIME WE TACKED I
HAD TO GO OUT SLOWLY AS THE SHOCK CORD WAS SO LOOSE (IT WAS TIED ROUND THE TOE STRAPS) THAT THERE WAS NO
TENSION ON THE TRAPEZE RING TO KEEP IT ON THE HOOK, SO ONE FALSE MOVE AND I COULD HAVE GONE SWIMMING,

JOHN ANO CAROLINE WERE ABOUT 200 YARDS AHEAD WITH THE TWO TREVORS AHEAD OF THEM, THE REST OF THE FLEET WERE
ABOUT 600 YARDS BEHIND US WITH STEVE GLYN CREWED BY RICHARD WILMOT (WHAT HAPPENED TO YOUR REAL CREW?)
NOTICEABLE AMONGST THE LEADERS, AS THE LEADERS REACHED THE BAFFLE THE WIND SUDDENLY DIED, AND THE THREE
LEADING BOATS CLOSED UP, PAUL AND I HELD OUR DISTANCE, WHILST THE REST OF THE FLEET RAPIDLY NARROWED THE GAP,
ONCE AROUND THE BAFFLE, TREVOR ANNELS DISAPPEARED OFF INTO THE DISTANCE NE'R TO BE SEEN AGAIN, WHILST TREVOR
MILTON AND JOHN CHASED EACH OTHER ALL OVER THE RIVER, "I CAN'T SEEM TO GET IN THE GROOVE,” SAID PAUL. WHAT
WAS HE TALKING ABOUT? WE DIDN'T HAVE A DISCO UNIT ON BOARD! “IT WON'T GO DOWNWIND," HE ADDED. HAH, HAH!
I'D SUSSED IT, "STOP WATCHING THE SAILS ON THE PRINDLES AND LOOK THE WAY WE ARE GOING, AND WE MIGHT GET
THERE!" IT IS AMAZING WHAT CONCENTRATION CAN DO, AT THIS POINT, THE PACK BEHIND WAS ABOUT 50 YARDS BACK, BUT
WE RAPIDLY STARTED TO INCREASE THE DISTANCE. AS WE PASSED THE CLUB, We FOUND OURSELVES BEING CHASED BY A
PRINDLE 19 WITH A MASTHEAD GENNAKER, WE WERE BOTH SITTING INBOARD CLOSE TO THE MAIN BEAM, WHILST THEY WERE
TWIN WIRING WITH THE KITE FLYING, GRADUALLY THEY BEGAN TO OVERHAUL US, FIRST TO WINDWARD, THEN TO LEEWARD.
FINALLY THEY GOT THROUGH TO LEEWARD, ALTHOUGH WE WEREN'T TRYING TO LUFF THEM AT ALL, BUT WE WERE WERE NOW ONLY
ABOUT 200 YARDS FROM THE OSEA MARK, AND THEY DECIDED TO DROP THE KITE, BY THE TIME THEY HAD DONE THIS, WE
WERE ROUND THE TwO MARKS AND ABOUT 300 YARDS AHEAD, AND THAT WAS ABOUT AS CLOSE AS THEY EVER GOT AGAIN,

WE TACKED TOWARDS THE CLUB AND AS I SWUNG OUT ON TO THE WIRE, MY LEGS AND BODY STRAIGHTENED WHILST MY HANDS
STAYED INBOARD, WITH MY ARMS STRETCHING TO FILL THE GAP, MY SHOULDERS ACHED AND THE MUSCLES(?) KNOTTED, WHAT
IS HAPPENING I ASKED MYSELF, THE JIB FELT OVERPOWERING AND IT WAS TAKING ALL OF MY STRENGTH TO HOLD IT IN,
THE RATCHET HAD FLICKED OFF AND MY ARMS AND SHOULDERS WERE NOW TAKING THE FULL PRESSURE FROM THE JIB, WAS I
GLAD WHEN WE TACKED FOR THE LINE, AND DID I SUFFER THAT NIGHT WHEN, WHICHEVER WAY I LAY, I WAS IN AGONY FROM
THE STRAINED MUSCLES, ALTHOUGH WE DIDN'T CATCH JOHN, WE WERE NOT TOO FAR BEHIND AT THE FINISH, SORRY, DAVE,
I'LL NEVER CALL THE CREW A WIMP AGAIN! TREVOR ANNELS WON THE RACE BY A WIDE MARGIN, AND AS CLASS ASSOCIATION
CHAIRMAN I WENT TO ENSURE THAT THE CAPACITY OF THE ENGINE THAT HE MUST HAVE HAD HIDDEN IN EACH HULL WAS WITHIN
THE CLASS RULES! JAPANESE TECHNOLOGY IS WONDERFUL FOR, NO MATTER HOW HARD I LOOKED, I COULDN'T FIND WHERE THE
ENGINE WAS HIDDEN,

IN THE EARLY EVENING REG WHITE ARRIVED, SAILING THE NEW HURRICANE 6.5, COMPLETE WITH ELEVEN-FOOT WINGS ON
EITHER SIDE AND A RIG SET UP LIKE THE HIGH WIRE ARTISTS IN A CIRCUS, THE BOAT ATTRACTED A LOT OF INTEREST,
WITH HULLS WHICH SEEMED AS IF THEY HAD BEEN PUT ON UPSIDE DOWN, A TRAMPOLINE WHOSE SIDES WERE HELD OUT BY A

VERY TAUT WIRE THROUGH THE EDGE, AND A SPINNAKER POLE WHICH LOOKED MORE LIKE A GUIDED MISSILE! ROBERT WHITE
WAS SPORTING A GENNAKER ON HIS 5,9, LATER THAT EVENING WE VENTURED INTO THE CROWDED BAR -TO SOCIALISE WITH OUR
FELLOW SAILORS, THERE WAS A VIDEO SHOWING AND THE CREWS WERE CROWDED AROUND MAKING DEROGATORY COMMENTS ABOUT
EACH OTHER, NOT ONLY ARE THE PRINDLE SAILS LOUD, BUT THE CREWS ARE LOUDER STILL! THE THREATS WERE FLYING
THICK AND FAST ABOUT WHO WAS GOING TO MURDER WHO ON THE WATER TOMORROW, ONE LARGE HARDY FELLOW WAS BOASTING
THAT ON THE REACH BACK FROM WALTON, THE PRINDLE 19 FLEET WOULD BE SO FAR AHEAD THAT THE HURRICANES WOULD NOT
BE ABLE TO SEE THEM, EVEN WITH BINOCULARS! SO WITH ACHING MUSCLES AND THROBBING EAR DRUMS, I RETIRED TO MY
BED.

SUNDAY DAWNED THE SAME AS SATURDAY, TOO MUCH COLOUR TOO EARLY IN THE MORNING, WE HAD BREAKFAST AND I WENT TO
THE LOO ABOUT 25 TIMES (MUST HAVE BEEN WORRIED ABOUT THE PRINDLE FLEET!) BEFORE WE JOINED THE MERRY THRONG
LAUNCHING FOR THE DRIFT UP TO OSEA BEACH TO AWAIT THE START OF THE RACE, WHILST WE WERE ALL PREPARING, REG
WHITE WAS REMOVING THE GIANT METALLIC SNOW SHOES WHICH PASS FOR WINGS ON THE 6.5. HE WAS OBVIOUSLY NOT

EXPECTING STRONG WINDS,

AS SOON AS THE TEN MINUTE GUN SOUNDED WE SET OUT TO PICK A SPOT ON THE LINE, PAUL WANTED TO START AT THE PIN
END, WHILST I FAVOURED THE COMMITTEE BOAT END. IN THE END WE STARTED IN THE MIDDLE, ALTHOUGH NOT THROUGH

CHOICE, THE WIND WAS SO LIGHT THAT WE KNEW WE COULD NOT REACH THE PIN ENO IN TIME? SO FOLLOWING LOCAL

contd....

MW,

KNOWLEDGE WE TURNED TO THE COMMITTEE BOAT, BUT WE COULDN'T GET THERE EITHER! ALTHOUGH THERE WERE 118 ENTRIES
AND 114 STARTERS, THE LINE WAS NOT TOO CONGESTED, THE GUN WENT AND WE WERE STUCK IN NO WIND AND MAXIMUM TIDE,
WE TACKED FOR THE OSEA SHORE, WHILST I EXPLAINED TO PAUL ABOUT THE DIFFICULTY THE OTHERS WOULD HAVE IN
GETTING ROUND THE CORNER BY THE CLUB, JUST AHEAD OF US WERE ROBIN SMITH & LISA GATTON; TREVOR MILTON & KEITH
GURNEY; ROB STAHL & ANNETTE; TIM & MARCUS WALLACE; PAUL & MIKE SHAW; AND KEITH & NEIL SIMMONDS, I EXPLAINED
TO PAUL THAT WE COULDN'T ALL BE WRONG, HE WAS UNCONVINCED, WE SHORT TACKED ALONG THE
PIN SHORE, WHILST THE
END STARTERS QUIETLY SAILED AROUND THE CORNER BY THE CLUB WITH NO EFFORT AT ALL! ROBIN AND LISA FOUND THEIR
OwN PERSONAL WIND AND SAILED AWAY FROM US ALL ON THE OSEA SIDE. ‘THE REMAINING GROUP WERE SWAPPING PLACES ALL
THE TIME AS EACH BOAT FOUND AND THEN LOST WHAT LITTLE BREEZE THERE WAS, IT PAID TO STAY IN THE WIND ONCE YOU
FOUND IT, EVEN IF THIS MEANT STAYING IN THE TIDE. ONCE AROUND AND INTO GOLDHANGER CREEK + BOTH TREVOR MILTON
AND KEITH SIMMONDS FOUND A BREEZE AND PULLED CLEAR, ALTHOUGH TREVOR'S BREEZE PUT HIM INTO THE TIDE OFF STONE.

BY NOw THE FLEET WAS WELL SPREAD WITH THE LEADERS BEING EITHER CLOSE TO THE NORTH SHORE OR CLOSE TO THE SOUTH
SHORE. 70 MINUTES HAD ELAPSED SINCE THE START AND WE WERE ALREADY ABOUT A MILE BEHIND THE LEADERS AND JUST
OFF STONE, BUT NEAR TO THE NORTH SHORE, “TIME FOR LUNCH," I CRIED. “WHAT? IT'S ONLY 11 O'CLOCK!" REPLIED
PAUL, “ENOUGH IS ENOUGH," I RETURNED. "LET'S GIVE UP AND GO AND HAVE LUNCH." PAUL TURNED THE BOAT BACK
TOWARDS THE CLUB, “ARE YOU SURE?" BY NOW WE WERE USING THE TIDE TO HELP US HOME SO I SAID “I'M SURE," AND HE
REPLIED, “THANK GOD!" AS WE GOT TO THE HARD THE LAST BOAT (A DART 15) WAS JUST PASSING THE RACE BOX, 1
THOUGHT THAT WE WOULD BE THE FIRST RETIREMENT, BUT THERE WAS A DART 18 ALREADY ASHORE ON THE HARD AND AT
LEAST
A COUPLE OF BOATS IN THE CAT FIELD. IT WASN'T LONG BEFORE OTHERS FOLLOWED OUR EXAMPLE, AND WITHIN THE NEXT 30
MINUTES AT LEAST ANOTHER 20 BOATS RETURNED, INCLUDING A COUPLE OF PRINDLE 19's! WE DERIGGED THE BOAT, HAD A
LEISURELY LUNCH AND RETURNED TO THE CLUB TO GET AN UPDATE ON THE RACE, BY THIS TIME THE LEADERS HAD JUST
REACHED BRADWELL WITH THE TAILENDERS STILL ABOUT 2 MILES BEHIND,

THE COMMENTARY WAS COMING THICK AND FAST FROM THE CLUB, ‘THE FACTS WEREN'T NECESSARILY CORRECT BUT IT WAS FUN
SPOTTING THE MISTAKES, MALCOLM STUART HAS OBVIOUSLY BEEN TO THE MURREY WALKER SCHOOL FOR COMMENTATORS, A
CROWD OF US WAITED TO SEE WHAT WOULD HAPPEN NEXT, WHILST MALCOLM AMUSED US WITH HIS COMMENTARY, THE FRONT OF
THE FLEET HAD REACHED COLNE POINT, WHILST THE TAIL HAD NOT YET REACHED BRADWELL.

DESPITE THE FACT THAT THE LEADERS WERE ABLE TO TRAPEZE BEYOND BRADWELL, THE RACE OFFICER WISELY TURNED THE
FLEET BACK AT COLNE POINT, AND MALCOLM READ OUT THE FIRST 20 BOATS, IN FACT HE ONLY CALLED OUT 17, AND THE
BOAT WHICH EVENTUALLY FINISHED 2ND DIDN'T GET A MENTION! WE WANDERED OFF AGAIN FOR COFFEE AND RETURNED TO
HEAR THAT REG WHITE WAS JUST BEYOND STONE AND WOULD FINISH SHORTLY.

THE COMMENTARY WENT; “HERE IS THE WINNER OF THE 1990 EAST COAST PIERS RACE JUST CROSSING THE FINISH LINE
NOW... (MUMBLE, MUMBLE)...BUT HE HAS STILL TO GO AROUND THE BUOYS OFF OSEA,.. THE SECOND BOAT IS (MUMBLE,
MUMBLE)......" (MESSAGE ENDS.) BY NOW ALL OF THE BINOCULARS WERE OUT, AND WE COULD IDENTIFY ROBIN & LISA,
ROBERT WHITE AND TREVOR ANNELS AS BEING MIOWAY BETWEEN BRADWELL AND THE CLUB, ABOUT AN HOUR AFTER REG CAME
ASHORE, THE SECOND BOAT PASSED THE CLUB, THE COMMENTARY WENT "HERE IS THE SECOND BOAT IN THE 1990 EAST COAST
PIERS RACE JUST PASSING THE CLUB..." (IT WAS OFF THE RACE BOX) “...IT IS TORNADO 273 SAILED BY THE WILLIAMS
BROTHERS...." (IT WAS ACTUALLY DAVE WILLIAMS AND IAN RHODES) THEY WILL BE FINSHING ANY MINUTE NOW..."
(1T TOOK THEM A FURTHER 30 MINUTES TO FINISH THE RACE) "....AFTER THEY HAVE BEEN ROUND THE BUOYS OFF OF
OSEA," MURREY WALKER, EAT YOUR HEART OUT! GRADUALLY, BOATS DRIFTED CLOSER TO THE CLUB: “WELCOME BACK TO
ME AND MRS DODGSON..." (STEVE DOOGSON AND DEBBIE ROBERTS, WHO AREN'T EVEN MARRIED!)

THE LEADING CLUB BOAT (ROBIN SIGNED ON AS A MEMBER OF GRAFHAM) WAS JOHN NICKALLS, BUT HE DECIDED TO RETIRE AS
HE PASSED THE CLUB, KNOWING THAT HE WAS UNLIKELY TO COMPLETE THE COURSE WITHIN THE TIME LIMIT, BY THE TIME
THE 6PM TIME LIMIT EXPIRED ONLY 14 BOATS HAD FINISHED, ALTHOUGH ONE HOBIE CREW WERE UNFORTUNATE TO CROSS THE
LINE ONLY 60 SECONDS AFTER THE TIME EXPIRED, MEANWHILE, REG WHITE, WHO HAD TAKEN LINE HONOURS AND WON BY
MILES ON HANDICAP WAS BUSY SAILING THE HURRICANE 6.5 BACK TO BRIGHTLINGSEA, WE TRIED TO GET HIM TO TELL THE
OTHERS THAT HE WAS ON THE SECOND LAP, BUT HE WOULDN'T PLAY BALL! HE MUST HAVE BEEN REALLY PLEASED, FOR NOT
ONLY DID HE WIN THE RACE, BUT THE FIRST 12 BOATS HOME WERE BUILT BY HIM!

WHERE WERE THE PRINDLE 19's? THE LAST BOAT TO FINISH WAS A PRINDLE 19 WITHOUT A GENNAKER, THE REST BEING
EITHER ALREADY RETIRED OR BEING TOWED HOME, UNFORTUNATELY NOT A SINGLE DART FINISHED, SO THEIR TRAVELLERS
SERIES WAS DECIDED ON THE SATURDAY RESULTS. THE OTHER BOAT WHICH FINISHED WAS AN “A" CLASS SINGLE HANDER,
MEANWHILE THE REST OF THE FLEET WAS BEING TOWED HOME AND IT GAVE ME GREAT PLEASURE TO POINT OUT THAT THEY GOT
THE SAME RESULT AS ME, BUT I'D BEEN ASHORE FOR OVER 7 HOURS!

A PITY ABOUT THE LACK OF WIND SPOILING WHAT WAS A SUPERBLY ORGANISED EVENT, BUT HOPEFULLY THE SPONSORS WERE
HAPPY WITH THE TURN-OUT AND WE MIGHT GET WIND NEXT YEAR,

Many thanks to those members who attended the Regatta'91 Meeting held as the Marconi Athletic & Social Club on Friday, 21 September. They were:-

Neil Pembleton (Commodure) Mike Boreham (Rear Comm.) Mike Duckmanton Dave Fletcher Frank Bennett (Hon.Treasurer) Maggie Boreham Barry Newboult Val Fletcher
Mike Hellewell (Sailing Sec) Larry Botheras Malcolm Stuart John Weedon

The aim of the meeting was to seek volunteers to undertake the task of reviewing and defining the detailed requirements and actions needed to run Regatta'91. The ‘Basic Task List' for Regatta'91 (as published in Navigans, August'90) was taken as the minimum starting point for the review and definition.

The volunteers were requested to complete their review and definition in time for January, 1991 (say, by
15 January) so as to present their findings to the January'91 meeting of the Sailing Sub-Committee.

It is not intended that the volunteers conduct their review and definition in isolation of each other, or of others members of the club. It is intended that those who attended the meeting be regarded as a Regatta Working Group (reporting to the Sailing Sub-Committee via the (new) Rear Commodore and/or Sailing Secretary) and that they should meet before Christmas (say November and December) to liaise with each other and ensure they are moving in the same general direction for Regatta '91 (or reveal any glaring problems if they are not 'in tune' with each other). By consulting with other members of the club, it is hoped our volunteers will gainfrom both 'old' and 'new' ideas and experiences for Regatta.

Annual General Meeting, 1990.

The Marconi Sailing Club Annual General Meeting will take place at Stansgate on
Sunday 18 November 1990 at 1300hrs, to be followed by the Prize Giving.

AGENDA.

1. Apologies for absence.

2. Minutes of the 1989 Annual General Meeting.

3. Matters arising from the 1989 Minutes.

4. Commodore's report.

5. Hon. Secretary's report.

6. Hon. Sailing Secretary's report.

7: Hon. Treasurer's report.

8. Proposals:
8.1 Membership Rule Changes. Resolution 1.
8.2 Calling of Meetings Rule Changes Resolution 2.
8.3 Suspension of Rule 8.5 Resolution 3.
8.4 Amendment of Membership Fees Resolution 4.
Sed Amendment of Membership Fees Resolution 5.

9. Election of Officers:
9.1 Election of Main Committee. Resolution 6.
9.2 Election of Vice Presidents. Resolution 7.

10. Any Other Business.

Notes:-

1. Voting Rights. Ordinary, Family, Associate and Retired members have
voting rights. Permanent Guests do not have voting
rights.

Die Voting. All votes at the Annual General Meeting are by show of Membership Cards unless a secret ballot is requested by a majority of members present.

3. Majority Resolutions 1 - 5 require a majority of two thirds of
those present and voting to be opted.
Resolutions 6 - 7 require a simple majority.

RESOLUTION 1 Proposed by the Main Committee.

To remove the types of member known as Associate and Family, and allow those and similar prospective members to be known as Ordinary members, in accordance with the following rule changes.

RULE CHANGES.

6. MEMBERSHIP

Every candidate for membership should have an active interest in sailing or
boating.
There shall be the following forms of membership.
oO’OV NN Ordinary Membership. Open to all Group Ordinary, Ordinary, Family, and Honorary Members of the M.A.S.C. including their husbands/wives and children under the age of 21 years who shall be entered on the membership role as Permanent Guests of the member.
64:2:52 Honorary Life Membership. Honorary Life Members may be elected by a two thirds majority of the members of the Committee present and voting.
6.2.3 Temporary Membership. Persons deemed suitable by the Executive Committee and visiting Members of other Yacht Clubs recognised by the R.Y.A. may be accepted as Temporary Members for a period and a fee fixed at the discretion of the Executive Committee.
6.2.4 Retired Membership. Open to all Retired Members of the M.A.S.C. including their husbands/wives and children under the age of 21 years who shall be entered on the membership role as Permanent Guests of the member.
6.2.5 Unaccompanied Cadet. Open to any person aged 18 or under on the Ist of January of the subscription year who is not a permanent guest of an Ordinary or Retired member.
6.3 The cadet section includes all persons aged 18 years and under on lst January of the subscription year.
6.4 Permanent Guests shall be entitled to participate in all activities of the M.S.C. but shall not have voting rights. They shall be able to participate in the Sailing Programme and to receive prizes on the same basis as members.

DELETE Rule 6.5.

A View from the rear

My Word - if last month's 'View from the rear' was the penultimate one, then I suppose this ought to be
entitled 'The ultimate view from the rear', but that would sound rather too boastful. An alternative title
might be 'A final view from the rear' - but that sounds altogether too foreboding. 1 did give some thought
to 'A last view from......etc', but felt it sounded too much like a last Will and Testament. Oh! dear;
problems, problems.

Still stuck foratitle (but starting from the basis of ‘ultimate') I decided to consult Roget's Thesaurus in
search of a suitable expression to convey the sense of this particular ‘View from....' and came up with all
sorts of possible words. How about, for example:-

"An end view from the rear' - perhaps not; too open to misinterpretation

"An extreme view from the rear' - could be politically controversial. Is he too far left or
too far right ?

‘A distant view from the rear' - the further the distance the better ?

"An aloof view....++.+..-etc ' = SNOOLY vices tases ended

"A terminal - too suggestive of unpleasant consequences

"A cessational - sounds like something from a US Congress debate

‘A last gasp view from.......' - could be appropriate; I get out of breath walking to the Race Bo

In the end, I settled for 'A retiring view from the rear'; I'd like to think it offers some peace and quiet
after a 'Year in Office’. In addition, it leads me neatly into.........

Taking Early Retirement - someone remarked to me recently that they were surprized I was retiring after only

one year as Rear Commodore. By way of explanation, I said that when I was first asked to be R.C. I said ‘NO'
- and suggested a couple of other ‘names’. Clearly, they also said 'NO' because, with only one week to go
to the 1989 AGM, I was again asked (but this time along the lines ‘We're desperate; scrapping the bottom of th barrel; you're our last hope). Always one to succumb to flattery, I said 'YES' but with the proviso it would only be for one year initially and, during that year, I would decide if I could continue for the more normal
2nd and 3rd year. In the event, I decided I could not give the time and effort to the job in the same manner
as my predecessor; consequently, I advised the Main Committee at its June meeting that I would not continue as Rear Commodore. So there you have it.

What's my (start) line ? - ‘What's my line ?' used to be the title of a very popular quiz programme on both
radio and TV. The most famous 'line' (ie occupation) was that of 'A Sagger-makers Bottom Knocker' which, whatever the 'innocent' intentions of those who put it forward for the quiz, caused much hilarity and was the subject of much mis-interpretation.

Something else likely to be subject to much mis-interpretation, but precious little humour, is the report of the Start-Line Working Group.
