MARCONI SAILING CLUB - THE NEXT FIVE YEARS - From the Main Committee

In his 'View from the rear' last month, Mike Boreham commented on the future &wv direction of the Club.

Under Rule 2 the objects of the Club are:-

"SHALL BE THE PROMOTION OF AMATEUR SAILING, THE ENCOURAGEMENT OF SOCIAL FELLOWSHIP,
AMONGST ALL THOSE INTERESTED IN THE SEA AND THE PROVISION OF ALL POSSIBLE FACILITIES
TO THIS END"

The Main Committees interpretation of this rule is that we should be providing facilities for dinghies/cruisers, Racers/Non Racers, and "those who want to mess about in boats", and believe that this is the essence of the Club. Picking up from the article in last months Navigans on the financial relationship between the MASC and ourselves, the reason for the drive to increase membership to 500 was to enable the Club to meet its financial obligation and maintain the fabric without any major change in subscription level (except for inflation). This was based on a judgement made by the Main Committee in 1985 that this level would generate sufficient income to carry through some development to the overall facilities. It also recognised that to increase significantly above that number would require major capital developments such as extensions, safety cover etc. Generally the judgement has proved correct as witnessed by the total redecoration of the Club, rebuilding of the gate, filling of the ditch, new water main, new radios, repairs to the road, retiling of the Galley, building of the tender rack over the last two years. These have been achieved both by the additional funds from the increased membership and the effort of the members. Whilst this membership drive was in progress, the Main Committee have been looking further into the future to satisfy the likely needs. We clearly recognise the need for more accommodation and the question of safety cover. These plans had been developed sufficiently for us to approach the MASC for the necessary funding for an extension and second rescue boat. However the present financial situation within the MASC has come at the wrong time and we have had to carry out a major review of the situation within a number of significant constraints.

These contraints include the facts that we as a section cannot enter into any loan agreement, we cannot spend any of the reserve account without MASC approval, that any surplus income over expenditure that we generate each year must be paid into the reserve account, that any major capital spend must have MASC approval, and that the MASC does not have the available funds to assist us at present. It is also our opinion that such assistance will not be available for the next 4-5 years.

An obvious solution appears to be to purchase the site and sever the link with the MASC. Even if we assume that the MASC and the trustees would be agreeable to such a proposal, it will take a significant time to finalise the details. It will also be essential to ensure that the Club does not end up with a loan of such a size to finance the purchase that the capital and interest payments cripple the Club immediately. It is our opinion that such investigation, negotiation, raising of the finance and re-constitution of the Club will take at least 3-5 years even if we decided that this was an appropriate course.

For all the above reasons we have recognised that any prospect of large capital spend in the next five years is very remote. It has therefore been necessary to plan our way through this time period to improve the facilities and minimise the costs
involved.

As part of the planned extension provision was being made for a comfortable lounge, a verandah, increased storage/changing area etc. These needs still exist and we are planning to take a number of actions to resolve them. The initial key is to find a

low cost method of releasing the garages from acting as storage areas and we need as soon as possible three or four portakabins at no cost (except possibly the transport); these will then be used for storage until the Dutch Barn becomes available from MCSL and is erected.

During this winter approximately a quarter of the lounge at the West end will be converted into a comfortable area. At the same time the downstairs bar will be re-arranged to serve direct into No. 3 garage instead of under the awning and No. 3 garage will be improved. The comfortable area will be available for use by any members, guests or visitors in dry clothes; the majority of the lounge for those in wet clothes with an overspill available downstairs. Additionally we are finding out whether the roof over the changing rooms is strong enough to act as a verandah without strengthening. If this is the case we intend to erect a railing and staircase to allow access.

If we are able to find sufficient storage to release garages 4 and 5 as well, this will open up the possibility of expanding the changing facilities. It would also be very desirable to provide tables and benches on the grass to the West of the Club.

In order to achieve these plans we need your help and co-operation to find the materials and provide the labour. By doing this we can still continue to provide additional equipment etc.

Regarding the second support boat, the answer is not so easy. Based on a number of proposals that have been considered, the likely cost is in the order of £6,000.00 to £10,000.00 and we would have to have MASC agreement to the spend. The Sailing Sub Committee have asked for, and the Main Committee approved, the use of the Orkney as a second support boat next season. KNOW YOUR LOCAL AREA - ST PETER'S CHAPEL Dave Beane, 'Rodnigon'

The River Blackwater is reckoned to be one of the saltiest rivers in England, hardly surprising when you consider its lack of tributaries and how little fresh water flows into the river from the land. However, it is a river steeped in Essex history and it is interesting to reflect on this history while enjoying the pleasures of sailing its
waters.

Long before the bulk of Bradwell nuclear power station was built to daminate the eastern end of the Blackwater, St Peter's Chapel on Sales Point provided a conspicuous landmark for seafarers approaching the Colne and Blackwater Rivers from seaward. This chapel was built on the site of a Roman fortress and consecrated in AD 654 by Bishop Cedd. It subsequently was used by his followers to spread their gospel across southern England. In the ensuing centuries it was desecrated, used as a barm and allowed to fall into disrepair before being restored and reconsecrated in the 1920s. It is a very simple building which forms a fine example of a Saxon church. It is used for occasional services and is the destination for an annual pilgrimage which starts from the parish church in Bradwell, wends its way round the sea wall, and terminates with a gathering and service in the chapel.

Near to the chapel, almost hidden in a small copse right on the sea wall, you can see the small weatherboard cottage where Walter Linnet, last of the Essex wildfowlers, spent what must have been a rather lonely existence shooting and trapping wild fowl to earn his living. The cottage is now used by the Essex Wildlife Trust as a base from which to watch the prolific local bird life on the nearby marshes.

This area is
easily reached by the lane which is signposted from Bradwell village.
There is a car park within easy walking distance (about half a mile) from the chapel, and for the more energetic there are the options of walking further south along the sea wall bordering the Dengie Hundred and overlooking St Peter's Flats or of turning left along the south shore of the Blackwater towards the power station and Bradwell
village.

KNOW YOUR LOCAL AREA - OSEA ISLAND Dave Beane

With Osea Island right on our doostep, MSC dinghy and cruiser sailors alike will be fairly familiar with this little bit of Essex. Most of us will have completed the circumavigation across the Stumble at high tide and will know a bit about this island which can only be reached at low tide by wheeled vehicles using a narrow track which starts on the mainland at a point between Goldhanger Creek and Decoy Point and links across to the north west corner of Osea.

The Island, normally and currently a peaceful island farm, was the scene of much warlike activity at the end of the First World War and up to 1926 when it was a naval base for a range of high speed Coastal Motor Boats. These were all of Thormeycroft design and were hydroplanes powered by petrol engines. They were variously anned with with torpedoes, depth charges and mines, and were capable of speeds of up to 55 knots. If you think you have problems with wet bikes and speed boats, just imagine being confronted with a 70' motor boat approaching at 50 knots! All that now remains of all this naval activity are same of the sheds which have now been converted for use to house farm implements.

The large house on Osea was at one time a drying out haven for alcoholics but local legend has it that the return to sobriety of the inmates was somewhat hampered by the activities of the fishermen who ran a profitable sideline by smuggling in bottles for the inebriates, doubtless at a healthy premium,

It is possible, except at high tide, to land on the easter end of the island and to walk right round the island without trespassing. This walk takes you past the old wharf on the north shore where the Thames barges used to load the produce grown on the island. Once past the island end of the Causeway it is necessary to walk along the beach on the tideline past the fast-disappearing remains of Osea Pier and alongside the deep pool which provides a popular anchorage to the east of the pier. If you do decide to follow this route, please remember that Osea is privately owned and take care not to trespass on the main part of the Island. This stroll will take about an hour to complete assuming a fairly leisurely pace.

10,

no doubt put it stronger than that!) and I would welcome comments and suggestions for future improvement. I am sure, also, that same of you have been eagerly awaiting my approach to set you up with a duty only to be disappointed. This is because it is
not half so easy as it seems to track down all the willing and able - particularly
among crews - so if you would like to be considered for a racing duty next year,
having been overlooked this, please let me know.

John Salmon, [redacted]

A TAIL OF TWO KITTIES

I know, it gets worse, doesn't it? By the time you read this we'll be well towards decking the hall, etc. and the 1990 season will be a mere twinkling in our eyes, although the Winter Pursuit Races will still be going on for those hardy souls who want them from 4th November to the Osea Icicle, with the Last Fling as part of the series, and a day off (for good behaviour) when the Working Party is on (25th November). Me, I reckon that came November it's time to deliver the wet suit to the repairers, huddle round the log fire and plan for next year.

However, just to show what a selfless person I am, I've volunteered to be Race Officer for the whole series. Special instructions for the series do give me draconian powers though, and perhaps I'm just feeding the latent megalamania!!

Enough of all that cold and ice! Let's reflect on one of the balmiest years I can remember, with times when sailing in shorts and aT shirt in a Force 4 was not something reserved for California or the Med. Aaaaahh, warm spray!!!! OK, we may have had our share of light airs, but very few races were actually abandoned through lack of wind (something to do with Mick Warr and a vegetarian diet no doubt.)

We did see same very large turnouts, and even Pete Flook's version of a lime-coloured hot air balloon (but only or twice.) We also saw a very significant move towards twin trapeze boats with the aforementioned Sir Peter (yes he does trapeze sometimes,) Big John, Lee Harrison, Dave & Anna and The Two Micks all going for their version of exotica (or should that be erotica), from the Regular Racers.

Don't let that put you off, all you closet cat. sailors out there, there are still plenty of Darts around to race (if you want to.) Anyone who hasn't plucked up the courage to race yet (and wants to) don't hold back. With the 1991 start line being over by No.1, a lot of the fear of getting tangled in the cruisers should have evaporated. Racing is really the best way of developing your boat handling skills and therefore being able to get out of problems at other times. If anyone has any other fears, the Cat Fleet is a very co-operative bunch who only want to see you enjoying sailing. After all, twice the hulls, twice the rudders, twice the sail,
twice the speed - sixteen times the fun.

As mentioned in October Navigans, I do delegate, but as they say, a volunteer is worth a hundred pressed men, and our mate Peter “The Pink" Flook has volunteered to look after affairs in the Cat Park for me. Ta, Pete. Hopefully, we'll be coming up with a few ways of improving our use of the space for next year, but in any case, talk to Peter before you bring a boat in. Watch this space.

Finally, the Sailing Sub has suggested that it will be easier for the Race Officer if the Slow Cat Handicap fleet (i.e. PN 90+, plus Steeve Keeble) start separately fran
the Fast fleet, so that's wot you're going to get in 1991, a separate start at 11.05
and 13.35.
See You All Afloat, Larry Botheras

HELM OF THE YEAR, 1990.

Once again, the final of the Helm of the Year provided a close and exciting competition with the ultimate result held in the balance until the last race was completed. The eventual winner of the Helm of the Year Trophy for 1990 was:-

DAMIAN BOREHAM

This year, five finalists took part in the competition; they were:-

Ron Greygoose (Solo Fleet)
Steve Glynn (Catamaran Handicap Fleet)
Mike Boreham (Monohull Handicap Fleet)
Damian Boreham (Dart 18 Fleet)
Tom Ashley (MIrror Fleet)

There should have been a sixth finalist but neither the qualifier, nor runner-up, from the Sailboard Fleet could take part due to other commitments.

As usual, a catalogue of mini-disasters accompanied the competitors as they battled it out on the water. Ron managed to hit a mark (Race 3) and run aground (race 4); Damian found his outhaul disintegrating before his eyes (Race 4) and also managed the only capsizes (twice) before the start of the 5th race. Mike probably collected most mini-disasters; his outhaul also came apart completely (Race 1), his self-bailer refused to shut (Race 3) and he managed to clonk poor, innocent, Steve on the head with his boom (race 5). The said Steve did nothing particularly wrong - except to leave his head in the path of Mike's boom and, the most disasterous of all, to vote at the Catamaran AGM to use Toppers for this final rather than Dart 15s before he knew that he would be taking part in the final. Ah, if only we had the gift of foresight. Tom alone seems to have avoided any major mini-disasters - wise chap.

The Sailing Sub-Committee had decided to approach the Catamaran Fleet for the loan of Dart 15s in which to sail the final. However the Cat AGM felt it would be better (fairer) to use Toppers; after all, it was pointed out, Toppers were used for the 'Top Dog' competion of the various national dinghy champions. This arguement, coupled with Steve Keeble's offer of 6 Toppers from the International Topper/Hurricane Association, was something the Rear Commodore couldn't refuse. Amongst other things, it had the advantage of providing six boats of more or less even performance for the competition:-

The race results were as follows:-

Race 1 saw an apparent good start at the windward end of the line by Mike, Damian and Tom - but Ron and Steve were wiser to start at the leeward end in stronger wind, reached the first mark with a handy lead and were never troubled. Mike's problems with his outhaul excited the hearts of the rescue boat who thought they had a customer - but 'twas not to be, even Mike managed to stay upright in the Southerly Force 3 wind.

Race 3 saw Ron hit a mark at a crucial point in the race as he contested the lead with Tom and Damian, with Mike not far behind. The subsequent 360 put him well behind and he just failed to snatch 3rd place from Mike, who had a boat half-filled with water due to the faulty bailer.

If Race 3 was vital to Ron, then Race 4 was vital to Damian. He had only to win this race to secure the trophy and seemed all set to do so as he led the fleet. Unfortunately, his outhaul started to 'fall apart' and, as he tried to repair it 'on the move', he sagged off to leeward and allowed Ron and Tom to overtake him. He managed to claw back one place from Tom but failed to catch Ron, even though Ron did sportingly run aground as he approached the finish. Fortunately, Ron managed to extricate himself from the mud and won both this race and a chance to gain the trophy in the 5th race.

In race 5, Ron and Damian merely needed to finish ahead of each other in order to win the trophy. Ron had the better start and looked all set to win as he led the fleet around the buoys. However, nothing is ever certain and Damian overhauled Ron on the close-hauled legs to win the race - and the Helm of the Year Trophy.

12.

Commiserations to Ron who came close to adding a 2nd Helm of the Year win to his previous win in 1983. His demonstration of sailing technique and tactics on the water was well worth watching - particularly for those who found themselves following behind him for most of the time.

Congratulations to Damian who finally won the Helm of the Year Trophy in this, his 7th successive attempt, having previously scored a 'Did Not Compete', a 4th (ie. last), two thirds and two seconds.

Tom Ashley sailed consistently well to take third place. Sometimes he led the fleet and was never far behind Ron and Damian. We'll certainly be seeing more of Tom's winning ways in the seasons to come.

Mike and Steve sailed contentedly, but ruefully, at the back (but Steve had a good 2nd place in Race 1). In race 5 they sailed quietly side-by-side on the run when Mike's boom, guided in a downward arc as he came off a wave, clonked Steve on the head. "Ouch" said a surpized Steve; "Sorry" said an embarrassed Mike. A 720 followed, thus ending Mike's race for all practical purposes.

Before the event, the competitors agreed that one discard should be allowed, just to guard against catastrophic gear failure on what would be strange, non-club, boats. In the event, nothing went too seriously wrong (apart from the outhauls and self-bailer) and a good competition was enjoyed by all.

The use of Toppers for this year's competition seemed to work well. Ron, Tom and Damian were of comparable weight, whilst although Steve and Mike might be described as 'a little heavier' they were nevertheless 'in contention' for most of the time - until an error put paid to their chances on the short courses.

"What boat shall we use ?" is a question asked each year when considering Helm of the Year, and it is a difficul one to answer. Club boats, be they Mirrors, Lasers, Dart 15s or whatever, tend to vary greatly in performance due to various factors. It is also difficult to choose a boat which does not favour at least one of the finalists. Whatever is used is a compromise' - and this year, the Toppers seemed to be a reasonably fair compromise bearing in mind that none of the finalists were 'Topper sailors'.

First, I would like to thank all those who attended the Annual General Meeting and took part in the debates on the motions. At the start of last season, six Sigma 36 cruisers, each with an experienced skipper, were chartered for a weekend by members from this Club. FOOD FOR THOUGHT

At the 1990 A.G.M., during the discussion on increasing membership fees etc., there appeared to be a marked resentment from some quarters that the M.S.C. were not permitted to build up a capital reserve fund to be spent for the benefit of the M.S.C. alone : but had to abide by the rules of the M.A.S.C. whereby any M.S.C. funds are retained by the M.A.S.C. in a general account and any request for capital expenditure has to be approved by the M.A.S.C. and if approved, money is made available.

The objection to this procedure seems to be centred around the fact that, like so many organisations today the M.A.S.C. is itself undergoing a financial crisis and therefore is unable to finance our current needs, which, if I read the mood of the meeting right, the first priority was for a replacement rescue boat.

As I listened to the arguments both for and against 1 took stock of our surroundings and my mind went back to our first clubhouse on the river, the barge MAMGU, where we were restricted to sailing 2 hours either side of high water. It was only after intense negotiations plus the support and purchasing power of the M.A.S.C. that Stansgate became the new site for the Marconi Sailing Club. I say site because we did not have a clubhouse, but we did have a site from where we could sail at all states of the tide, which was a bonus.

A clubhouse was soon forthcoming in the form of a wooden hut, obtained from 1 know not where, a working party added to the existing foundations leit over from WWe and erected the first M.S.C. Stansgate clubhouse, the facilities were few, but it was a beginning.

Today we have a brick built clubhouse and although the facilities may be overstretched at present, with a little give and take on all sides we can probably manage, changes may be desirable but are they essential 7? What we have has been obtained under the present rules and from before MAMGU to
present day has been a big step - don’t knock it.

To replace the Jack-B may be more essential, I leave it to the better informed to decide, but do we have to purchase outright ? Is it possible to lease a suitable boat ? after all most companies lease all or part of their capital equipment, are boats available to lease 7

Alternatively is it possible for MSC members to become shareholders ina financial arrangement independent of the MSC with the objective of purchasing capital equipment (rescue boat 7?) that can be leased to the club, assets being retained by shareholders for the benefit of the club as a whole. If in time profits are accrued these could be paid back to the shareholders as dividends. It may take a financial genius to work out the pros and cons but I think it is worth looking into.

Food for thought if nothing else

Fred Partlett

Ed's note to clarify one point: The desired new support boat is intended to be used in addition to, and not as a replacement for, Jack B.

THE 1989 SUMMER CRUISE OF 'LADY VERL' MAMGU ENTRY

TO TAKE AN EXTRACT FROM QUR NON-EXISTENT LOG BOOK WOULD BE JUST A SERIES OF LATITUDE AND LONGITUDE READINGS,

WE, THAT'S MYSELF, HEATHER, NICOLA AND NEILSON SET OFF FROM BRADWELL MARINA. THAT IN ITSELF WAS A MAJOR

AND VODKA ETC., WERE STOWED ABOARD. IF WE'D HAD A PLIMSOLL
LINE, IT WOULD

TIME TO RANGE THE HOSE PIPE OUT WE HAD TO SHIFT, AS THE PERMANENT BERTH HOLDER WAS AT THE MARINA ENTRANCE.
PANIC ENSUED AS WE WERE DIRECTED TO THE END OF ANOTHER PONTOON JUST ABOUT LONG ENOUGH TO ACOOMMODATE A MIRROR

UP QUICKER THAN A COWBOY HOG-TYING AT A RODEO. IT WAS WITH MORE THAN A LITTLE SMUGNESS ON MY PART THAT I TOLD
THEM WE WERE LEAVING IN 3 MINUTES AND THEY WOULD HAVE TO SHIFT.

OUT IN THE RIVER WE MADE CONTACT WITH ‘FREYA', COMPLETE WITH THE ROBINSON QUARTET, WHO WERE TO BE SAILING
COMPANIONS
FOR THE NEXT THREE WEEKS. OUR ROUTE TOOK US OUT TO THE SPITWAY, UP THE KINGS CHANNEL, TURN RIGPTM
AT THE TOP, AND, LEAVING THE LONGSAND HEAD AND THE WEST HINDER LIGHTVESSEL TO STARBOARD, HOPEFULLY FIN.
COSTEND. THE WIND, WHICH WAS AT FIRST RANGING FROM 17-21 KNOTS FROM THE N.E., SOON FELL TO 13-16 KNOTS.
UNDER FULL MAIN AND GENOA THIS GAVE A SPEED THROUGH THE WATER OF 6 - 6.5 KNOTS FAIRLY CONSISTENTLY AND WITH IT
QNE OF THE BEST NIGHT SAILS I HAVE EVER HAD. THE AUTOHEIM WITH THE WIND VANE WAS PERFORMING PERFECTLY, THE
SKY WAS CLEAR, AND PHOSPHORESCENCE IN THE WATER REFLECTED GREEN ON THE TOPSIDES - PERFECT CONDITIONS. WE ALSO
HAD THE ADDED BONUS OF NOT MUCH TRAFFIC IN THE SHIPPING LANES. WELL, NOT MUCH FOR US THAT IS, BUT FOR 'FREYA'
THAT WAS A DIFFERENT
STORY. IT WAS AS IF ALL THE FERRIES, TANKERS, AND FREIGHTERS WERE WAITING FOR 'FREYA' TO
APPEAR ON THEIR RADAR SCREENS BEFORE BEARING DOWN ON HER. EVEN A TUG WITH A 200M TOW MANAGED TO GET IN HER
WAY. OOSTEND, IT IS SAID, CAN BE SEEN SOME 17 MILES AWAY. WE DID NOT SEE IT 17 HUNDRED FEET AWAY, AS THE
MIST THE NEXT MORNING TOTALLY OBSCURED THE COASTLINE.

THOSE WHO HAVE BEEN TO THE NORTH SEA YACHT CLUB AT COSTEND WILL BE AWARE OF THE 'QUASIMODO' IN THE CAPTAIN'S
CAP WHO PARADES FROM HIS VANTAGE POINT BY THE CLUB BUILDING, DIRECTING YACHTS INTO BERTHS AND GETTING QUITE

WORKED UP WHEN YOU DO NOT MAKE PROGRESS FAST ENOUGH DUE TO A 50 FT. FLOATING CONSERVATORY WITH TWIN DIESELS
ACROSS
YOUR PATH. 'FREYA' WAS THERE ALREADY - WE HAD ROMPED AWAY FROM HER DURING THE NIGHT, BUT THERE SHE IS,
TIED UP AND WITH THE KETTLE QN. I SPEND THE NEXT FEW DAYS MUTTERING ABOUT BEING A PURIST AND SAILING ALL THE
WAY. THAT EVENING ONE OF THE FINEST FIREWORKS DISPLAYS WE HAVE WITNESSED WAS HELD ON THE BEACH; FOR WHAT

THE NEXT DAY WE ARE VISITED BY THE BELGIAN MARITIME POLICE. WE HAD SHIFTED POSITION SO 'LADY VERL' LAY NEXT
TO THE PONTOON WITH 'FREYA' OUTSIDE. THE CHILDREN HAD GONE OFF OF THEIR OWN ACCORD, LEAVING US ADULTS TO

SHIP'S PAPERS SO I GO BELOW FOR MY DOCUMENTS. MEANTIME, HEATHER INFORMS BRENDA ON 'FREYA' OF WHAT IS REQUIRED
AND GEORGE GOES BELOW FOR THEIR PAPERS. THEN THEY ASK FOR THE RADIO LICENCE, S30 I G BELOW 70 FETCH IT.

INSIDE
LEG MEASUREMENT. FINALLY THE TWO POLICEMEN SEEM SATISFIED. BRENDA CALLS OUT TO THEM THAT THEY HAD ALL
THE INFORMATION THEY REQUIRED READY FOR THEIR INSPECTION, ONLY TO BE TOLD, "WE WILL GET YOU ANOTHER TIME."

THE NEXT DAY WE LEAVE BELGIUM. THE SAIL THAT TAKES ONE ALONG THE COAST PAST ZEEBRUGGE ALWAYS SEEMS TO TAKE
FOREVER, EVEN WITH REASONABLE CONDITIONS. THIS DAY WAS NO EXCEPTION. GRADUALLY,
AND AFTER WHAT SEEMED THE
HUNDREDTH TIME OF ASKING, "ARE WE NEARLY THERE YET?" DOES FLUSHING BECOME CLEARLY VISIBLE. ON ROUTE, 'FREYA'
WHO TRIES TO CONTACT 'STAGGERS' (WHO IS EITHER QUT OF RADIO RANGE, OR, HAVING CRUISED WITH US BEFORE, KNOWS
WHEN TO KEEP QUIET,) FINDS 'BLUCETTE'
ON THE LINE. WE ARRANGE TO MEET INSIDE THE OLD LOCK AT FLUSHING. ON
OUR ARRIVAL WE FIND 'BLUCETTE' ALONGSIDE THE DOCK, WE RAFT UP, FOLLOWED SHORTLY BY 'FREYA'. ALMOST
IMMEDIATELY AN ANIMATED DISCUSSION ON THE VIRTUES OF 'QRANGEBOOM' VERSUS 'GROLSCH'. AFTER WHICH, DEREK ON
"BLUCETTE' ANNOUNCES THAT HE INTENDED TO LEAVE EARLY, SO MUSICAL BOATS ENSUES BEFORE FURTHER DEBATE TAKES
PLACE. UP TO MIDDLEBURG NEXT, ALWAYS A FIRM FAVOURITE WITH THE FAMILY. YOU FEEL YOU ARE IN HOLLAND AS YOU
PASS BENEATH THE LIFTING BRIDGE WHICH LEADS INTO THE HARBOUR OVERLOOKED BY THE PERIOD HOUSES, ALL WITH THEIR
DARK GREEN DOORS. AT MIDDLEBURG
THE FAIR IS IN TOWN. NOT THE QUAINT HAND-PAINTED MERRY-GO-ROUNDS WITH
TRADITIONAL
ORGAN MUSIC, BUT GREAT BIG GAUDY CHROME AND PLASTIC RIDES, DESIGNED TO EMPTY THE CONTENTS OF YOUR

STOMACH AND WALLET AT HIGH SPEED TO THE ACCOMPANIMENT OF 'HEAVY METAL' AT 400 WATTS PER CHANNEL. STILL,
"FRITS MIT MAYONNAISE' GO SOME WAY TO MAKE UP FOR THIS INTRUSION. AS USUAL CHILDREN SEEM TO THRIVE ON THIS
SORT

THE NEXT MOVE IS INTO THE VEERSEMEER. AT BEERE WE TURN LEFT AND HAVE A SHORT BUT FINE SAIL UNDER MAIN AND

AND WITH THE WEATHER SEEMINGLY UNDER THEIR CONTROL TOO, WE STAY A FEW DAYS.

EVEN IDYLLIC SURROUNDINGS AND CONDITIONS BECOME TIRESOME AFTER

BECOMES A NECESSITY AFTER A FEW DAYS, SO BACK DOWN THE MEER, PAST VEER AGAIN, AND ONWARDS TO A MARINA DIRECTLY

OPPOSITE
DELTA MARINE. ON OUR ARRIVAL THEY HOIST THE RED ENSIGH, WE LOOK ABOUT
TO SEE IF THERE IS ANYONE

HERE IS SO CASUAL. PEOPLE OF ALL AGES SWIM IN THE MARINA ITSELF, LEAVING YACHTS TO NAVIGATE AROUND
THESE MOVING HAZARDS AS WELL AS THOSE FOUND NATURALLY IN A MARINA.

OUR NEXT FORT OF CALL IS BRUNIESS IN THE GRAVALINGENMEER, WHICH REQUIRES LOCKING QUT OF THE VEERSEMEER,
CROSSING THE COOSTERSCHELDE, AND LOCKING INTO THE GRAVALINGENMEER. 'FREYA' LEAVES QN TIME SIMPLY BECAUSE
THEY'RE
READY AND WE'RE NOT. WE ARRIVE
AT THE LOCK, 'FREYA' IS MADE FAST ALREADY. WE ATTEMPT
TO TIE UP, BUT
DUE TO THE CONGESTION
WE ARE TOLD TO LEAVE. WE DO SOME PRETTY SMART REVERSING, (PITY I CANNOT DO THIS MORE
OFTEN), AND WAIT FOR THE NEXT LOCK. ONCE THROUGH THE LOCK WE ENJOY A FINE SAIL TO BRUNIESS. HEATHER CORRECTS
THE LOCAL CHART WITH A NEW CARDINAL MARK. IT'S NORTH,
BUT FOR SOME REASON BEST KNOWN TO HERSELF SHE HAS DRAWN
A SOUTH CARDINAL
MARK. WHAT IS WORSE IT'S IN BALLPOINT
PEN. THE MISTAKE IS POINTED QUT AND A CORRECTION MADE
WHICH IS ALMOST LIFE SIZE. I MAKE A MENTAL NOTE NOT TO REMARK ON CHART DIFFERENCES IN FUTURE. FROM DELTA
MARINE AT BRUNIESS WE SET SAIL UNDER A DARKENING
SKY, YET STILL WARM ENOUGH TO WEAR SHORTS AND TEE SHIRTS.
OUR DESTINATION, THE TOP OF THE MEER. THE WIND INCREASES IN STRENGTH, REQUIRING A REEF IN THE MAIN. THE RAIN
STARTS
TO FALL. INSTEAD OF RUSHING FOR WATERPROOFS, WE STRIP OFF TO BATHING ATTIRE. LINE SQUALLS
WORK THEIR
WAY ACROSS THE WATER AS GUSTS UP TO 29 KNOTS ARE SHOWN ON THE WIND SPEED INDICATOR, AND WITH EACH SUCCESSIVE
SQUALL
COMES MORE RAIN. STILL WE SAIL QN IN OUR SWIMMING GEAR. AS WE FINALLY TIE UP TO THE PONTOON, THE RAIN
BEGINS TO EASE, ALLOWING THE BELGIANS AND THE DUTCH TO COME QUT QN DECK AND VIEW THE LATEST IN ALL-WEATHER
GEAR BEING WORN BY THE BRITISH THIS YEAR. AFTER A DAY OR SO WE DEPART, WITH THE AIM OF REACHING OUDE TOUNGE
ENROU
TO THE HARINGVLIET.

FOR OVER A WEEK NOW THE WIND HAS BEEN CONSTANTLY QN THE NOSE. EVEN WITH A 180 DEGREE CHANGE IN THE DIRECTION

ABLE TO CRACK THE SHEETS OFF, BUT ONLY A LITTLE. WITH ONLY 13 - 17 KNOTS OF WIND ON THE FLAT TIDELESS WATER,
WE ACHIEVE 6.5 - 7 PLUS KNOTS WITH MAIN AND WORKING JIB. THIS TIME WHEN THE RAIN CAME, AND IT REALLY DID RAIN
TOO, BOTH NICOLA AND I WERE IN THE COCKPIT. IN THE BEST TRADITION WE PUT OUR JACKETS OVER OUR SWIM WEAR AND
TOOK OUR SHOES
OFF. IT WAS HERE IN THE RAIN STORM THAT WE RE-ENACTED THE PARABLE OF THE LOAVES AND THE
FISHES. ONLY THIS TIME IT WAS A MUG OF TEA, THE RAIN WAS POURING OFF MY SOUWESTER AND BEING DIRECTED
STRAIGHT
INTO MY MUG. EVERY TIME I LIFTED IT TO MY LIPS TO DRINK, THE MUG FILLED UP FASTER THAN I QUID
SWALLOW. OUR ARRIVAL AT THE LOCK COINCIDED WITH THE IMPROVEMENT IN THE WEATHER, AND WE MADE QUR WAY INTO THE
OOSTERSCHELDE AND THROUGH YET ANOTHER LOCK WHICH BROUGHT US INTO THE ONCE TIDAL STRETCH OF WATER WHICH
CONNECTS THE OOSTERSCHELDE
AND THE HARINGVLIET. THE ENTRANCE INTO QUDE TOUNGE IS BY A VERY NARROW SHALLOW
CHANNEL, POORLY MARKED IN COMPARISON TO THE NORMAL STANDARD OF DUTCH BUOYAGE. ‘THE ROUTE TOOK US THROUGH
A
SMALL DERELICT LOCK WHERE THE CHANNEL NARROWED TO THE POINT THAT WE BEGAN TO QUESTION WHY WE HAD CHOSEN 10

FROM QUDE TOUNGE, NEXT ON THE LIST WAS HELOVLIETSLIUS. THE WEATHER WAS SUNNY AND THE WINDS WERE LIGHT AND
PROGRESS
WAS REASONABLE. THE HARBOUR PROVED TO BE VERY FULL WITH YACHTS. STILL, ROOM WAS MADE FOR US AND THE
MANY OTHERS THAT FOLLOWED. A STEAM FAIR WAS IN TOWN WITH STEAM DRIVEN TUGS, PADDLE BOATS,

AND FAIRGROUND RIDES. TO ADD TO THE ATMOSPHERE OF THE EVENT THERE WAS A DISPLAY OF MORRIS DANCING BY A GROUP

THERE WAS A
FIREWORK DISPLAY, FOLLOWED BY A PROCESSION OF YACHTS LIT UP IN CARNIVAL FASHTON PARADING AROUND THE HARBOUR.

BACK. HAVING SAID THAT, IT SEEMED A VERY FAST PASSAGE BACK DOWN TO ZIERIKZEE WITH JUST ONE NAIL BITING MOMENT

NOISE, (SORRY, SINGING) WELL INTO THE NIGHT. THE NEXT DESTINATION
WAS BRESKENS VIA FLUSHING. THIS WAS NO
EFFORT, MADE EASIER DUE TO THE CHILDREN TAKING THE INFLATABLE AND MOTORING THE ENTIRE WAY - WELL, AT LEAST TO
FLUSHING. WE HAD MISSED THE LOCK THAT 'FREYA' HAD TAKEN WHILE WE WERE STOWING THE DINGHY ON BOARD, SO WE HAD
A SHORT WAIT UNTIL THE NEXT LOCK,

THE TRIP ACROSS THE WESTERSCHELDE TOOK MORE TIME THAN EXPECTED, DUE TO THE STRONG TIDE, BUT THIS ACOOMPLISHED,
WE TIED UP BOWS~TO THE PONTOON AND THE STERN TO A BUOY. I HAVE NEVER LIKED THIS METHOD OF MOORING AND THE
FOLLOWING MORNING I DEMONSTRATED
WHY. WITH MOORING LINE FIRMLY CAUGHT BETWEEN THE FIN AND THE SKEG THE WIND
BLOWING ON TO THE PONTOON, AND THE REALISATION THAT TO ENGAGE GEAR ON THE ENGINE IS TO WIND MORE ROPE ROUND
THE PROP QUICKER THAN WINDING CANDYFLOSS QN A STICK. BY A PROCESS OF SHOUTING, KICKING AND SCREAMING WE
MANOBUVRE OURSELVES OUT OF THE MARINA AND INTO THE WESTERSCHELDE
ONCE MORE, THIS TIME BACK TO OCOSTEND. THE
WIND IS ON THE NOSE AGAIN, AND WITH A FRESH BREEZE AND A THREATENING SKY, WE PUT ON THE WORKING JIB AND PUT

ONE REEF IN THE MAIN.

COSTEND SEFMS TO TAKE FOREVER TO REACH, AND WHEN WE DO FINALLY REACH THE BREAKWATER WE HAVE TO WAIT FOR A
FERRY BEFORE ENTERING THE HARBOUR AND TYING UP BY THE NORTH SEA YACHT CLUB. DURING THE NIGHT THE WEATHER
TAKES
A DISTINCT TURN FOR THE WORSE AND WITH THE SWELL NOW REACHING THE INNER HARBOUR, LIFE QV BOARD BECAME

SO ALONG WITH 'FREYA' WE LOCKED INTO THE MERCATOR YACHT HARBOUR AND MADE OUR PLANS TO RETURN BY FERRY. THE

CONRAD BARNARD

MOORING ACCIDENT ARTICLE FROM MARCH 1985

The question has arisen as to the liability of a mooring owner who allows another member of the Sailing Club to use his mooring without charge, on the basis that the User is responsible for checking and maintaining the mooring,

In such a situation the mooring Owner is unlikely to be able to rely upon insurance, as the normal policy covers only damamge caused by the insured craft, and not damage resulting from an alleged defect in the mooring.

The first point to be made is that for a third party, (i.e. the owner of another boat whose craft is damaged by the moored craft breaking free) to successfully sue the mooring Owner, same breach of duty to such third party must be established. In the present case there is a reference to "the negligent failure of your mooring" which presumable means it is alleged by the insurers' solicitors that the Owner was negligent either in the laying or maintaining of the mooring. At this stage, however, the solicitors provide no details of how the negligence is supposed to have
occurred.

The evidence from the mooring Owner suggests that the accident was caused by a manufacturing defect in the shackle pin. If this is the case, there is no negligence on the part of the mooring Owner, who could not reasonably be expected to carry aut metallurgical testing on the pin, which was presumably bought from a reputable
chandler.

Contd... 's

ll.

It must be stressed that it is for the plaintiff to establish negligence, not for the defendent to establish that he acted with all due care. There are circumstances where it is presumed that no accident would have occurred without negligence, reversing the onus of proof; however, a yacht breaking its moorings would not fall into this category.

It would seem well established practice that a member of a club using another member's mooring without payment, accepts all risks of accident, howsoever arising. Indeed even where moorings are hired out by a commercial boatyard, it is normally m the basis that the boatyard disclaims all liability. the point of custamn and practice it would, no doubt, be useful to obtain the written opinion of a body such as the RYA. In the present case, the mooring owner's position is further improved since it was agreed specifically that it was the User's responsibility to periodically check the mooring.

On the facts as presently known, there would seem to be no liability on the part of the mooring Owner, and the next step would seem to be simply to repudiate the insurers' claim without going into details. If the insurers wish to pursue the matter, it will then be for them to establish how the alleged negligence occurred.

P.R. DAVIS, 21-3-85

NAVIGANS PAST

The Year
is 1957 - a hesitant beginning, and there's trouble with the troops

This is what will, I hope, be the first of a series of articles taking a look at Navigans Past. The aim of
the articles is to try to get some flavour of the development of the MSC - and to see if the apparent
problems of today are no more than replays of those of Yesteryear. I hope that those involved in the club's

development all those years ago will not take offence at any ‘tongue in cheek' remarks I may make; I can assure you I am full of admiration for the efforts you put in and which gave rise to the club we have today. Perhaps those involved ‘in the past' will be able to 'fill-in' the detail; I'm merely looking at Navigans which doesn't reveal the ‘goings on' behind the scenes !

Vol. 1 No.1 - January, 1957 - The very first Navigans, a single typed sheet on one side of foolscap ,
and edited by the Hon.Sec., W.J.Hodge. The first thing I notice is that it is the “Monthly Bulletin of the MASC Sailing Section"; clearly no thoughts of UDI here. The inevitable invitation for news and views and a deadline of the lst Wednesday in each month. The 1956 AGM was held in November '56 and apparently decided the annual subscriptions really ought to have been paid before the AGM, otherwise membership would "be deemed terminated". I should say so; the smart operators presumably could sail all season and then ‘be terminated’ without spending a bean. Plans to hold an EGM to hear reports on the possibilities of alternative
club accommodation - sounds exciting. Members of the club were serving on the Fleetwind Stand at the Olympia
Boat show in 1957 and, oh, yes, they need someone to look after Avril. Now who is Avril I wonder ?

Vol.1 No2. - February 1957 - The Editor hopes all members will subscribe to its contents; if they took
that literally he'd be somewhat overwhelmed but we know what he means. He reminds everyone the 1957 subs are
due and good news for Avril - someone offered to look after her. However, no romances in the air ‘cos
Avril turns out to be the club boat - shame. A note that catamarans are not eligible for handicap races
puts them firmly in their place and quite right too (oops, I'ma Cat owner so I'l] take that back).

Vol.1 No.3 - March, 1957 - Oh! dear, the Editor reports "your committee deplores the lack of support shown
by the Section to this bulletin" - ‘twas ever so I fear. He goes on to say “an aptitude for journalism is
unnecessary for your Committee promises that any material submitted will be re-written if the writer so desires". Of course, the development of our modern comprehensive educational system makes this statement
unnecessary - nowadays we'd just miss out “if the writer so desires". A meeting to hear Mr & Mrs Eric
Hiscock lecture on their world voyage costs 2/6 (124 p in new money); I must say I like addressing the
‘Mrs' half as Mrs Eric Hiscock - must try it on Maggie sometime. The Fitting-Out Supper at the Jolly
Sailor, Heybridge, is 4/- per person plus 2/6 return journey on the charabanc - assuming you want to return
to-thetmsford:——By-the way, the annual subs for 1957 are still overdue.

Vol.1 No.4 - April, 1957. - The annual subs are now considerably overdue and the Editor hopes to be over-
whelmed by contributions. At last, a real contribution to navigans entitled ‘Going Foreign' by Charlotte Cottam which, being marked Chapter 1, promises more to come.

Vol.1 No.5 - May 1957 - A note of exasperation from the Editor:- ‘To make the bulletin a permanent feature,
it is essential that the support of all members of the Section be forthcoming" That will get ‘em going - provided they read the bulletin in the first place. Part II of 'Going Foreign’ was published.

Guess what, annual subs are now long ovedue.

Vol.1 No.6 June, 1957 - Great news ! An implied improvement wher’ the Editor writes "In spite of
repeated requests, annual subscriptions are only trickling in”. Well, at least they are now trickling, the flood will come later. Chapter concluded ‘Going Foreign' and, even at this distance in time, Charlotte must be congratulated as being the trail-blazer for all future articles in Navigans. You can buy a newly
built Enterprise for £110 with racing sails an additional £26.10.0

Vol.1 No.7 - July, 1957 - Has the Editor's message finally got through ? Not a murmur about late subs.

A second article entitled 'East Coast Delivery by 'Goose' - Step' (the humour was as bad then as it is now).

Vol.1 No.8 - August, 1957 - Sorry, f got it wrong; many members remain on the books as unpaid. Surely they
shouldn't be on the books if they haven't paid ?

Vol.1 No.9 - September, 1957 - Laying-Up Supper at the Palm Court (don't get excited - its the Marconi
Luncheon Club) costs 9/- per person. GP boat cover at £8.8.0 and Hornet cover at £ 9.7.6. Nowt about
late subs, surely now all must be well ?

Vol.1 No.10 - October, 1957 - Alas, we still have transgressors re. late subs but now the Committee is
getting tough. Unless they're paid up in 3 weeks, their continued membership will be considered by the
Committee in session. I guess 10 months credit ain't bad - were they charged interest ?

14. —

Vol.1, No.1] - November, 1957 - Eric Cottam won the Fleetwind Points Series and the President's Cup
in 'Muggs'. Now where have I heard that name before ? Eric scored 178 points (how many ?) and the
2nd helm, Terry Hallam, scored 162 points. Ah! they clearly had a different scoring system unless the
results Secretary got it al] wrong (not entirely unknown !).

Vol.1 No.12 - December, 1957 - The editor has clearly given up on subs - either that or the Committee's
threat to “ex-terminate, ex-terminate" has had the desired effect. The Editor again begs for contributions including suggestions and grievances (he should have jumped into a time machine and transported himself to 1990 before he wrote that ). He goes on to say "all that's required is for a rough outline to be submitted to the Editor who will write up the details in the form of an article” Desperate situations require desperate remedies but it wasn't a bad service to offer was it ? How about it Maureen ?

So ends the first, uncertain, year of Navigans. Not much has really changed but the success of our club
pioneers is here for all to read. Next month - 1958, ah! a good year was 1958!

Mr and Mrs Mise Boreham

Looks familiar.

No doubt many of you, like Maggie and I, like to ‘browse around' the Battlesbridge 'Antiques Centre’
occasionally - just to see what's there. Much to Maggie's disgust I bought a few copies of old
Essex Countryside magazines
at 10p per copy - much better than the cheese dish that Maggie was eyeing
at £36 (we didn't buy it).

One of the magazines had a photograph which seemed familiar, and it turned out to be a photo taken from Stansgate looking towards Osea. It was taken by Mr.N.J.James and submitted for the magazine's competition for Essex yachting and boating scenes. Looking through the old copies of Navigans, I assume that the photographer was club member ‘Jimmy' James. Apart from the barge in the background taking my interest, it was the Enterprise dinghy in the foreground which drew my attention; undoubtedly a Marconi SC racing dinghy which, from the old Navigans, seems to have belonged to the Bigden family, but I don't know if if was Jack, Julian or Tim adoin' the sailing. The Enterprise sail number was £1563.

I'd like to think that Mr.James won the competition but, even if he didn't, I got a great deal of pleasure
in seeing the photograph for its own sake - and an additional pleasure knowing a little bit about its
source, I forgot to mention the date of the magazine - it was December , 1967.

CLUB NOTICE BOARD - BACSPA NEWSLETTER

Speed Limit on the Hiver Blackwater

There is 8 growing concern of all River users with the increasing menace of uncontrolled jet-skis and high speed power-craft now beginning to wreak havoc on our waters since the re-opening of the Public Slipway at Stone.

The Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association BACSPA who pursue 6 policy of active participation with the 31 Watersport Organisation Members, believe that the Maldon District Council should exercise strict control of the Public launching site at Stone, to defuse a potentially lethal situation.

At a recent BACSPA meeting it was agreed to pursue a policy with the MOC to set up zones for specific water sports such that the main Fairways would be left relatively free of unnecessary traffic.

The Council has responded in this latter case by moving speed limit bouys from Stansgate southern shore to Osea Island thereby protecting the time-honoured anchoring area West of the Pier.

Many of you will already be aware of a new organisation, The Blackwater Users Action Group BUAG, who have set themselves up to consider the interests of River users, including wildfowlers, bird watchers, ramblers, Osea Island, etc. They are proposing oan overall speed limit of 8 knots inland from a North/South line taken from a point near Stone Sailing Club.

This policy has an immediate attraction and deserves carefull consideration before any decision is made, one way or the other.

SPECIFICALLY, it must be realised that such control cannot be made for any particular type of craft and would have to include all River users.
It would change the way of the River and how we use it, at this moment in time.

It would become illegal to sail any performance dinghy when planing conditions prevailed (F3-4) as planing starts at 8 knots plus!

Likewise, catamarans would have to be excluded from the Blackwater.

Rescue Boats, of the planing variety, would be outlawed when everyone knows that speed in the time of an emergency is of paramount importance.

Sailing surf-boards could be a thing of the past.

BACSPA believes that the Aiver Blackwater is one of the most beautiful settings that any water user will find on the whole of the East Coast and should therefore be carefully preserved for the benefit of ALL users.

This will necessarily mean constraint in certain areas and perhaps relaxation in others to strike a balance that will allow us to live together with nature and with due respect and consideration of others.

The River Blackwater is your River and BACSPA believes that each Member Club or Association should address the current situation with its own Membership to guide BACSPA along that path considered to be the most equitable to its Membership and to provide the next step towards our childrens’ heritage.

Colin Lambert. Secretary, BACSPA. - 14th November 1990

BLACKWATER AND COLNE SAILING PROTECTION ASSOCIATION (BACSPA)
Representing the Yacht Clubs of the Blackwater and Colne Rivers

I usually write a short item about BACSPA's activities during the preceding year for the HBSC Newsletter. This year I am circulating it to all Clubs in view of the important issues facing us, and I hope that all Club Editors can find same space for
it.
Chairman

BACSPA - Firstly a word about our Organisation!

BACSPA is run by the Clubs for the Clubs. We have no commercial or private interests and, although from time to time we may find common cause with other River users, e.g. conservation bodies, the National Rivers Authority, Maldon District Council,
contd.

4.
BACSPA....

fishermen, local owners etc., we represent only the Clubs, and Sailing. BACSPA is in fact a member of the RYA in its own right, and we are very grateful for their steady support in these difficult times. BACSPA's policy is set democratically by the Clubs at Spring and Autumn General Meetings each year, and is carried forward by its small Executive Committee in between. The work usually includes representation of the Clubs at the River Blackwater Consultative Committee (where we have established excellent relations with Maldon District Council), calling meetings of interested parties where co-operation is needed or where disputes have arisen, and very importantly, lobbying influential parties such as local MPs to make sure that the interests of sailing people are properly represented. An election for the executive is held each Autumn.

COWBOYS AND ROGUE SPEEDBOATS. These have been causing continuing concern for a number of years but the problems are now more serious with the advent of jet-skis and wet bikes in our estuaries. At our Spring meeting we decided to submit to Maldon District Council, to all Clubs and to BACUAG (the new BLACKWATER USERS ACTION GROUP) our draft report on the very real problems identified by our members. The great majority of planing boat operators do act responsibly with consideration for other river users. Stone Watersports, who are members of BACSPA, set an admirable
standard.

The problems are _ twofold. 1. The Cowboys and the ill-informed (as ever); 2. Existing speed limits are largely ignored.

BACSPA's policy was against any sort of blanket ban since this could be a_ two-edged sword in unsympathetic hands. We strongly recommended stronger policing of the existing limits; this would, in our opinion remove 90% plus of the problem.
Education of newcomers is desperately needed, as is control at the launching sites of the offenders. BACSPA has had a generally favourable response to the report and MDC have picked up the suggestion of a temporary trial area at Steeple Creek dedicated to skibikes, as has been also done at West Mersea. Obviously we have to be extremely careful with such schemes, bearing in mind all the canpeting interests, but our last meeting confirmed the general view that there is room on the Blackwater for all current watersports with the present pattern of use. Clearly an explosion in ski-bike numbers (or anything else) would pose a new situation. On the Colne we now have a highly regulated situation, with 8 knots speed limit over most of the river, an area dedicated to waterskiing, and 4 knots speed limit in Brightlingsea harbour. The limits apply to all craft (including yachts etc.) and formal permission is required before holding any water events. We understand that there are major difficulties in policing the limits, which of course is the real problem.

LIGHT DUES. The British Ports Federation report has recommended: a) canpulsory registration for all seagoing pleasure craft above 21' with a view to b)extracting an annual fee of £100 to support the cost of lights and navaids. The RYA has pointed out sO many inaccuracies and incorrect implications in the BPF report, that it is pretty well discredited. We are nevertheless writing to our local MP to point out that among the maritime nations, Britain is almost unique in trying to fund its aids in this crazy and ineffective way. It is also cheeky to bring in this idea when so many useful marks have recently been abolished or reduced.

SALTCOTE MILL. The Maldon Plan envisages a “yacht harbour". This’ has been interpreted by developers in terms of a new marina and associated housing development. BACSPA, along with Blackwater SC and Saltcote SC have consistently opposed successive planning applications along these lines: We feel that a further increase in the number of deep draught yachts in the Upper Blackwater is totally inappropriate but that if the Plan policy is that it has to be, then numbers must be strictly limited. Moreover the implications of dredging, salt marsh disturbance and changed current flow are such that a major environmental study is essential before any work begins. We should also lose 12-30 swinging moorings, to be replaced by Marina berths at, perhaps, 30 times the cost.

THE UNIFORM BUSINESS RATE. From April 1990 all Clubs have been seeing severe increases in their rates. One has no less than 300%, the norm seems to be around 200%. This means that a considerble proportion of Club income will have to go on Business rates from effectively non-profit making sports clubs, paid by the members

BACSPA ...

who already have paid their poll tax. It is manifestly unfair and illogical and same small Clubs may well close. The Ministry's view is that discretionary relief should be available, but that this must be negotiated at a local level. Of 21 Clubs in East Anglia who responded to a recent RYA questionnaire, one had had 100% relief from its Local Authority, 4 had 50% and the rest Zero. In Scotland all Clubs receive relief! BACSPA is not aware of any such relief locally; one Club to our knowledge has been
turned down. Same have made progress on revaluation - a different issue. We need a
consistent sympathetic understanding of Club problems from our Local Authorities, and BACSPA is raising the matter vigorously. Meantime, as suggested in the RYA's
excellent guide, Clubs must keep hammering on the door - don't take no for an answer.

TAILPIECE. These are sane of this year's threats to us. Remember that BACSPA is set up to defend the Sailing Clubs, and no other organisation whatever, however high its motives! Good Sailing!

I am an occasional Club Member, isolated om Osea, but very concerned with the matters which originate with highspeed powercraft. My son, Charles Anderson, a better known member and a parttimer with the Coastguards, tells me that episodes requiring salvage services increase in frequency. Though not confined to the highspeed power boat, this type of vessel is often driven or piloted by persons less well tutored in, and less anxious to learn, the rules of the road. Alcohol is an additional hazard when travelling at high speed, and though crew of sailing craft are not innocent in the enjoyment of alcohol, they are running a risk of doing damage only to themselves.

Apart from partitioning the estuary to improve the safety standards, I believe that power boatdrivers should be insured against the cost of salvage (£2,000 to put a helicopter in the air), so that the use of public funds be reduced. They should qualify by testing for a licence and should be penalised for misdemeanours.

Should the same apply to sailboats? If so, it can only be an advantage if the hazards of the sea are recognised by more of us and avoided by those who are, by nature or lack of experience, not competent to go afloat.

I suspect I am one of the latter, but at 70 years of age I feel well qualified to fly kites, including this one.

May I comment on 'Food for Thought' (P7, Vol 35, Issue 1). Never likely to use the M.A.S.C. facilities, I would be much happier to pay my M.A.S.C. subscription into the M.S.C. capital reserve.

Yours, Tam Anderson

LOOKS FAMILIAR - more information

With regard to Mike Borehan's "Looks Familiar" in last month's Navigans, I thought I would write with my now sanewhat hazy recollections of Enterprise Sail No. E1563. The first Club owner of 1563 was Nomnan Palmer, who named the boat “Sue Ann" after his two daughters. He then raced the boat successfully for the Club's first one, two or three seasons at Stansgate. My brother Julian bought the boat, probably around
1966 or 1967 after somehow failing to emigrate to Barbados. Shortly after Julian
acquired 1563 fran Norman, the boat's name was changed to Argus II (or and the
colour changed fran white to black with a white stripe - the sort yachties call a
boot top. In 1968 Julian tried another foreign jaunt; this time he DID leave the UK but went the wrong way and ended up installing Marconi's radar in Germany.

While sitting out the sailing season in Germany, Julian did have the sense to lend the boat and crew (his future wife, Jill) to brother Tim (me) for a_ season's unremarkable racing. My recollection of the boat now becomes extremely hazy, but I can say that Julian raced her with reasonable success both at Club level and in the East Coast Nimbus Series. She gained new decks and a very stiff Proctor mast compared with its bendy (laterally 2-piece) collar predecessor; new Musto sails to replace the excellent but ‘past it' Windward ones. As for Julian, two Enterprises later he made another, third attempt at Barbados, this time missing by a mere few thousand miles and ended up in the States, and is yet to find his way back for a fourth attempt. I do know he recently got to Hawaii (warmer but not closer.)

I hope this is of same interest, no doubt others will have other recollections.

Tim Bigden

A WINTER'S TALE (Through the Eye of the Hurricane) - Part 1

Let's have a Winter Series this winter, they all cried together! You could see the tears running down their faces as the enthusiasm drained slowly away into ever shortening days. This was September 1989! Let's have a Winter Series (it is now
September 1990) whispered the valiant few prepared to brave the elements (and who
owned a drysuit!)

Race One. So here we were, a small group of intrepid Catamaran sailors on the first day of the series. Trusty (just let out of clink), Larry as our ever-efficient Race Officer (and general micky-taker). The wind, a mere northerly force 6, was ready to make an entertaining race as the first boats set out on a triangular course between number 2, Fisherman and xX. The two lads in the Dart 15 went first, brave souls! Peter Flook and Larry gave them an encouraging send-off, whilst remaining warmly

wrapped up against the weather and comfortably seated inside Larry's Volvo. A beat
to Fisherman and....They are turing back....It is lmping out _ there....two
down....four to go. The hooter goes for the Prindle 18-2s but Steve Glynn and Tan
Duckmanton are still helping put the two Micks' boat together! Dave Allen and crew are next away in their Hurricane 5.9 (at last the boy has seen sense!) followed by
the Prindles. Three away...one to go. Where is Lee and Jenny? The boat is on the
hard, but they are not to be seen. This is real confidence! Giving everybody such a generous start! At the end of lap oe, it is Steve Glynn with a big lead, followed by Dave Allen (pull the downhaul down!) and then the two Micks. Lee and Jenny decide to join in at this point. They pull past the two Micks, but are a long way behind
Dave.

On the Rescue Boat, Dave Payne has his camera at the ready and each time Steve Glynn passes, he tries to put Tam through the side of the cabin and wipe out the boat. Same people will do anything to have their photo taken! By the end of the second lap Dave was really into Hurricane Sailing, so much so, that he proceeded to demonstrate a pitchpole right in front of the Club! After three laps and an hour of racing, Larry decides to shorten course (I didn't know you could shorten a pursuit race, but the Race Officer knows best.) So it was a win to Steve Glynn in Race One,

Race Two commenced in more reasonable wind on the following Sunday. John Nickalls and Caroline were there to provide the opposition but after a very close race, it was Dave Allen who snook through to take the winning flash (kinky Larry again) from the
Volvo.

Race Three was cold with a light north westerly force 2. Attendance was down to three boats as only the hardy had dragged themselves from the warmth of their beds. Dave Allen had obviously decided to rest on his laurels, John Nickalls was sulking in same far away place (Japan), and Steve Keeble had finally run out of excuses and had came out to play! The two Prindles shot away, with Steve and Tom in the lead. Steve and Dave followed, a mere 3 minutes adrift. By Mark 2, the two Micks had been relegated to third, whilst Steve and Dave had decided to sample the water when Steve forgot to hold onto the mainsheet! The boat remained upright and calm, which is more than could be said for the crew! At the end of lap one it was very close, with Steve and Dave just sneaking through as the boats passed the Club. As the wind eased, they took an unassailable lead, so with three races gone, we had three different winners.

Race 4 took place on the Sunday after the big snow, so only the very brave, or foolhardy, took part. Again the fleet was reduced to just three boats, but Ian Caruth was one of them. Yes folks, big Ian has succumbed to the lure of a large pussy (so that's where the name Pussy Galore came from!) and is now the proud owner of a Prindle 18-2. Accompanied by the amazingly versatile Larry, he joined
Steve Glynn, sans Tam (us inland dwellers were snowed in...well, that's our excuse
for staying in bed) and the still "cold but not beaten" Micks in a pleasant Sunday morning sail. Dave Payne volunteered to be Race Officer. After an hour, with Steve Glynn leading, Dave decided to shorten course (but you can't shorten course on a pursuit race!) The finish line was laid between the Hard and a transit on the other shore (it may have been a Bedford, but who cares!) and just before he got to the line, Steve, sailing solo (but he's got a clean dry suit now!), gybed at, ran parallel down, but 10 yards from, the line from Osea towards the Hard. The two Micks, sailing like men possessed, managed to sneak around the Club comer and beat Steve across the line. Despite Dave giving the finishing signal, the boats chose to continue until the previously allotted finish time, at which point Steve Glynn had a commanding lead. So who actually won? The two Micks of course! The Race Officer is always right, and Steve gave in without a fight!

Race 5 looked like being another frostbiter, so all competitors (3 boats again!) assembled on Sunday morning, suitably attired. Steve Glynn & Tom in matching (but boring) overalls. What, no colour! Steve Keeble, complete with normal bright clothing, plus balaklava and bright yellow MARIGOLDS(!) over his sailing gloves, was doing a close impersonation of one of the seven dwarfs (Dopey? Grumpy? But certainly CMtd..s

1l.

never Bashful!), whilst the two Micks were wearing even less clothing than usual. "I've sold my main wetsuit, so I've got to make do with my second best," stated little (?) Mick. This was the short-sleeved summer one. “Ah well," we replied, "not enough wind to capsize anyway.

The course included Fisherman, which was not obviously visible from the shore; there being a sanewhat smaller buoy in its normal position. Having pointed this out, it was decided to use this as Fisherman was not to be found. Unfortunately, neither Steve Glynn nor "wonderful Larry" were paying attention. Off they went, with Steve & Tam taking the lead. By the first mark, Steve & Dave had already taken a minute off of the lead pair. At the end of the first lap, Steve and Dave were closing rapidly on Steve and Tom, and then Larry intervened! Having agreed the replacement for Fisherman (we thought) before the start, Larry dragged the latter pair back from that mark and made them go around another mark in the moorings! All of the boats had gone into the moorings on the first rounding, but all three had taken a different route, the only common mark being the one in the position of Fisherman! Steve & Dave were now back to where they were positionally at the start. Gradually, they began to close the distance again, especially when the wind eased. At the same mark next time around, they had a port and starboard incident with a fishing boat. They were on starboard and the fishing boat was definitely a lot bigger! Each time the cat pair altered course the fishing boat seemed to alter to maintain a collision course! In the end the Hurricane pair were forced to complete a 360 degree turn to avoid being run down. This left them back where they were at the end of the previous lap. Meanwhile the fishing boat was heading in the direction of Steve & Tam. Would it attempt to run them down. Yes, it started to run up towards. them! Suddenly it turned fully about and started heading back from whence it came! Obviously they had had their fun and more interesting pursuits called.

Meanwhile the gap was closing again. At number 2 the two crews split tacks. Steve and Tom going into the bay, whilst Steve and Dave headed across to Osea.

“They're over!" “Who are?" "The two Micks!"

Yes, the two Micks had decided to practise winter capsize drill in about a force 2. Suddenly Steve & Dave stopped dead, the sails were shaking, the water was going up and down in little points, just as if it was being subjected to a lot of vibration, and the windex was pointing just as it was before the boat stopped! Although the crew were on the wire, the boat made no attempt to capsize and no amount of tiller waggling would induce the boat to move. Steve looked up at the sails and the wind blew directly in his face! Just as suddenly they were sailing again. The whole incident might have lasted 30 seconds, and could oly have been a massive down draught. Maybe that is what caused the capsize? Meanwhile, Larry had rushed to the two Micks' aid in the Orkney, but they had righted the boat and proceeded to sail to the Hard, which was about 50 yards from where they had capsized.

The race finished with a win to Steve Glynn by about 50 yards, but the fun was about to occur. Barry Newboult had made a new Racing Buoy out of polystyrene and string and this had been placed just off the Hard. We were informed that there was no penalty for hitting this mark as it needed testing for survivability. So, having finished the race, Steve Glynn hit it. He aimed for a glancing blow with the outside of the hull, but owing to misjudging the tide he took it slap between the hulls! Larry rushed to his aid in the Orkney, and after 10 minutes of heaving and grunting (good job that there were no ladies on board), they finally freed themselves and brought the buoy ashore. The buoy had came apart slightly, but as a first attempt it was a success. Well done Barry!

So with the "Blue(s) Brothers" safe ashore and warmed up by same hot soup, we all looked forward to the OSEA Icicle!!! Sunday 30th December dawned clear and bright without any sign of the predicted gales and rain. So who was there? The regulars of the two Micks and Steve Glynn & Tom, plus Steve & Dave. Damian & Lucy emerged fran hibernation, whilst Ian Caruth had also come out to play. Lee & Jenny were there

12.

along with Rob & Annette. Lastly, we were treated to the sight of Paul Ellis sailing an 18-2 crewed by the redoubtable Larry! Chris Harrison volunteered to be Race Officer as he didn't know the Py for his jeep! With the lack of suitable marks being available, the course was set around the few remaining moored boats in the river. Dami@én and Lucy were first to go, and were well into the first lap when the Prindle 18-2s started. Ian and Paul were obviously confident as they chose to start with or slightly after the rest of the fleet. That is, with the exception of Rob and Annette, who decided to give everybody a start!

It was as if Damian had never been away! I understand that Damian is in the University 'B' team, so what must the 'A' team be like? (Who said four guys with a van and one all covered with metal work!) The faster boats were struggling to gain distance, whilst Steve Keeble and Lee Harrison were engaged in a two boat race which was probably slowing both of them up. Lee was definitely faster, but Steve was pointing much higher on the beat and gradually opened up a gap. With a lap lasting around 10 minutes, the fast boats had six laps to catch Damian, and on the 5th lap Steve Glynn & Tam overtook and passed Damien at the end of the beat to take an unassailable lead. Damian claimed second spot, with Steve Keeble & Dave Payne in third. What of the rest? Lee & Jenny were fourth. The two Micks were seen to be Sailing up to Goldhanger at one point, and this put them out of contention. Paul and Ian had given everybody too much of a start to be close, but Rob & Annette seemed to be flying as they closed the gap on the leading boats. If only they had started at the right time.

So, a most deserved win in both the Osea Icicle and the Winter Series to Steve Glyn & Ton Duckmanton. Was the Winter Series a success? With an average entry of 5 boats, 13 different crews and no problems, the answer must be yes. Let's hope that we can try again next year and that more crews will take part. It is not often that we get to sail on an empty river.

Thanks must go to all those who participated and helped run the Series, especially to Larry for acting as Race Officer/Rescue Coxswain/Butt of Some Jokes/Teller of Many. Now if only he would buy a real boat!

COMMODORE’ S NOTES

The closed season work to mairitain and improve the facilities cortinues apace. The
dignhy-equipment container is now being occupied, ard Garage 4 has been turned over to the
new Rescue Boat. I am assured that the planned improvements to the downstairs bar arid the
creation of the comfortable area upstairs will be complete by the end of March, ready for
the season.

Some of you may have read in the local paper of a planning application to exterd the
Clubhouse. This is the one which involves extending the main lounge to the South, i.e.
the dinghy park side, that we drew up about a year ago. Whilst this was being processed,
we also looked at the possibility of extending over the Changing Areas. We deliberately
left the original plan to complete the planning process so that we can incorporate any
comments into the alternative design. Both plans have advantages and disadvantages from
the functionality point of view, and one or the other may have a significant cost benefit.
At the present time we have made no firm decision about which we will finally adopt.

This leads conveniently on to the subject of the Discussion Meeting. At the AGM I made,
on behalf of
the Committee, the offer of a General Discussion Meeting in March or April.
The date of this meeting has now been fixed for Friday 1éth April at 7.30 for Bpm, in the
Conference Lounge at the M.A.S.C., Beehive Lane, Chelmsford. The purpose of the Meeting
will be for the Committee to describe its thoughts and plans for the future of the Club.
I hope that you will attend and partake in the discussion so that we can obtain a fair
cross section of the views of the Membership. Obviously, as this is a discussion Meeting,
there cannot be any formal motions, but your views are important to the Committee in
planning the future. I would also ask that we restrict the discussion to the future, and
not get bogged down in any of yesterday’s/today’s problems. If you have any points that
you would like to see raised for discussion, I would be grateful if you would send me a
note before 30th March 1991 to the address below.

Finally, I would urge you to support your Social Committee’s planned quiz right which is
replacing the Fitting Out Party. As you are aware, this has been less well supported in

knowledge. If you carmnot form a team beforehand, come along anyway and link up with

DINGHY FIARK

With Easter upon us it is time to think of opening the dinghy park for the new season. The layout for this year will be similar to last year, but with a few minor charges to ensure that we make the best use of available space. Last year at the peak of the summer (Aug/Sept) about 168 boats were stored in the park. These were made up of:

Mirror 48 Eriterprise 8
Solo 20 GF14 6
Laser 15 Club 4
420 10 Others 47
Wayfarer 10

Of the "Others", no class was represented by more than 5 boats ard most were ones or twos. The Park was very full at the peak, but with good co-operation from members, all the boats were fitted in. This year the plan is for a total of about 180 boats. With so many different classes it would be very extravagant to allocate standard spaces of the same size for all boats. It is clear from previous years that the best use of space is made when boats of the same or similar classes are placed together, ard placed facirg the same way. Examples of this are the Solo and Mirror fleets. This year there will be dedicated blocks in the park for:
