TRANSATLANTIC SUMMER CRUISE - GOSPORT TO NEWFORT

AT LAST YEAR'S AGM/PRIZEGIVING, NEIL PEMBLETON SAID THAT IN THE PAST THERE HAD BEEN
OCCASIONAL APPEARANCES IN NAVIGANS OF LOGS WRITTEN BY DINGHY SAILORS, AND THAT SOME
OF THESE HAD BEEN WELL RECEIVED. THEREFORE, I THOUGHT I MIGHT WRITE UP MY EXPERIENCE
OF THE LAST CRUISE THAT I DID BEFORE BECOMING A MEMBER OF THE CLUB’S CAT FLEET.

THE ROUTE WAS FROM GOSPORT TO NEWPORT, RHODE ISLAND, ALTHOUGH THE EXACT DESTINATION
WAS NOT DECIDED UNTIL WE WERE MOST OF THE WAY THERE. THE BOAT WAS CALLED
*NORVANTES', A 47’ SLOOF AND ONE OF THE LAST WOODEN BOATS BUILT BY CAMPER &
NICHOLSON. SHE WAS BUILT AS AN ADMIRAL’S CUP BOAT AND HAD SOME SUCCESS UNDER THE
NAME OF ‘CERVANTES’, BUT IS NOW ONLY USED FOR CRUISING. THE CREW OF SIX WERE A
COMPLETE MIXTURE OF NATIONALITIES AND OCCUPATIONS - PETER JAY (THE SKIPPER) AND JIM
FORMED ONE WATCH; MICHELE AND NELSON (HONESTLY!) WERE ANOTHER, LEAVING JOHN AND
MYSELF. OUR SAILING EXPERIENCE WAS EQUALLY VARIED, WITH MY TWO TALL SHIPS RACES AND
20-ODD CHANNEL CROSSINGS BEING ABOUT AVERAGE. ABOUT THE ONLY THING WE HAD IN COMMON
WAS THAT WE HADN’T DONE THE TRIP BEFORE. I SHOULD SAY THAT WE HAD DONE A SHAKEDOWN
TRIP TO IRELAND AT EASTER TO GET USED TO THE BOAT AND EACH OTHER.

SO WE SET OFF AT NOON ON DAY 1, A FINE JUNE DAY. WE WERE LESS APPREHENSIVE THAN THE
PEOPLE WHO WAVED US OFF, JUDGING BY THEIR FACES. WE HAD A GREAT SAIL OUT TO THE
NEEDLES - FORCE 4, LOTS OF SPRAY AND SUN. THE BOAT FELT VERY SAFE AND STEADY, IT
MUST HAVE BEEN ALL THOSE TINS. IF IT'S ALL LIKE THIS IT WILL BE A DODDLE. BUT, BY
THE EVENING, THE WIND HAD DROPPED AND WE WERE IN FOG. I SPENT SOME TIME LISTENING TO
TELEPHONE CALLS BEING MADE FROM THE GE2 AS SHE RETURNED TO SOUTHAMPTON, HIGHLY
AMUSING BUT FROBABLY ILLEGAL.

DAY 2. WE STARTED WATCHES AT MIDNIGHT AND JOHN AND I WERE FIRST ON, (WE KEPT UF 3-
HOUR WATCHES FOR THE WHOLE TRIF, (UNLESS IT WAS A NEW TIME ZONE WHEN THE UNFORTUNATE
FAIR HAD TO DO 4 HOURS). STILL FOGSY, PASSED CLOSE TO A SHIP THAT WE DIDN’T SEE OR
HEAR, BUT ITS WAKE WAS ALL TOO OBVIOUS. FIRST WASH IN SEAWATER - CONCLUDED THAT
*SEAWATER SOAF? WORKS NO BETTER THAN ORDINARY SOAF. WE HAD FITTED 2 EXTRA FLASTIC
WATER TANKS FOR THE TRIF, BUT FRESH WATER WAS ONLY USED FOR COOKING AND DRINKING.

DAY 3. SPOTTED THE FIRST SHARK A LOT EARLIER THAN EXPECTED, AND HAD QUR LAST SIGHT
OF LAND. NAVIGATION WAS TO BE BY DEAD RECKONING AND SEXTANT - PETER COULD DO SUN
SIGHTS AND STAR SIGHTS AND I WAS THE BACKUP WITH NOON SIGHTS ONLY.

DAY 4. A VERY ORDINARY DAY, EVERYONE NOW SETTLED INTO THE WATCH ROUTINE, (I.E.
PERMANENTLY TIRED). I STARTED BAKING BREAD WHEN THE OVEN WAS IN USE FOR SOMETHING
ELSE, AND STARTED READING *SURVIVE THE SAVAGE SEA’ (TRUE STORY OF A FAMILY’S SURVIVAL
FOR 38 DAYS IN A LIFERAFT) MUCH TO EVERYONE'S AMUSEMENT,

DAY 5. THE WIND GRADUALLY INCREASED TO 20 KNOTS DURING THE MIDNIGHT TO 3am WATCH,
BUT WE HELD ON UNTIL PETER AND JIM CAME ON SO THAT WE COULD CHANGE THE GENOA WITH 4
PEOPLE ON DECK. SAILED THROUGH A FLEET OF RUSSIAN STERN TRAWLERS LATER ON IN THE
MORNING. ONE CALLED US ON THE RADIO, IN VERY GOOD ENGLISH, AND GAVE US OUR LAST
POSITION CHECK. THEY ARE AT SEA FOR 6&6 MONTHS AND WERE VERY JEALOUS OF US. LATER ON
WE WERE ALL STARTLED RY A LOUD HANG, THE SORT OF *CRUMP’ NOISE THAT BIG GUNS MAKE.
IT WASN’T THE RIGHT NOISE FOR SOMETHING ON THE MAST BREAKING, BUT WE ALL WORRIED
ABOUT IT UNTIL SOMEONE REALISED THAT IT WAS PROBABLY JUST THE SONIC BOOM FROM
CONCORDE. WE WERE CERTAINLY UNDER AN AIR CORRIDOR, JUDGING BY THE VAFOUR TRAILS.

DAY 6. 3-6am WATCH. QUITE A BIT OF WIND NOW, WE PUT 3 ROLLS IN THE MAINSAIL AND
CHANGED TO THE STORM JIB AFTER A SMALL TEAR DEVELOFED IN THE NO.3 GENOA. I GOT VERY
WET DOING THIS INCLUDING A BOOTFUL OF WATER (WHICH STAYED WET FOR THE NEXT 3 DAYS).
BY THE MORNING THERE WAS A FAIR BIT OF CHADS RELOW WITH SAILING GEAR AND MASTERMIND
PEGS ALL OVER THE FLOOR, AND THE HEADS DOOR FLAPFING ON ONE HINGE. A COUFLE OF
PEOPLE WERE FEELING SICK FOR THE FIRST TIME, SO WE MOVED THE HAM AND THE FISH (SALT
COD) TO AN OUTSIDE LOCKER. I DID THE 12 - 3 WATCH ON MY OWN WHILE JOHN MENDED THE
TEAR IN THE NO.3. I THINK I HAD THE BEST OF THE DEAL BUT 3 HOURS WAS THE MOST I
COULD HAVE MANAGED AT THE WHEEL IN THAT SEA WITH THE WIND ON THE NOSE,

DAY 7. MORE OF THE SAME, WIND NOW 28 KNOTS. MICHELE RIGGED UP A LINE WHICH ENABLED
US TO FULL DOWN THE FORESAIL FROM THE FOOT OF THE MAST, AND HENCE SFEND LESS TIME
GETTING SOAKED ON THE FOREDECK. WE HAVE ALL NOW GOT USED TO CHANGING SAILS WITH JUST
& PEOPLE. HIGHLIGHT OF THE DAY WAS SEEING A STORMY PETREL, A TINY BIRD THAT FLIES A
BIT LIKE A BAT AND OCCASIONALLY FPATTERS ITS FEET ON THE WAVES WHILE FLYING. i ARE
SUPPOSEDLY AN INDICATION OF STORMS - A BIT LATE INA THIS CASE.

8,

DAY 8. WIND GRADUALLY LESSENED THROUGHOUT THE DAY. ENOUGH SUN FOR A SUNSIGHT, BUT
NOT ENOUGH TO DRY OUR GEAR. ENOUGH WATER UNDER US TO COVER MT. BLANC. LOTS OF
PETRELS AND POSSIBLY SHEARWATERS FLYING ABOUT.

DAY 9. THE LONGEST DAY OF THE YEAR, STARTING TO GET LIGHT AT 3am. GOOD DRYING AND
SAILING WEATHER AT LAST. SAW TWO RAINBOWS IN THE SKY, NOT INSIDE EACH OTHER, BUT
SEPARATE, AND WITH RED ON THE INSIDE OF ONE AND ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE OTHER - OR WAS
I SEEING THINGS? A S’ TEAR APPEARED IN THE NO.1 GENOA AND A REPAIR WOULD HAVE USED
UF THE BULK OF THE HEAVY SAILCLOTH, SO WE SWAPPED IT WITH THE SPARE NO.1 AT THE
BOTTOM OF THE SAIL LOCKER. AT THE SAME TIME WE ALSO NOTICED THAT TWO STANCHIONS HAD
BEEN BENT OUTWARDS. THE REASON FOR THIS, AND THE CAUSE OF THE SAIL DAMAGE, WAS THAT
ALL THE HEADSAILS WERE CUT FOR RACING IN THE CHANNEL AND NOT PASSAGE-MAKING IN
ATLANTIC STORMS. THEY ALL NEEDED A COUPLE OF FEET TAKEN OFF THE FOOT SO THAT THE
BULK OF THE WAVES COMING OVER THE FOREDECK WOULD PASS UNDERNEATH WITHOUT HITTING THE
SAILCLOTH.

DAY 10. MORE WIND AND WAVES. WE HAVE NOW GOT INTO A ROUTINE OF ONLY EATING TWO
MEA LS A DAY - A LARGE BREAKFAST AROUND 10-11am AND THEN DINNER AROUND 6-7pm. THIS
SAVED GAS AND SLEEFING TIME FOR THOSE OFF-WATCH, AND WE KEFT IT UF FOR MOST OF THE
TRIF. AROUND THIS TIME I DISCOVERED THAT SOMEONE WAS EATING MOST OF THE CHOCOLAGTE -
ME! I WAS AVERAGING ABOUT 3 MARS BARS A DAY, AND A BIG BAR OF FRUIT AND NUT MOST
NIGHTS. (THE TALE ABOUT CHOCOLATE GIVING YOU SPOTS IS OBVIOUSLY UNTRUE AS I KEPT
THIS UP FOR ABOUT 3 WEEKS WITH NO SIGN OF ANY). NORODY ELSE SEEMED TO MIND, AS LONG
AS I PROMISED TO KEEP ON MAKING THE BREAD.

DAY 11. WIND GUSTING TQ 35 KNOTS AND THE WAVES ARE ABOUT HALF THE HEIGHT OF THE
MAST FROM TROUGH TO PEAK. THAT SOUNDS A LOT, BUT THEY WERE WIDELY SPACED AND NOT TOO
STEEP. ALSO THE HELM WAS MUCH EASIER NOW AS WE WERE ON A REACH WITH THE NO.4 GENQA
UF.

DAY 12. NOW DOING S-HOUR WATCHES TO COVER FOR MICHELE WHO IS VERY SEA-SICK AND
STAYS IN HIS BUNK. EVERYONE WAS FEELING COLD, EVEN JIM, WHO HAD STARTED TO WEAR HIS
SKY-DIVING SUIT.

DAY 13. STORM JIB AND S ROLLS IN THE MAIN. THE ONLY GOOD NEWS WAS PETER ANNOUNCING
THAT WE HAD CROSSED THE 30°W PARALLEL - 40° TO GO.

DAY 14. AT LAST THE WIND HAD DROFFED AND WE WERE BACK TO NORMAL SIZED SAILS. IT
WAS RAINING HEAVILY THOUGH, AND I DID MOST OF MY WATCH FACING THE STERN AND HOLDING
THE WHEEL FROM THE WRONG SIDE TO KEEF THE RAIN OUT OF MY FACE, BUT BY THE AFTERNOON
THE SUN WAS OUT AND WE ALL SPREAD OUT OUR CLOTHES TO DRY.

DAY 15. ANOTHER FAST CHANGE IN WEATHER CONDITIONS - THE WIND PICKED UF QUICKLY AND
WE WERE MAKING 7 KNOTS WITH NO MAINSAIL AND JUST THE NQ.3 GENOA. JOHN AND I HAD A
BAD WATCH; HE DROPPED A WINCH HANDLE OVER THE SIDE AND I BLEW THE CLEW RIGHT OUT OF
THE GENOA. BY THE TIME WE HAD STRUGGLED TO GET IT DOWN AND THE STORM JIB UP, THE
WIND WAS A CONSTANT 38 KNOTS WITH GUSTS OF UF TO 45, (IT’S TRUE WHAT THE BOOKS SAY -
THE TOPS OF THE WAVES REALLY DO START TO FOAM AT THIS STAGE).

DAY 16. A BETTER MORNING AT LAST, BRIGHT SKY AND GETTING WARMER, THE MAINSAIL NOW
MENDED AND HOISTED. HAD A HUGE BREAKFAST (AS NOBODY HAD EATEN MUCH THE DAY BEFORE),
WASHED DOWN WITH A COUPLE OF BOTTLES OF CHAMPAGNE TO CELEBRATE THE END OF ANOTHER
STORM AND BEING PAST THE HALFWAY MARK. I REALLY ENJOYED JUST SITTING IN THE SUN AND
DRYING MY FEET OUT. LATER WE MOTORED FOR THE FIRST TIME AS THE BATTERIES NEEDED
CHARGING AND THERE WAS ALMOST NO WIND. WHILE WE WERE DOING THIS, NELSON SPOTTED A
WHALE, WE ONLY SAW A SFOUT OF WATER AND THEN ITS TAIL, THEN IT WAS GONE. THAT
EVENING WE USED THE AUTOPILOT FOR THE FIRST TIME SO THAT WE COULD ALL EAT TOGETHER
FOR A CHANGE. THE BEST DAY OF THE TRIP SO FAR.

DAY 17. A QUIET DAY DRIFTING ALONG WITH THE SPINNAKER UF FOR THE FIRST TIME. THE
ONLY EXCITEMENT OF THE DAY WAS SEEING A SHIF ON THE HORIZON, CALLING HER UF, AND
FINDING OUT IT WAS THE GEe. THEY ALTERED COURSE SO THAT WE COULD TALK TQ THEM FOR
LONGER - THIS SOUNDED ODD UNTIL THEY EXPLAINED THAT THEY WERE DOING 28 KNOTS. THE
RADIO OPERATOR WAS VERY CHATTY (BORED, I THINK) AND HELFED US WITH A WEATHER
FORECAST, TIME CHECK AND FOSITION,

DAYS 18-20. FIRST SUNBATHING WEATHER. LOTS OF DOLPHINS IN THE WATER, BUT DIDN'T
JOIN THEM. STEADY PROGRESS IN 15 KNOT WIND, AND A FEW MORE SHIFS ON THE HORIZON.

9.

DAY ei. AS WE APPROACHED THE GRAND BANKS OFF NEWFOUNDLAND IT SLOWLY GOT MORE AND
MORE FOGGY. A 25,000 TON FREIGHTER CAME WITHIN A MILE OF US BUT HE SAID THAT HE'D
SEEN US ON RADAR S MILES AWAY. HE TOLD US WE WERE JUST INSIDE THE MAXIMUM LIMIT FOR
ICEBERGS. BECAUSE OF THIS AND THE DENSE FOG, WE STARTED FOUR AND A HALF HOUR WATCHES
OF THREE PEOPLE IN ORDER TO KEEF A GOOD LOOKOUT. WE WERE ALL VERY COLD. I HAD ICE
FORMING IN MY BEARD AND THE PAIR OF NEOPRENE MITTENS HAD BECOME THE MOST PRECIOUS
ITEM ON BOARD.

DAY 22. A DUTCH CONTAINER SHIP REPLIED TO ONE OF OUR REGULAR FOSITION BROADCASTS
SAYING THAT HE HAD BEEN ON A CONVERGING COURSE BUT HAD SEEN US ON RADAR. WE ALSO HAD
ANOTHER QUICK TALK WITH THE GE2 AS THEY CAME FAST US AGAIN. THEY SAID THAT WE WOULD
BE OUT OF THE FOG IN 60 MILES AND THE ICE LIMIT IN 100 MILES.

DAY 23. THE SEA WAS NOW GREEN INSTEAD OF BLUE AND ABOUT 20 DOLPHINS WERE FLAYING
AROUND THE BOW. IN JIM’S HONOUR WE CELEBRATE YESTERDAY BEING THE 4TH OF JULY.

DAY 24-25. SUN AT LAST, AND WITH THE SPINNAKER UP, THE BOAT WAS FAIRLY STABLE, SO I
WENT UF THE MAST TO CHANGE A HALYARD AND TAKE SOME PICTURES.

DAY 26. NOW ABQUT 100 MILES SOUTH OF SABLE ISLAND - THE MOST INFAMOUS WRECKING
PLACE IN THE NORTHERN HEMISPHERE ACCORDING TO THE PILOT. A LOOK AT THE CHART
CONFIRMED THIS; THE ISLAND 1S SURROUNDED KY A DENSE LINE OF WRECKS AND A NOTE SAYING
THAT THERE ARE TOO MANY TO POSITION ACCURATELY!

DAY 27. AFTER ANOTHER RAF ID WEATHER CHANGE IT WAS NOW VERY WARM AND WE WERE ALL
SLEEPING OUTSIDE OQUR SLEEPING BAGS. A PLEASANT DAY COASTING SOUTH AT 7 KNOTS UNTIL
WE CALLED COASTGUARD RADIO HALIFAX (NOVA SCOTIA), WHO ADVISED US THAT WE WOULD SOON
GET MORE FOG, THEN VERY STRONG WIND FROM A LOW THAT WE SHOULD AVOID IF FOSSIBLE.

DAY 28-29. THEY WERE RIGHT OF COURSE, THE FOG ARIVED. THE WIND DROFFED AND WE
STOPFED MOVING COMPLETELY FOR A FEW HOURS. SAW A PLASTIC CUF AND SOME MATCHES, THE
FIRST SUCH DEBRIS FOR 3 WEEKS. WE MOTORED OUT OF THE CALM IN THE END,

DAY 30. ONLY A COUPLE OF HUNDRED MILES TO GO BUT IT WASN'T ALL OVER YET. THE FIRST
SURPRISE WAS A ROGUE WAVE. NELSON WAS AT THE WHEEL WITHOUT OILSKINS AS THERE WAS
ONLY ABOUT 10 KNOTS OF WIND, WHEN HE SUDDENLY YELLED SOMETHING, SPUN THE WHEEL, AND
GOT FLATTENED BY A WAVE WHICH COVERED THE BOAT FROM THE BOW TO THE COCKFIT. NONE OF
US HAD EVER EXPERIENCED ANYTHING LIKE IT. SOON AFTER THAT THE SEA STARTED TO GET
LUMFY, THE BAROMETER FELL, AND THE SKY WENT BLACK, WITH THE ODD FLASH OF LIGHTNING.
WE REDUCED SAIL AS FAST AS THE WIND CAME UF, STOPPING ONLY TO WATCH A BUTTERFLY GO
PAST AND SOON WE WERE BEING THROWN AROUND AGAIN.

DAY 31. SHAKEN EARLY TO HEAR THAT 3 PEOPLE ARE SICK AND A JUMPER STAY HAS FARTED IN
THE NIGHT. THE LOW MUST HAVE PASSED RIGHT OVER US, AS WITHIN A COUPLE OF HOURS THE
WIND WAS BLOWING EQUALLY STRONGLY BUT FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION. THIS WAS VERY
DISCONCERTING BECAUSE, WITH NO SUN OR LAND AS A REFERENCE IT SEEMED AS IF WE HAD
TURNED ROUND AND WERE SAILING THE WRONG WAY. OF COURSE THE COMPASS WAS THE THING TO
CONCENTRATE ON. EQUALLY STRANGE WAS A FISHING BOQAT THAT WALLOWED ACROSS OUR BOWS -
THERE WAS NOBODY ON DECK OR IN THE WHEELHOUSE, AND IT HAD A SMALL HELICOPTER LASHED
TO THE CARIN ROOF. IT'S ONE OF MY LASTING MEMORIES OF THE WHOLE TRIP.

DAY 32. WOKEN BY CRIES OF LAND AHEAD, AND SURE ENOUGH, AFTER 3600 MILES, THERE IT
WAS. ALMOST AS APPEALING WAS THE SIGHT OF JIM USING ALL THE REMAINING EGGS THAT
HADN’T GONE BAD TO MAKE TWO HUGE OMELETTES. WE SEEMED TO BE IN IN NO TIME, THE ONLY
PROBLEM WAS DECIDING WHICH TO HAVE FIRST - A SHOWER OR A STEAK. AFTER SAVOURING
BOTH, WE HAD ONE LAST SURPRISE - NONE OF US COULD RUN ON DRY LAND - IT WAS NO PROBLEM
ON THE FOREDECK, EVEN IF IT SEEMED MOTIONLESS, BUT ON SOLID EARTH IT WAS JUST
IMPOSSIBLE.

AFTER A DAY SORTING THE BOAT OUT WE ALL WENT OUR SEPARATE WAYS. I WAS SAD TO LEAVE
THE OTHERS (AND THE BOAT, AS IT WAS DESTINED FOR THE CARRIBEAN) BUT TIME WAS RUNNING
OUT AND I HADN’T SEEN ANYTHING OF AMERICA YET.

FAUL METCALFE

NAVIGANS PAST 10,

1959 - cursethe cat, stub your toes, and throw themover the side.

January - not a lot in this January issue. The Editor (W.J.Hodge), who also happens to be the Hon.
Secretary, asks that one and all should at least aim to keep one new year's resolution and send their subscriptions to the Hon.Treasurer as soon as possible. And who is the Hon.Treasurer yes, you've
guessed it.... poor Mr.W.J.Hodge. No wonder he gets a bit fed up with those members who keep their
wallets well and truly glued down.

February - the report on the National Boat Show states "a Cat craze had swept the industry" - and to
think I thought it had all happened within the last year or two. It seems that Sheerwaters and Swifts are the ‘in thing’ Cat-wise .

The Financial Accounts record that the hiring out of Avril brought in £11. 8s. Od for the year and, of course, Mr. Hodge again complains of the members' tardy response to the call to 'pay your subs pronto' (or words to that effect). It seems that Subscriptions brought in £25 during the year compared to £75. Os. 6d for the Laying Up Supper. It is clear the ‘members’ interests lie very firmly within their stomaches rather than within their conscience. ‘Potential Membership ' is, we are told, now 110 (ie. if they all paid up).

March - an article giving advice to those contemplating buying their first boat. The new ‘Enterprise’
is recommended for those who want to trail their racing dinghy on holiday (clearly the age of the semi- professional ‘circuit goer' has not yet arrived) whilst the Silhouette or Ballerina is recommended for the would-be cruiser owner of limited means (presumably meaning ‘financially limited' but, bearing in mind the oft-quoted image of owners standing under icy cold showers tearing up £50 notes**, the writer might have had something else in mind). The poor old Catamaran comes in for a bit of stick. "These are very fast (on certain points of sailing) and expensive. Thiswinter there seems to be more Sheerwaters on the second- hand market thanany
other 0.0. and they are all fairly cheap." Well, that's not too bad surely...but now
comes the cruncher....."they do not seem a very good buy". I bet that was written by a cruiser man.

April - A list of "Officers of the Day" and “Time Keepers" is published for the year and, would you
believe it, our Editor/Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas Mr.W.J.Hodge has been landed with not one, not two but THREE such duties. They really do put upon him but, as they say, one willing volunteer is better than 10 pressed
MEN..e

An article 'The art of Sailing' states " bare feet will usually provide the surest grip on deck and floor- boards". He must be joking ! That might have been OK in Nelson's day but, in my brief experiment with "bare-foot boating',
it usually provided stubbed toes, foul language and a distinct lack of concentration.

May - apparently the Fitting Out Supper held on board MAMGU during April was judged very successful both
financially and socially but, there is a sting in the tail (or should it be tale ?). I quote "Mamgu is now
well established as a centre for week-end activity - the general disorder and unhygenic conditions prove
the point". I think someone's trying to tell us something but I suspect the message was about as successful as the Keep Britain Tidy campaign.

The first of many articles by 'Barnacle' appears in Navigans. No doubt Barnacle, like Alistair Cook and his Letter from America, only expected to write a half-dozen (NB. this is the pre-metric age) articles but went on to produce a monthly article for many years. Now, I wonder who ‘Barnacle’ was ?

dune - the Editor (Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas/0,0./Time Keeper) again draws attention to the disorder and lack of
cleanliness on board Mamgu. It seems that if things don't improve, they might have to identify the
culprits and withdraw their keys - now that sounds very painful and that only for the lst offence.
At least with Mamgu, a whole host of possible sanctions could be applied. How about keel-hauling, walking the gangplank (with parasoles) or, when all patience and temper has been exhausted, pitch the untidy so- and-soes over the side (without parasoles).

July - clearly things are not satisfactory as far as OOD and Time Keeping duties are concerned and}I now
quote "Surely it's not much to ask members that they devote just a few hours of their time once during the course of the season in return for all the benefits provided by the club." Alas, not all members see it that way, either then or now but thankfully the present-day MSC has a pretty good bunch of enthusiasts able and willing to get things done. Come to think of it, they must have had a pretty good bunch of
enthusiasts in 1959 as well - after all, our present-day club is evidence of it.

A notice requests "..all members must identify and remove old clothing,etc....". OK for dinghy sailors
who usually change for sailing - but those cruiser chappies, why they seem to wear their old clothes
the whole time. Watch this space for further startling revelations. Actually, the notice asked that the clothing be removed "from Mamgu" and not bodies

** at one time it was £5 notes. Then is was £10 notes. Alas, the effects of inflation are felt everywhere. even in the metaphorical shower.

August - sound advice for the cruiser man - but equally appropriate to the dinghy helmsman. The
advice suggests that whilst rowing out to a mooring, the passenger should "press their hands together,
as if in prayer, and point the best direction to go". I know the feeling - and don't we all ? It
is usually accompanied by “for ---'s sake get that spinnaker up" or " quick, get out on the wire", or "“quick,come in off the wire", or "set the -------------- jib" or Yes, there are times when the power of prayer might seemingly be more effective. So don't forget you cruiser folks, in 1991
I shall be watching to see how many of your passengers are seemingly praying - and pointing back to the
clubhouse as the best direction to go.

September - a familiar lament. A notice asks "The last year has seen a big increase in the number of
larger boats and the family-type boat. Are we doing all we can to introduce youngsters to the pleasures of racing dinghy sailing ?".

October - the announcement of the forthcoming 1959 AGM makes it plain that Mr.Hodge will not be standing
for re-election as Hon.Sec/Hon.Treasurer - but will he continue as Editor ?

A charge of 5/- was made for use of the dinghy park during the year (they're a trusting lot, collecting the fees after the event) and, for those members who have obviously complained about exorbitant charges,‘it is pointed out this is approximately ld (one old penny) per week, and that it costs 10/- to moor on the
river. Ah ! The golden age when the air was pure and free - and the water very nearly so.

The season's sailing results reveal (1) that the sailing program was considerably less than it is now and
(2) P.Harris seemed to win most of the races. I also wondered why the Ladies Trophy didn't have a winning
name inscibed on it for 1959, its' second year of competition. I feared it had been due to lack of interest but it appears that it was cancelled due to bad weather.

November - my conclusions from the sailing results werecorrect. This month's leader comments on the
Laying Up Dinner/Dance and associated prize giving and states "If there was any boredom at all, it arose from the monotonous recital of events won by Peter Harris. Surely there is someone in the club capable of offering him competition ?".

Barnacle offers some advice on buying a cruiser ".......take the owner's judgement (on the excellence of
his craft) with a pinch of salt. It may be well to remember............they don't realise their boat
is just about everything that a cruiser should not be". Well, what would you expect ? If the average cruiser owner spends 80% of his leisure time scraping the bottom of his favourite possession, he's not likely to see anything but perfection.

December - W.J.Hodge took his farewell, not only from the duties of Hon.Secretary and Hon.Treasurer but
also those of Editor. At this distance in time, I say "Well done Mr.Hddge and thank you. If you'd given up the struggle to establish Navigans, our club today would be the worse for it".

In his report to the 1959 AGM Mr.Hodgewas able to list improvements achieved for Mamgu in 1959, such as electricity and water supply, furniture and "following a rather unfortunate mishap when one member, attempting to board Mamgu from a temporary structure, was unceremoniously ducked into the water,

a permanent access gangway was hastily erected". What I want to know is ‘was the member drunk or was he not ?! Anyway, they'd still better watch their step in 1960 'cos 'a hastily erected' gangway still sounds a bit risky to me.

Finally, Mr.Hodge returns to his favourite ssubject - who ain't a-payin' of their subs ? He reports
"Payment of subscriptions is still far from complete and quite frankly, we are worried".

Money, money, money - always worrying about money. Nothing changes. Happy retirement Mr.Hodge.

EXTRACTS FROM THE CONSTITUTION AND BY-LAWS.

GENERAL.

i. Officer of the Day.

An Officer of the Day shall be appointed on all appropiate occasions, and will act as the executive officer of the committee in
all matters relating to the conduct and welfare of members and the club during his period of office. In the absence of an
appointed Officer of the Day, any committee member at the club may assume the responsibility.

2. Insurance.

ALL boats brought to or sailed from the club shall be adequately insured against third party risks. All vehicles driven on club
premises shall be adequately insured against third party risks. The M.S.C. and M.A.S.C. will not be Liable for any form of
claim. (Rule 21).

3s Losses.

The club shall not be held responsible for any loss or damage sustained by a member or his visitor. (Rule 15).

4. Visitors.

ALl members except Temporary members shall have the privilege of introducing not more than three adult guests to the club at any

one time. The name(s) of the guest(s) and that of the introducing member shall be written in the Visitors Book.

SAILING.

I Identif ication.

All boats and covers must be named or numbered for easy identification.

2. Berths.

(a) No boat shall be brought to the club before registration and payment of the appropiate fees.
(b) Boats should only be left in their allocated boat park space as shown on the club notice board, or as notified by a club
officer.

(c) Any member contemplating acquiring a cruiser and wanting a mooring et Stensgate must first apply to the Moor ings
Secretary to determine if a mooring is available. Moorings will only be allocated to boats for which all relevant fees
have been paid. Purchase of a cruiser on an existing mooring does not entitle the new member to a mooring.

(d) Any member with a mooring at the club, contemplating changing his cruiser, must apply in writing to the Moorings
Secretary for approval before bringing the new cruiser to the club.
(e) Moorings shall be accurately positioned and laid down as directed by the Moorings Secretary, or Mooring Team Leader.
(f) ALL maldon District Council mooring fees shall be paid via the club.

SF Buoyancy and Sefety.

(e) ALL dinghies used from the club shall be fittef with bouyancy to Class Rules, or eas the Committee May reasonably
require. (Rule 25.1).

(b) Members and their guests using dinghies from the club should wear personal bouyancy at all times when the red flag is
flying. At all other, times personal bouyancy should be carried aboard all boats and wearing of this bouyancy shall be
the personal decision of the individual. (Rule 25.2).

In addition to (b), under 18 year olds using dinghies from the club shall at ell times wear personal bouyancy, except
with the permission of the parent or guardian who shall be responsible for any consequences. (Rule 25.3).
(d) Members, their families and guests are responsible for their personal safety and the M.S.C., the committee and the
M.A.S.C. cannot be held responsible for the actions of an individual. Advice given by any official of the club is of an

advisory narure only. (Rule 24).
(e) Parents and Guardians are warned that the club is only able to provide rescue facilities during the hours of club
racing. Outside these hours, Parents and Guardians have the sole responsibility for their children and wards end must
appreciate that the club cannot be expected to exercise control and supervision. Even during club racing the club

cannot accept responsibility for any person.
(f) Code Flags flown from the Clubhouse will indicate the following to members:

Flag N (Blue and White check): ALL club sailing abandoned. We advise no sailing at all.

Answering Pennant (Red and White): All club sailing postponed. We advise no sailing at present.

Flag L (Black and Yellow squares): We reccomend sailing only within sight of the Clubhouse.

Flag B (Red): Personal Bouyancy should be worn - see (b) above.

4, Speed Boats and Motor Boats.

No speed boats may be brought to the Club or operated from the shore. Motor Boats are only permitted by extraordinary

permission of the committee in writing.

5: Club Boats.

(a) Use of the club rescue boats and work boats is limited to persons authorised by the 0.0.D. except in emergency.
(b) The club sailing dighies may be borrowed at the discretion of the 0.0.D. or Bosun. Brazil may also be use by club
members at any time, provided that details are recorded in the log book and that other members are present on the shore

who are competent to act in an emergency. Instructions on the use of these boats are included in the log book.

(c) Personal bouyancy must be worn at all times when sailing club dinghies. These boats may be used for racing. Preference

will be given to Cadets.

6. Sailing Accidents.

It is the responsibility of helmspersons sailing from Marconi Sailing Club to ensure a responsible person is informed of any

collision with other boat(s) whether damage is apparent or not. To enable club control all helmspersons are rquired to inform
the Officer of the Day of the name or sail number of any boat with which they collide and brief details of known damage. If the

incident should take place when there is no Officer of the Day at the Club, it is the helms person’s responsibility to contact an
officer of the club and provide the name or sail number of any boat with which they collide and brief details of known damage.

In all cases, it is also the same helms person’s responsibility to contact the owner of any unmanned boat(s) as soon as is
reasonably practicable but no later than 21 days after the incident.

This byelaw will not apply to boat(s) racing from the Marconi Sailing Club when all the boat(s) involved in the incident are
also racing from the Marconi Sailing Club.

CLUBHOUSE AND PRECINCTS.

sy Hours of Opening.

The clubhouse shall be open to members subject to such Limitations as are imposed from time to time by the committee. With NO
EXCEPTION the last member to leave the site is responsible for closing of all windows, locking doors and turning off the
electricity.

Animals.

No animals shall be allowed in the clubhouse, or to run free on the site.

3. Car Parking.

ALL cars shall be parked in the allocated space. Parking on the hard, adjacent to the clubhouse and the boat park is forbidden.

4. Club Premises.

It is the responsibility of ALL members to:

(a) Help with general maintenance.
(b) Keep the saloon and changing rooms clean and tidy.
(c) Keep the Galley tidy, and wash and replace any crockery used.

(d) Report all instances of damage to club property to the 0.0.D., Clubhouse Secretary, or record it in the logbook.

5. Use of Galley.

The Galley, when not manned, may be used by individuals, for the preparation of hot drinks. Preparation of hot meals is not

permitted unless authorised by the 0.0.D..

6. CAMPING

(a) Camping shall be restricted to members and their Guests, except that it shall be open to members of R.Y.A. clubs
attending open race meetings at the Club. Camping shall only be permitted at times decided by the Committee. Before

establishing camp, members shall report to the camping marshall or the 0.0.D., to pay the appropiate fee and receive any
instructions on siting.
(b) No tent or caravan is to be on the site prior to 0830 hrs on the first day of camping and all tents and caravans must be

removed before 2100 hrs on the last day of camping.

ran Gate to the Site.

The gate to the site shall be kept locked at all times other than Open Events. Any member unlocking the gate is responsible for

ensuring that it is relocked. Keys must not be lent to non members.

8. Dinghy/Catamaran and Cruiser Parks.

(a) No motor vehicle shall be brought onto thses areas except for the purposes fo unloading etc..
(b) ALL dinghies and catamarans shall be securely tied down with no projections above ground level.
Members shall keep their allocated boat park space tidy and the grass cut.
(d) Winter storage: Dinghies left at the club over the winter shall be securely tied down with the mast removed.

9 Winter Storage,

(a) Only those boasts for which a Winter Storage fee has been paid may be left on the site between ist December and ist
March. All such boats are to be visiblably marked with the Class of boat, Name and Telephone number of the owner.
(b) The owner of any boat left on the site between the above dates for which Storage Fee has not been paid will be subject
to a fine not exceeding twice the Storage Fee which would have been payable.

PLEASE sign on (print preferably) with your full name (eg. Alay Mindbender) - its much nicer to be
able to refer to people by their first name rather than as A.Mindbender, etc.

PLEASE ensure that both helm and crew sign on in full - you might know who FREDA is but I've probably
never met him. Anyway, Crews earn points towards their own Points Series prize independently of the helm, and just because the helm has won a prize, it doesn't mean his/her crew also gets a prize automatically.

PLEASE ensure you SIGN OFF when you have finished racing. Either you have FINISHED or you have RETIRED. If you do not sign off, you are automatically disqualified (which is a pity if you won the race).

If you retire early from the race, please ensure you (a) tell the race officer before you go home or go off for your pleasure sail; if not, we may have the coastguard out looking for you 'cos we don't know where you are and (b) SIGN OFF (if a Signing Off sheet has not been put out already, get one out of the folder yourself).

Hello, playmates! Here we are (well, we will be by the time you read this) under full steam again with the New Season.

First, may I apologise if I repeat anything from the April issue. Having just moved house, that one has yet to catch up with me.

I must admit that this is the first year in my sailing career that I’ve only had a
lay off from 31 December to 10 March - yes, a number of nutters from the Cat Fleet
couldn’t wait (i.e. Dave & Anna; Steve & Tom; The Two Micks; Mick Jones & Don; Tan &
Steve Caruth; and Yours Truly - ably assisted by the redoubtable Chris Caruth) and

8.

had a Very Nice Sail on 10th. On 17th the numbers were bolstered by Steve Keeble & Dave Payne: Paul Ellis & Crew; and Bob Anderson trying out Cat Balou. Another good day was had by all, despite the lack of wind.

The first points races were extremely well supported with (I am told) fourteen in the Fast Fleet and three in the Slow. Racing amongst the twin trapezers was highly competitive despite it being a comedy of errors, i.e. Steve Glynn & Tom deciding to invert, me trying to plough furrows across the banks in Goldhanger (have you ever tried to bear away into deep water with your rudders up?), Dave Payne testing the temperature of the water with his head, and my noble crew trying to waterski off the
trapeze astern of the boat - and they're only the ones that I saw! (Yes, Chris, I
know I fell off as well!!) None of it mattered anyway because we’d all remembered that it was Rear Commodore’s benefit (you have to let him win sometimes).

The afternoon race was even better than the morning with that man Dave Allan & Anna proving that the practice over the last two weekends was well worth it. Just watch out Dave, those two 19’s are after you!! Steve Glynn & Tom managed to redress the balance following their a.m. swan dives. Mind you, they did only manage to pass Chris and me after we tried to nick G Mark tightly, and hit it. Everyone’s comment on the day was that it was the best day’s racing we’ve had for a very long time, and it bodes well for the rest of the season.

On a personal note I should like to add how pleased I was tao see rule infringers doing their 720s. I reckon if this close racing continues we’1ll all be experts on
them by the end of the season....

Easter Egg went quite well with (according to the Race Officer on Sunday) 22 Cats. I was sorry to miss it but the pleasures of driving the RIB almost made up for it!
It’s amazing trying to keep up with Cats going upwind even in light airs - we were
probably doing 5-6 knots, and we weren't tacking! Monday was a hooligan, and being April Fool’s Day we had a Keeble Special course. Well done, Steve Glynn & Tom for finishing in such style, and congrats on winning the series. As a sailor, I’d like to express my appreciation for the way in which the shore based organisation has improved through the closed season. It certainly shows on the water. Well done Mike D and the Sailing Sub.

January - the new Editor/Hon.Sec/Hon.Treas. is F.W.Garrett. One thing that has struck me when reading
these old Navigans is the steadfast adherence to formality. 'Mr.W.J.Hodge' or 'Mrs S Harris' It is
- and
articles are signed merely by initials, almost as though it would be pretentious or undignified to sign
the
author's full name. How very different from our 1990s Navigans where all are addressed by their first name
as though they were long-lost friends - and the trading of 'insults' (well, perhaps only "getting at' each
other with a gentle niggle) occurs fairly regularly. Anyway, the change of Editor brings with it a slip in the mask of apparent inscrutable correctness as I discover that W.J.Hodge is known to his friends as ‘Wally! as Fred Garrett (for Fred is his name) pays tribute to his predecessor.

February - Fred asks 'Wes you bin and gone ?' but not quite inthatiway. What he actually writes is "....it
would greatly facilitate the keeping of records......if members would advise the Secretary of any changes
of location." Yep, I guess it would ; it would also help to catch up with the ‘subs demand’.

The accounts for 1959 show an improved Subscription income of £45 5s Od and a reduced Laying-Up Supper income of £60 15s Od. Obviously, the membership not only shows a commendable pang of conscience but also a determ- ination to diet. The Fitting-Out Supper brought in £16 4s 2d (why 2d ?) with catering expenses of £3 (how
much ? What did they eat - dry bread and jam ?) and ‘other' expenses of £9 8s 9d. Now for the exam
question: Without taking more than five seconds, calculate the profit for the Fitting Up Supper ? NB. the answer is at the end of this article and, be honest, how many got it right within the time allowed ?

March - a revolution might well have been declared between February and March, 1960, or maybe even a coup
d'etat has been attempted - but I doubt if many people noticed. Until now, Navigans has always been
described as the "Monthly Bulletin of the Sailing Section, M.A.S.C". However, in the historic month of March, 1960, Navigans become the “Monthly Bulletin of the Marconi Sailing Club, M.A.S.C." Was this a deliberate
decision of the Sailing Section's Main Committee - or merely a unilateral whim of the Editor to declare UDI ?

With regard to the forthcoming sailing season, mention is made of team races with at least four visiting clubs. The Portsmouth Standard Handicap for the Enterprise is 98 (Terylene sails) or 103 (Cotton dails), whilst the
International Cadet races to 129 compared to the club's rating of 130 for ‘Avril’. Presumably, Avril falls
into the category of 'slow but steady’.

April - a new Editor, but the same old problem '".....many subscriptions remain outstanding". Formality has
been restored with "A considerable amount of work has been undertaken on our clubhouse under the direction of Mr.Bigden", These days, even those of us who did not know him would, I am sure, unhesitatingly refer to him as Jack Bigden and he subsequently did an awful lot more work for the club. The memory of Jack Bigden is . deservedly preserved by our main support boat ‘Jack B'.

The club dance is to be held at the Odeon (cinema ?) and tickets are 5/- each.

"Barnacie' writes an article "On learning to Sail" and recommends Peter Heaton's book "Sailing". At this time I hadn't even thought about sailing but when I did, sometime in 1961, the first book I bought was, in fact, Peter Heaton's book. I still have it and feel it is one of the nicest books to read on learning to sail
- I should know, I've read an awful lot of them !

May - instructions concerning the club 'flattie' (I first read this as 'fattie') and readers are instructed
"When mooring her, tie to the rope mooring line..... «-with a hitch that will not ride up the mooring line."
Now come on you dinghy sailors, how many of you could do that first time without having to think about it ? Come to that, how many cruiser sailors could do it ? Hang about whilst I take time off to read up on "Knots to tie and Knots not to tie ". P.S. What's a 'flattie' ?

An article on 0.0.D.duties ‘reveals that the 0.0.0. is also the Race Officer - now, what a good idea !
Apart from the ‘usual' duties, he has also to collect 2/- from each helm entering the race, except not from those who have paid a ‘block payment' for the season. Some years ago at an AGM, someone suggested that the club dispense with a hard fee and charge each time a member launched their dinghy. The heat generated by that one scortched the ceiling.

Anote about the America's Cup, reporting the NYYC's acceptance of a challenge from Australia for 1962. Now
I wonder what Alan Bond was doing at that time - and what chance a challenge by the MSC in 2001 ? Who
knows to what extent the MSC will develop; maybe we can take Dennis Connor's last 'defence' as a precedent and make a «challenge in a catamaran ?

Finally, a note about a visit by Dabchicks Sailing Club members - but a somewhat unusual arrival. tt seems
they came in a sailing smack - and abandoned the boat completely ‘some distance' downstream due to lack of
water, coming ashore in their dinghy. The smack itself was left to come in on its own with wind and tide

12.

alone to guide it. Apparently, it berthed itself very neatly alongside Mamgu. I must say, that's what I'd call a well trained boat. Of course, in recent years some of our catamaran members have had a go at training their cats to manoeuvre unattended on the river. Alas, although the cats glided off under their own guidance system very impressively, they failed to answer to their master's 'return' whistle and we had to send out the cat-catchers to retrieve them.

June - at last, another small crack in the armour of formality appears; Jack Bigden is referred to as
Jack Bigden whilst mention is also made of Stan Allerton, Pete Harris and Brian Partridge.

I think Maylandsea Bay Sailing Club won the team race held on lst May; at least the results show MBYC = 73.50 and M.S.C. = 46.0.

As far as I can tell, the main sailing programme seems to have consisted of a single handicap fleet series
- and not too many entries in the two races to date.

July - a reprimand to members, "Too many members are sailing without personal buoyancy in conditions that
demand more discretion". A visit to Ariel S.C. (BBC) at Teddington for "the return team races" is reported.
Alas, the MSC team '".....was hopelessly outclassed by the BBC who knew all the dodges on their home waters".
Well, they would, wouldn't they !

A report of a letter of thanks to Blackwater SC's rescue boat for rescuing a number of MSC capsized dinghies. Did we have a rescue boat then? From what I read, I get the impression we did not have a rescue boat, at least not one that went out as duty boat during races.

August - the Editor again chides members for lack of cleanliness, tidiness and hygiene on board Mamgu, and
is particularly concerned about the toilets. He states, " These (ie. the toilets) should only be used as a last resort and then only in a minor way" (72777) What, I ask myself, do you do whilst you await the blessed state of 'last resort’ so that you can legitimately use 'the heads’ aboard Mamgu ? By the time you do get to the 'last resort’ stage, what was presumably relatively 'minor' will more than likely have become 'major',
and you're still banned ! No wonder they don't get many ladies with parasols on board Mamgu - not for long
anyway.

First mention of a club rescue launch - a vessel is being acquired and is to be commissioned shortly. The
prime function of the launch is to be for rescue purposes and assisting members in distress.

Another duty for the 0.0.0. Apparently, when Mamgu was flying the Red Ensign, club yachts were suppose to dip
their own ensign in salute - and the OOD was supposed to acknowledge in like manner. What with acting
as Race Officer, unblocking the loos (sorry, heads) and generally looking after the clubhouse, the poor 00D doesn't get much time to relax does he ? No chance for him to put a coat of anti-fouling on his boat..in those days. By the way, is the saluting etiquette still required to be observed ? Certainly, I've never
done it when acting as 00D - there's never been time to look at passing cruisers
and, anyway, I'm not sure
I'd recognise the salute if I saw it. Fings definitely ain't wot they used ter be.

September - a Fleetwind team race against MBYC took place in bright and sunny conditions - but not for the
MSCteam. MBYC took lst, 2nd and 3rd places and MSC occupied 4th-6th.

An article by ‘Barnacle’ entitled "Helmsmanship and Seamanship" no doubt caused some considerable comment
amongst the members - especially the dinghy sailers. Maybe Barnacle had had a bad day at the office or, more
likely, a particularly harrowing experience the previous week-end but he certainly gives the dinghy sailers a roasting. He states, "The last few years has seen the rapid growth of an entirely new breed of 'sailor' -
the ‘dinghy boys'. Many.......are absolutely first rate seamen but.......many others cannot be called seamen
at all" He continues, "Having won a race or two they consider themselves fine helmsmen, as maybe they are, but they also consider themselves fine seamen, and that theymost certainly are not". Barnacle then goes on to blast the dinghymen with examples of lack of seamanship which, I must confess, I recognise myself as being a guilty party. However, some respite is granted the dinghymen when he re-directs his attack towards what he calls “marine motorists" (Ah! says our modern-day dinghyman, NOW we can relate to him !) and, perhaps surprizingly, he soundly belabours the ‘large racing cruisers’. Rather more in hope than expectation, he ends the article by saying he sincerely hopes no one will take offence ! Ah, well! He's a nice chap really and
just felt like ‘blowing his top' - but I think I'd have kept out of his way for a bit, just in case.

October - a winter meeting entitled 'Blackwater Mud' - now there's a subject to get stuck into.
Barnacle is still with us and presumably still acceptable. His article on ‘Laying Up' no doubt pricked the
conscience of those cruisermen who read of those things they ought to have done - and of those things they
ought not to have done - as winter approached. At least the dinghyman can hide his folly in the garage.

flovember -- the AGM reveals a paid-up membership of about 150, including 21 associate members.

December - a winter meeting not to be missed; an illustrated lecture by Hervey Benham. I love reading his
books and would dearly liked to have heard him speak. Sadly, 'The Sailing Barge Preservation Society’ is to be wound up, and, even sadder, 'they' plan to break up ‘Black Eagle', a sailing barge which had served as the home of a former Commodore of the Maldon Little Ship Club. What a shame. Is Mamgu safe I wonder ?

ADDERS ON THE SEA WALL

ADDERS HAVE BEEN SEEN IN THE LONG GRASS ON THE SEA WALL ALONG THE CRUISER FARK
RECENTLY SO WOULD MEMBERS, AND PARTICULARLY CHILDREN, AVOID WALKING THROUGH THERE,
BECAUSE THOUGH AN ADDER WILL NOT APFROACH HUMANS, IT WILL BITE IF TRODDEN ON,
I UNDERSTAND THAT THE PREGNANT FEMALE ADDER LIKES TO BASK IN THE SUN AND IS RELUCTANT
TO MOVE ON SOMEONE*S APPROACH -— WHICH IS THE REASON THEY ARE SEEN MORE OFTEN BY
PEOPLE AT THIS TIME OF YEAR. (THE YOUNG ARE BORN IN SEFTEMBER, ) BITES ARE VERY
RARELY FATAL, BUT DO REQUIRE IMMEDIATE MEDICAL ATTENTION IF THEY OCCUR. PREVENTION
IS BETTER THAN CURE, AND OUR NON-DISTURBANCE OF THIS PARTICULAR WILD LIFE CAN ONLY BE
A GOOD THING WITH SO MUCH LIMITATION TO THEIR LIVING SPACE CAUSED BY US HUMANS THESE
DAYS!

PIERS RACE UPDATE - Sunday 7th July 1991

As so many members are putting a considerable amount of effort into helping with the East Coast Piers Race, it would seem a good idea to explain exactly what the RYA
Seamanship Foundation is and what it does - as, like last year, this is the
organisation that will benefit from our Fundraising.

The Seamanship Foundation is a registered Charity (No. 265869) which works closely with the RYA but is funded only by the money it can raise, ard neat by RYA subscription. It has three specific aims:

- to provide opportunities for young people, particularly those from deprived areas,
to benefit from activities directly connected with sailing and the sea.

- to arrange training and to provide special equipment to erable handicapped pecfdple
to learn to sail and take part on equal terms with the able-bodied.

- toa enhance the knowledge and seamanship of yachtsmen and other pleasure boat
owners.

Its activities range from organising offshore cruising for blind sailors, to helping physically disabled sailors to sail, either as part of a crew on a cruiser, or sole ir a Challerger Trimaran. It is the latter activity that MSC has been able ta help with, by providing the funds required to buy a new Challenger. This boat is currently under construction at Reg White’s yard in Brightlingsea and it is planned

that the new owner will bring it along to bail at the Club on the Saturday before this year’s East Coast Piers Race. We hope that a few other Challenger owners will
make the trip to join him and race from the Club on the Saturday - although they will

Salmon sighted on the Blackwater

Such is the stuff of 'headlines'; it doesn't have to mean what it says, merely make you want to read what it implies it is saying.

The Essex Chronicle has recently introduced a weekly 'Sailing Report' and the MSC was asked to submit a weekly report which I was be pleased to supply. Unfortunately, the 1st report submitted was for the week 'they' didn't print a Report in the Chronicle. However, undaunted, I submitted a 2nd report and SUCCESS, 'they' printed a report in the Chronicle issue of 3 May - albeit they got one or two bits twisted around somehow. Never mind, its good to see an attempt to give sailing some publicity in the local press and even better when it features the MSC. However, for the record, here are the two reports I submitted (more or less).

Spring points 7 & 8 (21 April)

Marconi SC members enjoyed magnificent sailing on Sunday in SW force 3-6 winds, with a total of 8 Solos and 19 Catamarans turning out for Spring points 7 & 8. Marconi's Solo Fleet is always competitive, so new member Simon Liddington's two wins were particularly noteworthy. John Salmon scored two second places in his new boat, whilst 3rd place was taken by local helm Ron Greygoose in the morning and by Roger Smith in the afternoon.

In Marconi's ever growing Catamaran Fleet, David Allan and Anna Spittle (Hurricane 5.9) showed exceptional downwind speed to get 1st in the morning and 3rd in the afternoon in the Fast Catamaran Handicap race. The club's lady helm, Lucy Boreham (Dart 18), crewed by Tom Ashley, took 2nd place in the morning, whilst Fleet captain, Larry Botheras (Prindle 19), crewed by Chris Caruth, placed 2nd in the afternoon.

The Slow Catamaran handicap race produced a win for local helm, Dave Payne (Dart 15). The club's youngest regular catamaran helm, 12-years old Paul Harrison (Dart 15), crewed by Stuart Golding, took second place.

Spring Points 9 & 10 (28 April).

Forecast winds of NE force 3-4 turned out to be a very variable F1 and a bit. Unfortunately, this meant a number of competitors found themselves "out of time" in the morning races. Out of an entry of 16 Fast Catamarans (less than PYN 90), only John Nickalls/Caroline Hollings (Hurricane 5.9), Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton (Prindle 19) and Steve and Janet Keeble (Hurricane 5.9) finished the course in 1st, 2nd and 3rd places. Three others finished "out of time" and 10 retired, having been caught on the wrong side of the river with little or no wind and a strong adverse tide between them and the next mark. The afternoon race attracted 17 entries in Force 1 - 2 and this time 14 finished and 3 retired. This race was won by Paul Ellis (Dart 18), John Nickalls/Caroline Hollings (Hurricane 5.9) wnd and Lucy Boreham/Tom Ashley (Dart 18) 3rd.

The Solo Fleet attracted 8 entries for race 9 and 6 for race 10 and generally coped much better with the fickle, swinging wind than the catamarans. At one time, boats only yards apart and heading in exactly the same direction on a beat to windward were actually on opposite tacks. John Salmon, sailing his new boat, won both races with new member Simon Liddington 2nd each time, the afternoon race being a particularly close battle between them. Third place was taken by Roger Smith (race 9) and Peter Collis (race 10).

None of the Slow Catamaran Fleet(PYN 90 and above) finished in the morning and only Colin Kidner (Dart 15) completed the course in the afternoon.

In the monohull Handicap Fleet, race leader, Mike and Maggie Boreham (420) finished a minute 'out of time' in race 9, whilst Howard Rogers/Paul Wilkinson (Fireball) won race 10.

NB. If John Salmon had kindly capsized, the 'headline' could have read 'SALMON SIGHTED IN THE BLACKWATER'.

PS. The 'headline' in the Essex Chronicle was nothing to do with me; 'twas all their own inspiration.

NAVIGANS PAST

1961 - signs of dissent, and a very sad loss
plus plans to make the ladies flush with delight.
January - the Editor's Comments state "There appears to be many misconceptions about the true aspect
of club working days during the off season..........Bearing in mind our prime function is as a sailing
club we can, nevertheless, attend to our creative comforts as well. The club provides the material and the money (on a very slender budget) and a disservice is done to those individuals who give of their time and skill in this work by taking it for granted, or that the job is someone else's ‘pigeon', or we
keep a permanent ‘cinderella'........ cracks about ‘dirty old barge', or ropey dinghy park facilities do
not help. Those who think this way should ask themselves the obvious question."

February/March - two issues in one due to the recent indisposition of the Editor, Fred Garrett, who is
also Secretary/Treasurer, He seeks a volunteer to take over both the Editorship and the whole of the production of Navigans (ie. 200 copies). This means collecting,editing and preparing copy followed by arranging for stencilling & checking before printing, and the final chores of stapling and distribution.

Stan Allerton questions if it is fair for, say, two parents, two children and two friends to all sail on the basis of a single subscription ? Although he recognises that family sailing is a fundmental part of the club's activities, he feels that once the children become ‘earners' they should become members in their
own right. To this end he proposes a Junior Membership (16-21) be established - and he deliberately
avoids the term 'cadet' to avoid confusion (identification ?) with the Cadet dinghy class (and presumably its implications of a younger age group, 15 and under). He also feels the need to encourage Associate Members under the age 21, and suggests a subscription well below the normal Associate Subscription of 34/-. In this way he hopes toguide the ‘youngsters' into the club's adopted fleets of Fleetwind and Enterprises, thus maintaining these fleets and avoiding the introduction of other classes which, he feels, the club could not sustain.

The coming season offers fleet racing for trophies in Enterprise and Fleetwind (12 races, 6 to count), and
handicap racing for two Menagerie classes (103 and under; over 103), with a small prize for the winners of
each of the 12 races scheduled. Three starters are necessary for each race. The BJRC agree various adjustments to the ‘Portsmouth harbour speed figures' and our favourite club boat 'Avril' is rated 130,
putting her between the Cadet (Terylene sails) at 128 and Cadet (Cotton sails) at 132.

April - Fred (now writing under ‘Secretary's comments) announces that responsibility for editing and
publication of Navigans has been taken over by Nick Tovey and his Wife Daphne as Editor. I can't help feeling that he really ought to have said that the new Editor was Daphne Tovey assisted in the publication
by Husband, Nick - but it was in the good old days when it was a man's life at sea and the ladies were
presumably not too bothered either way.

Fibre-matting was fitted to the launching ramp to give a more secure foothold - anda stiff broom provided
to clean it down. Was the fibre-matting successful - and did the new broom sweep clean ?

Bad weather on Easter Sunday forced postponement of the 'Tuning-up race' until Easter Monday but even worse weather resulted in only a scratch race of two boats. Turnout for the first four Points races was 4,5, 3 and 3, with Peter Harris in his Fleetwind 'Muggs' winning all but the 3rd race in which, of the 3 entries, one sailed the wrong course, one capsized and one hit a mark !

The block racing fee for the season will be él.

Socially, it rained, but didn't it rain, for the Fitting Out Supper. About 70 people enjoyed a programme of colour films including
some about the English Electric Valve Company, surf boatmen of Ghana and Canadian sailing. This reminds me that when I was a very young lad, I used to go around to the local village hall for the once-a-week film show; some of them were silent movies and the local baker's wife used to play the

accompanying piano enthusiastically - but very badly. The Supper finished with, I quote, 'A gay
accompaniment .....provided by the 'Remo's' a local skiffle group at Heybridge’. How about a gay group
for the 1991 Laying Up Supper ? Oh! I forgot to mention; the Supper was held on board Mamgu.

May - a call for volunteers to operate the new rescue launch and training will be given. It will operate
under the control of the 00D (who is also Race Officer).

A team race against Ariel SC, Teddington (ie. the BBC) but, alas, it seems we learned nothing from the 1960 defeat. Once again the MSC ‘was hopelessly outsailed by the BBC who were up to all the dodges of the river
and knew where to expect the gusts’. Even more alas - we were beaten by MBYC in a team race and didn't
do too well in the Enterprise Open Team race competition, «lso held at Maylandsea.

The lst Picnic Cruise to Osea was not too well supported - only one boat made the trip and had to be towed
back to Heybridge due to steering trouble. However, a 2nd Picnic Cruise to Osea on Whit Sunday was more successful with 16 boats and 50 people making the trip to Osea. The youngest to attend was 8-month old Kerry Sims.

ji.
June - an evening working party resulted in the successful stepping of Mamgu's mizzen mast, plus
removal, and replacement, of the rescue launch engine to effect repairs.

Peter Harris came 2nd in the Fleetwind East Coast Area Championships and Maldon Little Ship Club beat us in a team race. A Maldon Little Ship Club boat also won the Marconi Cruiser Cup whilst a Hornet from Maldon Yacht Club won the Marconi Challenge Cup. It would appear that Maldon sailors rule the river; I wonder if it has anything to do with the aftermath of the Vikings' victory at Northey some
1,000 years ago - you know, all that rape and pillage they seemed to go in for in those days.

Robbie Sims organised a successful camping/cruising weekend with 17 people travelling to East Mersea, some going by road and some in one of the 5 boats that made the trip .

July/August - a sad day for the family and friends of Fred Garrett and a sad loss for the club. Fred
died on 18 August, 1961 after a short illness. There can be few members in our modern-day club who knew
or can personally remember him - but the name of Fred Garrett must be one of the most well-known to club
members through the Garrett Memorial Trophy which is awarded annually to the most outstanding cadet member of the club. In the tribute to Fred Garrett, we are reminded that he took a leading role in the conversion of Mamgu from a dilapidated old barge yacht intoaviable floating club house, and that he also provided a valuable link between the MSC and its parent organisation, the Marconi Athletic and Social Club.

As a result of the passing of Fred, Robbie Sims took over as. the MSC Secretary.

Robbie has clearly issued a set of ‘House Rules' for the club, although it it is not clear how they were circulated and advised to members since they don't appear to have been printed in previous issues of Navigans. Whatever 'the rules', he has caused John Scarlett (also a member of Maldon Little Ship Club) to write a letter of comment (some supportive, some critical) to Navigans. One of the rules presumably required each member to perform an OOD duty because Mr.Scarlett writes " I cannot see the inactive majority liking the idea of paying 10/- a year and being expected to spend one day every other year at Heybridge staying there until everyone else has departed, possibly in the small hours of the morning. Some of these
members might not bother to remain in the club......... Objections to the duty of SOD can be expected from **
the more responsible of the ‘inactive’ members but there is a risk of others just not bothering to turn up".

This has a very familiar ring about it; the current OOD duty roster is drawn from all members of more than 3 years standing and results in a duty roughly every 2 years but, from recent experience, not all members seem keen to 'do their bit’. Strange isn't it, even after 30 years, the same old problems and same old arguements rule the day.

September - a committee has been formed to organise a collection to purchase a permanent memorial to
Fred Garrett, initial thought being possibly a piece of furniture, a barometer or some other article for
Mamgu.

At last, team wins for the MSC, this time against Osea SC and MBYC - but don't celebrate too loudly 'cos
the return match (on our home waters) against Ariel SC (BBC) resulted in the BBC winning handily.

In the Points racing, race 9 is considered to have attracted a large turn-out with 8 entries - most races
seem to attract 3 - 5 entries. The Ladies Race, I suspect, attracted 3 entries and was won by Miss J.
Fairbains

October - MSC was beaten by Maldon Little Ship Club in a team race !

The Childrens’ Party held on board Mamgu attracted 30 children and ‘Uncle’ Peter Makins reputedly brought along his Performing Flea . This gives a whole knew meaning to ‘scratch race’.

Inflation is catching up; tickets for the Laying Up Supper are 15/- this year.

November - the new Secretary, Robbie Sims, asks for a good turn out for the 1961 AGM since "...(it) will
be very important for the future of the club; indeed, as a result of increased membership we have reached a turning point." Thirty years later in 1991, have we again reached a turning point ? Some believe so.

The last page of Navigans is a questionaire about possible club activities covering Sailing Activity, Summer
Evenings (ie, apres sailing), Winter Evening and the member's attitude towards the use of Mamgu - plus
space for ‘constructive suggestions’ (but not ‘destructive criticism’).

December - Arthur Adam (Commodore) writes a Christmas Message, dispells the gloom and doom expressed by
some members at the AGM, and mentions that some want to buy a shore-based site - but no available site

Know Your Local Area wt WEST MERSEA

West Mersea is famous in the annals of Essex Maritime tradition. Many of the skippers and paid hands for the well-to-do owners of racing yachts were recruited from the area in the 20s and 30s. Most of these men were fishermen in the winter ard paid yacht hands in the summer. Their exploits are recorded in many books dealing with this area.

Mersea Island itself is joined ta the mainland by a causeway which flocds at high spring tides. As yet there are no marina-type develcepments on the island nor are any plarmed. The facilities there are within easy reach for MSC yachtsmen, and the moorings in Mersea Fleet or Quarters give access to the sailing Clubs, pubs, shops and restaurants to be found on the island.

For the MSC yachtsman arriving from Stansgate there 1s normally enough water to allow a short cut across the Nass Shoal into the channel leading into Mersea Quarters. This charmel starts at the Nass beacon and is marked by port and starboard buoys until the first of the moorings is reached. Shortly after this the channel divides intca three branches; the Strood, the Ray and Salestt Channels, all three beirg heavily populated with moorings and navigable, depending or draught, for a reasonable distance. It is normally possible ta pick up one of these moorings, especially when local boats are absent. The West Mersea Yacht Club boatman will give advice as to the availability of moorings.

The best charnel with regard to proximity ta the landing stage is the first ta starboard as the Channels divide. It is fairly narrow, ard shallow at the edge, sa stay reasonably close to the line of moorings until you find a vacant one. This route takes you close to starboard of the old Oyster shed, a square shed with a corrugated iron roof. Having found a mooring you will have ta go ashore by dirighy, or by halling the boatman for a ride ashore. If intending to return after dark it 1s preferable to rig a riding light and to make careful note of the nearby boats as the crowded moorings can prove quite confusing especially in the dark ard with a different tidal state and alcohol level thar when you ventured forth. Price safely ashore you carn explore Mersea City with its picturesque clapboard cattages, have a drink in the Yacht Club or walk to one of the pubs.

The alternative ways to access the island are to sail across the Mersea Flats ard into the Colne opposite Brightlingsea and to anchor in the Fyefleet pool or ta pick up a mooring in the Pyefleet. Beware, though, the landing area in the Pyefleet is extremely East Coast muddy at low water. The landing from the Pyefleet pool is v ery much firmer. Both landings involve a mile or sco walk to the nearest pub, just ercugh to work up a thirst.

As with all the East Coast voyages in our local area, the East Coast Rivers handbook is a strongly recommended, indeed irivaluable, guide to pilotage. It is also very interesting if you carry books about this area on board with you. "The Salty Share” and "Last Days of Sail" are twa examples which concentrate particularly om the Essex area, as also do several of Hervey Berham’s books about sailing barges.

Dave Heane, Readnigen, April 1991

QUARTERS OF AN HOUR WAS SPENT POINTING AT °A® AND WATCHING IT RECEDE INTO THE DISTANCE UNTIL THE TIDE CHANGED. LOADS
OF PEOPLE APPEARED TO BE RETIRING (UNUSUAL, CAT SAILORS ARE NOT WHAT YOU WOULD REALLY CALL RETIRING PEOPLE...) AND THEN
- A GUST! WE ROCKETED ROUND A’ AND NO. 1 AND BREEZY, PAUSED FOR A LULL AND THEN TWIN-WIRED TOWARDS THE FINISH,...ONLY
TO DISCOVER THAT BOB HAD, WISELY, ABANDONED. UNFORTUNATELY MY PEN HAD OBVIOUSLY CAUGHT ME OUT BECAUSE THE TWO MICKS
WERE ON RESCUE DUTY AND WE WERE THE ONLY CAT NOT TOLD OF THE ABANDONMENT.... THANKS, GUYS, JUST YOU WAIT! BOB WAS VERY
KEEN, WE GOT ASHORE AT 1 O'CLOCK, POURED DOWN A PINT AND STUFFED DOWN A HOT DOG, TO BE TOLD THE AFTERNOON START WOULD BE
1.30. | THE FAITHFUL CHRIS NEARLY WENT ON STRIKE AT THAT POINT. WE LINED UP FOR THE START AND WERE POWERING UP BEHIND
ALL THE PEOPLE WHO'D DECIDED TO STOP CLOSE TO THE LINE TO CRIES OF "UP, UP" AND "YOU CAN’T BARGE IN”. UNFORTUNATELY
THERE WASN'T AN 86" PRINDLE 19 SIZED GAP FOR US SO CHRIS AND I HAD NO CHOICE BUT TO EXECUTE A 360. FOR SOME REASON ON
COMPLETION THIS GLUT OF SLOW MOVING BOATS WERE STILL MOVING VERY SLOWLY TOWARDS 'A’. WE, FORTUNATELY, WERE ABLE 10
GENERATE SOME SPEED AND BREAK THROUGH. JUST GOES TO SHOW HE WHO LAUGHS LAST, ETC. WE MANAGED TO GET THREE LAPS IN
WITH THAT MAN DAVE ALLEN & THE LOVELY ANNA SHOWING US ALL A CLEAN PAIR OF HEELS, MIND YOU, DAVE & ANNE, STEVE & TOM AND
CHRIS & I WERE ALL VERY SURPRISED TO NEARLY LAP A FEW BOATS. AS PEOPLE FINISHED, IT BECAME OBVIOUS THAT THE SAILING
SUB’S EFFORTS AND PUBLICATION IN NAVIGANS WAS WASTED SINCE HALF THE FLEET AND ALL THE SLOW CATS NEGLECTED TO USE THE
CORRECT FINISH LINE. READ YOUR SAILING INSTRUCTIONS CHAPS. STILL, WHAT A CHANGE FROM SLEET, SNOW AND GALES,

6.

AND SO TO THE FINAL BRACE OF THE SPRING SERIES RACES. IT BEING THE LAST WEEKEND BEFORE REGATTA, THERE WERE ALL SORTS OF
SLJs (SILLY LITTLE JOBS) TO DO AND WITH RESET TO NO WIND, OUR REVERED COMMODORE OF THE REAR SUGGESTED A POSTPONEMENT 10
CARRY QUT THE WORK PARTY BEFORE RACING. I CAN TELL YOU THAT THOSE OF US ALREADY CHANGED DID CALL HIS PARENTAGE INTO
QUESTION! SQ THE CAT FLEET DISAPPEARED ONTO THE ROOF TO GET THE AWNING BITS DOWN AND ERECT SAME. AS WE SUSPECTED
THOUGH, WITHIN MINUTES, THE WIND PICKED UP AND SO WE DASHED OFF FOR AN 11.30 START. UNFORTUNATELY THAT WAS PROBABLY A
BIT OPTIMISTIC AS A NUMBER OF US ONLY JUST MANAGED TO GET TO THE LINE IN TIME FOR THE GUN. THERE WAS AN ' INTERESTING’
FIRST BEAT TO 'A’ WITH SEVERAL SHALLOWS-HOPPERS TESTING THE DEPTH OF THE HARD AND THEN GETTING TANGLED WITH THE
STARBOARD TACKERS WHO'D GONE OUT FIRST. THE USUAL TRIUMVIRATE HAD GOT AWAY SMARTLY (NOTE: I MUST GET ON THE LINE AT THE
START SOMETIME) WITH, INITIALLY, BIG JOHN AND CAROLINE LEADING, STEVE & TOM AND DAVE & ANNA. WE MORTALS WATCHED THEM
SHOOT OFF INTO THE DISTANCE, AND I (CREWED FOR VARIOUS LONG-WINDED REASONS BY JOE EDOM, A NEW DART 15 SAILOR) SPENT THE
REST OF MY TIME TRYING TO CLAW MY WAY PAST DART 18s. SECOND TIME AROUND WE GOT TANGLED UP WITH THE SOLO FLEET TOWARDS
YE MARK AND UNFORTUNATELY COLLIDED WITH DAVE ONYONS & BEN. OUT CAME THE PROTEST FLAG, PLUS MUCH SWEARING AND GNASHING
OF TEETH - AIMED MAINLY AT MALCOLM STUART (BUT HE'S USED TO IT). LET US THEN DRAW A VEIL RAPIDLY OVER THE INCIDENT.
THE RECORD WILL SHOW NO CONCLUSION REACHED BY THE PROTEST COMMITTEE FOR VERY GOOD REASONS,

AS 1’VE SAID BEFORE, PROTESTING IS NOT 'UNSPORTSMANLIKE’, IT IS THE ONLY WAY TO GET A JUDGEMENT(!) IN A SPORT WHERE
THERE IS NO REFEREE AND IT HELPS ALL OF US LEARN MORE ABOUT THE RULES. BELIEVE ME, THAT IS NOW AN ESSENTIAL IN THE CAT
FLEET, WITH THE LEVEL OF COMPETITION WERE EXPERIENCING THIS YEAR.

AT THE FRONT OF THE FLEET STEVE & TOM EVENTUALLY TOOK LINE HONOURS FROM BIG JOHN & CAROLINE, AND THAT MAN DAVE ALLEN &
ANNA. THE WIND GOT UP A LITTLE FOR THE AFTERNOON EXCEPT FOR THE FEW MOMENTS AROUND THE GUN, AND SO SEVERAL PEOPLE WERE
VERY SHY OF THE LINE. 1 MADE MY USUAL ABYSMAL START, BUT DID ACTUALLY MANAGE TO POWER THROUGH A BIT. THE FRONT OF THE
DART FLEET SEEMED TO BE HIGHLY COMPETITIVE WITH JOHN TUCKWELL & CREW, TIM DE B & CREW, LUCY BOREHAM & TOM ASHLEY, DAVE
ONYONS & BEN , PAUL ELLIS (SINGLE OR DOUBLE HANDED), CHRIS PATMORE & JULIE MILLS, AND EVEN OUR VENERABLE COMMODORE OF
THE REAR BASHING IT OUT TOE-TO-TOE AT THE FRONT. WATCH IT THOUGH, GUYS (& GAL), BECAUSE THOSE CHAPS BEHIND YOU ARE
CLOSING FAST... IT ALSO MAKES, CONTRARY TO MALCOLM’S THOUGHTS, THE DART 18 THE BIGGEST RACING FLEET IN THE CLUB. STEVE
GLYNN & TOM CLINCHED THE SERIES FROM BIG JOHN & CAROLINE AND THAT MAN DAVE & ANNA, DESPITE THE LATTER'S WIN IN THE PM,
$0 THAT'S 17. ONE THIRD OF THE RACING SEASON OVER. AN OVERALL ENTRY OF 21 AND AN AVERAGE TURNOUT OF, IF MEMORY SERVES,
14+ BOATS (AND THAT INCLUDES THE RACES WHEN ONLY 2 OR 3 NUTTERS WENT OUT') LET'S LOOK FORWARD TO EVEN MORE CROWDED
START LINES FOR THE SUMMER SERIES,

THAT LEADS US NEATLY ON TO REGATTA. MANY TRUSTY CAT FLEET MEMBERS TURNED UP FOR THE FRIDAY WORK PARTY IN DRIZZLE AND
COLD, BUT FORTUNATELY THE WEATHER (NOT THE WIND) IMPROVED OVER THE WEEKEND. MARKS WERE CHANGED, WHITE LINES PAINTED AND
WE WAITED FOR THE ARRIVALS, SATURDAY DAWNED BREATHLESSLY, AND WE HAD THE THE COMPANY OF A VISIT OF A HNURRICANE 5,3
FROM THE ARMY AND A CONDOR (WELCOME TO THE CLUB, MATTHEW HERBERT). MANY OF OUR REGULARS WERE CONSPICUOUS BY THEIR
ABSENCE, WITH STEVE GLYNN CAVORTING ON A KEELBOAT IN SCOTLAND AND THE TWO MICKS LEARNING TO SAIL (SOME WOULD SAY NOT
BEFORE TIME!) WITH DON FINDLAY AT ABERSOCH. THE MARCONI DINGHY CHALLENGE ON SATURDAY AFTERNOON 1S BEST FORGOTTEN BY THE
CAT FLEET, MOST OF WHOM, EXCEPT LEE HARRISON & TOM ASHLEY WHO WERE FLYING THEIR KITE, WERE ACTUALLY LED AROUND THE
COURSE BY A SELECTION OF MONOHULLS. WE SHALL GLOSS OVER QUICKLY, BUT SAVE FOR LEE, THE LAST PLACES WERE FILLED BY...
THE 6 CATS RACING. (SOLIDARITY, 1 CALL THAT.)

SUNDAY DAWNED WITH A ROBBIE SIMS SPECIAL COURSE - THIRSLET, GOLDHANGER, DOCTOR AND BACK. WE ALL DUCKED THE TIDE ONCE
WE'D MANAGED, FINALLY, TO CROSS THE START LINE AND SPLIT INTO TWO FACTIONS; THOSE THAT STUCK TO THE SOUTH SHORE AND
THOSE WHO WENT NORTH, I.E. ME' I SOON DISCOVERED AT THIRSLET (REACHED IN AN HOUR) THAT NORTH WAS WRONG - ESPECIALLY AS
I WAS EMBARASSED TO SEE PETER FLOOK & MIKE STEELE ON THE 18-2 BREATHING DOWN MY TRANSOMS! WE THEN HAD A VERY
INTERESTING TACK DOWNWIND TO °C’ AND ALL ENDED UP FINALLY IN A HEAP AT 'S', THE REPLACEMENT FOR NO.1, STILL GYEING
MERRILY UP-RIVER IN A GAGGLE OF MONOHULLS. FORTUNATELY, I'D PAID MY DEBTS (OR SOMETHING) AND GOT MY OWN PRIVATE BREEZE
ALL THE WAY TO THE FINISH AND MANAGED TO MAKE MY HANDICAP ON ALL THE BOATS WE'D BEEN AMONGST TO GET 4TH BEHIND.
DUCKMANTON, NICKALLS, AND DAVE & ANNA - NOT NECESSARILY IN THAT ORDER,

WE PROVED HOW KEEN WE WERE IN THE AFTERNOON BY HAVING A GENERAL RECALL WHICH PUT OUR START BACK TO 3,50 ALBEIT ON A MUCH
SHORTENED COURSE (B, C, E, A, HOME) AND ALL TOOK OFF FOR BREEZY ON THE FALLING TIDE. HAVING HAD OUR OBLIGATORY RUBBISH
START, CHRIS & I ROUNDED 'B’ ABOUT 9TH AND SAW A GAGGLE OF BOATS MID RIVER STOPPED, AND DRIFTING OUT, WE POINTED TO MY
FAVOURITE NORTH SHORE AND SPED OFF AT HALF A KNOT. WAS IT THE BEER? WAS IT SUNSTROKE? WAS IT THE PROSPECT OF
LISTENING TO THE CRICKET? FOR SOME REASON PEOPLE STARTED TO RETIRE. (MAYBE IT WAS THE NUMB BUM SYNDROME INDUCED BY
SITTING THERE FOR AN HOUR AND GETTING NOWHERE.) WE EVENTUALLY TRICKLED UP THE NORTH SHORE DODGING MUD AND GRAVEL BANKS
(UNLIKE SEVERAL MONOHULLS WHO GOT THEMSELVES LANDLOCKED) AND GOT ROUND ‘A’ AT ABOUT 6.15 IN A SMALL PUFF - WILL WE MAKE
THE TIME LIMIT? AROUND ‘A’ TO THE DULCET TONES OF DUCKMANTON ON THE PA COMMENTATING ON OUR PROGRESS. REMINDED ME OF MY
ROWING DAYS WITH THE "CHEERS" FROM THE BANK. THE WIND DROPPED, WE DRIFTED BACK, COMING TATE A TATE WITH ‘RASPUTIN’ -
HOW EMBARASSING IN THE SIGHT OF THE COMMODORE - WE TACKED TO MISS IT, AND THE WIND CAME! NICKALLS TRIED TO PUT US OFF
BY COUNTING DOWN 1 MINUTE EARLY, BUT I SHOULD THINK WE MADE IT BY 50 SECONDS. THAT SET THE CLOCK TICKING ON THE ONLY
TWO REMAINING IDIOTS, MIKE STYLES AND OUR ARMY VISITORS, AND THEY ALSO MADE 17. WITH THE PROBLEMS OF SUNDAY'S RECALL,
AND AGAIN NO WIND, THE DECISIONM CAME TO PUT THE CAT START LAST SO THAT THE MONOS WOULD BE CLEAR. THE IDEA WAS A SMALL
COURSE WITH SEVERAL ROUNDS, SO WE WERE OFF TO BREEZY, S, A, E, A AND HOME ON A RIPPING INCOMING TIDE, STARTING INSIDE
‘D’, MOST OF US WALKED UP THE SHORE AND HELD THE BOATS WRITING FOR THE START. EVERYBODY 1S WATCHING LIKE HAWKS INSIDE
THE S-MINUTE FOR THE FERSON WHO PUSHES FORWARD RATHER THAN GETTING ON.... AND WE'RE OFF!

Ve

DECISION TIME
AGAIN, LOADS OF MONOS AND DISTURBED AIR FROM ALL THOSE ROLL TACKS INSHORE, SO WE SET OFF ON OUR NOW
OBLIGATORY NORTH SIDE FLYER, FOLLOWED BY TIM WALLACE WITH THE REST OF THE PACK INSHORE. WE GOT SOME SUPERE BREEZE AND
OVERSTOOD THE MARK TO ALLOW FOR THE TIDE, BUT THE WIND DROPPED AND WE WHISTLED BACK UPRIVER JUST IN TIME TO
SEE BIG JOHN
& CAROLINE JUST NICK ROUND THE MARK. CHRIS & I EVENTUALLY ROUNDED BY WHICH TIME BIG JOHN & CAROLINE WERE OFF
OSEA, SO
WE RESIGNED OURSELVES TO A POOR SECOND. BUT AT 'A’ WE WERE AMAZED TO SEE BIG JOHN TRYING TO
CLAW HIS WAY AROUND THE
SPIT OFF ALONG WITH SEVERAL MONOS. WE HAD CARRIED OUR OWN PRIVATE BREEZE AND SNACK AROUND IN FRONT! OK, I ADMIT IT WAS

WERE. THE

MASSIVE
TIDE AND INCREASED WIND OUR CHALLENGE BECAME SOMETHING OF A BUSTED FLUSH WHEN WE CLOBBERED
°E’ MARK AND HAD TO DO A 720,
STILL, A GOOD WEEKEND DESPITE THE COMPUTER HITCHES WITH THE RESULTS; CONGRATS TO EQUIPE NICKALLS,

WELL, FOLKS, THAT’S ENOUGH FROM NR FOR MAUREEN TO TYPE, SEE YOU NEXT MONTH....

The Challenger Trimaran funded by the MSC as a result of East Coast Piers Races will be visiting the Club on Saturday 6th July, the day before this year's race, it is hoped along with a few others. The following letter of thanks was received by the Commodore recently:

Tuesday 4th June

Dear Mr Pembleton,

Please allow me to introduce myself. My name is John King, wheelchair jockey and sometime future winner of the Admirals Cup. Recently I became the grateful recipient, via the RYA Seamanship Foundation, of the trimaran, "Marconi Challenger" and was given your name as the person to contact.

My sincere thanks to the Marconi Sailing Club for making possible the purchase of this Challenger and by it, the freedom that Sailing has brought me.

Bill Farrow, RYA ER Coach, tells me I am required to win a race at the Marconi S.C., Maldon, on 6 July. I will be there to do just that! I will be honest though, Sailing is relatively new to me and competitive sailing newer still. Methinks "homework" needs to be done. To this end would it be possible to have, if available, a copy of the Race-course plan together with its Starting Time. Any other brief but helpful points, e.g. winds, tides, currents, etc., pertinent to the Course and which you think it proper to give, would also be appreciated.

I eagerly await any reply you may care to have. Once again, many thanks for getting me Sailing.

Yours faithfully,

JOHN KING

1990 COASTGUARD INCIDENT STATISTICS PUBLISHED

Statistics published today showed that in 1990 there were 7,076 Search and Rescue operations co-ordinated by HM Coastguard, and 13,474 people received assistance from the Maritime Search and Rescue authorities.

Patrick McLoughlin, Minister for Shipping, commented:

"1990 was the busiest year so far for the Coastguard. Incidents ranged from co-ordinating assistance to fishermen and merchant vessels to holiday makers in trouble on the coastline and sailboards unable to cope with the conditions. As in past years, however, the main customer has been the recreational boat owner, who accounted for a large majority of the total calls for help.

"With the holiday season approaching, it cannot be emphasised strongly enough that the sea and the coastline can be dangerous to the unwary. I urge all who use the sea and coastline for pleasure or work to:

- get a brief on wind and tide
- be properly equipped for the unexpected
- if in doubt, call the Coastguard for advice."
