NAVIGANS PAST

1962 (January - June) - with official clots up-river and sinister plots down-river.

January - a note about the club's President, Mr.£.Eastwood, receiving the CBE in the New Year's Honours
list. Also, a note drawing attention to Barnacle's article about mooring; apparently several boats went ‘drift about' during the 1961 season. Then, of course, the inevitable note about the need to pay the annual
subscriptions on time - some hopes !

A number of ‘temporary’ sub-committees have been formed to help the (main) committee to run the club. These sub-committees are (a) the Sailing Sub-Committee (b) the Social Sub-Committee and (c) the Clubhouse Sub- Committee. I don't know about you, but I don't think they'll last very long, do you ?

The Commodore is A.M.Adams, the Vice Commodore is R.F.Sims, the Rear Commodore is 8.W.Partridge and the Sailing Secretary is A.Pratt. The Sailing Sub-Committee plan to offer sailing instruction to novice members, the training to be organised via the official club C.L.0.T. (Central Liaison Officer of Training).

By popular request, the former Menageries Fleet is, henceforth, to be known as the Handicap Class.

Information has been received about plans for a holiday camp downriver. Guess where ? Yes, you've guessed
it - on land adjoining the river near Stansgate Abbey. Also plans for an oi] refinery or store at Tollesbury.
Both this and 'the holiday camp' are to be kept under scrutiny through the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee.

Finally, the results of the 'Club Activities’ questionaire are published and, as far as the ‘Sailing Activities' part is concerned, the results were:-

Day Picnics 50 Longer Cruises 27 Cruiser Racing 12
Weekend Cruises 30 Learning to Sail 24

and the least favourite sailing activity ? I hardly dare reveal it:-

Dinghy Racing 3 votes (Oh! dear. Oh! dear. Oh! dear)

It looks more like the results of the European Song Contest.

February - the name of the Editor is missing from the title page of Navigans ! Is this merely a typing
error or has the club enforced a state of purdah on poor Daphne ? The new Hon.Sec. (G.Edwards) shows he
means business by issuing an ultimatum, effectingly saying 'pay your subs,...this is the final public warning !'
What, I ask myself, are the private warnings - and will retribution meted out to the transgressers be public
or private ? Mind you, I've no sympathy; they really ought to have paid up by now.

The dinghy parking fee is still 10/- per year; park one first come, first served basis.

A letter from Ken Beavins asking members to object to the proposed Tollesbury oi] refinery project by writing to various authorities and to the M.P. for Maldon.

A note from the Hon.Treasurer (J.H.Hind) noting, amongst other things, that the MASC own the capital assets (eg. Mamgu, Avril, ramp, etc) and that the sailing club owes the MASC £75 for the purchase of the rescue launch, and which will be repaid at £25 per year commencing 31 December, 1962. After that, the rescue launch will presumably belong to the MSC but, since the MASC owns the capital assets of the club, the launch will presumably
belong to the MASC - once we've paid for it. In the mean-time, whilst we pay our installments, the launch
belongs to the MASC. Are you confused ? So am I but I get the feeling I'm in a ‘heads you win, tails I lose! situation, but I'm sure it's all very logical to the accountants.

March - the Editor's name is restored to its rightful place - at the top of the lst page of Navigans.

A call to attend the MASC AGM in April "...to back, or oppose, as the case may be, motions tabled that may
affect the organisation of the sailing section." Now, I wonder what was going on ?

The dinghy park layout is published ( 4 rows of dinghies) with spaces allocated to the 32 members who
have
paid their fees to date. Those who haven't paid are out of luck - the dinghy park is full ! However, it
is hoped to negotiate an extension of the dinghy park with the owner of adjoining land. Cars are banned from the dinghy park and cannot be taken in even to deliver (or remove) dinghies. THAT rule applies today.

A list of BJRC handicaps shows the Solo as 102 (Terelyne sails) and 103 (cotton sails); now that's what I'd
call a sensible handicap for the Solo. The sailing programme starts on 7 April with Novice Instruction (sounds like a convent), followed by the Fitting Out Supper on board Mamgu. Sailing proper starts on 8th April with a
Tune-Up race (start 15.30) and lst Points races on 15 April (start at 11.30) - don't forget, they're tide-bound
at Heybridge. The Enterprise have an Open Series (all Blackwater club boats) of 6 (4 to count) and a club Closed Series for the Knight Cup (4 out of 6). The Fleetwind fight for the President's Cup with a series of 12 races (8 to count), whilst the Handicap Fleet sail individual races ( a small prize for each winner).

The correct title is probably spelt 'Mugg's', but our 'modern-day' spelling is probably more apt; after all, how else can you describe anyone who (voluntarily ?) sits at the wet end of a boat, takes all the spray full in the face, gets shouted at, blamed for all that goes wrong - and then has to stand second-in-line as 'the hero' receives the prize (assuming there is one).

A VERY LATE ENTRY FOR NAVIGANS - Typed by yours truely (so do not blame the Editor)

Saturday, June 8th 1991

At dawn there was no wind and rumour had it that an event "Try Sailing" would take place at the Club. Foolishly I decided that I would attend and explain that I had come to try these 'Two Hulled Things', that was safe enough as no one would want to go out with no wind.

Shortly after arriving I was standing around in an old wetsuit looking the part and very keen, when the Rear Commodore descended on me and, passing me a life jacket and harness, informed me that Lee was going to take me out. After realising that my plans as usual were going drastically wrong, I climbed on board with Lee and we set off. Lee obviously realised that Coomodores need treating with respect and took me
for a gentle tour of the river, No - He didn't put up the Reacher, No - He didn't
force me onto the trapeze. However we still seemed to cover an immense distance in no time at all.

On being safely returned to the Hard, I discovered that Pete Bloomfield was also
acting the school boy and pretending to enjoy all this crazy activity - I was
thankful for the support on at least one other person from the cruising fraternity.

At this point I was accosted by a glamorous blonde and asked if I wanted to try a Laser. I thought that I struck quite a good bargain; I would try the Laser if she would try a Sailboard. So off I went in the Laser and much to my surprise failed to tip it over but this business of hanging over the side to keep it upright is not so good for the old stomach muscles.

By the time that I returned Julie had also joined in the fun and been for a ride on a Cat. She and Pete decided to to try the Laser as a two person boat and I believe gave an excellent demonstration of the technique for righting such a boat.

I was now collared by John to try his Hurricane and who was I to argue with him. After looking at the river he decided that we should go towards Bradwell to find enough wind so that I could try the trapeze. All went well until we tacked to come back up river and mixing my legs, arms, and various bits of rope, found myself ‘skiing' beside the boat at the end of the trapeze wire. Once John had hauled me aboard and considerably shortened the trapeze wire (by golly his crew must be tall) we came up the river with both of us on the wire. I thought about suggesting that we return to the Hard but was too late, we had already passed the Club and were up beyond Osea Pier. I was able to have a breather while John 'Hove To' after Lee had the misfortune to capise, before we returned to the Hard. At this point Pete now went for another ride.

On behalf of all the others, Pete and Julie, and myself, who had a go on the boats available, may I thank all those who took the time to produce such an enjoyable day, and if you ever repeat it, I for one will definitely be there. (If I can do it, how about the rest of the cruising fraternity).

Finally I am looking forward to seeing the blonde on the sailboard sometime during the rest of the season when I am there, how about a special demonstration event by her at the Fun Day. (Mr Rear Commodore can arrange that I am sure).

Very many thaks to you all for a throughly enjoyable day.

Fun Day, Sunday, 23rd June - The rain did not dampen MarconI's enthusiasm for its Fun day entertainments for its members. Having recently held a very successful 'try sailing' Open Day, it was a the turn of the members to enjoy the amenities of the large club site and some fun and games on both water and land. The highlight was the catamaran 'fly a hull' competition which provided keen rivalry on the water and considerable mirth and admiration off the water. The practice sessions provided many capsizes, but gradually the competitors got the hang of it, the best technique seeming to be to place the the crew on the leeward side (also the wettest side!), haul in the sails to lift the windward hull and to sail as slowly as possible, the helm keeping the boat balanced as best he/she could. The first competition was sailed in westerly F4 wind and was for who could 'fly a hull' for the longest time. Steve Glynn (Prindle 19) won with a time of 3 mins. 23 secs, with David Allan (Hurricane 5.9) 2nd with 2 mins. 55 secs. So much fun was had by all that they demanded a second competition, this time who could 'fly a hull' for the longest distance. Once again Steve Glynn was the winner with just over 1 mile at his first attempt, and again David Allan was 2nd with a similar distance - but at his second attempt. However, of more significance was the time they took; each sailed on the single hull for well over 10 minutes and one unofficial time-keeper believed it was nearer 15 minutes of slow motion, slow progress sailing.

Whilst team of Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton undoubtedly won both events on Technical Merit, by popular acclaim the team of David Allan/Anna Spittle won the award for Artistic Interpretation.

And don't forget all the others; by the end of the day, many were 'flying a hull' well over 3 minutes at some time or other, and David Ball in his single-handed Unicorn was not far off rivalling David and Steve for longevity in both time and distance.

" THE MARCONI GUESSITTE"

A genuine imitation news-sheet to record the sailing reports submitted to the Essex Chronicle.

Sunday, 9th June - Marconi's Cadet Members are those who are 18 years and under on 1st January. Apart from organising Cadet winter lectures and a very enjoyable and comprehensive sailing instruction during the club's camping fortnight each year, a Cadet Members Handicap Series is also held, consisting of 6 races held at various dates during the summer months. Cadets Race 1 was held in westerly winds force 4/5 plus and an ebbing tide. Three laps of the relatively short triangular course of As 1s Fs Ds provided the opportunity for an equitable race for all entries ranging from the Mirror dinghy to the Hurricane 5.9 catamaran. However, the more experienced helms were sailing the catamarans and dominated the top places
The winner was Lucy Boreham (Dart 18) followed by Lee Harrison (Hurricane 5.9), Ben Holroyd (Dart 18) and David Ball (Topper). The less experienced helms found the wind and tide difficult to cope with but Alison Battle (Mirror) sailed particularly well to finish in 5th place. Both Rebecca Fowler (Mirror) and Clare Davies (Mirror) found the tide too much of a problem and retired, as did Stephen Caruth (Gull). Paul Harrison (Dart 15) retired after hitting a mark and three other entries decided not to start in the rising wind conditions.

For the main Marconi Summer Points Series, Race 3 started in westerly winds force 4/5 .. later rising 6/7, the Fast Catamaran Fleet found the going particularly difficult on their long course. With a number of capsized craft on the river, the Race Officer decided to abandon all races. Although this was unfortunate for the Monohull Handicap and Solo Fleets who appeared to be coping with the conditions without problems at the time, the wind continued to increase in intensity as the afternoon wore on and gusts of force 7/8 were observed on the windspeed indicator. Marconi's race support vessels performed very well and were pleased to be able to offer assistance to a neighbouring club.

Sunday, 16th June - Marconi's 5th Summer Points race was sailed in very light winds. The Fast Catamaran Handicap was won by Steve Glynn/Tom Duckmanton (prindle 19), Larry Botheras/Chris Caruth (Prindle 19) 2nd and Tim Wallace/ (hurricane 5.9) 3rd. First Dart 18 home in 4th place was the team of John Tuckwell and Lynda Chilton. In the Slow Catamaran Handicap, Willie Pitcairn/Joyce Allen (Dart 15) were 1st, Colin Kidner (Dart 15) 2nd and Paul harrison/Stuart Golding (Dart 15) 3rd.

John Salmon continued his run of successes by winning the Solo race, followed by Simon Liddington and John Rutherford. The Monohull Handicap saw a good win by Evan and Luke Davies (Mirror) with Mike and Maggie Boreham (420) 2nd.

When the time came for the 6th race of the series, the wind had virtually failed completely. As competitors walked their boats to the start-line, several continued to walk after the 5-minute gun and brought forth a bevy of protest flags. Having started the fast and Slow catamaran Handicap and the Monohull Handicap fleets, the Race Officer found himself with fleets spread out on the water with no wind to drive them. As thunder roared and lightening flashed over Maldon and threatened to make its way to Stansgate, the Race Officer decided to abandon all races, not having started the Solo fleet at all. Some disappointed competitors decided to go for a pleasure sail, but most had to be towed back eventually.

Sunday, 23rd June - the 2nd Cadet Members handicap race was held in winds SW F 4-5 over a course consisting of A (F 1 A D x 6), the small triangle giving the Race Officer the option of shortening the course, which he did after two laps. Lucy Boreham (Dart 18) scored a 2nd win in the series, followed by Lee Harrison (Hurricane 5.9) 2nd and Chris Caruth (Prindle 19) 3rd. Paul harrison (Dart 15) took 4th place whilst David Ball, having secured 4th place in race 1 in a Topper, took 5th place in his Unicorn cat. The monohulls again showed their inexperience in handling the tide, the temptation to 'strike out' for A-mark in an adverse tide immediately after rounding No.1 caused them to be swept down stream and left struggling to make their way upstream against the strongest tide stream just outside the cruiser lines. Mike Fletcher (420) took 6th place and Richard Battle (Mirror) finished in 7th place. Kerry Styles (Dart 18) unfortunately went the wrong side of D-mark and was disqualified and the remaining entrants retired.

Saturday, 22nd June - the Mud race over a 'shallow water' course, took place in very windy conditions WSW F5-6. and was run as a pursuit race. The event attracted only 4 entries, possibly because it was run on a rather dull and dismal Saturday - despite it being designated a 'Fun event and Midsummer Night Revels'. Only Malcolm Stuart (Solo) survived the course. Steve Glynn (Prindle 19) and Tom Ashley (Mirror) capsized and retired, whilst Lucy Boreham (420) attacked the boom of her boat - and lost the contest on a 'retired hurt' decision. Malcolm, having survived 4 laps and seeing no one else in sight, beached himself on Osea Island to 'wait out the time limit', launching himself in time to take the winning 'hoot' from the support boat. Malcolm's Solo victory could well have been a devine sign and could possibly be interpreted as justifying the ancient saying which goes as follows:-

"You might well call a Solo for 'water', but you can't always make it stick"

NB. only selected parts of the above reports were actually submitted over the telephone to the Chronicle

NAVIGANS ‘PAST
1962 (July - December) - kitchen sink drama, and "was there a link with the right man"?

July/August - this issue of Navigans has 15 pages, but it does cover two months news.

Mr.'Darby' Stebbens has been appointed the part-time club steward, presumably a paid post. Was he the first paid employee of the MSC ?

John Tillotson won the 2nd Cadet race with Julian Bigden 2nd; there were four entries.

A report by Miss S.P.Maxwell and Mr C.B.Hansford (both cadets ?) on the very successful camping weekend at Mersea Stone, whilst the MASC organised a Gala Day and Robbie Sims organised the impressive display of boats as the MSC contribution. In addition, an MSC Open Day attracted about 200 guests.

A letter from Peter Darney questions the amount being spent ‘on the few' at the expense of ‘the many’. He points out that only about 8 or 9 members take part in racing out of a membership of 200. That shows an interesting shift in the activities of the club; after almost 30 years, by 1991 the club membership
has increased by about 250% but those taking part in racing has (probably) increased by about 1900%.

Peter questions the need to spend more money on improving the facilities on board Mamgu, etc., in view of the possibility of moving the club to a new location. He suggests improving the facilities forordinary (presumably non-racing) members, particularly the appointment of an 00D during the ‘non-racing/non-programmed' days. He also wants such activities as picnics, cruises and camping weekends actually recognised as part of the ‘sailing programme'. Finally, he suggests that if it is felt that financial stringency does not allow
extension of facilities, an increase of subscriptions would not be amiss (since) "...ten shillings a year is
such a small sum..... - little more than two packets of cigarettes..... Ne Readers are invited to respond
to his ‘controversial letter’.

September - Daphne Tovey has had to give up the post of Editor and Phil Luke is the new Editor with his
name at the top of this issue of Navigans. A ‘set of rules' is published covering the use of the rescue launch. Amongst other things, on race days it is to be ready and tested 30 minutes before the race, but is to remain on its mooring until required by the 00D. Also, it is not to be used as a fishing boat, or for joy rides and “,..is out of bounds to members not on rescue duty."

Following Peter Darney's letter, the Committee have decided to appoint OODs for all Saturdays and Sundays
(during the season) - not just on ‘programme' days. Some of the ‘jobs needing doing', as highlighted
in the unquoted part of Peter's letter, have been taken up by ‘volunteers’ - and Peter has taken on some
of the jobs himself.

Great news - MSC have at last beaten the Ariel S.C. (BBC) in a team race event.

The Mona's cup attracted 9 entries, of which 7 capsized - and Peter Darney, no doubt weighed down by all
the jobs he's talked himself into, managed to miss out a mark. Pity the poor old Race Officer; he intended to shorten course, but got it wrong and, as a consequence, there was a ‘protest against the race committee’ which was upheld. By golly, I bet they didn't 'alf moan; with a little bit of imagination, you could almost
hear their outraged voices floating down the river on the wind - the ghosts of yesteryear come to haunt us.
That's one area of the club activities that certainly hasn't diminished !

The points races attracted 3 - 5 entries whilst the Ladies Cup attracted 4 entries and was won by Sarah Darney
with .sister/mother/daughter(?) Rosine 2nd and a certain Eleanor Eldridge 3rd. Now I'm sure I should know
who Eleanor Eldridge was, but I can't quite place her - or can I ?

An article by 'The Commodore's lady' about the delights of helping in the galley; I quote "It is a well-known principle that any sink is preferred, by wives of otherwise impeccable devotion, to that provided by her indulgent spouse, especially if a bit of gossip about the ways of said spouses be thrown in". Oh! Lord ! I hope Maggie doesn't ‘tell all' about me (signed ‘Worried, Billericay').

Finally, a ‘thank you' to the Cadets, especially the girls for helping in the galley (the boys, I suppose, had all the fun of splashing paint over themselves and each other, as well as over the club boats they were supposed to be painting).

October - Philip Luke re-introduces the ‘Editor's Comments'. Although recognising that the Main Committee
must expect to be on the receiving end of complaints, nevertheless he does wonder if some (members) regard the committee members as nurse-maids ?

MSC apparently beat the Osea S.C. in a team race event for the Beatty Challenge Trophy, but lost to Maldon Little Ship Club in another team race event. No matter, MSC helmsmen (yes, helmsmen, things were quite well ordered inthose days) took the first 5 places in a Blackwater (Sailing Club) event.

Alas, it appears that Darby Stebbens is no longer club steward - members will have to clear up after
themselves from now on.

10.

November - 200 people attended the Laying-Up Supper. Guests included the Mayor and Mayoress of Maldon
(after all, the Maldon sailors do seem to be winning everything), all the Commodores and their ladies from other Blackwater sailing clubs, plus those of the Ariel S.C. (BBC). Arthur Adam announces he will not be
standing as Commodore for the coming year - principally because he wants to start sailing again !

A certain Peter Wright, replying on behalf of the guests to Arthur's toast, reminded the assembly that his Father, G.M.Wright, (late Engineer-in-Chief, Marconi) had tried to buy Osea Island for the Marconi Company
for £4,000. I've heard of that before and believe it might have been in the 1920's or 30's.

Finally, Mrs. Lancaster (wife of the Commodore of the Maldon Y.C.),replying to the MSC President's toast
to the ladies, said " Man was God's first thought; Woman was only his second - but second thoughts are
always best".

December - at the AGM, Mr. T.W.(Terry) Hallam is elected Commodore, A.S.Bigden Vice Commodore, Peter Darney
as Rear Commodore (he must have done his particular jobs very well) and Nick Tovey is the new Sailing Secretary.

Clearly there has been some considerable ‘action’ regarding the possibility of moving to another site. Detailed reports ("based upon the report circulated to members") were given on the rival Stansgate and Maldon sites. A vote was taken to give guidance of the feeling of the membership (but will not commit the club to any particular action) as follows:-

"In the event of the club having to vacate the present site and position on the river, which of the two sites mentioned beforehand do the members consider best to move to ?"

Voting was : for Stansgate: 41 votes. Maldon: 8 votes.

Still, I can't really think anything will come of it. After all, who wants to commute to the far reaches of the river in order to sail ? No, I reckon they'll stay at Maldon, even if the tide does have a habit of leaving you high and dry at the most inconvenient times.

The last thing for December, and 1962, is an article about BACSPA (the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection
Association).

The idea for the Association developed at the beginning of 1962 when a number of planning applications, and rumours of applications, appeared to be threatening the whole future of the Blackwater Estuary as a plesant sailing area. Amongst the (then) applications and rumoured applications were:-

- a holiday camp at Stansgate
- an oil storage depot at Tollesbury

The alarm engendered amongst the sailing fraternity by the ad hoc and disparate "voice for sailing” at the Public enquiry re. "the holiday camp" so shocked everyone that, arising from an initial suggestion by the Marconi Sailing Club, the BACSPA was formed. It had its inaugural meeting at the Blackwater on
15 April, 1962.

Arthur Adam, who wrote the article, ends by saying "This club played an important part in the formation of BACSPA; we should continue to support it to the full in the future."

I know from my own brief experience on the Main Committee that the club has maintained that support by sending a representative to BACSPA meetings and getting reports of what is going on in our sailing area. I also get the impression that we might well be in need of BACSPA over the next few years,

Reading the 1962 Navigans, one gets the feeling that things are 'on the move' in more ways than one. If the size of Navigans is anything to go by, then the MSC is really getting going; most of the monthly Navigans must have had at least 10 pages and it seemed to contain a whole load of interesting bits and pieces about racing and sailing, socialising , boat and seamanship knowledge and, of course, ‘the club’.

Mike Boreham

D.I.Y. Whisker Pole

When running downwind, there is often a need to pole out the genoa or cruising chute. This is particularly so when running goose-winged as the foresail tends to be blanked by the main as the wind shifts.

Having investigated the prices of whisker poles, I decided to make my own. I bought a second-hand sailboard mast. This is made of fibre glass, is very light yet strong, and can easily be cut to length to suit. This mast is tapered and I fitted a dinghy spinnaker fitting to the small diameter end with a release cord leading to an eye fitted to the middle the pole. The thick end of the pole has a large diameter dog clip which attaches to the spinnaker pole attachment on the mast. Finally, I fitted an eye to the middle of the pole to which the spinnaker pole uphaul clips. A downhaul could be fitted if required but in practice does not seem to be necessary.

The whisker pole, complete with fittings, cost less than twenty pounds, a considerable saving on the cost of a commercial pole. I bought the mast from Jaguar yachts on Carvey Island but any sailboard dealer may be able to supply a suitable
mast.

Dave Beane, Radnigon

NAVIGANS PAST
1963 - farewell Mamgu, au revoir Heybridge, goodbye Avril, we've had to leave you now.
- welcome to Stansgate, the original ‘back of beyond'; the nearest bar's two miles away!

January - the Editor writes "This year...... may be more than ‘just another year' in the history of the
club; it may well be the year in which we move our headquarters to one of the sites mentioned at the AGM, it doesn't need a crystal ball to foresee the upheaval that will cause".

Barnacle's regular technical article is devoted to "leaks" - most appropriate for a club whose Headquarters
is a sailing barge !

February - the MASC Finance Committee has granted the Sailing Section £303 towards the expenses for 1963.

Michael Eyre has been elected Cadet Captain. Was he the same M.Eyre who took part in the 1962 Cadet races ?

If so, the Cadet Captain is, truly, a Cadet. Also an appeal for help in repairing and renovating Avril; the man-in-charge is John Scarlett. All members are reminded of the rules passed at the 1962 AGM including the requirement to have 3rd party insurance. Finally, Barnacle continues with his theme of January; in other words he's gone for another leak.

March - members are warned that sailing may be cancelled in April - and that the current dinghy park at
emTMHeybridge is only available up until May.

April - another sad loss through the death on llth April of Eric Cottam who was both a founder-member and
a past-Commodore . In the tribute to Eric, he was rated as a natural and very skilled helmsman, despite a handicap due the effects of polio at the age of 18. Our present-day link to Eric is through ‘The Mug's Mug! which , perhaps, should be more properly called 'The Mugg's Mug'. It was Eric who built the Fleetwind 'Muags' which has featured so prominently in the club's sailing results and history.

A Special General Meeting held on 10 April attracted 58 people. The Commodore (Terry Hallam) reviewed the history of the search for a shore-based site and advised that a draft lease for the Stansgate site was being considered by the Committee and (Marconi) company solicitors. The main features of the lease were:-

(a) 3-year lease with no option for an extension (e) (granted) exclusive use of the foreshore; (the club)
(b) sole use of the site restricted to MSC members to regulate its use
(c) "the club" (MSC or MASC ?) would support any (f) no boats to be placed on the sea wall
development scheme in keeping with sailing as (g) keep the site tidy, clear and circumspect with the put forward by the Landlord use of the road
(d) No high speed motor boats to be launched from (h) byelaws, when available, to be rather stringent
the site and no water-skiing to take place (i) the rent to be £ 150 per year for 3 years, with near the shore no road charges.

Not unnaturally, considerable debate ensued and it was revealed that there was no possibility of buying the eTMsite at the moment. Also, that Mamgu had been sold for £450 (subject to a surveyor's report), that all dinghies had to be removed from the Heybridge site by May, but could he moved to the new(ie. Stansgate) site from the

conclusion of the meeting (dinghy parking fees now £1 summer, 10/- winter; cruiser fees had still to be settled with the river bailiff).

It was proposed by Mr.Alan Pratt and seconded by Mr.D.Bedwell "This club changes its Headquarters from Heybridge to the Stansgate area of the river Blackwater". It was reported "there was no opposition. There were, however, two abstentions". This sounds very much like Hobson's Choice to me; what with (Mamgu's) floorboards being sold from beneath their feet, and their dinghies likely to be cast over the sea-wall, what else could the 56 members do but not offer any opposition ? I wonder why two people 'abstained' ? Faced with the choice of

‘owt or nowt', I'd have thought the real choice was really 'no choice at all'. Maybe faced with the reality
of the move they couldn't face committing themselves to the ‘short-term known" - and long term unknown. I'm
willing to bet there were many who had begun to wish they'd opted for the Maldon site instead.

Having presumably obtained the support of the club members for the move, the Commodore now reveals he has some work for them to do. He reveals that 2,000 bricks have been purchased, a lorry, complete with driver and mate, has been provided by a member and, hopefully, cement, sand,ballast and other building materials will be delivered to site. Coupled with the knowledge that the club had already secured a temporary wooden building at a cost of
£250 (and which was in store awaiting planning permission) what, I wonder ,;would have happened to all this stuff
if the meeting had decided not to support the move ? =| suppose ‘they’ would have had to keep calling Special
General Meetings until the proposal was 'successful'.

After all the excitement of the meeting and imminent move, spare some sympathy for Avril. It seems our Avril has bad leaks, split planks, broken ribs, needs re-caulking, re-filling, re-rigging and, surprise, surprise, she also need re-painting. Apart from that there's not a lot wrong with her; sounds like a candidate for a used-car mart.

However, rejoice, rejoice, for the honour of being the winner of the lst race from the Stansgate site goes to the official club-CLOT , Brian Partirdge, who won the inaugural pennant race on Easter Monday, 1963.

6.

It is worth noting that racing was severely restricted due to the need to hold working parties to complete the tremendous amount of work necessary at Stansgate. Whilst working parties were in operation, there was
to be only one race per week-end, starting at 15.30 - and even this would be cancelled if it was rough
weather due to the rescue boat not yet being in commission. Another intersting snippet is that the Sailing Instructions require all boats entering ‘internal club races' to carry a 41b.(minimum) anchor and minimum 6 fathoms of warp (unless stated otherwise in class rules) since “We think this is essential, to prevent boats being washed out to sea".

May - a very good 'fillip' to the MSC since I believe they again beat the Ariel (BBC) S.C. in a team race,
the victory being all the more sweet since the event was held at Teddington. A planned picnic on Osea was
not undertaken due to "brisk, cold winds" - sothey " sheltered in tent or car and drank their tea in comfort".

I don't blame them; our present day monohull handicap fleet had planned to have a cruise to Maldon on Saturday
15 June (1991) but it also suffered from “brisk, cold winds" and they didn't go. I personally "sheltered in
my front room and had my coffee and eccles cake in comfort" !

The first Points races from the new club site were not held until 26th May.

June - Associate Members of the MSC can now make full use of the MASC - jolly good ! On the sailing scene,
the Ladies Race was postponed due to lack of entries, the Mona's Cup was won by Brian Partridge. However, I was more interested to read that Ian Shaw and a certain Linda Partlett "capsized off Osea and were towed back"
Now, I happen to know that Linda Partlett is still a member of MSC - but under a different name as is the
wont of ladies who get married (at least is was the "wont" in those dim and distant days, but I find it all too _

confusing these days). Anyway Linda, what were you thinking about, letting the boat capsize ?

The Maylandsea Bay Challenge Cup was "rather dismal....". Apparently, 55 started but only 2 finished due to
Jack of wind. Also, the Mamgu Trophy was presented to the MSC by Mr and Mrs A.M.Adams.

August - there doesn't appear to have been a July issue, but John Tillotson won the cadet race on 20 July,
all other races being cancelled due to lack of entries. John also won the Pilot's Cup, raced from Stansgate to Maldon Promenade as a pursuit race so that the entrants would be in time for Maldon Regatta.

A note about the ‘anchor and warp' rule (sounds like a good name for a pub; perhaps we should call the MSC
the Anchor and Warp ?); | a reminder that the anchor ought, for best effect, be tied to the warp and, silly me,
the warp really ought to be tied to the boat for maximum efficiency during use ! Finally, what I believe might be the first 'lost' notice in Navigans, which was for a large V-necked pullover, with long sleeves in green/brown wool. Now, I'm certain I've seen that in the boiler-room recently.

September - alas, Avril is beyond it. Since the members didn't come forward in sufficient numbers, or with
sufficient help, to undertake the necessary repairs, Avril is to be sold since the cost of professional repair was more than her value. A much happier report that helmsman and crew, David Farthing and Rosaleen Littlewood, had changed status to "captain and mate" after the vicar had checked that no protests had been raised.

A party of Marconi Cadets visited MBYC Cadet Week in August and also the Blackwater S.C. "but couldn't compete with the easier handicapped Sprites". A few years ago, our Cadets visited the Blackwater S.C. to take part in One of their cadet races, but a sudden storm blew up, caused many capsizes and virtually obliterated the view of the scene to a few feet due to the intensity of the rain. Not one of our cadets capsized however, and all handled the situation in very seamanship-like manner, a tribute to the teaching of then-Cadet Captain, Derek Hall.

The Ladies Cup was won by Mrs Houlding (GP14) in Force 3-5, with 5 helms taking part. The Mud Trophy was won by Nick Tovey, MSC won the "Twin Flag" trophy by beating Ariel SC in a team race, and Eric Payne, in 'Rainbow', won the Stone Cruiser Trophy. Clearly, Stansgate is proving 'a lucky place' for the MSC.

October - Ian Shaw won the Cadet trophy, there being a total of 4 entries over the series.

November/December - Approximately 65 people attended the AGM. The sale price of Mamgu, at £450, was apparently
a 50% profit over its purchase price (presumably £300). We are told that the lease for the Stansgate site had been signed on 31 March, 1963, and the Commodore paid particular tribute to Alan Pratt and Jack Bigden for their efforts in getting the site fit for use. As a result of the move to Stansgate, club membership now stands at 282 (the reports says this is an increase of 82%, so I suppose many ‘original' members left the club when it was decided to move to Stansgate). One disadvantage of the new site is clearly the two mile journey to Steeple village, for we are told that the meeting, after much discussion, overwhelmingly voted for the club to apply for a bar licence. Presumably “the much discussion" concerned what beer to stock ?

Eric Payne, past-Commodore and donator of the Cadet Trophy, was voted a Life Honorary Member.

Thus ended Marconi's first year at Stansgate; a great deal of work has been achieved but a lot more remains.

In those days, did they envisage a brick-built clubhouse, 120 cruisers, some 160 dinghies and more than 60
catamarans? Of course they didn't, ; after all, they only had the site with certainty for 3 years. There must have been many who wondered if they'd done the right thing and, with all the inevitable hassle and arquement which goes with development and growth, must have looked back with nostalgia to the days of ‘the hut on the
wall' - and Mamgu.
Mike Boreham

The ‘Equal Time' Handicap Race Formula.

Formula C = —E x M x_ 100
N x A

Where C = Corrected Time; M = Number of laps completed by the yacht sailing furthest

—E = Elapsed Time; A = fctual number of laps sailed by the particular yacht
N = Portsmouth Yardstick Number

Each yachts' finishing time is adjusted in inverse proportion to the number of laps sailed, so that the adjusted time represents the time each boat should have taken to sail the same number of laps as the fastest boat. The PYN is then applied to these ‘adjusted times' to give corrected times.

SIGNING OFF

Just to remind you racing types that if you sign off as FINished, you are effectively declaring that you have completed the course as set down by the race officer and that you have complied with all the Sailing Instructions and racing rules. If you haven't, then you have no option but to sign off RETired - even if you have finished the race and received a finish gun. From my own observations, I get the feeling that sometimes helms/crews 'sign off' automatically under the FIN column without thinking, even though they meant to sign off RTD; it's an easy mistake to make but obviously could have a major effect on the results of the race and possibly deprive someone else of a well deserved 'place'.

Mike Boreham (Results Sec).

The 'Rumtub & Bung' - 21 July, 1991

The Rumtub and Bung is one of the oldest sailing events on the Blackwater, having been originated by the Mulde7 Yacht Club in the 1950s and open to all members of the BJRC clubs. For the last few years it has been run on behalf of the Maldon Yacht Club by the MSC and the race is traditionally to the Bench Head and back. Unfortunately, for the 1991 race, the lack of wind forced the Race Officer (John Salmon) to restrict the race to the Nass Beacon and back, the wind being approx easterly Force 0-1. Of the 23 starters, 7 were from

Osea SC, 5 from Steeple Bay SC and MSC, and 2 each from Maldon YC, MBYC and Blackwater SC.

With an easterly windward start and favourable tide, it initially appeared that those who started in the middle of the river had made the right choice, but soon lack of wind reduced everybody to being tide-borne only. Those close by the northern shore then whistled up their own private wind and pulled well ahead, leaving the rest struggling and frustrated. Eventually, the wind picked up enough to enable the majority of boats to make the Nass Beacon before the tide turned and helped us back to the finish in a lightish wind.

A VIEW FROM THE PIER

The 1991 East Coast Piers Race, Sunday 7th July.

The sheep went 'BAA', the cows went 'MOO' and the hens went 'CLUCK CLUCK' - but only the sheep were genuine. The cows and hens were passable imitations provided by Marconi S.C.s resident announcer Charles Anderson in his 'wakey wakey' call to the many overseas and UK visitors, and home-club members, who had entered for the 4th East Coast Piers Race held by the Marconi Sailing Club based at its extensive site on the River Blackwater in Essex. Amongst the overseas visitors were a team from the USA and three from Holland. With camping on site and breakfast provided, the entrants had no excuse for missing the 8 am race briefing ready for the 9.30 am start of the premier east coast catamaran race from Osea Island pier to Walton pier and back again. With so many other major catamaran events upset by either too much or too little wind in recent weeks, the ECPR had a particular attraction as one of the UK's major racing catamaran events.

From an entry not far short of 100, some 84 starters covering 23 different classes of catamaran actually crossed the start line in an easterly force 2-3 wind, a little less than the predicted force 3-4. The initial lead was taken by the Nacra 6.0 of Glyn Ruth and Martin Young, followed by Graham and Lynn Eeles (Hurricane 5.9) and the host Club's world class team of Robin Smith and Lisa Gatton (Hurricane 5.9). Former Olympic Champion Reg White and Stephen Olle, sailing the formidable-looking Hurricane 6.5, had to work hard to catch the leading bunch, but nevertheless had taken the lead by the time they rounded the mark at Walton Pier and started the return journey. At about 3.50 pm Reg had reached the final turning buoy just off Bradwell, some 23 minutes ahead of the Hurricane of Robin Smith who was followed at one minute intervals by the teams of Mark Barnes/Francis Ball (Hurricane 5.9), Thorn DeVries/Remco Kenbeek (Tornado), Glyn Ruth/Martin Young (Nacra 6.0) and Arie Van Der Plas/deYong Henh (Nacra 6.0). The actual line honours were taken at about 4.15pm by Reg White/Stephen Ollie (Hurricane 6.5) followed by very tight bunches of Hurricanes, Tornados, Nacras and Prindles. However, on handicap, the race was won by Robin Smith/Lisa Gaton (Hurricane 5.9); 2nd - Mark Barnes/Francis Ball (Huricane 5.9); 3rd - Brian Piggott/Terry Beech (Hurricane 4.9). The light wind unfortunately meant that most of the smaller catamarans such as the Dart 18 were officially 'out of time' at the limit of 6pm, but many still arrived before 6.30pm and the Race Officer timed them all in.

A particularly noteworthy performance was that of Tim Swinburn/Susie Pepper (Dart 18) who were the only Dart 18 to finish inside the time limit and achieved 7th place on handicap, just behind the Hobie 18 of Paul Pascoe/Guy Warr.

Just over 20 support craft covered the whole course. Of the 84 starters, only 3 retired and 2 others requested a tow back. The rest enjoyed a slight increase in wind as they approached Bradwell and had the immense satisfaction of completing the course, if not under their own steam, then under their own sail.

OF CATS AND CREWS

In response to requests from our revered editor, I am not going to report all the sordid details race by race (thank God, they all cry) in order to save space.

The Cat Fleet
continues to go from strength to strength with Sunday 11th August having a
turnout of 26 boats in superb Force 4-5 Westerly conditions. That is actually more than the Hurricane 4.9 Nationals, and as marly as several Open Meetings.
Entries for the Summer Series have reached the unbelievable level of 36 boats!! Racing continues to be as keen as ever, no longer is it good enough to turn up regularly to guarantee success, you now have to win or come second to have a sniff at
the overall prizes. Congratulations to Steve Glynn and Tom Duckmanton on their win in the Series and to Dave and Anna for the close second. Obviously, this sort of success brings its own problems, with much closer proximity between boats and the resultant increase in "incidents". I’m delighted to say that Sportsmanship (the capital letter is deliberate) has been almost without question. Having sailed in various big club fleets in the 70s I can tell you that it is very refreshing to see the level of responsibility adapted by the Cat Fleet. Well done, you guys!
Fortunately most contacts have resulted in nothing more serious than a 720 or possibly a protest meeting. Just beware though as you improve in standard through the fleet, increasing demands and expectations will be placed upon you rounding marks
etc. - that’s all part of learning to sail faster!! In previous articles I've
mentioned that you could catch up rapidly in a Cat if you dropped a clanger, that’s no longer the case. If you’re not somewhere close to the box seat at the start, it’s
goodnight!

The problem is now to decide where we want to go as a Fleet in the medium term. Several points need ta be considered and probably aired at the Cat Fleet Meeting
(which will be held late October/early November - watch this space) ard I'd like to
ask for you to think about items you'd like discussed and let me know. It is your Cat Fleet, and up to you to make of it what you want. I obviously include, in my plea for comments, those people who don’t race. I have come to recognize over the past year that the very strength of Marconi is based on its breadth of types of sailors all with very different priorities for their requirements from the facilities, so if I don’t see you down at the Club on a Sunday (or Saturday) please do your best ta let me know your thoughts.

Away from the serious for a moment, 80% of the Prindle Fleet spent August Bank Holiday in Sunny Weymouth at the National Regatta and I am delighted to be able toa report that the Club reputation was more than upheld. In fact I think we had the biggest single attendance from any Club. The weather was immaculate except that the ward was rarely above Force 2 (no real drifters though) and with all due modesty I have to say that Steve and Tom, Chris and I spent the whole time mixing it with the leaders. Corigrats ta the aforementioned pair for their fourth place overall (I'11 get you next year Glynn). It was an education ta sail at that end of a very competitive fleet where, although sailed very fairly, no quarter was given or asked for, and I’m sure all Club crews learnt a lot. Just watch out in the Autumn Points!!

Larry Botheras

FUTURE OF UK MARINE RADIO-NAVIGATION

(Press Notice No. 174 from the Department of Transport, 21 June 1991)

The Decca Navigator marine radio-navigation system is to be retained in United Kingdom waters, Malcolm Rifkind, Secretary of State for Transport announced today. Mr Rifkind’s decision follows a review of the position reached in the International negotiations on the alternative proposal to replace Decca with Loran C, together with consideration of revised proaposals from the Racal Electronics Company for automating the UK Decca chains at lower cost.

Answering a Parliamentary question from Dr Charles Goodson-Wickes MP (Wimbledon), Mr Rifkind said:

"The United Kirigdom has been negotiating over a period of time with eight other countries on the possible adoption of Loran C as part of a joint regional system of marine radio-navigation in north west Eurcepe and the North Atlantic. My right honourable Friend, the then Secretary of State told the House in April 1990 the conditions on which the United Kingdom would in principle have been prepared to eriter into an international agreement if it could be achieved by mid-1991. Some but not all of those conditions have been met. But a new factor has been a revised proposal recently put to me by the Racal Electronics Company to modernise and operate the existing Decca chains in the UK at a lower cast than in their 1988 proposal.

"IT have examined the proposal carefully and Racal have made further improvements to it. I now have decided to accept the Racal proposal and to withdraw from the Loran C discussions. Two main factors have led to this conclusion. First, it is now very doubtful whether an international agreement could be concluded and brought into effect which would both ensure a three-year transitional period before the closure of the UK Decca system (under the existing contract by early 1997) and avoid a price increase in the Loran C investment. Second, the revised Racal proposal means that the case has changed significantly in favour of retaining the Decca system, bath in the overall economic appraisal and in the effect on light dues. After taking account also of the casts of a change for users, I have concluded that, despite some factors which point towards Loran C, it would no longer be reasonable to impose this change of system on the UK user community. In reaching this caornclusion, I have had Particular regard to the representations made to me by the fishing and electronics engineering industries against a charge to Loran C, ard to the fact that the Decca system continues to serve the mariners’ needs satisfactorily within the overall requirements of marine safety.

Our partners in the international negotiations on the Loran C proposal are being informed of my decision. I now intend to invite the General Lighthouse Authorities to give effect to my decision by entering intca formal negotiations with the Racal company on a new contract for operating the Decca system."

NAVIGANS PAST - 1964

This chapter of 'Navigans Past’ is dedicated to the memory of Gordon Golding whose sudden and unexpected death on 14 August has caused his.family and many friends so much sadness and sorrow. Gordon's links with the club go back to its very beginnings and I know he enjoyed reading this Navigans Past series of articles. Equally, I very much enjoyed our conversations as he told me of his personal reminiscences of 25-35 years ago when he was a very successful racing helm. His name is on many a trophy throughout the length of the river from the Blackwater S.C. to Tollesbury. Part of the aim of the Navigans Past series is to remind us of how much we owe our present-day successful club to the efforts of the past members; Gordon was very active in the club long before I joined it and I am grateful not only for knowing him, but also for his part in the making of the club all those years ago.

January - an announcement of the names of the members of the six sub-committees of Finance, Clubhouse, Sailing,
Social, publicity - and Bar ! The Editor, Phil Luke, explains the recent deterioration in the readability
and quality of recent Navigans issues. Poor ‘readability’ is due to ".....a senile typewriter which has gradually
got worse and worse" and "...the poor way in which the copies have been run off the stencil." Poor ‘quality’
is due to ".....the almost complete lack of material; if it wasn't for Barnacle, Navigans would be almost non-
existent." Actually, I thought the content was pretty good but I guess he's complaining that not enough people submit material; as usual it is all down to 'the few'. Phil goes on to complain he has received no write-up on the Laying-Up Supper, Christmas Eve dance, talks by Charles Stocks and Kit Hobday or the Norfolk Broads film evening. However, he had received a separately circulated social news letter which obviously didn't
please Phil for he says "...this would seem to be the answer - let each sub-committee send out its own news
sheet and to the devil with Navigans". I get the impression all is not well in the hierarchy of the club ! Anyway, the exasperated Phil has my sympathy.

By the way, the good Barnacle wrote an article entitled "Steaming the ribs"; well, that makes a change from our modern-day predilection to barbeque the spare ribs. However, Barnacle was, of course, talking about boat building in the pre-GRP era.

February - The Hon.Sec (G.Edwards) writes that club pin badges are now for sale. Also, the club's Sailing
Rules are published.but the best announcement is that " the brewers have initiated the new bar - and it's
now ready for opening time." Three cheers everyone Hic! Hic! Hooray.

Rear Commodore,
Peter Darney, writes " in thecase of good sailing manners and consideration for others, our club
is noticeably at least as good as other clubs on the river..." He also comments on the racing rules and

(the raising of) protests; "...if you have a good reason to protest against a competitor, then do so, as it
will encourage others (and yourself) to stick to the racing rules...".

March - a "thank you" letter from Eric Payne for the retirement present of life-jackets from MSC members upon
his retirement from the Marconi Company; he is, of course, also a Life Honorary Member of the MSC

A successful children's party, masterminded by Jack Bigden but assisted by many others, was held at the clubhouse

at Stansgate for 25 children (4 - 10 years). If that was the old wooden clubhouse at Stansgate, it must have
been mightily crowded. I bet there'sa few late 30s /early 40s 'kids' who will remember uncle Jack dressed as a clown, surrounded by pirates and such. In the late 1970s, I can remember Damian and Lucy gojoying the club's Christmas parties at the MASC.

Thiswissue contajns ‘the MSC Racing Rules’ (as distinct from the Sailing Rules). A new points system is to be used ie. Ist = “4, 2nd = 2, etc, llth and over earns 11 points, non-starter/retired earn 11 points, and disqualified/non-entry earns 15 points. Races cancelled due lack of entries or bad weather, each entrant earns 7 points (why ?) and abandoned races = 7 points (again why ?)

I don't know whether a loose-leaf notice belongs to the March or April Navigans, but it announces the Marconi Regatta Day Cruiser Event, 2lst June, 1964, with an entry fee of 2/6. The event will be in the nature of a seamanship or obstacle race, the object being to have a pleasant day out. Was this the birth of the club's
Regatta - or merely an event of the same name ?

April.
- Mr Sawyer of Steeple Post Office has kindly agreed to hold 3 sets of clubhouse keys - but no
unsocial hours please ! The club has bought a brand new 14ft dinghy for use as an inshore rescue boat at a price of £114.5s.0d with a 5 h.p. Seagull at £38. The MASC paid £75 towards the cost (of the boat only)
and the MSC has to find the remainder - plus the cost of the engine. Commodore Terry Hallam hints that
4/- from each of the approx. 300 members could meet the sum - one voluntary basis !

Clubhouse Rules include:-

(a) no children under 10 allowed in the clubhouse unless accompanied by an adult
(b) no dogs allowed in the clubhouse or to roam free on the site
(c) no gambling on club premises.

8.

Barnacle continues with his series of articles, the latest being entitled "Any fool can screw". Sometimes our friend Barnacle surprizes me; 1 wonder who he (or she) was ?

May - John Perrin is the new Editor for Navigans. John, being full of enthusiasm and hope, says he wants
more articles and club news from members, a possible (new) front cover for Navigans - and he hopes to be
able to maintain the magazinets tiigh standard. Hang about, I thought Phil Luke had been complaining about the poor quality, etc ?

June - Terry Hallam's appeal for donations toward the new rescue boat engine has raised £15.17s.0d towards
the £60 target sum. On the sailing side, the club obviously hosted the Graduate Southern Championships since a "thank you" letter from the Graduate Association is published. The Ladies Cup race scheduled for 20 June has been postponed to 4 July due to only two entries being received.

July - John Perrin's wish to adopt a new front cover has been swiftly fulfilled. The new design incorporates
the capital letter 'N' of 'Navigans' with the outline of a sailing boat - but I feel the effect is not quite
right. I keep seeing the left-hand side of 'N' as a pot-plant, whilst the rest spells ‘lavigans'. However, we should not decry the good efforts of our predecessors. With the benefit of hindsight, it is interesting to see , little-by-little, the departure of the club from being merely the ‘sailing section of the MASC' to becoming the Marconi Sailing Club with its unique and recognisably separate identity. How long, I wonder, before full independence is achieved ?

Mrs Sutherland (whose husband was Managing Director and Deputy Chairman of Marconi Co.) has presented a new boa to the club; it is called 'Brazil'. We still have Brazil asa club boat, along with Idlevice and the two mini-
sails - plus presumably the sailboard. A total of £28.17s.0d. has been raised towards the target of £65 to

On the sailing side, 10 entries for the Ladies Race which was won by Jane Cottam. Ian Shaw (Fleetwind) and a Mr.Whiffin (Kestrel) did well in the Blackwater & Colne Dinghy Championships (200 entries, plus alarm spread by a fleet of 'Hell Cats'). to Osea for a picnic, some 9 people crowding into Jack Bigden' causing Jack some consternation apparently. Finally, "beware of venemous snakes" by the gun emplacement !

August - Stan and Margery Allerton held their Silver Wedding Anniversary at Stansgate, the event being
celebrated "more uproarously than usual" - and ending in midnight sailing and swimming. Marconi cadet
members took part in the MBYC Cadet Week, and won the team race against the MBYC cadets. Also, an obviously very sincere ‘thank you' to the club's cadet members for their hard work and assistance with club events, both sailing and social.

Arthur Adam and crew came 6th in class and 7th overall in an East Anglian 0.R.A. race from Harwich - Ostend, with

Considering that in April, we appeared to have approx. 300 members, the number of boats registered appears to be surprizingly low; I wonder why ?

September - 'The Committee' (main or Sailing ?) have discussed the adoption of a 3rd racing
dinghy class and
Commodore Terry Hallam writes an article on the subject. The club's original adopted class (Fleetwind) "seems to have developed into a class for Cadets", whilst the 2nd adopted class (Enterprise) appears to be relatively
expensive (£200 + £30 for sails) and ",..requires a certain amount of agility to keep it upright, and to race
Properly the average person would have to be on the right side of 40". (NR. Now you modern-day Enterprise sailors, read that as you will; I'm saying 'nowt !). Terry's article quite clearly favours the Snipe class, on the basis of growing fleets at nearby Stone, Maldon, Maylandsea and Burnham
- and that one local helm was
apparently National Champion at 69 and, at 70, is still going strong. Well, that's encouraging; move over, Lucy, I can't wait to get at that Dart 18.

Peter Darney follows up with a letter to the Editor on the same theme but seems to favour two new classes.
He
leans towards the Snipe for the “older member" and another (less expensive ? more exciting?) class for "the
younger and probably impecunious racing tyro". Mind you, there are no Snipes in the club at present but the Commodore can/will arrange some demo-Snipes at Stansgate for 4th October.

On the Social side, the Laying Up Supper is to be held on 13 November at the Marconi Research Laboratory Dining
Room (sounds very exotic - "whatcher wan’ deaarh ? am an' chips or plaice an’ chips?"). However, it's good
value for money with dancing to the Blue Ramblers Orchestra and tickets at 18/6 inclusive (but they don't say inclusive of what ?).

A notice draws attention to the fact that, under the terms of the lease, we are not permitted to use the east

side of the hard. It's just as well we only had 5 catamarans in those days.

9.

We finish with a note on the successful Cadet Weekend (22/23 August) in which we were joined by Cadets from
Maylandsea and Stone clubs. I quote "....the cadets on the river all know each other well both on and off
the water, and this produces some very keen racing". Clearly the local sailing scene was very different from that of today and I wonder what 'state of development' the Stone SC had reached to still find time to send its Cadet members down to their near neightours; would it work today ?

October - A correction to last month's notice re.use of hard; we can use the east side. It appears it is the
west side we can't use. Ah ! A very easy mistake to make by the informant but let's hope he (or she ?) is not navigator on your boat for a time.

Re. the laying-Up Supper, someone else must have asked ‘inclusive of what?' because we are told the 18/6 includes dinner, wine, free buffet and dancing.

Terry Hallam's 'Buy a Snipe ‘cos it's a snip’ article has, I fancy, touched a few raw nerves amongst some members in the club. Ken Beavins (signing himself very formally as Kenneth S.Beavins) takes Terence Hallam to task for his obvious bias towards the Snipe. Ken states "To my mind it would be about as reasonable for him
to advocate the adoption of the Blandford Twelve Footer - we do at least have one of these boats in the club
already". I get the impression there's a bit of heat being generated around the club.

On the actual sailing side, the Mud Trophy is to be held on 25 October. Apparently the Sailing Committee had a problem since the 'traditional course' around Northey is rather a long way off now. It has been suggested that the mud banks between the MSC and Mersea be used.

You can buy a 2nd-hand Enterprise (Terylene sails) for £120, or buy Eric Payne's GP14 (cotton sails)

November/December - two issues in one. Dinghy Park fees for the 1965 season are to be £1 (1 March'95 -
30 April'66) or 10/- (1 September'65 - 30 April'66). The mooring fees (paid to the club thence to Maldon
Borough) are to have an additional 10/- to the club itself for dinghy space for tenders, previously, cruiser Owners managed to get away with it free of charge.

Commodore Terry Hallam's ‘Christmas Greetings' state "...this has been the best season for many years...." but
I think he means 'weather-wise' rather than 'sailing-wise'. In his Commodore's report, we read we have a total of 513 subscription-paying members made up of:-

237 Marconi Employees; 78 Associate Members; 46 Cadet Members
101 Marconi family Members; 51 Associate Family Members;

This shows a remarkably rapid growth since the club moved to Stansgate, and particularly since April'64 when
we apparently had approx. 300 members. However, Terry points out that out of the 100-odd dinghies in the
dinghy park, only a few supported the racing. In fact, the results sheets show 32 different dinghy helms took part in the Points and Handicap Series, whilst there were no cruiser entries except 4 in the Cruiser Cup.

The race results show that 'the younger elements' (ie Cadets) were as big a 'pain' to their ‘elders and betters’ in those days (in that they would keep winning the non-cadet races) as they are today. I sometimes think the term 'Cadet' gives the wrong impression i.e. that of young children ‘mucking about’ in boats to the superior amusement of the 'real' (ie.adult) sailors. Our Cadet Members are, by definition, aged up to and including 18 years of age, effectively covering a range from guininely ‘very young children' to ‘young adults'. In fact,
as I recall the exploits of ‘Cadet Members' such as Colin Harper, Chris and Robert Weedon, and Caron, Heather and Penny Stuart, I can't help feeling we need a designation other than 'Cadet' to cover the age range. When I hear the term 'Cadet', my mental image is of 8-12 year olds charging around in Opies rather than the real vision of the Hornets, Lasers and Solos of Colin and Co., or the Hurricans and Darts of todays 'Cadet' members.
Has anyone a better term than 'Cadet' to describe the ‘up to and including 18-year old' members ?

compare, I wonder, with today, taking account of inflation ? A big ‘thank you' to ".......the unsuspecting

now

Snippet Corner

Bob Fisher's column in Yachts and Yachting (30 August, 1991) threw up two interesting ‘snippets’.

The first concerned ‘starting techniques’ but the interesting bit was not so much the ‘techniques’ but the name he mentions. The forename 'Simon' is not all that common, nor is the surname ‘Darney', so when the

two appear together, it is likely to be even less common. It appears Bob was sailing (crewing ?) for a Simon Darney in the Hornet world championships in Holland “some years earlier" and I wondered if this was the same Simon Darney who featured so often in the Marconi prize list also “some years earlier" ?

The second snippet from Bob's column concerns what might be called ‘starting technicalities’. It is of interest because of the recent club protest raised when a competitor, before the actual start signal, passed the club's Quter Distance mark (G) on the correct side but, because G was some considerable distance on the pre-course side of the start-line, the competitor was able to effectively start ‘outside’ G in the slacker tide, having followed the course instructions as laid down and broken no racing rules. Bob Fisher writes:-

"The partial failure of the ground tackle of the inner distance mark........could easily have negated
Kolius's starting advantage. As (the inner distance mark) had drifted well behind the line, there were a few smart sailors, Lawrie Smith and Harold Cudmore amongst them, who realised that in the light air they could come up to the mark with a couple of minutes to spare and tack ahead into it to go into the area the race committee has sought to deny the fleet. Perfectly legitimate. It also gave them the

opportunity to tack early....... ..out of the adverse current ".

Well, it's nice to know some of our home-grown helms are at one with the champions.

Our race officers had better watch where they place those start-line ‘distance markers' from now on; you can imagine the whole fleet jostling for room to start ‘outside* the mark, all shouting “what's

good enough for Harold is good enough for me" - or words to that effect !

light-wind skill to score a well-deserved win in his Mirror dinghy to win the race which was shortened at Osea
Causeway.

With a westward start and incoming tide, a little bit of wind before the start encouraged some of us to move
well onto the pre-course side of the start line, the plan being to sail, with whatever wind was availble at
the time, down to the start line, reaching just inside D mark in the strongest part of the helpful tide just
as the gun sounded. Alas, such plans went awry when the wind virtually died completely, and we merely drifted
slowly with the tide, whilst those nearer the line also drifted with the tide to A mark - but considerably
ahead of we who 'got it wrong'. I believe Damian Boreham (Prindle 18.2) was first around A mark, but Richard
Battle's Mirror was close behind in second place. The course required Osea to be passed to Port, so the fleet
struggled to cross the tide to Osea island. Some of the monohulls made it to Osea shore and crept slowly towards
No.l in the slack tide. I, being more hopeful, stayed out in the tide hoping (a) wind would come and (b) the
tide would turn any moment. Alas none of things happened and 1, together with others, paddled our way back to
the MSC. Of course, as we neared the club, the wind got up, the tide turned and we had the best sail of the
day - but no longer in the race. Those made of sterner stuff (or not too worried about packing up their

caravans/tents) continued in the race and were rewarded with the same increased wind. Unfortunately, the race
was shortened at Osea Causeway, it being feared (not unreasonably) that Northey Causeway would be ‘high and dry'.
However, some boats continued the whole course - and just made it across Northey causeway with a bit of pushing
and shoving.

By chance, Maldon Y.C. also held their Figure-of-Eight on the same day, but shortened their race to ‘round Northey'
only.

HOLDIAY RAMBLINGS

We took *Rodnigon’ down to Brittanny again this year, or rather, Rodnigorn took us. This time we determined ta get a bit further south than last year when we were frustrated in our attempts to get to L’Abervac’h. Sa off we went via Dover (rally but friendly); Newhaven (what a rip-off); the Hamble; Alderney; Guernsey; the
Treguier river to Roscoff - our ultimate point of last year. From Roscoff it was a
rice sail in not very nice weather along the racky Brittanny coast and so into L’Abervrac’h. This was as we had imagined the entrance, dramatically rocky but very well marked, although we were not able to use the advertised transits as the visibility was only a mile or so (Thank you, Mr Decca. )

From L’Abervrac’h we pressed on south to the Cheval Du Four. Again, this was well marked although not as dramatic as we had imagined, although we are told that wind versus tide conditions can give problems. Once through the Four we set course far Camaret which is a popular kicking off point for yachtsmen heading to south Brittarny via the Raz de Sein. It can get very crowded here in the holiday season but we were lucky and found a pontoon berth with no problems. Camaret is also a fishing port and the town itself has plenty of small shops and restaurants. We then decided to explore the area around Brest and so proceeded eastwards through the Goulet de Brest and south of Brest itself before anchoring for the night in one of the many bays. This area is one of great French naval activities with warships ard shore establishments in all directions.

The next day was sperit on an exploration of the River Aulne, very pretty with steep wooded banks and a high road bridge, with lots of clearance.
the We then returned ta marina at Brest and a cycle round the town. Subsequently we paid another visit to Camaret before turning back north to Rosceoff via the charmel that leads between L’Isle de Batz ard Rascoff. We then motarsailed from Roscoff to Guernsey St Peter Port and then up to Alderney. On this leg we had a close view of the Casquets, quite a frightening sight even in relatively calm weather. This time Alderney was bath very crowded and rally in Braye Harbour, we had quite an uncomfortable right at anchor trying ta stay in our bunks, thank heaven for lee cloths.

Setting off on the afternoon tide en route ta Brighton we had a favourable SW wind and were soon bowling along under spinnaker with eight knots groundspeed showing on the Decca and reached Brighton early the next morning. The entrance to Brighton was quite rough in the Force 5 Southwesterly, so it was nice to get inside the relative calm of the marina. Much better value here than Newhaven, with all kinds of nice facilities, shape, restaurants nearby. Aryway there we were, 2 hours out of Brighton Marina en route to Ramsgate on the penultimate leg of our return to MSC. We had a rice following wind but the genoa was getting blanked by the main. Sarah was aff watch below asleep (I thought) in her bunk. Time to try the cruising chute, so autopilot on, roll in the genoa ard hoist the chute. At this stage came the realisation that I had underestimated the wind strength and Rodnigon rolled into a fairly dramatic broach which laid her well over. Strange noises from below indicated that all was not well, and having sorted out the broach, a glance through the hatch gave sight of a white, somewhat frightened face peering out of the heads compartment. I told Sarah that in future she should keep the helmsman informed of her movements, but this instruction was rot well received. Still, never mind, at least we were an speaking terms by the time we were dodging the hovercraft which were squirting out of Dover harbour at amazing speeds.

As a sort of hardy hint to MSC intrepid travellers, we found out the hard way that anyone intending to cruise in the Channel the Islands area should fit a stripper to propeller shaft. The area seems to attract a lot of flotsam and on three separate occasions we had encounters with bits of net, the first being a twelve foot length of cargo net. Even if you do not have the misfortune to meet any bits of net, the local seaweed is both prolific and tough, and tends ta form a ball around the propeller. This can often be cleared by rurming astern, but does manifest itself by a mystifying loss of power as the weed builds up. The alternative to fitting a stripper is to always carry a mask and flippers, but with the proviso that diving underneath the boat in the open sea is not recommended.

Dave (Beane) & Sarah, Rodnigon

Gordon Gelding - Family Man and Good Club Member

I am sure that many members, particularly those of you who date back to the early days at Stansgate, were deeply shocked to learn of the totally unexpected death of Garden Golding. It had been only a week previously that we had been reminiscing together over the old days and the beauty of the Stansgate location.

I first met Gordon in December 1967 when he became Club Coxswain and I became Hosun. Jack Bigden was Commodore, Dennis Byatt Fleetwind Captain, and Terry Hallam Cruiser Captain. Our roles and our sailing Sub Committee work brought us into close ccarntact. Every weekend he was there, either keeping a watchful eye on the proceedings, or at the tiller of Rescue Boat No.1 (still in business as the Cruiser Workboat.) I also remember him organising Barbecues with Jack Bates at the M.A.S.C.

It was during this time that a certain young lady, Leonie Carlisle, was racing and winning pennants in the family Heron "Misterbloac",

Our sympathy goes cut toa Leonie, her family and friends, in the hope that the fellawship ard memories provided by the Club will provide comfeart and support in the difficult times ahead.

Ron Greygoase

RIVER BLACKWATER DEVELOPMENT - THE CURRENT SITUATION

1. Speed limits can only be set by the Maldon District Council at 250 metres from the
shore. Water ocutside these boundaries have no speed restrictions.

2. Further speed restriction could probably only be achieved by Act of Parliament, or
by a River or Harbour Authority. The cost of setting up the latter would be in the
region of £500, 000. 00.

3. In general, it could be agreed that so far the vast majority of River users have
enjoyed their sports/pastimes withsout serious interruption except for that small minority of unthinking or ill-informed users.

4. All recognised Clubs and Water Sport Activities generally regulate their
respective Membership in an exemplary manner.

5. The main problems on the River seem to stem mostly from casual visitors who gain
access via Public Launching sites.

& Lack of manpower and policing of the River, particularly at weekends, does not provide the degree of safety and control which we all believe necessary on the water.

7. Maldon District Council states that it is powerless to control Public access to
the River and has, to date, resisted all requests to control entry at these points, although it has the power to do so.

8. Residents local to these access points have their own problems, especially at
Stone, of illegal parking, noise and abuse from the casual visitors as no facilities are available for car and trailer parking close by.

3. Unless we, the River Users, can agree on our own requirements for leisure and
water activities, it seems likely that the Authorities will be satisfied to make na changes. Only consultation on agreed policies for recreation on and around the River is likely to achieve any degree of safety or an improvement in our environment.

NOTE: IF YOU AGREE WITH THE ABOVE PRECIS, WHICH IS BELIEVED TO BE A FAIR
REPRESENTATION OF THE CURRENT CONDITIONS CONTROLLING SFORT AND RECREATION ON AND
AROUND THE RIVER BLACKWATER, PLEASE LET US CONSIDER THE OPTIONS AVAILABLE TO US
TODAY, ACT ON THEM ACCORDINGLY AND NOT WAIT FOR WHAT MAY BE POSSIBLE AT SOME TIME IN
THE FUTURE.

THESE WOULD INCLUDE:

A. SPECIFIC REGULATION AND MANNING OF PUBLIC ACCESS POINTS.

B. LOCALLY AGREED ZONING OF SPECIFIC AREAS SET ASIDE FOR SPECIFIC SPORTS AND
ACTIVITIES BOTH ON AND OFF THE RIVER, BEARING IN MIND TRADITIONAL PATTERNS OF USE!

C. AGREED RULES OF CONDUCT FOR RIVER USERS.

D. IMPROVED RELATIONS WITH THE POLICE, MDC AND OTHER AFFECTED GROUPS AT LOCAL AND
DISTRICT LEVEL TO WORK OUT WAYS AND MEANS OF ACHIEVING THESE OBJECTIVES TOGETHER.

result from the overall score. You have been warned..........
