S" FOUR-DAY VOYAGE
"GEMMA?

We had originally planned a week in France - ALONE. Those of you who know the
Bigden tribe will appreciate that the chance for the adults to escape without the
various combinations of kids is rare. However it was not to be - one link in the
babysitting arrangements fell through at the last minute and we were left with just 4 precious days on our own. As our boat Gemma is a 2aft. Corribee, we don’t go far with the gang on board, so Tim likes to sail to new places and had always had a yearning to try the Haverngore route into the Thames. We are quite the "Maurice Griffiths" fans, and prefer the quiet creeks and unspoilt areas to Marinas etc.

Friday Sth June saw us arriving on board with enough supplies for a fortnight —-Tim
always complains I take too much. At 07.40 next morning we left with the ebb under
blue skies, white clouds scudding across in the stiff breeze - perfect conditions for
sailing - except the frosty conditions aboard due to a difference of opinion. That
was soon resolved and conditions were so good we arrived at the Wallet Spitway with the tide out of the Crouch still against us (nothing to do with the Captain misjudging, you understand). So we decided to dry out on the edge of Huxey for lunch. Mind you, that was misjudged too and we ate our lunch bumping up and down,
testing the keel plates on the hard sand - not good for the nerves. Just as we
motored off, when we could no longer endure the grinding, a friendly seal _ kept circling the boat and popping his head out of the water every so often, he kept us company for a while. We stopped off at Burnham for supplies (more?), namely a chart and mango chutney.

Once into the Roach we motored into Yokesfleet Creek, Middleway and Narrow Cuts to take a look at the bridge. A chat on the VHF with the bridge keeper confirmed the bridge could be opened in the morning 1 hour before High Tide when we planned to leave (he keeps a listening watch on Ch 16, or call on Ch 72, call sign Shoe Bridge.) Our main concern was the depth. Jack Cootes’ excellent book ‘East Coast Rivers’ recommends the passage only in High Water Springs, but it was approaching Neaps. Gemma only draws 0.8m so we weren’t too worried as long as the water was calm. Weather conditions affect the depth too, with less water in settled High Fressure. We motored back into The Middleway and enjoyed a superb curry (hence the mango chutney) accompanied by the call of various wild life and a magnificent sunset - Maurice Griffiths was right.

The captain recalculated the tidal heights and announced we might not make it in the
morning. Next morning dawned - another beautiful day - just the early mist lifting
off the marshes in the morning sun and we passed through the bridge at approximately 07.40 with the water like a mirror, tide still flooding. The bridge keeper was more
than helpful - you must keep as close as possible to the line of cans on the port
side until well over the broomway (the shallowest part). The echo sounder was
reading 1.2.... 1.1.... and stopped registering, and we expected to ground any
moment. However, with the keeper talking us through the guiding us, the echo sounder started to read again and we were over. Once ofer the broomway we headed for the black beacon, whilst
eating a celebratory breakfast. Just before we passed over the edge of the sands,
a salutory reminder of how unkind the sands can be - a _ yacht’s
mast, complete with shrouds intact, sticking about 3-4ft. out of the water. Can’t have been long ago she came to grief.

Our plan was to cross the Thames to the Medway and it was just a matter of buddy
hopping - South Shoebury, Sea Reach No.1, Medway, and then parallel with the coast,
inshore of the marked shipping lane. A glorious run most of the way, sunbathing in the cockpit. We kept well in to the East Shore in the entrances to the harbour, until a ferry got rather agitated at us as he was trying to leave his berth. As we
tacked toa get out of his way, the yacht behind us did the same - he seemed to have
been doing our favourite in a new river - following someone who locked like a local
and knew his way in. Into the Swale and Queensborough seemed like the best place ta
stop for lunch - but it was hot and crowded and we had to share a mooring with
someone’s dinghy just off the causeway so we didn’t go ashore.

Set sail again to explore the Swale; on the last bend before Kingsferry Bridge, Tim went to start the outboard and the starter cord pulled out. We had to anchor while he fixed it. After we finally got going under power we then had to wait for the bridge to open, amongst a large crowd of jet skis and motor boats whining up = and down. So far, the lack of scenery combined with this assault on the nerves, had decided us that the river is not one of the best on the East Coast. By the time the bridge lifted at 16.20 there was a queue of boats waiting to pass on both sides, not without some jockeying for position I might add. Once through the bridge the scenery didn’t improve and we decided to motor, although the outboard was playing up -

9.

speeding up slightly and then dying on us - fuel starvation diagnosed, but no obvious
cause.

After a chat with a local from Oare Creek we decided to follow him and either = anchor
at Harty Ferry or in Faversham Creek. Following him found us aground - and him as
well - sc much for local knowledge again. AS we passed Harty Ferry we could see the
Ferry House Inn on the hill, but weren’t happy to anchor under the north shore as the ward was from the N.E. and not recommended with the fierce current on the early ebb, ever though this is the most attractive bit on the Swale. Soa, into Faversham Creek, and after advice from the local fishermen we tied up against a Cornish Crabber just
inside Oare Creek. Ashore is the Shipwright’s Arms - no electricity, gas or running
water and an atmosphere all of its own - low ceilings, a curious mix of odd chairs
and tables and a simple menu - 3 assorted fillings in french sticks, meat pie or the
house ‘speciality’ Garlic bread and salar OR Garlic bread with melted cheese and salad. Sweet (or rather pudding) was Bread and Butter pudding and that was it. Still the beer was good and the locals friendly. We walked along the creek up to Qare and admired the variety of boats on their mud berths, from rotting, neglected hulls to superb, gleaming expensive yachts. Settled down in our bertths after another spectacular sunset, which added to the old world charm of the place, we awoke
sometime during the night at an odd angle - sco much for local knowledge - we had
dried out half way up the edge of the chanrel.

Monday morning was grey and gloomy and the wind freshening, forecast 4/5 with 6
later, but luckily from'the south so we set sail early, already having decided toa cross the Estuary to Brightlingsea, as Havengore would be impossible under these conditions. Once again it was mainly a buoy hopping exercise, although the variable Visibility meant compass steering some of the time:- coming out of the Swale, head for the Pollard Spit light buoy, Columbine Spit and then 335 to S.W. Oaze.

Tim's bit....After about an hour of heading for the S.W. Oaze Janet announced
she could see trees on the starboard bow. "Silly ------ ; there aren’t any trees in
the middle of the Thames Estuary," I says, hastily checking the chart. However they appeared off and on out of the mist and the Red Sand Tower did look like a line of poplars. By the time we reached the S.W. Oaze the wind had freshened to a good FS but we managed to take in the jib pole and gybe onto starboard for the broad reach across the Warp to S.W. Swin and then up the Swin. Janet, true to form** had taken to her bunk at the sight of large grey waves. What a glorious sail, the boat often surfing at 6 knots plus, under fully reefed main and half rolled genoa (by now the wind was a good F6é.) The navigation went well, too, with S.W. Swin, Maplin, Maplin Bank and W. Hook Middle Buoys coming up or cue. This was a good thing as, with the crew prostrate** I couldn’t leave the tiller to do chart work; all I could manage was to grab the chart from the cabin ard raid the goodie box for chocolate and coke.

¥¥Janet adds......In mitigation I rarely get sea sick and never take tablets these
days. However my body has a built-in defence mechanism just in case, and I tend to _sleep if conditions are such that queasy feelings might start, sc I missed a chunk of
‘he passage in peaceful dreams. I awoke ta find Tim slightly lost (SORRY - we've
both learnt from our yachtmaster course that one is not last - just unsure of one’s
position. ) We were due to arrive at the Swin Spitway very close to law water, but
the expected buoy had not appeared - instead Tim was confused by a cardinal mark and
had turned 90° to port. He is very good at passage planning and following through but he won't mind me saying that my instincts are better in a crisis. So it was instinct (or common sense) that told me that heading towards Bradwell Power Station would land us (literally) on the sand somewhere, and we returned to our original heading and were relieved when the familiar Swin Spitway materialised. From there it was home territory, there proved to be plenty of water in the Swin, even though the sea was confused with fairly large waves. We arrived at
Brightlingsea about 16.30 having logged 39kn miles over 8 hours - not bad for a Pift.
boat. After tidying up we went ashore and persuaded mine host at the Anchor to start cooking early for two extremely hungry sailors. Tuesday dawned even windier and we spent most of the day listening to the gusts howling through the rigging, worrying about alternative means of getting back to the club (we had to return) home Tuesday evening). However the wind started to abate about 15.00 and we set off up the Blackwater, ending up motoring back just after Bradwell.

It may not have been ’foreign’ but we thoroughly enjoyed the trip.

Janet Bigder

"HITS NOT FAIR"

The Equal Time Handicap Race Formula - a purely personal view from Mike Boreham

The Prologue

Handicap racing is never ‘fair'. At best it isareasonable compromise acceptable to the majority; at worse
it is a lottery in which some will become convinced they will always be the loser. However, having said that,
handicap racing is a necessity if (a) you do not have enough boats of a particular class to form a separate
racing fleet and (b) you are sufficiently curious to know 'how well' you can sail against boats of other classes.
The trouble is, when you win, it's all due to brilliant sailing - but when you're last, it's due to an
incompetent race officer, a ridiculous course and/or an 'unfair' handicap system which is long past its sell-by
date and in drastic need of revision. I know how they feels I'm long convinced the 420 (PYN = 115) ought more
properly be 151, whilst those Solo flying machines (PYN = 122) are treated too leniently and ought to be racing
off 100 - or less.

The biggest ‘gripe’ against the ‘traditional’ dinghy handicap sailing is that boats do not all sail in the same
conditions of wind and tide. For example, a Cadet dinghy (PYN = 152) ought to take twice as long to sail a
set course as a Tornado (PYN = 76). However, in a physically long race of 1-2 hours duration around a ‘normal'
course, the tide (and almost certainly the wind) will vary in strength and direction, both in time and space.
Thus, if the Cadet dinghy experiences 'favourable' variations of wind and tide when the Tornado is safely
finished and on the hard, it clearly gains an advatage not necessarily connected with ability to sail. Conversely
‘unfavourble' variations will place the Cadet in the 'no hope' category, with the Tornado (now nicely put away in
the Cat park) left. the winner and the proud helm downing a pint, whilst the poor old (young ?) Cadet skipper is
still trying to get around No.2. Again, not necessarily any reflection of ability to sail as such, merely
‘a victim’ of the circumstances on that particular day. Maybe that's why some people prefer to sail on
non-tidal waters.

Therefore, the ideal might be for all boats to sail in the same conditions of wind and tide for the same length
(and period) of time. "Good idea, Mike" I hear you say “How do you arrange it ?" "With great difficulty" is
my unhelpful reply, but help might be at hand via the Equal Time Handicap Race Formula.

Equal Time Handicap Race Formula

C = 5 xM ) xy where C = Corrected Time; E— = Elapsed Time
N = PYN A = Actual number of laps sailed
100 = 100 (surprize ?) by the boat in question
M = Number of laps sailed by the
boat sailing furthest.

Essentially, for a given boat (eg. our struggling Cadet dinghy) we work out the average time it has taken
to sail one lap = seconds/lap) . Then we work how long it would have taken to sail the same number of
laps as the fastest boat (ie. x M seconds). Now we apply the normal handicap number to get the relative
performance (ie. corrected time) for each boat. Hey Presto! We have found the worthy winner against whom
nobody can complain, grouse or shout "Hits not fair !" If you believe that, you'll believe anything.

The snags

To start with, to be reasonably fair, all boats ought to sail for more or less the same actual time period
(eg. 11 a.m. - 12 a.m.) as well as the same elapsed time (eg 60 minutes) and, in addition, sail in the same
general physical area. In this way, all boats ought to experience the same variations of wind and tide in
both the space and time domains. That's the snag!

Time considerations

In my opinion, the race Officer should aim to finish all boats within a time period not more than 20% of the
‘planned duration’ of the race. I.E. for a planned duration of 60 mins, the finishing time-span should be
12 minutes, whilst for a 2-hour race it would be 24 minutes ‘time span' in which to finish all boats. Clearly,
this is difficult for the race Officer to judge - and achieve.

Space considerations

Boats a 100yards apart will often experience quite different conditions of wind and tide, so boats %-mile apart
will certainly experience different conditions and be affected quite differently by changes. If the wind dies
towards the end of the race, the Cadet dinghy is affected longer than the Tornado. The solution would be to
keep the laps short (say F, No.1, A, D - *but that's not fair’says the Tornado) rather than long (eg. B, C, No.1
No.2, D - “that's definitely not fair’ says the Cadet dinghy).

11.

How many laps ?

In my opinion, each boat ought to sail at least two laps (another reason for keeping short laps). Consider a race in which, say, a Laser, 420 and Solo are well ahead of the field. They complete one lap and the Race Officer sends them on for a 2nd lap. However, the rest of the field, including 420s, Lasers and Solos, he stops after one lap and then applies the formula as described. Our leading trio are not best pleased; after all, they have sailed twice as far for twice as long - if they're lucky. If the wind drops on the 2nd lap, they'll finish well down the results list, even though they were clearly the leaders. If the wind increases, they don't necessarily improve their position since they were leading anyway. For this reason I feel all boats ought to sail at least 2 laps, more if possible, in the planned duration of the race.

The Epilogue

If the Equal Time Handicap Race Formula was adopted by the club, I feel that:-

(a) short laps should be set rather than long laps
(b) a minimum of two laps should be sailed by all boats
(c) a 20% 'time span' should be the criteria for the Race Officer to judge when deciding at which point to start finishing boats.
(d) the 1992 Easter Egg Series and May Day Bank Holiday Series would be ideal for 'testing' out the system and finding the practical problems of administering it
(e) maybe we should forget the whole thing and stick to the 'normal' handicap race system.

NAVIGANS PAST

1965 - Arthur Adams writes an epic tale of an epic voyage
- what really happened on the Norfolk Broads ?
- the Committee tells us 'how it is' and lays it straight
on the line; you can ‘Work or Pay' !

January - a statement to the effect that, interms of effort needed to produce it,and the cost of posting it,
" ...2..the cost of producing Navigans is becoming uneconomical". With a circulation of 330 (with some
88 posted to Associate Members) there will be a ‘postage levy’ for all members who require Navigans and other circulars to be posted to them. The levy will be 4/- per year. Membership subscriptions are due and they are Ordinary members 10/- (but with wife/husband 15/-); Associate Members 36/- (with wife/husband 41/-), non-MASC
Cadets 20/- or 5/- (10-15) and MASC Cadets (10-18) 2/6. A ‘block Racing Fee of 30/-, otherwise 2/6 per race,
collected at the end of the season; by the way, “many members" have not yet paid their 1964 race and dinghy park fees !

MBYC held a 5-race Winter series andattracted
50 boats, 9 from Marconi. lan Shaw/Linda Partlett (Enterprise) were 6th whilst David Perry/Eleanor Eldridge capsized in December. That sounds as though they still haven't got
it upright yet - what a way to spend Christmas! It appears that, amongst the cadets, "girl. friends and boy
friends change" (they do ?) but “in the next generation, congratulations to Ian Rogers and Henrietta Wellings whowere engaged on New Year's Eve". Not capsized I hope; if David and Eleanor get their boat up in time, perhaps they can join in the celebrations.

A letter from Brian Tillotson re "the third class". He basically says that a 3rd class should grow spontaneously and not be dictated. He feels ‘the Executive’ should only exercise any jurisdiction over classes sailed by restricting admission of new members whose boat(s) do not conform but existing members won't change boats.

February - a successful Burns Night Party was held at Stansgate with haggis provided and cooked by Robbie
Sims - he's nay a scoot, surely ? Arthur Adams writes Part I of his 'Mamgu prize-winning’ log recounting
buying, collecting and sailing his new yacht in Holland. The Sailing Sec responds to Brian Tillotson's letter " If there is evidence of 5 or more regularly racing in any one class, separate races will be started
for them..... The club should not consider adopting the class....until it has proved itself for at least a
year. Similarly, if one-design classes are unsupported for a year or more, the club should consider dropping
that class...." He goes on to say "....The whole point of having club one-designs is to concentrate interest
into those classes..... The committee would be failing in its duty ....if it pressed classes that were similar
to the constitutionally adopted classes, consequently the official programme will only show the races for the constituted classes".

March - Part II of Arthur Adams' log. Don Budds writes a bit about 'Sea Shanties’. He ends by saying
"It is the shanty tunes rather than the words that are interesting. At best the words give glimpses of life On board the old sailing vessels. At worst they are merely obscene doggerel." 1 must admit my recollections of 'sea shanties' from my ‘service days' don't include any interesting tunes; are there any 'clean' sea
shanties ?

April - A notice appears in Navigans:- "Wanted: Ladies for work as galley slaves. Ability to row not
essential - in fact, no earthly use at all". Now does he (I suppose it's 'he') mean 'row' as in ‘row the
boat ashore, alleluia" or ‘row' as in having a humdinger of an arguement (as at some Main Committee Meetings I've known !). I won't embarrass the 'he' who (I suspect) penned the ‘Wanted' notice but I understand he does a good turn with the haggis ! Part of Arthur Adams' log is published.

May - a hosepipe ban from lst April - no boat washing. As far as I know we still have a hosepipe ban.
Mind you, I reckon with the absense of a hose-pipe on the hard, things are ‘less cluttered up' especially at the end of racing. Perhaps we don't really need a hosepipe if a bucket of water does the trick ?

Club ties are now on sale at 10/6. The last time I bought a club tie, I reckoned it was probably from the original stock, at least judgingfrom its width. Jack R@eve proposes organising a series of Torch races.

Part IV of Arthur Adams' log is published.

June/July - Jack Reeve is the new Editor - and Part V of Arthur Adams' log is published.

Yet another engagement; seems like a regular marriage bureau is in operation at Stansgate.

It appears a large party of MSC members took off for the Norfolk Broads with 8 hired Blakes (sailing) boats and one private 'Felicity'. Clearly a very good time was had by all and Eleanor Eldrige recounts the tale, admitting to running aground (that's a change from being capsized over Christmas around MBYC). Eleanor writes "The majority of the fleet were happily drinking "; well, what else would you expect from a load of rowdy

Marconi sailormen and sailorwomen (actually she goes on to include the word ‘tea’ on the next line, but that’s not now I read it first time}. John Hutchings had his 18th birthday with breakfast provided by Leonie

(Carlisle ?), Dave Young and John Witter, followed that evening by celebrations in the local hostelry (but don't try to convince me you were drinking tea again ).

TS
John, Dave and Leonie appear to have been the ‘entertainments committee’ for theywrote the verses of "On the Norfolks Broads" to the tune of the Quartermaster's Stores:- "There was Con, Con, with her apron on, etc. There was Jack, Jack, motoring at the back, etc The was Mike, Mike (Sissons) quanting up the dyke, etc. There were boats , boats, 9 Marconi boats, etc ".

I assume 'Con' and 'Jack' were Connie and Jack Bigden.

A young lady named Sue Palmer (who presumably should have been tucked up in bed and soundly asleep) spent several evenings with her headpoked through the open windows whilst she learned the words to "Oh ! Sir
Jasper!". If you're reading this Sue, can you still remember them - and how about an encore at the Laying-Up
supper ?

Members' boats are listed:- 33 Enterprise, 9 Fleetwinds, 66 Handicap, 26 cruisers, 6 ‘cats' and 6 motor cruisers
launches or o/b dinghies. The handicap fleet included an 11' Challenger dinghy belonging to Dennis Byatt; is this the same Challenger we have as a club boat today ? Four club boats are listed, namely Rescue Boat No.1
(16'), Fisherman (14') a Walker (8') and Brazil.

August - Under sailing notes there is a complaint about the number of boats without means of identification -
a problem not unknown tous these days. The club is to supply (at 2/6) brass plates upon which can be painted the name and number . A whole host of racing results are published covering several pages, and Terry Hallam writes an article entitled "Flags and Burgees".

September - a notice to remind everyone that, under the River Authority bye-laws, it is an offence for anyone
to walk on either side of the sea-wall, especially the landward side.

A special announcement, under the name of Jack Bigden, of a Veteran's race (40 and over) with a course from clubhouse mark to the Jolly Sailor and return (if capable). Although not stated, clearly a ‘stop-over' is
intended. This, presumably, was the first 'Jackpot' race - but without the actual 'Jackpot' (trophy).

Also, the rules of the first Helmsman of the Year Trophy event (the 'Costain Cup' presented in 1965 by Sir Richard Costain to mark the opening of 'the new pavillion’ at Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, 17 July, 1965). The event was run as a twoeday series consisting of 5 races, approx. l-hour per race and the same course for each race. The event seems to be open to anyone willing to pay the 7/6 entry fee.

Winner of the Ladies Cup was (Mrs) D.R.Darney, but I see Leonie Carlisle was2nd and Linda Partlett 3rd. Of course, Leonnie nowLeonie Golding whilst Lindais Linda Chaplin.

There were 60 entries for the Marconi (Dinghy?) Challenge Cup with MSC = 22, MBYC = 14, SSC = 12, OSC = 7,
MYC = 4 and 3 ‘unknown'.

October . a very weighty tome this month, due to the upcoming AGM. Articles entitled "The Club Future" (Commodore), "Policy Statement " (Committee), "The 3rd Racing Class(es)" (Sailing Sec.), "Work or Pay" (Commodore) "Proposals for the AGM" (Committee) and the AGM Notice/Agenda. For the Club Future, Terry Hallam reminds us that the club's 3-year lease at Stansgate runs out at the end of this year. The "Marina Scheme appeal" has been resolved in that the Min. of Housing and Local Government has allowed the appeal and outline planning permission has been granted to Mr.Sparrow (our landlord). Club membership has grown 5-fold in the 3 years
~from about 120 to some 600. Consequently, stress, creaks and groans are issuing from the present administrative
ystem. As to the Policy Statement, A.J.Stong (Hon.Sec.)
states the terms of lease renewal have been in doubt all year. However,
following sanctioningof the Marina proposals, discussions between Terry Hallam and Mr.
Sparrow have resulted in the lease being extended under the current terms for one more year. The Committee will, in the year to come, enter negotiations which, they hope, will result ina strong and stable club with a permanent clubhouse and improved facilities. For this reason, the Committee will recommend that Terry Hallam be elected for an additional year, despite the fact that his normal 3-year term of office will have expired. The 3rd Racing Class theme jis taken up by John Witter. After much debate, the Sailing Committee recommend Points Series racing for GP14, Hornet and Snipe classes as well as the existing Enterprise and Fleetwind classes. Torches and Mirrors will also be able to have their own races but will not be encouraged as racing classes. The Handicap Class will continue to have races but Points Series races will be held for any other class able to raise sufficient support. Terry Hallam takes ‘the stand' again on Work or Pay. He outlines the usual problem of ‘lots of work and lots of things to maintain; lots of members but too few helpers’. In fact, he points out that ‘the workers’ are largely the same people, and same number, as when the club moved to Stansgate 3 years earlier. Terry reminds everyone that over the 14-year (?) existence of the club, the subscription has remained at 10/- (full Marconi Members) compared to increases of 2,3 or 4-fold for other clubs. The question is posed; do we remain a ‘do it yourself' club or do we employ full/part-time staff ? Terry points out that managing the club of our size (600 members) "..is a business and requires the application of proper management principles”. I think we've had echoes of that in recent years. Finally the Committee recommends the members to accept the choice
of "TO PAY" - now that is a surprize.

November/December - the Laying Up Supper switched from Baddow to Waterhouse Lane "where the manageress and
chef produced a most excellent meal". Well, do I detect some disatisfaction with the Baddow venue ? Was my ‘jibe' in last month's Navigans Past 1964 a bit nearer the truth than I thought ? However, do I also detect

14.
a note of disatisfaction with 'the style' of the Laying Up Supper ? I quote "....within seconds of the band
starting.....several couples were dancing". That must be good surely ? Maybe it depends upon how they were
dancing, for the reporter goes on to say "What a pity then that so much of the remaining 2% hours, especially
the last %-hour, was taken up with the buffet, raffle, Knees up Mother Brown, Hokey Cokey, Conga, etc.." Now
I remember fromthe late '70s and early '80s, some (well, most) Laying Up Suppers became somewhat 'boisterous'
particularly one year when 'the antics' of the Mirror crowd drew forth a letter of ‘comment’ in Navigans.
However, apart from the ‘Mirror Mob', the real noisey ones were the ‘Hornet Hustlers'; a tendency to ‘over
indulegence' might be the way to put it. Nevertheless, the reporter ends by saying "Thank you, the organisers,
for a most enjoyable evening". - apart, I suppose, for the last 2% hours !

On the sailing front, a notice asking anyone interested in forming a Hornet Fleet in the club to contact Julian
Bigden and/or his crew Mike Turner. Julian Bigden ? Mike Turner ? Hornet Fleet ? Ah! Now that explains all
the commotion above. Those two quiet, gentlemanly, ‘family members' we saw at the club in 1991, were not always
so - at least, not from the tales I've been told of the ‘good old days' in the ‘60s when the club was a bit
younger, and so were they.

An extensive prize list shows that Ian Shaw not only won the Cadet Trophy, the Enterprise Points Series, and was
lst winner of the Helmsman of the Year Trophy, but also was 2nd in the Pilots Cup and 3rd in the Marconi Challenge
Cup. As I've mentioned before, Cadet members throughout the club history have had the temerity to show little
respect for our feelings by winning our trophies. No wonder Jack B initiated the over-40s race, and even that
is threatened these days with the unofficial 'under 40s' race at the same time. Ah! Well! Maybe we'd better
stay in the clubhouse and be wise from the comfort of the bar. Peter Darney actually won the ‘over 40s'race
with Brian Tillotson 2nd and Mrs J.Reeve 3rd. All received 1 dozen Export Ale as a prize, so who needs silver
trophies, just hand me the opener.

At the AGM, Terry Hallamwas (re)elected Commodore, Nick Tovey Vice Commodore and Stan Allerton Rear Commodore/
Hon.Treasurer combined. John Witter was re-elected Sailing Sec.

Yet another note stating that an extremely large number of people have still not paid their 1965 racing fees.

Finally, a happy end to the year with the announcement of the engagement of John Witter and Eleanor Eldridge.
So that's who Eleanor Eldridge is ,but I must admit I had my suspicions. Anyway, it just shows what a Norfolk
Broads holiday can do to people. Congratulations Eleanor and John.

S NOTES
COMMODORE’

By the time that you receive this edition of Navigans, we will have held this year’s Annual General Meeting. You will have elected the new Committee to manage the affairs of the Club for the next twelve months.

It seems that it was only yesterday that I wrote my first Commodore's notes and it is hard to realise that three years have passed since then. Now that the time has come to step down, I would like to reflect on some of the events of the last three years and the reasons why I have enjoyed serving the Club, despite the occasional
frustration.

I believe that one of the main reasons is “the occasional frustrations". Obviously it is disappointing to the Committee when its ideas are not backed by the Membership, and sometimes I have allowed this to show, but in our Club it is very rare for this to happen. The two instances that come to mind are firstly the problems over the bye law and the start line. Sometimes it is necessary for the Committee to go ‘over the top’ and for the Members to bring it back in line. I believe that this was such a case and that the resulting compromise this year has improved the situation a lot although there is probably more work for next year’s Committee to do.

The second was the plans to develop the site. In this case the response was all positive in that, at the Meeting we held in April this year, you clearly indicated how you would like to see us proceed. Again this has given your future Committees a clear way to proceed.

I think that these 'frustrations’ demonstrate one of the main reasons that I have enjoyed serving you. It is the fact that when there is a problem, the resulting discussion is made in a positive and constructive manner and not done in a derogatory way. Such situations do demonstrate that we are all able to act together and discuss opposing views to the benefit of the whole Club.

Another aspect which has made the job enjoyable is the tremendous support that all of you have given to myself and the various Committees. This has varied from supporting sailing events; supporting by helping at such events; helping at working parties; and helping with all manner of other projects. It is noticeable that in our Club, people approach the Committee and say "I have this idea for the Club and would like to organise it’; too often elsewhere it would be expressed as ’I have this idea, why
doesn’t the Committee do.....’

Lastly it comes from the mixture of sailing that we offer and our joint desire to ensure that we continue to offer such a mix. There cannot be many Clubs today who cater for Cruiser and Dinghy sailing from the keen racing to the mucking about. Any Club that can provide for its members events such as East Coast Piers, Regatta, Camping Fortnight, Cruising in Company, Creek Hopping, etc. and satisfy the needs of so many different types of sailing must have a great future.

I hope that I hand on to my successor a healthy situation and that we all give him and his Committees the continuing level of support that I have enjoyed.

I will close by thanking every one of you for this help and support and wish you all good sailing for the future.

Thanks WV.Pe,
N.T. Pembleton

1991 HIGHLIGHTS OF A SOLO YEAR

1. Winter Project. Not one but two Portakabins have been cleared out, made
weatherproof and fitted out for Race Control. Great fun demolishing the old wooden
one with the Cat Fleet Chair Gang - we nearly burnt the cold Revenue Hut to the ground
with our bonfire.

&. Social Do’s Dirmer at the Cross Keys, Roxwell; Ten Pin Bowling at Southend Pier and the Dinner at Stansgate started the year. The latter was hosted by our Entertainment Manager Tim Sweet and Master "Italian’ Chef Martin Hall. Summer BBQ's, hosted by Ron Greygoose and Geoff Josey gave us some pleasant evenings after Sunday
sailing.

3. Team Racing 8 Saloists, 1 ex-Scale Helms person, and 5 guesting Cats made up four
teams for a six race series on Saturday 20th July. The event turned cut to be one of the best team racing events I can remember at Stansgate. On the water, judging by Mike Boreham, several interesting penalties, mainly due to superb luffing by Simon Liddington, I’m trying to forget that Larry Botheras’ team won, but it was close.

4. Marconi Open, 21/22 September Our Oper Meeting attracted 11 regular Solo helms
and 4 visitors. We also persuaded Tom Ashley, Damian Boreham and Jane Williams to join in with borrowed Solos. To complete our total entry of 19 boats, Graham Richmond brought along the Solo he had just finished building. Strong winds, gusting Force 6 at times, made it difficult for the inexperienced helms but made very interesting sailing for the fleet. Our Race Officer, Steve Keeble, gave us good Clear starts with his no-go box and set excellent challenging courses for the conditions. Unfortunately Graham Richmond bent his new mast on the Saturday sea we don’t know how fast his new boat is yet. The visitors went away happy with first and second prizes:

lst Malcolm Gandy - Halfway YC; 3rd Roger Smith - Marconi SC
end Alan Husk - Halfway YC; 4th John Salmon - Marconi SC
Sth Simon Liddington - Marconi SC

3. Points Series The serious bit is all about Club Racing, so congratulations to
our main Points Series Winners:

Jahr Salmon - Spring "Meteor Trophy"
Johri Rutherford - Summer "Qne Up Cup"
Ron Greygoose - Autumn "Captains Trophy"

6. Solent Cruising The Sola Fleet manned half the fleet of three Sigma 36's in
this year’s Solent thrash. Good sailing on Saturday and Sunday in severe Gale Force 39 winds , Saturday’s beat up to Yarmouth 1.0.W. was exciting but the surfing run back on Sunday was even better. All who helmed reckoned they had acquired a little extra life experierice.

Thanks ta Mike Hellewell for a super weekend - pity about the two sails we tore = and
the winch that flew to bits under the strain.

7. Qper Meetings Marconi Soloists were present at the following open meetings:
Thorpe Bay; Inland Nationals at Rutland Water; Fishers Green; Ardleigh; King George; Half Way; Bewl Valley; and Hayling Island. Johri Salmon got third place at beth Fishers Green and Ardleigh in light winds.

At the Thorpe Bay World Championships with 65 entries, Simor Liddington came 3énd, followed by Roger Smith 39th and John Salmon 41st. Ex Marconi Soloists also did well
- Malcolm Gandy coming 6th. Colin Wilsmore getting a £150 cheque for the most
improved helm and Dave Nixon coming well up the fleet at 20th.

Malcolm Stuart

Food for Thought

I was afloat on an October gale and saw the Cruiser Fleet bucking and riding to a northerly gale. It made me realise the enormous strain put on Scopes, Mooring Buoys and Pennnants. Yes, I was out trying to rescue a breakaway yacht.

We must be mad making large investments in our boats and then leaving them out there to the mercy of the elements!

Our problems, it seems to me, have this year come about by breakages on top parts, not the ground chain. Is your Gear strong enough to withstand full gales, are your Shackles man enough for the job, is your Pennant of the right quality rope? We are beholden to each other to do the strongest job on our moorings and it saves the aggravation afterwards of damage to other boats in the Club hit by breakaways. Think
about your 1992 gear, if you are not sure ask advice. Me - I’m a belt and braces
mari.

Derek Hall, Continuing-in-1992 Cruiser Fleet Captain

Extracts from the log of "Bidwell" - Westerly Storm 33 - being sailed by the Gardner
family, normally of "“Blucette": The date of departure soon arrived. We were plarming to cruise the Northern Brittany Coast in our friends’ boat "Bidwell" from Plymouth to Biscay. He would join us after two weeks to bring the boat back; a highly illegal thing to do, according to the RYA!*

3rd August. Forecast was good but very poor visibility, less than 200m. After
fueling and storing up we left Queer Anne’s Battery, Plymouth at 1315. Wind virtually nil SW. First problem was finding the gap in the Plymouth Sound (big barrier wall.) We followed the breakwater until we sighted the Lighthouse. Turned onto 180'm. According to Decca we passed Eddystone Light half a mile off, but couldn’t see it. Eyes and ears strained, we pressed on being sure it would clear
soon. Then the sun appeared and - disappeared. After three and a half hours it was
clear, bright and sunny, only a SW 1 so we motored on. The highlight of the trip was about 1730, when we spotted several gannets feeding in the water, and the next thing we knew, about six dolphins swam alongside for 10 minutes or so, much to the delight of all on board.

Settled down for the night, wind up and down, engine on and off several times! Beautiful quiet night, all children crashed out on the saloon floor! At one time we counted 18 sets of ship’s lights but at 0300 after having picked up Ile de Batz light, it disappeared as visibility dropped again. Decca going well, and we soon picked up the Lighthouse again when one and a half miles off. Being an East Coast man, we weren't used to seeing these huge dark shapes rearing out of the sea all
around - yes, rocks, hundreds of them. Soon we were lying to anchor fairly close to
the Roscoff Ferry terminal ready for sleep. 0530 and 100.4 miles on the log.

4th August. Visited Morlaix briefly, but we got the tide wrong - one hour out. Soa
scorn headed back and picked up a mooring off the Chenal de Ile de Batz in blazing
sunshine.

sth August. Surmy hot day, had to wait for tide to rise sufficiently to tackle the Chenal (Channel) de Ile de Batz. The narrow channel running between the Isle and the mainland being a very tortuous, not well buoyed, track betweer rocks. Bit exciting
in one place when depth read 0.00 but no bump - only the bumping of the heart beats
as they rapidly increased. Through and out into the sea, wind SW 4ish. Our first taste of the full Atlantic swell about 2-3 metres, a little like being on a roller coaster. Headed for L’Abervrach and negotiated the entrance, again, rock strewn. The biggest problem; the boat was going so fast now we had difficulty slowing down in the very narrow channel (Blucette normally has max speed of 6 knots, we were managing
8 knots).

7th August. Forecast NW 4-5 so it’s off through the Chenal du Four. One lock at
the chart is enough to get the heart racing as there are so many little rocks. Pretty unrestful passage as wind dropped and we motored again. We could just see Usharnt off to Starboard, as visibility not too good again. A lot of tide here. Decca’s giving us 9.5 knots S.0.G. and only 5.0 on the log. We shot through the Chenal like a cork in a river bobbing all over the place. Tremendous overfalls could be seen, I’m glad the wind was light! Sailed on to Cap de la Cheval and into the Bay de Downanez. Decca not very accurate row so more traditional navigation methods had
to be used. Arrived Norg at 2100 with 47.3 miles on the log.

8th, 9th, 10th August. The whole of the Bay is really beautiful and we spent a few
days, Swimming, visiting local beaches and even being boarded by the local maritime police one evening. The off-putting part was the gunboat standing half a mile off. They proceeded to ask us lots of questions and finally circled the boat in their dinghy taking photos!

contd.
2s

7.

1tith August. Raz du Sein today. Departed 0615 from Treboul, light airs, visibility half mile. Decca pretty useless now. We stood well out as we approached the Raz and the tide was pulling us hard towards the rocks. After all the stories one hears about the Raz it was most disappointing, water very confused, but once through, it was a boring 30-mile sail down an uninteresting coastline. Few rocks now and land much flatter. Arrived in Loctudy after having completed 55.3 miles. Weather still glorious, again local trips made for an interesting couple of days.
contd.
13th August. Today Iles Glenans. A beautiful archipeligo of about 10 islands
seven or eight miles off the coast. Still weather red hot. We found a beautiful anchorage off Ile de Penfret. Beautiful gold sands and beautiful water. You could
see the anchor in the bottom at a depth of 11 metres - not quite the same as the
Blackwater? Spent a grotty night at anchor as the wind changed from blowing off the land to blowing off the sea. Poor ’Bidwell’ was a bit short on chain and all night the chain snatched and banged.

14th August A quick trip to Cancarneau today, only a few miles away. Beautiful
town and lovely Marina next to the Castle. Almost too hot today, water had ta be thrown on the decks to cool things down.

15th August. Spirmaker up today. With only Hilary and our two girls (9 and 11) we
hadn’t flown it yet. 1,000 sq ft seemed a bit daunting but she flew well as we headed further South to Ile de Groix. Wind increased and we eventually pulled the spinnaker dawn as we reached 8.5K with 18 knots of wind over the boat. Exciting, though! Into Port Tudy on Ile de Groix, certainly the most crowded port of all the holiday. Anyhow moules (mussels) and wine scon made up for that.

16th August. Short hep to L’Orient (mouth of the Loire) where we had decided after
frantic phone calls to meet the ’new crew’ on Saturday. Total of 328 miles on this trip. A wonderful holiday as the weather had been so hot and sunny, combined with cheap wine and good food. A superbly beautiful coastline enjoyed by all the family. Sc nice it was to come home by Brittany Ferries and not have the worry of getting "Bidwell" back. "Bidwell" did have a good trip going South to beyond Morhiban and back. The final leg from L’Abervrach ta Flymouth, they had 40 knots of wind, but did arrive safely back in Plymouth a fortnight later.

Derek and Hilary Gardner

*Ed’s note: I’m puzzled as ta why it can possibly be illegal to swop skipper/crews, before a boat completes its round trip, can anyone enlighten me?

NAVIGANS PAST

1966 - the politics of office and is 'one more than three' just one too many ?
- the "syndicate" moves into the catering trade; has 'the mob' arrived at Stansgate ?
- Fred and Mark visit the Pirates (but they're not from Penzance)

January - The Editor (Jack Reeve) points out that many people have still not paid their 1965 racing fees, mooring fees and/or dinghy park fees. "Pay Up", says Jack - or the Committee will have to 'name names'.

Attendance at the 1965 AGM was 120. Amongst the Committee's proposals was one to employ a paid steward for cleaning and maintenance of club premises and site; also care of the club's rescue launch and Brazil (but not run the galley !). 69 voted 'for', none against and 4 abstained (I often wonder why people 'abstain' on such relatively uncomplicated issues ?) A proposal to allow Terry Hallam as Commodore for another year over and above his alloted 3-year stint appears to have been much debated. Some thought a sub-committee should be formed to negotiate the new club-site lease and that the Commodore should not carry out the negotiations. Another suggestion was that Terry be elected a Vice-President and lead a sub-committee to conduct negotiations. Others felt that club rules specifically aimed at preventing anyone continuing in office over and above the 3-year span and, given the onerous task of Commodore, felt the 3-year period was the limit of anyone's efficiency. However, others equally felt it permissable to change rules that were found 'restrictive'. Up to this point, Terry had chaired the meeting, but "Mr Millett" took the chair and a secret ballot re-elected Terry Hallam as Commodore for an additional year by 60 votes 'for' and 20 votes 'against'. Also elected were Nick Tovey (Vice-Commodore), Stan Allerton (Rear Commodore/Hon.Treas), John Witter (Sailing Sec) - and Jack Bigden as a Vice-President .

Part 1 of the Mamgu Trophy prize-winning log by C.S.Molyneau, giving an account of his single-handed cruise across The Channel. A notice reminds us that all members should observe a 10 mph speed limit along the approach road to the club. Finally, an invitation to a 'get together' (pub binge ?) for the embryo Hornet Fleet, the notice describing the Hornet as "the Aston Martin of dinghies". A new Hornet (less sails) costs £265 (wood) or £295 (GRP) with sails an extra £43 or so. Apparently 4 new boats have been purchased which, with the 2 existing club Hornets, brings the fleet to 6 before it has even got on the water.

February - Jack Reeve is looking for an Assistant Editor. Leonnie Carlisle is congratulated on reaching her majority whilst Olive and Brian Partridge expect to acquire a 'new crew' in the coming summer. Congratulations to Peter and Marlene Lawrence and to John and Eleanor Witter, each of whom clearly 'tied the knot' (presumably a nautical one) during February.

A Handicap Fleet meeting promises racing for GP14s, Hornets, Mirrors and Torches whenever possible, all hopefully encouraged by the news that no race fees will be charged for "closed club events". The Hornet crowd also held their own 'convivial evening' and reveal another 5 members express interest in buying Hornets.

Part II of the prize-winning log by C.S.Molyneau. Finally, Jack Bigden is selling a Graduate for £100.

March - Alas, no volunteers came forward to help Jack Reeve with Navigans production. However, the paid steward (Tom Polden) has been recruited and "is certainly giving us value for money".

"Notes for Swinging Race Officers" require the R.O. to have (a) absolute patience (b) ability to decipher handwriting in Hindustani written by a Chinese whilst planing in a Force 9 on the way to the start of a race and (c) a good command of basic english to explain why the 10-minute gun was 5 minutes late, and the 5-minute gun was 10 minutes early ! I'm sure we can all 'identify' with the sentiments ! Essential RO equipment includes (i) a whitewash brush (to obliterate all personal blame whatsoever), (ii) a clock (to tell when the bar is open) and two guns (one for starting, the other (preferably a colt.45) for the RO's personal use).

K.N.Littlebury writes an article promoting the Snipe dinghy - a lost cause I fear but the article will, I suspect, resurrect the 'third class racing' controversy. In the meantime, Jack Reeve reports upon the inaugural meeting of the Torch Class Owners Association, which was attended by the Torch designer, Mr Bert Keeble who I believe lived in Maldon. Also an unsigned article about the GP14 is also published.

Also published is a summary of the basic racing rules in readiness for the coming season.

Part of C.S.Molyneau's prize-winning log.

April/May - a major Marconi Company 're-organisation' (oh! dear! more dis-organised chaos so beloved of the 1960s 'high flyers') has delayed the issue of Navigans, hence the 'double issue'.

Peter Croft is trying to organise a Cruiser Class Whitsun Cruise, whilst the expected 'resurrection' reference Hornet v. Snipe has materialised; Peter Jennings quite clearly took exception to the claims made concerning the attributes of the Snipe over the Hornet, and challenges the Snipe sailors to a race. Peter points out the Hornet Fleet is now 10 boats strong.

A "Galley Syndicate" (Chris Allerton, John Hutchings and Paula Jones) has been formed to manage (and run ?) the galley. They will open Sats and Suns 11.00-14.00 and 15.00-17.00 (plus extended hours if customers await).

3.

The ‘syndicate’ (sounds rather sinister) will serve tea, coffee, sweets, etc, plus hot pies and sandwiches. They will also take over the catering for club parties. In addition, tea,sugar and powdered milk will be
available mid-week on a ‘serve yourself’ basis - but don't forget to put your money in the till.
An announcement by the Cadet Captain (Simon Darney) that, for the first time, there will be a Cadet Week at the club (instead of a cadet Weekend) in the 2nd week of August. This will fall "in line" (does he mean between ?) the Cadet Weeks at Stone SC and Maylandsea bay SC.

On the sailing front, the 'man to beat' appears to be John Tillotson in the Hornet Class, with Julian Bigden not far behind.

The 'Club-house Rules' are published and Jack Reeve draws attention to the Rule concerning ‘Transistor Radios’. No guesses as to what that rule said.

Part IV of the prize-winning Mamgu Trophy log by C.S.Molyneau. Presumably it is the last because he ends by
stating "....only a Customs Officer can fall out of bed at 5.30 in the morning and start drinking neat rum !"
But I thought that was what cruising was all about ?

June Stone SC apparently had "rescue launch problems" this year and it was literally the MSC to the rescue.

Good comments on the Regatta (was it the first Regatta ?). However, only 12 Marconi entries out of 79 in all. Robbie Simms (who else ?) controlled the Race Box with 9 starts at 5 minute intervals. Robbie and family have been doing the Regatta starts ever since. One Mirror apparently missed 'C' mark at Goldhanger and continued all the way around Osea, taking 3's hours instead of the expected 1+ hours. You'd have thought he wondered where the others were, wouldn't you ? The Mona's cup was “a bit of a tragedy" with 3 out of 13 finishing, the rest capsizing or coming to other grief. The Marconi (Singhy) Challenge Cup attracted about 50 entries but not much wind. Best Marconi boat was Nick Tovey (Enterprise) in 3rd place. Seven Shearwater Cats (6 from Stone, none from Marconi) seemed to have a special separate race. The Sailing Sec. publishes the names of members who have either (a) registered their boats but not paid the fee or (b) paid their fee but not registered their boats or
(c) neither registered their boats or paid their fee. I bet there were a few red faces around !

Finally, Olive and Brian Partridge took delivery of their new crew and Mark is his name - most appropriate for
a dinghy sailing family. Would he become a racing Mark do you think ?

July - Warnings of 'Spot Checks' on membership status. Apparently “unauthorised people" have been using the
site. So what's so different ? You have been warned !

What happened to the much-praised new steward Tom Polden ? A notice says "thanks" to an even newer steward, Mr Underwood. Confirmation of the Cadet Week “under canvas" which will apparently be run along “navy lines" with "messes" etc. Oh Dear! Will it work I wonder ? Anyway, ‘tis all under the control of the Cadet Officer, Tom Gaskell.

Fred Partlett writes Part 1 of his "Visiting the Pirates" adventure. He and son Mark took a Wayfarer up to Frinton and back over a long week-end. I'm not sure what he means by "Visiting the Pirates" but he was not welcomed by the fisherman at Walton Pier who prefered he keep at least }-mile away. Cor, I wonder what they think about our East Coast Piers Race ?

August/September - a 'one-page' Navigans due to Holidays and work-load taking up a very large slice of the Editor's
time, Apparently, the club was broken in to but not much was taken.

A letter (attached to this Navigans ?) was circulated to all members concerning club discipline (or rather the lack of it). Complaints about blatant wrong-doing & disregard (for the rules), including "non-authorised" use of the club by non-members, and possibly a hint of abuse of the definition of ‘visitors’.

October - another single-page ‘temporary Navigans' only. Unfortunately Jack Reeve had to resign from the post
of Editor due to pressure of work and ill-health and none had responded to his appeal for an Assistant Editor.

November - Eleanor Witter is the new Editor. She states " I wouldn't exactly say that I'd been Jumbered with
the editorship - I sort of volunteered - with a bit of pushing’. I wonder if the Sailing Sec. had a hand in
‘the bit of pushing' and gentle persuasion ? An announcement of a Cruiser Owners “Jug UP" - apparently
ladies are (also) welcome ! Sounds like a bit of an afterthought, that one.

A write-up of the laying Up Supper (written, 1 suspect, by Eleanor). Although things started out OK, a ‘hiccup' occurred when more people turned up than suppers provided. The guest of honour was Mr F.N.Sutherland who presented the MSC with the model Arab Dhow which is on display over the stairwell at Stansgate. In his speech he explains why ships are called "she" (unpredictable, often in stays and involved with sheets) which, whilst not original, usually guaranteed to raise a laugh. More laughs from Jack Bigden (MC) and his ‘games’. Eleanor confessed she laughed so much she got hiccups; mind you, she does confess to being fed canned beer from her "2nd ladies Race" prize (small ladle) by her crew, Bernard Tillotson and consequently not being able to remember
who won (but does she mean “who won" the games - or the ladies Race ?). The ‘supperless' presumably didn't
entirely relish the whole evening - but Eleanor says she thorughly enjoyed it, and no wonder !

10.
The Prize List includes prizes for Enterprise, Hornet and GP14s but nowt for Fleetwinds or the Torctr & Mirrors.
Only one handicap race was held and that was won by Leonie Carlisle. Susan Tillotson won the Ladies Cup,
Norman Palmer won the Helmsman of the Year (with Jane Cottam finishing 5th, having won the last race of the
series) and Jack Bigden won the over-40s race. Charles Holding won the Mug's Mug (spelled that way); was this
the first award of the Mug's Mug ?

A notice to say that a boat shed was to be erected at the club and Jack Bigden would like all the help he can get.

December - Our new Editor chides those who do not circulate 'their' Navigans around their family. She also
praises the enthusiasm of the Hornet sailors and their writer-of-articles who signs himself/herself as "H.Ornet"

The Commodore's report for 1966 is not entirely ‘upbeat’. The failure of the Marina project to ‘go ahead’ has
had indirect reprocussions in that the club lease has not yet been renewed - merely extended for one more year.
Social events at the club, although successful, have barely broken even. A sad "lack of interest of the Cadets"
(in racing ?) is reported whilst the rest of the sailing is described as "patchy" despite the removal of race
entry fees. However, he praises the Hornet fleet. The Steward/handyman (Mr Underwood) is praised, particularly
for services performed beyond the call of duty e.g. he turned out at 3 a.m. during a gale to check that all was
well at the club. An ex-EEV Co. building (presumably wooden) has been obtained to replace the current clubhouse
(assuming the lease
is renewed) whilst a smaller building will be used for the boat shed. Also, a new 20' rescue
launch has been bought.

The new Commodore is Jack Bigden (does he remain a Vice-President ?) with Stan Allerton (Vice Commodore) and
Nick Tovey (Rear Commodore). John Witter remains as Sailing Sec. and two names familiar to me appear on the
Committee ie. Pat Black and Cyril Drakeford.

On the sailing side, a Hornet team race against Saltcote SC resulted in a win for Marconi.

Fred Partlett and son Mark complete their return journey to Stansgate, take two days rest, and then apparently
sailed around to Burnham-on-Crouch. Arising from the lack of ‘Cadet activity’, Tom Gaskell has been appointed
as the Cadet Skipper with a view to organising a programme of events to encourage the cadet Section. Previously,
I believe the cadet captain was, in fact, a Cadet member. was Tom the first Cadet Skipper ? I suspect so, and
surely we can reflect with pride upon what has been built upon his initial efforts.

So 1966 ends with a bit of a ‘sailing wimper' - but we've always got the Hornet Fleet to ginger things up;
rather like our present-day Catamaran Fleet.

By the way, I still can't work out what "Visiting the Pirates" had to do with Fred and Mark's voyage of discovery
or am I looking too deeply ?

KK
Keak

Helm of the Year - 1991

"Beware the femme fatale nautique"

The Helm of the Year final was sailed on Saturday, 12 October, 1991, and it is congratulations to:-

Lucy Boreham

who became the first lady to win the "Helm of the Year" trophy in the 27th year of the competition.

The trophy was presented to the Sailing Section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club in 1965 by Sir Richard Costain to celebrate the opening of the new MASC pavilion at Beehive Lane, Chelmsford, on 17 July, 1965. It was inscribed as to be awarded to "The Helmsman of the Year" but, in recent years, we have tended to call it "The Helm of the Year" - a move initiated by Malcolm Stuart (if I remember rightly) in anticipation of just such a result as seen in 1991.

This year, six fleets were represented in the HoY final and they sailed 6 races in Toppers, with 5 races to count. The finalists were:-

Steve Glynn (Fast Catamaran Fleet)
Paul Harrison (Slow Catamaran Fleet)
Lucy Boreham (Dart 18 Fleet)
John Salmon (Solo Fleet)
Jane Williams (Monohull H'cap)
Mike Boreham (420 Fleet)

Unfortunately, the Mirror Fleet didn't sail enough races to qualify for a representative in the HoY final.

The forecast Southerly Force 3 failed to materialise and the competitors had to be content with Force 1 - 2. Race Officer, Mike Turner, set an olympic-style course of several short laps ( each 'lap' being a triangle and sausage) for each race but shortened course as he thought appropriate). As a consequence, a steady nerve on the start line was necessary, a good start highly desirable - and the failure to avoid 'tactical errors' became almost 'sudden death' to the competitors.

At 12-years old, Paul Harrison has done particularly well this year to qualify. I don't know if he is the 'youngest ever' to take part in the HoY final but he must have a very strong claim to the honour and it was a just reward to Paul for the regularity with which he turns out for the racing and the effort he puts into his sport. I've no doubt we'll see a great deal more of Paul as he gains rqcing experience.

Race 1(start 11.15 - one lap) All very shy of the line at the start and Jane Williams was first away, but Steve Glynn reached the windward mark first. However, he lost the lead to Lucy after he went too far down-tide and Lucy went on to win.

Race 2 (start 12.08 - one lap) Again everyone was well back from the line at the start but Lucy led from start to finish. Mike Boreham mis-judged the adverse tide conditions and wrapped his main sheet around the wing mark (followed by 720). He then compounded the error, and threw away 4th place, when he fouled John Salmon on the final beat (another 720).

Race 3 (start 12.54 - one lap) Jane again had the best start with Lucy close behind. Jane led to the wing-mark but Lucy overtook to reach the 2nd windward mark in the lead and she went on to win. Steve and John had an 'inside overlap' clash at the wing mark - and Steve did his 720 but still managed to come 3rd.

Race 4 (start 15.40 - two laps) Lucy had the best start and led from start to finish. Mike thought he'd got a good start but again misjudged the tide and hit the outer-distance mark (another 720 and 6th place followed). Jane and Steve swopped 2nd and 3rd spot all the way around but it was Steve to finished 2nd and Jane 3rd).

Race 5 (start 16.18 - two laps) John had a good start but, much to his chagrin, the R.O. signalled a general recall since everybody was over the line. Mike was pleased; he'd been heading the wrong way against the flow of traffic when the gun sounded. The second start again saw John over the line, but Mike surprised himself by finding himself in the lead. However, it was Jane who reached the windward mark first, followed by Steve, Mike and Lucy 'trailing' in 4th place - but all were close together; but then Lucy and Mike had moved into 1st and 2nd places by the time they reached the wing mark. On the way round, Steve hit a mark and John fouled Steve ("15-all"). Lucy and Mike held their places to the finish with Jane 3rd.

Race 6 (start 1700 - one lap) Lucy had a good start and very quickly established a clear lead. Mike also had a good start and trapped John and Jane on starboard tack when really all they wanted to do was to tack on to port. Alas, he 'let them off the hook' too soon and John secured a good 2nd place in this race. Lucy, having won all 5 of the previous races, had quite clearly won the HoY trophy but both Steve and Jane knew that they were tied for 2nd place overall - and each needed to finish in front of the other. Steve came 4th to Jane's 6th place, and so secured 2nd place overall.

Steve Glynn could probably claim the prize for being the heaviest competitor (an admitted 13½ stone); nevertheless that didn't stop him from frequently being in, or close to, the lead and his 2nd place overall was particularly noteworthy. Steve has had very little experience of sailing monohulls.

COMMODORES RAMBLINGS

Over the last three years the reputation of the club has soared. We are providing, good sailing, enjoyable activities on and off the water and organising open events to a very high standard. The support of all club members has contributed to this, but I think you will all agree that the lions share of the credit must go _ to our Commodore during this period. Neil Pembleton has provided a very positive lead, pulling together the varied interests and aspirations of the club’s membership. This has meant a lot of hard work on his part, thinking about, organising, attending meeting , and being in attendance at events to provide a lead to the club. But Neil wouldn't have been able to carry this out without the support of his family.

On behalf of the club I wish to thank Neil's family particularly Barbara for their patience and tolerance. Thank you Neil too!

At the AGMs of the various fleets, site security was a common issue. Dinghy's, cats, and cruisers have all been subjected to theft or vandalism. It is in all our interests to ensure we help each other by being more aware of this problem and taking’ steps to reduce the risks. The gate must always be shut. Open meetings are the only exception to this. Please make sure you always close the gate. Don't leave valuable items on your boat which will attract attention. Challenge anyone you don’t recognise, particu- larly if they are wandering around any of the boats. The footpath is along the road not through any of the boat parks. Report any damage or theft to the police, who will be making regular patrols to the club. Note Steve Hill's comments on keys in this issue of
Navigans.

We need your help for the Working party on the 27 =December. Please try to come. We will be clearing the ditch, so you will need old clothes, gloves and strong footwear. Tools would be useful too. Team leaders on site will show you what needs to be done. The work will be the first stage in preparing to lay drain- age pipes in the ditch . In carrying out the work we intend. to retain as much of the existing hedge as possible.

On the 4 January 1992 the club will have a number of boats taking part in the Maldon Rowing race. I will be taking part myself, which should provide some merriment so please come and support.

On behalf of all the officers of the club I should like to wish you a

MERRY CHRISTMAS, AND AN ENJOYABLE SAILING SEASON IN 1992

Mike Duckmanton

Well, what else could it be called? You will undoubtedly have read elsewhere through the pen of Mike Boreham (welcome to
the Cat Fleet Hike & Maggie) the analysis of the 1991 season. What a fantastic growth in the Cat Fleet, and, you may be
interested to know, as auch a result of people racing more frequently as new entrants. However, every set of figures
tells a story, and the other story of 1991 has to be the sad reduction in the Handicap Fleet. The overall effect has been
a reduction in the total number of people participating in Club racing from 200 to 190. I am very conscious of the fact
that racing is not everyone’s cup of tea and that several boats “cruise”, but I wonder how good a return see people are
getting when their boat doesn’t appear to aove from March to November. Any comments or ideas gratefully received...

As most people only know me as Spot’s appendage!??7) and the twerp that suffers from verbal diarrhoea in Navigans, I
thought I’d just give you an idea of my sailing background before you get Duckmanton’s (his hearing aid batteries are on
the blink anyway!). I learnt to sail with ay school in Penzance in the boat I hate the most, the Enterprise (sorry Lan,
but you try sailing one on the open sea!). This was at the tender age of 1! in 1966...... After a couple of years in
which I crewed in everything - Redwing, Hornet (sliding seat version), 1928 International 14 (they're a bit different
now), Uffa Fox Jollyboat and Ospreys - a mate of mine built one of the first Fireballs in the Club (Sail No 4437!) and we
spent a couple of years learning how to sail that. In the interia I’d sold ay electric train set and bought a Cadet for
£25 -built in 1947, sail no. 197 and should have kept the train set!!! As a gentle aside I had ay first intro to cat
Sailing and Reg White’s companies via a Mk I Iroquois that we sailed when there was too much wind to dinghy race.
Seventeen knots in that was impressive surfing across the Runnel Stone on the way back from the Scillies! In 1973 ay
parents hoped to Exeter just as I was off to university, and after helping run the Enterprise Nationals (213 boats) as
Gate Launch Driver. I found a new club at Topsham, on the Exe, where they sailed Hornets and (wait for it) Solos, and
you could only sail four days a fortnight (tidal). I crewed again for a bloke who still had a sliding seat and had no
spinny chute (those were the days). Mind you if you had the bottle to wind your legs under the seat in a blow you
certainly had an advantage over the trapezers! Having been spoiled by sea and estuary sailing I didn’t fancy puddle
jumping in Larks when I went to University and so only sailed in vacations (including the Fireball Nationals in 1974)
whilst rowing in the terms. In 1975 Father moved job back to Piymouth (the things they did to avoid !) and I became a
member of the Royal Plymouth Corinthian. The first couple of seasons were in what is my favourite mono - the 505. Three
Sail reaches (20 sq. m. kite) were ‘ansua, and have only really been matched by the 19. Then came a season at the back
end of an Albacore on loan, better than an Enterprise, but really the two aan version of the Finn followed by ay second
foray into boat purchase, a Laser (No. 7357). That was extremely good fun downwind in a blow (splash) but flaming hard
work uphill. At the same time I was co-opted as Sailing Sec - with no other people to help out! J was involved with
organising Plymouth Regatta Week, Scorpion (I think) Nationals, and (of all things) the Silhouette Rally! By this tine I
had developed the urge to be one of the property owning class so I outed the Laser and bought a flat. That meant a hunt
for a new berth which I found on an Albin Gallad for round-the-cans (roles - start tactician, main trimmer, spinnaker
trimmer) and some passage races (role - up-chucker in chief). Unfortunateiy the owner died(!) and I found another home on
a Sonata, and, if you've not heard it already, I’m quite prepared to tell the story of The Broach. During this latter
berth I'd managed to get myself entangled with a female to whom I got married, stopped sailing and took up horse riding
(dressage for the cognoscenti)....... Which brings me up to date. The wife went with the horses, the new boat was going
to be a Dart 18 as 7 thought 1 was getting on a bit for slogging a Laser round, but thanks to our new Commodore, that was
stopped in its tracks-just like a Dart would be if I was sailing it!

On a personal note, I’m a Physics graduate from Magdaien, Oxford and have worked for British Rail and Lex Service in
General Management positions before becoming an Executive Search Consultant 5 years ago. Any questions?

CLUB NOTICE BOARD - BACSPA NEWSLETTER

River Blackwater - the 8 knot speed limit proposal for the Blackwater has been
raised in various guises but Maldon Council require some form of practical capability before any change can be implemented. A parking ban for beaches is also required.

The old gravel pit at the back of Maldon designated as a watersports recreational area. Some 25% of the area will set aside for nature conservation.

River water tested at West Mersea has been found to be well below the level required by regulations.

A plan of the proposed Salcote Marina does not show what dredging/channel facilities are required into the River. In spite of several attempts by Blackwater SC to obtain further information, they have received no replies about navigation, dredging activities or spoil dumping.

River Colne - the coastal protection scheme barrage at Wivenhoe will require
about 16 boats being moved so that work can procede.
Generally, good relations have been held with the developers who have arranged a reasonable deal for Wivenhoe SC Clubhouse.

Considerable problems occur with dangerous water skiers and they seem likely to deteriorate further with a statement from the police saying that they are not going to prosecute further as warning notices are inadequate at Stone Point opposite Brightlingsea.
It was noted that the Harbour Authorities do not have budgets for provision of bouys, etc. for the various water activities.

RYA - Bob Foster has given up Chairmanship of the RYA Eastern Region but has
agreed to carry on as RYA representative for BACSPA for one more year.
His appointed successor is George Baker.

The Sports Council has put aside £10,000.00p for the Topper Fleet if this ammount can be matched by the Clubs. An appeal is to be launched for this.

It was noted that a new two person dinghy is required particularly for small/young people for training purposes.

Robin Duchesne, RYA Chairman will be present at the annual Semina at Belstead House, Ipswich, on Saturday 23rd November.

Conservation - a document produced by the RSPB is considerate and sensible.
They particularly make reference to the importance of the Blackwater and Colne estuaries as "staging posts" for migrating birds. Specific "quiet" areas set aside during migration, should not be encroached upon further.

Their findings suggest that yachtsmen and birds can get along together but

jet-skis and birds Don't.

They would welcome designated areas to protect the interests of both sportsmen and wildlife in general.

The jet-ski section of Stone Watersports Club are requesting an area for races, etc. and would like an officially designated area for their activities. BACSPA Delegates agreed in principal to an area East of Stone as previously

suggested in the BACSPA 1990 proposal of designated areas. This area would, it was hoped also be acceptable to the RSPB.

1. All MSC members must be members of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club (MASC) and must
have a current MASC membership card and number in order to open or renew their MSC
membership.

Every candidate for membership must be proposed and seconded for election by a Full or Famil Member of the Club, both of whom must be personally acquainted with the candidate. ( Rule 11)
2. CLASSES OF MEMBERSHIP (Rule 6)

Full Being a person who, at the date of election, or renewal, is over the age of
eighteen
Family Being a married couple, or one or two parents, and all their children who are under eighteen years of age
Junior Being a person who, at the date of election, or renewal, is under the age of
eighteen

the highest Hard Fee. Subsequent boats under 10 ft (e.g. tenders) are free.
6. Winter storage fees are payable, in advance, at these rates on boats, trailers and cradles to be kept
at Stansgate during the period 31st November to 1st March, following the renewal date. Cruiser Owners must also ensure in advance that space is available for their boats.

A tribute to our friend, Navid Greenhalah

Many members will be saddened by the news that David Greenhalgh died on Christmas Eve, aged 70.

David and his wife, Marie, were familiar figures at the club, particularly during the camping fortnight, and consequently their absence, during the last camping fortnight, from their usual spot just inside the site gate first alerted us to David's illness during 1991. The subsequent "Get Well" card and best wishes sent to David and Marie by 'the regulars' was, I know, very much appreciated.

David joined the staff of the Marconi College in 1950, and he and Marie joined the Sailing Section of the
MASC in 1963 . They initially "pottered" around the Blackwater in an Enterprise, E8201, and I believe
their son, Peter, still has the boat in Shrewsbury. David claimed he knew little about tides in those days and so they always carried an anchor to await 'the turn of the tide’ when they inevitably got ‘caught out'. However, having observed how much they enjoyed "“pottering" in the club boat “Idlevice" and their own Topper in recent years, I suspect their being ‘caught out' was rather more deliberate. David and Marie were often to be seen setting out for Heybridge or Maldon "to buy an ice cream" and I often wonder whether, at literally the end of the day, they achieved the greater sailing satisfaction compared to my own habit of racing around the restricted area of the club'$> racing marks.

David wrote to me last November to express his pleasure at reading the 'Navigans Past' series of articles.
He recalled Frank Savill as an apprentice - and Eleanor Eldridge (later, of course, Eleanor Witter) as a
graduate apprentice and also Nick Tovey as an early fellow Enterprise owner. Before joining the club, David and Marie sometimes visited the club as guests of Bert Brewster, and David remembered the very successful social evenings onboard Mamgu and also the ceremony at the Heybridge ‘Hut on the Wall' club-HQ when the ashes of Fred Garrett were spread on the waters of the Blackwater.

In his letter, David not only recalled the names of many old friends and colleagues from ‘the early days' but clearly reflected the great pleasure he and Marie had received from sailing and from their long membership of the club. To those of us who knewDavid only in more recent years, that pleasure was obviously as stong as ever and much to be admired. Characteristically, David had asked me not to reply or acknowledge his letter and, to my shame, I allowed time to slip by, intending to contact David in the new year to gather more ‘background information’ of what he recalled of the club's past. Alas, that is now not possible, but I value his recollections and his letter will be part of the club's recorded history.

I'm sure all members will join with me in expressing their sympathy and condolences to Marie, to son Andrew and granddaughter Katie who are also members of the sailing club., and to other members of David's
family.
Mike Boreham

The Club entered five boats in this year’s RNLI Rowing Race at the Maldon Little Ship Club on 4th January.

Pride of place wernt to the Marconi Essex Girls (alias Melanie Keeble, Lucy Herehan, Jenny Ball, Sarah Starling) who won
It was first prize in the Fancy Dress.
definitely a time for parents toa disown their daughters whoa had managed ta accumulate (and squeeze themselves into) an assortment of fishnet tights, white high-heeled shees ard tight skirts; finished off with very tasteless jewellery and hairdos. Apparently they ever appeared briefly on TV on Saturday afternoon.

Tan Caruth and our Commodore Mike Duckmanton, crewed a Gull dinghy. The Commodore, as befits his rank, was resplendent in a lounge suit topped off by his familiar flat cap. AS there was a risk of serious diserder in this boat, Pat Stuart went along ta keep them under control.

A very rice result (as they say in The Bill).
