NAVIGANS PAST - 1967

"It's no fun anymore". Maggie's anguished voice arose from the kitchen - and she was obviously not
happy. “What's no fun ?" I asked, rapidly running over a number of possible "It's" and coming to some alarming conclusions. "Your 1967 Navigans Past" says Maggie, "It's too long and ton detailed. Why don't you scrap it and start again". Well, you can imagine the effect that had on me. What would Leonardo have said if someone had told him to “put a really bright ‘toothpaste’ smile on the face of your lady friend," in place of the Mona Lisa's enigmatic smirk ? However, I'm not Leonardo, so I tore up the 27 pages of closely
typed observations of the 1967 Navigans issues - and started again.

January - The Sailing Sec (John Witter) confirms that the 1966 Regatta was the first, but that we need more
club entries for the 1967 effort. Of course, many members regard Regatta as a good excuse to do somethina else, and more than one cruiserman high-tails it for Tollesbury over the week-end. On the other hand, many
other members get ‘pitched in' to Regatta and have a fine old time. You pays your money - and has your choice.
The Editor (Eleanor Witter) reminds everyone that subs are due on lst January and not at the start of the sailing season in March/April. On the social side, Jack Bigden and Joan Gaskell apparently demonstrated the
Tango - or maybe it was the Foxtrot - but whatever it was, I suspect our modern day ‘younger set' now rate
it alongside the Valeta. Ah, the good old days when the lady of your choice would, one hoped, save the last dance for you. The Hornet Mob also tried to look cherubic as the Hornet Choir, but clearly failed, for their rendering of “Pennies from Heaven" was rated as “hardly a polished performance".

February - A write-up of a working party sounds pretty familiar. You know what I mean, assorted people
leaning on spades lookingabit lost whilst those with a conscience attack bits of grass at the road edges and hope that coffee time is not too far off. Come about 3 p.m. people start to slope off, hoping no one will notice, whilst the tractor driver, and those who seem to know what's going on, look set to last it out to 10.p.m.

March - Apparently several people claim they haven't received a subscription renewal form, but Eleanor rather
scornfully points out it's at the end of the January Navigans. She tersely states " If Navigans is so boring that you didn't read that far, please let me know". I can't help feeling it would be a brave man to say so; personally, I'd plead I'd lost it which, as well as possibly true, would certainly be safer. I certainly
wouldn't say I hadn't read it. A note says "Handicap racing is very light-hearted.....Don't be afraid that
you may look a B/F as most of the others are in the same boat". Well, if they're all in the same boat, no
wonder it's fun - all nice and cosy like. Mind you, they'll] look very much like B/Fs when the boat sinks.

April - Eleanor confesses to "...feeling awful". Maybe she had a twinge of remorse for her "If Navigans is
boring...." bit - or maybe someone was fool enough to say "Yes, it is". But Navigans is not boring, at least
not to everybody and I thought the 1967 Navigans were particularly interesting in many ways. Elsewhere in

the issue, a party night is described as successful with the THREE Gs much in evidence. No, they're not a 1960s pop group but stand for "GRUB", “GUZZLE" and "GABBLE".

May - Mick Turner and Paul Catanese are given some advice. "If someone calls starboard on you, it is much
more advisable to go smartly about....than to tip your boat over and go for a swim". Is this the same Mike
Turner who, in our modern times, performs a great double act with Mike Battle as the TWO MIKES during the Cadet Camping Week. I remember once calling "starboard" on a port tacker as we sailed close in-shore and very shallow. The other helm promptly jumped out and claimed he was anchored. I tacked and became firmly

June - Eleanor the Ed. and John the Sail capsized in the Pilot Cup. Eleanor writes "Estimated water
temperature - low. Have read A Doctor's article (on hypothermia) and know I have only a few minutes to live".
Well, I know how she feels; I ofter wonder what I'm doing out there ‘enjoying myself’ when I could be doing something more civilized like wreaking havoc amongst the worms by digging the garden. By the way, Regatta
attracted 106 boats, of which 21 were Marconi which was, I believe, an improvement on 1966.

July - Mick (or is it Mike) Turner and Rosemary announce their engagement - many belated congratulations.

Fred Partlett, with daughter Linda and Allan Polley, went ‘sail about’ up to Clacton (or rather ‘down' to Clacton as the old bargemen would have it) in their GP14. Fred was clearly a rather adventurous member, having previously been up (sorry ‘down') to Frinton and round to Burnham-on-Crouch in his open dinghy. Simon Darney was selected to represent the Marconi Hornet Fleet at the World Championships in Holland.

September - Eleanor says she is setting a precedent by missing out the August issue. She also advises the
club lease has been extended for two more years, so we're safe until end-1969. Also, the Laying-Up Supper is to be held, for the first time, outside of Marconi establishments. It is to be at the Heybridge Country
Club. The cost will be 32/6 per ticket (limited to 230 tickets).

In the Hornet Worlds, Simon finishes 9th out of 45 (best result 4th), but his crew (Jane Cottam) unfortunately Jost a toe nail and he had to have a substitute crew. Was 'the substitute’ the Fisher-man of Yachts and Yachting fame ?

8.

Former Commodore, Eric Payne, is obviously a man after my own heart, for he wonders how many members have kept their copies of Navigans since it was first issued ? Like me, he feels they are worth keeping for they are a record of the club's activities. behind the pen -name
Hé.also asks if anyone knows who is the person of "Barnacle" and he praises Barnacle forhis brilliant series of articles. Well, I'd certainly like to know the real name of Barnacle (but only in strictest confidence). At least Eric has answered one question for me; I had thought Eric was Barnacle but this clearly is not so. ew Beavine = Ed,

October - The introduction of 'the Breath Test’ results in a coach being hired for the Laying-Up Supper
at a charge of 6/- return. The Over-40s race is now called ‘The Jackpot’ and "....was sailed in two parts
following the inability of more than half the entrants to sail unassisted to Saltcote. Perhaps Saltcote's
beer revived them - more finished the return race".

November - Linda Partlett won the Ladies race whilst, alas, echoes of former years as we were beaten by the
Ariel (ie. BBC) S.C in a team race at Teddington. After the Laying-Up Supper, Jack Bigden (Commodore) was
apparently stopped by the police on his way home - but he was not ‘breathalized’. Apparently the boot of
his car was partly open. However, I wonder why his boot was partly open ? Did he start the journey with half-a-dozen ‘worse for wear’ companions from the Laying-Up Supper, and they fell out of the boot along the way ? The mystery definitely deepens !

December - In the Commodore's Report, Jack Bigden judges 1967 to be a successful year. Having lost our
radio operating licence due to non-complient equipment, the MASC granted 50% towards the cost of new radios whilst the remaining 50% was donated by members, with a particularly generous donation from the club President, Dr Eastwood. The Laying-Up Supper at the Heybridge he judged as the best ever.

Unfortunately, three burglaries during the year resulted in substantial loss of cash, etc. and Jack raises the
the point about site security, particularly as it is known that "....not all the people seen at Stansgate
are members of MSC". During the year, the MSC took steps to begin repairingthe road to the club and the AGM approved the levy of an additional 10/- subscription for 1968 to help pay to finish the job. It was also suggested that those who used the club most might wish to volunteer an additional donation or two. Discussions
with Mr Sparrow (the landlord) for a lease extension continue. The Marina Project "....has not been shelved but
it may be modified to be developed in stages". It seems the MSC is involved in the first stage, whereby the club might then secure a very long lease. The club already have various planning permissions granted in anticipation of a longer stay at the site and this demands serious thoughts about financing. With this in mind, the MASC have now undertaken to pay the clubs' fixed expenditure such as rent, rates, sewerage, insurance etc, thus allowing the MSC itself to start to build some ‘surplus funds' for possible future developments.

The Sailing Sec reports that during 1967 we had 114 dinghies and 44 cruisers registered, of which 4 cruisers
and 50 dinghies took part in racing. Since the inception of Helmsman of the Year Trophy, it had been run as a two day series of 4-5 races. However, the bad weather played havoc with the 1967 series and there is thought to spread the series throughout the year in future.

The AGM elected Jack Bigden (Commodore), Stan Allerton (Vice Commodore), Nick Tovey (Rear Commodore) - and
Mick Turner as Social Sec. Names familiar to me on the Main Committee are Pat Black, Dennis Byatt and, of course, John Witter.

Socially, the MSC reputation as a good place for ‘boy meets girl' continues unabated as Julian (Bigden ?) and Jill announce their engagement.

Lastly (and the mind boggles) it is reported
that a bullock sat (yes, sat !) on John Witter's car as he drove about the ‘smaller roads’ between Marconi sites. Actually, a similar thing happened to a friend of mine many years ago as he met a herd of cows on the way to work. He decided to ‘nudge’ one along a bit and the cow
similarly ‘sat’ on the bonnet - but added a vital additional letter to the word ‘sat’ !

wee Mike Boreham
eek
KEKE

PS. to Navigans Past 1967

I happened to mention to Pat Black that in the 1967 Navigans he got ‘an honourable mention’ about his alleged difficulties in getting back into his OK dinghy after a capsize. Instead of an embarrassed denial, Pat's face broke into a very broad grin as he recalled the strain he put on the club's rescue resources in those days. He built the OK himself, including mast, but it was so buoyant, he never did manage to clamber back
in - he claims it had nothing to do with the bar-opening times.

The November '67 Navigans has a ‘for sale' notice for "MUGGS Fleetwind No. 150 - £65 - can still show
new boats the way home". It's rather sad, isn't it, when the boat which has featured so prominently in the club's early history and lends its name to our present-day MUG'S MUG (even if spelt differently) should be
‘for sale' at £65 - and presumably was actually knocked down for a little less. What happened to MUGGS
in the end ?

CONSTITUTION AND RULES OF THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB.

SECTION 1 - Name and Objects.

The name of the club shall be "Marconi Sailing Club" (hereinafter referred to in these rules as “the club").

2. The object for which the club is formed is to promote and facilitate the sport of yachting and also to provide
social and other facilities for members as may be determined from time to time.

SECTION 2 - Officers.

(a) The Officers of the club shall be Full or Family members of the club and shall consist of a Club President, a
number of Vice Presidents, a Commodore, a Vice-Commodore, a Rear-Commodore, an Honorary Secretary and an Honorary
Treasurer. Officers shall be elected at the Annual General Meeting in each year and shall hold office for one
year, retiring at the termination of the Annual General Meeting in each year. All Officers shall be eligible for
re-election except that the Commodore, Vice Commodore, and Rear-Commodore shall not serve more than three
consecutive years in any one post.

(b) The Commodore, Vice Commodore, Rear Commodore, Honorary Treasurer and Honorary Secretary shall be deemed to be the
Executive Committee.

The Honorary Secretary shall:-

(a) With the Registrar keep a register of club members names, addresses, boats and fees paid;

(b) Conduct the correspondence of the club;

(c) Keep custody of club documents;

(d) Keep full minutes of all meetings of the club, the committee (as defined in Section 4) and, with the sub-committee

secretaries, all sub-committees which shall be confirmed and signed by the appropriate chairman upon the agreement
of the club, the committee or sub-committee at the following meeting of the club, committee or sub-committee;

(e) Administer such insurance policy or policies as may be needed fully to protect the interests of the club, its

officers, its members and its property;

(f) Maintain contact with the club’s legal adviser to ensure that the club’s affairs are managed in accordance with

the current Law.

The Honorary Treasurer shall:

(a) Cause such books of accounts to be kept as are necessary to give a true and fair view of the state of the finances

of the club.

(b) Cause all returns as may be required by law in relation to such accounts to be rendered at the due time.

(c) Prepare an Annual Balance Sheet as at 31st December in each year and cause such Balance Sheet (and accounts as

necessary) to be audited at least once annually and shall thereafter cause the same to be exhibited in the club

premises at least fourteen days before the Annual General Meeting.

SECTION 3 - Membership.

6. There shall be the following categories of membership with power to vote at all meetings of the club as indicated
hereunder. Each Full members and one member of a Family unit must be a paid up member of the Marconi Athletic and

Social Club. The rights and privileges of each category of members are as defined in the Latest edition of the
bye-laws of the club.

A FULL MEMBER - being @ person who, at the date of election, is over the age of eighteen shall have one vote.

CONSTITUTION AND RULES OF THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB.

A FAMILY MEMBER - which expression shall include:-
A)Married couple
B)One or two parents (as may be) and all children under eighteen years of age.
The family unit shall have one vote, exercisable by one person over the age of eighteen.

A JUNIOR MEMBER - being a person who, at the date of election, is under the age of eighteen shall have no vote.
Such member shall be one who at the commencement of the subscription year joins the club other than as a full
member or a family member.

AN HONORARY MEMBER - who shall be nominated and elected in the manner described in Rule 46 shall have one vote.

A TEMPORARY MEMBER - who shall have no vote.

No member except a Temporary Member may use the club premises, or any of the facilities of the club until
forty-eight hours have elapsed from the date of posting of notice of election.

The rate of Entrance and Subscription Fee for each category of Membership shall be proposed by the committee to
the members at the Annual General Meeting in each year. Any member in any category of membership and being over
the State Retirement age shall pay 50% of the appropiate MEMBERSHIP subscription. Any proposed changes shall be
approved by a majority of those present and entitled to vote and shall become operative on the first day of
January in the year following. The current rate of Entrance and Subscription Fee shall be prominently displayed
in the club premises.

Members shall also make the following annual payments as appropiate:-

(a) An Annual Boat Permit fee of such a sum as the committee shall from time to time prescribe which shall entitle a
member to sail his or her boat from the site at any time of the current year; and to store the boat at the site

between ist March and 30th November of the current year.

(b) A Winter Storage fee of such a sum as the committee shall from time to time prescribe which shall entitle a member

to store his or her boat at the club between 31 November and 28 February of the following year.

(c) An Annual Mooring fee of such a sum as the committee shall from time to time prescribe which shall entitle a

member to use the mooring as allocated by the Mooring Secretary.

(d) An Annual Postage fee of such a sum as the committee shall from time to time prescribe to cover the costs involved

in distributing the club magazine “Navigans".

(e) A Penalty fee of such a sum as the committee shall from time to time prescribe which shall be payable by any

member who has not given notice of resignation in accordance with Rules 15 and 16 and who has not paid the

appropriate fees by 31st of January.

(f) The rates of the above fees shall be proposed by the committee to the members at the Annual General Meeting in

each year. Any proposed changes shall be approved by a majority of those present and entitled to vote and shall
become operative on the first day of January in the year following.

ALL Subscriptions and Annual Fees cover the period January to December.

A view from the Rear.....

With the new season, when you read this, just a few weeks away, the Sailing Sub and I thought it worthwhile to reiterate a few points for everyone's benefit.

Early Season Sailing on the Blackwater

Water temperature in March and April is at the low point of the year, and with a fair amount of fresh water sluicing into it upstream giving a constant flow with very little chance to stand and warm up, probably sits at around 6° C. That is around 31° lower than body temperature and is a very effective method of cooling. No matter how hot the sun, it is extremely likely that anyone immersed without a wet or dry suit for protection will start to suffer the effects of hypothermia within about 10-15 minutes. More relevant is the fact that the temperature will much more quickly reduce the power of your muscles, and so whilst you could expect to right your capsized boat easily within that time you will find your capability to do so dramatically reduced. This of course means that someone else will have to save your life, either (if you're lucky) a Club Support boat that will be with you within a few minutes or the RNLI or Police, which takes much longer. THE MORAL IS TO WEAR APPROPRIATE PROTECTIVE CLOTHING FOR YOUR OWN SAFETY.

Support Boat Duties This relates to the above, only more so. Any one rostered as crew on either the RIB or Jack B must expect to go over the side to assist in a recovery operation. Bear in mind that you will also generally be very inactive and (on the RIB in particular) relatively exposed. PLEASE ENSURE THAT YOU ARE PREPARED WITH A WET OR DRY SUIT TOGETHER WITH ALL THE OTHER BITS FOR SUCH DUTIES.

The Rule Book I am very aware that for the vast majority of people the Rule Book is a daunting publication (131 pages, 78 Rules, 16 Appendices (2 RYA, 14 IYRU for the barrack room lawyers)) and is enough to put all but the brave off starting to race. For your information, only a very small proportion of it is requisite knowledge for club racing. The basic Right of Way Rules (31 to 41) are completely contained in 4 sides (pages 34-37). The slight complexity added when at a mark or obstruction (Rules 42 to 46) take up about 1/2 a page more (pages 38-42). There are numerous books which include pictures of examples and explain the situation in detail (e.g. The Rule Book by Eric Twinname, updated by Brian Willis). However, even this can be a bit daunting so in the spirit of making things simple my in-house expert (AKA Spot) has developed a fair amount of expertise discussing things over the winter. Watch for his articles in the august pages of future editions...

Formation of the M.A.S.C. Yacht Section.

A fair number of yachting and boating enthusiasts attended a meeting called by L.L.Jackson (8addow) for Friday, March 28th, to discuss the formation of a Yachting Section of the M.A.S.C. Mr.Hallam took the Chair.

The following Committee of organisers was chosen :-

Mr. Gill Hon. Organising Secretary and representative of New St.

Mr. Nichols ) New St.
Mr. Greatrex )
Mr. Quill New St. and Rivenhall
Mr. Quilter E.E.V. Co. and Waterhouse Lane
Mr. Colchester Bedell's End
Mr. Hallam ) Baddow
Mr. Jackson )
Mr. Sharpwel] Marconi College and Apprentices
Mr. Tyler Broomfield

A number of matters were discussed and it was agreed that a meeting of the Committee followed by another General Meeting should take place in the near future.

At 30 March, 1952, Mr L L Jackson sent the above brief resumé of the initial meeting (to discuss the formation of a Sailing Section) to the Secretary of the Marconi Athletic & Social Club, Mr Impey. In the covering letter, Mr Jackson explained that they hoped to hold another general meeting on 18 April at the MASC, and also pointed out that one main principle decided upon by this first meeting had been that anyone wanting to join the Sailing Section must become a member of the MASC. In another letter, to Mr Gill, I am struck by the formality shown by Mr Jackson. You would have thought that, having met together to plan the formation
of the Sailing Section, he would at least address the Hon. Organising Secretary as ‘Mr Gill' - not so,
for he addresses him as ‘Dear Sir' and formally sians off by ‘Yours faithfully, L.L.Jackson'. A sharp contrast to the informality of 1992.

My meeting with Maurice Greatrex.

One of those who attended the initial meeting to plan the formation of the Sailing Section was Maurice Greatrex who, at 88, is still a member of the MSC. Maurice has been following the ‘Navigans Past' series with great interest and I was pleased to accept his invitation to meet him and his wife to talk about the early days of the club. Unfortunately, Maurice was unable to offer any information on any 'informal'
sailing section before 1952 or why our Commodores Board shows the names for 1950 and 1951. However, he
believed the first meeting might have been held in the Blue Lion. Amongst the many anecdotes he recalled
was when Eric Payne, sailing his yacht Electra II, left his mooring at Maldon - only todiscover that his
keel remained firmly behind in the mud !. Others included Geoff Wardell loosing his wallet, and all his money, inacapsize and our old friend, Robbie Sims, driving around in a Rolls Royce (now thems was the days, Robbie !). Joe Gill (presumably the Mr Gill above) produced the winning design for a club burgee and received a glass ornament as a prize and which was created by Eric Cottam (who was both an MSC member and a glassblower within Marconi). We finally got around to talking about the river Blackwater in general and

the traditions of Maldon, Brightlingsea and Tollesbury. It was then that Maurice claimed a somewhat distant
Kk
relationship with Captain Edward Carrington Heard (born 1879) who was possibly one of the most successful of
the professional 'J' class and 12-metre class skippers between 1919 - 1939. It was Capt. Heard who sailed
the America's cup 12-metre Endeavour I back home across the Atlantic, through storm and hurricane, taking some three weeks and being given up for lost with all hands.

Maurice was a Rear Commodore of the MSC during the mid-1950's and sometimes pays a visit to the club.

I suggested he try to visit us on the East Coast Piers Race day on 26 July as, hopefully, it will be a sunny day, fair wind and a sight well worth seeing.

SEAMANSHIP AWARD

The Seamanship Award 15 a new award, donated by our retiring Commodore, Neil Fembleton in November last year, and is ta be granted annually to a Club Member who has performed a feat of outstanding seamanship. Many stories have been told over the years of the skills shown by some of our members in times of difficulty and danger wher, afloat, and it was decided that these feats should have some recognition.

The 1991 Seamanship Award goes jointly ta two younger members of the Club, Andrew Rabirsorn and Nielson Barnard, both aged 16 at the time in question, and here is the story, supplied by Corrad Barnard, of their achievement.

Ori our Cruise this year to France we chanced ta meet up with an elderly couple who had taken their Westerly Tempest on an extended holiday from the Fambridge Yacht Station toa Holland, and then on through to France. The lady was very = sprightly for her age; being the driving force behind their sailing, and in fact conducted all the functions necessary to sail the yacht, save the navigation. The man, a retired doctor, was unable to venture ontca the foredeck due to a physical disability. He had great problems in getting on and off his boat, and as a result was rarely seen anywhere except in the cockpit.

_ We had been in their company off and on during our Cruise and during that time had become aware that he suffered from a number of quite serious complaints, apart from the disability.

It was in Boulogne, on preparing to make the crossirig back ta Ramsgate, that he called me cover and asked if they could travel back in convoy with ourselves, and could we keep ar eye out for his wife. He explained that his health had taken a turn for the worse, he could not get off the boat to take the ferry home which he dearly wished tea do, and he had an almost venomous distrust of French doctors and refused to call one.

What he did agree readily to do was to accept extra crew for his yacht. For this purpose beth Andrew Rabinson and my son Nielsen Barnard showed no hesitation in wishing ta help. As a direct result both boys, who are 16 years ald, a took
strange boat and sailed it from Boulogne across the English Channel to Ramsgate -
a 7 hour trip - helming i hour on, 1 hour of Fs utilising all the instruments,
radio, etc. without any assistance, thus allowing the lady toa concentrate her attention or her husband. The bays in fact beat George and myself into Ramsgate by quite a respectable margin.

Adventures like these may well happen away from the view of interested Club so Members,
we will be relying on the participants themselves their famil companions to let us know their stories. —- Ed.

The list of club dinghies shows 26 Enterprise, 25 GP14s, 12 Hornets, 4 Fleetwind (the demise of the club's oldest and original fleet ?), 6 catmarans (since then they've bred like rabbits), 12 Mirrors and 37 other assorted dinghies, including Gull 575 (H.A.Taylor) which in recent years, I believe, was given to the club by Mr Taylor and is currently in the tender loving care of the Caruth family.

August - true to her word of a previous year, there is no August Navigans from Eleanor due to holidays.
PS. Maggie and I were on holiday too; our honeymoon to be exact.

September - Mr AD Currah writes to complain of finding a hole in his Mirror and, from the tone of his letter,
he clearly believes it must have been "someone" who failed to confess it. However, although sympathetic, Eleanor points out that damage to other dinghies can occur when storms or high winds blow a dinghy over, or a dinghy's own trailer might cause such damage. The problem of boats not being tied down securely has been a problem since the club was founded and I understand that quite recently one of the catamarans went ‘blow-about'
and sustained considerable damage but apparently did not damage any other boats - as luck would have it !

A 'write up' by Connie Bigden of her advertures of crewing for husband, Jack, in the over-40s race which seems to have included the (now) traditional 'stop-over' at the Jolly Sailor for re-fueling. Connie, being well aware of the mud at Heybridge, decided to 'stay put' until her helm had pulled the boat well into the sea wall. However, Tom Gaskell asked his crew (and wife) Joan to ‘bring the anchor'. Joan gaily jumped out up to her
knees in mud - and Connie joyfully recalls the pleasure of hearing crew tell the helm well] and truly ‘off! in
no uncertain terms. Things don't change; in the 1991 race I asked Maggie to jump out - and she did, almost
up to her armpits in water and mud. After that, I turned my hearing aid off; after all, how was I to know it

was deep and dirty ? It looked quite near the sea wall to me .

Jack Bigden proposes a whole week of club “organised activity" (presumably for the 1969 programme) with racing, cruising and picnics. Was this the first thoughts of camping week, to eventually turn into camping fortnight ?

October - a request from "the anxious wife of a harried organiser" for people to buy Laying-Up Supper tickets.
It seems 'the organisers' had a fixed price in mind when they visited the Heybridge Country Club to discuss arrangements but couldn't resist an “absolutely superb menu which cost just a little more", plus an "extra good

band". The result - they need to sell 60 extra tickets to pay for it all. The price of the tickets was
an astronomical 32/6.

A note tells us that
the last (ie. September) Navigans was sent to 354 members (including 84 Associates, etc) at a postage cost of 21/=; this October issue has cost 28/= in postage.

Dudley Currah (of letter fame ?) reportsthat 9 Mirror members have decided to form a Mirror Fleet with Murray Todd as Fleet captain. Murray later was a stalwart of the Hornet Fleet. On the sailing side, Ken Beavins won the Mona's Cup.

Finally, the GossipColumn states "Robbie Sims was seen driving Joan to church in his Rolls-Royce decorated with wedding ribbon. Is it Robbie and Joan that we should congratulate or Julian and Jill Bigden who were married at Galleywood later the same day ?" So Maurice Greatrex was right when he recalled Robbie and his Rolls-Royce.

November - Leonie Carlisle and Gordon Golding announce their engagement. Sadly, Gordon died in August, 1991,
but Leonie is happy to share the celebration of her engagement with us some 23 years later.

December- the 1968 AGM was attended by more than 100 members - who agree a levy of 10/= Joining Fee for
new ordinary Members to help the Road Fund. Nick Tovey is elected a Vice President (a note says " to add young blood to the three ancient marinas (?) of Jack Bigden, Terry hallam and Eric Payne). Membership in 1968 increased by 80 to 599 . With 7 new Associate Members admitted, the waiting list for Associate Membership continues to increase. 1969 will see the new posts of Dinahy park Secr etary i i the post of Social Secretary for 1969 has not yet been filled.

if someone's broken a tule you still give them the same treatment for Right of Way

flule 36 Opposite Tacks - Basic Rule
The shortest rule in the book, Port keeps clear of Starboard!

Rule 37 Same Tack
When the two boats are overiapped, windward keeps clear of leeward. When not, boat astern keeps clear of boat ahead.

Rule 35 Same Tack - Luffing after the start
If you are a Daginner at racing don’t pass close to windward of someone! (see diagram)

Stay out of the way until you've got used to “mixing if on the start line!!

Minutes of the Inaugural Meeting held on 18 April, 1952

The Meeting opened at 6.0 p.m.

In view of the interest made evident at the preliminary meeting held on 28th March, 1952, the above meeting was held with the express object of forming a Sailing Section of the M.A.S.C. Some 23 interested persons were present, and the business of forming the Section was proceeded with immediately.
Since only a short time had elapsed from the initial thoughts on this subject, and as it is too early to have decided the full scope of the activities of the Section, at an early stage of the meeting it was obvious that a working committee should be formed whose function is would be to plan those activities. This action was agreed by all present.

As to the constitution of this committee, it was unanimosly agreed that it should comprise the fol lowing:- Chairman, Hon.Secretary, Hon.Treasurer (and) 6 Committee Members. The meeting duly proceeded to elect these officers and committee members as under:-

Chairman: Mr Hallam proposed by Mr Greatrex seconded by Mr Garrett
Hon. Treasurer: Mr Nichols ? i ?
Hon.Secretary: Mr Gill ? ?
Committee Members: Mr Jackson * "Mr Colchester " "Mr Mercer
Mr Tate ‘i "Mr Baines i "Mr Nichols
Mr Quilter . "Mr Greatrex * "Mr Frost
Mr Colchester 4 "Mr Garrett " "Mr Quilter
Mr Daines , "Mr Quilter 8 "Mr Greatrex
Mr Christensen * "Mr Nichols as "Mr Garrett

The Working Committee having been achieved, the meeting went on to discuss certain essential matters which
comprised:

Name of Club - By a majority vote it was decided that as a section of the M.A.S.C. it would be known as
the "Sailing Section". When operating in its own field the section would be known as the "Marconi Sailing Club". This was also agreed on a majority vote.

Object of Club - It was unanimously agreed that the object of the club shall be to promote the sport of boat
or ship sailing in every form, embracing social and instructional aspects. There should be facilities for repairs, and design and construction should be encouraged. It is to be hoped that during the winter months lectures shall be arranged covering all fields of the sport, such as seamanship, navigation, and design. Perhaps the most important aim that was expressed was that there should be full co-operation between members so that they can work to their mutual benefit.

Subscriptions - It having been generally agreed that all members should automatically pay their membership
of the parent club, namely the M.A.S.C., the meeting went on to consider the subscriptions of the sailing section. The result, after some alternatives had been debated and put to the vote, was as follows:-

Subscription Amount Proposed Seconded

Full Members (with or without their own boat) 10s. Od. Mr Garrett Mr Thomas

Associate Members Not more Mr Daines Mr Byatt than 17s.6d

Family Group (to include wife and children only) 5s. Od Mr Garrett Mr Christensen

The matter of guests was deferred until a further meeting.

Next Meeting - It was agreed that the next general meeting of the Section should take place on 15th May,
1952, at 6 p.m. Before then a meeting is to be arranged for the committee.

WELL’S DISEASE - notes from RYA Information Leaflet, 1989

Between SO to 60% of rats carry and excrete the organism Leptospira ictera- haemorrhagiae in their urine. Infection with the crganism causes an illness which has been known to result in death of 10% of cases. There has been a recent increase
in the incidence of the disease - 133 cases notified in 1988 compared with 68 in 1987
and 32 in 1986. Formerly occurring mainly among sewage or abbatcir workers and miners, recent records show that the majority of fatalities are now related ta water activities. Ir 19859 there have beer 19 deaths of which no fewer than 13 were associated with water users. The nature of leisure water activity means that the average of this at-risk group is fairly young, with most cases occurring in the 13 - 42 age group.

ABOUT THE ILLNESS The organism enters the human body through breaks in the skin such as cuts, blisters and abrasions or via the lining of the nose, throat or alimentary
tract. The incubation period is 7 - 13 days and the disease starts with a_ fever,
muscular aches and pains, lass of appetite and vomiting with prostration. It is vital that the doctor be told of any water-borne activity as the symptoms are easily confused with those of flu and if the patient has a ‘clean’ occupation the possibility of Well’s Disease my be overlooked in the early stages. Subsequent bruising of the skin, sare eyes, nose bleeds and jaundice may occur. The fever lasts about five days amnd may be followed by significant deterioration. Treatment is usually by Penicillin Antibiotic.

(In 1989 the advice was: Laboratory testing of blood will confirm the diagnosis, but this may take undue time in an ordinary hospital. Send samples direct to: The Leptospirosis Reference Unit, Public Health Laboratory, County Hospital, Hereford,
HRi 2ER. Tel. 0432-277707, here they will be tested within 24 hours.)

RATS AND THE ILLNESS The rat is a creature of the water’s edge. The leptospira organism is passed im urine and, while it does not live lang in dry conditions, it can survive for some time in water. Salt water scon kills off the organism but there is a Significant risk in tidal waters such as the lower parts of the Thames and other rivers. The risk increases upstream and is greatest in canals, ponds or areas caf slowly draining water. There is a Significant risk to users of river banks or reservoir edges.

WATER USERS Sailors, board sailors, canoceists, carsmen, swimmers or fishermen are at risk in any area with a population of rats. Any skin wound ar blister, old or row, may be infected if immersed in water polluted with the organism.

GENERAL CARE:

Handrails, steps and walkways should be checked for gaps, nails or rough edges that may Cause minor wounds.

All Members should make every effort ta see that food residues are removed = from Clubhouse, boat and trailer parks or picnic areas. A happy well-nourished rat will produce more rats.

Wear shoes to protect the feet from cuts.

Dor’?t allow water to collect inside your dinghy, it may be wet but it may not all be water! (The same caution also necessary with pools of water collected on the outside of boat covers, i.e. don’t let it come into contact with any wourds. )

Cruiser Owners: if you ever have to come ashore clutching at the jetty from your tender, you toca are at risk.

Waterproof surgical plasters of an adequate size should be used to cover old skin wounds before going afloat or ta the dinghy park. Such protection will also apply toa club working parties wher members may be clearing old structures or other hazards.

Every sailing club should have available to members at all times a supply of clean fresh water tec wash wounds, ard a shower for those wha may have fallen into suspect
water.

Poussin .

Once safely back in England and looking forward to the activities and adventures of the forthcoming sailing programme, I wondered if some of the club's amateur artists would like to ‘get together’ at the club during 1992 for one or two days collective painting ? I haven't done any ‘serious’ painting since my school days, but I've recently taken it up again and would like to try some 'Stansgate scenes'. Dear Maureen,

Despite the fact that I've written many Navigans articles in the past, I've never before written a letter "tothe Editor’. So what has inspired this particular personal 'first' ? It is simply that I wish to Propose that, as a club, we should abandon marriage!

Those who know me well will, I suspect, detect a certain amount of ‘tongue in cheek' in this letter and, indeed, it is not intended to be read too seriously. Nevertheless, I feel that the club's policy on marriage is not entirely logical and maybe it is time to change it. "What policy on marriage ?" asks a bewildered
and bemused Executive Committee. "What's he on about now ?" Read on, friend - al] will be revealed.

The new MSC Rules adopted at the 1991 AGM include a definition of Family Member as a "Married Couple". Now, what is a "Married Couple ?" In the club's founding year of 1952 most people probably had a quite specific idea of what "married couple" meant and would expect to have a certificate to prove it (curiously, few, if any,
have it framed and displayed on the wall - I wonder why ?). However, I suggest a 1952 concept of “married
couple" carries little weight in 1992. How would you, the reader, define a married couple ? Would you demand certificated proof of ‘marriage’ or is it sufficient that people live together to be recognised as a de facto married state ? If not, why not ? As a matter of interest, has anmyMSC member every been ‘drummed out' for falsely claiming married status? Has a Family Membership application ever been refused on the grounds "but you are not married" or lack of proof of marriage ? The other curiousity of our membership rules is the inclusion of Married Couple" under Family Membership. What is a 'family' ? Can vou have ‘a family' without children ? If not, how come a (childless) Married Couple can be Family Members ?

Why don't we simplify the Membership Rules by allowing each Full Member to nominate (at membership application or renewal date) a 'Permanent Guest' for the year, thus treating the married and unmarried Full Members in exactly the same way (for the same basic membership fee), abandon the meaningless ‘Married Couple' category but continue to rank children of Full Members to be Permanent Guests (but restore the age limit to
18 and under on 1 January of the membership year) - and maybe restore the privilege of Student Membership
(for full-time students under 21 at lst January) at a particularly cheap rate so that they can 'legitimately' continue to use the club during the holiday periods, or maybe the previous privilege of including full-time students up to age 21 as 'Permanet Guests' under the single subscription of their parent ?

Mike Boreham

(married (with certificate), with children - and poor)

Well, folks, despite your attempts to stop these articles by electing me as Rear Commodore, the start of the new season
and a few little incidents put me back in the mode of gossip columist. After all, who could not be driven to SOMETHING
by the sight of our venerable Commodore getting into the 40th Anniversary swing by dressing in an imitation 50s schoo)
uniform at the Fitting Out Party. I mean, I have to report on it due to the fact that so few of you were there.... an
Caruth was also brave enough, but can you imagine the sight of lan and Mike playing CONKERS! The weekend had the tin
hat put on it by gale force wind on the first Sunday of the season. Yes, I fully admit that I wimped out as well!!

Fortunately weekend number 2 came to a good deal more with a nice southerly 3-4 in the morning followed by a slightly
more strident 4-5/6. Team Nickalls provided the support services particularly capably, and set some fairly intricate
little number to exercise the grey cells. It was extremely fortuitous that neither race lasted much more than an hour
for this time in the season. I’m actually sitting here completely cream-crackered with pieces of spaghetti for arms.
You see, the gusty conditions involved a fair old degree of mainsheet pumping and no one told me | needed a multi-gym at
home in the closed season to keep the muscles going!!

Anyway, the racing was pretty good, albeit not brilliantly supported. Lee and Jenny appeared to have eaten something
for boat speed, but it also had a nasty wet side-effect!! John Tuckwell and Linda also seem to have been doing the bizz
over the closed season, proving to be a real handful for the faster boats on a boat-for-boat basis. The course gave us
some really good reaches - definitely Cat sailing “as she is spoke". I was knackered enough after that without the need
for the gutsy increase in breeze in the afternoon. More capsizes, Lee and Jenny again, Pete Flook and David, just to
name the ones I knew about. Caruth and I had our share of disasters; running aground, getting the jib snap-shackle
caught on the diamonds, and finding the knot coming out of the traveller line.... Better checks next week!! Having
said that, more mind blowing reaches with one or two tests of the reserve buoyancy in the bows of a Prindle 19! Let's
hope that the rest of the season gives us more like this.

Spring Points 5 & 6 gave us more of the same with a jolly Force 3 NW. This gave us Fast Cats the chance to try out the
route to Number 3. Following Caruth and I giving an example of how to stall on the start line and to make a real pig’s
ear of things, we all legged it into the middle distance. Having mucked up, we decided to split tacks with the rest of
the fleet and found an ’ansum little lift. Fortunately, nobody else seemed to notice after rounding 3 and left us to
our own devices inshore under Osea....in a superb private breeze!! L’equip Nickalls seemed not to have lost any talent
over the winter but they had to hold second best to a certain Prindle 19 that modesty prevents me from naming!!
Unfortunately, the success was short-lived because my tiller extension JUST touched the flag at Breezy....

Anyway, a super morning’s entertainment for all concerned. Nice to see a steady fleet of 5 Dart 15s showing regular
attendance at this stage. Keep it up chaps. The afternoon looked from the shore to have a bit more breeze, possibly
Force 4, a quick look aloft for the meteorologists amongst you would have revealed a bunch of nice little cumulus
bubbling up (that means wind underneath, folks) and the cause of our enjoyment. Same course (plus an extra lap A-1-C-B)
saw an interesting time with Nickalls again doing the bizz from the start. Another tight fight ensued between Lee and
Sam Ashley, Steve Glynn ard Stuart Golding, Caruth and I, and, pleasingly, Vince and Andy. Caruth and I had an
interesting time when, approaching C, the mainsheet caught on the shroud. I flicked it free and saw the remants of a
split ring disappear into the briny!! A quick panic and fumble around, with Chris locating a replacement whilst my
thumb remained strategically placed on the pin!

Still, it was another superb day, Keep it up all, and let’s see the season go from strength to strength.

Larry Botheras

FORTY YEARS AGO - May, 1952

In May, 1952, the General Committee of the Marconi Athletic & Social Club accepted the proposals for the fledgling Sailing Section and was “ready to give every encouragement and support to such a new and promising Section of the Club". Thinas moved pretty quickly and by the end of May a draft agreement had been secured for the rent of a shed (described as a Shipwright's Workshop) on the seawall by the canalentrance of Heybridae Basin. The shed was approx. 70' long and 20' wide and already had electric light and power laid on, but its use was restricted to that of a workshop and store; it could not be used as 'a clubhouse’. The rental was £1 per week and the MASC had promised to provide £25 towards the total annual rental charge.

A General Meeting of the prospective club membership aareed that the current 1952 subscriptions would commence
from lst June. It was also agreed that a competition be held for a design of the club burgee - entrance
to be 1/- (ie. 5p) with the proceeds going towards Section funds and a auarantee that the winning design swuld be adopted.

R.I.P. to "The Tree"

(a tribute to an old and well-used feature of the MSC landscape) alas, suddenly cut-off and sadly terminated.

At the working party on 15 March, Magaie was approached by a very young lad (of about 5) who lamented that "the bridge" had been removed from across the ditch and hoped it would be put back. "The bridge" was near to "the tree", andperhaps the lad was too young to also notice ‘the removal’ of the climbing tree which had stood by the telegraph pole which, itself, formed 'the bridee'. The tree had been used by generations of
‘pre-sailing' children who had climbed up, swung on, sat in - and occasionally fallen out of - its Sranches.
When parents 'missed' their children , the first place to look was ‘the tree' and Mother's initial relief that all was safe and well was soon replaced by anxiety at the precarious nature . of their offspring's position. "Be careful up there" was the unhelpful advice; "Stop fussin' and let them play " Father would say, silently praying that the silly so-and-so's would not fall and break their necks.

A modern climbing frame, carefully constructed and fitted with safety in mind, is a poor substitute for one of
nature's own designs; rather like replacing the tea-lady with the high tech drink dispensing machine - that is
before the tea-ladies all became tea-persons and the mid-morning tea-break lost a little of its charm and zest.

"Thank you tree for all you did and the joy you gave. That you ‘had to qo’ there can be no doubt. You had clearly grown old and weary and seemed ready to fall as you swayed in the wind and rain. You looked far from your prime of life, and your limbs creaked and groaned as you fought to support the youthful loads which, in former years, you had accommodated with ease."

Thus it was that "The Tree" was humanely put down, literally cut-off as it approached the winter of its life which had to be terminated in the interests of all concerned.

I'm glad I'm not a tree.

Mike Boreham

Cambridge).

May - Stan Cambell hopes to establish a "Cadet Corner" as a regular feature of Navigans. He was pleased
with the turn-out for the (1st Cadet) Points race - but apologies for the short course ! For the next
race, he hopes Julian Bigden will ‘follow round' to observe and then afterwards point out the errors to the cadets and offer useful tips, etc., so as to improve the quality of sailing.

On the 'car denting' front, Dennis Boswell (Herald), Bill Mortimer (1100), Mike Jennings (MGB) and John Witter
(in what was described as "an old Austin" - but how old ?) all suffered ‘bangs' or engine trouble. All
this goes to show that, if you really try, troubles always come in several thousand.

By the way, Cadet Race 1 was won by Colin Smith, with Alan Hoy 2nd and Tim Bigden 3rd (I wonder if elder
brother gave him any 'tips' afterwards - and how were they received ?).

June - Regatta is reckoned to have been quite successful (only 'quite' ?) with a total of 155 boats entered,
which is an increase of about 20 over the previous best. The entry of 40 Marconi boats was about double that
of 1968. The 1969 Regatta also saw the hiring of a marquee and band.

Stan Campbell says he is disappointed at the (lack of) response to his cadet ‘cruiser trips’ and ‘lend us

your dinghy' appeal.

July - Eleanor warns there will be no September Navigans, whilst Jack Bigden warns members of the folly of
connecting the name of the MSC with any correspondence they might enter into regarding proposed developments at Stansgate (presumably ‘correspondence’ to the local press, etc). The club's public policy was, I believe, governed by terms of our lease which prevented any opposition to development plans of our landlord.

Another note from Jack states "For some years now members have been able to enjoy the facilities of Stansgate in comparative ease and privacy. In recent weeks, however, this situation has ceased by the influx of guests and non-members who have had little or no right at allto be at Stansgate". Jack then goes on to

8. j
quote an example of a member arriving at the club with his wife and family in one car and later two more cars arriving with his guests. Jack reminds us of the rule limiting guests to not more than two in one day. He also reminds us that a swing gate has been installed at the club entrance and members are expected to close it after use. Finally, he warns that periodic checks of membership will be made and that membership cards will have to be produced. Did I say this was the 1969 Navigans ? It could be almost any year since we arrived at Stansgate and certainly ‘the problems' are no less now than they were then; in fact ‘the problems'
may be worse now that more people ‘have wheels - will travel’.

The dinghy park boat register reveals 26 Enterprise, 26 GP14s, 13 Hornets, 18 Mirrors and 58 ‘'others'
(including about 5 catamarans and one lone 420).

August - our Eleanor has presumably received ‘some feedback' for she reminds us that the ‘Editor's Comments'
are exactly that. She writes "If anyone objects to what I write about, I do wish they'd send me a stinking letter to print in Navigans". How about a "Fishy Corner" feature in NaviganSwhere members could put in
‘two liners' of comment about the club and the way they perceive it is run - plus the response from those
who run it. Maybe the ‘two liners’ could be anonymous if they wished.

Eleanor is clearly undaunted by 'feedback' 'cos she goes on to refer to the rule that ‘Cadets shall wear
personal bouyancy when sailing at Stansgate' - including rowing and motor-boating. She winds up the
Editorial by stating "There must be other byelaws and rules that are not adhered to and my own view is that the committee would be pleased to hear from members who wish to suggest amendments or new rules". I think
that what she jis really saying is that if people don't like the rules they should seek to change them - not

ignore them. Did I really say 1969 Navigans ? It must!be more recent times !
A ‘general chat' article called SAPWOOD (written by The Gribble) reports Geoff Wardell being in trouble in
an Old Gaffer's race (presumably ‘Old Gaffer' refering to boats(?) - Geoff is an ex-Commodore of the MSC)
Apparently one of his crew had to be taken off by the Stone SC rescue boat and a replacement crew was provided
by a boat aground on a bank - the same bank Geoff had grounded on two years previously. Also, it appears
one of our GP14s towed in a motor boat whose outboard motor had fallen off.

Finally, it is congratulations to Mick (Mike) Turner and Rosemary on their marriage. I bet they didn't think
they'd still be getting congrats some 23 years later - or be regarded as ‘part of history'. Being mentioned
in Navigans Past might be a pleasant surprise - but takes us nearer to our pension books.

October - not much in Navigans this month. The Editor suggests that dinghies left for the winter at the
club should consider taking the mast down to avoid being blown over in high winds and also suggests the boat be tied down. Of course, she should really say ‘the owners should consider..etc' but we know what she means.

November - it is reported that several boats have been blown over in the dinghy park - don't say you
weren't warned ! Eleanor announces she is thinking of ‘retiring’ from the post of Editor and thanks Avril Stevens for doing all the typing for Navigans. Since Avril was also the Social Secretary, she must have been kept pretty busy on club affairs. Anyway, she can claim some credit, for it is reported that the Laying-Up Supper went off very well. Anthony Wedgewood Benn, MP, had been invited but was unable to attend and wrote
a letter of apology. In it he says, "....the presence of the Marconi Club on the Blackwater is very welcome
to all who have the interests of the river at heart, and I hope there may be many more years of sailing for you all". "Here ! Here!" say I. "Resign ! Resign" say others. Oh! Well! you can't please everybody.

On the sailing side, it seems that every Hornet Class regatta or open meeting on the Blackwater and Colne has
been won by a Marconi helm with one exception - and no Marconi boats took part in that event. Amongst the
club prize winners were Sue Tillotson (Cadet Series), Eleanor Witter (Ladies Cup), Julian Bigden (Helmsman of the Year) and Jill Bigden (Mugg's Mug). Finally, a note states "The Marconi Company still seems to be losing
people at a great rate....". Alas, the same situation exists
in 1992 but presumably for a different and much
more significant reason. Where, I wonder, does that leave the future of the MASC - and the Sailing Section ?

December - Eleanor supports an RYA article encouraging more women to become involved in sailing club
activities and writes "Let's have more women joining in the excellent sport of sailing on dry land and in
the organisation. If you.........don't like racing in a dinghy.....there are plenty of other ways of..... .
feeling part of things".

At the 1949 AGM, Jack Rigden (Commodore) reminds us of the lack of securityof tenure of the site. Nevertheless he and Stan Allerton have spent considerable time on preparing plans for development of the club at Stansgate, including a new clubhouse. During 1969, our landlord (Mr Sparrow) had sold his two farms (including the club site) to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. It was proving difficult to discover what plans our new landlords had for the development and use of the site. However, Jack is optomistic that it will all turn out
right in the end. Jack thanks Avril Stevens and Eleanor Witter for their work - and also his wife, Connie,
for being very tolerant and helpful over the years, especially at times when club work came before the home. The new club officers are Stan Allerton (Commodore), Dave Polley (Vice Commodore), John Witter (Rear Commodore) and Peter Crick (Sailing Secretary). Amongst the Main Committee members is the name of Ron Greygoose. Finally, an article by B Martin (crew) decries the fact that whilst, at club level, helmsmen have at least 13 trophies to fight for, crews have only one (Mugg's Mug). He wants equal rights for crews.

Mike Boreham

"MAMGU" - Forward and Aft

I have aver 3 months or so, during the Winter period, attended a series of very interesting talks and field trips an the subject of Thames Barges. These talks were given by Mr Roger Beckett, the owner of Maldon-based "Reminder" and also of the still-surviving barge works at Maldem.

The talks covered the history of Thames Barges, design considerations, construction, rigoing, sails and how they are sailed. During the talks there was the opportunity to read various books on the subject supplied far the course. Having enjoyed the articles by Mike Boreham in Navigans under the ‘’Navigans Fast’ heading, I
particularly remembered the description during the late 1950s and early 1960s of the
acquisition of the barge "Mamgu" for use as an M.S.C. Clubhouse.

Towards the end of the series of talks I was browsing through a publication when, hey-presto, the word "Mamgu" appeared on one of the pages. I am not certain how many existing Club Members were around when "Mamgu" was the M.S.C. Clubhouse, or if they were aware of some of the history of the barge prior to M.S.C. taking it over in
May 1958. However I contacted our hard-working editor and the Club's
official historian Mike Bereham, and they both felt that some further information would be of interest. Sa here goes, and I quote -

"She was laid down in 1904 at Rochester, being designed and built by Gill & Same. Although ceanceived as a working barge, she was sold before completion ta a yachtsman, Mr R. Hill-Dawe, who had a counter stern fitted and accommodation built into the hull. She was launched as the "Cawana". The dimensions were 37ft. long overall x 22ft. beam, and as a yacht her draught was 473", which contrasted with a loaded draught of had she been a working barge. Hecause of this difference in draught, 40 tons of iron ballast was stowed in the bilge, hung from the floors so as nat ta touch the bottom planking. (See ’Navigans Past’ for February and August 1958, when members removed a considerable amount of this ballast.) The model from which the "Cawarna" was built is now in the Science Museum, London.

She carried 5,272 sq ft of sail on a ketch rig. The masts were stepped in tabernacles and a gaff mainsail was laced to a hallow boom. On deck a 16’ sailing cutter and twa 13° dinghies were carried in davits, and a lighting engine ard dynamo were housed in a small deckhouse. She was ofter sailed by just the owner and his wife. (There was no engine installed at this time.) In 1908 two petrol motors were fitted, driving electric prepulsion motors which turned the shafts of her twin screws. The motors were by the Pierce Arrow Co. of New York and the electrics by the Lancashire Dynamo & Motor Co. The "Cawana" was one of the largest craft of the time (except submarines) to have that form of propulsicm. The installation was removed in 1920 when she was owned by Major C A J Younger. Twa years later a 25 bhp Kelvin engine was installed and her rig had been reduced ta a bocmless, brailing mainsail; a foresail set to the stemhead and a gaff mizzen. A topsail was not carried and she was deliberately undercanvassed to the cawner’s
desires.

In 1924 Major Younger presented the "Cawana" to the Portsmouth Sea Scouts for their use aS a training vessel. Hy 1930 the "Cawana" had been sold ta Mr RVE de &. Crawshay, was renamed "Mamgu", ard became a motor yacht, at first with one engine and later with two. The leeboards were retained to aid steering when making a passage. The "Mamgu" remained in his ownership into the 1940s, being based at the Town Quay, Maldon, but she made few passages, her cwrner preferring to be on beard in the Blackwater, using "Bee" his 29°’ motor cruiser.

Sc far, despite several enquiries, I have not been able ta discover her owner/s or
use between the 1940s until 1958 when the M.S.C. tock her over, (does anybody have
this information?) To bring matters more up to date for Members who may not know —- the "Mamgu" was sold in 1963 by the Club to the London Borough of Newham, whoa retained her at Heybridge as an outdoor pursuits centre. Sadly in September 1980, after 76 years, she had deteriorated so much that Newham decided to sell her. In the meantime Newham had the "Haybay" which was to replace "Mamgu". However, before she left around this time, "Mamgu" sank at her moorings owing to a skin fitting ta the saloon sink failing. It tock 48 hours to be repaired and pumped out. She had been purchased by Mr Vernon Harvey, a Thaxted farmer who had owned another well known barge, the "Edith May", at that time for 20 years. The "Edith May" can still be seen arcurnd the Essex coast. She was based in London/Maldon in 1991 and is back at Maldon now. Mr Harvey purchased the "Mamgu" for her fittings. The mast case, for example,

I've been checking our own copies of Navigans and realised that the Club's Ed. and Bosun have been MSC members for half
of the 40 years of the life of the Club. The June 1972 edition of Navigans shows Saturday Ist July as an Open Day at
Stansgate to which we went along - I think at the suggestion of former Commodore Stan Allerton who was my boss at the
time! Ray was teaching me to drive, and we managed to run out of petrol between Mayland and Steeple and had to walk
back to collect some (haven’t done that again, so far.)

We arrived at the Club eventually, and Ray enjoyed his first sail in Mirror No. 19799, pale blue hull, owned and helmed
at this time by Frank Savill, whose name also appears now on the past Commodores’ Board at the Club. It must have been
a nice day because we joined. We bought my boss's 6F14 in October, and when Jenny came along in time for the 1974
sailing season we decided that, somehow, we would all three of us go afloat. In July 1974 a 16ft drop keel boat with a
tiny cabin came up for sale at the club ard Jenny started her sailing in a carry cot wedged in beside "Dee Dee's” centre
board case inside the cabin. No mooring being available at that time, “Dee Dee" was launched and recovered with the car
at the beginning and end of Sunday's sailing, before and after the crowd of racing dinghies occupied the hard. 1974
must have been a nice summer because we turned our thoughts to a cruiser and in May 1975 changed "Dee Dee" for 21’
Ballerina “Coppelia". David began his sailing in 1976 in “Coppelia’s" more spacious accommodation. A few very bad
summers made us realise that a fibre-glass boat was essential if we wanted to cut down the many hours Ray spent fitting
out a wooden cruiser every spring with the reward of very little sailing because the weather was frequently so bad - you
can have some frightening experiences even while safely tied to your mooring - and, no, there was ro fleet of Cats
around then! We managed to acquire our Tupperware boat "Tara" late in 1978. In the mid-80s Jermy and David began
Mirror sailing as Cadets, and in the last couple of years graduated to crewing in fast Cats.

Jenny and David have enjoyed growing up at the Club, long may it continue being the unique place that it is, and I hope
many more youngsters will be able to follow the same path.
Ed.

40 YEARS AGO THIS MONTH - JUNE, 1952.

A third general meeting of the Sailing Section was held on 12 June at the M.A.S.C clubroom. They learned that Mr G R Tyler had offered the loan of his 18' sailing boat to the club; three members expressed their willingness to fit it out.

The meeting elected Mr (Eric ?) Cottam as the club's first Sailing Secretary with Mr (Geoff ?) Wardell and Mr (?) Robinson joining him to form a 3-man Sailing Committee. Judging to the 'Burgee Competition' was postponed for a month.

The M.A.S.C.(as the parent organisation ultimately responsible for the financial and legal 'welfare' of the new Section) was naturally involved in the negotiations for the lease for the proposed clubhouse at Heybridge Basin. The M.A.S.C. insisted on "dotting the i's " and "crossing the t's" and this meant the lease agreement could not be finalised in time for 1st June - the proposed 'move in' date for the Sailing Section. Because the Section could not move in on 1 June, they asked the owners if they would agree to a new 'start' date of 1st July, but the owners declined, pointing out that they had already made considerable efforts to clear the hut ready for occupation on 1st June - so 1st June it had to be, and the Section presumably had to eventually fork out the £1 per week for the month of June. Of course, we know now that it all came right in the end, but the delay must have been frustrating for our pioneer founder-members who wanted to be 'up and running' - or rather 'up and sailing'.

Howver, nothing daunted, they all agreed to meet again on 12 July at 'the clubhouse at heybridge, assuming the agreement had been completed and signed by then. Just to show their faith was complete, they hoped as many members as possible would arrive at the meeting by water.

Mike Boreham

This season, Support Boat Coxswains are having to do a minimum of five duties each. Being one of them myself, I consider this to be far too many and we desperately require volunteers to be trained in this activity, both for Jack B and the R. I.E.

Naw a word on Radio Communications. Having recently been listening in during a major everit, it became obvious that our radio procedures require a little polishing.

The equipment now in use is of an excellent standard, thanks in no small way to the efforts of Frank Bennett. It is however in the way that it is used that improvements could be made. Early in the day and then after lunch, the links between the four stations (Base, Race Box, Jack B and RIB) should be established. Therefore messages should be passed in the following manner:

"Race Hox ta Jack B, what is your position, Over."
"Jack B, South of Osea, Out."

The following points should be noted:

1) It is not necessary to establish the link before passing the message, as seems ta
be universal practice currently, e.g.

"Race Bax ta Jack B, Over."
"Jack B to Race Box, Over."
"Race Hox ta Jack B, what is your position, Over." etc. etc.

Comparison with the preferred method shows how unnecessarily verbose this one is.

2) The word "aut" at the end of a transmission signifies that the conversation 15
cover. The other party ta the conversation should now shut up. Such transmissions as "Race Hox standing by", as was recently heard mean nothing and can confuse other stations on the ret who are waiting for an "out" to signify the end of the conversation before transmitting their awn, possibly urgert, message.

3) If you pass a message to another station and do not receive a reply, don’t must
leave it at that. The correct procedure 15 to transmit:

"Jack B, nothing heard, Out"

This lets him (if he can receive but not transmit) and the other stations know what is going on and an alternative route for the message can possibly be found.

4) Official call-signs are: Marconi Base
Marconi Race Box
Jack B
Marceani RIB

5) A telephone link exists between the Clubhouse and the Race Box, ard all messages
between these two locations should be passed using this facility and not the radi
link.

40 YEARS AGO

DURING THE MONTH OF July, 1952

A committee meeting on 3rd July reveals that the Shiowrights Shop at Heybridge Basin is now ‘ours' with only the formality of signing the contract remaining outstanding. The solicitor's bill amounted to the sum of £4, 3s. Od. for their "charges and disbursements". The committee meeting also revealed the plan for the next General Meeting on 12 July at which it was Droposed to judge the Rurgee Competion (hy a show of hands from all present) and then follow up with two races. Race 1 was to be for dinghies, half decked and open sailing boats of any type whilst Race 2 was for sailing cruisers of any description. Handicaps were to be assessed by the Sailing Committee "on inspection of the entering craft" and later adjusted (if necessary) on actual performance in this and future events. N®. Any boat (presumably ‘cruiser') towing a dinghy instead of carrying it on board would be allowed 20 minutes in the hour in addition to her fixed allowance.

The course for Race 1 (ie the dinghies) was from the Start Line (between clubhouse and a suitably placed mark) to Hilly Pool Point Buoy (No.9), then to the red can buoy off Herring Point, and back to the starting line which was reckoned to be about 1s miles. The number of laps and direction of start to be decided (just ?) prior to the race. Race 2 (the cruisers) were to sail from the start line to Bradwell Creek main entrace (7 miles), all boats keeping to the main channel "as marked by Corporation Buoys"and leaving Osea Island to port. The ‘finish instructions' for race 2 make interesting reading ; "The first boat to finish will anchor as nearly as possible on a line perpendicular to direction of main channel and level with outermost beacon on spit extending north-east from Pewet Island. All succeeding boats will be timed over the line by the first boat, who should not neglect to time himself. (In the event of a close finish between two or more leading boats, all should anchor. The winner will be determined by a darts contest to be held later). "

"On July 12th the Sailing Section of the MASC held its first sailing meeting at the Clubhouse at Heybridge Basin. Many members came by boat over distances from 30 yards to 30 miles. The Chairman, Mr Hallam, in his voyage from the Crouch "took the chair" on the Buxey Shoals before reaching the Blackwater, and so arrived rather late. Mr Christensen brought a starting gun and his assistant Tim Tate managed to prevent casualties.

Two races were held. Four dinghies sailed a short race to decide future handicaps .».won) and will be heavily handicapped in future races. Secretary Joe Gill showing great skill in finding calm patches finished

third - we expect him to do better when prizes are offered. Four cruising yachts then raced to Bradwell -
first boat home was i but as Jim Gould and Ron Hume brought up the rear 18 minutes later, it was decided to allow them a 20 minute handicap.

The day ended with the toast to the Marconi Sailing Club being drunk in the bar of "The Green man", "

Either I had become more used to the noise and the motion, or the elements had grown less boisterous. We hoisted the main and tore off dowrwind, but this time I decided that I had to learn how to deal with the conditions and not merely to fear them. Boats, I reasoned, are designed to float; Matilda didn’t wart to visit the sea bed any more than I did and I had to
learn how to help her avoid this. It was wild. Planing, surfing - I don’t know what
the technical term for it is, but she went like _ (supply your own phrase).
All I had to de was to keep her away from the wind as her stern rose, and she would tear off in more or less the right direction. I was standing up and so had a wider horizon, being able to see beyond the wave-tops and thus to know what was coming
next. A more positive atmosphere resulted - we were back in control! Pat ever
managed a smile after a while, but demurely declined the offer to have a go at the helm. About an hour later we were crossing the mouth of the Colne quite close inshore, and it was very bumpy. We were clasehauled now, getting quite a few big greer visitors onto the foredeck and showers of rain out of evil-looking clouds were sweeping dawn from the North. Needless to say we were very wet but, strangely enough, confiderice was quite high. I always feel more in control when on the wind; the only trouble is the difficulty of keeping a good lookout to leeward, a fact we discovered when a blast on a very loud hooter prompted a peek under the boom which revealed a freighter about half a mile away heading straight up the Colne. We had beer absolutely unaware of its existence until then, in much the same way I suppose, as a hedgehog on the M25 is unaware of the approaching juggernaut.

The second memorable moment of this stage of the voyage was when I wished for three or four arms in order to be able to steer and take a photograph at the same time. Pat was leaning out as far as he could go, hanging on to the sheet with one hand, his other arm waving around above his head like a cowboy on a wild bull. We had just broken through the top of a wave and the whole front half of the boat, together with his body from the knees upwards were suspended above several feet of boiling-white and ard smooth-green emptiness. We were making a lot of leeway and not much progress, with quite a bit of the river on the wrong side of the hull, so once we gat out of the mountains and into the foothills we hove-to for a rest and emptied the boat as best we could. The sky had cleared, there were spells of bright sunshine and the wind, still strong, was gusting even stronger. We were tired and wet but extremely happy toa be back in home waters again and in the shadow of Bradwell Power
Station. (Now isn’t that a strange thought - to be happy to be near a nuclear power
station ?) We hailed a passing beat and found cut that it was lpm and near high water so we got under way again, this time with a soldier’s wind all the way = up. What a sail that was! From the moment we freed sheets we were off on a plane up the river like an arrow from a bow, the long smooth wake hissing away astern over the flat water. The spray was shooting out horizontally from amidships and sparkling like diamonds in the sunlight against the dark green of the river water, and Pat and I were screaming and laughirg like maniacs all the way.

When we stepped ashore at Stansgate at 1.30 somebody casually asked, “Had a good sail?"

I didn’t know what to say.

Andy Ochecki, Moro’, Cruiser Fleet

"HELM OF THE YEAR" - How can YOU qualify for the final on 10th October ?

The Costain Cup is awarded to the winner of the 'Helm of the Year' final series. The finalists (one from each of the club's 'official fleets') are the helms who win the Qualifying Series for the competition. The qualifying races are all those Spring and Summer Points Series races plus those races of the Autumn Points Series up to the end of September. The number of 'races to count' is the nearest whole number above half of the qualifying races. Since there were 10 Spring Points races sailed, 15 Summer Points races are scheduled and 6 Autumn Points races up to the end-September, the total of qualifying races is 31 and thus the 'number of (your) races to count' could be 16 - so it pays to 'turn out regularly' if you want to qualify for 'Helm of the Year'. The 'Fleets' are Sailboard, Fast cats, Slow Cats, Dart 18, Monohull Handicap Solo, 420 and Mirror but your fleet only gets a qualifier in the final if ONE THIRD of the qualifying races for your fleet have been raced. So, not only must you 'be regular' - but so must your fellow fleet members !

Following the article on Radio Communications between MSC Base, Race Box and Rescue, Dave Beane would like to add the following information for members who might be
interested.

Correct procedure is that the station called is always first in the message preamble, and the correct proword is "This is" and not "to".

Therefore the correct format would be:

"Jack B, This is Marconi Race Box, Request your position, Over."

and the reply:

"Marconi Race Box, This is Jack B, Position Osea Pier, Over.”

followed by:

"Jack B, This is Marconi Race Box, Understood, Out."

Having done my pedantic bit, I would like to suggest that either or both of Michael Gale’s books on VHF R/T and the appropriate RYA booklet be made available to users of Marconi Club radios. May I also offer to give ai short teach-in on radio procedures should that be considered useful.

I suppose this sailing club could in a way be considered to be MSC*’s tiny baby sister, or perhaps cousin. It has been in existence for a couple of years with no more than 10 members, but this has lately dramatically increased to a membership of about 20. The club has just moved to Haversham Lake, north of Milton Keynes, where it shares a smart new Clubhouse and site with various other Clubs.

At the moment none of the members individually owns a boat, the membership shares a tiny fleet of 3 boats which they hope to expand in due course. One member gives instruction ta those new to sailing who wish to be shown the ropes.

My interest stems from the fact that my sister (who once had the privilege, shared by many, of being capsized by my daughter Jenny at Stansgate) has allowed herself to be bulldozed into the post of Hon Secretary, and is also considering starting the club’s Magazine in order to help the members to keep in touch with each other.

I hope that perhaps one day in the future a few members of the new Club might be able to come and visit us, and have a sample of tidal salt water sailing which is quite a different experience from inland water sailing.
