The Renewal of Subscriptions Forms and the Discount Paint information makes the January edition of Navigans a very bulky
one every year. This has meant holding back one or two contributions that are of general interest. Next month I intend
to catch up with Navigans Past, sailing rules quiz (a pity this couldn’t be fitted in the Christmas edition,) a marine
ecology article, and a cruise log.

A DART 15 NEWS article, 2 or 3 months overdue because the original was lost, can be found on the last page - don’t miss
it now it is here!

I would like to add my thanks to those of the Commodore to three hard working volunteers who have recently stepped down
from their posts. Thanks again go to Leon White who (for the past 8 years I understand) has taken care of the folding,
enveloping, addressing & posting of all our editions of Navigans - quite a task each month of the year. Once Navigans
was typed and delivered by me for printing, I could leave the rest of the task safely to Leon, a great relief on some
occasions! Navigans Distribution is one of the Club tasks that goes on totally unseen (apart from its result) by the
membership. (Some other duties are only seen being carried out if you visit the Club in deepest winter!) Warmest
thanks also go to Mike Turner and Mike Battle, our Cadet Fleet instructors who have over several years (winter as well
as summer) taught all they could to any Cadets who came forward to learn about sailing. All their planning and hard
work came most vividly to our notice when huge fleets of Cadets took to the water each Cadet Week. We would love to see
some more of those Cadets sailing around on other sumer weekends,

I would like to mention the wives of our volunteers, who help considerably either by actual involvement, or simply by
giving their men the time and space to do their work. From what I’ve heard in the past it is often the much-desired
wallpapering and decorating around the home that suffers most! So thank you also to Norma White, Rosemary Turner and
Janet Battle.

R.Y.A_ NEWS

Having been volunteered as MSCs representative to the RYA, I find I have some catching up to do in passing on
information received from RYA Eastern Region meetings as far back as June, and whilst some of it is water under the
bridge, the contents may still be of interest.

Items of local interest were as follows:
1) That the Marina development at Salcott had been turned down by the D.0.£. - I am trying to find out more about this.
2) Maldon Lake - slow progress due to the developer going slow on account of the current slump in house building.
Maldon Council are putting some pressure on to get the Lake deepened and have debris removed. They also expressed their
thanks to the RYA Eastern Region and the Blackwater SC for advice and support. Maldon Council Planning Review,
Blackwater Estuary, BACSPA, RSPB, Wildlife, all being consulted.
3) Wivenhoe Barrage now well under way.

Sailing in Holland
1) Dutch yachtsmen are not allowed by their laws to have a hand-held VHF set on board a yacht. These are quite
acceptable in the UK providing a valid licence is held on board. The suggestion is, when in Dutch waters, don’t wave
your hand-held set about!
2) Yachts that carry pyrotechnics that require a UK Firearms Certificate (Very pistols, some Mini-flares, etc.) should
always carry the Certificate on board, as the Dutch Authorities may well demand to have sight of it.
3) There is also the extraordinary situation where the Dutch Authorities require all vessels more than 15 metres long
or capable of more than 20 Kmph to carry a Dutch Certificate of Competence, obtained through a written examination in
Dutch and taken in Holland! The RYA is continuing its efforts to get RYA qualifications recognised by the Dutch
Authorities and has got the full submission from the UK Department of Transport. In the meantime the RYA still advises
yachtsmen sailing in the Netherlands to carry the Helmsman’s Overseas Certificate of Competence.

Wreck Marking Trinity House has asked the RYA to publicise the fact that their ships may now exhibit a RACON when
involved in marking new wrecks. This will be in addition to signals displayed under Rule 27 of the COLREGS (Collision
Regulations?) The RACON will have the characteristics: Type Agile Frequency 'X’ and 'S’ Bands; Code: Morse 'D’;
Nominal Range 10 Miles.

UK__Keep Low Diesel Rate HM Customs & Excise and the UK Goverrment has managed to maintain the present duty on diesel
fuel for marine use. Along with Belgium and Greece, the UK has decided not to accept the new minimum rate from
January 1993, This is good news, since the cost would have increased by £1 a gallon.

I will be in touch with representatives of the RYA Eastern Region Council and will be pleased to take up with them any
points of interest, be it in relation to Cruising or Dinghy sailing and, of course, the environment.

Derek Kirby, [redacted]

Sorry Folks, but the sense of humour (!) doesn’t change with the exalted position!!

I hope to keep the general light-hearted tone that you’ve come to know and love me for in "A View From the Rear", but obviously there will be a reasonable degree of gravity from time to time in accordance with "wot’s going on". Initially, we'll be starting off on the latter footing as I outline our initial thoughts as a new Executive and Committee on where we go from here.

Obviously our existence is inextricably linked with that of MASC, and with all the fun and games going on with GEC we are very firmly watching events and putting in place contingency plans to cover all eventualities in that direction. We (the Exec) had an interesting meeting with Norman Cox (Chairman) and Gerry Wignall (Manager) that put things into perspective and removed any of the immediate anxieties we had (particularly with the resignation of Mick Elliott from the MASC Committee).

Any good organisation has a "vision" statement (all you BS 5750) people please note!) and although we have not discussed one in detail there is one implicit in both the Exec and Main Committee. I think it can be best summarised as follows:

"To improve and develop the resources and facilities at MSC incrementally in order toa enhance the enjoyment of sailing of all members, and, whilst recognising that 1t is a self-help club, to reduce the demands on individuals with respect to their investment in time and energy."

There are a number of critical areas that we looked at after the working party, such as the state of repair of the road, the Cruiser Park and the state of the roof and windows of the Clubhouse that are under immediate and urgent consideration.

We are also looking seriously at the social calendar, although there has been little response about the Barr Dance. The Laying-Up Supper at Channels was a very erjoyable right and, what is more important did not run up the huge losses of the past. Watch this space for developments in that respect.

I can’t finish this without a few wards of thanks to a few people who have’ finished periods of involvement in various respects. Firstly, Leon White has been stuffing Navigans into envelopes for ever as far as I can make out, and he’s decided that crouch is enough. We often get work teams together to do things like the AGM notice or membership packs, and we then realise what a job it is. Leon has done it twelve times a year since rineteern canteen. (Ed’s note: through 6 years, seeing off 5S Commodore’s 1 believe!) Thanks a lot, Leon, you deserve the rest!! (Best of luck to Keith Starkey as his replacement!)

Also the Two Mikes, Turner and Battle are stepping down from their role as Cadet Fleet Captain and Chief Deputy. Their effearts which have gone largely unsung in Camping Fortnight deserve special mention. Thanks for all your efforts!! (PS Ar:
volunteers for 1993, please ring Colin Kidner!!)

Arid last, but by no means least, Mike Duckmartorn. I know Mike was particularly unhappy at having to step down late in the day but in the past two years that he has served as a Flag Officer, Mike put a lot of thought and energy into consolidating the direction of the Club, and has left an indelible mark on "the way we dco things". I mean, where else did you see a Commodore wearing a tatty flat hat and sailing in
pink!
!

There’s an awful lot that goes on behind the scenes ard I am pleased to have a very active and energetic Executive to help sort it all out. You very often don’t know the full extent, mainly to avoid undue heartache. The Exec, Main and Sub-Committees pick all of that up and deserve your thanks for making your Sailing Club work in the way that it does. Give them your support and let them know when they de it right as well as when they do it wrong!

Sorry for the long diatribe, but I felt it important to set the stall out.

Merry Christmas and A Happy New Year to everyone.

Larry Botheras, Commodore

CRUISER FLEET AGM 1992

The Cruiser Fleet held their AGM on Sunday 15 November 1992 at MSC Stansgate toa which 23 members (representing 23 Cruisers) and also the Rear Commodore attended. The meeting opened at 1200 hours, chaired by Fleet Captain Derek Hall. Matters arising from the previous AGM held November 6th 1991 were incorporated in the discussions for this year which were as follows:

SECURITY: The requirement that ladders be padlocked to trailers while Cruisers were laid up in the Cruiser Park is still not being carried out by some members. This not only causes a danger to their boats, but also to those belonging to other members. It was suggested that a sweep of the Cruiser Park be carried out, and any ladders not secured be gathered up and be padlocked together until claimed. This is being investigated. In the meantime would members take note. Members are also reminded that the gate must be closed after entry and exit.

PAINT Malcolm Shaft has again agreed to purchase antifouling, paint etc. on behalf of members and details will be in Navigans (this edition). He reminded members that all cheques are to be made payable to M. Shaft.

CHAIN and MOORINGS Dave Thomas will again be purchasing chair on behalf of members which will be half-inch and three quarter-inch, as well as shackles. Watch Navigans for details. Concern was expressed at the state of some Moorings. It was suggested tighter scrutiny be carried out whereby persistent offenders forfeit their Mooring space tao members on the Club’s waiting list.

FLOTILLA SAILING Events this year were seriously affected by the weather. However the Club finished on a high note with an excellent evening at Bradwell (some don’t
remember much about it) on Saturday 10th October. After some 4 - 5S years of
organising these events, Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman finally finally decided to stand down. Both received a hearty vote of thanks for their efforts over the past few
years.

FLEET CAPTAIN It was at this point that Derek Hall arnmnounced that he was = standing dawn and that Derek Kirby had agreed to take over. The appointment was agreed unanimously, at which point the Chairmanship was handed over. The incoming Captain proposed a vote of thanks to Derek for all his work on our behalf. Two members were also required to sit on *Clubhouse’ (Derek Kirby agreed) and ‘’Soacial’ Committees (Barbara Holdsworth agreed).

GENERAL Winter Meetings were yet to be arranged (see dates below) one of which will include a visit to Bradwell Power Station (a comforting land mark when returning home
sometimes) - watch Navigans for details. Early notice is given that the Piers Race
will be held om 15 August 1993 and we look forward to your support for this worthwhile event. We are looking into the possibility of purchasing a new TOEJACK, preferably hydraulic, also now that the Hosepipe ban is off, the merits of renting/buying a High Pressure Hose will be investigated.

RYA information is to be reported in Navigans as and when received.

The Meeting closed at 1310,

SIGNING OFF = WITH APOLOGIES.

After 9 years as the Results Secretary, I handed over the Results Box to Willie Pitcairn (new Sailing Secretary) who will, presumably, in turn hand it over to Mike Hellewell (new Results Secretary). It
would probably have been more logical to give it to Mike in the first place - but I happened to see
Willie first, so I ‘dumped it' on him and, anyway, Mike was up to his eyebrows in prizes and trophies.

Mike, I understand, plans to 'computerise' the results for 1993, so I guess we will ‘await the results’ with interest. I must admit that I tend to view the magic of ‘computerisation’ with a certain amount of scepticism. Like many another poor soul, my office is adorned with WPC, Database, Windows and Accounts Package, all contained in a grey box which insists on sticking its computerised tongue out at me (ie. the Drive 'A' floppy disc). The Accounts Package presents me with several thousand ledgers, whereas I was more than happy with the 60 provided by the old-fashioned manual system. At the touch of a key, I can see that the computer's Balance Sheet 'balances' and the Profit and Loss Account ‘profits’ ina very convincing way, although I am also certain that the computer's bland statment that our Current Bank
Account contains £356,726,532.26 must be incorrect - but, since the computer says it is so, then I guess
it must be right and I am wrong.

] must apologise to Martin Newman for forgetting to put his 'Muggs Mug’ win on the ‘major trophy' part of the Prize List, just below the Cadet Trophy listing. Unfortunately, I only had about 3 evenings in which to work out the Autumn Points Series results, compile the Prize List, assemble the Sailing Statistics
and list all those who took part in the racing programme during 1992. - and all so that it could get into
the December Navigans and be ready for the AGM.

Maggie and I have greatly enjoyed ‘the results' task which, like many another support job in the club, has more often than not proved to be a thankless one. Nevertheless, it gave us a great deal of satisfaction and pleasure and that is the most important thing about it; once a club job ceases to give personal enjoy- ment, it's time to let someone else have a go.

Computerisation is , without doubt, inevitable, desirable and wonderful, so I wish Mike ‘ben Voyage’ as he sets out on his journey through the software equivalent of the Sargasso Sea.

Mike and Maggie Boreham

DART 15 NEWS

(With apologies to all concerned for delay in publishing - first submissian to
Navigans appears to have gone missing somewhere in the system —- Ed.)

Following the excessive winds on the 30th August, the Dart 15/Solo Open meeting saw ideal weather for sailing, but not if you were Race Officer, particular on Sunday!
Saturday saw 11 visiting Dart 15s and one Sting - mast boats coming from Grafham -
arid 8 Club Boats competing. Nick Dewhurst arrived minus prizes and decided to go off ta Maldon at about 11.15am leaving the rest of us to put his boat together. The TT regulars maintain that he doesn’t know how to assemble a Dart which is why he keeps pulling these stunts. Those who know Nick will not be surprised to hear that he gat the prizes, made the start, and was first standard boat across the line!

Saturday and Sunday saw some close racing between the visitors’ and Club boats,
particularly in the last race. Larry set the course to go once round the marks = and then round Osea, leaving it to port before completing the race by going round the marks three more times. Jim Jeffery led Willie Pitcairn, Nick Dewhurst and myself as we started the first of the last three laps. The first three boats stayed in mid charmel, your truly bore off to sail close ta Osea shore. This tactic paid
off....madesty forbids that I go on.

The final results were:

SPRINT STANDARD

1. Mike Cemm Dart 15 1. Nick Dewhurst 6. Tim Dieu de Bellfontaine
&. Gerry Reeve Sting 2. Phil Meal 7. Bob Anderson
S. Paul Berry Dart 15 3. Jim Jeffery 8. Debbie Yorstan
4. Willie Pitcairn 9. D. Davies
5S. Colin Kidner 10. Nick Pavitt
li. Dave Bladon

A superb weekend’s Sailing and many thanks to all those Club Members who helped aut, particularly those who volunteered at short notice to drive support beats. A special thank you ta Larry who ran the shaw.

The Autumn Points Race 3 took place in light airs. For once yours truly got it together from start to finish! By the way, Paul is not invincible! The afternoon race was a drifter. I still don’t know why I bothered.

The forecast for Sunday 27 promised a Force 4 to 5 so we got another drifter in the morning. Six Dart 15s started, those who used the bottom of the Blackwater managed to start the race without going via Maldon! Paul won and the rest of us retired for lunch. The afternoon saw a better wind and same close racing early on, and Dave gat a place, he was third!
Colin Kidner

marine Ecology and Sailing 1s solely concerned with the relationship oetween sailing and nature, it does not endeavour
to resolve anthropocentric and terrestrial conflicts with leisure boating resulting from a suburdan vision oF the coast
and sea - 1.e, landscape value.

A View From the Sea To gain an insight into the basic principles of estuary management it 1s vital to take a historical
perspective. Sailing and boating have been integral to the ecology of the coastal waters of Europe, ano estuaries in
particular, for many centuries, mainly for commerce with the facilities required developed on ari evolutionary basis. At
the turn of this century there were probably more sailing craft occupying the coastal zone than there are today.
Sailing barges, fishing smacks, winkle brigs, oyster dredgers etc. proliferated around the coast. Virtually every
sheltered creex and estuary provided a natural harbour for these craft when not in use. Therefore this fac 1s
inseparable from any overall concept of estuary management.

As commercial sailing craft oradually disappeared so the traditional facilities once used by them were utilised
increasingly for leisure purposes. Very little changed until the severe flooding in the early {950s with the decision
to embark on an extensive prooramme of hard surface sea defence works. As a result many Dlaces which once provided
traditional moorings and berthing for small boats were no longer available due to enclosure. This coincided with
preater interest in leisure boating, coupled with the introduction of new forms of water sport. The increased demand
for moorings in pupular areas has been satisfied by purpose built small poat harbours. To maintain craft afloat at all
states of the tide a cill was required at the entrance, sterilising the enclosed mud for wading birds to feed, unlike
traditional harbours which are tidal. Also the placement of sea defence works crasticaliy reduced the inter-tical zone
diminishing the distance between boating activity and wild life.

Ir a traditional context, it can be argued that leisure sailing has minimal impact on nature. Most locations for
sailing are sheltered low energy coastlines were saltmarsnes and mudflats predominate. It is also clear that wildlife,
especially birds, are attracted to these areas for similar reasons and for the ricn food source available in the mud.
The abundance of wild birds appears to suggest that a symbiosis has evolved. Indeed it may be the presence of small
boats which is a positive factor. There are many examples where wading birds are content to feed within close proximity
of moored leisure craft. Fernaps the shelter a moored boat provides from cold winds enables birds to survive where they
minnt otherwise perish. Also, smal] boats and their rigging provide convement resting places. It is not uncommon to
see a Little Tern resting on a mooring buoy between fishing expeditions or in wintertime a a Twite hanging on to a yacht
forestay.

It has peer said that saltmarshes are mainly of interest to ecologists, botanists and secimentologists etc. however,
this 12 not entirely sc. Sailors also are deeply concerned that saltmarsh habitats remain intact and 1t has been the
pressure py them to preserve their mooring facilities which has often prevented land-claim for agriculture, rubbish
Cumpinc and coastal cevelopmernt. Furtnermore the presence of smal: craft offers protection to a saltmarsh by acting as
a brake to the dynamic effect of waves, especially at the fringe.

Nonetheless recent developments in leisure boating can have an adverse impact on the ecolony of coastal waters. Water
skiing and jet skiing, of which power and speed, with the attendant noise and wash are significant factors, clearly nave
2 disturbing influence on wildlife. Landing from seaward by the novice onto what may appear to oe a deserted stretch of
shingle may inadvertently destroy a nest site for Little Terns or other coastal nesting species. Clearly, tacking a
Salling craft in & narrow creek with the resultant flapping foresail may also create a visual and noise disturbance.
The speed of modern life inevitably results in a detachment from nature and this lest affinity 1s difficult to recapture
Instartiy in readiness for the weekend sail. Therefore, easv access to information 15 paramount to the contemporary
Sailor to develop the necessary empathy with wildlife wher: using congested estuaries and coastal waters.

A further attitude which has exaceroated the pressure on coastal waters 1s the anthroporentric terrestrial perspective
exemplified by the Heritage Coast concept. The almost fanatical opposition to any form of development, irrespective of
of how environmentally benign it may be, sterilises long stretches of coastal water for the leisure sailor. The
coastline of the UK car be extremely treacherous and it is therefore vital that refuges, in the form of smal! boat
harbours, are accessible within a few hours’ sailing time to provide convenient shelter from the rapid onset of bad
weather. Heritage Coasts Coasts are invariably chosen for their dramatic scenic quality where wildlife may be somewhat
sparse, Also, these coasts are often some of the most hazardous, Wher planning permission for smal) boat harbours or
launching facilities are refused, this inevitably results in confining leisure boating to the more sheltered but already
conpested semi-encicsec estuaries which are also important wildlife hapitats.

Proposals for the Future Any proposals intended to resolve what are perceived to require a manafement initiative must
recognise the realities of the marine environment. The sea is at times ar unforgiving task master and all seafarers,
including leisure sailors, go to sea on these terms. Therefore any attempt to impose planning or management systems
which have evolved from a terrestrial background nave no place at sea.

These requirements may consist of public launching ramps and landing places located where minimal impact on wildlife

There are rumercus other needs ashore which car help minimise the adverse impact of leisure boating on the marine
environment put which car: only be determines by all parties involved. Finally, however, 1t is worth reflecting on why
leisure sailing 1s enjoyed at all considering how brutal the sea can sometimes be. It is a romantic search for freedom
otherwise lost in the dead habit of everyday life. To go sailing at sea where one wishes, or as determined by the
natural elements, is to recapture a lost spirit of adventure and sense of remateness for which so many of us feel 2
need. Management systems which in any way compromise this vision for leisure sailors will mean, for them, the end of

NAVIGANS PAST

1972 (June & July) Would that the Commodore the giftie gie us; To see ourselves as others see us.
- In what image should we build ; & new clubhouse in our spacious field ?
- What shape, what size, how high, how low ? ; How much, who pays ? Oh! wail ! Ah! Wow !
- If Solomon in his wisdom decided ; You can bet the result would be soon derided.
- No matter what the "How, Why or When ?" ; It's bound to be beyond our ken (or Jane or Tom
- We'll all keep quiet and await results ; too shy to speak or point out faults.
- BUT when 'tis done - this monstrosity ; We'll blame it on "The Powers That Be".

June - Amongst the "baby! announcements is Jonathan David Craig (Bigden), grandson of a, no doubt, delighted
Jack and Connie Bigden who subsequently donated the Jonathan David Craig cup for a Mirror Open Meeting. Alas, the Mirror fleet has shrunk in size since then, but Jonathan (David Craig) is now a lot bigger and lives in the USA with parents Jill and Julian Bigden, and has proved to be a very welcome and engagine visitor to the club in recent years.

With his ‘Ordinary Member' hat on, Stan Allerton writes in support of Pete Foreman's "New Clubhouse" comments in the May Navigans, noting that the original (ie 1968) idea was for a single storey building on pillars with storage underneath. He points out that building on the river -side of the sea-wall would not be entertained,
not least because of the problems of a shifting foundation !| He also supports finishing races off the club-
house, but feels they couldn't start there because of the unfavourable (tidal ?) conditions.

With his ‘Commodore's hat' on, Stan also writes a long article on 'Planning and Development' and it is evident “that “rumour and mis-information" has been circulating which Stan attempts to put to rest. Stan’s article is -00 long to cover all his points here, but I am impressed by the straight-forward and succinct manner in which he informs the Members, via Navigans, of the current situation. One interesting ‘snippet’ is that our current
day 'Cat' field had only just had the two concrete access bridges built - but we had no planning permission
for its use other than as agricultural land. It is worth, however, quoting Stan's closing remarksr-

Remember - without prejudice - that whatever we build can only be built with our money and will belong to
the Sailing Section of MASC.

Remember - without rashness - a decision to raise subscriptions.... to build a £10,000 clubhouse within
four years could deny membership to someone else.

Remember - with gratification - we must continue to pay our dues .... of £1,000 increasing by £100 per year
for the next 4 years to our parent club against the debt of £21,300 incurred for the purchase of the site...

Remeber - without flamboyance - the need for a "Club-house in character with our image".

Ken Beavins writes a letter stating that one of the club's two fields should be kept as a ‘green space’ for the
many club children under sailing age but without special play equipment - only clean grass and open air.
He is also keen to retain existing hedges and trees along the roadside of the ‘dinghy park' field - alas the
once thick hedge there has long since gone. Ken is not too keen on improved facilties for campers/caravans and is, in fact, against any camping at the club except for the 3-day Regatta. He fears that camping would turn he open, airy and pleasant Stansgate site into a “sort of waterside slum only too common along the Essex rivers and coast". Ken is no longer with us, but I wonder what he would make of both the site and the sights
these days ? Would he be relieved that his worst fears were not fulfilled ? - or would he be saddened at
what he saw ? ] suspect it would be a bit of both - but you can't stop ‘development and progress', especially
if it creeps up on you unnoticed. However, Ken praises Navigans and particularly enjoyed some of the "thought provoking items in recent issues".

A letter from J W Pletts reveals that he and his architect son had put forward similar ideas to those postulated by Pete Foreman but, it seems, they had been rejected. Overall, he felt that everything was “already cut and dried" and there wasn't much point in making suggestions. He feels the lines of communications between “the Powers that be" and the ordinary club member leave much to be desired and asks for a special meeting to discuss
(a) the current status and future plans for Stansgate and (b) what actions are needed to enable ordinary members
to be informed of progress and be able to express their views.

Finally, our new ‘old friend’ Observer comments on Regatta which was sailed in strong winds and recounts that

“,..the (Marconi) crew of a leading boat in one of the races left his boat and deliberately entered deep water to render urgently needed help to a family of two adults and two very young children whose Mirror has capsized. Sacre ..the following boats in the race, who had of course caught up with the erstwhile leading boat, then deliberately delayed so as to allow it to resume its former position after the rescue operation has been completed." Observer comments that "The incident reflects credit on all concerned, except (it has to be said) on the helmsman who took two small children for a sail in such patently adverse weather conditions".

16.
July - An appeal by Pete Foreman (Cruiser Social Secretary) to the dinghy sailors; "If you should hit a
cruiser, please tell the owner as soon as possible either through the OOD or directly". Apparently, three cruisers has recently been holed. Now, I wonder where I've heard that message before ? I wonder if the
dinghy sailors got ‘all huffy' that their seamanship should be thus questioned ? Even more intriguing, |
wonder who made the holes ?

Well, the ‘Clubhouse debate' is well under way and battle has been joined. Four letters are published in the July Navigans and maybe there are more to come.

In her letter, Jane Long briefly reviews features of ‘local' clubhouses, including the Royal Corinthian where
"....ties will be worn after 7.00 p.m.". She is somewhat critical of the new clubhouse of our near neighbours
at Maylandsea Bay for she writes "Anyone who has known the club for some years will tell how it has changed
from a jolly glowing "who's-going-to-be-Race-Officer ?" club - much the same as ours - into an uninteresting
spiritless place. Why ? - they built a new clubhouse". Well, I know what she means. Maggie and I
met at the Penzance Tennis Club when it had no clubhouse and everyone gathered together on the grass banks

by the tennis courts, everyone was friendly and mixed well. Then they built a nice new clubhouse - and the
whole atmosphere changed. Those who formerly freely mixed in a friendly bunch no longer did so, and it was all
down to the clubhouse. Mind you, I expect the standard of tennis improved - but I couldn't play anyway.

Jane goes on to praise the spirit of the existing club, despite lack of hot water and showers, the presence of the smelly cess pit and the need to shout "Shut the door" as the last person out of the Ladies Changing Room (closet ?) exposed those ladies inside to the keen-eyed view of those on the outside. Jane is not against a
new clubhouse as such - she merely fears a change of atmosphere. She writes “What I hope is never said to
sailing members is "You can't come in for a drink - you're wet and you'll ruin the floor" After all, it is
a sailing club". How close have we come to that position in recent years ? It was only a season or two ac that I argued against confining the wet sailors to the newly created ‘overload bar' in the garage downstairs. Let us hope the 'overtoad bar' doesn't become the ‘wet bar’ by default. Would it be progress if it did ?

Dr R T Jones writes to support Ken Beavins view on campers and caravans and fears the club will] become a
Caravan Club with sailing facilties. However, Margaret Farnie writes in defence of limited camping/caravaning, perhaps limiting the number of camping units to 3 or 4 and definitely ‘for members only'. Oh dear ! How does that measure up to the 50 or 60 units (including non-members) of recent years ? Is it progress ?

However, Tom Gaskell] must take the prize for the most forthright letter of 1 pages in which he doesn't mince his words. He writes "I have read one of the most bigoted and conservative letters which it is possible to write on the subject of preventing people from enjoying themselves after their own fashion without interference with others". I think he means he doesn't agree with some of the viewpoints of another member .

Tom then goes on to dispute/disagree with Ken's viewpoints, but supports limited camping and is, surprizingly, against a new clubhouse, although he supports a more economical scheme of "an ablution block somewhere" with a SWIFTPLAN building on top to act as a clubhouse, He finishes up with what I feel are two rather 'deep'
sentences :-

"It would be interesting to know what our ‘image’ is - to see ourselves as others see us - or should
we remain enchanted with our own reflections. The facts are that we are running the club on a shoe string with heavy overheads and exploiting the willing few to run or ruin a valuable asset."

I guess the ‘ordinary member' found the whole thing quite confusing - maybe we should have stayed in the Hut
on the Wall at Maldon where all was simple, pure and friendly. (Oh yer? If you believe that, you obviously haven't been reading Navigans Past !).

Observer laments the fact of queues of cars at Stone and fears they'll all descend on Stansgate. He feels that unless the club enforces the "no vehicular access" notice, then the steady trickle of uninvited gate- crashers will become an unmanageable flow. He proposes a ‘locked gate’ system with keys for club members (keys to be paid for).
Finally, Pete Foreman's Grand Draw winners were lst Mr D Byford (presumably the dishwasher - let's hope he
is a sailor), 2nd Miss S Keep (Tape Recorder ?), 3rd John Witter (presumably the Mixer - with bowl) and 4th
Mrs Perry (prize unknown). I wonder if John made any Upsidedown cakes to go with his Enterprise dinghy (also
known to be of the Upsidedown variety - so I am told). Pete tells us that approx. £170 was raised towards
the cost of a new rescue launch, which he felt disappointing in view of the prizes offered. Never mind, it
was a bold try and Pete is to be congratulated on the attempt - and at least I assume it did, in fact, make
a contribution towards the purchase of the new rescue launch.

On other matters, the Southern Area Police Regatta was held at the MSC, whilst an Open day on lst June resulted in 12 new members enrolled, which was two more thanthe target of 10. A ‘sample handicap race' was won by Frank Savill in his Mirror, which is described as the club's fastest growing smal] boat class. How times have
changed !

There will be no August Navigans, but Editor , Mary Greygoose, asks everyone to “read and inwardly digest al] the letters and comments I have received and have your answers ready for the September issue". It was on this note that Mary ‘wrapped up' the July'72 issue at 1.05 in the morning !

Mike Boreham

Commodore's Notes

A business trip to Cheshire last week just showed me how simple it is to have one's equilibrium upset beyond measure by a simple everyday event i.e. having one's briefcase nicked!! I'm now absolutely bereft of the 1993 diary and address book, so my apologies if I promised to do something and haven't. I can only suggest that you call to remind me! However, out of every crisis comes a
"benefit" - the old Casio Digital diary has been replaced
by a Psion 3, and that enables me to write CN's (Commodores Notes) on the train!!

Enough excuses, to business! After a great deal of vacillation, it is mow clear that the NRA are going to start work on the sea wall around Easter. Our preliminary meeting on site indicated the high degree of disruption to which we may be subjected, and you may rest assured that we shall be keeping on top of the problem in order to minimise the effect on club activities. Initially, I feel it important to warn you all that this could be a difficult period. The first blockbuster is that we have to empty most of the cruiser park by Easter. Bearing in mind the number of weekends available, that is going to be a fair old task. The only choice we have will be to park them on the car park behind the dinghy park pro tem. If you have a boat in the park, then expect to be contacted with a view to arranging to move.

The stalwarts on the Sailing sub have wrought their magic, and we have a few amendments to Sailing Instructions for this season. Of particular note (queries to Colin Kidner or Willie Pitcairn please !! are the removal of average points and the further splitting of the Cat Fleet start into Fast (PY<80) and Medium (PY80-90). The hope is that this will do for the Dart 18's etc what starting separately did for the 15's. It will certainly help the
nerves of the Cruiser Fleet between 10.50 and 11.10 on
Sunday mornings. Just one point of etiquette, if you are
starting after Class X then you should stay clear of the immediate area of the line until after their start.

Well, that's yer lot, soon see you afloat,

Larry Botheras

Many members will be sorry to hear of the death recently of Albert Pearce. Albert joined the Club in the early 1970s, gave a lot of help with building work at the Club over the years and served for several years on the Committee. Many of us will remember him for organising and helping with the cooking at the Annual Outdoor Barbecues we used to hold in the summer, when I seem to remember that the cooking was done in a S-sided canvas shelter, sometimes set up on the hard, and anchored down to girders. Albert moved his Cruiser sailing to Tollesbury about 3 years ago where it was less physically demanding, and became an Honorary Member of MSC. The sympathy of all Albert’s friends in the Club go to his wife Shirley, and to daughter Leslie, and son David at this sad time.

THEFTS - ALL MEMBERS, ALL FLEETS.

As I am sure has been mentioned elsewhere in this Navigans, several Cruisers were broken into during a seemingly well-organised single operation last month, = and property was stolen.

This, as all thefts at the Club, causes great concern to the Officers of the Club, and in order that we carn do as much as possible to help the police, can I ask ALL MEMBERS to do the following:

1) If anyone is infortunate enough to be the victim of theft of any kind, after
reporting the incident to the police, please let me know in writing, including any information you may have on time of theft, item/s taken, and name of Folice Station at which theft was reported.

2) If you've seen anyone, or any activity, either on the Club site, or cut on the
water (both winter and summer) that causes you to be suspicious, please also let me know.

Steve Hill, Hon. Secretary, [redacted]

Ed’s_ note: I understand Steve would now like a written report of any thefts (even if considered not worth reporting to Police) for his records. Also a description of a doubtful person/make and registration of a car/ description of a boat showing interest in the Club (some unwelcome visitors may arrive by boat) if you noted it, may be of use even after a theft. If really suspicious call the police, some thieves were apprehended on a busy sailing weekend a couple of years ago by this means thanks to watchful people down at Stone.

Where our Cruisers are concerned, my personal feeling is that the only hope we have of discouraging future winter visits to the Cruiser Park like the last one, is toa ensure if we possibly can that our Cruisers should be rendered virtually *bare boats’ during their annual Winter Lay-Up. Because as long as it is believed that there is even a chance of some boats yielding some booty, all our boats will continue to be at risk. We need, if we can manage it, to earn the reputation that none of our boats stored at the Club’s Cruiser Park are worth the attention of the thief.

SEA WALL HEIGHTENING

The NRA (National Rivers Authority) recently made their decision to start the long- expected work on the Sea Wall at our Club at around Easter, (Easter Sunday = 11th April). I understand that we will end up with the same sort of Sea Wall as we have now, but higher and wider at the base, encroaching a little more on our space. One advantage we will have is a much better system of gates instead of floodboards to close the gap in the sea wall.

As Commodore’s Notes warn us this work is likely to have a very noticeable effect on the comfort of our preparations for sailing and on our activities on land at the Club this summer, so please be prepared to make large allowances for how the Site may have to be organised at its busiest times. Some property (e.g. Cruisers) will have to be moved very soon now (before Easter) and stored in another part of the site until they car. be launched, and I’m sure that some more of our precious space will be temporarily taken up by NRA equipment while the work goes on — probably until late October. The work may also affect the comfort of Camping Fortnight to some extent as
well.

Lastly, there is the question of safety. I do feel that as our site is likely to be turned into something of a building site, Members will need to exercise more care for their own safety, and I think it will be important that Members impress upon their youngsters the importance of keeping away from any deep holes, heavy machinery and NRA property in general, that will be nearby.

I suppose we should be grateful for all the hassle! I’ve read of questions asked about the huge cost of protecting a particular number of acres of now ‘surplus’ agricutural land, and I suppose it could yet be decided to leave the water’s edge in some places to its own devices. An article in Maldon & Burnham Standard about a continuing experiment on this on Northey Island will be on Club Notice Board soon.

Ed.

GET THAT STITCHED!

Apologies to all those who follow the yachting or medical press, who have already read about Frenchman Bertrand de Broc’s achievement in the Southern Ocean. But if you haven’t, and you’ve also wondered how you would cope with a medical emergency
when afloat read on...... De Broc suffered a severe facial injury when his boom
broke in a storm while competing in the Vendee Globe Challenge non-stop solc round the world race. The tip of his tongue was almost severed but he proceeded to put three stitches into it while looking into a mirror with a badly swollen eye and taking instgructions from a doctor on-shore via a telex (because conditions were too bad to hear the radio clearly.) Having done that he took some pain killers, rested and made a good recovery. I don’t know if he will win the race, but he certainly deserves a prize for bravery. Lick that!

Paul Metcalfe

1972 (August - December)

- As the sweet smells of the farmyard get mixed up with club politics, Stansgate's rural and
marine charm comes under the scrutiny of some members.
The question is “are they revolting" ?

- But the cruiser crowd club together to clobber the clommittee (well, you just try saying
it quickly).
August - no Navigans published in August because everyone is on holiday.

September - a brief note entitled "Enterprise Champion Again" congratulates Roger Hance on his great success
at Helensburgh - presumably he won the national championship but it doesn't actually say so. Amongst the
cruiser folk, Pete Foreman mentions two cruisers went adrift due to poor tackle and expresses concern that it seems some members are not insured.

Observer talks about the Jackpot race as follows:- "The conduct of this race has always been somewhat slapdash 1 guess we've had a ‘problem or two' in recent years as well !

As far as the ‘clubhouse debate' in Navigans is concerned Observer laments "....the sort of emotive language
which adds nothing to reasoned debate." but is sympathetic to Jane Long's fears thata new Clubhouse will bring
with it a changed atmosphere "....almost overnight by efficient but soul-less development" I guess one
person's ‘reasoned debate' is someone else's ‘emotive language’ - and vice versa - and presumably ‘the powers
that be' must try to accommodate everyone and be damned forever afterwards. Ah! well ! Pity the hierarchy who will presumably get their reward in some kind of ‘sailor's heaven'; at least the Commodore gets his name
on the board, although I'm not sure if it is as a 'reward' - or as a warning to others ! Nicholas Benwell
adds a very brief letter, saying he was "....dismayed....that they are going to try to get planning permission
for caravans on our site". and he feels such permission would be "....inconceivable..." and "...fears the club's
rural and marine charm will be destroyed". Mind you, I'm not sure if our modern day 'farmyard' containers, cruiser mast derrick, gas holder and children's play equipments add to the "rural and marine charm" of Stansgate or not. Atleast the tractor shed and accompanying tractors are in keeping with ‘the farming scene' but perhaps we should replace the tractors with some Shire horses, bring in some free range hens, a cow (milk for the galley) and a couple of goats (get rid of the rubbish). However, on second thoughts,maybe we shouldn't; the last time we tried being 'rural' and imported sheep onto the site, they played leap-frog on the boats, ate the boat
covers - and deposited from one end the derivative of what they took in at the other ! Accusations. that we
were a ‘stuck up' club might well have been true (literally) had they been made ! I wonder what Stansgate
and the river Blackwater were like 1n the 1920s and 1930s? Hard graft, I wouldn't wonder, full of rural charm.

October - The Laying-Up Supper is to be at the Chancellor Hall in Chelmsford , and offers a 5-course dinner
with wine for £2.50 per ticket.

The Cruiser Section news reveals the need to form an action committee to "...plan and cost the erection of
scrubbing posts and the second access by the racebox". Did they really plan to bash a great hole in the sea-wal]
by the pill-box - and did they erect the present-day scrubbing posts ? I thought those posts had been there
from Cro-Magnon times, whenever that was.

A Marconi team of Roger Hance, Julian Bigden and Norman Richards won the Enterprise “East Coast Area Team Championship” at Broxbourne S.C.

November - the Agenda for the AGM is published and includes the Committee proposal "The committee propose
that a clubhouse be erected on the Stansgate Site of similar design and style to the type presented". Also proposed are membership fees for Ordinary (ie Marconi employee) Members of £3 which includes husband/wife and children under 15, Associate members (ditto) at £6, dinghy hard fees £7 and cruisers £10 (drying mooring) and £12 (deep water mooring). Well, I reckon most of that will go through ‘on the nod' apart from a few people who are worried about 'the atmosphere'. They will, no doubt, be reassured that ‘the committee’ are well aware of their concerns and will watch that the nature of the club will not change. In fact, I would imagine that the only piece of really contentious business will be over the Mirror Fleets proposal that a new rescue launch be purchased for the 1973 season.

December - Wow ! What happened at the AGM ? The committee proposals were rejected - and one consequence
was that the Membership Renewal Forms couldn't be sent out. It seems an Extra Ordinary Meeting is now required to sort things out. Presumably not all the proposals were defeated because Dennis Byatt is the new Commodore. The AGM reveals present membership stands at 266 Ordinary and 84 Associate Members.

Observer comments on the AGM as follows:-

"Some may tell us that the defeat of the outgoing committee's proposals OnClubhouse and subscriptions at the recent AGM is a sign of a healthy and active democracy in the club. On the other hand it may simply have been the effect of active pre-meeting lobbying among an already fairly tightly-knit and highly articulate group of members with a common interest. Certainly there could be no doubt of the strength of the antipathy with which cruiser people viewed the proposal that their hard fees should in future be greater than those for dinghy sailors. One suspects , however, that they may have felt just a little abashed at the ease with which they succeeded in

11.

toppling the Establishment, or (choose your own flavour) rejecting the carefully thought-out work of the committee. with proposals for Clubhouse and means to pay for it defeated at the AGM, we have no policy on these matters. However, nature abhors a vacuum, and I do not think it will be long before the new committee comes back to us with an unaltered clubhouse proposal and somewhat modified subscripti proposals." Observer then goes on to thank Stan Allerton (retiring Commodore) for his work and Mary Greygoos (retiring editor). In reply, Mary writes "Thank you, Observer, for your concluding remarks. Your articles
have caused quite a 'stir' this year - much stronger words have been used by some." However, Mary issues
a mild rebuke to Observer, for she continues "Anonymity however carries with it the responsibility to ensure that your 'Observations' are wise and will strengthen fellowship and club spirit amongst the members. On balance I think you succeeded but next year I hope you will make the Editor's job a little easier".

I must be honest and say that, reading Observers remarks at some 20 years removed in time, I haven't found them
particularly contentious - but perhaps that is because I have no feel for ‘the mood' of the club in 1972.
The fact that 'Observer' felt the need to put his/her ‘observations' on record seems to me to point to a mood of uncertainty and apprehension amongst the members. Although, no doubt, the rejection of all the hard work of the committee was very annoying and disappointing (to the committee), it was probably 'no bad thing’ for’ ‘the membership’ to flex its muscles and show that ‘the powers that be' cannot always expect to get an a easy
ride from those whose interest they (the committee) are supposed to serve.

So, as 1972 closes for the MSC, Avril Stevens retires from the post of Social Secretary after many years of service (Pete and dT" Foreman take over) and also Mary Greygoose passes on the post of Editor to Dorothy Renshaw . The club said ‘thank you' to Mary in 1972 and has said ‘thank you' many, many times since then for her continued practical support of the club in many way§. It was most appropriate that Mary was the first winner of the Commodore's Trophy and I am sure that we are all delighted that she should now be the club's ‘first lady' as Ron becomes President at the 1992 AGM.

Afterthought - when I visited the club in January ('93) I noted that our present hierarchy have clearly taken
Stansgate's ‘rural and marine charm' very much to heart, for they have built what appears to be a very nice sheep-pen which, by happy chance, also encloses the gas tanks. All it needs now is a low thatched roof; then the free-range hens can perch on the roof top, the local Brent Geese can be encouraged to 'honk' all over the Commodore's lawn and the sheep left to 'bah' contentedly all night within the safety of their compound. Then, of course,. there would be. the Shire_horses and Daisy the cow-to add. to the-cacophony:.of rural sounds which, together with Daisy's cow-pats and Dobbins droppings, would create a ‘rural and marine’ idyll in which we would all have to tread very carefully indeed and few campers would enjoy an uninterrupted night's sleep. That's the trouble with ‘rural charm's; its full of creepy-crawlies, cow-pats and cockerells "doodle-doing” all night. PS. Maggie has reminded me that it was in 1972 that we paid our first visit to Marconi SC as a guest of Mike and Jennie Hart. We eventually joined as Associate Members and bought Mike's Mirror. Later on we renamed the Mirror ‘Lars Tinn' to reflect our usual finishing position (but someone did once ask me if we hadsScandinavian connections !). Mike Boreh

40 YEARS AGO - MARCH, 1953.

Nothing much in the files for March, 1953. A letter to the River Bailiff seeks permission to put down some mooring off the clubhouse, asks if there would be any objection to using the channel markers as racing buoys and enquires if he is the right person to ask about putting a Starting Line Withy on Northey Island.

The Sailing Section Report (presumably to the MASC AGM ?) recalls the formation of the club on 18 April, 1952
and the fact of having 50 members by the end of the year. It also refers to the clubhouse as "....an almost
ideal club house right onthewaters edge at Heybridge Basin. This building, an old shipwrights shop, is some 60 ft long by 18 ft and is located on the sea wall. It is noteworthy that during the recent calamitous
floods ........ although surrounded by water, none entered the building. Any Sunday or Saturday in the winter
months found members busy on their craft which practically covered the whole floor space available, and the view of the river from the wide windows made it pleasant for those working within."
The Report finishes up by thanking the MASC for its contribution towards the rent of the clubhouse and for the loan to purchase a club boat.

Mike Boreham

Park. Hopefully, we will still have had not problems - the first two sessions went
well - thanks to the efforts of Pat Black who has masterminded the whole oaperaticmn.

informed....

The distressing news for all of us is that we have had a number of security incidents since the New Year. Apart from the Club taking advice from the police, I suggest every single person reviews their own security since cone success for ai raider encourages them either to come back or to look for more. The general view is that the less there is ta nick, the less likely we are to have problems. Obviously there
are two major areas where we can all help each other - keeping the gate shut = and
ensuring every ladder is locked up. It only takes one person to put everyone else at risk. Don’t feel guilty about challenging strangers on site either. I krow there’s a public footpath, but it is pretty good cover for someone locking over the prospects. As we all know, there is no way to stop the determined thief, but what we can stop is the opportunist. A final point about making your own personal effort is, that whether you get burgled aor not, your insurance premium will suffer.

Related to the above is the renewal of the key system. Wher the GEC system was installed it was pretty much the best that could be done at the time, but with keys running at £7 each to buy, being limited to 1000 combinations, and running out of that number row with defective or missing keys, we were at a stage of needing to lock at alternatives. Frank Bennett, being the electronics whizz-kid that he is has
irvestigated and built a new system. Cards will be issued - much like a credit card
but unmarked - and these will be sent out with Membership packs. The cards are much
cheaper (15p) and we shall consider re-issuing every year, and cancelling the old card cade, Initially both systems will run in tandem. This will obviously help improve the security situation, with old keys no longer being an issue. Frank has put a note in with the membership pack, but please ensure that you keep the new = card
safe.

Social everts have been a bone of contention for a long time, with the limited support from a membership of around 500. The view of both the Executive and myself is that we are no longer prepared to see the effort put in to organisation, all for S0O-60 people. We asked for comments about the desire for a Barn Dance and Roseanna received several calls in support. Surprise, surprise when we find that a number of the *supporters’ were conspicuous by their absence at the event. If it had net been for the sterling efforts of one ar two who brought along parties of friends we would have been embarassed once again. Consequently, there will be no Fitting Out or Midsummer Event organised or financially supported by the Club. If anything is arranged it will have to be on an independent Fleet basis, with permission from the Committee. We are prepared to continue with the Laying Up Supper, which in 1992 at least "washed its face" and shows signs of some regeneration. This year’s event will be on Friday 1léth November (we get a discount) at the Three Rivers (Cold Norton). We are aiming at a ticket price in the region of £15 (don’t hold me to that too much). That means that since 1991 the price will have been reduced by 40%! I suppose you'll have to dream up some other excuses now for not going! You might be interested ta know that most of our neighbours on the Blackwater make a healthy profit from their annual dirmners!

This whole sorry saga is part of a syndrome that seems to affect the Club throughout its activities, i.e. the few doing the majority of the work for the benefit of the many. You only have to start locking for Committee and Sub-Committee members to see the evidence. Last year, we had only one willing candidate for Handicap Fleet Captain, wher we have aver 100 boats in the park. This year we went through the entire Cat Fleet to find a Captain, and came down to only two or three options, all
of whom required a degree of coercion - mind you the Cat Fleet is currently very
involved throughout the Club with the Piers Race (time for fresh faces there - no
volunteers?) and the Main Committee, as is the Cruiser Fleet. I am not going tea perpetuate the principal. If you don’t want to get involved, then expect tca see activities scaling down. If you do, then stand up and be counted and help spread the load away from the few. Involvement is relatively light with no more than one or two meetings per month. Help contribute to the future of your Club.

Enough of the heavy stuff... by the time you read this, sailing will have kicked off
again, ard Sailboat '93 will be done and dusted. Let’s hope 1993 will see a healthy turnout and keer racing. Has anyone seen the revised Rule Bock yet? I hope there's nothing too difficult to digest!

AVERAGE FOINTS AXED - sent for March Navigans, but lost by Ed - apologies.

After much discussion, the Sailing Sub Committee has decided to abandon the award of average points to racing members performing duties during the Club Racing events. The following reasons contributed towards this change of policy:

1) No system for average point calculation has yet been proposed which is considered
*fair’ tec all competitors. For example, the proposed new system of average points was mathematically biased in favour of competitors sailing in fewer races. This meant that the less you competed, the more points you were awarded for carrying cut duties. This was biased toa the extent that the awarding of average points could lead to someone being favoured with a prize in preference to someone else wha had actually competed in more races.

=) Net all duties performed at the Club would qualify for average points therefore there was an unfair bias according to event. For example, duties performed during a ‘normal’ series were rewarded with average points whereas the same duties performed during a ’weekend’ series would not qualify. Given this anomaly, sailing ccompetitors would have a vested interest in seeking sailing duties during ’rnormal’ rather = than *special’ sailing everts. Theoretically, it was even possible for certain members who had duties assigned to them over more than one weekend series ta ’lose out’ in the meting out of average points.

3) All competitors are required to carry cut approximately two duties per year. This
should rot affect the outcome of any series as each member will still have the chance of competing in a requisite number of races ever if they choose to arrange to conduct their duties in the same series. By abolishing average points, the incentive to use the system for unfair accreditation of points is removed and calculating places is purely or a *races sailed’ basis.

Willy Pitcairn, Sailing Secretary.

RAFT FLEET NEWS

A couple of excellent books, suitable for kids from 8 to 80, on the subject of boats. One is the Eyewitness Guide entitled ‘Boat’ going through the development of vessels from Rafts to Liners and Tankers, from rowing and sailing, to engine power. Lots of illustrations and a surprising amount of information for something so easy to read, and it has
been produced in association with the National Maritime Museum. There is also a book called ’Ships and Sailing’ - one
of the ‘Eyewitness Visual Dictionaries’ and each book in this series goes into detail on the construction of the subject
item and ‘naming of parts’ - again with clear illustrations and easy to read. Well worth looking for in the Library,
unless you want to splash out and spend 28.99 per book to have them on your shelf at home.

After suspecting for a long time that a Windsurfer couldn’t be classed as a Heat (well, they can’t be if they have a nose and tail instead of a bow and stern and have no port & starboard to speak of, can they?) it seems the Windsurfer is really the latest development of the Raft. Rafts are not watertight structures, but float because of the natural buoyancy of the materials they are made of. You usually sit in a boat, but you sit/stand on a raft. The Windsurfer is the fastest sailing vessel ever made, clocked at over 50 mph, and no doubt that record continues toa be broken by ever faster Windsurfers as time goes by.

At this time of the year Cruiser Park(s) are beginning to blossom spring-like with paint-hued Cruiser owners temporarily taking on the red and blue colours their boats will bear in the new season. The sea fever is becoming rife, claiming more people with each fresh morning, and blowing awake the winter weekend’s lie-in.

We go out aon the grey river ta re-anchor our summer roots in the mud and to saw the surface with the colourful patterns all laid in neat rows, carrot-like, awaiting our craft. However there are those who are already awake to this year’s sailing, contrasting their bright sails against the grey water.

It was whilst taking a break from the above pursuits that I watched several starts of our Club’s racing for the day. A bitterly cold day, with a 4, occasionally 65, gusting icily from the South East, which seemed not to daunt these hardy folk, some of whom were no youngsters. And this was not even the first race of the year!

The Cat classes and the Solos were virtually the only boats on the river, and the clarity of the helmsmen’s planning, positioning and handling was a pleasure to watch
- free of moored craft and other river users.

I shall never forget the thrill of rounding a mark in a good wind having approached or the beat, cutting close to the buoy, freeing the sheets and bearing away off the wind, just ahead of an opponent, the wind accelerating the boat to the plane in one powerful flowing movement. There is nothing else like it!

So I offer an appreciation to our Cat and Dinghy racers from a Cruiser owner who well remembers the excitement and fervour of racing in a small boat. The skill and commitment of these racers is great to see and gives watching families, and many like myself, a great deal of pleasure.
Limpet

FAST CAT NOTES
It has been suggested that in volunteering to write these notes at last year’s Cat Fleet
AGM| was simply acting in defence of the Hurricane sub-fleet (and | do not use ‘sub’
as an abbreviation); personally | cannot remember my motives (indeed | all but forgot
volunteering at all), but for better or worse | now find myself attempting to follow in the
hallowed (if somewhat deep) footsteps of our Commodore. Please bear with me as
| attempt to document, in a vaguely accurate way, the successes and (probably more
interestingly) the failures of the Fast Cat Fleet members through the season. The season started gently for those who ventured out for Spring Points 1 and 2, with a mild Force 3 greeting the 5 starters in the fleet. It has to be admitted that the Prindles impressed with their strong turnout, whilst the bulk of the Hurricanes were not
to be seen on the water; | look forward to this anomaly being corrected in the near
future. The first race was won by John and Caroline with a new livery for the 1993 season, taking advantage of Steve’s broken tiller bar (crew-beating never helped anyone); however the Prindle 19s made a strong comeback in the afternoon with both Steve and Tom (Ashley, not Duckmanton, who was stricken by ‘flu) and Larry and Chris vanquishing the lone Hurricane.

The second weekend was, well, different. I’m not sure whether to thank the gang for pitying us on our ‘duty weekend’, or to point out that, in general, we should try to emulate the other fleets and finish races. For a variety of reasons (gear failure, exhaustion, confusion, more confusion) the entire fleet elected not to complete the
course set by Caroline in either race. Contrary to suggestions | must insist that this
was not a Nickalls replacement for the average points system, wherein the course set is sO complicated that none of the entrants can successfully navigate it, thus guaranteeing no penalty to those manning the racebox. Particular condolences must go to Mick Jones, who retired out of consideration for his very cold and tired crew, only to discover that a few more minutes sailing would have brought him a deserved
1st place. No condolences whatsoever are deserved by the heavyweights of the
Prindle 19 fleet: both Steve and Larry broke their trapeze lines.

Spring Points 5 and 6 brought a return to sanity, and a return of Grant and Martin's winning ways. As became a regular sight last season, they convincingly won both races, with Steve and Tom and John and Caroline second in the two races. Dave Onyons returned from winter grazing to push the other Prindle 19s hard; it looks as if they can look forward to a close season's racing. It was also interesting to see the medium cat fleet start with the fast cats; it’s quite a dilemma, whether to satisfy those who are Sailing, or to encourage those who are not. Either way, I’m sure we all view declining numbers in the medium cat fleet (and, more significantly, the monohull fleet) with considerable concern for the future.

As | close I’m looking forward to the Easter series, in hopeful anticipation of some
more of the Hurricanes coming out of hibernation and justifying the RYA’s confidence in us. As often seems to be the case, the RYA has made some minor adjustments to the relevant handicaps over the winter, and it will be interesting to see whether the Hurricanes can live up to their new turn of speed. What a pity we don’t all sail the same boat, be it a Hurricane or a Prindle.

John Nickalls

The first boat I owned on returning to sailing had an outboard as auxiliary power ard, whilst quite efficient when used for short duration, it was awkward to say the least wher cone had to refill the engine mounted tank with the slippery petrol mixture. I was looking forward to enjoying the advantages of an inboard diesel with its alternator power and low consumption of a cheap fuel when I got the rext bcaat. The previous owner of my next boat had described its engine as ’adequate’ and as we left Maylandsea Creek in a flat calm, the accuracy of this description became clear. It was as if the propeller had fallen off! No swirls from beneath the transom, just a barely discernible increase in forward motion that built gradually to a maximum of about four knots! Flat out at four knots, the smoke was black and smelly, therefore to avoid the smell helping one to get sea-sick, three knots was the effective cruising speed. On the plus side, engine use was generally an easier operation with fuel being more available and starting more reliable, and a better alternator allowed a full electrical system ta be supplied.

On reflection, the tousled pages of the workshop manual bearing the greasy signatures of the previous owner’s attempts ta improve engine effectiveness should have told me that my effearts to effect any improvements would be in vain. The engine was used a let in the first year and extra problems really began with my ill-advised attempts toa squeeze mare power by over-fuelling the ald motor. Shortly afterwards we took a trip to Ipswich and following a broad reach up the coast to Harwich with that short sea rolling the boat along at 5 knots, I started the engine ta enter Shotley Marina. The motor always started well, but on this occasion it seemed ta start too well and, kneckirg heavily, it revved as if jammed on full throttle with me frantically working the control lever. I assumed that the throttle had stuck but no amount of pulling, even orn the engine end of the cable, had any effect.

My imagination was beginning to run wild, did the diesel devil have it in for me, having overheard my aft-repeated comments about its inadequacy? I was not keen for the engine to aver speed to the point of destruction sc I left it in gear ard we rushed about like a hunted destroyer making full smoke! Through the smoke I think I saw 5 knots on the lag, the fastest ever under power! After what seemed several minutes the engine dropped back to idle, but not before I’d broken the stop cable in the attempts ta arrest the revving. The smoke cleared and all seemed normal. Later, a thorough inspection of all aspects of the ergine and its controls showed only one strange thing. The engine oil level had increased by aver an inch on the dipstick. With the boat anchored we went ashore and all was soon forgotten in the haze of the Shetley village pub which was serving a very special whiskey at half price!

Time for aur armual summer cruise with engine serviced and running normally = and slightly better, if anything, after breaking its own rev limit. An excellent run ta Ramsgate via the Roach ard Haverngore. The channel through Havengere is as shallow as reported ard, with 4’ draught, quite a close run thing needing careful prior calculation of tidal heights and a let of echo-scounder pilotage. One previous year in a foggy moment I had miscalculated by looking at the tidal height instead of the range for the day wher assessing it to be a spring or a neap tide. This and other errors resulted in many hours spent high and muddy at the very mouth of the inlet toa the bridge. Whilst sat on the mud there I remember noticing the number of cars that crass the bridge contd the island, presumably due to the MOD preserice. I find Foulness Island and its military secrecy somewhat fascinating, and the tales of Deccas having their memories wiped in this vicinity a few years age make it all the more mysterious. B will not have completed her tack until she is lying (whether moving or not ) in the direction of a close hauled
course (definition of tacking). While she is stil tacking , as defined , she has to keep clear of a yacht on a tack, be it
port tack or starboard tack (rule 41.1)

In a protest hearing , it would naturally be B's case that she had completed her tack before the collision occured. If
she can satisfy the protest committee, then it will be have been A who infringed, as A will have become either clear
astern and required to keep clear under rule 37.2, or windward boat required to keep clear under rule 37.1.

In this situation, it is B which has to to prove she completed her tack far enough away from A. (Rule 41.)

41.2 TRANSITIONAL.

A yacht shall neither tack nor gybe into a position that will give her right of way unless she does so far
enough away from a yacht on a tack to enable this yacht to keep clear without having to alter her course
until after the the tack or gybe has been completed.

41.3 ONUS.

A yacht that tacks or gybes has the onus of satisfying the protest committee that she completed her tack
or gybe in acordance with rule 41.2.

How far is ' far enough away ' ? This is a matter for the protest committee. If it finds that A started to take avoiding
action within a couple of seconds of B having tacked, but cannot avoid collision, then B will probably have tacked
too close. The burden of proof is on B. If A alleges that she was forced to start tacking off to avoid a collision,
before B had completed her tack, B has to show that A did 'nt have to do this, and that B would hva completed
her tack wel before A was obliged to take avoiding action. If, as usually happens, the protest committee is faced
with two equally credible but contradictory tales, it will have to beleive A.

So the general rule is Tackers Beware ! If B is sure she has tacked in time, she should hail‘ close hauled‘ as
soon as she is pointing on tht close hauled course and then count the seconds out loud. If a collision occurs , say,
five seconds later, then A should have had enough time to take avoiding action. Experience shows that those who
find the need to hail ‘close hauled ' are often nowhere near close-hauled , but are still tacking. A should be hailing

FAST CAT NOTES

Looking back over this month to catalogue the activities of the faster elements of the Cat Fleet I notice that there really have not been many Spring Points races completed since I last put finger to keyboard; it's been a month of 'specials', with the Easter series and the Solo / Dart 15 Open dominating. The Commodore seems to have run a very tight (only with the sun over, or is it under, the yardarm) ship for the Open Meeting; Larry's liking for long races was in evidence at the event, when both the Solos and the Darts had an energetic weekend in strong winds. Thanks must go to all those Fleet members who turned out to support the club in many different ways throughout the meeting.

One sad happening in the month was the disappearance of traveller cars from 4 boats, all of which were of the Tornado/Hurricane style; apparently Robin Smith's vanished from Grafham around the same time. Unfortunately it seems it is almost impossible to guard against the theft of these items (which requires removal of the main hull attachment bolt), but the greatest vigilance would not be wasted.

Following my lament for the absent Hurricanes in the last Navigans, I am delighted to be able to report that four 5.9s ventured down river to Stone for the Open meeting, including Steve and Tom, having borrowed Steve Keeble and Dave Payne's boat. I am less than delighted to have to admit that on their first serious outing in the class they showed the way home to Caroline and myself! Grant and Martin led the Marconi boats overall (managing to be the only one not to enjoy a top-to-bottom salt rinse), showing that even when they manage to launch Grant's 'new' Hurricane they will still be the team to beat.

Perusing the results of the Easter series, I thought it would be interesting to conduct some modest analysis of the results and see what turned up. I have shown below the corrected times of each entrant in each of the four races plotted against that entrant's handicap. The group of Solos is identifiable toward the right of each graph; note their good performance in Race 3. (Statisticians amongst you please note that I have normalised the length of the races so that the distributions seen in each race can be compared.) My impression of these graphs is that, in general, the faster cats did better (on corrected time) than the slower cats; indeed, I was surprised to see the degree of correlation. Why might this be? It must be remembered that these results are based on one particular set of conditions (although there was a reasonable variation of wind strength over the weekend), a particular set of sailors, and of course a small sample. Nonetheless, they do seem to indicate that, for this event, the handicaps of the faster boats should have been generally decreased (to between 55 and 60 for the Hurricanes/Prindle 19s/Tornados!) if the aim is to ensure that all the boats finish level on corrected time. Of course, it could be that the more experienced helms sail the faster boats... but is that not true in most clubs, so should the Portsmouth numbers not reflect this difference already? I would be delighted to hear your views.

John Nickalls
