BOAT ENGINES AND ASSOCIATED EXPERIENCES - continued from last month

The next passage from Ramsgate towards the Swale was largely an engine-driver leg. However in the fickle marmer of wind and weather a breeze piped up as scon as we had decided to lay to anchor for some food and a kip in the lee of Margate Hook. Later the beat into the dusky sunset over the East Swale was a joy, finally bringing up off Shellness, an excellent anchorage made tenable by the now complete calm and affording views across the estuary with its myriad of flashing lights. Several times since I have used anchorages out in the estuary when windless nights have made it possible and have found new dimensions in sclitude whilst laying to anchor. In the morning the Swale was used to get to Queenborough to meet to meet some friends and ari anchorage in Stansgate Creek provided shelter for that night.

For the next passage to Walton Backwaters we chose to leave around midday, providing the chance to use our new-found night sailing confidence. Very light winds in the afternoon made the early use of the engine essential but after some hours a fine following breeze came up and we chased along at 4-5 knots with the chute set. Later the wind built up further and the chute was stowed to make way for jib and pole. The decision to reduce sail and then carry out the operation in time toa avoid the problems borr of late reefing, etc. is a sign of true seamanship, as is the full appreciation of those small signs that help to show the following wind’s true strength. However, on this occasion the wind held steady and as darkness arrived the wind died away to nothing. Having reverted to engine power, the course into the Stour tock us along the rolling swell that had, for some distant reason, increased in level since the wind died. Perhaps the lack of stabilising sails made it seem toa increase, but certainly my little craft rolled along most uncomfortably at her 3 knots, often increasing revs in time with the swell. The strange increase in revs got worse the longer we rolled along and nothing could stop it. The passage had become most unpleasant and wher we were approaching Harwich the engine slowed down alarmingly and it seemed to be straining. I closed the throttle and nursed it, but
it stopped after a while. I checked the diesel - plenty. I dipped the oil to find -
no ail!

Harwich harbour entrance is not the ideal place to drift about especially at might and due ta the number of shore lights it is very difficult to pick out shipping movements. The lights appeared to be straight aut of an RYA training book! I tried adding more oil to the engine and managed to spill some onto the hot exhaust causing
billowing smoke to belch from the engine bay hatch - things were not improving! I
finally managed to get some oil into the beast, in fact managing to overfill the sump. The motor complained into life enough to get the boat to a suitable anchorage just inside the mouth of the Orwell where we dropped anchor. We continued up toa Fox?s at Ipswich the next day with many items of cabin upholstery outside trying toa get rid of the smell and dirt of diesel fumes. At Ipswich I drained the gunge that used to be the engine oil, changed the filter and ran the engine on new oil. Once again all seemed well, and placated by lunchtime ale we dozed all afternoon. Once again the ’interest’ of the old diesel continued!

Despite the ‘interest’ provided by the engine, I could see in my mind’s eye a new goal. A clean, new engine, installed in a sound-insulated engine bay, with no diesel leaks. With clean new paint all round and no smells or fumes, this area of the boat could actually be a pleasure. At the finish of the season I made the decision ta fit a new engine, the original having done well considering it had functioned for &7 years in the boat. The strange behaviour of the old engine was now virtually proven to be due to excessive piston clearances, combined with my overfuelling of the injection system. This resulted in diesel fuel washing intca the sump via the bore, diluting the oil and then being forced up past the piston as the sump overfilled and increasing the compression ratio. The removal was a dirty but satisfying job, the removal of components triggering a variety of memories from its chequered history, and involving yet more cily expletives as cold hands slipped and fingers got nipped. I often dream of having the boat laid up indoors, and what a total luxury that would be! The boom was used to hoist the motor out and drop it straight onto the waiting tralier for transport to its new location, and to a much needed overhaul prior ta fitment in a small open fishing boat.

contd....

9.

Having decided to spend out or a new engine, the research into types was a_ pleasant exercise involving ringing all the main suppliers of diesel inboards for their literature, then drawing up a comparison table in the marmer of the yachting press. The first consideration was size, not only for basic fit, but also to gain some space ir the main cabin. With most modern engines being considerably smaller than their Similarly-powered predecessors, it seemed likely that I could achieve this space saving. I looked at Sole, a twin cylinder unit I had had experience of in a friend’s boat and that was very smooth, and with its fresh water cooling, a desirable unit, but even with a good discount being offered it was too expensive. Bukh would not fit due ta its size, and the weight was considerably more than any other 8-10 hp engine, as was its price. It was, however, the only engine manufactured solely for marine use, and many of its design features shawed it to be the most worthy unit. A Vetus
twin was very similar to the Sole - both being marinised industrial engines cof
Oriental orogin, but there was some difficulty in supply at the right discount. Valve would fit but was expersive relative to the Yarnmar, and I could not forget the spares price concerns expressed in the yachting press, whether they proved groundless or not! Discount was also not negotiable enough to make it competitive. The ever- popular Yanmar was small, was lightest and cheapest, and a deal could be done. So the engine, along with new single lever controls, exhaust system components and ancillaries were unpacked and inspected in the comfort of the dining room, another thoroughly pleasant wiriter exercise only slightly marred by the realisation that, in commer with many things boat, the cost of the project overall was rather more than originally thought!

The fitting of the new Yanmar involved making a modified engine bed for which I obtained some oak which was machined to form a long wedge shape as the angle of fitment was quite different from the original engine. This was epoxied and screwed to the existing beds and ten inch studs for the mount fixation installed. The motor was now four inches further aft and, combined with it being shorter, the gain in space allowed me ta make the cabin step unit into a useful cupboard. The engine was fitted and roughly lined enough for the prop shaft to enter the drive coupling when slid towards the engine. The final alignment was achieved by sliding the prop’ shaft in and out of the drive flange until little or no resistance was felt. This was repeated while turning the flange to various positions ensuring absolutely correct aligrment. The confined space in the engines compartment made the conventional method of alignment virtually impossible. The old dry exhaust system was scrapped and the Vetus plastic and rubber units installed, saving more space, as the exit was now in the transom with the system running under the cockpit sole, a previously wasted area. This also made much more space in the main rope locker which used to be the home of the silencer.

The fitting of a new engine had many obvious benefits in terms of user confidence plus the gain in space in various areas. After some of our recounted experiences,
I’m sure you agree! The only mistake was to choose a two-bladed prop - my thoughts
being that it could then be aligned with the deadwood toa reduce drag. Th: “faet seldom bothered to line up the marks painted on the coupling, and the prop also caused vibration as the tip clearance was not sufficient and turbulence resulted. A three-bladed prop has now cured the problem and increased the speed to a respectable 5.5 knots, so the mouth of the Deben or Alde cannot play games with us any more!

Solos at Marconi —- Jim in the Hunt

Marconi SC held an open meeting for Solos on April 18th which was an Eastern Area qualifier, and attracted an entry of
17 boats. These boats enjoyed close and exhilarating sailing with the wind recorder indicating gusts in excess of
Force 6 during the second race. In the first race the lead changed a number of times up the first beat, but Hunt was
first round shortly followed by Cook, Barclay and Burrell. By the next mark Garner was in second. The order remained
until Garner went swimming at the last gybe mark with Hunt well clear to win, followed by Burrell, Cook and Husk.

The second race was a beat against the flow of the tide which had turned, and which made the downwind legs very
interesting for those who kept upright. Burrell was first round opening up a huge lead which he held from Hunt and Husk
until he went for a swim, letting Hunt through, who went on to win. Burrell held Husk off up the last beat for second
and Cook was fourth. The wind dropped off slightly for the last race but was still strong enough to force Burrell out
with a broken main sheet block. Garner was first round and pulled away from Cook, hanging onto the lead in spite of a
blowout at the gybe mark. Cook suffered the same fate going round the wing mark, allowing Husk, Barclay and Ede
through. Garner went for his second swim of the race and eventually it was Husk first, Barclay second and Ede third.

Overall results: 3883, Jim Hunt, Beaver SC; 2nd 3741, Alan Husk, Halfway YC;
3rd 3757, Allen Burrell, Halfway YC; 4th 3808, Gordon Barclay, Dell Quay SC;
Sth 813, Tony Cook, Littleton SC; 6th 2290, Simon Ede, Marconi SC.

The Force 6+ wind created difficulties for me, every time the race box door opened my
position/time sheets blew all over the place. On a more serious note, the idea of
moving the Solo Open to a ’ane day’ date that did not clash with other Solo Open
Meetings seemed to have worked with regard to visitor numbers, but may have proved a
little too early in the season for some of the Solo Fleet (me included). Plan for
next year is still a one day event (Sunday) shared with the Dart 15 class, but with
date moved to later on in the season. This has yet to be organised.

40 Years Ago - June & July, 1953.

T would imagine that 'young' John Eastwood will remember what he did on Coronation Day in 1953 - and what
he did the day before! A report, presumably for the Marconi "house magazine’, tells a dramatic tale:- "On the Monday before Coronation Day, 2 June, 1953, the Sailing Section were honoured by a visit to their headquarters of their new President, Dr. Eastwood, and his son John. ‘here were to have been races, but the weather beingof a very doubtful nature it was not surprising that only one other boat put in an appearance. Regardless of the adverse weather, the President and his son were initiated in the art of sailing, having sailed up to Maldon in the club boat ‘Avril', skippered by Terry Hallam, Commodore of the section. They returned to the club house just as Fewel in 'Seamew' arrived by sea, and the Hon.Secretary by land.

There was no chance of organised racing, so it was decided to sail again in Avril, particularly as the President and his son appeared only to have their appetites whetted, and this time the crew was augmented by Mrs Hallam and the Hon.Sec. ‘Avril' followed out ‘Seamew', and the two boats sailed in company for a while. This particular time coincided with a temporary lull in the wind, and it was observed by those less familiar with small boats how steady 'Avril' was. At about the same time the skipper expressed the view that it was
time the reef in the mainsail was shaken out - but five seconds later, after a quick glance to windward at
a particularly vicious looking cloud, with a long black curving edge to it, he thought again. Just as Avril was halfway across the reach leading up to Maldon, the squall struck. Almost immediately the gentle undulations of the river were converted to row upon row of angry whitecaps, and no longer was progress smoth and leisurely. Only by careful spilling of wind from the minsail was anything like an even keel maintained, and at each gust a violent flogging of the sails took place which sounded like machine gun fire.
Young John Eastwood was on the helm just then, with the skipper close at hand, and for one so new to the art he certainly seemed to have mastered some of the tricks, in particular how to manoeuvre so as to catch the foremost crew member, the Hon.Sec. in this case, with bucketfuls of spray.

The strength of the wind made it difficult to go onto the other tack, a necessity as Avril was closing the river bank rapidly, but like the good lady she is she never hesitated and came round obediently, and through clouds of spray set off back again. A capsized craft was then spotted, but on approaching closer it was
apparent that no assistance was needed - the crew were sitting on the upturned boat eating sandwiches !
The ferocity of the wind soon abated and Avril returned to her harbour as serenely as she left. Our new President seemed duly impressed and we hope to see him often down at our clubhouse.”

I notice it doesn't report what young John felt ! Avril's log records that 10/-
was duly collected for
the trip, but it is not clear who paid ? ES See a

Commodore’s Notes

As you can tell from last month, timing one’s bit for the press can get a little awkward with events occurring post submission. Apologies to Charles Anderson for the lack of recognition of his great contribution in accepting the challenge of Cadet Week. From my perspective the prospect of sleeping in a field for two weeks and then
to volunteer to surround yourself with brats is a sacrifice above and beyond... It’s
a good job we’re not all cynical, miserable b’s like me!!

The NRA saga continues, with a letter from me to try to gee things up a little. Their reply was full of thanks for all our co-operation and an undertaking that the job will be done this year, taking 26 weeks in all (between Steeple and Store), starting ‘late summer’ and the work on our site being completed in the first six weeks, avoiding Camping and Bank Holidays, and aiming at avoiding any inconvenience
ta boats laying up.... Watch this space.

One subject about to be considered very closely is the "“Wraysbury Lake" scenaric. For those of you who do not know, the Borough Environmental Health Officer issued a Prohibition Notice on Wraysbury Lake Sailing Club under the Health & Safety at Work Act (HASAWA) banning them from carrying out any activities until certain ‘improvements’ had been carried out. These included ensuring someone was availabl to carry out Support duties any time that activities were happening ard (in my opinion) several other equally idiotic and senseless restrictions on a voluntary sports club. Obviously the chief concern of everyone on the MSC Committee is safety, but our philasaphy has been to draw attention to, or moderate, risks and ensure that
everyone understands the periols inherent in in our sport - 2.5 times less dangerous
than athletics/30 times less dangerous than horse riding). We are seeking Clarification and guidance from the RYA and any appropriate actions will be taken.

It’s been good over the past few weekends to see the sunshine bringing all the fine weather sailors out of the woodwork. As usual the Cat Fleet is looking pretty healthy, but what has happened to the Moros? I can’t understand the point of spending £47 per annum to keep the sun off a patch of grass, which is what the vast majority do. Boats deteriorate more quickly ashore than they do by being sailed. Let’s see a few more of you cut there!

Larry Botheras

RNLI’?S WEST MERSEA ATLANTIC 21
ON SERVICE ON THE BLACKWATER SOTH AUGUST 1992

Local Knowledge Essential in Arducus Service
Multiple Casualties for Atlantic 21 in winds up to Force 10

‘The wind was SW Force 8 gusting to Force 10 creating very difficult conditions as the wind was against the tide.’

Ar, arduous service by the West Mersea Atlantic 21 lifeboat, carried out in very rough conditions with the crew using their initiative and local knowledge to asist a large number of casualties, has led to helmsman John Frost and crew members Matthew Haward and Javis Wenlock receiving framed letters of thanks from the Institution’s chairman Michael Vernon.

At 1155 on Bank Holiday Sunday, 30 August 1992 crew members John Frost, Matthew
Haward and Javis Wenlock were near the lifeboat station listening o communication between Thames Coastguard and the Bradwell sector officer. This in dicated that a number of small beats could be overcome by weather conditions near Osea Island in the estuary of the River Blackwater.

Contd.

De

They telephoned the honorary secretary who authorised the launch of the station’s Atlantic 21 ’Himley Hall’ to go to Osea Island, investigate and give assistance if required. The wind was SW Force 8, gusting Force 10 which was creating very difficult conditions as the wind was against the River Blackwater’s strong tide. The lifeboat was launched with helmsman John Frost in command, accompanied by crew members Matthew Haward and Javis Wenlock.

Best speed was made from West Mersea into the River Blackwater where conditions were found to be very difficult with a very short steep sea, blinding spray and visibility further reduced by dust blowing off fields to the side of the river. The six miles took approximately 15 minutes, and by this time the Bradwell sector officer had asked that they go to Osea Pier on the south side of the island where a 3eft motor boat was reported ta be in difficulty with an elderly man aboard. His son was ashore with their dinghy and it was considered too dangerous for him to venture cut to the boat to collect his father.

Helmsman Frost took the lifeboat to the jetty and picked up the son, and then put crew member Wenlock aboard the motor boat, to secure her and transfer the man ta the lifeboat. The casualty vessel was rolling very heavily in the rough conditions and the Atlantic 21 suffered damage to her navigation light. The two people were then taken to the Marconi Sailing Club, nearby on the opposite side of the river.

The lifeboat was then asked by the Coastguard to check numerous other small craft anchored in the area.

At 1309 the yacht ’Scloist’ with five people aboard was taker to the safety of a mooring orn the windward side of the river, and her crew also transferred toa safety ashore at Marcori SC.

At 1347 they approached the 35ft yacht Ruskina which was anchored rear Osea Pier and
had radisced a request for assistance - as all four people aboard were suffering from
seasickness and one needed medical treatment. Crew member Haward boarded the yacht and raised her anchor and then helped the skipper to manoeuvre to moorings off Stone Point, some two miles to the west. During the passage Haward examined the injured female and advised the Coastguard that an ambulance might be needed. With assistance from the Atlantic 21, the yacht was put on a mooring, but before they could transfer
the crew the lifeboat received another call - to a boardsailor a mile west of their
position. The injured person volunteered to stay aboard the yacht and the lifeboat went to the boardsailor, advising him to make his way ashore as he was not in need of
assistance.

While with the boardsailor the lifeboat was asked to attend another yacht west of Osea pier with two elderly people aboard. The yacht had fouled her keel on her anchor warp and crew members Wenlock and Haward boarded her to help. With Wenlock slacking out the warp Haward used the engine to manoeuvre her and clear the fouled warp. This yacht was then taken to a mooring off Marconi, secured and the two people taker, ashore by the lifeboat. The lifeboat then returned to ’Ruskina’ to transfer the four crew, but during the passage the casualty last cansciocusness and was immediately transferred to the ambulance which had remained at Marconi Pier. (sic)

A further sweep of the moorings between Osea Fier and Stone Foint discovered five people and their dog aboard a yacht who asked to be taken ashore, and they were duly landed at Marconi Pier (sic) at 1430. Having carried cut these evacuations in very difficult conditions the lifeboat crew left Osea to return to West Mersea, but on the way they heard that a motor cruiser had been reported in difficulties in Mersea Quarters, not far from their location. The lifeboat found the motor cruiser very quickly, the skipper having lost control of the vessel in the adverse conditions. She was helped to a mooring at Stone where the four people aboard were taken ashore by the lifeboat.

The lifeboat then returned to West Mersea, helping another small boat ta her mooring near West Mersea lifeboat station before taking the crew ashore to the lifeboat
station.

The lifeboat was rehoused at 1554, her crew exhausted after a four-hour service in severe weather.

FAST CAT NOTES

A Clean Start
The latest occupancy of the race box by the Nickalls clan may have failed in its prime objective (that of ensuring that none of the competitors finish the races, thus removing the points penalty to those on duty) but it did bring home to us the dramatic improvement in the quality of the starts being made by the fast cats. That the leading craft was not over the line was only due to the thickness of the mete when projected out to the far end of the line; by my estimation the considerable diameter of the pole provides an invisible zone about six feet (or 2m, as they say in cookery books) deep in the region of G mark (when it’s there, Paul). Larry took full advantage of this in starting, and we, with considerable generosity, gave him the benefit of the doubt. In days gone by one could achieve ‘a good start’ merely by having the sharp end of the boat pointing toward, rather than away from, the line when the flag dropped (and one might observe that this is still a valuable maxim in certain fleets). This seems no longer to be the case with the fast cats, and the bulk of the fleet are not far from the line (and going the correct way) at the start.
Moaners’ Cup
If only we could all keep going the correct way after the start (or rather, if only we could all agree on which way was the correct way). Mona's Cup is becoming the occasion for the annual contention over courses: last year we had the 'wrong way round the island’ dispute, and this year it was ‘when is a course not a course?’. Perhaps it is inevitable as the fleet as a whole becomes more skilled at the basic control of the boats sailed that the differences separating boats will become smaller. Thus the level of competitiveness within the fleet increases, leading in turn to competitors making careful use of the rules to ensure no disadvantage is suffered by failing to take the best legal steps available. Even after a protest committee has found that no infringement has been committed, it is a very fine line between on the one hand perceiving a competitors actions to be an unfair exploitation of loopholes in the rules and on the other hand recognising that whoever sails, legally, the fastest race is the deserved winner. For the enjoyment of all it is essential that this progression toward a greater level of competition is made at the same pace by all those racing, to ensure a common understanding of what is ‘fair and therefore to reduce the personal slant that can sometimes be seen creeping into disputes and protests. Of course this applies equally (if not more so) to knowledge of the rules of Part IV and the use of the right-of-way rules to gain a tactical
advantage during a race. Never have | heard so many cries of "water" or "mast abeam" on the
Blackwater as in recent weeks (although | cannot vow that all were used correctly!) and personally
| believe that a more developed knowledge and use of the rules can only be good for the standard
of sailing at the Club. This knowledge must, however, be used at a similar level throughout the fleet to avoid much splintering of fibreglass and so much work for Brian that he can’t find time to come and beat us every week (or perhaps that’s not a bad idea). Those whose knowledge of the rules is greater than most should help to raise the average by advice and example, and those who concentrate purely on boat speed should recognise that the quality of Club sailing has improved to the point where good speed is no longer a guarantor of victory, and that improved tactics can gain many places in a tightly bunched fleet.
Men (and women) in a Hurri
On a personal note, |’m delighted to see four more Hurricane 5.9s joining the fast cat fleet this year.
After Julia and Ashley Machin added the 5.9 to the family fleet ("the Dart is for sale" they tell me "honest") we welcomed Philip Longhurst and Brian Grimshaw with their (lookalike) 5.9 and a mean-
looking Hobie. More recently both Brian and Grant Piggott have migrated to 5.9s, and | am delighted
to see that the numbers on the water, and the quality of the racing, have shown a dramatic
improvement. | only wish | could say that the change of boat had slowed Grant down little!
East Coast Piers Race
Those of you with diaries (or wives) will have realised that the Piers Race is drawing ever closer.
By the time this goes to press | guess it will be about three weeks away. | hope the new format this
year, offering a shorter course for those who feel the trip to Walton is simply too far, will attract some of those who to date have not felt that the event is for them. You can even decide which course to sail after you've set off (although of course those who opt for the shorter course will not be competing against those on the long haul). It's a good event; if you've been put off before, think
about giving it a go this year.... and remember, it’s all for charity.
The Piers Race was filmed last year for Anglia TV’s 'Sailaway’ series, and the episode is due to be screened in the Anglia region about ten days before this year's race. At the time of writing I’m not sure of the details, but you might like to keep a look out for it in the schedules (and if you see the trailer, look for the jolt as our centreboard hits the top of the cameraman’s head)).

John Nickalls

A note from former Commodore, Eric Payne, records the death of Cecil Stebbens aged 71. Cecil had been, wntil aged 69, the Water Bailiff and had been a good friend of the club and was particularly helpful during the club's Heybridge days. It was he who towed the barge Mamgu to her mooring off the original 'hut—on—the-wall' clubhouse at Heybridge on 20 April, 1958. In addition, it was he who built several access ramps to the water for the club, ie. for the original clubhouse, later for the dinghy park a little further down river and for Mamgu itself. Cecil was a Trinity House Pilot and it was he who presented the club with The Pilot's Qup for an annual all- in race which still features in our sailing programe.

Alf Cottam entertains us with a tale of a trip to Brightlingsea with Frank Savill in the Mirror ‘Frantic’. Starting off in a Force 6 blowing from behind and an adverse tide from ahead, they took 23 hours to arrive just off Brightlingsea. Taking a look around Brightlingsea, they arrived back at the (untethered) Mirror just in time to stop it floating
off. Leaving at 3.45, they had a long hard slog back towards Stansgate, arriving off Stone in the dark from where they could see car headlights and much obvious activity at the Marconi Sailing Club. ‘Thinking a search party mustbe under way to find them, they curtailed their voyage at Stone S, interrupting a dinner party in progress and phoned their loved ones with both reassurance and a request for wheeled transport. Alas, it seems nobody had really missed them, for the lights arose from a barbecue - not from the launch of a rescue party!

Walter Standing. We were sad to hear that Walter Standing died on Friday 20th August 1993 at his home in Paignton, Devon.

We send our sincere condolences to his widow Rebecca and to his daughter Michelle.

COMMODORE’S NOTES

The Bank Holiday weekerd has had about the only good weather for the summer and saw
the doubty (doughty? - Ed!) Prindle/Nacra Fleet decamp to Lake Bala for their
National Regatta. We again had a brilliant showing and, but for a nasty accident ta Steve Glynn that prevented him and Tom Duckmariton sailing in two races, may well have wrested the 19 championship from the Bala local wizard. Despite that he came second, followed by the well-known "Dark Horse" combination of Vince Talfourd(!) and Damien Horeham in third, and the Onyons brothers in fourth. Steve Caruth and yours truly had what is best described as a mixed event, with lightning speed in the light stuff and emulating a backward sailing Mirror in the heavy! Still, an excellent showing, particularly when you add Olly Harris and Judy Garham in their Nacra 5.2 (Lilo-Lill) doing the bizz in the Nacra event. The sailing was only marginally less important than the social events, with the Monday night Bunk House Barbecue giving everyone the opportunity to take incriminating photoes of a high ranking flag officer of the club in his cups (see, chaps, if I admit to it, blackmail won’t work!!), closely followed
in, degree of inebriation by a certain Mick Richardson - who nobody has ever seen get
really drunk before. I can’t remember...... My personal thanks go ta Peter
Richardsern’s wife Barbara for stuffing copious quantities of water down my throat prior to being escorted ta my pit! The reckoning was it beat the best of camping fortrights by a distance.

It was a glorious weekend in a glorious setting. The way that a club of 43 members rallied round to cater for a similar number of competitors was very impressive.

Also needing report this time is the ECFR which was a great success. My congratulations must go to the ECPR committee who produced an event this time that surpassed all those previously. The atmosphere at the prize-giving for me told the whole story. The majority of people stayed and were vociferous in their support for all the factions. From a sailor’s viewpoint the event was absolutely perfect. The Inshore Series balanced well against the Main Event. The attendance of around 15 Dutch competitors also shows what a first rate event we run. Most of the comments compare it very favourably with "Ronde om Texel" (Round Texel) which attracts annually nearly 1000 Cats but is shorter. The successful running of this sart of event is one of the best pieces of publicity for the Club and has been responsible for the recruitment of a number of new members aver the years.

Particular mention must go tao the Glynn youngsters and their friends who over a couple of days offered to open the gate for you in exchange for ccin of the realm. The result was around £40 contributed to the ECPR funds. A nice bit of work from the Brat Pack!!!!

That’s yer lot, see you next month.

LARRY BOTHERAS

RYA NEWS

A meeting of the RYA EASTERN REGION was held on the 16th June. The following are extracts of the minutes which I consider may be of interest to MSC Members.

Federation of Eastern Counties Sports & Recreation: Concern was expressed on the increasing activities of the ‘Environmental & Conservation Lobby’ and its possible interference with existing and potential waterborne recreational activities. The Chairman had been sympathetic to our concern; he heaped that common sense would prevail and that it would be possible for harmonious relations to be developed with such bodies. There had been increasing pressures on all sporting activities, however, Dr Smithson of English Nature had rather changed the stance of his organisation and co-operation was now thought to be an essential factor.

Crouch Yachting Federation: It was reported that part of the river had been affected by a sewage problem, it seemed that a particular gate had been opened at an unsuitable time; steps were being taken to regularise the problem. Speed restriction buoys are now in place on the river.

Harwich Area Sailing Association: The importance of RYA’s active involvement in local matters was stressed, commenting on the conflicting pressures of commerce and jobs in sensitive areas. One spokesman for the bird lobby was on record as being in favour of the complete shutdown of Ipswich and Filixtowe Docks on the grounds that both areas belonged to the birds. It was reported that Walton & Frinton YC were concerned about spoil dumping in the Dovercourt area, which could perhaps cause silting of the entrance to the Backwaters. Details of dredging and dumping are showr separately in this issue of Navigans.

Any Other Business: Two Southend yachtsmen had been asked for dues after anchoring in Stansgate Creek, River Medway. This is thought to be an illegal act, ard the matter is being raised with the Medway Authority.

HARWICH HAVEN AUTHORITY — Dredging Bulletin

The £20 million contract ta deepen the main deep water Approach Channel ta Harwich Harbour was awarded to Westminster Dredging Ltd. and signed on 30th June 1993. The dredging contract is expected ta take at least a year to complete.

Or, 27th July 1993 the first dredger "WD Mersea" took up position near the Cliff Foot buoy to commence working northwards. "WD Mersea" is a bucket dredger, and remains static within the cut as the buckets cut into the clay and reck. The spoil tips into a self-prepelled hopper barge to be taken off to the dump. At present two heppers are working with the dredger, the "WD Clyde" and "WD Tyne". Spoil is being dumped at the Roughs Spoil Ground.

In order ta maintain position, the "WD Mersea" is moored by two anchors on each side, plus a stern anchor and a head anchor. On the Harwich side of the dredger the anchors are marked by twa lit pontoons, but the Felixtawe side and the stern archor are not marked. As the dredger moves across the 50 metres cut, the side wires alternately take the weight and then slacken off, so it is most inadvisable for yachts to pass close.

The head wire holds the dredger against the face of the cut, and therefore has toa have immense holding power. The cable runs from the tap of the dredger aver a
pentoorn about 300 metres ahead and then to arn anchor a further 700 metres ahead. All
yachts must avoid passing between the dredger and pontoon, ard give the pontocan an extremely wide berth if passing ahead.

During the course of the project it will be necessary at times ta reposition certain buoys toa facilitate the dredging. At present the Cliff Foot buoy is 160° T x 45 metres from its assigned position. Information regarding dredging is braadcast by Harwich Harbour Radio on Channel 11 at four-hourly intervals to follow the weather broadcast from Thames Coastguard. Attached tae this bulletin is a chartlet [see below] showing the approved dumping areas and the route that will be used by the hoppers. Further bulletins will be issued during the course of the project.

FAST CAT NOTES
There can only be one subject for this issue’s notes, and that is the coming of age of the East Coast
Piers Race. It is easy to say "thank you to all those who helped in...." but it is also easy to overlook the
magnitude of what we as a club have achieved over the last 6 years. From Robin Smith's suggestion in 1987 the Race has grown into the best known event in the UK multihull calendar, and it is now taking on a European angle as our Dutch colleagues recognise that life does not end at Texel. The profile of Marconi S.C. has been dramatically raised and it is now seen nationwide as a focus of catamaran sailing; we can attribute a large part of the rise in Cat Fleet membership to the success of the Piers Race. The team of organisers who have made the event so successful must indeed be thanked, and
heartily congratulated, but | hope that all who have the club's interests at heart will consider whether
there is anything they can do to take a little of the burden (and the credit!) next year. In my opinion Steve Glynn and his team made this year's Race the best yet; the land-side organisation seemed to go off without a hitch, the number of competitors was up on last year, a new (optional) shorter course was introduced to appeal to those who sail the smaller catamarans and (in my mind most importantly) the race management itself was fluent and most professional. The Race has now reacheda stability which allows those involved to step back from the day-to-day panics (a little!) and to consider possible strategic improvements (for example the new shorter course), as well as changes in emphasis; should the Race develop more overtly as a charity event, or should it take on a harder competitive image? To ensure the healthy growth of the event, ideas, and assistance, would be welcome from all.

IT’S A LONG WAY TO FEPPERARY THAMES ESTUARY

(ar hew a little bit of needlework can help you along)

(through the Eye of theHurricane)

There I was, leaning om the front of my car whilst the garage mechanic completed the last few checks of the 54,000 mile service when this little voice behind me said, "Fancy sailing a boat back from the Isle of Wight after Cowes Week?" I turned around to be greeted by Keith, garage owner, motor enthusiast and ex E-Boat World National Champion. "Well?"
"Wher, in what and with whom?" came my rapid response "First weekend in August, a class 4 racer and with me ard whoever you can rustle up," came the equally swift response. Well, it wasn’t to be quite like that, but close enough.

With three days to go, Dave Fayne and I had our bags packed to go, but no idea where we were going. Cowes is a big place and there must be some thousand plus boats in
the River Medina. Time ta seek help - Keith’s wife, wha confirmed that our
assistance was still required and gave directions to the Marina.

Saturday morning, sitting on the tube as it trundled towards London, thinking to
myself "Needlework, well there is an effeminate name for a boat, if ever I have heard one!" But I suppose that I had visions of a 40ft cruiser/racer, with all mod cons, originally owned by a devoted and loving couple, but subsequently purchased by a group of bay racers. Meeting Dave on the train from Waterloo to Southampton, we discussed which navigation aids we would use and how effective the Radar might be in position fixing if DeccaNav wasn’t available.

Crossing Southampton Water and the Solent, we admired the small cats and goggled at the Round the World yachts as they cruised back to Southampton crewed by professionals but with the "out for a jolly" crowd sipping pink gin on the after deck. We walked along the streets of East Cowes to the Marina and then realism struck us in the face like a wet fish! Needlework was a 27 foot, plywood built, quarter tanner, whose only navigation aids were two cabin wall-mounted compasses, a couple of hand-bearing compasses and three large-scale charts of the South Coast and Thames Estuary. However, brave intrepid explorers (or fools) do not shy away) from
adversity but persevere....

It was Spm when we crossed from the mouth of the Medina into the Solent, ard with a following (westerly) force 4 wind, we attempted to hoist the spirmaker for a pleasarit sail down to Portsmouth. Well, the sea was a-rolling, the boat was a-rockirng, the sails were a-heaving and the spirnaker decided to wrap itself around the forestay! Sa down it came ard we headed across the channel, keeping our eyes peeled for 20, 001 tom blocks of steel which might be headed our way. Once on the northern side we goose-winged the genoa and relaxed as wind and tide tack us rapidly down towards the forts between Portsmouth and Bembridge.

"Whoosh, whoosh!" "What the....!" Suddenly we found ourselves in the middle of a
Windsurfer race, with high performance men and women (and the boards went well, tac) passing us on every side and, seemingly, from every direction. "Look out, skipper!" "Dor’t worry, we have right of way as they are all either overtaking, on port, or windward boat!" "But doa they know that?" Obviously they did as we didn’t collect any, and subsequently passed Ge without going to jail! We passed the forts in good time ir, a slowly falling breeze; it was only just after 7pm and we set course to pass
Selsey Bill. "Time for tea said Zebedee...." What a disappointment. With only a
one burner cooker, dinner was coffee and cold Cornish pasty! But the night was young, the sun still shone and life was idyllic.

By 9pm we were past Selsey Bill and headed towards Brighton. With the dusk came the desire to wear safety harnesses, but the wind had dropped to a steady force = ard the Number One Crew (Dave and Brian, the skipper) stood down, whilst the Number Two Crew

19.

(Keith and me) tock command. We took bearings on various lights and shore = stations to check that we were on the lay line, but a lack of compass lights made exact riavigation difficult as we reed to shine a torch on the compass and this ther destroyed our night vision. To make matters worse, we were on a dead run with a following sea, and the corkscrewing motion made for the occasional involuntary gybe! We did actually try the spinnaker for a while, but the concertraticn needed ta fly it properly in the dark was too much.

Brian had disappeared below to sleep, but Dave decided that he preferred to sleep on deck, so he lay on the floor of the cockpit (more like a mouse pit really) and fell instantly into a deep sleep. By the time the crews changed watches (fam) we ceauld Clearly see the light from Beachy Head, although the mist had come dawn and the tide was preventing any major progress. By Sam we had made it as far as Eastbourne = and our next target was the Royal Sovereign Light Tower, which we duly passed at about Bam on Sunday morning. According tae the tide tables, the tide was generally giving us some degree of assistance, but at times we seemed ta be making little progress. We were generally close inshore ard may have been suffering from same degree of back
eddyirig.

At this point we began to have some navigational difficulties! The mist was still about so it was not easy to get a good accurate fix on any object other than the Sovereign Light and although we were on our lay line, we could not clearly establish how far we were from the Royal Sovereign. For some time we thought that we were aff Rye, but were confused because we couldn’t see the power station at Dungeness. At this point we gave up trying to plot our position and settled for breakfast of Hread and Marmalade, with Tea. As the sun came up to clear the mist, we could see the power station still on the horizon, although at first we mistock it for the channel tunnel workings at Folkestone. In fact we were actually off Hastings, but as the tide turned (?) in our favour we rapidly came up on Dungeness Point passing the point about SO metres from the shore. Most of the morning we had been flying the spirnaker, but suddenly the wind arrived and with a force 5 dead astern and a following sea, it became too difficult to manage and we returned to a goose-winged
gernca.

New at this paint you have tec use your imagination about the boat. It is 27 feet long, but the first five feet is taken up by the pointed bit and fittings and then a large bow well for the crew to stand in whilst "doing things". There are two quarter berths below the cockpit floor, but na mattresses (toa much weight) and the tap three feet caf each berth was being used as a storage area for bags and the chart table. The bit between the bow and the cockpit consisted of the forward 6 feet containing spare sails, anchor, water containers, cupboards containing the food, the cocker and the sanitary system (a large plastic bucket!) Behind this area were the ends of the quarter berths separated by a small companicrnway (four feet) which was the only place you could stand upright (provided you kept your head in the open hatchway!) The cockpit flocor was about eight inches above water level, whilst the side decks were about 12 inches higher. Needless to say, cooking ard washing, etc., were extremely difficult and accordingly we lived on Pot Noodles and sandwiches.

By 4pm we were off Dover, hands clasped in prayer that we wouldn’t get run down by the Haver Craft or Ferries which seem ta charge about at 20 krnots+. We were aiming at the South Goodwin Light Ship, but had passed it before we saw it. It was rot a problem as we were only about a mile from the coast so navigation was fairly easy.
Suddenly disaster....no wind. The tide continued ta sweep us towards Ramsgate but we
were ricw travelling at about 1 knot. "Out with the engine!" said the skipper, ard a small 4HP Mariner was clamped ta the transom bracket. Off we go! However, nobody had ever run the engine for more than 10 minutes before, so we had no idea of haw long it would run on a tank of fuel, and we only had 3.5 gallons on board. Worst case was that we would push on until we had one gallon left and then anchor until the wind returned.

Up past Ramsgate with the bigger yachts creaming past us on their inboards, past the North Foreland and out into the estuary. Navigation is not easy when you have na alternate points for bearing taking. We were looking for a small buoy about 3 miles almost due north from the North Foreland, but we were probably less than a mile from it wher we saw it. We had originally planned to take a fairly straight route across the estuary, but the difficulty of finding the buoys made us change our mind ard head towards ane of the better lighted channels, although this may mean a closer

20.

involvemert with commercial traffic. By the time we reached the big old gun tower off of Margate, it was dark and it was low water.

For those of you who have never sailed at night in a small yacht, there is very little depth perspective when looking at light buoys. Although they flash ta set patterns, the patterns are repeated and picking out the correct Buoy can be quite difficult. If you aim for the wrong one, you run aground! We reached the Edinburgh Charmel and became confused as to which buoy we should aim at, having passed the channel entrance almost without seeing the appropriate buoys. On our way through we managed to touch bottom, but by putting all our weight on one side ard boosting the motor, we were quickly off and heading in the right direction again.

At this point the gremlins struck. The navigation lights went cut and despite studious joggling by Keith, we only managed ta get the bow lights working. At this point we were in the process of creassing the Black Deep, which is a main shipping channel ard wherever a large vessel seemed ta be headed towards us, we shame all of the toarches ante the sails, at which paint they all altered course to avoid us. Naw according ta the chart, the choice was ta go up the Black Deep until we were off Clacten or to cut across the Sunk Sands into the Sunk Channel. A difficult process as at low water the whole area dries out. About half way up the sand sthere is a tower, which locks a bit like a miniature Eiffel Tower, and by which is ai narrow channel which we thought we might scrape through. Now this tower is unlit ard we could only see it by silhcuetting it against the lights of Clacton and Jaywick. After much bumping on the bottom, much screaming and shouting of "Over there! Turn left!" (note the nautical terms) "Watch out!" we finally made it into the Sunk Charmel and from there across ta the Swirway.

The motor had been on for 7 hours and had been refilled twice, sea we had done about 3 hours to a tank full, about 3.5 litres. Not bad for a little motor! But row the ward came up and Dave was fighting the helm against the tide, waves and wind. We sailed under main alone and the boat leaped forward like a shark chasing a kill. We headed for the Swirway. It was now midnight, the stars were hidden and the navigation buoys blended in with the coastal lights. We are not sure we took the correct channel, but at tam Monday we were in the mouth of the Colne having crossed the spit totally blind. We quickly identified the Nass Beacon and headed towards it, missing the Hench Head by about 20 feet, as the tide tried to sweep us back out ta sea. Hy 3 am we had reached the Nass, despite having to tack several times and fight the last of the tide rushing out of the Blackwater.

We had planned to go straight in to Mersea Roads, but it was dark, we were net sure of the charmel ard we were tired, sc we moored up to the buoys by the Nass and started to tidy up the boat whilst waiting for daylight. Once we had everything stowed and packed for taking ashore, we sat and relaxed, whilst Dave did his normal I-can-sleep-arnywhere trick and crashed cut! We decided ta staw some of the gear ta be taken ashore on deck, and, despite having two very large ard heavy bags thrown ante him, Dave coantirued to sleep peacefully. With the arrival of daylight we motored irntca West Mersea and because the tide was rising were able ta tie up ta the pontoon to unload, before putting the boat on its mooring.

Not a bad trip! Total time 34 hours, total distance about 160 nautical miles, average speed 4.7 knots.

Dave ard I have talked on several occasions about doing the trip again. We have concluded that we would only agree if the boat was at least 60 feet lorg, had two or, preferably three hulls, full satellite navigation, decent berths (not that he would use them) and heat shewers! Sc if you have a boat which fits that description, you are welcome ta give us a call!

Steve Keeble.

FASTNET ?93 -— A Racing Tale from a Cruising Man
This is the story of an out-and-out cruising man suddenly finding himself part of the frenetic racing scene. Most MSC members will be familiar with Natasha IV, a Westerly Fulmar on Mooring BS. Many will remeber Natasha a Contessa 28, and Natasha It, and Galion 22 which returned to the Club owned by Ray Hillman. Few perhaps will remember Natasha I, a 20 foot Vivacity, but over the years Jackie and 1, plus or minus Nicola and Mark, have cruised extensively along the North Sea and Channel coasts, aided by such non-racing items such as jib furling and spinnaker socks. Imagine our surprise ther in the Autumn of last year, wher: my company, GPT, asked me if I would like to take part in the Fastnet race this year on a yacht sponsored by BT and their Industrial Suppliers. I was therefore presented with a challenge, and of course, a marvellojus opportunity, but I recognised that I would need to change my relaxed cruising attitude to one of being part of a hard working, dedicated racing
team.

The team turned out to be seven from BT, and one each from Ericsson, Northern Telecom, GPT, Sun, Amdahl, Tandem and Hewlett Packard, plus the yacht owner’ s representative and Stuart Quarrie our tactician and coach. Stuart writes in Yachting World and Yachts and Yachting, and has taken part in all the Fastnet races since the fateful one ir 1979, when he was on one of the yachts that foundered. That year is uppermost in people’s minds, but before and since then the safety record has been good, though it is recognised as a tough off-shore race, and one of the world’
classics.

So we had a team of 16, and the BT members where chosen by a selection within the BT Off-shore Sailing Club. Many of the team had taker part in previous Fastnet Campaigns, but this was a first for GPT. The yacht chosen was a 57 foot Swan called "Noonmark V", but named "Teamwork" for the racing.

We had to become a hardened racing team, which for the cruising members was a change iri mind set, and meant learning many new skills. This started last autumn with the team split betweer two Sigma 38 yachts for a weekend, practising sail changing techniques and tuning the yachts for maximum performance. We also "practised" some involuntary broaches wher putting up the spinnaker in the heavy wind of that weekend, losing total control of the yacht on a number of occasions. On the Sunday it was gusting 45 knots, so we practised staying on the yacht!

For winter study we were giver some video tapes produced by Stuart, and in the spring had two training weekends or Teamwork. This really brought home the magnitude of the forces at play or a large yacht, and the sheer weight of the sails. It took at least three people to lift the largest sails, and we had four sizes of genoa and three spinnakers to contend with. On the second weekend we went off-shore, and got used ta living a dual-watch system, which is like having two crews which change place ever three hours at night, and four hours in daylight.

Since 1979, the Royal Ocean Racing Club (RORC) has insisted that in order to take part in the Fastnet, at least half of the crew must have undertaken three off-shore races that year. During the run-up, Teamwork took part in the Cerventes Trophy race to OQuistreham, the Morgan Cup channel race and the Cowes-St Male race. In the first we did particularly well, coming 3rd in class, and 4th overall out of 95 starters. Ir the Morgar Cup we came Sth in class and 9th overall out of 93, but could only manage 43rd in class in the St Male race where conditions favoured the lighter boats, and 194 yachts took part.

During the races we ran a system where the bowman and Stuart were always or call, and seven of us were in each watch. The bowman needed to be a masochist, who actually enjoyed retrieving halyards from the top of the 70 foot mast, and who felt it was quite natural to climb up the spinnaker pole downhaul, 15 foot up and 20 foot out over the water, in order to put up a new spinnaker ard peel off the old.

For a cruising man, the frequent changing of sails takes some getting used to, and at night at 30° on the foredeck in rough conditions it is physically very demanding. The tasks of putting up a new Genoa, two of you hauling on the halyard and one tailing on the winch, followed by dropping the old sail and bagging it by flaking into a long racing bag, takes at least half an hour. The peeling of sails in this way means that the boat is always driving under full sail, but of course the wind

With spinnakers it was also necessary to stop the sail before bagging, which entailed gathering the sail together from the head and = each clew, and tying with wool stops at 6 foot intervals. This prevents the sail filling prematurely when hoisting, which can be disastrous wher it wraps around the forestay ard is impossible to get down.

On an out-and-out racing boat with a well practised team, everyone would probably have a specific job ta do, but we tended to split between the younger ones on the foredeck, handling halyards and sail changing, ard the colder ones steering, trimming and tailing, with bursts on the coffee-grinder winches. However, everyone helped wherever necessary, apart from bowman activity, which in addition toa requiring a certair agility, is also frequently under water.

Sleep in 3 hour slots does not come naturally. To start with half an hour is last getting waterproof clothing off, and more particularly on, and the general noise level of sail trimming and changing sounds very loud below deck. In the end one becomes so tired that sleep for short periods becomes very deep, to be rudely = broken by your wake-up call from the watch above. My toes still feel the effect of skidding the full width of the boat on one foot while attempting to pull oan waterproof trousers. Sacks are lethal on wooden floors.

I have to confess that for all the hardships the yacht was extremely luxurious, and having a deepfreeze, we had really excellent pre-prepared food. We had a strict rota for the cook’s job, and for me it was not easy juggling with three red hot trays of shepherds pie in rough conditions, but very rewarding for a hungry crew.

With all our training we now felt ready for the Fastnet; 605 miles from Cowes to the South Western tip of Ireland, going either side of the Scilly Isles, round the Fastnet rock to part, and back ta Flymouth outside the Scillies. The course instructions were simple enough.

Just before the race the bottom of the yacht was cleaned and polished by the crew, and then on 7th August we joined the other 240 yachts off Cowes. These included 23 Admiral’s Cup yachts from 8 nations, and 13 Whitbread yachts working up for the Round-the-World race starting in September. With Press boats and helicopters as well, the atmosphere was electric, and the start was something I will never forget. The various classes were started at 10 minute intervals, but even so the congestion was incredible. The start line had a bias that favoured the Cowes end, and everyone was there, sailing at 9 or so knots with nowhere to go. A collision occurred in front of us causing quite bad damage to two boats, and then the gun fired at 2.40pm ard we were off ta a good start. Five minutes later the Italian yacht "Nocorette" that caused the earlier crash was totally out of control, heading straight at us. We ran along the deck to escape the impact, but somehow they recovered control and missed us by inches. They were, of course, disqualified.

Adrenalin continued to flow as we short-tacked cut of the Solent, through thge Needles Channel, and then we settled down to the long beat down charmel, the wind generally Westerly. The forecast suggested heavier weather coming, which would favour a Swarr compared to the light-weight flyers, where crews need to sit aut on the side deck for their weight, ever sleeping there! By Portland Bill the fleet had spread right cut, and we were only see about 10 yachts for the rest of the race.

By the evening of the second day we had rounded Land’s End, and were well into the Irish Sea wher we heard a Mayday call from a Japanese Admiral’s Cup boat, which had lest a crew member overboard. It was 11 o’clock at night, Force 5 with a moderate
sea rurming, and we were the nearest boat - about 4 and a half miles away. We were
Just about to abandon the race and start the search, when he was recovered by his own yacht having beer in the sea for about 20 minutes. He was very lucky. He had a torch but dropped it when struggling in the water to get his heavy clothing off. Or Teamwork we all double-checked the security of our harnesses.

£4 hours later we were rounding the Fastnet rock, 5 miles off the coast of Ireland, having sailed around 400 miles with the Force 4 to 5 wind right on the nose. At night it looked very menacing, with sheer rock walls and a lighthouse perched on the top. The RORC staff on the rock told us that we were 49th round, and we celebrated with a specially made cake with a picture of the rock on top.

The wind had backed as expected, and was increasing, giving us an exhilarating spinnaker run back ta the Scillies, and on to Plymouth. The yacht was automatically giving its position back to BT every 6 hours and this was then faxed on a map to each Company, keeping everyone informed.

With gusts up to Force 7 we absolutely flew, and the effort and concentration needed to steer was such that we changed helmsman every 30 minutes. Running down the wave fronts, we reached 14 knots on several occasions and great care was needed not toa lose control and broach.

8 o'clock in the morning, after 4 nights at sea, we crossed the finish line under St Annes Battery in Plymouth. 46 yachts were in front of us, but those included 36 Round-the-World and Admiral’s Cup racers. We were 14th in Class 1 out of 70 and
entered the marina with our built-in hi-fi blaring out "Simply the Best - better than
all the rest: from Tina Turner. Our wives were there to greet us and champagne flowed. It was an emotional moment.

Of the 240 yachts that started, 21% failed to complete the race, some with mast or boom failures. We had relatively few problems. The most severe was a 12 foot tear in the No.1 Genoa, solely caused by letting the sail back or to the spreaders wher tacking. On a large yacht racing sails are much more fragile than one might imagine. This was repaired by hand-sewing and taping over the next 24 hours, but probably cost us the Swan Cup, as there was only one hour between us and the winner. The or other breakage was a halyard snapshackle that fractured under strain at the top vu:
the mast. Our bowman saw toe it! The fastest yacht, a Whitbread, was 27 hours ahead of us in real time, and the last yacht to complete the race was 88 hours behind us, almost double our time.

Sc what are the memories? Great comradeship, hard physical work, living life in 3 hour slots, lack of sleep, cooking dinner for 16 while heeling at 30 degrees, dolphins playing round the bow, and the thrill of a fast spinnaker run. But above all, a sense of achievement, and grateful thanks to my Company for giving me the
opportunity.

Brian Bowsher, 26th September 1993

COMMODORE’S REPORT

1993 has beer an interesting year in many respects. The outward appeararice 1s that not much has happened, but much has occurred that has helped to clarify the Club’s Situation for the future.

Going into the year, our relationship with MASC and the calculation of the "Contribution" were items of great concern, particularly with the avowed intent of GEC to ensure that the majority of members were GEC employees. This situation was exacerbated by the pace of redundancy within the Company. Fortunately, our dogged determination to resist the imposition of a draconian rise in contribution was successful, and has brought into sharp focus the relationship between MASC ard its Sections, so much so that a sub-committee has beer set up to investigate the way forward for the organisation as a whole. FPerscenally, I have high hopes for the outcome of this group.

The degree to which we are able to carry out improvements toa our facilities is totally linked with the foregoing. We are unable to make capital expenditure without the (proper) agreement of the MASC Committee, or to take action tao raise money for specific projects. Consequently, our financial plan is based on a break-even target, with minor repairs or renewals only allowed for. Major development will have ta await clarification of our position. However, we have managed to improve facilities in a number of ways. Firstly, our hot water capacity was extended over last winter, and nobody need now fear the dreaded cold shower. Even at the ECPR it was still bearable at the end of the queue. My thanks go cut to Steve Glynn and Frank Bermnett for their activities in that respect. Secondly the access control system has been renewed with something that has already proved much more successful. Frank Bennett designed and built the system for a tiny fraction of the cost of commercially available alternatives. Currently, plans are in hand for the essential repair of the ground floor windows of the Clubhouse, installing security lighting in the Cruiser Park, and for the repair of the Workboat.

Much of my personal objective this year has revolved around making the tasks undertaken by individuals in the daily rurming of the Club less onerous. We now have a laptop PC that is used by Frank Bennett for Accounts, and doubles as our major event-results machine. We shall be further investigating the systems used for Membership records and Navigans production ta try to relieve the loads on those
people.

Another item of note has been the poor response of OODs this year. Very few plecple have turned up to do their allocated duty, which only crops up once every four or five years. Consequently, several parts of Club facilities have been unavailable at times of high demand —- particuarly the Bar. The repurcussions of this are more widespread than may be apparent, since decreased bar opening equates with lower sales and thus lower profits. This will only result in one outcome, a further increase for all in subscriptions. The Executive and Main Committees have spent a great deal of time discussing possible alternatives, with no great success.

I cannot let the opportunity pass without mention of the NRA. The work in raising the Sea Wall is important to all of us, but the problems of dealing with ai large bureaucratic organisation are plain to all of us. Unfortunately, we have very little recourse other than to play on their sympathy toa gain other spin-off benefits from the contract, but I do record my thanks for the forbearance for all the members of the Cruiser Fleet who have been inconvenienced over two winters. However, work is now under way, and will be complete by the start of next year. From the New Year access to the Hard will be limited, to allow construction of the new entrance.

I reserve my final remarks for my colleagues on the Executive and the Main Committee. The support and initiative of these people makes my job much easier and enables the Club to operate smoothly. At the moment I am privileged to have the immediate team of Steve Glynn, Colin Kidner, Steve Hill and Frank Bennett to work with and they are all characterised by the ability to intercept problems and get on with things without a word from me. The members of the Main Committee have given their time and contributed toa much healthy debate over the year as well as picking up individual jobs as required. I place on record my thanks to them all.

Larry Botheras

Manceuvred as close as I could, which wasn’t very close at all, but Laura made a heroic leap and secured us. A heavy scerd was coming into the harbour, and the wind soon got up. We ended up secured with at least three bow lines and several springs for a very windy night.

Day Nineteen - Still extremely windy with local forecasts promising gales for the
next 24 hours at least, with the possibility of a short lull. The lull only came in the evening, too late for us to go anywhere, sc had a day in the very pleasant port. We bought smoked fish from the quayside, and the skipper made history by deaing his awn washing. Walked cut towards the headland, and visited a tiny but extremely well stocked maritime museum. The curator was an interesting chap wha, a few years age, had sailed a 7 metre Maxi singlehanded to the West Indies and back. Hrought the log up to date in the evening. Weather still guiet with the promised resumption of the gale yet ta materialise.

Day Twenty - Very windy, sco we went for a walk, looking out over a very windy Sound.
A slight lull in the afternoon, so we decided tao brave the waves rolling into the entrance ard made the short trip across the entrance ta the Sound to the lovely little fishing port of Gillejie in Dermark. We managed to tie up next tao a trawler in a very creawded harbour.

Day Twenty One - We spent the morning shopping, intending to move on at midday, but
continued strong Westerlies would have made the intended progress due west uncomfortable toa say the least!. Sc we settled down for another enforced lay day, giving the crew a rest, particularly Helen who was just recovering from the effects of her bug.

Day Twenty Two - Made an early start in flat calm and very sunny conditions.
Attempted to sail with the spinoa, but everitually had to admit defeat and researt to the engine. We rounded the long peninsula of Sjaellands Odde and across ta the the lovely little island of Sejero. We tied up to the harbour wall and ate cut at vfery reasonably priced harbour cafe.

Day Twenty Three - Made another early start toa try to make up for the limited
progress of the previous week. Good sail into the Breat Belt, ther headed by falling wind, so we motored into increasingly misty conditions. The surrounding islands soar disappeared completely. We decided to head for the almost deserted island of Mushalm, and had just located the island and were heading cautiously in, when Laura discovered that our water tanks were unexpectedly empty, having been filled only twa days earlier. We decided ta go somewhere with facilities, and crept into the tiny fishing harbour of Reerso with very little shewing on the echo sounder. We tied up in ar empty berth by the diesel pump and started filling up with water only ta find that water was pouring from the calorifier under the cockpit. Emptied the two level cockpit locker and climbed in and under to inspect the calorifier ard discovered that one of the water pipes had worked loose and come off. At least we knew where the water had gone! Started to tighten up the pipes wher the Harbour Mistress arrived. Asked if there was a chance of getting diesel and she said there was. Went back under the cockpit. Just then a large German yacht arrived and tried to squeeze into the small space behind us, necessitating us moving MUNA forwards. I was still trying to fix the calorifier when attendant arrived to give us diesel. Filled up with diesel and then went back to work. It now decided to rain. Eventually the calorifier was sorted cut and the contents of the locker returned to their rightful Place. Collapsed down below to very welcome supper.

Day Twenty Four - Yet another early start in ever worse visibility, and motored south
for unseen bridge-building operation. Contacted Information Service on VHF toa discover there was a special small ship channel taking you through the bridge building works ret shown on our chart! Helpful chap gave us the position of the first buoy and we got through without seeing anything of the bridge building operation whatsoever, apart from very indistinct misty shapes. We heaved a collective sight of relief only to discover a huge ferry hurtling out of the mist towards us and spent a very anxious couple of hours until we were safely clear of the ferry and shipping lanes. What was particularly frustrating was that we had passed through some reputedly very attractive scenery without seeing any of it! We located the island of Largeland, and the wind got up and gave us a very pleasant and therapeutic sail down the coast towards the little port of Snodsberg, the only port

9.

on the east side of the island. We arrived a year to the day and almost the hour that we had last beer there. We discovered that water was once again pouring out of the calorifier and further probing under the cockpit resulted in me being soaked with extremely hot water and revealed that the water was coming from the safety valve indicating that there was a fault with the thermostat. Feeling less than enamoured with hot water systems, I decided that I would have to isolate the system before we left in the morning.

Day Twenty Five - Got up early to do necessary adjustments to hot water system, then
the tricky manoeuvre to extricate MUNA from the tiny harbour. Laura was confined ta her bunk for a second day, being seemingly second victim of the mystery virus. Fresh Westerly giving a superb fast sail down the remaining Langeland coast, and across ta Kiel, tying up once again at the British Kiel Yacht Club for sumptious hot baths for the female members of the crew and a cold shower for the male!

Day Twenty Six - Motored round the corner and locked into the Kiel Canal for an
undemanding day motoring through the fifty mile length of the canal, enjoying rare sunshine. We arrived at a lovely little, incredibly cheap (less than £4), marina just inside the lock gates. We spent the evening trying to solve the twin’ problems of haw best to leave the tricky waters of the Elbe and how to get Laura home, who was leaving us early to get her A level results and sort out a University place. Eventually having talked to a friendly Dutchman tied up alongside, we decided to lock out at first light ta take the extremely strong tide the 16 miles or sa down ta Cuxhaven where we would try and sort Laura’s travelling arrangments out.

Day Twenty Seven - A quick trip to Cuxhaven, entering sideways with four knots of
tide sluicing across the entrance, and tying up by half past nine. Into Cuxhaven to find a very helpful travel agent. As the next ferry to take Laura from Hamburg to Harwich wasn’t until next day, and the weather forecast indicated that the best time for MUNA to leave the Elbe was that afternoon, arrangements were made, with some difficulty, for Laura’s overnight accommodation at Cuxhaven. So with some trepidation we left Laura on the pontoon and filled up with diesel from the fuelling barge (that had closed but kindly reopened long enough to give us fuel and incur the wrath of a following German a powerboat who understandably expected the same treatment). We were just in time to capitalise on the fast flowing ebb and covered the 25 miles to the Elbe Light Vessel in some 3 and a half hours. Our first night passage as a three-man crew was comparatively pleasant, most of it being taken up with steady motorsailing. The morning however was one of those dawns that somehow never quite manage to happen, bringing with it the forecast, but somewhat premature, cold front. Last year’s experience of a Force 9 gusting 10 off the German Friesland Island of Borkum had resulted in distinct feelings of unease when approaching this area for the second time. Now these fears were being partly realised with rising head winds, confused angry seas and little visibility. Although conditions were nothing like last year, there followed several hours of extreme discomfort until we finally tied up in Borkum some 120 miles and 22 hours afer leaving Cuxhavan.

Day Twenty Nine - Weather dictated a lay day in Borkum enlivened by the discovery of
excellert, reasonably priced German food in the restaurant, and a phore call toa England revealed that Laura had arrived home safely and had gained her University
place.

Day Thirty - A very early start at 0400 to discover that the lights at the rather
tricky entrance to the Yacht Harbour had been switched off. Somehow we managed to feel our way out and followed the long channel out through the shallows. Still lumpy seas and dawn brought with it drizzle which stayed with us in varying entensities all day as we motorsailed along the Friesland Islands. Then in the afternoon as we approached the narrow gat between Tershelling and Vlieland, a NE 6 that had been promised for the next day but decided to arrive 24 hours early, sprung up behind us and made the entry in wind-over-tide conditions agains a fast flowing ebb decidedly interesting. At one point we were surfing completely enveloped in spray. We tied up in the picturesque island of Vlieland after a somewhat exhilarating end to an 86 mile day’s passage.

Day Thirty One - By unanimous decision we agreed to have a lay day pleasantly spent
wandering round the little town and along the beach. Jenny spent most of the afternoon doing her washing.

10

Day Thirty Two - A pleasant trip, after a lively exit from Vlieland, through the
Waddenzee toa Der Helder. Very pleasant accommodating Yacht Club in the middle of this very active military base. Good forecast with, unbelievably, North Westerlies
going Northerly - unheard of for the trip home.

Day Thirty Three - An early start intended, but just casting off lines wher the
engine stops, and an expert is required. The yacht club aobligingly contact the local engineer who turns up promptly at 0915 to diagnose that one of the valve springs is broken because of some emulsifying of the engine oil. A Spare needs to be sent from Dortrecht ard worn’t arrive before Friday morning at the earliest which is all rather frustrating particularly having ta watch these rare Northerlies blow aimlessly away. Still, spirits improve as the day wears on, and even more so that night when the rain starts, so we lie in bunks feeling slightly relieved we’re not out in the North Sea after all. Also feeling that if the engine had to fail, it did soa before we'd finished urntying the lines.

Day Thirty Four - Enforced day of leisure sport on a pleasant wander around Den
Helder, with a lunch of bread and roast chicken.

Day Thirty Five - After an anxious wait the engineer arrived with the spring, and
with much muttering and sucking of breath, combined with thoughtful puffing on roll- ups, the spring was duly fitted and the engine reassembled. All ready to geo at mid afternoon, winds blowy but still favourable. We cast off about 1530 and had a speedy departure with Northerly 6 and fair tide. Heavy seas but tremendous progress of at least 98 knots, and great to be moving again. Jenny once again proved herself extremely competent at transferring accurate positions onto the chart from the GFS in difficult conditions. A long night at the tiller, but it was very rewarding in terms of progress. Dawn saw us clear of the shipping lanes and an easing of the winds down to a light North Easterly. By late morning we can see Sizewell, and from there a slow but pleasant run in brilliant sunshine to Harwich, motoring the last part. We decided to make our first visit to Shotley Marina ard almost regretted the decision after jilling about in the entrance and touching bottom for the first time in the whole trip. Eventually got in and enjoyed a good meal at the club.

Day Thirty Six - Little wind, but we managed to start sailing just outside Harwich
Harbour. The tide turned against us off Frinton, but we managed to keep on sailing. Gradually gained ground and in the end managed superb sail right back to the Club.

Day Thirty Seven - Slight panic when the engine wouldn’t start, then it responded
just ain time for us to lock in at Heybridge Basin some 1,581 nautical miles after locking out just over five weeks before, having visited some twenty ports, enjoyed some superb sailing and spent a week each in Norway, Sweder and Denmark. Arrived back in the middle of Bank Holiday Monday mayhem, 30th August.
