(an ordinary sailor's guide for sailing on the Blackwater)_
Ref. Maureen's comments in the November '93 Navigans, I don't think she is being over—sensitive about
good manners between sailors on the river - but I do think she might be a little naive to think it
will be any different in an age of 'the professional foul', 'gamesmanship' and 'the will to win at any cost' -— assuming it was really any different in the 'old days’ anyway. Over the years I have experienced, as a dinghy-racing helm, similar incidents of blatant ‘ignore'(ance)' of 'the rules', some of which might be due to genuine ignorance but most due to 'gamesmanship' sometimes accompanied by varying degrees of verbal abuse. To be fair to Stone S.C., with the number of Open Meeting, National Championships,
etc., 'the abusers’ of language and/or rules need not necessarily be members of the Stone SC - merely
visitors for the event. Fran a dinghy—racing viewpoint, the remedy would be to raise a protest for each incident but, apart from the difficulty of finding witnesses, it is unlikely that regular protests would be popular with our own Marconi hierarchy, let alone be viewed with much sympathy by Stone, and anyway, who wants to hang around in the evening whilst a joint Protest Committee is formed ?

On the other side of the coin, I fancy there must be quite a few cruiser owners (and Stone dinghy-racing members) who have as great a jaundiced view of Marconi sailors behaviour as we might have of that of our neighbours. Not too long ago whilst on an air journey, I struck up a conversation with a very nice fellow traveller who turned out to be a keen dinghy-racing member of Stone. He was clearly unimpressed when I
mentioned I belonged to Marconi (but envied us our 8 acres) and appeared genuinely surprized that we had a racing programme; he firmly thought weconsisted of 'potterers' and cruisers whose moorings had encroached upon Stone's traditional sailing waters. He was, however, very much aware of our catamaran fleet, particularly in the vicinity of Breezy and, I imagine,had much the same opinion of Marconi's ability to follow the rules as we have of Stone's.

What is disappointing is the apparent 'knee—jerk' reaction of the Stone SC hierarchy in taking the stance of ‘not our members'; it is unrealistic to believe that the members never break, or ignore, the rules or that they never display bad manners or use abusive language to others who ‘get in their way’. I would hope that our own hierarchy, should they receive a similar complaint, would treat it with both courtesy and sympathy and assure the correspondent that, whilst only due to a very small minority, the Marconi Glub strongly disapproves of such behaviour and would always do its best to discourage it.

Over the years I have often voiced my view that the Marconi SC should not seek to ‘develope’ along the same path as the Stone SC but should remain essentially a ‘casual sailors' club in which a minority (albeit, a significant minority) choose to arrange a racing programme for their own amusement and pleasure. ‘The danger I foresee as the club ceases to be the Marconi Works Club sailing section and becomes a 'regular' sailing club is that-it will be taken alor- the path of promoting an ever—increasing number of Open Meetings and National Championsitips on the basis of ‘improving' the quality of sailing and ‘earning revenue' to avoid the necessity of increasing the membership fees 'too much’. With two such clubs in near proximity to each other on the Blackwater, I fancy it will be relative hell for the cruiserman as he tries to thread his and her way through the melee of racing dinghies trying to reach the next mark by the shortest possible route. In fact, we'd became just like any other club on any other crowded waterway.

In times past (mid-1960s) there was probably rather more 'mingling' of the Stone SC and Marconi both amongst the sailors on the water and the Officers of each club. Since those days the two clubs have developed along different paths with (hopefully) quite different aims. However, perhaps it is time for our hierarchy and that of Stone to meet a little mre informally a little more often and, by virtue of personal contact, perhaps cane to appreciate each others problems (and aims in sailing-life) a little better. At one time, there was a degree of intermingling of the cadet fleets (members, not Cadet boats); that could be revived to some extent, perhaps by inviting the Stone SC to hold their cadet week at the same time as our own and at our site ? Qk , so there might well be good reasons for not doing so, but unless actual contact between the two neighbouring clubs is improved, the relationships on the water can only deteriorate.

Or maybe there is no probelm? Maybe we (or at least some) are being too sensitive ? I think not.

Mike Boreham

16.

NB. Whilst looking through the list of dinghies, I noticed Colin Harper had an Optimist at the club. Did he really race in the Optimist at Marconi ?

Dennis Byatt (Commodore) reveals plans for the formal opening of the clubhouse with a "Filling Out Party’ in March, 1975. He also reminds everyone that if boat owners hit another boat (particularly the moored cruisers) then they should report the fact to
the owner - or at least to Vic Tate (Moorings Sec). In addition, Dennis tells us
that Minutes of Committee Meetings are put up in the clubhouse in order to keep members informed of the business of the club. What a good idea !

Sadly, the club's first 'official' Commodore, Terry Hallam, died suddenly on 1 July, 1974, at the relatively young age of 54. This series of Navigans Past has revealed to me many of the tensions, arguments and ‘battles behind the scenes' which went with the growth of the club and undoubtedly Terry Hallam was often in the thick of it. In his obituary to Terry, former Commodore Stan Allerton writes:-

"Many spendid and sometimes infuriating episodes form the backcloth of my memories of Terry but at the front of stage stands the man so many of us admired and will continue to remember with much pleasure and a little sadness".

Terry Hallam was, of course, Commodore on two separate occasions, both of which could justifiably be regarded as the two most crucial stages in the club's history. These were the founding of the club itself at Heybridge and the tremendously ambitious decision to move to the virgin Stansgate site. I understand that initially Terry was not in favour of the move but, once committed, worked hard to ensure its success. As Stan Allerton says of Terry “His experience and success will never be equalled in the club, for he led during the days of ‘do it yourself' when each member contributed to its work and growth, when unity and friendship were taken for granted".

In 1993, the club is still essentially a 'do it yourself' club but the membership is a lot bigger and no longer has the cohesiveness of being almost entirely 'Marconi' and, of course, there is a greater diversity of sailing interests within the club. One wonders what Terry would make of it all now ?

Finally, the Editor quotes John Witter (Vice Commodore) at the last Main Committee Meeting as saying "The question of an extra window in the Ladies Changing Room will also be looked into" (presumably via the existing window?).

August - it was Marconi's turn to run the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships

catamaran.

colloquially 'push off' and say nowt. Now, where have I heard that one before ???

WHERE HAVE THEY GONE?

For those of you who may have read my enquiry published in last October's issue of Practical Boat Owner regarding the removal and whereabouts of the Wie guns emplaced on the Tongue Sand Tower, the following may be of interest to you. Although a reply has not been published by PBO I did in fact receive several interesting responses, the most informative
being the one below. Should you wish to see the articles referred to in this response, please contact me - Malcolm
Yeoman, [redacted].

GUN, THAMES ESTUARY FORTS. I read with interest your letter in Practical Boat Owner concerning the above. Both the two guns which were on the Tounge Towers, and the two which were on the Knock John Towers were removed last year. Of the four guns, three are now in Orkney at the Scapa Flow Visitor Centre, and the remaining one is at Coldharbour, Gravesend, in the care of the Kent Defence Research Group.

By way of explanation as to how this came about: I am a native of Herne Bay but have lived in Orkney for the past fifteen years. Part of my job with the local authority

contd....

3.

was to create a visitor centre/museum on the site of the old naval base at Lyness, Scapa Flow. I had been looking for heavy Guns for the museum and recalled that there used to be some on the forts. I made enquiries with the Air Vice Marshall’s Office in Pitreavie who arranged for a helicopter to go from Manston to check if they were still there. The next step involved me going to Manston where the Air Vice Marshall kindly placed a Sea-king and crew at my disposal. I was taken out to the Tounge and Kriock Johri Towers to look at the guns. I then made arrangements with the Ministry of Defence to release the guns to Orkney Islands Council. The Biggest hurdle was yet to come. I obtained the assistance of REME at Colchester but had to wait (because of the Gulf War) for the use of a Chinook helicopter from 7 Squadron. The project finally came together last June when I flew ta London and sperit a very interesting day with the RAF at Manston. A Sea-king took a party, including myself, out to the forts. Technicians from the REME and Joint Air Transport Command cut the guns free and they were airlifted to Manston by a Chinook from 7 Squadron RAF Odiham.

I hope this answers your questions. Please find enclosed complimentary guide books and copies of photographs taken at the time of the recovery.

Yours faithfully, R.D. Hughes, Special Projects Manager.

BROUGHT UNDER TOW BY KELLY’S EYE - an account of the incident which brought about the
taking into tow the vessel Varuna II by Kelly’s Eye during the summer of 1992, for which Pete Sayer was awarded MSCs Seamanship Trophy.

Or, August Bth 1992 Margaret and I, sailing Varuna II in company with Pete Sayer on Kelly’s Eye, set aut from MSC to commence a two-week holiday bound for Zeeland via Belgium. Our outward ports and places of call were Bradwell, Nieuwpoort, Ostend, Breskens, Middelberg, Veere and finally Zierikzee, arriving on Friday @2ist August. After a two-day stay at Zierikzee we commenced our return passage which included stops at the Delta Marina, Middelberg and Vlissingen. All the passages sea far had been without incidents.

We departed Vlissingen on Wednesday 26th August at 1430 hrs. In the ship’s log we recorded that at 1600 hrs we had a large reef in the main, no headsail, and under engine. The sea was very lumpy and arrival at Blankenberge could not come = soar enough. At 1700 hrs disaster struck when the engine started to lose power and we could smell diesel fumes. Thoughts of limping along and sorting out the problem at Blankenberge were shortly ruled out when the engine finally stopped. Our position was about half a mile east of Zeebrugge harbour mole where at this particular time numerous vessels were frequently entering and leaving the harbour’ entrance. We considered a number of options to overcome the problem, these being:

a) To take long tacks out to seaward, but with little favourable tide remaining, and
the prospect of entering the marina under sail, this option did not appeal tec us.

b) Anchoring in shallower water was ruled cut because it would be on a lee shore.

c) To turn about and go back to Breskens, be it with a more favourable wind was an
option we did not want to take since our destination, Blankenberge, was just 5 miles away.

We decided to radio Pete on Kelly’s Eye who by row was about to cross the buoyed channel to Zeebrugge harbour. Having discussed our options with him, he offered to assist us by taking Varuna II in tow so the engine problem ccauld be investigated and possibly repaired.

The job Pete had of getting Varuna II under tow was no mean task. He was single- handed and we were close to a busy harbour entrance where a strong tide was running. He had to organise locating a suitable tow line (I had not got one of sufficient length on board) and then control his vessel at close quarters to enable a tow line to be thrown to us.

All these tasks were carried out calmly and expertly with an excellent throw of the line which was secured to Varuna II.
CONntGs-6

4.

Under tow, with the large swell persisting, our vessels’ positions relative ta each other were, to say the least, quite nerve-racking at times. However, with some skilful steering by Pete and Margaret, we avoided collision.

The outcome of it all was that the engine problem was due to a leak on the injector fuel feed pipe, and fortunately we had a spare pipe on board. The repair was carried out and within 20 minutes of coming under tow the engine was running again.

Fete ther released the tow line which was recovered on to Varuna II and we were theri able to continue our passage safely, arriving at Blankenberge at 1915 hrs.

Thank you, Fete!
Malcalm Yeoman.

HANDICAPS

Many Dinghy and Catamaran races are handicapped using the published Foartsmouth Yardstick Numbers. These numbers are purported to be an average performance figure obtained from club returns. Presumably this means that the average boat in a class, Sailed by the average crew in average weather conditions will be equally handicapped compared to any other boat sailed in the same circumstances.

Let us consider that last variable - weather conditions, this being wind strength and
tidal flow. At low wind speeds the relative performance will depend upon waterline length and the hull’s wetted area. but as the wind picks up, then all-up weight = and underwater shape will determine the point when the boat starts ta plane. A boat on the plane has a substantial speed advantage over one travelling at displacement speed. Eventually as the wind speed increases further then the average sailor will lose control. As the threshold at which both the above occur is at different wind strengths with each class of boat, then the average potential handicap cannot be a constant factor across the wind range.

Wher, it comes to tide, however, it is possible to give an illustration of a_ typical Situation, simplified for convenience. A race consisting of a circuit rounding two marks one mile apart with a one mile an hour tide flowing along the line of the
course.

Yacht °’S’ with a handicap of 150 sails at @mph. Yacht °F’ with a handicap of 75 should therefore sail at 4mph under average conditions.

Yacht ’S’ will travel at 2 + 1 mph over the ground with the tide, and at 2 - 1 = mph
against the tide.
1 1
This gives a lap time of = + 1 + 2 2 2535 Are.

Yacht ’F* will travel at 4 + 1 mph with the tide, and 4 - 1 mph against the tide.

i 1
Giving a lap time of 4+1 + 4-1 = QO.53 hrs.

In still water however, yacht °S’ would have taken exactly twice the time of Yacht ‘FF’ to finish level on handicap. In the example above Yacht 'S’ exceeded this time
by 25%!

Why do we use the present handicap system, ther? I suspect it is because there is nothing else that could be easily applied which is better. There may be a set of circumstances that allows your class of boat to be favoured at some time, especially if it is a fast handicap class in tidal conditions (i.e. Stansgate).

A Different View from the Rear.............

I am sure that those of you who experienced the Laying Up Supper will agree with me that it was an excellent evening. The food, entertainment and company were first class and I am sure there will be a rush for tickets for next year’s event once the word gets around. Many thanks to all those who helped to make the evening a great success and especially to Steve and Debbie Glynn.

The fruits of the year's sailing were presented to a large number of people on Sunday 14 th November by our President's wife, Mary Greygoose. I was pleased to see a number of different people receiving prizes for the first time. A complete list appears elsewhere in this issue. Those of you who could not be at the prize giving will have to get in touch with me and arrange to collect your trophies. My congratulations to all prize winners in 1993.

Willie Pitcairn has decided to step down as sailing secretary due to pressure of work. I am sure you will all join me in thanking Willie for all his hard work in making this year's sailing programme work extremely efficiently. Tom Duckmanton takes over, he has a hard act to follow!

The work for next year’s events has already started and the sailing programme has been drawn up and agreed by the sailing sub committee. The main changes are as follows:
First race coincides with BST.
Mid week series starts mid May.
Pilots Cup replaces Rum Tub and Bung.
Handicap team race against Osea Sailing Club.

The Codes of practice for the activities of different sections of the club will be reviewed in the coming months to ensure that our activities are as safe as possible. Sailing instructions for racing are also being reviewed and modifications will be made. Rotas for Race Officer and Support boat crews are also being drawn up. If you know that you will not be joining the club next year and you took part in this year's race programme, it would be very helpful if you would phone and let me know.

Is there any one out here who would like to become a race officer? Perhaps you have given up sailing and have some time on your hands on a Sunday! It would be a great help if you could lend your support to this aspect of the club's activities. Give me a ring if you can help.

I have heard that some people may be reluctant to start racing because they find the thought of being rostered for race officer or support boat driver duties too off putting! If you start racing then you will only graduate to these exalted positions after you receive adequate training. If you don't race but would like to become involved in either of these activities then please contact me as soon as possible.

In the recent stormy weather a number of boats were not adequtely secured because they were blown about. Please check your ground anchors and the rope used to tie the boat to it's ground anchor. Why not spend a few pounds one length of high quality rope to secure several thousand pounds worth of boat securely! There are still a large number of boats and trailers in the cat park which are not clearly identified with the owners name and telephone number. It makes the job of the fleet captain a lot easier if boats can be easily identified. Vacant pitches should also be identified otherwise they are likely to be reallocated next year.
Colin Kidner.

COMMODORE’S NOTES

Hope you all had an excellent festive season, and I am in the fortunate position of having a little more time to pen (or should I say word-process) some deathless prose. Firstly, I should like to welcome all the newcomers to the Main Committee. We didn’t get the right number of nominations for the AGM, but a number of volunteers have come forward to be co-opted. Thanks to Tom Duckmanton, Peter Flook, Derek Kirby and lan
Carruth.

The wettest year for a decade has put the NRA into (literally) the thick and slimy. Hopefully they should recover time and enable us to launch at the beginning of the season. We are most definitely on their case.

We have had a_ large number of instances of the Clubhouse being left open. Ir discussion, we have decided to remove the hold-back bolt from the door and to fit a Closer to it. The upshot of this will be that the Clubhouse doors will be permanently closed outside the normal season or special events (Moorings, Working Parties etc.) Let’s see if this works!!!!

Keep on taking the tablets,

Larry Botheras

CRUISER COMMENTS

42 Members, representing 25 Cruisers, attended the Cruiser AGM on 15th December. The Meeting opened with a review of events held in 1993 which included:
a) Fitting Out Supper at Stansgate held on Saturday 24th April 1993.
b) Assistance to the East Coast Piers Race in aid of the Seamanship Foundation.
c) Club Cruise to Walton Backwaters & supper at Walton & Frinton Yacht Club.
d) Cruiser End-of-Season Supper at Stansgate on Saturday 25th September.
e) A good attendance at the MSC Laying Up Supper held at Three Rivers Golf Club.

Launching & Hauling Out: As there is a limit to the number of Cruisers that can be dealt with in one day, it was agreed as a trial that a ’Notice of Intent’ Board be placed in the foyer for the Cruiser Owner to notify date of intention to launch/haul out his Cruiser. This will enable each Tractor Driver to know in advance how mary
Cruisers will want to haul out on his particular day - and a phone call to the
Tractor Driver in addition to a booking on the Board will ensure that one particular day is not over-booked. The Board would also be useful for booking the Scrubbing Post. Please contact Derek Kirby for more information.
Trailers: Attention was drawn to the poor condition of some trailers and Members were urged to ensure these are properly maintained, especially after immersion in the water at launching or recovery. A broken-down trailer can seriously jeopardise the completion of the whole day’s operation not only of the boat concerned, but of all the others being handled on the same day.
Security: The question of security was again stressed. Remove as much gear as possible from the boat; ensure ladders are locked up; Clubhouse and Gate are locked. Always assume you are the last person to leave the site.
Sea Wall; NRA are now working on the Clubhouse area, and access through the sea wall will be closed end December to approximately end February. (Ed’s note: Delay to this timetable is likely due to wet conditions which has brought work to a halt for a
time).

Election of Cruiser Fleet Captain: There were no nominations for this, so yours
truly agreed to carry on - no one seemed to object to this.

Paint Orders; Malcolm Shaft has again agreed to take this on, for which we thank him. Details will have been published in last month’s edition of Navigans.
Club Sweatshirts & T Shirts: Murray and Ann Bates are taking orders for Club wear and brought along samples to the meeting for members to see. Ordering was brisk, sea get your orders in. (Ed’s note: They were very nice sweatshirts and more details later, hopefully).
Chain & Shackles: Dave Thomas will be taking orders for Chain and Shackles again, watch out for details in Navigans. The use of anodes on moorings has proved successful, details of availability will be given later.

RNLI ROWING RACE, MONDAY 27TH DECEMBER 1993

Once agairs MSC was well represented both on the water and on the promenade at the armual RNLI Rowing Race at Maldon. Over £6,000 was raised by the event for the Lifeboat Service .

It is not known how much the MSC boats raised in total, but congratulations ge to Nicola Gardner who rowed on her own and collected £120. The other lone entry was David Ball in the Club tender. The rest of us rowed in company.

The MSC Ladies’ Team rowed in Charles Anderson’s boat, dressed as Cinderella (Lucy Boreham); the Fairy Godmother (Jenny Ball); and the Two Ugly Sisters (Claire Davies and Maggie Boreham). Special thanks to Maggie for stepping in as a last minute substitute and to Charles Anderson for the loan of his boat once again.

The Marconi Gentlemen in the Club Fisherman consisted of two reindeer (Malcolm Stuart and Mike Helliwell) and two Father Christmii (Tom Asnley and Ray &all). Tom was

of the Blackwater out. Name boards and flags on the boats proclaimed that Marconi SC was out in force to support our friends at the Maldon Little Ship Club who organised the event.

THE LIFEBOAT FLEET

In 1986 the RNLI- announced a 7-year plan to complete the modernisation of the Lifeboat Fleet, with a fast Lifeboat at all 210 Lifeboat Stations.

On 30th November 1993 the last of the ‘traditional’ displacement lifeboats was replaced at Aldeburgh, thereby fulfilling the RNLI plan. However, Lifeboat replacement is a continuous process as some of the older fast Lifeboats are nearing the end of their lives and new classes of boats are being introduced.

Ray Ball

Handicap Fleet

Many of you, no doubt, have decided that this is the year you will find more time to sail your dinghy. Furthermore, you have resolved to come down and join in the Sunday races and extend the fun you get from sailing. If you’ve not raced before then read on for arn easy lessor.

One fellow sailor has said he might have entered the races if he’d known what he had to do and what the flags meant. Well I’ve beer racing for twc seasons and have managed without knowing too much about all the details. I?ll try to give a basic
summary.

First, the races on Sunday usually start with the Fast Cats at 11.00am and ©&.00pm. In the hour before, you should find the course and start-time for each race written up on the blackboard outside the portakabin in the Cat Field. The course will tell you which marks to go around and whether to leave them to port or starboard. Having decided to sail, go inside the portakabin and sign on for the race, i.e. find the form for the Handicap Fleet and enter the name of your helm and, if you have one, of your crew, then your class of boat, sail number and finally, if you know it, the handicap number for your boat.

Be or the water and on the right side of the starting line in time for your start. The order of sailing is; a) Fast Cats, b) Medium Cats, c) Slow Cats, d) Handicaps and Mirrors, and finally d) Solos. The starts should all occur at 5S minute intervals. A gun (hooter), if you can hear it, should be fired at each start and for the Fast Cats there will also be a 10-minute and S-minute warning before their start time. There are also flags at the Race Box, if you can see them, which go up and down.

Watch out for the ‘3’ flag (this is not square, not triangular, but tapered and coloured red at the wide end, blue at the narrow end, and white in the middle) because this goes up 10 minutes before your start and goes down at the start. The Handicap fleet and the Solos start inside the D buoy, whereas the Cats start outside it, so you have the best chance of hearing the gun and seeing the flags. If you are not sure of the racing rules, which none of us are, then you’d do best to keep a little clear of the other boats at the start to begin with, although there aren’t usually that many other starters to worry about anyway. If you sail the right course and stay upright then you stand a good chance of winning. As you cross the finishing line the gun will be fired; this might be Don't a lap or two early if the race is taking too long. Note the start line is the continuation of the line from the line from the triangle on the race box to the ‘mete’ (a pole in the water), whereas the finishing line is from the triangle on the race box to the D buoy; the difference between the two lines is not a lot. Finally, don’t forget that when you’ve finished you must sign off in the portakabin; this is done on another form for the Handicap
Fleet where you enter whatever it asks for - similar to the signing on form.

It’s all very simple, isn’t it? For more details look at your copy of the MSC Sailing
Instructions. Oh, one other thing - it helps if you’ve got a watch but, even if you
haven’t, you can always ask your fellow sailors on the water how long it is to your
start.

1975 (January - June) - Marconi's Mirror—batchelors go sail-about round the Isle of Wight with many a tale

- Maureen and Ray have a mighty row in the middle of the night. We know 'cos it

January - on the front cover is a photograph of the new clubhouse, whilst inside are four photos showing
the progress of the building of the clubhouse during 1974. Of particular interest are the photos showing the old clubhouse, whilst one shows both old and new clubhouse together.

It appears from the Editorial that same "uninvited gifts” from the German airforce during World War I have been lurking in the muddy depths around Northey, Osea and Thirslet Spit. As the Editor says "The Mud Race seems to take on a new meaning." Perhaps that is why, in some of the years since 1974 "the traditional mud race' adopted a marked reluctance to go anywhere near the mud.

More on the clubhouse from the new Commodore, John Witter. He thanks the MASC for the investment, the Committee of the MASC for accepting the proposal to build, Ron Rider and colleagues of the (Marconi)
Building & Facilities Group, Mike Taylor and team for the actual construction - and the members
of
the MSC who gave many hours to basic planning and final design.

Further notes from John on the public right-of-way through the site - and a note that The Daily
Telegraph (6 December, 1974) had featured an article entitled "Wedgies wailing wall stops riverside stroll." Now that brings back same memories !!!

Alf Cottam suggested that Mamgu's ship's wheel be mounted on the wall "...in the passage directly
opposite to the main entrance doors, with suitably enscribed plaque." Is the wheel still in the clubhouse? I expect it is but we're so used to it ‘being there’ that we don't notice it or appreciate

A note records the death of Fred Taylor, the Maldon sailmaker, whose sail loft had consequently been taken over by McG JH Dennis. ‘The note (by Eric Payne) records that Fred never used a measure but
judged a fathom of line by the span of his arm(s) and was "...only a little bit out even when long
lengths were involved."

February - The Main Committee decided that a club log-book should be kept all year around. It was
also decided that the memorial to Terry Hallam should take the form of a light on the new clubhouse and which would serve as a navigation aid to all river users. I believe it is shown on charts as ‘THe Hallam Light’.

On the social side, Sam Poulton of Maldon gave a talk on spritsail barges and on the characters who sailed them, both past and present. Sam, it seems, had bought a spritsail barge for £50 (presumably "years ago') but high maintenance costs caused him to have it broken up even though the current price of such a barge was nearer £6,000. A second speaker, John Jowers, spoke about the fishermen of the Essex coast. Drifters used ‘shoot nets’ up to a mile in length and were known to drift up the Blackwater with the tide when fishing. A pair of Drifters working together could cause the ‘amateur
sailor' some considerable problems if he came upon them and "...got caught between them........and the
chances of loosing mast, boat and finishing up on a slab at Billingsgate wasn't right out of the question it seams.

Rick Anstey (Cadet Skipper) hopes to initiate a busy cadet programme for 1975 with tuition, training, practice and competition in the Points Series races. He also wants the cadets to take part in the Race Box duties and rescue boat duties.

go to hell for a pastime can certainly be applied to some club members who braved the elements and were
sailing in a snowstorm on Easter Sunday."

HANDICAP FLEET - Reply to Don’s article in the last issue encouraging more of our
Dinghy sailers tea start taking part in racing - plus a few
general points relating ta those who already race at the Club, arid elsewhere.

Dear Mr Gill,

I couldr’t help noticing your plea ta Dinghy sailors. I would like to point cut that it iS possible that your sailors are at Oper Meetings, sailing under the Marcari Harmer, oar sneaking a few hours’ enjoyment on a Cat rather than going slowly ain a race. (I always find it strange when people who are interested in racing dinghies, presumably ta get round a course faster than someone else, then do it in slow craft - perhaps it is to prolong the enjoyment?)

Enough frivolity on the advantages of one kind of craft to another. To return to my first point, there is little incentive or recognition from the Club to do Open Meetings, and no recognition or inclusion in Points Series when away waving the flag. The net result of this is that many keen sailors see no real reason ta bother with the Sunday series on a serious basis, which inevitably leads to questicning whether it is worth being a member of the Club, as the open circuit can now take 40 weekends
of the year - as much or more sailing as most sailors manage at the Club.

Add to this the need ta take a duty ar two during the season, no chance of inclusion in the Points Series, and a really crowded Club when one doesn’t want ta be far from home due toa maddening crowds (Bank Holidays) and the membership can seem a little odious, I know I felt this at the begirnming of this season. I enjoy MSC but if I am contemplating the merits of paying the membership I feel others must have had the same thoughts. This then must detract from the racing fleets, beth from a numbers and skill point of view.

Also, what about the good sailors we have at University? Is there communication with them tao make them feel it is worthwhile turning up? So at the very time when people would be part of the mainstay of the Club (i.e. when they have graduated ard got a job) there is no incentive to continue.

Might I therefore suggest that MSC seriously consider the inclusion of Members far average points when they are away at Class Open Meetings, or sailing at other Clubs due to commitments like University?

I hope this provokes same thoughts.

Regards, Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine.

At right the natural silence experienced at a sheltered creek anchorage feels like the mud and marsh are helping the night to suppress the light and sound of day. The clarity of the might sky encourages me to seek the end of that vast heavenly spectrum. Looking up at the constellations and catching the odd meteorite trail that burns earthward towards the end of its lonely journey, the mind struggles to grasp the infinite spread above. Ofter we stargaze while at a dark, silent anchorage arid enjoy the feeling of the mind stretching to accept the vastness caf this
contemplation.

Wher. one first takes over a yacht, there is a whole range of new sounds that the skipper should become familiar with as they talk of the craft’s health and fouridation. The quest to locate and silence all unnecessary sounds from the craft 1 have owned is a vocation that lasts forever, as conditions and time extract their price from her structures.

Sometimes they provide you with arn early warning of chafe and fray, of locsening arid seizure, and at others, they toy with your dozy senses whilst the yacht gently moves and tugs at her anchor.

The noises of wind tell of the need to reef, the change in sound of the craft's passage through the water tell of speed maintained or increased.

This array of sounds awaits the attentions of a good skipper who, via his excellent human sensory array and his awareness ard perception, will achieve oneness with the sea arid his craft.

February - a notice in the files advertises Fast Coast Cruises between the Medway and Orfordness for 1955
under the auspices of the Maldon Youth Hostel. Cost per person for a 7-day cruise for 9 people was £ 6.00

March — 2] members attended the 1954 AGM of the MASC Sailing Section. Eric Payne felt the name should not
be the ‘Sailing Section’ but it was explained that the 'the club' was one of many groups belonging to the
parent MASC -—- hence it remained a Section of the MASC. Eric also queried the cost of insurance for the club
boat,Avril, but he was assured it would be less in 1954 and the years after because 1953 had to cover the journey
from Hullbridge to its moorings in the Blackwater. Eric Cottam said that as they were starting a Fleetwind
Class, they would need a Race Officer "...someone not interested in racing...but willing to fire the gun..... ‘
The Club President, Dr Eastwood, offered to be Race Officer if and when he was available, but the offer seems not
to have been taken up since it was proposed "...each skipper (and crew) take it in turns to act as Race Officer
or Officer of the Day..." It was also proposed to mm races only on Saturdays.

It was revealed that 8 Fleetwind kits were being purchased via the MASC whilst 2 others were being purchased
ready built. The MASC 'scheme' provided a loan for half the cost, repaid over two years without interest.

Membership of the club had now reached 60 and the club was now "..officially recognised as one of the Blackwater
Clubs". A suggestion to look for another site (since the present site was rather inaccessible) was not taken up,
it being pointed out that sites were difficult to find, particularly since building on the sea wall was not now
permitted and, anyway, the present club was within easy reach of The Jolly Sailor. The AGM elected Terry Hallam
(Commodore), Geoff Wardell (Vice Commodore), E C Talboys (Sec.) G W Nichols (Treasurer) and Eric Cottam (Sailing
Sec); surprizingly, they seem to have dropped the post of Rear Commodore.

COMMODORE’S NOTES

There are two incidents that I believe require my comment before the season gets much further under way.

On Good Friday a Club official was harangued and brewbeaten by a group of worried Windsurfers ta release the RIB, or failing that Jack B, to enable them to goa in search of one of their colleagues who had drifted off and couldn’t be located. There had been a strong wind all day and they may have had cause to be worried but this must not happen to a Club Official again.

I would like to inform the Members concerned that Good Friday was not a "Club Day". There was no OOD/Support Roster for that day. Therefore it falls intca the same category as any other weekday, and the Code of Practice operates. This states that the second course of action, once the Baddow Star is not operational, is ta call the
Coastguard.

Secondly, the Easter Marday events that led to the comments in the Daily Telegraph and the Daily Mail on Tuesday. I don’t know just how much people really know the work of the RNLI op Coastguard, but I have a sneaking suspicion that there is
an
attitude that says "if there’s a support boat out there I’1l be OK, and if not the RNLI will be there". I don’t krow how many of you will recall the name Union Star, but that was a coaster that suffered engine failure in Mount’s Bay on 19 December 1981 in mega winds. They did not accept a tow from a salvage tug (to save money) and went oan the rocks. The Penlee lifeboat Sclomon Browne was launched and never came back. I had two school mates on that boat. It might seem a bit heavy to make these sorts of comments, out my earlier remarks are aimed at showing that with that attitude you are not just risking yourself, but other people as well.

There is far tac much bravade afloat these days. It’s not clever or macho to go aut mrs weather you can’t handle, and if we weren’t estuary-based there would be much more frequent problems. Dern’t be fooled by the excellent seamen who can handle their boats in extreme conditions; that comes with years and years of experience. And keep
mrs mind the prospect of something happening further out ta sea - the sight of land
disappearing as you Swim with with a capsized unrightable boat is rot one ta be recommended (and I’ve experienced it).

The watchword then, whatever your activity, 15 aim to be entirely self-sufficient and sail within your limitations.

Larry Botheras

Those MSC sailors not making it quickly back to the Hard had a lengthy and cold session getting their boats beached, still having ta keep them from blowing along the beach, and getting themselves ard their craft back to the Club by one means or another. FAST CAT NOTES
"30 rescued as winds capsize racing fleet"; "...the clubs should not have put these people at
risk."; "Some of the boats ... from the ... Marconi Sailing Club, were blown up to three miles along
the river." (Daily Telegraph, 5th April 1994.)
On one thing most of us can agree: incidents attracting such publicity help neither our club nor
our sport. Writing these notes in the aftermath of the carnage | am equally sure that we have every
reason to be thankful that Easter 1994 did not see serious injury (or worse) on our sailing waters. What could we have done to avoid the incident? The start of the morning race was delayed to allow an earlier storm to pass by; perhaps unfortunately, it slipped away to the north and we were given
no indication of the fury that might lurk within. Personally | was aware of the existence of the threat of
strong winds, and | believe that most of those sailing recognised the probability that the glorious
conditions pertaining at the start were unlikely to outlast the race. It is an oft-quoted truism that those entering a race do so at their own risk, and that the decision by the club (or more accurately those of its members who happen to be on duty on the day) to run a race in no way absolves competitors of the responsibilty to decide for themselves whether or not to take to the water. Fair enough, but would Larry have liked (finding himself perhaps in the position of Stone’s Commodore Harry Elias) to have explained to a press inquisition that it was not the responsibility of the club to ensure the safety of its racing
members? | suspect that would have appeared as lame when printed in the Telegraph as Harry's “It was
just a Force Two when we set out." | believe we have to take great care to protect our members, our club
and our sport both from the threatening elements of wind and water and from the shadow of those who might wish to add further bureaucracy to our sport, possibly demanding formal qualifications (for competitors as well as support boat drivers), or impractical levels of support cover. Most of us will remember the Health and Safety official who last year succeeded in closing Wraysbury Lake Sailing Club for safety-related reasons.
Should the race have been run? | believe so; if we were not to venture afloat when inclement
conditions threaten then we would lose a large part of the season as well as fail to develop our sailing skills in stronger winds. It does not seem to me that we should consult the Coastguard as to the advisability of racing; to do so would place the coastguard in a difficult position, from which he could only escape by making an extremely conservative recommendation, one against which the club would be
foolish to go. Given that, how could we have acted to limit the subsequent damage? | did not notice a
forecast (including the strong wind warning) posted in the Clubhouse; neither did | notice an empty
forecast board, and | do not know whether it is the formal responsibility of any of the 'duty members’ to
post the forecast. | suggest that having a specific board (clearly identified) for a current weather forecast,
and assigning a clear responsibility to post a forecast on each morning on which club sailing will be held, would allow those intending to race to better assess the risks to which they are exposing themselves, and as a consequence help the Club’s position.
On this occasion was the rescue cover adequate? Certainly we only had one vessel immediately available (the RIB), although the Jack B abandoned mooring-laying to join the clear up operations after the squall hit. The area of the course had been deliberately restricted with this in mind; it became clear however that restrictions obeyed by boats racing were not necessarily recognised by the same vessels when they were cartwheeling before a Force 9/10. It seems to me that although the provision of further support boats would have reduced the time to attend each of the craft following the impact of the squall,
it is not obvious that there was an unacceptable shortage of cover. | believe we all accept the
impossibility of guaranteeing instant attention from a support boat, and that this is one of the risks (for some, possibly the attractions) of our sport. Could the rescue (sorry, the politically correct epithet
‘support’ doesn’t seem to fit) operation have been better carried out or managed? | believe we owe a
great debt to those members who played a part, either on the water or the land, and from my perspective
| would like to thank especially Mick Richardson, whose driving of the RIB was both skillful and
reassuring. Some of the radio traffic seemed temporarily to reveal an element of confusion as to the whereabouts of some of our competitors, although whether on the part of our members or those of Stone was not clear. Without a detailed post-mortem, in this case perhaps only by chance metaphorical, it might be difficult to identify areas where improvements could be made.
In the event, the more serious consequences were avoided (or avoided us). Several large insurance claims will now no doubt be submitted, another fact which should concern all those who each
year face increasing premiums; | wish those involved good luck. Easter Monday's storm has cast a
shadow over the new season at the club, after a sparkling first weekend with some excellent racing in
fine conditions. | hope and trust that the Fast Cat Fleet, having licked its wounds, will soon return to the
water, older, hopefully wiser, but undeterred.

Tip of the month, from Caroline at the height of the storm:
“Now don't get too competitive, John...". Seemed fair at the time.

The cost of the weekend is £89 and includes breakfast, lunch and accommodation oan Sigma 36’s. Extras are pub meals Friday night at Shamrock Quay and Saturday night at Yarmouth (1.0.W.) Handicap Fleet and its Handicapping

So what is the Handicap Fleet? It is the name given to those monchulls in the Club which race against each other under a handicapping system. In fact, the various catamaran fleets race under the same system. Only the Solos, being a one class fleet, have no need for handicapping.

The handicapping scheme used for racing is Called the Portsmouth Yardstick Scheme. Each class of boat has a handicapping number, the Portsmouth Number (PN), associated with it. This is used very Simply to scale the race time of a boat so that each boat has in theory an equal opportunity to win a race when the adjusted race times are used.

The adjusted time is calculated by the formula:

(adjusted time) = (actual time) x 100 / PN

Usually you just leave it to the race box to de this calculation. You can see why they measure times in seconds! Here are some PNs:

B7 305 116 Wayfarer
99 Osprey 117 Laser Radial
103 Hornet 118 Eriterprise
105 Fireball ) B Wanderer
109 Laser II 119 GP 14
110 Kestrel Let Eurape
111 Cherub ize Solo
114 Laser 136 Topper
115 420 144 Mirror (single handed)
146 Mirror

Notice that if I, in my Laser II (PN = 109), finish in a time of 109 minutes, and the
GF 14 (PN = 119) finishes in 119 minutes, then we tie because our times beth adjust
to 100 minutes. Thus, finishing in 109 minutes, I beat him if I finish ahead by more
than 119 -109 = 10 minutes. This PN difference is a good guide for catamarans because
they often finish their races in a number of minutes roughly equal toa their PN number. For monohulls, sailing a shorter course, they usually finish in some lesser time and sao would have to proportionately scale the margin given by the difference in PN rnumbers. For example, if I finish in 75 minutes, I would need to beat the GP by
10x75/109 = 6.88 minutes. Note, if we divided by 100 instead of our PN number, we
would get 7.5 minutes; incorrect, of course, but probably a good enough approximation for deciding if I beat her or not. Hence for monohulls, whose FPNs are fairly close ta 100, we have: the margin between us and the other boat that would cause us to tie is approximately given by our time divided by 100 and then multiplied by our PN difference. We could probably do this caiculation in our head!

I’m afraid I’ve got bad news for the slower boats. In our tidal waters the handicapping system will favour the faster boats. This is because the slower boat
suffers more than the faster boat sailing against the tide - the slower boat may not
ever manage to beat the tide! She will then gain sailing with the tide, but unfortunately it will not be enough to compensate. John Wooden did arn article on this subject in the January 1994 issue of Navigans.

Oh, for the joys of a lovely Mackintosh and a fancy printer... | can'tresist taking the opportunity of typing this on a
borrowed outfit, and if | don't finish it before the deadline for its return there will need to be a change of printing style

T antic Crui

David Cole owns the Arthur Robb designed wooden 55' ketch ‘Anatina' and very kindly asked me to join for a cruise across the Atlantic to Venezuela in November 1993.

The boat was lying at Villamoura Marina in South Portugal in the capable hands of ‘Johnnie’ (who had spent the last three months applying approximately 16 coats of varnish to the masts and almost every piece of teak in sight) and Dick (who had been over every possible item needing maintenance) and we arrived there by air on 20th November. Three fairly frantic days of storing ship and preparing everything ensued, and then we departed on a sunny evening into the empty wastes of the Atlantic. There were five of us on board, David, myself, Philippa Anderson, David's younger son Adrian, and Adrian's friend from
Harvard Business College - Pip Woods (26) an Anglo-American who had never been sailing before.

As we drew away from the mainland coast the wind and waves increased. We set watches of three hours each, and we were rather dismayed to find that a full rig of oilskins was needed. Water was occasionally finding its way on board, and even into the cockpit, and it was essential to be clipped on with safety harness at all times. The only saving grace was that it was not particularly cold, and the wind was fair on our South Westerly course.

We went to Porto Santo (Portuguese), a small island a few miles from Madeira which we decided would be preferable for us to visit as it is not beset by tourists. There is a small artificial harbour which protects from most of the swell where we anchored at dawn on the fourth day amongst about twenty ocean voyagers - mostly French. The sun was lovely, the solid ground between our feet. We ordered a bottle of Madeira at the harbourside and drank it rather quickly. The island is volcanic. Columbus lived here for a bit as he fell in love with the daughter of the first governor. We went to see a sma/l museum in his house. We hired bikes and went round the island which is about the same size as the Isle of Wight, quite poor, but simple and agreeable. Enough rain to have some green vegetation and some palm trees. After four days we left.

Again we were somewhat dismayed to find the weather very boisterous as the yacht drew away from the island in late afternoon and it was necessary to get back into the routine of night watches and sharing cooking duties, not very onerous as several people felt sea-sick. The worst aspect of the cooking was that the motion was very violent in 20' seas with a cross-sea running and the boat corkscrewing along on a fast
reach. Every single item one used - the coffee grains, the milk, the cooking oil, the cups - everything
needed to be wedged all the time or else it would fall to the cabin sole and join the general ice rink there beneath our bare feet. It was necessary to keep one's foot on a floor cloth or one would start to slide to the far side of the cabin down the polished teak. After four days and nights the fantastic clouds on the horizon at dawn resolved themselves into the volcanic peaks of Gran Canaria. It was breathtakingly beautiful, and not just because it lay there in the midst of the vast ocean but because it made one realise a bit what those first voyagers must have felt as they came across them for the first time beyond the empty sea-horizons which since the dawn of history had been the only known boundaries of Europe. As we approached the island the wind and waves died down and eventually the ship was becalmed and everyone bathed. For the rest of that day we skirted the vast volcanic cliffs and mountains of the uninhabited West Coast where there is no coastal plain and no sign of human habitation. In late afternoon we came to the small marina at Puerto Mogan (Spanish). Although it was only built in 1977 it is extremely well designed and agreeable with masses of well tended flowers and small dwellings and shops in an excellent town plan from which cars are largely excluded.

Here we spent about four days swapping crew members, getting some electronic instruments put right, doing some mechanical maintenance, trying to mend the decaying genoa by hand, buying all the stores for the big hop, topping up water tanks and bottled water. The best thing was the wonderful quality of the
fruit and vegetables grown locally, best | have ever seen anywhere. By contrast the local chandler was
worse than hopeless, anda ridiculous, self-important, (Swedish) so-called 'maintenance engineer’ actually succeeded in delaying us from getting essential last-minute jobs done. Luckily we managed to find a wonderful English ex-regular soldier in his own small cruising boat who came on board and dealt with everything most competently.

14.

Philippa Anderson left us to catch a plane for England, and Davia's elder son Martin arrived with his friend Nicholas Morse. Soon it was time for us to leave and once again there was a moving moment as the yacht drew away from the quay and a tiny waving figure on the shore grew smaller and smaller astern. (That was Philippa Anderson! She'd missed her plane.)

The passage to the Islas do Cabo Verdes took eight days, and once again there were big waves and
strong winds. The genoa | had stitched began to come unstitched along a further section of the foot due
to the strain imposed each time it collapsed and re-set itself with a loud crack like a whip. Luckily the wind was fair still and we were not obliged to beat to windward, but the rolling motion was as tiring as ever and should we lose anyone overboard in those rough conditions there would be no chance whatsoever of beating back, relocating him, or being able to manoeuvre anywhere near to reach down, secure and pick up the body. We navigated with a new Magellan GPS instrument whose only failing was that it seemed to eat dry-cell batteries rather fast and there was some doubt about whether we had enough replacement batteries on board. Occasionally we took sun-sights by sextant and worked them out with a small Japanese computer, taking about ten minutes to do the calculations, but mostly it was far too rough to even take sights as the horizon would be obscured by heaving waves. We started a watchkeeping routine. Each day one person would be excused watchkeeping and would cook all the meals, wash
everything up, sweep the cabin floors and wipe everything in the heads with disinfectant. | may say this
was a counsel of perfection which we did not always manage to fulfil, especially as all these tasks are very difficult when the weather is not good and the motion of the boat in the waves is violent. It is all one can do to keep one's balance below-decks and hold on to prevent oneself from falling, let alone clean as well, or perform a tremendous juggling act in the galley getting all the ingredients together from the various stowages for cooking and all the crockery and cutlery together from their various stowages for serving each of the three meals for six required each day. Meanwhile, the other four would keep deck watches,
usually alone, three hours on and nine hours off. | did not much enjoy the night watches as the weather
was not good, large waves, strong wind, overcast sky and quite frequent line squalls. However watchkeeping was not too onerous while the Autohelm did all the steering. Sometimes the waves and wind would become too much for the Autohelm and the watchkeeper would have to start steering by hand, andsometimes there would be a line-squall coupled with a shift of wind which would require hand steering to prevent a gibe.

After eight days of strong weather we reached Puerto Grande Islas San Vicente in the Cabo Verdes Arquipelago where we anchored next to the battered-looking old town of Mindelo, all very exhausted and glad to be in a relatively sheltered open anchorage, though the rolling continued all night and day. The pilot books all warned about the Cape Verdes, saying the natives were so poor they would board yachts
and steal anything not secured - dinghies, outboards or anything else you care to mention. This was
reprehensible as it has prevented, at any rate English people, from calling here. Only twenty British yachts visited last year. There were some Australian and Scandinavian and French voyagers there, and one Italian with a broken mast. No British. In our experience the natives were courteous and, as far we we could see, as honest as one can possibly expect. The are poorer than we can imagine, coming as we do from a prosperous country, and if one leaves things lying about unattended like expensive dinghies with
expensive things in them, as far as | can see it ought to be understood that it is the fault of the rich for
leaving things around and not the fault of the poor for taking them. Things representing untold wealth to the locals left about carelessly by visitors may be assimilated. That's all one can say on the subject. The inhabitants of the Cape Verde Islands are descendants of African slaves mixed with Portuguese, many very good-looking and athletic, and some with really beautiful faces. Some can understand French, but the local dialect is a kind of Portuguese which unfortunately few Europeans can understand.

We stayed four days and managed to get the genoa sewn up after a fashion by a tailor (‘Charley' who could sort of half-understand French) with a Singer hand-wound sewing machine and using our sail-bag to cut up to make patches, and the last of our reel of sail-twine as he had none of his own. Little piccaninies
would surround the dinghy at each landing and beg for your hat, your watch, your shoes - even your
rubbish, but we soon got used to them, and in the end grew quite fond of them. They were press-ganged into carrying hundreds of bottles of mineral water for us. There was no water available on the islands for replenishing the yacht's tanks. It had not rained there for three years. All the Island's water has to be made in a de-salination plant from the sea, and the plant itself keeps breaking down. All electricity comes from winamills, many of which are no longer revolving in the perpetual wind.

After four days we departed for the Atlantic crossing. Once more we sailed out into a huge sea and a strong wind -not the gentle Tradewind we had hoped for. Before the end of the first day we came up with six tiny open boats in a little group hand lining. They looked so lonely and vulnerable out there tossing up

15.

and down in the immense waves, sometimes lost to view and sometimes flung up as on a peak. At the same time we were joined by a wonderful school of lively porpoises who zoomed in and out round the bows as we thundered along at about eight or nine knots with huge carpets of foam spreading out each side of us to mark our passage through the seas. No ships appeared on our horizon during this part of our voyage. Once we saw a lonely little flock of white egrets going roughly North-west. What on earth were they heading for? Were they lost? At about the half-way mark a beautiful tropic-bird with long plume-like tail feather trailing astern came and flew quietly round us as if asking us to drop a little of our rubbish
overboard for it to inspect. Twice | saw plastic bottles floating miles from anywhere, horrid evidence of
untidy and careless civilisation. Flying fish took off at our precipitate approach and sped away, but sometimes they landed by mistake on our deck and got fried and eaten. Something enormous took my huge flashing metal lure, wire trace and shark book and broke my 5 Ibs breaking-strain mono-filament line and swam off with it, unfortunately. It was usually too rough to trail a line over the stern and the waves made it inadvisable because there was no means of preventing it from getting tangled in the log-line on the opposite side of the taffrail. We saw storm-petrels and boobies and pair of sinister killer-whales
powered past us looking like nuclear submarines hell-bent on a distant prey - luckily not us.

We could not celebrate Christmas Day as the weather was too rough. The Christmas presents | had
brought were stowed for convenience in the foc's'| and as that compartment was separated from the after
part of the vessel by a water-tight bulkhead and no one was able to leave the cockpit with any safety | was
not able to get the presents until 28th December, so it all fell a bit flat. The only thing worth mentioning about Christmas Day was that the Autohelm failed. This was a great blow. Up to then we had managed to keep watches (three hours each) singly, but now it became necessary to steer all the time and we decided to keep watches in pairs because we found it too tiring to steer in the heavy seas for more than half an hour at a time.

Unfortunately Nicholas Morse was not experienced at steering a sailing boat, and at about seven in the morning in the dark during a particularly severe line-squall he sensed that something was wrong as he felt the force go out of the mainsail. He knew he should take immediate drastic action to prevent a gibe, but he turned the wheel the wrong way and the boat, which was travelling at more than eight knots, took a wild sheer to port and heeled over too far to starboard. The heavy wooden boom carried away the wire fore- guy and the metal rail to which the four-part downhaul tackle was secured pulled the whole of the lower half of the boom off, splintering the wood like a strike of lightning and letting the top half of the boom and the mainsail smash over to starboard. He then lost his head and turned the wheel hard the opposite way, gibing the broken splinters of the boom back again and causing the yacht to heel over even further to port, burying the side-deck which picked up a quantity of water. Unfortunately someone had decided the cabin was too stuffy during the night and had unscrewed and opened all the scuttles which consequently spouted all this into the cabin. Here it began sloshing about on the cabin sole which was so beautifully fashioned that it was unable to get away into the bilges beneath, contributing considerably to a distinct lowering of morale.

Luckily daylight was breaking. We continued to run before the strong wind and David went forward and managed to pull the mainsail down the track and secure it and the two splintered parts of our boom. We ran on under the genoa, but that was slowly disintegrating before our eyes. During the day we lowered the genoa, set the yankee which was smaller, and also set the small boomed stays’! on the other side to balance it and make steering a bit easier. And so we carried on, and on the twelfth day it was 'Land Ho!" and lovely Barbados hove up over the horizon to leeward. Never had green trees and and yellow beaches and white surf looked more beautiful.

We had a lovely stay in Barbados and |! surprised myself by falling for the Bajans. They are so happy on
their island! It made me realise how sad it is that they are really not happy in London, and to some extent it's our fault, though of course it's much easier to be happy in a land of sun and plenty than it is in a land of fog and dearth. Adrian, Martin, Pip and Nicholas Morse left by plane. We managed to get the boom and the Avohelm mended and the genoa sewn up. Unfortunately we left the Zodiac inflatable in the sun on the hot beach one day and while we were away having lunch in the local Hilton Hotel it astonished the drinkers round the bar at Val Knowles's Boatyard Restaurant by exploding with a loud report. It proved impossible to mend, but Val Knowles managed to find a rather beaten-up Hutchinson dinghy which David was able to acquire secondhand from a Bajan and that had to serve as our tender from then on, unfortunately just a bit leaky in wind and water.

Hilary Cole arrived by plane. Michael Richie arrived too, owner of the wooden sloop ‘Secret’ which had been built for him at Aldeburgh and 'Sani' Fogel from Maine, owner of a very handsome Hinckley 35 sloop.

16.

After Barbados, a boisterous overnight passage took us past lovely Saint Vincent to Admiralty Bay, Bequia. We hada lovely time at Bequia which is wonderfully green, mountainous and fertile. A few years before, ‘Sani' had built a house on the other side of the island and she took us to Friendship Bay in an old Chevrolet pick-up truck so she could show it to us, and we could all bathe in the surf off the white beach. She very kindly gave us a wonderful lunch in a very jolly open-sided palm-thatched restaurant beside the sea where we Sat in the shade drinking rum punches and pina coladas, kept cool by the trade wind blowing through the spray from the surf. Next day we had a glorious sail past the active volcano at Kick 'em Jenny to the ‘Treasure Island‘ anchorage at romantic Tobago Cays, sheltered from the spume of the thundering Atlantic swells only by the shallows of the coral reef.

That was followed by a short sail in dull grey weather between reefs and palm-fringed islands to Union Island. The Union Island Yacht Club Hotel seemed rather sinister because it was fronted by a small sea- water lagoon containing about a dozen large brown nurse sharks. On the terrace here we were joined for lunch by some friends from England, the Powers, and Mary Barton (widow of Humphrey of “Vertue V" fame) came and sat next to me. The anchorage at Union Island was uncomfortable and full of swell and we all felt rather sad because ‘Sani’ left us here and departed by plane from the small airfield for Maine. We weighed anchor and left for Canouan Island. Here we anchored off the ferry pier. It was not well sheltered and the swell was continuous. We landed with difficulty. There are not many trees on Canouan. It was very hot. We walked a short way to the only place we could find where we might be able to get /Junch. It was a sad littte modern ‘Bed and Breakfast' establishment run by a little old bird who told us she had been a nurse in Scunthorpe for twenty years before coming back to her home island with her husband and spending their savings on setting up their small establishment. She gave us what she called ‘English cooking’ but unfortunately it didn't flatter us much. Lateron we all began to feel a bit ill and we came to the conclusion we were all suffering from heat-stroke spending too much time not in the shade during the heat of the day when we were not quite acclimatised to the tropical heat.

We left next day without regret and set sail for unbelievably beautiful but poor, romantic Carriacou Island.
This was the one | liked almost best of all the places we visited. We had supper ashore in a fairly dot-and-
carry-one establishment run by a large jolly local called ‘Bubbles’. Next day he took us for a tour round the
island in his old mini-bus. For lunch we stopped at the Cassada Bay Hotel. Quite the most beautiful place |
had ever seen in the whole world | thought, and now | cannot wait to try to visit it again.

Next - the Spice Island! Grenada. Prickly Bay. Everything you could possibly want grows wild here in
profusion - bananas, coconuts, oranges, lemons, limes, avocadoes, mangoes, guavas, grapefruit,
nutmeg, mace, peppers, cocoa, coffee, not to mention flowers and trees of the most exotic colours, ferns,
orchids - it's paradise! No wonder the horrible Americans invaded it and tried to wrest it from the British
under the Presidency of perfidious Reagan! All were sad to leave there. An overnight dash took us to the remote Testigos Islands which really are small and poor, about the same size as Eigg, Rum and Muck, ! should think, but stony and sparsely vegetated and swept by unceasing wind. Final hop was to Islas Margarita, Venezuela proper. Here once again there was no shelter other than the open roadstead at Pampatar, and nowhere to land except through surf on the open beach where the dinghy would almost invariably get upset, and everyone soaked either when landing or leaving. Luckily, as the water was warm, this usually only led to a good deal of laughter and was not at all worrying. In fact, in a funny way everybody began to enjoy it.

Trying to get away from Venezuela was a nightmare, involving having things stolen, losing my luggage on internal flights, being frisked by very unpleasant Veneauelan ‘soldiers’, drunken agents, desperately
dangerous driving in huge clapped-out American cars - a taxi, but | only found out too late that the ‘driver’
had stolen it just before | got in! He would insist on going at ninety miles an hour (to imitate ‘Alain Prost ha!
ha! ha!). Being overcharged for an air ticket, being charged 1000 Bolivars by a porter, being refused
twice at weighing-in by officials after | had bought my tickets (were they hoping for bribes?) and finally
being refused exit until | paid a rotten tax just to get out (having already paid yet another tax at the
Venezuelan Embassy in Grenada just to get in!) Due to the fact that a sheaf of Bolivars had blown away
across the tarmac on the wind when| tried to extract my boarding card from my pocket, | found | had not
quite enough Bolivars to pay the exit tax. It was then a question of racing across the International Airport building to try to find a money-changer (how do you do that in Spanish?) and racing back again in time to catch the plane. Miss that and it would have meant spending two nights in the airport building waiting for
the next one, and perhaps even forfeiting my fare. Not surprising | was relieved finally to catch it at the last
possible minute - it was late leaving, needless to say. Don't go to Venezuela unless you're good at
Spanish!

Owen Laurence-Jones

Handicap Fleet News

Receritly, I have had reason ta believe that there are dinghy sailors at large in the MSC who get a great deal of pleasure from their sailing without racing. 1 must admit I’ve missed out on this more relaxed form of sailing and their letters published in Navigans make it sound very enticing. I look forward to joining forces with them
sometime, but ... I am not attaching any outboard motor to my Laser II !

I also have reason tao believe that some of this non-racing fraternity would very much like to have the use of winches to help them pull their boats up the hard. Well, the good news is that there is a winch you can use. This information comes ta me from the upper echelons of the MSC and, further, it was suggested I wrote a few words here on usirig 1t.

Now for the bad news! I thought I had better get some first hand experience of using this winch by pulling up my boat. I pulled the winch cable (half inch diameter?) ta my boat off the end of the hard. Halfway down, I thought it would be easier to pull the boat up to meet the cable! Then I operated the winch. Every turn of the handle, around a two foot diameter circle, brought the boat up about one inch. Same considerable time later, the boat was up, I was exhausted, and everyone else had gore home. My sailing gloves were ruined, worn out and covered in dirt ard grease. Further, a lot of people who saw me doing all this think I must be a bit simple. They’re right! I have row asked Roger Nex to do some research on winches suitable for dinghies. If anyone has useful information on this subject, then contact him on [redacted].

If you ever find the winch is the only option open to you, then here is some advice on how to use the wretched thing. First, the winch that 1s suitable for dinghies (ha, ha!) is the small one that is nearest the entrance to the hard. The winch is covered by a box, as are each of the other three winches alongside it. Roll the box back cut of the way. Release the ratchet, which is held down by gravity so just flip it back. You will most likely have to free the ratchet first by winding up the cable slightly. Disengage any cogs from the large fixed cog that turns the cable axle. Do this by first lifting a greasy bar, that crosses the top of the winch, to allow the cags to move. Remove the handle if attached. Now pull the cable down to your boat. On the way, it will probably necessary to route it through a pulley attached to a ring embedded in the hard about 30 feet in front of the winch. You will find the pulley with a chain by the winch. Carry these (only about one cwt) to the ring and chain the pulley ta it. Having attached the cable to your trolley, walk all the way back to the winch. Engage gear. There are two gears. The cone you want you get by lifting the greasy bar and sliding the handle axle, which carries a small cog, so this cog engages the large fixed cog. Flip the ratchet over to its operating position. Attach the handle and wind, and wind, ad nauseam. There are some instructions on the side of the winch that you probably ought to read.

Let it be known that I represent all the Handicap Fleet, racers and norn-racers alike.

Finally, on behalf of the monohull Fleets, I would like to give a big thank you toa the Cat sailors and others who put so much work and time into running the Regatta. Their best efforts were frustrated by a lack of winds, but we appreciate very much what was done and a good time was had by all.

Dor, Gill, Handicap Fleet captain, 0245 [redacted]

40 Yeara Ago - May, June and July, 1954

May - The hulk of an old mine-sweeper had shifted and was obstructing the beach in front of the clubhouse in Heybridge Basin. The Water Bailiff suggested the club ask Maldon District Council to move it - but the Council replied they'd already asked the owner to move it and would, if necessary, try to enforce its removal. Eventually a letter from the Council intimates that a sufficiently high tide to move the hulk would not occur until late August/early September (1954), but the owner had been advised he should remove heavy timbers beforehand so as to make it easier to move the (lightened) hulk when the time came.

In the meantime, the club had also written to Maldon Distruct Council about the use of a nearby earthen wharf. Again, the Council were not able to help directly but were helpful (to a certain extent) by advising that ownership was "....rather vague." The wharf was, in fact, owned by May & Butcher (from whom the club rented its clubhouse) but it seems that (i) the Catchment Board were responsible for the sea wall, (ii) the River Authority were responsible for the foreshore. However, the 'demarcation lines' and appropriate proportions of who was responsible for what was, so it seems '...rather vague'. However, M & B had no objection to the club using the wharf provided they were willing to vacate it if, and when, M & B wanted it for ship-breaking work.

The suggestion was made to hold a rally during July; was this effectively the fore-runner of Regatta ?

Similarly, the circulation of a News Sheet to all members might well be regarded as a somewhat remote precursor of Navigans.

Mike Boreham

Handicap Fleet News - Jackpot and Mona's Cup

Another Sunday of glorious racing. What’s more, we had a half decent turnout of eight boats on the start line. In the second race, Claire Davies managed to rig her Laser and we were nine! Laura and I put in a creditable performance at long last. Home for a barbecue, a bottle of wine, and life seems worth living again. Please keep it up! It was so nice to have enough boats out that everyone was competing with someone.

Welcome back to Howard Yourig in his Fireball. His last year was a sabbatical racing cruisers. He’s got a new crew, through Navigans, Mark Johnson. Good luck to you both. I should also mention Peter Woodhouse, new this year, in his green Laser. He began the season going for my number of capsizes record, but is now staying upright = and looking for race honours. Graham Richmond in his Hornet is losing his crew Sam Ashley with trapeze-knees, but he hopes to get a replacement in quick-sticks. Jack Rusbridge at last had his GP 14 out today, although I hardly recognised it; he’s painted and varnished and it looks a real treat. Mind you only three layers of varnish, whereas Laura’s dad used to do six layers every year with rubbing down between each layer! And Claire rigging a Laser? Yes, she’s now got a Laser Radial and is getting to grips with it. I’m sure she’1l soon be giving us, and particularly Mark Bulkeley with his Radial, a bit of stiff competition.

Oh, I'd quite forgotten why I’m writing this article. Yes, it’s to tell you about some races and why you must sail them. Two races, the Jackpot (Sunday 24 July) = and Mona’s Cup (Sunday 18 September) both go to Maldon and back. Those of you who do not want to sail in circles and triangles, these races are for you. They are also ideal for the slower handicap boats because you arrive at Maldon at high tide and therefore you do not battle against the tide going there or coming back. The tide is unfair toa you in normal Club races, but here it is definitely in your favour. All boats take part in these races and you can still join in the Jackpot even if the helm is not over 40 years of age, although if you aren’t you won’t win the trophy. Basically, these races take you down between the channel markers until you get ta No 10 = buoy that you go around leaving it to starboard and then come back again. Your ‘Sailing Instructions for Club Racing’ details the course, but it makes it look complicated which it is not. Is there a No. 5S buoy? It’s shown opposite No. 6 on the back of the Year Book, but my chart of the river shows this buoy to be Na. 7. By the way, the ever numbers are the red port laterals and, guess what, the odds are the green starboard laterals. Oh, I nearly forgot to mention that the Jackpot is in two legs since we stop for lunch at the Osea SC. This means we arrive like a Normandy landing on their little sandy beach, much to the amazement of the sunbathers, where we pull the boats out of the water. And why is it Mona’s Cup? The Year Book says it is in memory of the landlady of the Jolly Sailor at Heybridge Basin. I think the race once used to goa ta the Jolly Sailor where the competitors stopped for lunch.

One boat that should enter these races is Toby Hampden-Acton’s Drabscombe Dabber. This boat fascinates me. It has, apart from the jib and mainsail, a little sail on a mast (the mizzen?) at the stern of the boat. He told me it had a loose-footed mainsail and I said mine was loose-footed as well. But then he told me it didn’t have a boom, and I thought he was pulling my leg. Apparently, this was common on the old working boats where the mainsail could be dragged over the cargo when they tacked or gybed. One problem, if he races, as the boat hasn’t got a Partsmouth Number! Alas, he intends to sell it; he has problems getting it in and out of the water and doesn’t want to use the winch.

Jackpot and Mona’s Cup, don’t forget!

Don Gill, Handicap Fleet Captain, 0245 [redacted].
