FAST CAT NOTES 9.
Maybe thick fog will be the next variety of weather to be thrown at Piers Race entrants, or possibly
snow... with the ridiculous wind against tide conditions this year’s race brought, many competitors will
be hoping for an improvement next year. However for those that were lucky enough to avoid both gear failure and collisions with either the emerging spits or other boats, the Force 6 easterly with the rapidly ebbing tide led to a challenging race that few will forget quickly. It has been fabled that spinnakers lift
the bows of catamarans... | remain to be convinced.

The fleet of 103 started with the expectation of sailing the full course, but it quickly became apparent that although the conditions were quite sailable for the leaders there might well prove to be problems in ensuring the safety of all competitors. The severe and very short chop making conditions difficult for the mother boats on their stations across the mouth of the Colne conspired with the high number of early casualties to convince our Commodore (whose company on the water was sorely missed this year by the few Dart 18 sailors present) to shorten course at the Bradwell gate. Although the significance of the
various signals to be made by the Race Committee had been very clearly explained at what | thought
was an excellent briefing, it was not until a number of the leading boats had reached the gate that a lemming-like urge to brave the waves and turn back downwind gripped the fleet. Paul (Metcalfe, who,
being not pregnant, had kindly agreed to crew with me) and |, observing with some concern as we
approached the windward mark the extreme spinnaker-induced bend in the mast of one of the leaders,
decided not to fly the kite, a decision which lasted only until we remembered the aforementioned fable...
clearly the spinnaker was going to make the ride home much more relaxing. Perhaps relaxing was not the right word, but it certainly proved to be a memorable experience, although at the time we felt that we had failed to make up the handicap penalty of 2% that our sail plan cost us. Probably our performance was not helped by the need, with our sadly limited sail handling ability developed in many hours of practice, to start the spinnaker-dropping process half a mile before the leeward mark.

Again, in spite of Larry and Charles’s excellent briefing, the leaders showed some hesitation in returning up the course for the signalled second lap, but apart from the minority who, perhaps wisely, decided that one ordeal was sufficient for what might otherwise have been an unremarkably pleasant Sunday, the fleet thrashed its way back up to Bradwell and enjoyed another sleigh-ride to the finish line.

The full results are printed elsewhere within these covers; my congratulations go to all who finished either one or two laps of the course, and my commiserations to those who were unlucky enough to suffer
damage.

My particular interest in the race was the handicap system to be used; for the first time in a significant UK event we used the ’French’ system adopted by the IYRU Multihull Committee, which gives time correction factors based upon measurement of the vessels only, and not upon past performance (unlike
the PY system traditionally used in the UK). To ask which system is ’fairer’ is, | believe, to miss the point.
Different classes will always have sailors with different levels of skill, will perform better in different conditions, and will prefer different courses; it will never be possible, to the precision needed to distinguish the two systems, to measure the accuracy of the performance predictions they offer. However
| believe the IYRU system can dispense with the argument that under the PY system, for example, "the
Prindle handicap is falsely increased by the low standard of its sailors" (palpably true though that may be) and, in addition, can readily allow handicaps to be calculated for a variety of boat configurations, thus allowing the IYRU system to be perceived as fairer and more equitable. Conversely the I[YRU system, like the IOR before it, could lead to designs being evolved to take specific advantage of its peculiarities, leading perhaps to less manageable or less seaworthy catamarans. Also, the Portsmouth Number of a
class can vary from year to year, whilst its |YRU TCF will not; whether this is an advantage or not | am
not sure. Inspection of the results shows what | feel is a healthy mix of classes at the top of the fleet,
although the two Hobie Miracles were convincing in their victory. On balance | feel that the [YRU system
is the way forward, being widely used on the continent, and the majority of those competing this year seemed to welcome its use. Further analysis of the figures must await a later edition of Navigans.

As always at this time, thanks must go to the band of organisers who again managed to make the event
a thoroughly enjoyable, well-run and professional affair. Although | will not attempt to mention them all,
| must especially thank Steve and Debbie Glynn for all that they have contributed over several years of
Piers Races. The race has become a major event in an international calendar - this year 16 competitors
crossed the channel to enter - and the organisation has evolved to match it. As always, the RYA
Seamanship Foundation stands to gain from the event, and through it the Piers Race has become, over the years, the single largest supporter of Sailing for the Disabled. Next year Steve and several others are stepping down from the ECPR committee, and Mike Duckmanton (or Duckman, as he is known to his many television fans) is taking over as chairman; please, if you feel you can offer a little of your time in any part of the race organisation, give Mike or Steve a call.

John Nickalls

Certainly | heard no complaints

How hard to compete?
Some months ago | mused over how strictly we should apply the rules when we are racing, and suggested
that we have to be careful that the competitiveness of our sailing and the extent to which we seek to exploit the rules for tactical advantage, whilst adding a valuable extra dimension to our sailing, should not vary so
much across the fleet as to lead to ill-feeling or even damage. Over the August Bank Holiday weekend |
clearly misjudged the mood of the fleet sailing at the time and | apologise to Brian and Roy for the violent luff |
made when they started to overtake our boat to windward on an offwind leg; although | hailed loudly, the luff
was Clearly felt to be unnecessary (although no contact was made between us). Judging from the comments
made in the bar afterwards, however, perhaps | ought to explain why | did what | did, and why| felt justified.
Rule 39.2 reads "After starting..., a yacht clear ahead or a leeward yacht may luff as she pleases unless the
windward yacht has been mast abeam at any time during the overlap". Rule 35 reads the right of way yacht
shall not alter course... except... when luffing as permitted by rule 39.2.". All text books on the subject cover
this area in some depth, and will show that a leeward yacht may luff as abruptly as the helmsman wishes and
without warning (until the mast abeam position, or an obstruction, is reached); certainly no hail is required. |
am not suggesting that we should go onto the water with the intention of hitting each other, but the point of these rules is to allow the leeward yacht a defence against a boat overtaking to windward and blianketing it; the result is that, to pass successfully and in safety, the overtaking yacht must position itself a considerable distance to windward. To quote Mary Pera, "If W is so rash as to put herself in a position where L can hit her, she has only herself to blame." In previous races at the Club, applying these rules (without hailing in some cases) has been accepted without comment (and I'm sure many have heard me assault them with a cry of
mast abeam as| try desperately to overtake). | know there are others who will use these rules; | suggest that
the only safe way to overtake to windward (certainly if one leaves the sheltered confines of club racing) is to keep a safe distance away and a good lookout under the sail, hailing mast abeam when the leeward yacht's mast is abeam the helmsman in his normal position (but see Rule 39, and others, as well as the definition of mast abeam for details), at which point the overtaken yacht must bear off to a proper course.
It is worth noting that luffing applies also on windward legs; if on a light wind day you are drifting close-hauled and some fiend catches a puff and starts to overhaul you close to windward you may luff and touch him. If you succeed, he faces a 360° penalty (although you may only luff as far as close-hauled, that being your proper course, unless you have remained ahead of mast abeam). Again, the moral is keep your distance when overtaking to windward. There are plenty of people competing both within and outside the Club who will use the freedom the rules very deliberately and specifically give.

7MORNING FLIGHT’ —- 1994 CRUISE

Hi Everyore. We are just about to set sail for Spain so it seems a good time to let you know how we are getting on so far. We left Suffolk Yacht Harbour on the 7th June for what should have been a gentle shakedown cruise across the Thames Estuary, but turned into something more challenging. We hastily put in a reef, dug cut the seasick pills ard got into a more seamanlike mode! We called in at Ramsgate for a well-earned rest and then went on to Brighton pausing only ta wait for the tide in Dover. The Weather was really grotty, cold, wet and grey. Sarah’s dad came down tea Brighton for a couple of days for a final briefing (and to bring further essential Supplies, namely, 48 bags of crisps for Dave and 1550 teabags for Sarah!)

We left Brighton with the wind abaft the beam for the first time all trip, and headed to Dartmouth. All was going beautifully until we switched the engine on to motor into the river and our brand new engine disappeared in clouds of smoke and steam!! It would have helped if the engine-overheating light had worked. We got towed into Dartmouth by a Hurley 22, anchored up the river and set about fixing it. We were anchored up the river above Dartmouth, it was brilliantly hot, quiet (except when the tripper boats went by giving an amplified commentary) and very pretty. Unfortunately we then discovered that the engine problem was recurring and the boatman kindly put us in touch with a local marine engineer. Even more unfortunately he needed the beat out of the water to work on it, and the yard where he was based was owned by the dreaded MDL. Before we had time to take out a second mortgage, however, we
discovered that they had a special offer on - lift out, up to 2 weeks on the hard and
lift in for £60 all-in - so it ended up cheaper than if we had stayed anchored in the
Dart. Although it was a bit frustrating, particularly being out of the water, the weather continued ta be glorious and we took the chance to get a lot of jobs done as well as cycling and walking and going to the pub to commiserate with other people who were Similarly stuck in the boatyard.

It 1S Surprising how long it takes to do the simplest jobs when it’s hat, the telephones aren’t ringing, and you have as much time as you want. I found it could take me all morning just to cycle up to the village shop for fresh milk ard bread! Dave managed ta fix the heads (which had not been working since we set off), installed a refrigeration unit in the cold box and a fan. I made the canvas cover for our bimini tap (a sort of fixed umbrella which covers the cockpit area at head height for keeping the worst of the sun off us when we get to tropical climes) and various other sewing jobs. We also made shelves and more storage for the forecabin, and I sorted out all the stores, made copicus lists, and goat the forecabin into a reasonably habitable condition.

Those of you who came to Suffolk Yacht Harbour to see us off will remember that we had to keep the door toa the forecabin firmly shut to prevent all the stuff piled up in there escaping, but now there’s room for Derek to get in his bunk when he = arrives to sail with us across the Atlantic! We also spent a lot of time fixing the various small but irritating deck leaks we have. Not entirely successful and I suppose that eventually we shall have toa take off the toerail and reseal it, but we are trying to put off the evil day, as it’s rather a big job on our boat.

The last evening we were in the Dart we came across Brian and Jacky on Natasha IV from MSC. Small world!! They have retired too and are spending the summer cruising the West Coast. We were sorry to leave Devon because we liked the places and also the people who seemed very friendly and helpful but decided we must press on and spent the next week or so cruising the Cornish rivers. We found Salcombe somewhat yuppified but loved the Yealm River and also enjoyed Foawey ard the Helford River. Both banks of the Yealm are forested and owned by the Woodland and National Trusts so that you can walk in them. We have found that a lot of the coastline and river banks are privately owned, which makes it jolly difficult ta get ashore legally sometimes (though Dave doesn’t worry unduly about that!) let alone walk.

We bought a brand new outboard in Fowey, Dave having only just been restrained from chucking our old one into the sea when, as well as either not starting or stopping
for no apparent reason, it started giving him electrical shocks. I was safe - it
wouldn’t do anything for me at all. Our new one is a Mercury 2.5 and I have no trouble starting it and it runs fine. No doubt it won’t last but it’s pretty
luxurious at the moment - I haven’t had ta row anywhere for days.

Contd. ....

14.

We spent a couple of days in Falmouth getting some last-minute chandler y, restocking food and booze and doing the laundry. That all becomes quite a chore when you have to lug everything ashore, onto bicycles , uphill ta the laundere tte and back. — The weight, particul arly of the booze, 1s enough to make you teetotal !! We fourd the chores day far more exhausting than sailing in our current rather laid-bad k style.

We then sailed on to the Scillies, highly recommended to us and living up to tide it. The
islands are a series of jagged rocks - some inhabited and some not. As the goes
out the landscape changes dramatica lly as more sharptoot had rocks appear, giving an
almost lunar appearance - I could sit and watch for hours! The islands have a lot of
visitors but have managed ta avoid becoming touristy mainly because the attractions are the scenery, flowers, birds, and fishing. Surprisingly most of the yachts here are French, and their anchoring techniques have led to a slight cooling ain the "“entente cordiale", Dave having started off by calling me intolerant and ended up swearing (under his breath of course, preserving his stiff upper lip) as we re- anchored yet again. We met up with an old colleague of his, Gordon Bilsborough from Nimrod days, who is now assistant harbour master in St Mary’s here. Not only that, but it turned out that he and Jane used to live in St Albans and their solicitors were --- Woolley and Western!!

Dave has row got his SSB rig set up after a few experiments with different aerial arrangements and is chatting away happily to the world (mostly Europe, although contact with the UK is patchy. We usually catch the Maritime Mobile net either ir the morning or evening and have joined it. Our callsign is GOTAG if anyone wants to call us. We have listened out for Stan in the Med on Tuesday mornings but haven't
yet heard him - we shall keep trying. Sarah’s dad has been provided with a receiver
sco he should be able to hear us transmitting sometimes. We won't really start transmitting much until we get down to Spain. It’s certainly a way of making friends. Last night we were sitting in the main cabin when there was a knocking on the hull and a couple from the next boat appeared. It transpired that they were keen radio hams, had heard us transmitting from the Scillies and had been keeping a bit of a lookout for us. They have certainly taken to the cruising life. They first went to the Med in a 31 ft boat with their 3 small girls and stayed for 9 months. wher:
the money ran cut they came back, saved, bought a bigger boat and set off again - for
three and a half years before having to return. Later they managed another couple of years and have been in the UK for the last 3 years getting ready to go again! They
always took the girls and taught themselves using correspondence classes - one of the
girls took her O Levels in the British Embassy in Turkey! Just shows what carn be
dore if you set your mind to it - also shows how you can be bitten by this way of
life! Their current boat is called "Dreamer".

Sc far most of the yachties we have met have been on holiday, but at Falmouth we found a truly international meeting of boats, many of whom seemed to be long- distance. Ir, particular we met a very pleasant Dutch couple who are setting cut to cruise Spain, and then South America. The bloke spent 2 years sailing 20,000 miles in the West Indies a couple of years ago, so he was very interesting and gave us some
new ideas - particularly as he felt Venezuela knocked spots off anywhere in West
Indies - but currently we still plan to sail north from St Lucia via various WI
islands to the USA.

Dave and I are both fine - not arguing more than usual, and in fact pretty relaxed.
It’s a healthy sort of life, although you do get aches and pains in the most peculiar places and both of us had quite a lot of backache while our bodies adjusted toa sleeping on 1" thick mattresses. I am also covered with bruises, but that’s nothing unusual ! Both of us have nice brown arms, legs and faces, but the prevailing cool
breeze means we are usually wearing shirts and shorts - we have had less baking hot
weather than those of you in the South and East and the last two weeks have been very overcast and quite chilly. BETTY BEAVINS

Betty Beavins passed away peacefully in Monday 24th October 1994 after a short illness. the Marconi Sailing Club was her second home and after sailing a Blandford twelve-footer with my father at Heybridge we as a family followed the Club to Stansgate. Dinghy racing became local cruising for Mum and Dad in their Pandora. When Dad passed away 16 years ago, Mum continued to come to the Club and seemed a permanent presence at the top of the Hard, sitting with her sister Connie and their friends, and ever ready to chat to anyone and everyone.

Everytime we returned to my mooring, Jan and | would look for Mum. She always watched us come and go,
and if we got any manoeuvresa little wrong, we would discuss the reasons later! She was always interested in everything and everyone.

| will always look for her when | return to the Club with warm memories of a wan person and remember her
wonderful understanding of life's patterns and how, when the shock and grief is past, she would want all of us to celebrate the quality of her life.

Thank you all for your expressions of sympathy. Nik, Clare and Sarah Beavins.

Batty Beavins - ...... The Funeral Service, which took place on 1st November was a celebration of her lively
and cheerful approach fo life. She was involved in many charitable and supportive activities, as well as being a longtime member of the Marconi Sailing Club. Some of our older members will remember her husband, Ken, who died in February 1979. He was a keen GP14 sailor, and Committee Member, and wrote the ‘Observer’ column in Navigans. Together they did much to create the family atmosphere of the Club as we know it today. A measure of the regard with which they were held was the presence at the Service of some of our longest serving and past members, including Stan Allerton, David Polley and Fred Partlett together with
their wives; Elsie and Leonie; and other members of more recent times. Mary and | will remember her most
for her indomitable spirit and her infectious laugh as she took her weekly swim from the Hard.

The Club has made a donation on behalf of the general membership, but if inidviduals would like to make a personal contribution, the family request was that any donations could be made to the "Macmillan Nurses Fund" and sent c/o the Co-Operative Funeral Service, 13-15 Market Hill, Maldon.

Ron Greygoose

COMMODORE'S REPORT

Last year | commented on the fact that there appeared to have been no major material enhancements to our
facility. | think that you will all agree with me that this year, the comment is totally the opposite. We can all
see the benefit that the laying of the tracks around the site will give us through the year, with the lack of churning up of grass. Obviously we had a “one off" chance to carry out this work when the NRA finally completed their activities, and some forthright negotiations took place with the MASC in order to expedite
almost £20,000 of unplanned capital expenditure. | am indebted to the contribution made in this respect by
Pat Black and Neil Pembleton. The whole project was managed by Pat, and from an idea at a Committee Meeting in early September to project completion in mid October, is an excellent achievement. Unfortunately this may well impinge upon our capital expenditure for the rest of this financial year (ending March 1995) but
| am sure that you will agree that the results are worth it. In addition this year has seen the replacement of
the downstairs windows with uPVC units and the further refurbishment of the downstairs bar (at no cost to the Club). Thanks are due to Steve Glynn and Mike Smith respectively.

Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This took a significant turn for the better when Peter Woodhouse
replaced Norman Cox as Chairman. | was suddenly able to talk on a more business-like basis and to get my
voice heard in a different way. We have just concluded an honest and open agreement with MASC that covers our contribution until 1999.

My other colleagues will comment on the events of the year, but | feel that there are two areas on which |
must comment specifically. Firstly the Laying Up Supper. In 1992 this was an event that was dying, but die to the efforts of Steve and Debbie Glynn in 1993 the event has become once again a "proper Club occasion. This year as well looks like being another enormous success. If we only get together socially as a Club on one occasion per year, then this has to be the occasion. The mix of attendees from the various fleets is excellent and shows that our true strength as a Club lies in our "diversity with a common purpose”. Secondly,
| should like to comment on the ECPR. This event is the major flag-waving event for the Club, and has made
us the largest continuing contributor to the Seamanship Foundation. It is now an international event, and has
placed us in the forefront of small multihull Clubs. | am not taking for granted the huge amount of support
and effort given by everyone to the ECPR committee, and would like to publicly thank every member of the Club for the support that they give.

Having undertaken this position for two years, | am about to enter my final year as Commodore. My personal
mission is to continue to make life easier for all the volunteers who contribute to the Club by their efforts. In this respect we already see the installation of a powered winch on the Mooring Barge, and a new Membership
PC (with hopefully a new system soon to follow). | promised last year that the investment in continuing to
ease the load of individuals would continue, and within the constraints of the issues of capital, this will remain. However, no matter how much kit we buy, the jobs are ultimately done by people. At the moment the difficulty comes in planning possible successors for particular positions. Next year we will be faced by the end of Colin Kidner's term of office as well as my own. To ensure true continuity it is vital that possible successors are identified early in order to immerse them to some extent in the activities of the Committee. This is not a "Committee stitch-up" but a genuine desire on the part of every one of us to see the Club Management having some form of stability. Projects and policy take time to develop, and a Parliamentary
swing from right to left and back every few years is a waste of resources. | am very happy to talk to anyone
on a strictly confidential basis about any ambitions they may have in this respect.

There is one particular subject that | have left until the end, and that is my personal thanks to all my
colleagues on the Executive and Main Committees. Each one of them has contributed in a positive and thoughtful way to debate throughout the past year. Some of them have carried out an enormous amount of
work on our behalf, and | have no hesitation here in singling out Frank Bennett. It is the end of one era,
though, with Steve Glynn coming to the end of his term of office. During the three years of his tenure, the practical advances within his portfolio are legion. Not only has he carried out many of the activities himself,
but his pragmatic input at the planning stages has been invaluable. | place on record my gratitude for his
efforts. Obviously | have singled out a couple of colleagues for special thanks, but it would be iniquitous were
| not to thank them all for their continuing support and efforts over the year. Thank You.

Larry Botheras

This chapter of Navigans Past is dedicated to the memory of Betty Beavins whose recent death leaves not only
many sad friends and relations, but also severs yet another link with what many might regard as the heyday of the
‘old-style’ Marconi Sailing Club.
Maggie and I cannot claim to have known Betty for many years. Indeed, we have only really got to know Betty
and her sister, Connie Bigden, since the publication of Navigans Past and then only in the sense that we always
took pleasure in passing a few minutes chatting with Betty and Connie on most Sundays at the club during the
season.

Betty always seemed to be full of fun and the enjoyment of life; she was always a joy to talk to and pass the time
of day. Such was her sense of fun and humour that I am sure she would have been delighted, and in agreement
with, the mis-typing in the October Navigans which described her as 'Batty' Beavins; Betty would have liked
that.
Betty will be missed. Maggie and I will always think of the area on the hard by the winch box-covers as ‘Betty's
place’ and remember her with great pleasure.

1976 (July - December) - Marconi's Mirrormen made their presence felt in more ways than 'won'.

- In the meantime, we think it was Eileen who again exposes the

July - a rather thin Navigans issue with not much exciting content to comment upon some 18 years later. Rick
Anstey (Cadet Captain) reveals that the Cadet Series is ‘wide open' with 3 different winners in the 3 races held so
far.

August - no Navigans due to the holiday period.

September - Brenda Tate records the entry of two new members to the club, quite literally ‘just born to it'; they
are Colin Cherry (introduced by Wendy and Tony Cherry) and Nicholas David Turner (nominated by Rosemary
and Mike Turner).

Marconi Cadet Member, Malcolm Hutchins, won the Sea Cadet Mirror Sailing Trophy for his Division and then
went on to win the Sea Cadet Midland District Trophy.

Mersea Week saw much success for other Marconi Mirror sailors. Marconi's Mirrors were not only Ist, 2nd and
3rd in the Dabchicks Points Series but also in the Round Mersea Race (Mirror Fleet), Dabchicks Regatta, Mersea
Town Regatta and the West Mersea Regatta in which Frank Savill also took Ist in the Solo class and John
Weedon (presumably in the 420) came Ist in the Handicap Fleet.

Still with the active Mirrormen, Marconi held a Mirror Open in September which attracted 27 entries and in
which Ray Hampson took 3rd overall.

Outside the sailing activity, a more somber view of the club is revealed as John Weedon (Commodore)warns of
the cost of repairs to the road and other expenses about to be encountered:-

Road Repairs £ 250
Hard Repairs £ 400
Workboat Engine (replacement) £ 450
Current engine repairs £ 100

This is to be Editor Brenda Tate's last Navigans issue and we can still say "Well done and thanks, Brenda" to a
member of a ‘club sailing family’ who were always at the centre of sailing and social activity during their time
with the club. The new Editor is to be Shirley Wood.

October - Shirley admits to not being a very active member to date and thus she seems to have ‘jumped in with
both feet and into the deep end’ all at the same time.

Again, Marconi's Mirrors feature in the sailing results. In the club's Mona's Cup race to Heybridge and back,
the first 3 places were filled by Mirrors with Ray and Katie Hampson (1st), Roy and Richard Battye (2nd) and

price will rise or the club will have to absorb the deficit (all sounds familiar, doesn't it; ‘problems’ are obviously
cyclic in nature). The venue had, in recent times, been the MASC in order to accommodate the numbers, but a
smaller venue might have to be considered in the future.

If I remember correctly, Maggie and I went to this Laying Up Supper with Mike and Jennie Hart. As I also
remember it, the 'Mirror Crowd’ were (shall we say) rather noisy and perhaps a little (or a lot) ‘into their cups’.
This ‘noisy lot’ (plus dissatisfaction with 'the Group’ hired to provide the music) gave rise to a letter of complaint
to Navigans. I must admit that, although we were ‘Mirror people’, we were rather glad we were on the opposite
side of the room to both the Group (Mirror) and the Group (Music) for, despite their 'best' endeavours, neither
Group were too melodious with their rendering, although both were full of enthusiasm for their performances.

themselves, for several of their number went on to become Flag Officers, including two Commodores at least.

in a borrowed boat called "Ace of Diamonds".

(or I missed it out when photocopying Maureen's archive set; perhaps our Editor could tell me ?).

A letter from the Local Valuation/Rating Office states that the Yacht Store & Workshop (ie. the MSC clubhouse)
had a gross value of £ 20 and ratable value of £ 12.

The club had obviously written to the Maldon Borough Council with regard to the possibility of a permanent
mooring for a barge. In reply, the Council invited an application but warn that permission would probably be
refused in the vicinity of the present clubhouse at Heybridge, but might be agreed for a mooring opposite on
Northey Island. On the strength of this, the idea of a barge HQ was abandoned and a sub-committee formed to
(a) review the potential of the current clubhouse and (b) seek possible premises/sites for a clubhouse between

Heybridge and the Blackwater Sailing Club. Presumably, as part of this task, a letter reveals that the owners of
the present clubhouse were not willing to sell clubhouse and adjoining cottage at this time.

Alas, the owner of the minesweeper hulk failed to float it in August and is being pressed by the Council to lighten
it even more so as to float it off in September. It was, indeed, finally removed from the foreshore in September.
In addition, rumours suggest the Essex River Board plan to heighten the sea wall at the clubhouse and this
obviously causes some concern to the club.

It was decided that the President's Cup would be contested by a series of races on 16/17 October, 1954.

A Newsletter (26 October) reveals the Laying Up Supper planned for 19 November at the MASC. Unfortunately,
the Maldon Little Ship Club had to decline an invitation to send two representatives to the Supper since they were
holding their Annual Ball on the same night.

The AGM in November saw Geoff Wardell elected Commodore and Eric Cottam as Vice Commodore/Sailing
Sec. A proposal to add the post of Rear Commodore was passed on the basis that since Commodore and Vice
Commodore planned to race their Fleetwind dinghies most weekends, 'someone’ had to stay ashore to 'mind the
shop’. It was thought a non-Fleetwind (therefore presumably non-racing) member serving as Rear Commodore
would fill this need. Thus it was that Maurice Greatrex was elected Rear Commodore.

The planned purchase of a 'club flattie/dinghy' for use as a tender to the club boat Avril was also ear-marked as a
possible rescue boat if provided with outboard motor !

The Heybridge Basin Yacht Stores offered to pay the costs of material to renovate the slipway if the MSC
provided the labour free-of-charge.

It was decided that the new committee would meet on the Ist Tuesday of each month in the MASC TV Room.
Presumably it was 'tough' for any MASC member who happened to want to watch TV that night !

One over the Eight is Intoxication
but Three under the Eight is Confusion

The recent death of Mona Clark marks yet another link with the club's origins which has slipped quietly away.
Mona was landlord of The Jolly Sailor at Heybridge and no doubt enjoyed a good relationship with the MSC
crowd for she donated the Mona's Cup for what was then a long distance down-river race, and is now one of our
two up-river long distances races. No doubt some of our predecessors in the MSC managed to achieve ‘one over
the eight’ whilst cementing our good relations with the locals at The Jolly Sailor. 1 had hoped to quote some of
the ‘write up’ about Mona from the local Maldon paper but unfortunately I cannot lay my hands on it - and
Maureen's deadline is today !

I would imagine the original concept of the down-river race was that it would be open to dinghies and cruisers.
Thus, not only would it have been more convenient to specify that all channel markers should be observed, but
also a ‘fairer playing field’ (if that's the right expression in this case) in that dinghies couldn't take a short-cut
across the shallow parts whilst cruisers had to stay in the middle. Like other of our long distance races, the
Mona's Cup now seems to be a ‘dinghy only’ race along with the Jackpot.

It is still customary to specify “all channel markers to be observed" to this day. Unfortunately, one of the
starboard (ie. green) markers is missing and has been for many years; do you know which one? _In addition, it
is not uncommon for some of the competitors to accidentally miss out marks. This is not surprising for few of us
sail regularly to Heybridge and the dinghies do not need to develop the habit of observing the marks as would the
cruiser sailors. When I looked after the Sailing Results it was not uncommon for someone to phone me during
the week after to complain that such-and-such persons did not sail the course because they missed out a mark
(usually Number 7 or Number 8) and what was I going to do about it. "Note lot”, I'd say, "you should have
protested.”

8.

So what's this about "Three under the Eight" ? Well, in all good faith and working on the best advice and information available to him, our 1994 race officer specified Number 5 (starboard up and Port down).
Unfortunately, Number 5 hasn't been in place for years and years (I think) and he should have specified No.7. |
cannot say I was particularly aware No.5 wasn't there; nor, presumably, did anyone else. Thus, not only did some boats sail ‘inside’ No.7 (not a mark on the course) but nobody could possibly have passed No.5 correctly - it didn't exist but no-one seemed to notice! I guess that, like myself, most competitors "observed all channel
markers".

I wonder if it would be fairer to merely specify channel markers Nos. 3, 8 and 10 for the up-river (and back) races? I'm sure we don't want to see Mona's Cup and Jackpot reduced to protests over alleged course violations; at the same time we all want to compete on a metaphorically level playing field whilst sailing through rather more real stormy waters to Heybridge and back. So where does this leave me’? Technically speaking, I
suppose the 1994 Jackpot could be deemed ‘null and void' and I didn't win the 1994 Jackpot after all - shame
really.

Mike Boreham

To All Marine Watches: At the end of the season, just a reminder for you to remove as much property from your boats as you can. Marine crime is still commonplace (as many of you know) and it is up to all of us to do our bit to combat the criminals that prey upon us.

Property marking kits are in circulation at many clubs....if you haven't seen them, ask. If your club hasn't
seen a kit yet please contact us and ask to loan one. We will put you on the list and get it to you as soon as one is free.

Please take a look at the attached stolen property list. Unfortunately it contains only a fraction of the property stolen in Essex this year and is only a drop in the ocean of crime that has occurred throughout the country as a whole.

If you recognise any of the items mentioned, and know were they currently can be found, please tell us and w will do our best to get it to its rightful owner.

We would like to remind all of those with dinghies that these need to be clearly and permanently marked. So many of them look alike that it is almost impossible for anyone other than the owners themselves to identify them. Paint names can be washed off. Screwed on plates can be unscrewed. Details need to be literally carved into a fixed feature if we stand any hope of getting them returned if lost or stolen.

If you are doubtful about any purchase you are about to make we will be only too happy to check it against the stolen lists for you. It could help us in cutting down on crime and satisfy you that the sale is genuine.

We at the Marine Police would like to take this opportunity to wish you all a happy and crime-free 1995.

TOM ASHLEY

It is with the deepest regret that we report the tragic death in road accident of Tom Ashley on 13th January.

During his earlier years as a Cadet at MSC Tom sailed a Mirror Dinghy, from which he progressed to being a keen member of the Cat Fleet.

Tom was a very popular member of a close-knit group of MSC Cadets who have grown up together at the Club. Despite outgrowing Cadet status, and scattering to various jobs, colleges and universities, this group has stayed together both on the water and socially. Tom will be sadly missed.

Our sympathies go to Hilary, to Tom’s brothers Sam, Ben and Joe, and to Mike and all the family at this time.

Some highlights from the solo boat in this years Southampton based cruiser weekend.

The general plan was to meet at Shamrock Quay on the River Itchen near Southampton at 18.00hrs on Friday evening. After a night on board the Sigma 38 cruiser we would sail around the Isle of Wight clockwise reaching Yarmouth late on Saturday evening. Sunday would be the final leg with racing along the Solent and Southampton water reaching home base at 16.00hrs on Sunday.
The Friday night on board gave us a chance to meet our skipper Andy and generally get used to the conditions etc on board. Bunks [berths?] were selected and alarm clocks set for 06.00hrs for a 07.30 departure [groan] was required by the plan. After a good meal and a few drinks at the local it was lights out for the magnificent seven. Bunks were interesting, I "had" to tread on Malcolm Stuart's head to get out of mine.
Saturday was a 2-3W with drizzle but we were the first of the three Marconi cruisers out into
the river Itchen. The tide tables dictated our future for if we did not make Bembridge Ledge [Eastern up of How to you] by 11.30hrs we would miss the tides and possibly fail. Motoring along we soon discovered the engine gave only 1/2 max speed, the three Ford engine experts [?] were sent below and after much discussion/adjusuments our speed was further reduced. The other two boats were way in front by now.
A near dead run down Spithead allowed the foredeck crew a good lesson in spinnaker drill as we passed huge Napolionic forts and the impressive IloW cliffs. The lead boat was a hazy image in the
distance.
Bembridge Ledge passed before schedule, we had a chance of getting around! Past Sandown, Shanklin and Venmor now on a reach we seemed to make good time. The power and complexity of the tide was evidenced by many dramatic changes in sea state, from calm water into very turbulent water all within a few feet!
Passing St Catherine's Head the southern most tip of the loW at about 14.00hrs we began to beat down towards the Needles. The cooker only worked on one ring and the "Yarmouth arrival time "
sweep [£1.00 a go] we ran had times ranging from 19.30 to 22.30hrs. Our dinner this day was hot
coffee, sandwiches made by me [tuna + mayonnaise or tinned ham inc. the wobbly jelly bits] and nice bright sunshine.
By Compton Bay we had caught and passed the second boat and although viewed at a distance we were sure of being level with the first. The Needles were a hazy vision about two miles away when darkness fell, the lighthouse now guiding our course. Night sailing must be tried, a constant watch was kept on the lights of the other two boats as well as the gigantic Stena Sealink ferry that passed us. As we rounded the Needles they were silhouetted by the beam from the lighthouse - quite spectacular. During this period skipper was quite active, looking at the pretty variety of red and green lights that marked our intended course through the narrow gap twixt loW and Hurst Castle. Another 30 minutes and our wheezy engine took us into Yarmouth harbour at 19.45. To mark our arrival the locals had light a huge bonfire and were giving a firework display, only later did others discover how exceptionally friendly the IoW'ers were. Skipper expressed slight concern as we watched the pretues and ignored the bits of string and other tubs. After a detailed review of all parking slots we moored about 20 boats out from the harbour wall.
Great place Yarmouth, good food and beer, nice atmosphere.
Sunday departure was scheduled for 09.00hrs which allowed an easy breakfast/start. Sunday
was an odd sort of day, the weather was great, force 3-4SW and bright sunshine. However the skipper surfaced in a rather competitive mood and on this boat were six helms plus him, not quite in the mould of an experienced cruiser racing team. I picked an easy job, the mainsheet, this allowed me to hear skipper's detailed and continuous opinion of us, especially the foredeck crew! After a few doubtful spinny hoists + a tulip it was alleged that skipper had a discussion about motivation with John S!
Race one was between channel mark, Yarmouth to the mouth of the Hamble. Lunch was great: a pub, a chance to read news in the Sunday rags + a pint. Skipper seemed relaxed but that compettive spirit came up in him again for race two and the foredeck crew were once again getting it a bit wrong. Geoff J and I on helm and mainsheet proved to be the best team. Once under the Itchen toll bridge [aim for the middle!! he kept saying, we thought there was plenty of room] the faithless motor coughed into action and our tremendous circumnavigation of the loW was complete.
It was a great weekend, good sailing, good company and our target achieved.

Tim Sweet

PS. As I write this, I have just been given a possible explanation of why 'No.5' channel marker doesn't appear on the charts or, indeed, physically in the river. The explanation is as follows:-

If it is true that channel markers traditionally are numbered going up-river with odd numbers (green) on the starboard-hand and even numbers (red) on the port-hand, then the natural progression of 1(st.), 2 (pt), 3 (st) and 4 (pt) follows quite logically. There appears to be a need for two port channel markers (Nos. 4 & 6) to be quite close together but no need for a starboard marker ‘between’ them; _ this starboard marker would have been No.5 if it had been needed. However, there is a need for a starboard marker up-river of No.6 and this, logically would be No.7 (green) since it is up-river of No.6. Thus No.5 has probably never existed because it was not needed up-river of No.4 or down-river of No.6.

Follow it so far ? It's all quite simple really.

Ah! Well! It all sounds very convincing but why didn't I think of that ?

Does anyone out there have another explanation ?

Eric Payne writes an article about Mona's Cup which is worth repeating here:-

"I wonder how many of our present members know the origin of Mona's Cup ? In the early fifties, when our headquarters were situated at Heybridge Basin, we made frequent visits to the Jolly Sailor whose proprietress was Miss Mona Clarke, who inherited it from her parents.

As she was a very friendly soul, and took a special interest in our sailing activities, she kindly presented us with a fine challenge cup to be awarded to the winner of an annual all-in race, and this is still included in Our programme.

On one occasion, Mona actually came aboard Mamgu and fired the gun starting this race. In later years, this has tended to be supported by dinghies from our present premises at Stansgate but in future, more cruisers should be encouraged to participate and it is suggested that Mona should be invited to be present for the occasion.

On one occasion when this race was sailed from Stansgate the first mark of the course was up river, and the Southey Spit Buoy had to be rounded but as the tide was falling some cruisers found there was insufficient water to make it.

Mona now has retired but still lives at Heybridge and The Jolly Sailor is now run by Eric Priestley, incidentally an ex-Marconi man.

Incidentally, our first Laying Up Supper was held at The Jolly Sailor in October, 1957; we hired the large inner room and ate our sausages and mince pies standing up, and went through to the bar for our drinks; there was no music to drown our exchanges of events during the past sailing season, and it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening.

Amongst our guests was Douglas Thompson, Commodore of the Blackwater Sailing Club and Sam Poulton from The Maldon Little Ship Club. The price of the tickets was 4/- (20p in 1994), or 6/6 (32.5p) including the price of the coach which brought us.

Our first formal Laying Up Supper was held at the New Street canteen, which we were pleased to call The Palm Court, on Friday, November 1, 1958; most of the Commodores of the clubs on the Blackwater were present as was Bill Hillman, Commodore of the B.B.C. Ariel Club, whose premises are on the Thames at Teddington. The price of the tickets was 9/- (45p in 1994-money) including the band, but not the drinks.

We used to race against the Ariel Club at Teddington and, in return, they came to Heybridge the following year, but eventually it was dropped largely because of the distance and absence of boats available. However, a trophy consisting of our respective burgees mounted on a plinth still exists, but as the Ariel S.C. were the last to win it, they are retaining it."

Alas, Eric Payne is no longer with us. I met him a few times in the early '80s when I first joined the Main Committee for a year or two and exchanged pleasantries with him. In retrospect, I would very much liked to have got him to talk about the early years of the club, in particular the days of the 'Hut on the Wall' and Mamgu years at Heybridge; at that time, of course, I had little or no idea of the history of the club. 1 am sure there can be few who had such an intimate knowledge of the club of those days and, like most organisations, it is the bits that were not recorded in the Minutes, etc. that are the most interesting or revealing. I am sure Eric would have been able to shake some dust off some ‘old bones’.

Mike Boreham

1995 MSC PAINT ORDER

In these times of ever increasing accountability even the humble club paint order is no longer immune. To comply with regulations laid down and prescribed by the Office for Club Reallocation of Antifouling and Paint (OFFCRAP), I am obliged to publish a report on the quality of this year’s orders. Fortunately this year a general appraisal will suffice, but I am reliably informed that next year League tables will be mandatory, so be warned, next year you could find yourself under the table. As far as this year’s orders are concerned this was the situation:-

General Presentation was of a very mixed standard. There were several examples of clearly presented orders whilst some members had clearly given little if any thought to layout. items appearing more than once on the same order and other items being squeezed in with seemingly gay abandon. There are still members who seem to expect me to know without being told, the colour Antifouling they intend putting on their boats. My propensity for burrowing round the undersides of boats might lead some members to assume that I can be expected to remember the colour they used last season, but surely does not imply an ability to anticipate their future intentions.

Spelling continues to be a problem. Danboline causes much confusion, both to you and us. We were prepared to accept Danbolin and even Danblin. Polwax also appeared as polywax which conjures up images of some kind of beauty treatment for parrots or even worse some concoction made from parrots. We will be keeping a careful watch on the behaviour of one particular member during the coming season to see whether the two and a half litres of Antifooling that he ordered has the desired
effect.

Arithmetic. There was a much appreciated iraprovement in overall standards attained in this department. It was however distressing to see the same silly mistakes dropping up as they have done
year after year. | would remind certain members that 33% is not a third ! I would point out that Size
and Quantity are two entirely different concepts. There is perhaps some justification for putting 750ml under quantity instead of size, but little I would have thought for putting 2 (as in two cans of Antifouling) under size. On a positive note, all cheques were correctly completed, and in all cases matched the amount listed on the order. This in itself was a great improvement on previous years. Having said that, not all the totals on the order forms were correct, some members attempting to procure additional discounts and one or two generously donating what I can only assume to be gratuities or even bribes to the examiners.

User Friendly Rating. Many members scored well in this department, and endeared themselves to the examiners by concentrating on larger simpler items that are the easiest to transfer to the Master Order. I don’t like singling out particular individuals for criticism, but one member scored particularily badly in this department by putting in no less than three separate orders and another who had already scored badly in many of the above areas, compounded everything as far as the examiners were concerned by ordering two dust wipes. Once again I have cause to be concerned about what can only be seen as one member’s unhealthily obsessive desire for three tins of Swedish Wood Oil.

There was I’m pleased to report an overall improvement as far as the concept of time is concerned.. The majority of members had their orders in before the closing date in spite of the deliberately misleading ploy on the part of the examiners to print the closing date on the order form as !£th
January 1995. Extra points were awarded to those members who spotted this. There were of course
the inevitable latecomers, and if the experience of previous years is anything to go by, I will be approached at least once in late February to be asked if I am doing the paint again this year. Anyway now we've just got the annual process to go through of uniting member’s with their paint orders, but that’s another story. Thanks for your co-operation and please excuse my self indulgence!

Malcoln Shaft

NAVIGANS PAST

A tribute to Tom Ashley, aged 20 years, who tragically died in a car accident, 13 January, 1995.

The gathering together of so many of his family, relatives and friends for a celebration of his life was a fine tribute to Tom Ashley. The time for mourning came when we first heard the news and in the days after when we reflected, in isolation, upon the event. When she heard of what had happened, Maggie
wept; when I telephoned my daughter and son to tell them what had befallen their friend, | wept; as
they heard the news, many others must also have wept. However, when we gathered together on 24 January to take our farewell of Tom, it was an event specifically to remember and savour the good times
of his life - but it was hard not to weep, and many did so.

Tom was one of the group of youngsters who have come to their maturity at the sailing club over the last few years, enjoying their life and each others company as they pursued their sport in keen competition but always in friendly rivalry. As each started to go their separate ways, either to a job or to higher education, they nevertheless ‘kept in touch' and came together during the holiday periods, sharing their companionship and experiences and always maintaining their friendship. Sometimes ‘the group’ would spend the evening at our house, staying overnight with boots and bodies seemingly everywhere, but always well behaved and always welcome. In this way we have formed an attachment to these friends of our own offspring. Alongside this has developed our own interest in their personal hopes, plans and achievements. Sometimes we have been allowed to hear the tales of some, but I'm sure not all, of the things they'd been up to in the recent past.

Thus it was that we came to know little of Tom and came to like him a lot for his sense of humour, his pleasant disposition, his 'laid-back' manner. At the same time, we knew he had a serious side to him and that he had plans and a determination to fulfil them. He had many qualities which were both admirable and likeable and which were, I am sure, clearly recognised and appreciated by those who knew and loved him. _His talent for sailing was apparent to all and he easily deserves to be ranked amongst the very best of the sailors at the MSC within recent years.

Tom was a fine young man. It was because we knew him to be a fine young man that we all felt such a personal anguish at his death. Not only do we extend our sympathy to Hilary, Sam, Ben and Joe, but also our love and support for a family who are very much part of the MSC way of life.

"...slower classes are at a disadvantage when there is a large proportion of beating against the tide,
particularly in light winds, but when the beat is with the tide they have the advantage. Things are further complicated when large mixed fleets are racing together causing disturbed air to affect relative speeds. The RYA ‘averaging’ system of producing class handicaps also means that it should be more difficult to succeed using a boat whose average helm is of a high standard (e.g. Laser) and V.V.(vice versa), because this will be reflected in its rating, but when the spread of performances in a class is large, then the better boats would be favoured. All this goes to show that although you may have thought you sailed the best in a handicap event and then did not finish first when the results were calculated, other things have been loaded against you. Nevertheless your turn may come and anyhow over a series of races conditions should average out for a fairer overall result.”

START OF SEASON CAUTIONARY REMINDERS

ADDERS In April Navigans it is traditional to caution members (who should remind any children they bring to the Club) that at this time of year there is the possibility of coming across the occasional adder lying in the sun, often concealed in long grass. The sea wall work has reduced the amount of long grass we have for the time being, but it’s worth being careful where you tread, and if you do come across one, please do not disturb it. It’s a part of our wild life population which is harmless if left alone.

THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season, even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats are out during all Club Races, it may happen that for some reason that you can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. Navigans has offered the following advice over the years:

Wear adequate clothing i.e. wet suit/dry suit etc.

forPo
Make sure your boat and its gear are sound.
Ensure personal buoyancy and the boat’s buoyancy are both adequate.
If you are inexperienced either with sailing or with our sailing area, please ask advice from the OOD, Fleet Captain, or other experienced helms.
—y If you start to feel cold and tired, return to shore straightaway, rather than wait till you are too cold to think rationally.

IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day’s prevailing conditions, having spent years building up their skills by going cut in gradually more testing weather, but less experienced sailors could have a difficult and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races, you should aim to be entirely self-sufficient, sail within your limitations, and remember on all occasions that the decision to go float, whether ta race or to potter, 1s always made on your own responsibility.

Thank you for joining us today, thus enabling the members of this Branch to show our appreciation of the help given to the Lifeboat Service by your members and friends aver the past year.

This is a social occasion, but thanks to the efforts of similar Clubs, Associations, Regatta Committees, etc. throughout the British Isles who organise events, plus subscriptions, donations, legacies, house to house/street collections, plus a great variety of fund-raising events too numerous to mention, today some 1442 pecaple are still alive who otherwise would have perished at sea during 1994.

This involved in excess of 5400 service launches from the 210 Lifeboat Stations
located around the coasts of the United Kingdom and Ireland. All this was achieved by a charity totally dependent on public donations and (with the exception of the Humber Lifeboat) on volunteers to crew them and in many places also ta launch and recover the boat after a service.

1977 (March - May) _ - the class struggle continues.
- presumably, whatever it was that Vic cooked up, it didn't go down
too well with some people !

March - a nice action photograph on the front cover shows Mike Turner with a grim smile on his face
as he hangs on the end of a Hornet trapeze amidst much spray and rough water. He looks very wet
indeed - and is clearly enjoying a hard sail; even his helm is smiling.

Commodore John Witter reveals that the sale of Stansgate farms to a dutchman who has purely agricultural interests in the land seems to indicate that the projected marina development on Ramsey marshes will probably not go ahead. He also tells us that a threat to establish a rubbish tip at Stansgate had also diminished; it appears that the Maldon Council had changed its mind and now intended to enlarge the existing tip at Maldon.

John also reminds everyone that the "which club class ?" debate was a discussion which had arisen on
previous occasions during the club's development - but this time there was a particular difference. At
this time the club already had four established classes (Enterprise, Mirror, Hornet and Handicap) with possibly a Sth class if the GP14 was included. Previous discussions had been conducted when only two classes existed (ie. Enterprise and Handicap) discounting the ‘original club class', the Fleetwind.

John makes the very good point that the MSC is basically a family club, and it was not the custom to make membership conditional upon ownership of a particular class of dinghy. Nor was it the custom to stipulate that members must race a certain number of times each year. Thus the Committee itself could not dictate which classes were to be adopted by the club. The Committee could only recognise ‘trends’ and steer people towards a particular class which might be adopted if there was sufficient support. He feels there is a need to either re-establish the GP14 or to establish a class such as the 420, as well as look into the perceived demand for single-handed sailing. He states "In the final analysis, however, the choice of classes must be arrived at by examining the track record of those offered. This means that a common and proved desire for a particular class must be demonstrated so, if we really need a new class or two, some effective lobbying will be necessary to establish a class that meets the specification required by the majority seeking a change."

Contributions to this Navigans issue from Cadet Members of the club included this one from Sarah Lingwood (aged 10):-

FAST CAT NOTES

IYRU Handicap System.

Handicap racing is a dead loss. If we want to know whether we can sail better than the next man we'd better
make sure we're sailing the same boat, or we're simply measuring how badly the handicapper got it wrong...
or are we? Handicapping of small boats has, in the UK, traditionally relied upon the Portsmouth Yardstick scheme managed by the RYA, in which handicap race results are returned to the RYA annually for analysis. The results of the analysis are used to amend the ratings given to the boats in the scheme (which, according to the apparent soundness’ of the data held can be Primary or Secondary Yardsticks, or Recorded Numbers). This scheme has always been seen to be flawed: changes in the ratings between seasons demonstrate that either the old rating or the new one was wrong, and there is often no real reason to suspect it was the former; only a very limited number of multihulls have Primary Yardsticks, and indeed many craft are not rated in the scheme at all; the perception that better crews gravitate toward particular classes leads to the perception that the ratings of those classes are unfairly penalised. These problems led to the adoption for last years Piers Race of the ‘French’ system, one based purely upon measurement and not upon race results. At a practical level the system allows the handicapper to accommodate very easily deviations from standard configurations, as well as in principle overcoming the complaints about the PY system. Given the success of the scheme at the ECPR, the high level of acceptance that it seemed to achieve and the more general move toward the ‘French’ system (since adopted by the lYRU for promulgation as a handicapping system for small catamarans) the Catamaran Fleet AGM supported the new scheme (now luxuriating in the title ‘International Small Catamaran Handicap Rating System’, or ISCHRS) for Fast Cat racing, chose to retain the current level rating system for the Dart 15s and referred the Medium Cat choice to the Sailing Sub-committee. Since then the Sailing Sub-Committee has detailed the system (see the notices displayed in the Reception area at the Club); the key points are as below:

The ISCHRS applies for the Fast and Medium Cat races, and for all-in catamaran races.

No trophies will be awarded for mixed monohull / catamaran races (i.e. there will be separate trophies for monos and multis).

Once you have entered a series in a particular boat or a particular configuration of boat (e.g. with / without a spinnaker) changing the boat or configuration will result in a new entry to the series. Note that this applies to all catamarans, including Dart 15s.

Dart 15s will continue to use their PN ratings for Dart 15 races, but will adopt the ISCHRS ratings for all-in cat races.

A measurement-based system has the deceptive advantage of being beyond dispute (save perhaps for the very principle upon which it is based); surely there can be no disagreement over the figures plugged into the equation which produces the rating? Although the IYRU has accepted the scheme we are still seeing some teething problems, some of which are real and some the result of unintentional misinformation. The figures upon which the ratings are based were submitted by the various manufacturers and published by the French Sailing Federation (FFV); these figures are currently being confirmed by the IYRU and will then be formally published. As with all things voluntary this is taking rather longer than expected, but as the people involved are those who produced the figures for the French scheme there is no reason to expect any change to the list displayed at the Club. There are however a number of flies in this ointment!

1 Until a genuinely official list is published it will always be possible for a person to measure his own
boat, find it heavier (or shorter!) than the list specifies and complain that his rating is punitive. | believe
that such problems can only be avoided by quoting certified measurements from the manufacturer and avoiding the measuring of individual boats for which such measurements exist.

2 Questions have been raised about the accuracy of some of the measurements in the (unofficially) published list. A particular, and rather high profile, vendor of probably the most popular catamaran has published sail area figures for his 15’ craft which do not agree with those on the ISCHRS table, and when questioned apparently supported the company figures. Further investigation with the sailmakers revealed that actually the ISCHRS figures were correct (and the brochure figures were not) but the ISCHRS figures incorrectly omitted the area of the rotating mast, causing an error in the rating. (As a result the ratings for the Dart 15 will have been amended by the time this goes to press;
| have removed them from the table shown below.) The other Dart figures are correct, and although
we have no reason to suspect them, it is possible that similar problems will exist elsewhere.

3 Boats not in the list but which are raced at the Club must be measured and rated. This should be done by reference to the class rules wherever possible for the reason given in 1 (above), but typically several of the required parameters are not quoted. Clearly the measurement of waterline length is not an easy task, but even some of the simpler parameters would appear to pose problems: the ISCHRS and the Texel tables quote different overall lengths for the Dart 15! The class which poses the greatest problems at the Club in this respect is the Hurricane 4.9, and we have tapped every source of information we can find. Unfortunately the class rules do not agree with the report from the sailmakers, and the "well-known" length of 16ft 4%in does not agree with the figure measured at

Texel. As a result we have been forced to compromise by choosing values which, within the RATING typically small range of uncertainty, seem fair. CRUISING DOWN THE PAN?

The morning was beautiful. coming out of Plymouth harbour in our new yacht. a slight mist wisping over a smooth sea. the
boat glistening with the morning dew, rigging taut. ready to enjoy the breezes that would surely come later.

Leaving the idyllic scene I went below to enjov contemplation and early ablutions. Somewhat later - Oh no. not again. the
pump on the marine loo seems to be jammed. Now when you have been experienced in marine toilets and their problems as
much as I have. you get to realise that the next hour may see the blasted thing in bits as you try to effect a repair to the often
dubiously fragile components within. A history of several boats behind me. and with every one a problem loo.

Many years ago. the first. a 22 footer giving the worst moment of all. Moored for the night to the quay just below Haven
Bridge in Great Yarmouth and on route to Norwich next day. I turned over and noticed the time as 0305 hrs and as |
sleepily tried to stretch away that small boat stiffness. my hand flopped out of my berth and onto the cabin sole. My hand
found a carton of margarine as it floated past. Floated Past!!! As the realisation hit me that my hand and a large proportion
of my arm was underwater a reflex occurred that must have blocked the memory that | had little headroom in that small
cabin. and attempting to get out of my sleeping bag the thump of my head on the coach roof. followed closely by a large
emission of blue language immediately woke my normally slothful companion! Chaos ensued as two people scrabbled
blindly to get out of a cabin that resembled a floating larder and get into the cockpit to get to the bilge pump. bucket. sponge
and anything else that would remove water from the boat. Outside we could see that the boat was low enough in the water
to result in some of the mooring lines becoming tight!

Having removed most of the water we now looked for the leak and found that the toilet bowl had cracked where it was
bolted to its plastic base unit and. as the sea cock had been left open this was the cause of the morning's early action. The
location of the toilet also made 1 difficult to have the approved system of an anti-siphon loop. (Which of course is only a
true anti-siphon loop if it features a vented loop at its highest point). From then on it became a rule that never would the
large toilet exit sea cock be left open.

On the next boat the loo kept me busy with the end of the piston often falling off until | replaced the circlips with a split
pin. In the end I fitted a complete new unit. having learnt a lot about the insides of this unpleasant but essential piece of
equipment. As I already had found out. many pump cylinder plungers have circlips to retain the piston assembly and this
can be a source of trouble. the best systems being those with nuts to the top and bottom of the plungers. On the cheaper
heads. the small lever often featured on the top of the plunger to provide the flush function is made of a highly dubious soft
alloy material and soon gives trouble.

Some people advocate the use of vegetable oil to keep the plunger working smoothly but I have found that this oil will
eventually attach itself to the walls of the pump cylinder and cause more problems. The only oil to use seems to be Baby
Oil. and a very small quantity only to get over an immediate friction problem that indicates the need for a strip down. Also
the juddering operation of the plunger can be down to little more than the top water seal being dry. An application of
Vaseline to the exposed portion of the plunger rod can often cure this.

It seems that there is no substitute for some units other than an annual clean out and its re-assembly. lubricating the moving
parts with Vaseline.

Back in Plymouth I realised that I had forgotten to open the exit sea cock with the excitement of the new boat. etc. Having
done so. the pump handle still seemed jammed. Out with the tool kit and to bits with the thing! Diagnosis - an inverted
Aortic Joker Valve - Nasty! This can occur if the sea cock is left shut. As the exit pipe becomes pressurised and then. as
the plunger is raised for another stroke. the valve. intended to stop liquid returning to the toilet. is blown inside out.
Sometimes the valve will return to its natural state and sometimes not. depending on the age of the valve.

On my return to Essex I rang Cleghorn Waring. the suppliers of the Par toilet unit and they were familiar with Aortic Valve
Inversion! An overhaul kit contained the valve. and all is now well.

Given my personal experiences over the last 10 years. the Par is the best of the cheap units of its type with all spares readily
available, but the £650-odd that a Baby Blake costs is probably justified as one still sees these units around in their original
state after many years. and I have met owners who have never touched them in that period!

Limpet M.S.S.E. Rel. (Marine Sanitary Systems Engineer - Reluctant)!

MARCONI SAILING CLUB REGATTA

The Regatta opened on Saturday 27th May with the RNLI Pennant Race. As it’s name suggests the entrance donations
competitors choose to make go to the RNLI. The event was sailed in a strong southerly wind. The gusty conditions caught out
several boats on the downwind leg where concentration and discretion paid off. After five laps of the triangular course Nigel
Skudder and Keith Hills sailing a Laser 2 finished first. The first BIRD boat across the line was the Laser 2 sailed by Gavin and
Jason Mills.

Sunday saw the start of the Regatta with a strong south westerly together with bright.warm sunshine. There were sufficient
boats to give the Kestrels. Solos and Gulls their own class starts. The remaining boats were divided into Fast and Medium
Handicap. The helms of the faster boats were asked to sail a large triangle sausage triangle course whilst the slower boats sailed
a similar course inside the larger course. Conditions in the morning were such that some of the Fast Handicap boats and Gulls
decided not to race. The remainder found the wind conditions a good test of their skills. The afternoon race was run over a
similar course but with the wind casing and blowing more from the south west.

Monday dawned with a Force + from the south west which increased during the morning before casing during the afternoon.
The courses were adjusted to give competitors longer and faster reaches.

The Fast Handicap event was won in convincing fashion by Michael Taylor and Jonathan Willey. Medium Handicap saw Stuart
Curtiss and Shaun coming home first. The Solo class was a close affair between Ron Greygoose and John Salmon. Ron
taking the honours by a whisker after taking into account the discards. Malcolm Gandy and Graham Richmond won the Kestrel
class with Gordon and George Wiiliams winning the Gull class convincingly.
