NAVIGANS PAST

1977 (June) - as we plunge ‘hell for Leather’ into wild waters, a salty outsider gives us a
‘narrows viewpoint’ of the Marconi Sailing Club.

June - obviously, the 1977 Regatta was a ‘blustery event’ both of weather and organisation. Editor, Shirley
Wood, says "...it seems that the question of its future, if it has one, must be asked and looked into’.
Commodore John Witter possibly makes the understatement of the year when he says "...this time the elements
were less favourably inclined towards us with most of the period challenging sailing during the races we were able
to hold". Tom Gaskel judges the Regatta to have been a success despite the weather but writes "At what cost
though to the few members who actually did the hard work - before, during and after. Their numbers get less
every year and each year we have an ever increasing plague of people". Tom goes on to point out that the bank
holiday was meant to be a holiday for everyone, that the commercial profit arises from the fact that the regatta
helpers (e.g. behind the bar) receive no wages for their work and that the number of helpers seems to get fewer as
the event gets bigger. Tom continues "Our resources are inadequate - 3 ladies loos and 2 gents for nearly 1,000
people. The drainage is inadequate and the memory lingers on - the big ditch will be foul for the rest of the
season". However, Tom is not ‘negative’ about regatta as such; he continues "To be constructive - there is no
need to abandon a spring jamboree, Mardi Gras, festival regatta, Stansgate Week or W.H.Y. (what have you) but
let's make it a closed event. Members and guests by invitation".

Ray Battye (Social Secretary) says "The weather could have been kinder for the regatta and the succeeding cadets
week".

As a by-the-by, it is amusing to quote from John Leather's book "The Salty Shore" in which he recounts his
experience of sailing through the Stansgate 'narrows' at what we can assume was the time of the regatta:-

"One day during the summer of 1977 a friend and I were beating his small cruiser through the narrows at
half flood, against a strong westerly wind, rising to gale force. Suddenly, scores of sailing dinghies were
launched off from a sailing club at Stansgate and within five minutes the whole narrows and the river south
of Osea was covered with capsized boats, drifting to leeward, their crews clinging to them, rescue boats
thrashing about in inadequate numbers and manoeuvring under the bow of sailing cruisers finding as much
as they could do to keep clear of the melee. "Looks like the battle of Trafalgar," muttered my companion
grimly as he put the helm down and we plunged about to avoid a capsized dinghy with her helmsman
sitting on the upturned bottom, clutching the erect centreboard blowing him to leeward like a sail. Such
are the modern perils of the narrows, which have been known to shake up ten toppers in a gale."

Oh! Dear! What is that quotation? "Would that God the giftie gie us to see ourselves as others see us" (or at least
something like that).

Many thanks to Malcolm Stuart who reminded me of the John Leather item. The book 'The Salty Shore’ is all
about the river Blackwater and well worth having on your bookshelf.

Amongst the cruiser fleet news is that of Russ Fuller who reports "My thanks go out to John Witter and others
who helped out on the Friday before the Regatta when one of our friendly Thames barge owners did his best to
move Kalinka's mooring with the boat still attached. It would seem the barge lost some tar in the process but
without John's prompt attention the result could have been far less happy".

The adventures (or misadventures) involved in the delivery voyage of the Victoria are continued from the previous
month and are illustrated by the following quotes:-

- “So far che weather had been warm and the sea slight, but a remark was made that whereas the wind had
been steady it was now tending to gust to what one would call 5 plus".

- "I will make no guess as to the strength of the wind for the next six or seven hours, but the sequence of
events should give some idea of the weather conditions prevailing".

It is probably worth quoting most of the remaining article:-

10,

- "To begin with, it was the noise of the wind and rain that made conversation difficult, shouting being the
order of the day. Steering by compass was now very difficult indeed and we needed to get sail off. We
had the following sails on - mainsail fully up with no reefs in, genoa (heavy) fully up but we could do
something about that as it had furling gear worked through a drum anda series of lines from the cockpit. A jib with reefing gear was bent on and secured up forward ready to hoist to replace the genoa. It was decided to furl the genoa and hoist the jib which should have been quite simple at that point in time, but it was stuck and just wouldn't move. By now we were sailing on our ear and John went forward to try to release the furling gear without success. Later, whilst John and I were trying to release the furling gear from the side of the cockpit, there was a most almighty crash and the boat heaved over the other way. In the dark and confusion nobody knew immediately what had happened except that 'yours truly’ was shot across the cockpit and unable to move. We had gybed. A torch brought from below shone on to me to show that when we gybed I was trapped by the mainsheets, which by some freak of fate had entangled themselves in the snaphook attached to my harness at the chest end of my lifeline. Two and a half parts of the sheets had entangled and it took four or five minutes to free them (the half had been cut into by the hook and a knife needed to free it). 1 was scared stiff that we would gybe again and I would repeat the performance perhaps with fatal results. I could feel no serious damage, which was a miracle considering I had been flung violently across the cockpit completely without control, in the dark and with no warning. When I was extracted from the mainsheets, we had the genoa aback and needed to gybe again to get on course. The quickest way was the most dangerous and put the mast under very severe strain in that we wanted to put the stern through the wind under engine to save going through a 360 degree or thereabouts
under the prevailing conditions. This manoeuvre was executed successfully...... ;

- "Attempts were still being made to furl the genoa when with no warning whosoever there was a terrific
crack and a shudder and the genoa tack came adrift, the sheets became detached and the genoa shot up the forestay to within twenty feet of the masthead. We had an uncontrollable thirty feet or so of jumbled up sail flying out almost horizontally from the masthead and exerting goodness knows what strains at the point not designed for such. It was urgent now that the main should be reduced to lessen the risk of losing the mast, but we soon realised that it would have to come right down as the reefing gear was incomplete and therefore no reefing was possible. This was executed with some difficulty, which I will explain later, for at this time a searchlight shone on us from two or three hundred yards astern, and a loud hailer blared out something which due to wind, rain and general conditions could not be deciphered. I did however wave and after three or four minutes the ship veered off and continued on its way. In retrospect 1 consider this is what happened. Our 'masthead genoa’ was in fact an indication of distress according to International Maritime Law, in that it constituted something conspicuous flying from the highest point of the ship. Some very alert lookout had seen it and true to tradition had closed us to see if we were in need of help. When close enough to see that a sail had carried away and that the man at the helm waved ‘casually’ they assumed that we were capable of looking after ourselves and departed".

- "By now the sea was such that to look over ones shoulder could cause fear, for all that could be seen was
the white curling tops of the next line of waves. Poor Jimmy had to look, for his Dad was at the wheel and looking ahead and he was looking for lights and timing them with a stop watch, for which he deserved a medal”.

hate but let's get back to why we had trouble getting the mainsail down. Our lee rails were under the water at times and we had to get it up on the wind and with the genoa gone, she didn't want to do it under sail alone. This meant starting the engine, which was, as I said, a heavy vehicle road one which had a shallow sump, and therefore heavily healed there would be no oil in the sump to circulate. This risk had to be taken so the engine was started and the oil pressure monitored. We did get into the wind, the boat did come upright (and the sump) so we could get the main down and the engine running. How John and I did it I'll never know".

- "What to do next ? The situation was as follows:- the genoa was thrashing halfway up the mast, but
still acting as a steadying sail. The main was down, but the engine was running, so we could ‘relax’, review the situation calmly and decide our next move".

- "There was a unanimous decision to re-establish our position, which isn't surprising since for a couple of
hours we had been at the mercy of wind and sea. It must be pointed out that we knew we had plenty of sea room to leeward so at no time had we been in danger of running ashore".

- "It might be worth noting here that conditions were such that all crew members had life jackets or
buoyancy aids on (life jackets being blown up) and all were secured by some means or other to the boat. This was mainly because of the darkness and the atmosphere which noise, movement, spray, torrential rain and general uncertainty created. At times there was considerable confusion but at no time was there
panic”.

- "Back to positioning ourselves. We knew that we were somewhere in the vicinity of the North and West
Hinder so the helmsman (myself) steered as straight a course as possible, Jimmy had the stopwatch and the navigator was at his chart table below. Most lights, even if different colours, normally flash 'X* number of times in so many seconds. Jimmy's job was to look for lights, start the watch on the first flash of the next sequence, let it go through its sequence and stop the watch on the first flash of the next sequence. He
then handed the watch down the hatch and said '4 reds every “that"' or '3 whites every "that"’ - the
"that" being the time (of successive sequences). 1 added "fine on the port bow" or "on the starboard beam" whichever was appropriate".

- "Within twenty minutes we had a light and two light vessels looms to look at, but the waves were big
enough and we were small enough to blank out whole sequences for quite long periods. We did however know that the two light vessels should have been the North West Hinder which were about twenty miles off the Belgium coast, and about 8 to 10 miles from us. They were roughly where they should be but too distant to confirm without doubt. It was decided to close to what must be the West Hinder which we did, and within an hour could clearly count the light sequence. In fact we closed to within three or four hundred yards to get a good point of departure for the next buoy”.

- "It was almost light by now and we were over the Hinder Shoals with the seas very big and confused
which made steering even with a huge wheel quite difficult. They were by far the worst seas any of us had seen from a small boat, except maybe Bill, but he was below".

- “We were very weary, very tired and those that had spent the night on deck, very wet (in spite of all the
weather gear) and cold".

- "It should be remembered that all this time the genoa was flogging at the masthead, for even with
lifelines it would have been too dangerous to work right up forward in an effort to get it down, even if we could see how whilst it was dark".

- "At about 8 o'clock, after passing Middlekirk and Ostende Bank West Buoys, we could see the coast
quite clearly, visually and on radar, from Neuport in (the) south to Blankenburg in the north, with Ostende a welcome sight in between".

- "Perhaps readers have wondered why we couldn't pick up the lightships on the radar. The reason was as
follows:- on very small ships with the aerial say 25ft above sea level, spray, sea clutter and heavy rain all help to interfere with transmission and reception so much that the equipment ceases to function efficiently. The fact that the buildings ashore were much higher, more stable and had a greater reflective area did enable us to see the coast when we were fifteen miles off and yet not see the two lightships at three or four miles distant".

- "The seas were more pronounced in direction as we got clear of the Hinder and it was decided to try and
get the genoa down as we would have fouled everything had we tried to run up into the harbour".

This adventure story is continued in the next Navigans Past.

Mike Boreham

From the NATIONAL COASTWATCH INSTITUTION

The Reinstatement of Coastal Watch Stations

At Padstow and Cadgwith seven fishermen lost their lives when their vessels foundered within sight of the shore. At Lands
End four school children lost their lives when they were washed off the rocks into the sea. Another four died in the Lyme
Bay canoe tragedy.

All of these tragedies. and many others in various parts of the UK, might have been averted had an experienced eye been
watching and the Coastguard watch service maintained instead of being cut for purely financial reasons.

With the support of the fishing industry, commercial shipping and boating. yachtsmen, powerboat owners and public
opinion, the Sea Safety Group (UK) has launched Operation Coastwatch. To do this we are setting up a Charitable Trust
under the name of ‘National Coastwatch Institution’,

A phased plan has been developed in order to reinstate 29 selected Watch Houses around the United Kingdom coastline in
the immediate future, with another 14 to follow at a later date. All will be complete with full standard Watch House
equipment but with the addition of both Radar. VHF and 121.5MHz Direction Finding equipment.

Phase One covers the reinstatement of four Watch Houses in the South West, it is envisaged that these will be at Swanage.
Cape Cornwall. Gwennap Head and the Lizard (Bass Point). Phase two covers the coasts of East Anglia and two stations on
the South Coast. with phase three covering the wild and dangerous coasts of West and North Scotland including the Minch.

All Watch Houses will be manned 24 hours a day for 365 days a year. by fully trained volunteer personnel drawn initially
from the large corps of ex-Auxiliary Coastguards. We will be employing a full-time training staff to both carry out initial
training and to ensure standards are maintained. The principal role of these stations will be to:

* re-establish a visual watch in all coastal areas around the UK.
* co-operate with search and rescue organisations.
* assist the Coastguard when requested.
* keep the Meteorological Office regularly updated on local conditions at each site.
* provide a telephone service on local weather and sea conditions to anyone who requires it.
* by means of Radar. assist with vessel tracking for the MAREP (Merchant Ship Reporting Scheme).
* assist the Customs and Excise when required.
* assist in the reporting of the MEPA (UK) “OSREP’ pollution watch.

Funding will come principally from industrial. corporate and similar sponsorship. Stations will be named and call-signed
under long term sponsors’ names. It is estimated (1994 figures) that it costs only an average of £25.000 per year to man
and maintain a Coastwatch Station. What price if one life is saved?

Further support will be sought to cover off-station training for personnel and for some local Watch Houses from public
donation and national fund-raising. For the 29 Watch Houses planned under the seven phases we need an income of one
million pounds per year. This is not only attainable but essential for the safety of our inshore waters to be enhanced to cover
all craft not fitted with radio or those that suffer rapid and catastrophic disaster which gives no time for a distress message
to be sent out as has happened all too often in the past. with the resultant loss of life.

Footnote

The Chairman of the NCI has given us the following up-dated details of developments. Base Point Watch House on the
Lizard was opened on 18 December 1994. The immediate programme is to open (or re-open) Watch Houses at Peverill
Point. Swanage, Cape Cornwall and Gwennap Head: Hurst Point and Shoreham: Great Yarmouth. Gorleston and two
others in East Anglia. Contributions and other offers of help can be sent via the Chairman at: [redacted]. Brea. Nr.
Camborne, Cornwall, TR14 [redacted]

Commodore’s Notes

Well. we've finally had a few days of summer and doesn't it make a difference? Lots of things on the horizon. like the
close of nominations for next year’s committee - Commodore and Rear Commodore included! Any volunteers?

difficulty in filling the OOD duty, and the fact that this duty has become less of a “safety role” over the past few years and

ISLE OF WIGHT IN PASSING

David (Ball) took the opportunity to keep up his sailing instructor's skills by accepting an invitation to spend 2 weeks
instructing at a sailing school on the Isle of Wight. So it was home from Bristol on the Saturday and off to the Isle of Wight
by train on the Sunday. The short crossing on the ferry from Southampton to Cowes had its interest for him - seeing a
former MSC Cruiser (the catmaran ‘Roving Red Admiral’) flying a German flag: and a car ferry trying to get out of the
way of a sailing race that insisted on starting no matter what the passing traffic consisted of! I wonder what would happen
if a yacht race got in the way of the car ferry out of Harwich? No doubt David will learn a lot from sailing in completely
different waters, and will have a lot to talk about when he gets back.
Ed.

CRUISER COMMENTS

Six Cruisers. SURUCA, GREEN PANTHER, ANGEL II. SEA BRUME. SILVER PEARL. & HAPPY MEDIUM, plus two guests
from T.E.Y.C. namely, REBECCA & MRS MALATROP (that’s the name of the boat. not the guests) made the trip to St
Katharine’s Yacht Harbour. Originally it was planned to leave on Saturday 17th June. but the weather was not conducive. so we
stayed put. However, the day was not spoilt since we made up for it with a pleasant get-together in The Dell Bar. Sunday was a
much better day, so at 06.30 we slipped our moorings for what was supposed to be a passage to Thurrock Yacht Club for a stop-over
before making the final leg up to St Katharine’s.

As it turned out we made such good progress, albeit motoring. that we were able to continue up to St Katharine’s arriving at 18.10.
just ten minutes before hight water London Bridge. All. that is. except for Sea Brume who would have none of this motoring
nonsense, so they stopped over at Thurrock Yacht Club, joining us the following evening. We spent three nights there. everhone
doing their own thing, meeting up on each other's boats for refreshments! - followed by a get-together supper Tuesday evening in the
Yacht Harbour’s Clubhouse.

NAVIGANS PAST

1977 (July) - where there's a (Regatta) will, then there's a (Regatta) way
- and where's there's a wind, then there's a wave (with 'stormy weather' in the
offing in both cases).

The 1977 Regatta - Club Commodore, John Witter, summarizes the results of a committee meeting which 'went
over’ the views and comments arising from the organisation of the 1977 Regatta, and which were:-

(a) Sailing: well covered with good distribution of help. Minor problems with spotting due to inclement
weather. Rescue facilities stretched but coped.
(b) Galley: good preparation and supply of food, etc. Some people spent more time in the Galley than
ideally we would like, but this was often at individuals own insistence.
(c) Bar: good service given by Brewers. Generous support behind the bar during peak periods but in
general too much for one person outside the peak periods. Some spells of duty, particularly during
Saturday evening party, became stretched and more advance commitment required to spread load.
(d) Clubhouse Facilities: This was the area in which we were most stretched to meet the demand. There
are, however, problems with providing extra facilities but these are under consideration. Despite the
shortcomings, many people return each year knowing what to expect.

The Committee apparently reached no conclusions as to the future of Regatta, since the views received had been
more on the ‘organisational aspects' and expressed mainly by people who were not particularly pessimistic about
Regatta. The views of the sailors, along the lines of "what do they want from Regatta ?", are also required.
John states "The question of Regatta is clearly an emotional one and unless some of those who enjoy it and want it
(to) continue say so, the view will be one sided and it will surely die."

John continues "It should also be borne in mind that the problem of getting voluntary help to do things at the Club
is not unique to the Regatta but is present throughout the year and is an older problem to which we have to find a
solution if the Club Officers and Committee are not to become disillusioned. "

John goes on to outline his personal perspective of Regatta which was:-
(i) to provide good competitive sailing and an opportunity for our members to sail against members of
other clubs on our home waters. He points out that 1/6th (presumably approx. 35-40) of the 225
entries were members of the MSC and were represented in 9 fleets.
(ii) to offer an opportunity to sail from our unique and much admired facilities to members of mainly local
clubs on the river and in Essex and thereby reciprocate the facilities available to our members at other
clubs.
to limit the disruption of Club life to a minimum of weekends in the year and to avoid opening the
Club to all on too many weekends in the year. This was in deference to the wishes of the members
who are not competitive sailors and who like to enjoy the privacy the Club can offer for the majority of
the year.
(iv) making a profit from Regatta was not the main objective, although naturally a successful one does
make a substantial profit...... Ditti cess he would not spend the time supporting the event if profit was the
prime motive.
(v) did not support Tom Gaskell's suggestion of a ‘closed jamboree’ rather than an open sailing event since
it would be against the interest or tradition of the MSC and would be a recipe for disaster for the
competitive sailing interest of the club. The idea of cruiser members racing with the dinghies within
an essentially ‘closed’ event was an ideal of the early Regattas which had died very quickly.
(vi) Holding several (single class) open meetings during the year in place of the (multi-class) Regatta
would still require a great deal of organisation and commitment and it would be difficult to interleave
club racing with open events without rescue launch support from other clubs.

John reports that analysis of the entries showed that the help for the Regatta organisation came mainly from the
(club member) entries themselves and their families with additional support from the fleets on a rota basis and
goes on to say:-

"The question of size and how to limit it and still offer open sailing is one to which there appears to be no
easy solution but 12 years ago (ie. 1965) we were equally worried about size when we had 80 boats and
since then we have held Regattas with more entries than this year's without the benefits of our present

clubhouse...... The main differences I think now really arise from our ability to accommodate more people
under canvas than previously and not from the sailing organisation".

John rounds off his extensive ‘Commodores Notes' by saying:-
"I do not expect my personal views to be supported unanimously by the members or the Committee, but
the Club consists of a lot of minority interests making up the whole and one of the jobs of the Committee
is to try and cater for all these interests over a period of time and a balance has to be struck.......... In
conclusion I would say I have no regrets about the many hours spent on the Regattas since they first started
and my reward is knowing our members and visitors are enjoying good sailing."

Note from Mike: I believe I am right in saying that John and Eleanor Witter helped (in a big way) in running
over 20 successive Regattas and, despite being keen racing sailors in (between them) the Enterprise,Solo and
Mirror classes, never (or at least rarely) managed to actually sail in the Regatta themselves. They are, of course,
not alone in this and in similar fashion the Greygooses and the Weedons have always been well to the fore to help
with Regatta over an equally long period of time and others, no doubt, are also worthy of mention. | However,
one of the most remarkable of records must be that of Robbie and Joan Sims and family who carried out the role
of Race Officer/Race Box team for 24 successive years and only missed out on the 25th anniversary event by
virtue of Robbie being Commodore and having to perform other duties. Even then Robbie, Joan and family
again completed additional 'tours of duty' as Regatta Race Officer before their move 'up country’ brought their
record run to an end.

John Weedon (Sailing Secretary) says "As far as future years are concerned | will be willing to assist in any way
and I am sure that others will do also - provided we have the support of the Club".

Roger Smith writes in to say "...as a fairly new member...... whilst I appreciate that the lions share of the
organisation of such an event must fall on a few experienced people I wonder if the Club makes best use of its
resources...... I was prepared to help....but have not been contacted........ I hope we continue to stage a Regatta."

A view from a cruiser member (Freddie Harrison) highlights the very real problems arising from the presence of a
large number of people at the club during Regatta. Not all of them were entirely honest and upright (at least,
not in the context of competitive sailing when otherwise sober honest citizens seem to think ‘anything goes' and
everything is excusable in the quest to compete and win). Apart from the annoyances of pilfering of boat items,
etc., Freddie writes "Like many others I removed my cruiser from Stansgate the week before the Regatta to give
the racing enthusiasts more room at the start line....... I returned to Stansgate to find crowds of strangers, a drunk
at the bottom of the ditch and, to crown it all, my poor old banger with its paint work deeply scored fore and aft
plus a flat tyre...... next to me was a shiny ‘R' registration which might have got the same treatment if it had not
been for the vigilance of two Marconi members." Freddie goes on to basically support Tom Gaskell's viewpoint
of a closed 'Club Regatta’ with open meetings during the year to attract the visiting experts.

No debate about Regatta would be complete without a contribution from Malcolm Stuart who has, by word and
deed over the years , always been an enthusiast for 'the open Regatta’ no matter what the perceived problems.
Malcolm puts forward similar arguments to those of John Witter in favour of Regatta. Malcolm writes "As
regards the work entailed one would expect to find, as in all things, a pendulum effect whereby the trend shifts
from lots of willing helpers one year to fewer the next. No amount of prior organisation will completely
eliminate this...... (I) hope that we can continue with an event that requires no further justification than that it
attracts World Champion Helmsmen to our Club." _ He then presents us (in line with his irrepressible sense of
fun and humour) with a ‘formula’ for working out some statistic or other which appears to have a great deal to do

The maiden voyage of Victoria - The July, 1977, Navigans contains the concluding episode of the adventures and
misadventures of the delivery trip of the Victoria to Holland (or was it Belgium?). Those who have not read the
previous two episodes of this story from 1977 Navigans will need to read 'Navigans Past’ in the April and July,
1995, issues of the present-day Navigans. We take up the tale with the Victoria's genoa flying wildly out of
control from the mast like a giant streamer, and life for the crew being generally uncomfortable:-

"The skipper went right up into the bows....and after inspection he called for a knife.....the necessary rope was
cut, the sail dropped low enough to be got at and was eventually stowed. This is an over simplification for the
job took almost an hour under impossible conditions........ This then was our first bit of luck in a night of
setbacks....... With our large (pennant) down, which had acted in some ways as a steadying sail, we began to roll
violently. Frightening noises below subsequently proved themselves to be tool boxes and provisions. A
thorough inspection below showed that we had made water, but nothing serious.....It was confirmed later that the
water had spilled out several time (from the toilet) when we were healed or were tossed about.”

"...we decided to put the mizzen up as a steadying sail. | One had to experience the change to appreciate the
difference a very small sail can make.."

"After an hour or so we had come inside the shoals off Ostende and we were comparatively sheltered. All hands
came on deck and, with great relief 1 am sure, watched as ‘yours truly’ (because he had been on the helm most of
the time) was given the great privilege of taking Victoria through Ostende breakwater to make her first landfall.
That was one of the most satisfying moments of my life. Within an hour we were tied up and asleep."

"Inspection showed the following:-

(1) The Genoa was only slightly torn and damage marginal to one seam and the eyelet where the sheets
were attached.
(2) There were two deck leaks, one caused by the strain put on the handrail protecting the steering console
and one round the forehatch.
(3) A starboard side stanchion was bent as was the guardrail running from it. Its base screws had also
gone and the angle plate strengthening damaged. It was where the end of my lifeline was attached
when I was flung across the cockpit!!!"

Other than the above, no damage was found.”

"In retrospect it is very difficult to know how some of the problems could have been avoided as it is easy in
hindsight to hold a post mortem....... Again in retrospect I feel that no maiden voyage should have had such bad
luck. However, it proved the boat for the owner and proved the crew to themselves."

"The following advise could be given as guidance should somebody wish to make a similar passage:-

(1) Do a short night sail prior to the crossing to see that the compass is adequate.
(2) At the same time familiarise the crew with working on deck in the dark for sail changing and other
necessary activities.
(3) Have an alternative destination well planned should the original not prove feasible.
(4) If there is a chance of sea sickness, take all precautions for avoidance well in advance.
(5) Remember that cold fronts invariably mean foul weather, so don't be afraid of them but be ready for a
change of plans and some very uncomfortable sailing.
(6) If it is ever intended to cook or even boil water on the passage, a fiddle rail and gimbals on the cooker
are most essential even if only for safety.
(7) Make sure that some of the crew has enough experience to take care of the boat under any conditions
that might be experienced on passage.
"I think apart from the compass, which was essential, and the cooker, which wasn't, Victoria's crew fulfilled all
such requirements and a successful passage was made even if the original destination had to be changed. Would I
do it again tomorrow? Of course I would."

written by ‘Anonymous’ for I can see no attribution of an author given with the articles

TRITON OF OSEA,, Port de Plaisance, Rochefort France

To Doreen & Derek Kirby

Rochefort. Wednesday 6th April. As you see I’m having a practice with the PC. I'm probably one of the few people who
take longer to type a letter than write in longhand. but at least this way you can decipher it! The weather here improved about
midday, and the sun came out for the afternoon. We spent quite a while poring over the charts and almanacs trying to make sense of
the firing range problem, and are now much clearer about the areas involved and need to get more information about their firing
times. We don't seem to be able to pick up Arcachon Radio clear enough here to make head or tail of the broadcast. perhaps we will
try the automatic message on the phone. Ray made a valiant effort today and had a look at the grill! Upon dismantling it he
discovered it did not have a control screw as he had expected - however with a little adjustment of the angle of the dangle and a good
fiddle he put it back together again. At least the cooker got a thorough cleaning and | think it has improved a bit.

Monday 10th April. Phoned the repondeur and got a very short message ‘Aucune zone engager’ (No areas engaged). however
the next day I tried again and got a great long fast spiel far too fast for me to understand. I went to get my recorder but Daniel saw
me and insisted on phoning himself (he has a phone on board). He listenened to the message. writing it down. then explained it to
me - and then phoned again so that I could hear it again and (hopefully) understand the message. The gist of the message was of
course times, days and positions (Lats and Longs). It started off with ‘Du centre d’essai’ which referred to the centre of the test
area. I'll try a few more times and see if I can get the hang of it.

The weather seems to have settled into a pattern. It's often chilly first thing. then warms up through the morning. then is really hot
in the afternoon. Long may it continue! We've been keeping busy plodding through our list of jobs. Ray's installed the new VHF.
which involved some tricky wire threading almost standing on our heads trying to get it under the floor and up through the battery
box! The SSB is also installed (quite differently than planned, but it looks fine). haven't had time to use it much yet. On Saturday
8th we went to a Classical Concert here in Rochefort at the Coupe d'Or Theatre, which we are told is built as a miniature copy of
the Paris Opera House. It certainly is miniature! There are only ten rows in the stalls. and only three rows in the circle! You felt
there were almost as many people in the orchestra as in the audience. However it was really beautiful. very ornate with a domed
ceiling with painted cupids, gilded pillars and great draperies. It certainly made a change from our pontoon!

Tuesday 25th April. We are nearing the end of our stay here and intend to leave some time through the coming weekend. The
weather has been quite changeable for the past week and we have had some rain on the majority of days. We are amazed by the
speed with which it alters, within minutes it can go from cold and damp to glorious sunshine (and the reverse). Our list of jobs has
been worked upon steadily and most of the important things are sorted out. although there are a few things we hope to get in La
Rochelle. The English chap from the boat behind us. the Moody Eclipse. went to La Rochelle by car and asked about a lift-out at the
place we had been given a quote in November when we were here before. It is now obvious that we had been given the winter rate.
which was almost half what it is now! Also they were getting very booked up. so once again, Daniel to the rescue, he phoned and
sorted out the current prices, and booked us a lifi-out for 15.30 on Tuesday 2nd May. We are considering leaving a few days before
then and having a good sail to test everything. and then staying on one of the islands for a couple of nights before we go to La
Rochelle. However unless the weather improves we'll stay here. There was a Force 8 forecast for Biscay yesterday and it is certainly
blowing at the moment. After all the research with the firing range we have decided to make life simpler by going directly to
Santander (at least that is the plan at the moment!) It is about 200 miles to Santander from La Rochelle. so depending on our speed.
somewhere between 5 to 6 knots. it will take 33 to 40 hours. We have planned to be out of the water for a week in order to allow for
any wet days when we can’t antifoul. but after that we will be looking for a settled period of weather to cross the Bay.

Monday Ist May. Well the weather has certainly improved. the last few days have been hot and sunny, real shorts weather, but
we are still here in Rochefort. dt is the May Bank Holiday and the favourite mooring spots are apparently very crowded, so we have
decided to go straight to La Rochelle tomorrow. We have managed to sort out the wetherfax programme and can now get daily
charts and analyses, all we need to do now is understand them! We have heard on the grapevine that Dave and Joan (Thomas) left
about two weeks ago and hope to arrive at St Helena this weekend. they are averaging about 120 n. miles per day.

Santander, Sunday 14th May. Well here we are in Santander. After being lifted out at La Rochelle on the 2nd May. the
weather turned really warm and we sweltered for a week on the shore. antifouling and generally getting the boat ready to leave.
There was virtually no wind and the temperature was well into the high 80s. We were reading the weather forecasts each day and
the chap in the Capitainerie suggested we visited the Meteo Office which is actually in La Rochelle. They were extremely helpful
and showed us the predictions for the coming week. These showed a deterioration from Thursday 11th with gale force winds by the
Friday and Saturday. As it turned out they were pretty accurate. which is why we are still here in Santander. We decided to start off
on the Tuesday morning about 6 am. and went out to St Denis on Ile dOleron. a bit further north than Port Douhet where we drove

11.

to with you. We picked up a buoy on Monday afternoon intending to get a good rest in order to leave about 6 o clock on Tuesday
morning. However the current whips around the corner there and it was really uncomfortable. We were obviously not going to get
much sleep. so about lam we let got the buoy and set off. We are sailing in company with Brian and Joan Lee who own the Moody
Eclipse which was on the same pontoon as us in Rochefort. Although the wind was OK strength-wise it was almost behind us.
which made rather a loppy motion. and impossible to set the sails. so we motorsailed the whole journey. It was reasonably
uneventful. except Brian picked up a fishing net around his rudder miles off shore and in 100 metres of water. He went to great
lengths to try and free it, hanging off the back of the boat at one time. Also we tried to tow him around to see if it would drop away.
but to no avail and after an hour and a half he cut himself free. In spite of this delay we arrived at Santander at 8.30: 198 nm. in
31.5 hours. At one time during the crossing I heard an enormous bang. and looking at the chart. realised we were very close to the
firing range. I noted in the log that I had heard this explosion: mentioning it later. I was informed that it was. in fact. Concorde
flying over!

Everyone was very friendly and welcoming at Santander. although when we arrived it was quite early and there was no one at all
who spoke any English. There was great hilarity as we did our best with the phrase book. then the Capitanio arrived (a lady) who
spoke French so we got by all right. It was a good marina with free hot showers and electricity. but a long way from the town and no
public transport. One of the marina workers insisted on giving us a lift to town and we were having a good mooch round when the
heavens opened and we got pretty wet. We are just getting used to the hours kept here by the shops etc. It seems even later than
France. with nothing much opening in the afternoon until 4pm and the restaurant here doesn’t open in the evening till 9pm.

Gijon, Wednesday 17th May. After a few storm bound days in Santander we heard a forecast for a SW force 4. so we set off
at 6am on Monday bound for Ribadesella about 60 miles away. By midday we were in enormous seas with wind gusting up to 34
knots. We discussed about 6 different options. none of them ideal, and luckily about 4+ pm the wind eased and an hour later we came
to the little entrance between the mountains and popped into Ribadesella. There is no marina. just a quay along the main road. We
moored to the best bit which had a notice saying ‘Reserved For Fishing Boats’. just to sort ourselves, but a chap whizzed up in a car
and said (in English) “Good evening. this is good. OK here 2 metres OK”. He gave us some leaflets on the locality and disappeared.
never to be seen again. We were there two days and there was no charge. nor formalities. We have seen the Aduana (Customs) in
Santander and here in Gijon. They copy down information from passports etc. but are not too sure what they are reading. We now
have our address as 7 Southview. Hockley. as this was an address in our passports under “Emergency Contact’. also when they asked
where we had started from. I said Rochefort. and they wrote down Oxford!

The forecast for Biscay this morning was SW v NW 5 to 6 rising to 7 occasional 8 (on Radio 4). however the local one was 2 to 3
and we had a lovely summer sail today, 29 miles here to Gijon. The scenery on the trip was really stunning. The Cantabrian
Mountain Range runs parallel to the coast here, and they drop right down to the water in places. with steep rock faces. and
sometimes come down in tree-covered slopes or fields. The highest mountains are snow covered and the whole picture is quite
breathtaking at times. In the clefts of the rocks you can see small sandy beaches and the occasional little village. hidden from view
except at just the right angle from the sea. We feel we should have taken longer to cover this area as we are sure we are missing a
lot. Perhaps we'll come back again some time. Here in the Marina at Gijon we are on the International pontoon with a British Cat.
a small Swedish boat on the way to the Canaries. and a few French yachts. all travelling south as we are. The facilities here are
excellent: showers. water and electricity all included in the price of £7.25 per night for us. Brian's 33 footer is £4.50 so we can't
complain about the costs so far. Also everyone. harbour officials, the Authorities and the public in general have been very
welcoming and helpful. We were a bit anxious due to the trouble with the Spanish fishermen. as we are right in that area at the
moment, but haven't had any problems at all, touch wood.

Well. that’s brought you up to date with our travels. we are making our way along the north coast and around Cap Finisterre to be in
Bayona by 8th June to meet up with the Rally Portugal mob. and will later be in Lagos on 20th June. We are picking up the English
end of the UK net on the SSB and have heard them speak to Joan, though we can’t hear her reply. They left St Helena almost a
week ago and are on their way to Ascension Island.

Hope you are well and enjoying life. please send our best wishes to Barbara and Don and anyone else at Marconi. I'll try and write
again later, if not, you'll get an occasional postcard!

Hazel & Ray Becket

USE OF WIRE STROP WHEN HAULING OUT CRUISERS.

These are being damaged and written off by incorrect use.

chain and shackle at the trailer end. and by the eyelet at the tractor end. /t is the Tractor Driver's

A brief view of MARS
as seen in its environment of green,red and white light.

Despite the introductory title, this is not an exploration of the Red Planet. This article is very much Earth-
bound, or should I say ‘sea-bound'. In this case, MARS is a non-government confidential and voluntary
reporting scheme for seafarers to highlight ‘incidents’ which they have experienced and which might otherwise
go unrecorded and/or not receive widespread circulation amongst those who would find them of interest and
benefit. Sometimes the reports include two (or more) very different viewpoints of the same incident at sea, in
confined waters or simply alongside in harbour. I find the reports very interesting to read even though I am not a
seafarer.

Thus the following appeared in the publication Seaways, June, 1995, (The Journal of The Nautical Institute) and
is taken from the MARS (ie. Marine Accident Reporting Scheme) Report No. 95024 and is reprinted with the
permission of Capt. Robin Beedel, FNI, Compiler of the MARS.

a
2 2

Not that t

"A recent nation-wide ITV feature programme showed the work of Gosport and Fareham Inshore Rescue Service.
In the programme, one of their rescue craft, a high speed, semi-inflatable took a dis-masted Catamaran in tow.
In the process, the young lady crew member made the tow rope fast to the rescue craft's towing bollards with, if
my memory serves correctly, what seemed to be a superfluous number of ‘figure of eight’ turns, but more
with a final locking turn.
dangerously,

For obvious reasons, a tug must always be able to free itself quickly from its tow and where a quick release hook
does not provide this facility, then the simple Towing Hitch, which can be quickly and simply thrown off, should
be used to make the tow fast to the tug. I am sure that if sea-going members of the G & FIRS were to contact a
traditional tug boat or an RNLI lifeboat, someone there would demonstrate the correct hitch.”

IR KK

I quote from another MARS report in the same issue of Seaways.

An illuminating Experience

This report was submitted by ‘someone’ on a large container ship travelling at 20 knots on a dark but clear night
somewhere between Sydney and Auckland.

"We were keeping a vigilant watch............. suddenly presented with a single green light....... it was obvious ...it
had just been switched on. No discernible radar echo.....1 estimated the vessel was 4 miles ahead. We deduced
Sees a yacht.......running with the wind and therefore crossing ahead of us. | As the bearing remained steady, I
was just about to alter course when the green light changed to white (and deduced the yacht was coming about and
would show red any second). After two - three minutes (no change)...decided white light must be stern
light.....and (yacht) was turning about. Just then an anxious voice came on Channel 16 VHF "this is yacht
******* calling vessel in front of me, do you see me....... I have put my deck light on so that you can see me"
(having switched off the combined lantern). The ‘big ship’ reporter deduced green would still be showing (if not
switched off) and made a considerable course alteration accordingly and ".....(the yacht) altered his course to
pass safely round our stern. I courteously but firmly chastised his action............. twenty minutes later I heard
a further confrontation on the VHF between the same yacht and another vessel”.

Most of the MARS Reports are written from the point of view of the ‘big boats’ and concerned with the
professional side of the international maritime activities. However, it might be interesting if some of our cruiser
members were to write an account of their encounters/experiences (from the point of view of a ‘little boat’ and
the leisure side of things) and send it to MARS. Their views might not be right as seen from the bridge, but they
could be illuminating!
Mike Boreham

act on the river Crouch during Burnham Week. Jenny Ball, Lucy Boreham and Stuart Golding crewed on a Contessa 32 and helped bring it into 3rd place in its class, scoring two 2nds, four 3rds, a 4th and a Retired, despite not being too familiar with the boats’ bits and pieces (although they had no trouble with sail trimming). It is understood they have an invitation to go back next year; let's hope they can make it.

An even older generation - Malcolm Gandy finished 4th in the Kestrel nationals at Weymouth. Earlier this
year, Malcolm said he was back into sailing to "sail just for fun" - he's obviously having a great time even if he's
not taking it too seriously !

On top of the world in the far North West - former MSC member Damian Boreham earned himself a gold medal
when his team won the first 'YRU World Dinghy Team Racing Championships held at West Kirby in late August. Damian and his 5 team mates from the Spinnaker Club (Ringwood) had earlier this year won the UK Selection Trials and thus represented the UK as the UK 'A' Team in the World Championships together with a UK 'B' team from West Kirby which included Russell Peters, recent winner of the televised Ultra Series. Amongst the competitors were national dinghy champions and others in the top level of their national sailing scene.

Mike and Maggie Boreham went up to watch the last 4 days of the week-long event and found themselves witnessing some of the most riveting and exciting close quarter, dynamic and fast sailing action you would wish
to see - and it was all very spectator friendly with viewing stands at the side of the marine lake right alongside
the West Kirby clubhouse.

The UK 'A' team finished top of the initial Round Robin elimination series, losing only one race (to UK 'B’). Thereafter the UK 'A' team won all their remaining races, beating UK 'B' in the Quarter Finals, USA 'B' in the Semi-finals and Ireland 'A' in the Finals after a tense and exciting series of races not without their near disasters and nail biting endings. Eleven teams took part in the event; two from each of the UK, USA and Ireland and * one each from Australia, Canada, Czech Republic, South Africa and Japan. JACK B DRIVERS

Please Note the following points:

Laying Race Marks: A lot of work was needed recently on Jack B_ to restore varnish and paintwork damaged whilst
laying and recovering temporary racemarks. Thanks to the ‘Two Micks’ some additional protection has been
applied to the gunwales of Jack B to make the job easier. It is appreciated that preserving fingers comes before
woodwork. but please ensure that as far as possible the protected areas of the gunwales are used for laying and
recovering temporary racemarks.

Fuel: Please ensure that the fuel tank is left at least half-to-three-quarters full. It was recently necessary to take Jack B
out at short notice to assist the Coastguard. The fuel level was low. but fortunately sufficient to do the job.
Whilst the incident was not an emergency as such, it would have been embarassing to make the coastguard
wait another half an hour whilst the boat was refuelled.

Pick-Up Buoy: On mooring up, the rope on the Pickup Buoy should be wrapped round the foredeck cleat to prevent
the buoy hanging over the side. Leaving the Pick-Up Buoy dangling over the side unravels and ruins the rope.

Many thanks, Ray Ball.

whose performance was not merely ‘good’ or even ‘excellent’. for it was “here comes glorious Daddy” that his arrival

Blossoming Reachers (or Blooming Reachers?)

I must admit to being delighted that Steve and Tom have seen the light and decided to trv a reacher. Caroline and |
have found that it has revealed a whole new aspect of sailing catamarans, and downwind has been elevated from a

After last year’s Piers Race I reported that we'd seen no sign of the kite ‘lifting the bow’. contrary to claims from

Wandering Around The Western Approaches In A
Month Of North Easterlies

After the traumas of the '94 season when following a comprehensive winter refit Muna had got just as far as Dover
before the engine decided to give up the ghost. our aim for the '95 season was fairly straightforward. Simply to get
away. get some decent sailing in and hopefully see a few interesting places on the way . Not having previously explored
the English coast beyond Poole or the French coast beyond St. Male we settled on the general idea of exploring the
West Country and Brittany. The plan was to get down to a line somewhere between Cherbourg and Poole as quickly as
possible. and then take it from there depending on wind and weather. By the start of our trip the prevailing South
Westerlies hadn't been much in evidence for several weeks so we were anticipating their likely return before too long
giving us a slog westwards and hopefully an easier run home.

The saga of last summer's enforced stopover in Dover had lasted until we had finally got away at Easter this year. The
whole sorry tale could only have been called 'Depression Over Dover' including as it did a collision whilst under tow
and a near sinking following removal of the engine. Not surprisingly perhaps Helen had developed a phobia about
going anywhere near Dover but it was something that couldn't easily be avoided. if we were going to get down to the
West Country.

With both our daughters on college vacations and in need of holiday work we weren't entirely sure of the composition
of our crew until just before we left. In the event Laura came with us and we left Jenny behind with some fairly
tentative arrangements for her to catch up with us a couple of weeks later. We locked out of Heybridge Basin at half
past ten on Sunday 23rd July with the intention of starting with a gentle sail to Harwich allowing us to skirt round the
top of the Estuary the next day. As it happened we had such a good sail down the Wallet that we decided to keep going
and ended up after a lively sail. in a falling wind and foul tide desperately trying to continue sailing to Ramsgate in the
small hours. Finally resorting to the engine we made harbour and securing to the Refuelling barge snatched some sleep
before it opened in the morning and we were able to fill our tank. After a walk round Ramsgate we felt somewhat
revived and decided that in spite of Helen's misgivings it would be sensible to make the most of the afternoon tide to
potter down to Dover which we duly did. anchoring in the outer harbour.

contd....

12.

So it was that early the next morning we prepared to leave for Brighton just as we had done a year before. Fortunately
this time the engine roared into life and a ghost was hopefully laid to rest. We were blessed with an Easterly three that
soon built up into a healthy four or five and ensured rapid progress down the coast. With the genoa boomed out we
goose winged in blazing sunshine towards Beachy Head. The only drawback to a perfect scenario was the limited
visibility. At this point I suggested that it was a shame to waste this favourable wind. So we decided to keep on going
and give Brighton a miss. As the afternoon wore on the wind increased and the seas built up to give us an ever more
exhilarating roller coaster of a ride. Once or twice Helen expressed some concern that we had too much sail up but |
felt that we had things under control. As we approached Selsev Bill. well offshore. warnings came on the air of Force
Sevens. We were getting apparent wind speeds in the upper twenties and the seas were building up appreciably. |
began to consider how we could get some sail down with the genoa poled out and the mainsail on its preventer. Then a
particularly violent wave rolled us into a gybe. The preventer parted like a bit of rotten cotton and the mainsheet
snatched across the cockpit catching Helen's shoulder and jarring her neck quite badly. With Laura on the tiller |
managed to get the main down with the wind behind us and set about de poling the genoa which we eventually
accomplished by rolling the genoa up bit by bit until we managed to take the pressure off the pole. We then carried on
sailing under staysail alone still making good speed. while Helen aimed some deserved and extremely meaningful looks
in my direction. and tried to relax her neck. With the wind registering a constant force seven and very lumpy seas it
wasn't the pleasantest of night sails but it was extremely satisfying plotting our progress south of the Isle of Wight and
into Poole Bay arriving off the entrance to Poole Harbour at dawn. The wind dropped and we motored into the harbour
and picked up a buoy. We'd just tidied up when a thunderstorm that had been threatening for some time finally hit. |
have to admit that it was extremely pleasant lying on our bunk under the forehatch watching as lightening flashed and
torrential rain hammered down on us.

After a rest in Poole where we met up with my parents. we sailed with them the next day to Weymouth only to discover
that we had picked the last firing day of the summer in the range off Lulworth. Our enforced detour six miles out to sea
combined with the still poor visibility ensured that we saw little of the Dorset coast. Having left my parents in
Weymouth the next morning we tackled the delights of rounding Portland Bill in a stiff South Westerly (one of the few
we were to have all summer) without catching more of a glimpse of it in the extremely murky conditions. Once round
however the sun came out. visibility improved and we settled on a fairly reasonable slant across Lyme Bay. It was a
thoroughly relaxing afternoon with the wind vane doing the steering and Muna making a steady six knots. There were
no ships and little else to worry about. | kept scouring the chart for hidden dangers waiting to ensnare us. which I was
convinced must be there somewhere. but couldn't find any. Helen decided that this particular chart was a thoroughly
bad buy as there was virtually nothing on it. Having laid the other side of the coast off Exmouth just as it was getting
dark. the wind dropped to nothing and we motored along to Torbay feeling our way right into Torquay courtesy largely
of Decca and then into the Marina. tying up just after midnight.

Just before we left Torquay the next day. Dave Steward arrived in Swiftsure on his way back from Dartmouth having
left the club the day before us. We pottered around to the Dart on what was to prove to be the first of several hot
windless days. not so good for sailing but almost ideal for exploring the rocky shoreline and rivers of Devon and
Cornwall. Once through the impressively narrow entrance of the Dart we were carried rapidly on the flood past
Dartmouth and up to Dittisham. a peaceful and really lovely spot where we picked up one of several visitor's buoys.
Nearly all the West Country rivers we visited were equipped with a healthy supply of these.

Now very much in pottering mode we carried on round the coast in brilliant sunshine but limited visibility to the
breathtaking Yealm and on past Plymouth to Fowey. taking advantage of the settled conditions to anchor in a bay near
Polperro for lunch and a swim. and venture close under the craggy cliffs. Both Helen and I thought that we knew the
West Country well but we were amazed at how different it all was when approached from the sea.

As we motored in flat seas towards Falmouth I began to contemplate the possibility of taking advantage of the settled
conditions and pushing on further than we had originally intended and perhaps get to the Scillies. In the meantime.
suffering from the heat and the continued drone of the engine. we switched it off as we rounded the Dodman and swam
from the boat. This gave us the rare experience of swimming in fifty metres of water and swimming round an
apparently motionless boat whilst the Decca continued to register our speed over the ground as somewhere approaching
two knots. The Fal Estuary had been one of the places we particularity wanted to visit and we weren't disappointed.
We arrived in the middle of an evening race which made things interesting. We spotted Red Admiral and picked up a
visitor's buoy off the Royal Cornwall Yacht Club.

13.

From Falmouth we made our way with just a littke more wind but still poor visibility round a suspiciously quiet Lizard
into Mount's Bay. We considered anchoring off one of the harbours for the night but in the end made for Newlyn
where we rafted up against a fishing boat in for repairs. The pilot books aren't very keen on Newlyn but from our
experience and observations it was a pleasant interesting stop and far preferable to neighbouring Penzance.

We were woken just after midnight by one of the most spectacular thunderstorms we have ever witnessed. It seemed to
remain almost dead overhead and accompanied by torrential rain continued unabated until about eight in the morning.
Somewhere along the line we decided that it would be prudent to delay our departure from Newlyn. It turned out that
the whole of Newlyn had been deprived of electricity and at least one fishing boat had had a direct hit and had lost all
its electrics. Tragically the Seaman's Mission were unable to provide the hot showers and cooked breakfast that had
been highly recommended to us. We later walked into Penzance where we once again basked in brilliant sunshine.

The next morning we were up bright and early and with a North Easterly three to four occasionally five given for
Plymouth on the six o'clock forecast we cast off and headed out of the harbour eagerly anticipating a fair wind and fine
sail to the Scillies. Even as we left the harbour it was obvious that the BBC hadn't got it quite right. We were
confronted by a blustery wind and short heavy seas that even with Muna's weight. we were having problems powering
through. A sizeable fishing boat that had left the harbour ahead of us turned back. Watching his re-entry through the
narrow harbour entrance quickly dissuaded us from trying the same. We were committed. Once we had fought our
way off the immediate lee shore we set about getting some sail up. With some difficulty we had the main up double
reefed and the staysail set. Hard on the wind to bash our way out of the bay. the motion was now far more comfortable.
Then amendments to earlier forecasts started coming over the radio. Talk was now of Easterly sevens that we were
already experiencing. continuing and possibly increasing for the next two or three days. Although once out of the bay
the Easterly would have given us an easy run to the Scillies. the Pilot Books make so much of the lack of good shelter
in The Scillies and that in a good blow you should make for the mainland as quickly as possible. it seemed rather
foolhardy to consider running there in a near gale. Also we now only had a couple of days before Jenny was free to
meet us and so our stay in the Scillies would have been an extremely brief one. All these considerations were debated
as we made our way as best we could across the bay. The only reasonable alternative was to make for Falmouth which
we did thereby committing ourselves to a long slog hard on the wind around The Lizard. Under her snug rig Muna
handled the conditions extremely well. steering herself most of the time without need for any assistance from the wind
vane. and making between five and six knots into extremely heavy seas. As we closed the Lizard the tide turned
against us and our tacks became less and less favourable. On each tack the Lizard would loom out of the mist as if to
haunt us. As evening drew on the wind dropped and we were able to motor sail into St. anchoring in a
sheltered spot just off the quay.

We had arrived back in the Fal in the middle of Falmouth Classics and the next day we explored the Estuary with the
added excitement and interest of admiring and avoiding legions of Falmouth Working Boats. The wind died as the day
went on but apparently thunderstorms centred over The Scillies continued. so we weren't too upset by our decision not
to go there after all. We followed the Fal right up to Malpas and just about managed to avoid running aground in
pushing up far enough to reach the yard at Malpas where Muna had been built. We were staggered by just how
beautiful the whole Estuary but particularity the upper reaches are. We then went to Falmouth Marina where we tied
up between two Saga's also designed like Muna by Alan Pape and we were immediately told that the manager of the
yard had an Ebbtide 33. We also did our bit of celebrity spotting seeing Libby Purves and Paul Heiney on their new
boat. We also saw their old boat Kate O'Malley which was now sporting a German flag.

The next day Jenny arrived and we set off to explore more of the Fal Estuary picking up a visitor's buoy at Malpas and
enjoying a superb walk through the thick forests. From the Fal we made the short trip to the Helford River which lived
up to its reputation as a magical spot. Relaxing at anchor and drifting about in the dinghy. we considered our options.
If we were going to get to Brittany we needed to go soon. Our problem now was once again too little as opposed to too
much wind. Also we were all in an extremely relaxed state and it took a bit of an effort to consider a longish passage.

In the event we left in the morning and were blessed with clear skies and a fresh Easterly. Once clear of the river we
got a slant which took us Clear of The Lizard and which we were able to hold all day, making good progress. We

hardly saw a ship and our only scare was a sudden burst of three very loud reports followed by a dull roaring when
there was nothing at all in sight. and which we eventually decided must have been Concord. The wind died as night
came on but we managed to keep on sailing until about one in the morning when we resorted to the engine. As we
homed in on L'Aber-Wrac'h, the last place on the Brittany Coast before Ushant. the dawn which seemed to be

contd...

14.

extremely late in arriving brought with it a drastic reduction in visibility. With the aid of Decca we located the off
lying buoy but were concerned about proceeding as all the information we had on board emphasised the importance of
picking up the right leading marks and of the folly of entering in fog. Eventually I called up the Harbourmaster who
was extremely helpful and gave me the confidence to proceed. We only really saw the place once we were safely in but
once the visibility had cleared a bit we could see what a spectacular place it was.

After exploring the rocky shore and pressing further inland we decided we had to spend another day there. In the
morning we were pleased we had decided to stay. because visibility was if anything worse. Then out of the murk
Natasha I V came into the harbour. Brian later demonstrated how useful his Yeoman Plotter linked to GPS was in such
conditions. They were in the middle of an extremely comprehensive tour of Brittany and having wintered in
Dartmouth last winter were intending to winter further down the coast prior to entering the Canal du Midi next season.
We then spent most of the day exploring upriver in the dinghy.

Leaving L'Aber-Wrac'h as we had found it. unseen, the mist closed in even more severely and we had a worrying
couple of hours when we could barely see a few yards. until things improved somewhat. We were also contending with
spring tides which were certainly making their presence felt. As the day went on the wind increased from the west and
we had a lively run. with the Decca giving us eight or nine knots over the ground. We rounded Ile De Batz in fine style
close enough to see the rocky shoreline in graphic detail. We then crossed the bay to the newish Marina at Trebeurden
which has been created by building a sill in the opening of a rocky cove. The entrance is dramatic and the whole area
is enchanting. We spent a fascinating day exploring the immediate coastline.

From Trebeurden we had another lively and stimulating sail in better visibility passing inside Les Sept Iles and entering
Riviere de Treguier after some confusion with the marks at the entrance. We made our way up the narrow and
beautiful river arriving at the old town of Treguier a short while before low water. It was fortunate that it was no
sooner, because arriving and departing at the marina. at anything other than slack water. is extremely difficult. The
steep walk into the town proved to be well worth the effort. The remarkable cathedral with its hollowed out spire and
the market square are particularly noteworthy.

After dropping down the river again and spending the night at anchor just inside the entrance we delayed our start long
enough for the morning mist to clear slightly and then set off in a total calm for Guernsey. The long motor was
enlivened by a period of balloon spotting. We managed to retrieve one minus its label and then one intact before
agreeing to ignore the rest. We stayed overnight in St. Peter Port before braving the Alderney races where we recorded
ten knots over the ground under sail before struggling into Cherbourg having gone too far inshore too soon and fallen
foul of the inshore eddy. We were very impressed with the revamped marina at Cherbourg which seems to be capable
of coping with a seemingly never ending stream of visiting yachts.

From Cherbourg we rounded the Pointe De Barfleur and went into St Vaast de la Hougue a tidal fishing port that by
building a single water gate has managed to create a sizeable marina whilst remaining a lovely little spot. We had a
swim in incredibly warm water and caused all sorts of mayhem in a restaurant when I decided to be adventurous in my
eating habits.

An early start saw us hard on the wind and just holding a course for Le Havre which we reached in the early evening
after a satisfying sail. The next day we decided on a shortish afternoon hop round the corner to Fecamp. As we left the
harbour and came out of the immediate shelter of the headland the North Easterly was quite stiff and still motor sailing
Muna set off with a vengeance. As we left the harbour Laura got stung by a wasp. The sting later turned out to be
quite nasty. In the confusion while that was being dealt with we became aware that a woman sitting on a sailboard was
trying to attract our attention, waving her arms frantically. We circled round and made our way over to her and Helen
went on the foredeck to try and communicate. This wasn't easy but it became clear that she wanted to get off. She had
obviously come out of the shelter of the land and been unable to get back in. Now she had had enough. and had
apparently given up. We still had our sails up and were drifting away so we circled round to get the sails down. She
seemed to think that we were leaving and put her head in her hands. We got the sails down and closed in again. By
this time I was aware that she had drifted into the main shipping channel and a ferry was heading straight for us. As
we closed in she got off the board and made to swim towards us. We told her to get back on the board which she did.
We then threw her a line which she eventually secured to the board. We then pulled the board in and helped her onto
Muna. Once she was safely on board we set off to get out of the ferry's way and made our way back into harbour with
the board in tow. We eventually managed to call up the harbour authorities and tell them what was going on. and a

contd...

15.

launch came over to see if the woman was all right. As we passed the beach she seemed to make a recovery and asked
us to drop her on her board near the beach. We felt happier taking her into the Marina. We wanted her to rest but as
soon as we had got the board on the pontoons she went off. When she came back later in the day to collect her board
she indicated that she had gone into shock after going ashore.

Later that day Jenny decided that it might be a good time to get the ferry home. so she left on the night ferry and we set
off for Dieppe. We were once again plagued by poor visibility and little wind. what little there was being North
Easterly. A long motor was temporarily disrupted by a large sack round the prop. which necessitated a tmp over the
side to clear it. Fortunately no damage appeared to have been done and we made our way into the surprisingly pleasant
port of Dieppe. The ferries have now moved to a new outer harbour and the inner harbour is being developed as a
marina right in the centre of things.

After a much needed lay day when I almost scuppered things by draining the fuel filter on the engine and breaking off
the tap on the filter (fortunately I was able to get a replacement with the help of marina staff). we continued our tour of
ferry ports and headed for Boulogne. a place with more interest than its initial facade suggests. In spite of a very early
start that day to optimise the tides. Helen insisted on a walk up to the old walled city which was in fact well worth the
effort in spite of my protestations at the time.

We were now fast approaching the Bank Holiday Weekend which was our intended deadline for getting back. Things
were looking rather more unsettled but the words South Westerly. which we thought had vanished from the English
language were beginning to reappear in bulletins. Leaving on the tide with a West South West Six we raced down to
Cap Gris Nez. We held a right angled course across the lanes and tore across some pretty lumpy seas. By the time
we'd cleared the lanes the tide had swept us nicely up to the Goodwins which we rounded and enjoyed a brisk sail to
Ramsgate in what had now become a North Westerly seven. In Ramsgate we took advantage of the newly installed
marina facilities. the days of rafting up now seemingly over.

With an unsettled forecast we crossed the estuary in mixed weather. A strong North Westerly died away and became a
weak South Westerly giving us a gentle run down the Swin, getting back to a North Westerly Seven as we sailed up
The Blackwater. which seems to be pretty well par for the course. The next day Bank Holiday Sunday was even livelier
as we locked into Heybridge Basin and we had our first full gale warnings of the entire trip. five weeks to the day after
leaving.

1977 (August-December) - links with the past gradually fade as Dugdale-Bradley reminisces

August - a front cover picture of a low-tide scene from the 1977 Regatta describes it as "cold and windy”.

Breeze II - and very pretty too.

As Maggie and I leaned casually against our Wanderer on the hard, patiently awaiting the start of the afternoon
race during mid-July, we cast our eyes with a great deal of admiration, and some envy, at the pretty tan-sailed,
gaff rigged, clinker built dinghy with its smart yellow painted hull and varnished deck and interior fittings. I'm
sure we've seen it a few times before and admired it for the very pretty craft that it is. We didn't recognise the
insignia or, indeed, the helm and crew as they prepared to launch their little craft on what was, by any standard, a
marvellous day to be cruising about in the Blackwater. We watched them launch and plucked up courage to ask
them what class of boat they were lucky enough to sail. "It's a Tideway'", they said, "It's 35 years old". It
certainly looked to be a credit to those who were responsible for its condition (presumably those who were sailing
it) and it gave us great pleasure to watch the duo sail their little craft off through the cruiser lines. The scene
was, | thought, almost idealic with the whole appearance of Breeze I/ (for that was its name) very much a part of
my image of 'the traditional Blackwater’ as a 'waterman's river’ rather than the hurry-scurry of our modern-day
motorised and plastics era of convenience boating.

Imagine, therefore, our pleasure when we read in Yachts & Yachting that Breeze IJ had finished 3rd in the
Tideway Championships (the 28th Challenge Trophy meeting) in June, 1995, at the Dabchicks Sailing Club. The
description of the racing with "...the run down to Packing Shed Island...... The beat back up the Ray channel...."
was evocative of the romance of the Blackwater as portrayed in books. It brought into my imagination the
beautiful sight of these lovely little dinghies racing each other in close company, rather like a group of graceful
water fowl going about their business in their natural habitat. I don't know if those named in the report (Nick
and Sue Hillman) are the same as those we've seen sailing it at Stansgate, but we must congratulate you on the
fine appearance of your boat - and on your fine performance in the Championship.
Mike Boreham

Cadet Week 1995

It may seem a little late in the day to be reviewing Cadet Week. The truth is that it has taken until now to regain sufficient
strength to be able to put fingers to keyboard.

What a wonderful way to start the summer holidays! We have already heard in these pages of the inspiration brought to
Cadet Week by The Remarkable Family Anderson. but what of the rest? Did Hugh Davies survive to the end of the
holiday? Did Dee May get sent to yet another Cadet Week? Did Nadine Debney eventually speak to her mother in French?
Did Mitch Glynn finally find a solid area on the Mirror for his Dad to fix to? Did the King twins at last come across one
adult who could tell them apart?

The weather was so kind to us: Charlie and I weren't sure that we could really cope with so much real live sailing in one
week. All our preparation (who am I trying to kid?) had gone into research for the twenty or thirty pencil-and-paper
exercises that we usually need during extended hurricanes. We completed capsize drill in double quick time. worried more
about sunburn than wind-chill and had to put up with the odd complaint of “Surely we're not sailing again?’ As usual we
were presented with a collection of boats in varying states of “fettle’ - Malcolm Stuart's confidential inspection reports are
available for a modest sum - but the better weather ensured that we did not break as much gear as in previous years.

The noticeable effect of the better weather was the blossoming of both enthusiasm and skills in cadets who in previous years
Just occasionally appeared to be with us under duress (perish the thought!) It was interesting to observe. over just a couple
of days. a growing realisation that there might just be something in this sailing thing after all.

Once again we had wonderful support from proud parents. cordial cat sailors. fine first aiders and itenerant instructors.
Yes. that motley band of students reassembled to form the highly disciplined. articulate and beautifully-groomed Instructor
Force that distinguishes Marconi Cadet Week from the rest. They did a superb job. the kids enjoyed their company and they
even admit themselves that they enjoyed it - at times!

Chris Davies
