SOLO NEWS

Open Meeting. The traditional Solo Open was held at the Club on 10th September 1995. The event was attended by 11 visitors and 11 Members of the home Club, making the largest Solo Fleet at the Club for some years. The morning race was postponed for an hour due to lack of wind. The race started in a light and shifty SW breeze. The order at the first mark was, Gordon Barclay (Chichester SC), followed by Mark Holland (Stewartby Water SC) and Steve Ede (ex MSC now Ardleigh SC). By the start of the fourth and final leg Holland held the lead, followed by Barclay and Ede. Holland held on to win the race, but Barclay was passed by Ede on the way to the line.

During the lunch break the wind shifted from the south to the east and picked up to a force 2-3. For the second race the wind strength proved ideal for Alan Burrell (Ardleigh), he was first to the opening windward mark, followed by Holland and Jerry Garner (Halfway YC). On the third leg Ede moved through the fleet to third spot, then on to second place during the second beat and passed Burrell on the second run to lead at the last mark. However on the final beat to the line, Burrell pegged him back to take line honours with Barclay coming in third.

The rain came in for the third race, killing off the wind. Disappointingly, the race had to be shortened to a single lap with Holland, having pulled away from the Fleet on the run, easily winning from Ede, with Burrell finishing third.

NAVIGANS PAST

1978 (January - June) - Snakes alive ! If a small boy had been a cat with a magnetic personality, would he
had lost most of his nine lives around the Medusa Buoy?
- Red flares (in the sunset?) over Goldhanger offer something far from tranquil in
narrows.

January - The Handicap Fleet notes written by Fleet Captain Pat Black reveal that he retired as Fleet Captain only
to find himself elected 420 Fleet Captain, even though the 420 had not yet been granted Fleet status. Another
group seeking self-rule was the Solo crowd who elected Frank Savill as their Fleet Captain, again before they had actually been granted Fleet status by the MSC. Perhaps they know something we don't?

420 Fleet notes are, not surprisingly, written by Pat Black who explains the 420 fleet had its genesis during 1976
and now boast some 10 boats in the club. John Weedon donated the Blackbird Trophy for the 420 fleet. Pat also predicts the downfall of the Osea SC in the forthcoming season's 420 team racing against that club.

Pat also announces that his favourite series, the Jugs Series, will start at 20.30 hours on 3 February, 1978, in the
Dog and Gun at Great Leighs.

February - Ron Greygoose (Commodore) notes the "night of the big storm" resulted in the river breaking over the
sea wall and flooding the dinghy park and garages to several inches and completely surrounding the clubhouse with floodwater. However no significant damage was done to the building although the sea wall itself was badly eroded in two places and part of the clubs new breakwater (ie. the planks in the seawall gap ?) were washed away.

| also suspect our Commodore has joined the 420 fleet and I can't help but wonder if an anonymous ‘ditty’
entitled Four and Twenty Thoughts might have been penned by Mary Greygoose ?

Four and Twenty Thoughts

"As ‘the boss’ is hovering on the brink of joining Pat's Birds in the drink,
I prepare myself for another season of watching (plus nokkies), with very good reason.
He'll be braving the storm in an unknown boat, I'll pray to heaven he'll keep afloat There'll be our ‘little breeze’ on the trapeze, raring to do with two good knees.
What a lot they'll have to learn - to set the Spinnaker, while fingers burn.
Anyway, good luck to them and everyone who sets off from Stansgate to have some fun.
A
Faithful Onlooker

Russ Fuller writes a cautionary tale about what befell a work colleague of his as follows:-

"Having gone out for the day with a friend who keeps his boat in Walton Backwaters, a day's fishing was completed somewhere near the Medusa Buoy off Walton. The boat carried a compass and torch but not alotmore. The return passage, under outboard power, was commenced in conditions of slight mist.
The owner knew the vicinity pretty well. Pye End buoy came up through the mist, then No.2 Buoy appeared, steering mainly by compass due to the mist. At this point buoys are closely spaced -
everything should be fine. Compass bearing OK - where is the next buoy ? Time passes - open sea
- more time passes - drop anchor. Kept warm in small cabin - 2 adults - 2 young boys. A shore
rescue service noticed parked trailer and starts searching.

Through mist my friend identifies Medusa buoy flashing. Darkness fell - good torch carried, several
passing ships signalled - not seen. Eventually boat passed close - flash SOS. - its the lifeboat -
rescue. Marvellous attention from the lifeboat crew, eventually everyone home safe and well.

Several days later small boy seen playing with magnets. Yes, they were in his pocket that day! Do
some tests, boy moves across cabin - compass swings about 120 degrees. Have your children got any
magnets?"

Ray and Maureen Ball wrote an article describing an RNLI rescue at Stansgate during May, 1977, where two (chartered) yachts ran aground in rough weather on Goldhanger Spit at the eastern end of Osea. We sail this area

so often that it is hard to believe it offers any real dangers but, as Ray and Maureen point out, “it was eerie, and perhaps a little sobering, to see red flares coming from Goldhanger Spit which is the site of such innocent pursuits as our Mud Race". It seems the two yachts had run aground in weather of north-east winds force 6, gusting 8, a strong ebb tide, short, heavy waves up to 6 feet. The crews were taken off by the West Mersea Atlantic 21 ILB and landed at Stansgate. After the rescue. the ILB went upriver to warn other yachts to remain westward of Osea and not attempt the passage through ‘the narrows’. The incident was reported in THE LIFEBOAT magazine.

Rick Anstey (Cadet Skipper) reports more successes with Intermediate and Elementary Day Boat Certificates and
announces that "in keeping with tradition....Cadet Camping Week (will be) immediately after Regatta." with
some navigation tuition on cruisers around Bench Head.

March - Steve Evans (Enterprise Fleet Captain) bemoans the fact that many Enterprises lie in the dinghy park and
never seem to shed their cover (so what's new ?) and Russ Fuller (Cruiser Fleet Captain) reminds everyone of the need to be aware of the Code of Practice for use of Tractor and Winches.

April - The Commodores's Notes records the club's thanks to Mike Taylor and Mr J A Cottam Snr for providing
their services and ‘concrete moving’ equipment entirely free of charge; presumably this arose from the requirements of the work party, Unfortunately, what was intended to be a ‘thank you’ to the Ladies of the club for their help ("Thank you one and all, especially the ladies") went slightly awry as it came out as "especially the
lasies".

Hornet Fleet news records Mike Turner and John Tillotson finishing "a very creditable 7th overall out of 28 entries in very difficult conditions” in the Burnham Easter Egg event.

May - The front cover picture shows Commodore, Ron Greygoose, sailing a Mirror (single handed) in the
Helmsman of the Year Final.

Alas, the Young Peoples party planned for the Friday night before Regatta was called off due to lack of 'pre- booking’ support and it will be replaced by an informal party.

A diagram of the cruiser moorings shows some 76 moorings allocated (included the two club rescue boats).

June - Commodore's Notes records the undoubted success for the 1978 Regatta, with the remark that "for the first
time in living memory, the ‘domestic’ facilities survived the weekend..."._ A special thank you to Cyril
Drakesford (Clubhouse Secretary). It seems Cyril had just decided to take a well earned ‘sit down’ on the sea wall when it started to rain! Alas it seems the water pipe to the Portaloo had developed a leak and started to spray a jet of water right onto the spot where Cyril had chosen to rest his weary bones.

A total of 233 boats entered the Regatta (with 37 from Marconi, 32 from Maylandsea Bay YC and 24 from King George SC) with over 40 clubs represented. The Enterprise Class was the biggest with 43 entries.
Unfortunately, it seems someone had 'borrowed' Dave Lawson's cruiser tender and let it go ‘drift about’,

Amongst Regatta results were Chris Weedon (2nd) and Colin Harper (3rd) in the 420 class and Mike Taylor (505)
3rd in the Fast Handicap Class. Otherwise, Marconi members didn't feature in the 1978 prize list.

Ken Beavins was invited to write an occasional article by the Commodore. He writes "...it would be all too easy
to infuriate members by perpetually lecturing them about conduct (litter, dogs, kids and shut the gate). Have you
noticed how the quality of...bar staff varies from week to week" (Ken's point being that it was good when Jack
and Joyce Reeve did it but not so good when he (Ken) did it). He goes on to mention some of the other tasks which have to be done at the MSC and says "I do wonder though how much longer we should go on without having some more formal arrangement which spreads this work more widely amongst the membership".

A note of dissent in the Mirror Fleet with an anonymous note lamenting the lack of Mirror Fleet news in Navigans. To be honest, I wouldn't have noticed for, truth to tell, we rarely bothered to read Navigans in 1978 even though we had been members of Marconi SC for some 5 years by that time. That was probably because we didn't sail very often and raced even less!
Mike Boreham

Commodore’s Report

The last year has seen further consolidation of the Club's position, with littke material change since 1994, However. as the
investment in 1994 was so great. this is perhaps no great surprise.

In continuing efforts to improve the facilities available at the Club. and to overcome the OOD problem. we decided to recruit a
Steward to run the Bar and Clubhouse on Saturdays and Sundays. I think that the consensus is that the experiment was a great
success, despite the short term duration due to the individual's financial circumstances. With the term coming to a close in
August. the Committee decided that it was not appropriate to recruit a replacement at that stage. but to hold off until the start of
1996.

Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This has been fairly much “on hold” for most of the year. due to Peter Woodhouse
leaving the company and having to step down from his post as Chairman. In addition. recent changes with the departure of
Gerry Wignall. new MASC trustees. and a review of the relationship with other sections bode well for us for the future.

As far as 1995 events go Regatta was undoubtedly a failure. with only some 60 competitors. The Committee has taken the view
that this event will go “on IceTM until demand turns round and we can again man a viable event. On the other hand ECPR was
again a major success. The Club has been mentioned extremely favourably in correspondence in the Yachting press which has
covered the ability of clubs to organise successful multihull events. Other clubs have been criticised (notably Stokes Bay and
Rutland) whilst we have been held up (along with Texel) as an example. This is obviously excellent PR. and probably has
greater value than any advertising that we could do.

Last year I made a plea for “successors” to come forward and outlined the reasons why we needed fresh volunteers to bolster all
the committees, With very few exceptions this has been a complete failure. As a group the membership MUST realise that the
future of your enjoyment of these facilities is dependent upon their successful management. It is no excuse to say that you only
use the Club “a bit” and can’t contribute. That attitude will eventually lead to the gradual and then speedy decline of the
organisation. I believe that every single one of us realises what a precious sailing site we have. and that none of us would wish
to lose it. My warning may appear alarmist. but the average attitude of individuals will lead to this situation. Please search
your conscience and if you can for goodness sake volunteer.

At the end of my term as Commodore, I must place on record my thanks to all the Executive and Committee members that |
have had the pleasure to work with over the last few years. The standard of discussion and sometimes lively debate at meetings
has resulted in several good ideas and decisions coming forward. The Committee is no longer a real talking shop. but very
much an action oriented decision making body.

As last year I have no reservation in thanking a few individuals. Firstly. Jean Flook has decided to hang up her apron after a
number of years of providing an excellent service from the Galley. I should like everyone to show their appreciation in the
traditional way, Secondly, Colin Kidner. who is now passing into retirement as Rear Commodore: his organisational abilities
have been of huge assistance. I hope he enjoys the “rest camp” of the Commodore's role! Finally. again. Frank Bennett.
Frank has again carried out a huge amount of work unseen by the vast majority; from tractor maintenance through the club
radios and electrics to the sewage plant. as well as counting the beans. It has been a great privilege to work with someone so
committed to the future of the Club. and someone whom we should all look to with gratitude.

As you see. I do not escape entirely scot free. some people think that after making this mess I should still be involved as a Vice
President - just as I thought I could put my feet up for a while. You never know, Alex and I might get some more sailing in! It
has though been a great pleasure and privilege to hold the position. and to see the way in which the various interest groups have
become united over the last few years. I wish Colin and his new team all the best. and thank all of you for your support over the
last three years.

Larry Botheras

NAVIGANS PAST

This is the last of my series of Navigans Past. The first of the series was published in the Navigans of January,
1991, and was inspired by the turmoil arising from ‘the problems' of 1990. It set me wondering if the club had
passed through similar phases of divided and entrenched views. I'm rather relieved to discover it had, indeed,
had its problems. The purchase of the floating clubhouse barge Mamgu, the move to Stansgate, the purchase of
the site, the design and building of the clubhouse were all major turning points in the club's history during which
harsh words were uttered and sailing friendships strained. Navigans, of course, only presents the public face of
the debates and the rather more interesting ‘hidden agendas’ and real ‘goings-on’ rarely had even a faint glimpse
of the light of day. In other words, what really went on behind the scenes? Alas, we will probably never
know.

Although I have attempted to collect together as much club archive material as possible, much of the more
interesting items remain within the minds of those who took part in the events of the past. Sadly, many of those
concerned are no longer with us and by the nature of things these sources will get less and less as time progresses.
Eventually we will finish up with a bland formal record of the Marconi Sailing Club which masks the real drama
of what went on behind the scenes and we will have lost all the scandal and gossip for ever - what a pity!

A total of 40 episodes of Navigans Past have been published since January, 1991. I hope you have enjoyed
reading them as much as I have enjoyed writing them.

1978 (July - December) - birds of a feather flock together but wise old birds are clearly hard to beat.

July Shirley-Ann Wood (Editor) takes a philosophical line as she writes "Come rain or shine, the show must go
on". It seems that no sooner had the charcoal chefs started to cook at the annual barbecue and the music had
started to play than the rain it did fall...and fall...and fall...until everyone was too wet to notice any more.
Shirley says "The midnight dip was well supported...(all completely mad)". J must admit I had to re-read this
comment just to make sure I hadn't read what at first glance I thought I'd read.

Mirror Fleet Captain, Deborah Harper, responds to the previous month's appeal for Mirror news with not only
congratulating Vic and Kim Braybrook on winning the Spring Points, but also Malcolm Gandy on managing to
break not only his own centre board but also Deborah's centre board all on the same day. Deborah was still at
school and at an important point in her exams so it was rather difficult for her to give a large amount of time to
fleet captaincy duties.

A note from coxswain Norman Kerridge reminds all (rescue) duty drivers and crew that they should be available
one hour before the races (together with the Race Officer) but also on the water at least 30 minute before the start.

On a rather more light hearted note, Norman also reports on some of the 'birds' he has spotted on the Blackwater
from the comfort of the rescue boat. They are, of course, club members and some of you ‘old hands’ might raise
a wry smile or two as you perhaps recognise a few of them - perhaps even yourself? Norman's list of
"feathered friends" are:-

The Great Bearded Bates - One of the Hornet family. Has great difficulty in flying back to the
clubhouse without injury. Usually flies up the opposite end of the river to the rescue boat. Has a
mutual attraction to fishing lines and hooks. (Murray Bates)

The King Moth Eater - A wild untamed young bird. Spends more time in the water than it does in the
air. Probably won't live to a great age. (Not sure who this is; anyone like to tell us?)

The Orange Savill - A solo bird with an unusual habit of standing up in the water. The female of the
species spends all her time collecting food for all the other birds of the river. Frank Savill and Jill Savill
(who ran the galley in those days)

The Curly Headed Windypeg - This jovial bird is easily recognised - usually amongst a flock of female
birds of another variety. It’s speed across the river is mirrored in the deep red plumage of its female
offspring. The latter looks after the older members of the flock - usually from the rear. (Now who is
, these particular 'bird' family?)

The Blackwater Grey Goose - A difficult one to spot as it's a quiet type but through intelligent use of its
enterprise (sorry) has become the King Bird of the river . (In later years it was renamed the President Bird, sometimes also as the Helmeted President Bird; its faithful companion can often be seen anxiously watching from the bank for its safe return, hopefully with a trophy or two to offer as a peace offering).

Sailing Secretary Bird - Not often seen on the river as it prefers to spend most of its time with its mate in
the clubhouse. Has a distinctive call of "It's a Rojer - It's a Rojer". (Mike Vaughan ?)

The Black and Blue Bird - The colourful female of the species is often seen wrestling with a flying
spinnaker and heard cheerfully chirping under trying conditions. The adult male stays well away but the male chick is a leading member of the fledglings whilst the young female sits gracefully around. (another
‘bird’ family which someone might recognise - and expose ?)

What birds can you spot in 1995 - and what are their chief characteristics ? No prizes for the best ‘spotters’ but
maybe Maureen would allow you to remain anonymous ?)

Dennis Byatt is struggling as Cruiser Racing Captain as he writes "No one could accuse the cruiser
members.....0f being racing fanatics. A cruise across the North Sea to Holland or Calais - yes, but a thrash
around the sticks - not really." He then goes on to try to whip up some enthusiasm for the Barnacle Points
series. One simple race to Herring Point (Please don't say "Where's that"!) and back was supported by only two boats; Dennis in Bill Buchanon's E Boat hotly pursued by Ken Beavins. Ken writes a short piece about his
holiday cruising ".....long tacks all the way home from the Wallet Spitway.....with a stead force 4 in the late
evening and small hours, topped off by a successful night mooring pick-up will take a lot of forgetting”.

A letter of thanks from Sir Robert Telford (Managing Director of GEC-Marconi Electronics Ltd) , upon being congratulated by Vice-President Eric Payne on the award of the knighthood.

A log of the summer cruise of Ace of diamonds describes some pleasant scenes of drift net fishing, rigging the accompanying Mirror dinghy and socialising on neighbouring yachts. It all sounded rather restful; even the
mention of having finished some varnishing....." has, at least for me, a suggestion of an unhurried cruising
holiday in peaceful surroundings on the east coast.

August - the cover picture features the steam tug Brent making her way up to Maldon with Chris Cooper and
Mirror on the hard in the foreground.

The format for Helmsman of the Year is changed for 1978. This year one boat from each class will qualify, with each qualifier's own boat being used on a round-robin basis with only the helm changing boats.

The death of Byron Bridges (boat name /dle Vice) was reported; clearly a man of quiet humour and sadly missed.

The Sailing Sub-Committee agreed (after requests from members) to grant average points to those performing the duties of O.0.D., Race Officer and Assistant Race Officer and Rescue Boat Crew, with a maximum of two such ‘average points’ races per series.

Norman Kerridge (coxswain) reports the new mast on the rescue boat broke after only some 200 yards of its first trip. He also reports that the radio is the worst on the river and seems to suggest some irony in that this should be the case for the Marconi S.C. ! However, the club's ‘radio reputation’ on the river must be reasonably good since we were invited to man the Bridge Radio and co-ordinate the rescue services for the Blackwater & Colne
Championships.

September - in an earlier 1978 Navigans, Ken Bezvins revealed that Commodore, Ron Greygoose, had invited
him to write an occasional series of articles for Navigans. Ken's latest contribution again highlights the eternal problem of a club such as the MSC which tries to cater for all tastes in boating. Ken writes "Last weekend the

tides were right for bottom scrubbing. I was all for beaching near the club but wiser counsels prevailed. Betty's
advice was good for although we were a long way down towards Stone the starting guns, public address
commentary and other noise overspill from the open meetings in progress at our Club were clearly audible to an
obtrusive degree. Anyone who has spent nights afloat on the Blackwater knows that it is often anything but quiet
even in the small hours, and we all know how much din is created by speed boats, but I wondered last weekend
whether it was necessary or desirable for us as a responsible club to contribute so readily to the general noise."

I might add that Ken had been, in the past, a keen dinghy racer and now supported the club's cruiser racing
program so he was not ‘anti-racing' but he was, I think, very keen to preserve the tranquil image of the river in
general, and of Stansgate in particular, as a quiet sailing backwater.

Cruiser Captain, Russ Fuller, points out that, whilst in the older design of cruisers it was normal to pick up
mooring under sail, the modern design of cruisers made them rather less steady or, put another way, they are now
"so skittish" as to make it wiser to pick up moorings under motor power.

October - Commodore's Notes announces that the club's current (and founding) President, Sir Eric Eastwood, is
at last to be allowed to retire after some 25 years in office (having intimated for a number of years that he felt it
was time to do so) and MrJ A Pateman (Managing Director, Marconi Avionics, Rochester ?) was to be invited to
become the new President. Sir Eric had served since the foundation of the club in 1952 and must have been a
very useful ‘contact’ in the early years in getting things done. Sir Eric and Lady Eastwood, and presumably Mr
Pateman, were invited to the 1978 Laying-Up Supper (tickets £6 adults; £5 Cadet Members).

Rick Anstey reveals that Helmsman of the Year was won by a Cadet, Chris Weedon. I'm not sure if Chris was
the first cadet to win HoY ? Deborah Harper won the Ladies Cup which was another triumph for the Cadet
members.

On a person note, I was interested to see that Mike Bees (Brightlingsea SC) won the Marconi Mirror Open (24
entries of which 11 were MSC) in his boat Bumble. Mike Taylor was the highest placed Marconi entry (3rd)
with Malcolm Gandy (5th) and Malcolm Stuart (6th). Those were the days when the Mirror Fleet reigned
supreme - or at least were a force to be reckoned with in the MSC. This might have been the year that Mike Bees
finished 3rd in the Mirror Nationals with Bumble and| still see his name reported by Yachts & Yachting in rather
faster competitive sailing circuits. Later on, we bought Bumble (from a subsequent owner) as our second Mirror
and still have it in our garage.

The cruiser racing fleet's Barnacle Points series was won by Colin Leverage's Bluster, with Ken Beavins 2nd
(Spiridion) and Dennis Byatt 3rd (Roanoke) out of 12 entries.

November - the front cover shows a crowded seawall at the top of the hard on what must have been a very hot day
during the 1978 Regatta. The 'White Hut' looked spick and span in those days and even had a full compliment
of 3 chimney pots. Now, in 1995, it's nice to see it restored to good order. Let us hope it continues to remain a
landmark on the Blackwater. Does anyone know the true full history of the 'White Hut’ (not just myth, legend
or supposition).

A slightly exasperated note from Dave Lawson (Social Sec) who points out that those who think the Christmas
Dance tickets are expensive (£1.20 each) should bear in mind that a professional dance band (how nice, not a
disco) costs in the region of £135 which together with hall charges, electrician, doorman, etc. results in ticket
prices based upon a no-profit budget.

writer concludes we all felt our holiday cruise had been a pleasure, we hadn't covered a great distance but
we had met some nice people, which is probably what a cruise is all about.”

He remarks that some 300 races had been conducted (excluding Regatta) but warns he detects that some of the enjoyment might have gone for the diminishing band of stalwarts who continued to offer their services rather than see standards of the club fall.

Amongst other items of interest, Ron reported that Maldon District Council had requested payment of a licence fee for the siting of the concrete hard and scrubbing post on the foreshore. Other clubs had received similar requests and a combined negotiation team through BACSPA had resulted in a more acceptable licence agreement. As for camping at Stansgate, legal objections to camping had been overcome but he warns the club must be very circumspect in how camping on the site is to be regulated. He pays tribute to Jim and Corrine Coy for organising and laying down the foundation for good camping behaviour. Some problems with our neighbours had occurred due to complaints of trespassing on neighbouring property during busy camping weekends.

The Retiring President, Sir Eric Eastwood, was presented with a small parting gift and also with Honorary Life Membership of the MSC.

David Urry won the Garrett Memorial Trophy and I finish up this series of Navigans Past by quoting the poem written by "a budding young sailor" who was aboard Eric Payne's boat Hullabaloo when he won The Blackwater Cup. The poem was actually given to Eric Payne on his 80th birthday; Eric was, of course, both a founding member and very prominent member of the Marconi Sailing Club:-

Happy Birthday racing Mr Payne
Sailing up and down again.
Hullabaloo, that nice boat,
Winning some of the races afloat.
Captain Payne at the helm of course,
Trying, trying do his crew,
With all their might to sail the course,
Triumphantly over the winning line."

To those old enough to remember ‘the good old days' (whenever you think they were), I hope you have enjoyed being reminded of them and that they bring back fond memories of races won, arguments lost, friendships sustained and enmities forgiven and forgotten.

To those relative newcomers to the MSC, I hope the series has served to convince you that the Sailing Section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club has always been a club of individual high achievement, best endeavours, hard work, great fun but, most of all, a grand place to sail whatever the boating interests and aspirations of a widely diverse membership. Let's keep it that way.

Mike Boreham

Connie Bigden

Many members will be sorry to hear of the death recently of Connie.

Connie Bigden nee Chapman and sister Betty Beavins were always very close. Connie's husband Jack and Betty's husband Ken
were both outgoing characters with a passionate love of sailing. This passion is shared today by their children and grandchildren.
Both Jack and Ken held office in the Club and contributed enormously to its development at Stansgate and to its family atmosphere.
Connie and Betty gave Jack and Ken their loyal and steadfast support and were always seen to be happily chatting on the Hard and
watching over their progenies. Tragically, both Jack and Ken died prematurely. Connie was extremely proud when the new Club
Support Boat ‘Jack B’ was named after husband Jack. Mary has known the family since Betty used to take her to school. Jack
invited me to become Club Bosun in 1964 and persuaded us to try camping in France: and sons Julian and Tim got me started in the
Enterprise Fleet. An era has passed but the family names of Bigden and Beavins will live on in the annals of the MSC for
generations to come.

Ron Greygoose.

CRUISER COMMENTS

The Cruiser Fleet AGM was held at MASC on Wednesday 29th November at which 35 members attended, representing 26 boats.
The Meeting opened at 194Shrs and a resume of events is as follows:

1. Apologies: Colin Kidner (Commodore), Mike Turner, Fred Hawthorne, Brian Court, Ron Phillips.

2. Review of 1995 Sailing Season: Three Cruising-in-Company events were organised: 27-29 May - Shakedown Cruise to
Burnham at which 11 boats attended, staying at Burnham Yacht Harbour, with an evening meal at Crouch Yacht Club. 17-25 June
- St Katharine’s Dock at which 6 Club boats + 2 guests attending making a total fleet of 8. Three days were spent at St Katharine’s
Dock with members doing their own thing, i.e. sightseeing, etc.. with us all meeting up up for supper on the Tuesday evening before
locking out for a trip into the River Medway before returning to the Blackwater at the weekend. 26th-28th August - Walton
Backwaters which was attended by 19 boats. Once again we enjoyed the hospitality of the Walton & Frinton Yacht Club for an
evening meal on the Sunday. Of the above events, 3 boats attended all three events, whilst 6 boats attended 2 of them.

3. Nominations & Election of Fleet Captain & Vice Captain No nominations were received for either of these positions, so yours
truly. ably assisted by Malcolm Yeoman agreed to continue for a further year.

4. Sailing Proposals for 1996: A copy of the letter sent to the Commodore by Ray Hampson resigning as Cruiser Racing
Representative was read out. This post will now be held by Mike Turner who, whilst not at the meeting for business reasons. had
contacted Derek Kirby to confirm this and requested that the question of Cruiser Races be mentioned. This was done and whilst
most Members were not too keen on serious BJRC-type races, there was interest in a more light-hearted approach to ‘port to port’
races, say, three a year for which some form of trophy/trophies may be awarded. Derek Gardiner said he had already spoken on the
subject to Mike Turner and has agreed to speak to him again on the response of the Members present. With regard to ‘Cruising in
Company Events’ it was generally felt the shakedown cruise to Burnham with an evening meal in the Crouch Yacht Club be
arranged for the Spring Bank Holiday, 27th May. With regard to the Late Summer Holiday, 28th August. it was felt a change of
venue would be popular, therefore arrangements are trying to be made for a visit to Woolverstone Marina on the River Orwell with
an evening meal in the Royal Harwich Yacht Club. Watch this space for details of both events plus any others that may be
organised. Members were reminded that notices regarding Cruiser events are now displayed on ‘dayglo’ signs on the Cruiser Notice
Boards both in the Clubhouse and the Dell Bar.

5. Dates for Cruiser Winter Meetings:
Wed 17 Jan, 7.30, MASC. ‘Cruising to the Mediterranean taking the outside route. Ray & Hazel Beckett.
Wed 21 Feb, 7.30, MASC. Details to be advised.
Wed 20 Mar, 7.30, MASC. Details to be advised.

6. Any Other Business Malcolm Shaft said he had again been successful in negotiating a 33% reduction for paints. antifouling
etc.. details in this Navigans.*** Tony Holbrook asked if the Security lights were working properly. I stated that both Mick
Richardson & Steve Glynn had been asked to look into this, and I will check to see if this has been done. Malcolm Yeoman asked if
it were possible to have ring bolts fitted to the scrubbing post to facilitate easier. therefore safer, securing whilst alongside.
Enquiries will be made. Don Holdsworth stated that he has chain & shackles currently in stock, however, early notice of any
demand would help in ensuring this is sufficient for next year’s requirements . He is out of stock in respect of anodes. Should
anyone require these, would they let him know since he will shortly be ordering some more. He also stated that. if fitted correctly,
they do save wear on the chain. The feasibility of organising a coach to attend the Boat Show in January was discussed, but not
favoured. Brian Court who could not attend the meeting had phoned me at home to query the statement made in Navigans under
‘Notices & Reminders’ stating that Winter Storage Fees were to be paid by 30th November. It was pointed out that this referred to
dinghies in particular situations, and that Winter Storage Fees for Cruisers have to be paid at the beginning of each year when
members are paying their Subscriptions. Mooring Fees, etc. next winter's Winter Storage Fees paid by 28th February 1996). It
is hoped we will again be holding a Cruiser Fleet Fitting Out Supper in the Clubhouse around April/May next year. Space, tables
and chairs limit the number to about 60 - watch this space for details.

There being no other business the meeting closed at 2130hrs with the Chairman wishing everyone a Happy Christmas and New
Year.
Derek Kirby - Cruiser Fleet Captain

Letter to the Editor

Cruiser Section Query.

Could the Club hierarchy inform us if any considerations have ever been given to a well-known problem peculiar to
the Cruising Members, albeit not of their making? I refer to racing events through our expensively rented moorings
where never a year goes by without some superficial damage appearing between visits. Of course these events are
rarely witnessed or reported, so proof is not easy, except when they are witnessed!

However, trying to relax on a nice day on the moorings during racing events (as was once the norm) soon puts the
picture in perspective! The general conclusion seems to be that supersonic Cats, i.e. twice the beam, three times the
speed, with corresponding reduction in reaction times, represent the main threats to our expensive pride and joys!

Now I am the first to admit the Blackwater river and our Club location is an ideal site for this rapidly growing fleet
and I enjoy their races and assist in the mid-week racing rescue services on some occasions when I think extra hands
may be necessary. However, with all that water opposite, as well as up and down the river, to allow or to want to race
through our narrow strip of moorings is illogical and shows nothing but contempt for the risks imposed on other
people’s property! Perhaps the state of affairs is down to us, only a load of wimps would do nothing except whinge
about it amongst ourselves!

My 1995 experience when ACCORD (now sold) was bashed, witnessed and reported was interesting! To summarise:
Not so much as a “sorry, mate” telephone call from the attacker’s owner and when I later tried to obtain the insurance
data of the offender from the relevant Club Official, it was refused for reasons you wouldn’t believe!

Any comment from the management?

Ronald V. Phillips

COMMODORES NOTES.

Greetings and may 1996 bring us all whatever we desire! As a Dart 15 sailor I would like at least Force + winds, sunshine
and no rain on every Sunday during the coming season. It would also help if my work load meant that I didn’t have to work
at the weekend so that I could sail more often.

Once one starts with wish lists one can. of course, get carried away to the point when one forgets about other folks and what
they would like, which more often than not is rather a different list!

Can I remind members of a few fundamentals:

|) All craft have the right to use the full width of the river for navigation.
li) The MDC 8 knot speed limit down all the shore line applies to all boats at all times.
ili) The start line for the Catamaran Fleet was moved outside the mooring area.
iV) There is no legal requirement for any boat to be insured. Whilst the Club requires all Members’ boats to be
insured and requests details to confirm that the rule is observed. there is no legal requirement for parties to
exchange insurance details in a marine accident. It would be a breach of confidence for the MSC Registrar to
pass details of one Member's insurer to another.
V) All Club Members benefit from each other.

Perhaps you will allow me to make the following wish: Can we all resolve to be considerate towards each other, both on and
off the water.

If any member feels that they have a grievance may I suggest that if it cannot be resolved informally in the first instance. then
submit the problem to the Main Committee rather than air the problem in Navigans. One could of course put oneself forward
as a Committee Member (or even Commodore)! A volunteer is worth ten pressed men they say!

Best wishes to you all for 1996.

Colin Kidner.

P.S. 1 am looking further into the kind of problem that lead to Ron Phillips” letter in January Navigans. The Cat Sailor
concerned also had some problems getting hold of the information he required immediately after the mishap because it had
been removed from the Notice Board at the Club. It is hoped to look at better ways of ensuring that in any future similar
situation the required information will be more easily available. Watch this space.

Flat Out Fishermen

Last year, whilst in Calais and relaxing after an exciting crossing, I was rocked into reflection over the behaviour of the fishing
boat and its occupants.

It seems that fisherfolk, bastions of the time-honoured marine community, weatherbeaten, windswept. sou wester'd seers of all
things nautical. sons of salts. all own or operate powered craft that have common features. Firstly. as I am constantly reminded
at ports and rivers all around. these craft cannot travel at a speed that produces little or no wash. whatever length they may be!
In the Basin de | Ouest the French pecheurs seem to love shaking their visitors up as much as possible with excessive wash at all
times of day and night.

Eastbourne Marina recently provided us with an English example of full throttle fisherman’s disease with regular wash-induced
rock and roll sessions and. as I watched the phenomenon from the safey of land. a good half of the basin was suffering this
annoyance with some boats nearly touching spreaders.

I sent a letter to the Marina management suggesting a speed limit and perhaps a word with offenders at the lock - No reply was
received,

Has their lot become so bad as to make them join the ranks of the unpopular water user? Are they so used to the roll and pitch of
their boats’ decks that they don't realise the havoc their washes cause’?

Are they always late for something? Can‘t be for the fish because. by all accounts, there arent many left to be caught!

Limpet

CRUISER COMMENTS

Sailing Events: Well, here we are again at the beginning of a new year with all the anticipation that it brings. First. may I wish
everyone a healthy and happy New Year. coupled of course with enjoyable sailing. Arrangements are in hand for two Flotilla
(sailing in company) Events to be held on the Spring Bank Holiday and Late Summer Bank Holiday weekends. Watch Navigans
and the Club Notice Board for details nearer the time. In addition to these it is hoped to organise other get-togethers. some
probably on an ad hoc basis. These are more likely to be picked up from the Notice Boards in the Clubhouse and the Dell Bar.
since we may not have time to get them in Navigans.

Winter Meetings: It is possible that by the time you read this we may well have had Ray & Hazel’s talk on “Cruising on the
Mediterranean’ for which I would like to thank them. Our next meeting will be on Wednesday 21st February when Brian &
Jackie Bouwsher will relate their experiences whilst sailing from Dartmouth the the Channel Islands. and on to Rochefort on the
west coast of France just north of the Gironde. and Bordeaux where they laid NATASHA IV up for the winter which.
incidentally. is where Ray & Hazel started their journey into the Med. Not bad continuity. ech? The last of this year’s Winter
Meetings will be held on Wednesday 20th March. and I am delighted that Nigel Harmer our River Bailiff will be coming along to
give us an insight to his duties. problems and how we can help each other in protecting our environment. He also hopes to bring
along a member of the Policy Planning Department to enlighten us about the Estuary Management Plan and perhaps the River
Warden to explain about his role along the waterfront. I believe the March Meeting to be of interest to all Club Members, and
therefore extend the invitation accordingly.

Lastly. two points of interest from the RYA Eastern Regional Committee Meeting:
a) The Walton Backwaters High Hill buoy in Hamford Channel now has a light. characteristics: Fl R 10sec. position 51° 54°03N.
01°16°07E. This buoy and others in the immediate vicinity are maintained by the Walton & Frinton YC at their own
expense and to the considerable benefit of all yachtsmen who use the waters.

b) CEVNI RULES. Any vessel navigating on French Inland Waters must carry a copy of the Rules. A booklet containing an
extract in English. French and German is now available from the RYA. Entitled “Vagnon Carte de Plaisance”. it costs
£7.50 plus £1 posgtage.

That's all the news for now. I guess I will have to start setting to on “Happy Medium’ now that Christmas and New Year's
holidays are out of the way, albeit I have not yet got round to doing the jobs around the house that I promised Doreen I'd do
during the winter whilst the boat was laid up! Hey Ho!

Derek Kirby. Cruiser Fleet Captain.

Going on from last month's homily. the Code of Practice for Dinghy Owners has been amended. Any member helming a boat
which collides with another must contact the third party with all necessary details. There is a membership list in the bar where
telephone numbers can be found. In case of any difficulties then the Club Secretary should be contacted to obtain telephone
numbers. I have also asked that the Sailing Sub Committee should discuss the problem of High Speed Sailing through the
moorings to seek a solution(s) to this problem.

It seems that there are folk who use the club site who cannot be bothered to get out of their cars and close the gate after they have
entered. If you leave the gate open then the ‘light fingered brigade’ have a golden opportunity to enter the site and leave with
boats and or trailers. I shall not be nice to anyone I see leaving the gate open! You have been warned.

The membership level is causing concerns. We need more members. Larry has kindly volunteered to produce suitable advertising

perhaps you would let me or fleet captains have your views.

and dinners. all at very reasonable prices.

CRUISER DAMAGE- Reply to Ron Phillips’ letter in January Navigans.

Asa novice Race Officer, and an often erratic Dart Sailor, I have a lot of sympathy for Ron, who is concerned about Cruiser
damage from racing boats and Cats in particular. However I think that. with goodwill, sense can prevail.

I find that as RO the easy option of sending the starters to “B’ Mark is usually prevented by the prevailing wind, and I’m obliged
to set a course starting up-river. I understand that all Cats will still be starting outside ‘D* mark in 1996. Most of us hope that
we can send them on a long beat up to but I'd love to put a dog-leg in to keep them clear of Cruisers. However if a mark
to achieve this is put near the pillbox on Osea, then the beating boats can cause chaos crossing the boats coming downriver.
Laying temporary marks just outside the moorings is a problem due to drifting. but could be tried.

5.

Having achieved a start. via No.2 etc.. I'd be tempted to use the space over towards Goldhanger more. (depth allowing) and
would ask that “X° mark is moved downriver to add variations. However even if most of the course is set off the Moorings. those
of us with little (proper) Cats will always want to keep out of the tide if it’s against us, and we do tack in and out of the Cruisers.
especially at the finish.

Committee Boat starts away from the site are not feasible week in, week out, and setting courses a long way from the Club does
reduce the safety factor, especially when one Rescue Boat has to stand down. It has also been pointed out to me that we would
improve our performance in Open Meetings if we had much shorter ‘legs’ as they do at Grafham, but this does mean the Race
has to be near to the Race Box. (If my own legs get any shorter I won't be able to launch the Dart at all.)

I have to confess to putting a hole in a Tender last year. but telling the owner my name and address on the next lap was no
problem, and he kindly repaired the damage to his boat and my pride. His generous and reassuring salutations confirmed my
view that we have an excellent spirit at MSC, and I’m sure I’m not the only one looking forward to next season - not only for the
sailing but all the camaraderie that goes with it.

Best Wishes for 1996 Dick Davies

VAT ON MOORINGS AND STORAGE

The RYA acting on behalf of Swansea Bay Yacht Club has succeeded in a trial case against HM Customs & Excise with regard
to the payment of VAT on members’ Mooring and Storage fees. This anomally has existed since the general removal on sports
activities in 1994. Until we have official confirmation from our local VAT office, the Club must continue to pay VAT on these
items, but I confidently expect to be able to discontinue the charge within a month or so, and then to submit a claim for back
payment as was done with the other Subs components in 1994. It should be realised that some of the gain will be offset by our
inability to reclaim input VAT on associated expenditure. but there is certain to be a net advantage. Assuming a satisfactory
result from the claim I anticipate refunds to individual members for the whole of their VAT for the period from when the tax was
removed from the other Subs. components, plus a useful contribution to Club funds from the earlier period back to 1990. This
will bring uniformity to the treatment of the VAT refund for all subscription components.

THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season, even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats
are out during all Club Races, it may happen that for some reason you can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important
that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. The following advice has been
offered in Navigans in past years:

Wear adequate clothing, i.e. Wet Suit/Dry Suit etc. and Personal Buoyancy.

pnSeBDet
Make sure your boat and its gear are sound.
Ensure Personal Buoyancy and the Boat’s Buoyancy are both adequate.
If you are inexperienced, either in sailing or in our sailing area. please ask advice from
other experienced helms.
: 5. If vou find yourself beginning to feel cold and tired, return to shore straightaway, rather
than wait until you are too cold to think rationally.

IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go
afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day's prevailing conditions, having built up
their skills over the years by going out in gradually more testing weather, but less experienced sailors could have a difficult and
and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races, you should aim to be
entirely self-sufficient, sail within your limitations, and please remember on all occasions that your decision to go afloat, whether
to race or to potter, is always made on your own responsibility.

USEFUL FORESHORE

We have all got used to the Club’s Hard being used to receive casualties as its vantage point and access both from the sea and the
shore makes it invaluable to the Emergency Services. Already this year the Coastguard has co-ordinated several shouts from the
Club.

The first was on 20th January when three gents were lost in their 15° dinghy. convinced they were behind Osea. Having set fire
to some rags soaked in oil on a biscuit tin lid to attract attention (not to be recommended) it became clear from the reports that
they could not be near Osea at all. As the West Mersea Lifeboat proceeded up river it was immediately dispatched to Northey as
this seemed the most likely location. Indeed. they were found and, being cold. were brought back to the Club where they were
warmed in the Coastguard Landrover while we recovered their dinghy.

The second job was on Sunday 25th February when, just after 0230, my pager went off. I am often feeling these days more like
Victor Meldrew and. as I rolled out of bed. I heard myself saying ‘I don’t believe it’. The call through to Thames Coastguard
briefed me to join Dick Townshend (Sector Officer) at, again, the Club. A pregnant Mum on Osea was contracting every three
minutes and with the causeway closed by the tide for several more hours the extrication would have to be by sea or air. By the
time I had stumbled into my trousers and as many warm clothes as I could lay my hands on in the dark. I ended up following the
Landrover and Dick to Stansgate. The decision had been made to use West Mersea Lifeboat again as the on’scene time had been
calculated to be quicker. and as the sea-state was calm. the crossing would not be too bad. As we opened the Club's tide gates.
the Mersea LB and crew went past upriver on their way to the Captain's House steps on Osea. This was shortly followed by the
arrival of the ambulance at the Club and we made ready to receive the patient. The casualty arrived on the Hard considerably
relieved to see the ambulance and waiting Paramedic. Between contractions she was chair-lifted ashore and into the warmth and
horizontal comfort of the ambulance. As it turned out it was someone I know. and she was soon delivered of a 9Ib 20z boy. Ned.
Exactly 30 minutes had elapsed between the initial call and the arrival of the Lifeboat at MSC: my congratulations to Amanda
and Ben as well as to the crew from Mersea LB for a brilliant response time.

My thanks to the Club for maintaining such an excellent facility, but you probably don’t need to be reminded of that.

Charles Anderson

The Tideway Challenge Trophy - Hosted at the Club 25th-27th Mav

Readers may remember that. some months ago. Mike Boreham did a very complimentary piece about my Tideway Dinghy
entitled “Breeze II - And Very Pretty Too’. I was able to thank him when he visited Sailboat *96 and the Tideway Owners
Association Stand at Alexandra Palace. Some 18 months ago I was inveigled into becoming Chairman of the Association and so.
naturally. it was “Breeze II” that was chosen by the rest of the Committee to represent the older boats in the Class. In the event it
Was a most enjoyable. if tiring. weekend. The Tideway seemed to be well received at the show. perhaps this was because it was
the only ‘traditionally built’ boat there amongst the high-tech racing machines that seem to predominate these days.

For those of you who sail these hi-tack (sorry) tech fashion accessories. I will give a brief description of our class. The Tideway
was originally built by L.H. Walker & Co of Leigh-on-Sea. It is a 12° clinker built hull of Mahogany planks on Canadian Rock
Elm timbers. It has a galvanised steel centreplate and . ready to sail. weighs in at about 300 Ibs. A stable and safe boat! The sail
plan is gunter sloop with about 81 sq ft of sail - 90 with the genoa instead of the standard jib!

We often do well at Handicap Racing. helped by the huge P.Y. of 152! Some 500 such wooden boats were built by Walkers.
Tepco Boats of Leigh-on-Sea are the current builders and have built one wooden Tideway which was snapped up by an American
to be sailed at Rhode Island. New York. and over 50 GRP Tideways which are now accepted by the Association and race with us
with no apparent advantage or disadvantage. There is an almost fanatical following for the Class as a cruising dinghy and
training boat. They also seem to last well, with the oldest boat known to the Association still sailing having been built in 1954.
My own was built in 1960.

On 28 previous occasions the Class has met up to race for The Tideway Challenge Trophy. This year Marconi Sailing Club has
kindly agreed to be the hosts for the 29th Challenge on Saturday 25th - Monday 27th May. Racing will only take place on the
26th and 27th, with free sailing on Saturday 25th.

Some of the members of the Association would like to extend an Invitation to anyone who would like to try a sail in a traditional
Wooden or GRP Tideway on the Saturday of that Bank Holiday weekend. So if you are about and fancy a very relaxing sail in a
boat that turns heads because of something other than the speed at which it goes past, COME ON DOWN.

Nick Hillman, TW 42

MORNING FLIGHT’S ‘1994 CRUISE’ - Further Progress - Fourth Newsletter.

Just to bring you up to date with Morning Flight's travels on the other side of the pond. Sarah had to go back to work after her
one year sabbatical was up so she flew back from St Martin in June 1995 and I set out northwards for Bermuda so as to be well
clear of the Caribbean in the hurricane season (a wise move in the light of later events as it turned out to be a very bad year for
hurricanes in respect of both frequency and intensity). Bermuda was very tidy and organised after the vagaries of the Caribbean
Islands. Martin my crew member. described it as looking like a very large golf course. The itinerant yachts in the harbour
seemed to be almost equally divided between those returning to Europe via the Azores and those going as far as Maine for the
summer. We spent ten days relaxing and sightseeing in Bermuda before continuing north across the Gulf Stream to Newport.
Rhode Island. This trip was fairly uneventful except for being threatened by the tail of Hurricane Alison, albeit by then degraded
to a tropical storm. However, by the time it caught up we were safely tucked up in Newport Harbour.
contd....

he

Morning Flight then pointed her bow north again and eventually arrived in Penobscot Bay. Maine. by way of the Cape Cod canal.
We did get sight of one whale north of Cape Cod. Martin had to fly back to UK from Maine. so since then I have been single-
handed except for two occasions when Sarah has flown out to join Morning Flight for holidays. I spent most of the summer in
Maine which is a very friendly and pretty place with a very active sailing community, There was also a number of British boats
in the area with whom I stayed in contact with via the magic of SSB.

With the onset of autumn and after spending six weeks in the UK, with Morning Flight tucked up in Rockland Boatyard. it was
time to head south back through the Cape Cod canal and thence via Mystic Seaport and down Long Island Sound into East River
and Hudson River to moor virtually in the heart of New York and what an experience it was to sail right alongside the famous
skyline. From New York I sailed down to Cape May and through the Cape May Canal and up the Delaware River as far as
Chesapeake and Delaware Canal. This is the entry to Chesapeake Bay which I spent some time exploring before entering the
Intra Coastal Waterway in Norfolk Virginia. The 1.C.W. is a wonderful facility extending all the way down to the Florida Keys.
but it is both narrow and shallow for much of its length. so it is quite wearing to navigate. especially so for a single-hander. and
Morning Flight touched the putty on several occasions and towed other yachts off on others. There are also lots of bridges.
especially so in the south. For this reason Morning Flight’s progress down the US east coast consisted of some trips using the
I.C.W. punctuated by longer legs in the open sea where one could relax a bit and gain some distance on route to Miami. One
highlight of this part of the voyage was a visit to the Kennedy Space Centre at Cape Canaveral with a guided tour of the centre
which included a visit to the launch pad.

Sarah came out to Miami and we spent Christmas 1995 there while waiting for a suitable weather window to cross the Gulf
Stream to the Bahamas. This we eventually achieved and arrived in Bimini to check in before crossing the Great Bahama Bank
to Nassau for Sarah to fly back to the cold of the UK. The water in the Bahamas is beautiful. but also very shallow over the
banks with lots of coral heads. Navigation is therefore mostly by eyeball and only in good light. The tidal range is a maximum
of three feet so it was quite normal to anchor in nine or ten feet of water (Morning Flight drawing 1.8m). After spending time in
the Bahamas and in particular in the Exuma Islands I headed south via Turks and Caicos and thence to the Dominican Republic.
a very poor, but also very green and lush country with extremely friendly people. I had been learning some Spanish en route and
this turned out to be extremely useful in the Dominican Republic and in Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico lies across the famous Mona
Passage from the Dominican Republic. However despite its reputation I had a good sail across to Mayaguez in 15-20 knots of
NE wind. The direction of the trades in this part of the Caribbean means that travelling east invariably involves a windward
passage. After travelling in short hops along the South Coast of Puerto Rico, mainly at night or early morning to take advantage
of the offshore night wind and calmer seas. I arrived at my present location in St Thomas in the Virgin Islands.

The immediate plan is to sail via the British Virgin Islands to St Martin and then to be in Antigua for Classics Week in April
where both Sarah and I are booked in as crew on the S & S (Sparkman & Stephens) Classic Yacht ‘Stormy Weather’ for the
Classic Series races. (Ed's note: She won the 1935 Transatlantic and Fastnet Races according to Oxford Companion to Ships
and the Sea.) Then John Todds will come out to Antigua and will sail with me via Bermuda to the Azores before he flies back to
UK in order to bring Chimo to the *96 Classics event in Brittany. Hope you enjoy this potted account of Morning Flights travels
since we last sent you a letter. (Apologies for the handwritten script but my printer has succumbed to the sea air.)

Please give or print Best Regards to my many friends at MSC and tell them that the kami-kaze Seagull (somewhat
patched) is still alive and well at the port cross trees.

Regards. Dave Beane, Morning Flight (St Thomas. Virgin Islands)

Commodore’s Notes

Sorry about the lack of these over the last few months but pressure of work has meant that I have been tied to my desk writing
material which I hope will help the less fortunate amongst us. This writing commitment has also prevented me sailing.

I hear that the sailing has been excellent this year which is good news. The Galley arrangements seem to be working well, by
and large, but the bar ‘could do better’. We do have this item on the front burner and I will let you know of any developments.

The bad news is that the Club has been targeted by the ‘light fingered brigade’ once again. The compressor has been removed
from the fuel store following a break-in. This follows the thefts, over time. of three tractor batteries and the heat exchanger from
Jack B's engine as well as her radio. Before you say that the insurance covers these losses, be aware that there is a £250 excess
on all claims and this cost has to come from Club funds i.e. from all of us through our Subs.

This is one reason for keeping the Gate closed at all times. Thieves are less likely to remove relatively large items if they have to
lug them all the way to the gate before being able to load them!

If you do hear anything about these thefts, let the police know.

I look forward to being able to get down to the Club to sail during the May Bank Holiday weekend. I hope we will be able to get
down to Weymarks Beach on Sunday 26th May for some fun (and a beach Barbecue?) | think the visit by the Tideways, as well
as a good number of Club Boats on the water should make for a Fun Day Out.

See you on the water. Colin Kidner

COMMODORE’S NOTES

Perhaps a word in the ears of those who go racing on a Sunday and their relationship with Support Boat Crews:

Please remember that Support Boat Crews have a duty to save ‘life’ before ‘property’. I am sure that none of us would want to
put them under pressure to ‘save my boat/help me save my boat’ (especially in conditions where they might be soon needed to
help occupants of other boats in difficulty).

The mind plays odd tricks on us when we are tired. wet and cold. and it’s very easy to lose sight of reality when it’s blowing a
hoolie: there's a four foot chop: the Support boat is on a Ice shore and all one can visualise is one’s pride and joy (the boat) being
lost. The boat can always be retrieved later. Please don’t put lives at risk by insisting that Support Boat Crews rescue your boat
and not you - they know better!
Colin Kidner

WEDNESDAY EVENING PURSUIT RACES

Why not take a break half way through the week with an informal and friendly challenge! The format is an upside-down
handicap race with the slowest classes starting first and the fastest last. The aim is to sail the furthest around the course by the
predetermined finish time.

Starting from the Hard. the slowest class goes at 7pm and. with sufficient boats. the Dinghies and Catamarans can be separated
into two events. This allows the faster Catamarans having too long a wait before their ‘off, Interesting courses guaranteed. but
the wind is not always under our control. The normal Finish Time is 8.15, or 8.20 for Catamarans if racing separately.

When circumstances warrant. the bar will be open after racing. See you there - John Weedon

Well. yours truly is afloat at last. just in ume for our shakedown cruise to the River Crouch. stopping over at the Burnham Yacht
Harbour. | must say their rates are very reasonable: £8 for Happy Medium (9 Meter) per night. also the facilities are superb.

INSURANCE OF OLDER CARAVANS - Article missed from last Navigans.

Dear Fellow Campers, Having enjoyed Camping Fortnight for the past few years in our aged but functional caravan. I was
Shocked to be told by my insurers that now it’s 20 years old they won't cover it. Neither would most companies I spoke to. If it
was a total insurance loss it wouldn't be the end of the world. but I had no Third Party cover either - even as an extension of the
household insurance. Total panic!

What if one of our calm and enjoyable bridge evenings ended with a gas explosion spoiling the Boreham’s chances in Mona’s
Cup? Would they sue? Fears resolved. either go through Caravan Club if you're a member (ta, Bob) or Charles Anderson has
contacts everywhere. I have the number of a Gloucestershire company who will insure older vans.

** But for your own peace of mind why not check your Third Party status for tents and caravans before the red wine starts to
flow.
Dr Dick Davies

CRUISER COMMENTS

Having just returned from a three week cruise to Holland I was reminded by Maureen that this will be the last Navigans for a
couple of months. so | thought I had better get cracking with this report. Firstly may I say Doreen and I enjoyed our cruise even
though the weather could have been better at times. It was a pity we did not have time to acquaint the crews of *Suruca’ and
‘Kelly's Eye’ with some of the information gleaned whilst in Holland, likewise to ‘West Marie’ who we met en route to Ostend
whilst we were going in the opposite direction to Dunkirk. However in each instance we conveyed what we could over the VHF
radio.

Briefly. for anyone intending to cruise the Delta, especially the Veerse Meer and Grevelingen Meer. there is now a charge for
staying overnight at any of the picnic areas or islands. The charge of 7'/; Guilders (about £3) is not unreasonable for the
facilities provided. the problem is how to pay. It seems you are required to purchase an electronic card. rather like a telephone
charge card (and which. incidentally, can be used to make telephone calls), Thus armed you locate one of these machines to
purchase your ticket. It seems most of these machines are near car parks since they can be used for car parking as well. I must
also add the tickets purchased for the Veerse Meer will not do for the Grevelingen Meer, these have to be bought at locations in
the Grevelingen Meer. We were fortunate in arriving carly in the season when things are quieter, I feel it is going to be
mayhem during the height of the season, since many yachtsmen. including other nationals seem unaware of the situation. It is
difficult for

me to cover it clearly in Navigans. but if anyone is going to Holland and wants some information in more detail. please contact
me. or failing that. enquire on arrival at somewhere like Middelburg. There is an excellent publication (free of charge) called
‘Recreational Navigation 1996° which provides information of VHF channels. Locks. Bridges, weather forecasts. etc. I have a
few copies if required.

As mentioned at the beginning there will not be a Navigans next month, therefore may I draw your attention to the August Bank
Holiday cruise to Ipswich on 24th-26th August. The plan is to leave the moorings at 08/30 on Saturday and lock into “Neptune

On Sunday | have arranged a tour of Tolly Cobbold Brewery starting at 12 noon which includes lunch after which we leave the

Brightlingsea or West Mersea has been arranged at short notice.

RNLI - Local News

The Burnham Lifeboat Station is being allocated an Atlantic 75 inflatable Lifeboat scheduled to arrive on the Crouch just before
Burnham Week (the last week in August). It will be housed in a floating boat house in the Marina, and the existing Class D Boat
will be retained in its Boathouse behind the Royal Corinthian. The suitably modified Severn Class Lifeboat (a new Class that has
had a few teething troubles) will be on its station at Harwich in the autumn and in the meantime the Waveney continues in use
there.

Two recent editions of °999° on BBC TV showed Walton Lifeboat becoming entangled with the mast of a yacht breaking up on
the Gunfleet Sands - what a baptism for the new Cox'n - and another Service at Palace Pier Brighton. Having many years ago
played wave-dodging in that last area I could well understand how it occurred. The state of the Atlantic 21 and the fact that three
medals were awarded for the rescue gives an idea of how horrific the conditions must have been. (A risky operation for all
concerned when two girls were plucked to safety from the supports of the pier in rough seas - this was after the Lifeboat’s bow
and port sponson had been punctured and deflated).

You will not need reminding that the entire cost of running the RNLI is met by voluntary contributions - not by the government.
Amongst many ways of contributing to funds is buying from the RNLI catalogue. To help the Maldon Branch, within whose area
you sail. can you add to your Order Form our Branch Reference 61 42 54. It will not cost you anything but it will help us. If you
are not already a member of the RNLI then please consider joining and supporting what is sometimes described as the ultimate
insurance policy.

Commodore’s Notes

I am sure that some of you will be aware of the incident which occurred off the Club foreshore during the East Coast Piers Race
when the helm of a yacht suffered a severe heart attack. the crew were extrememly distressed and needed help. Fortunately the
River Warden, Christopher Reynolds-Hole was passing the yacht and was able to go aboard and make a call for help to the Club
(the crew of the yacht being unable to use the radio or distress flares). I have spoken to the River Warden who was very
complimentary about the assistance which various Members of the Club gave. I have also received a letter of thanks from Dick

YOUR CLUB NEEDS MORE RACE OFFICERS AND ASSISTANT RACE OFFICERS

Like all voluntary organisations, this Club needs the active co-operation and help of all its Members. Without the Race Officers
and their Assistants no racing would be possible. and racing is the reason most of the dinghy and catamaran owners joined the
Club. The number of qualified Race Officers has dwindled to such an extent that many are doing 3 or 4 duties this season. I
think that is too much. A similar problem exists with Assistant Race Officers, we desperately need more people to help out.

In an attempt to address the problem I have produced a revised list for the last part of the season. I know those concerned will
say it is short notice and the day nominated will not suit for lots of perfectly good reasons. However, if you have a problem.
please swap with someone else. Leaving me a message saying you can't do a duty on a particular day does not help me or the
Club. and I am NOT going to spend hours on the phone trying to find a substitute - that is your job.

The situation would be helped if those sailors who know they have not done a duty, or enough duties, could contact me and
VOLUNTEER. Many of you, I know are on the Support Boat Roster and will not wish to do another duty. However, no racing
can take place at all without a manned race box.

On a personal note | feel that having 5 people manning 2 rescue boats every Sunday is excessive. The responsibility for safety
lies, in my view, entirely with the helmsman of the dinghy or catamaran. Rescue Boats should only be required in extreme
situations and then only for saving life and limb. Salvaging boats is a bonus, not a necessity. By taking so many members for
rescue duties, the pool available for the Race Box is dramatically reduced. Surely in winds below 15 knots we only need | boat
with | or 2 crew. If the wind does pick up I am sure we could find volunteers on the day who did not want to go out, but would
be happy to help in a Support Boat.

Finally, perhaps some of the Cruiser Fleet might want to help out at the beginning or end of the season, or if the wind is too
strong or too light to sail.

This all sounds like the usual grumble from a Committee Member but I, like all of you, joined the Club to sail. After allowing
for work and domestic commitments it is frustrating to find that you have duties on perhaps 20% of your available sailing days.
Remember, there are only 41 race days in a season.

So please contact me, either at the Club, Dart 15 Sail No. 1704, or by plane 04 G1621-826953.

Rob Davies, Sailing Secretary.

CRUISER COMMENTS

In spite of the dubious weather forecast. 18 Cruisers made the trip from MSC to Neptune Marina, Ipswich, on the Saturday of the
Bank Holiday Weekend. making a formidable flotilla on entry to the Marina. In fact other visitors calling up the Harbour Master
on VHF requesting entry were requested to wait until the Marconi fleet had entered, such was the effect our collective arrival
made. We even had a reception committee waiting to take our lines by way of Peter Clayton (‘Peace’) and John Todd (*“Chimo’)
waiting to take our lines.

Monday was a lay day with a tour of Tolly-Cobbold and lunch organised, followed by a guided tour of the historic Dockyard for
which we were joined by the crews of “Silver Pearl’ and ‘Two Jays’ who came round by road. Sadly. some of the fleet had to
return home on the Monday: however it was great that 11 of the Cruisers were able to join us for the rest of the week for a trip up
the River Deben to the Tidemill Yacht Harbour at Woodbridge. It was while there that we had the mother and father of
thunderstorms and gale force winds which kept us holed up there until the Friday, but if you have to be weather bound, I cannot
think of a nicer place to be.** The only problem was, it put paid to the Bar B Q planned to be held at ‘The Rocks’ just above
Ramsholt on the Thursday. However. we made up for it with a good meal and get-together in “The Bull’ at Woodbridge. Most
of the fleet stopped off at Brightlingsea on the way back on Saturday: we on the other hand had a family engagement on the
Saturday and had to hot foot it back to MSC. the rest of the fleet arriving on Sunday in glorious sunshine. It was great to see so
many boats and members attending and clearly, from the feedback received, everyone enjoyed themselves.

Whilst on the sailing mode, I am arranging an end of season (for me at least since I intend to lay up ‘Happy Medium*® on Monday
30th September) Cruise to Brightlingsea, including dinner in the Colne Yacht Club on Saturday 28th September. High water is
about 14.00 so I expect we will leave the moorings about mid-day. Exact details yet to be confirmed with the Harbour Master
with regard to berths. Also the water taxi will be running so you need not take dinghies. The only point I would make is that
should the weather prevent members from sailing to Brightlingsea, they make arrangements to go round by road for the evening
meal.

Cruiser Winter Storage: As intimated I am sadly having to turn my mind to the Winter Lay Up, and from indications received
so far, there is an increased demand for the space available in the Cruiser Park. The chart for Cruiser Winter Storage 1996/7 will
be displayed on the Cruiser Notice Board by the end of September, together with the “Hauling Out List’. Please make sure when
hauling out you have made arrangements with the Tractor Driver in advance. Please don’t just turn up and expect it to happen.
As far as space allocation is concerned may I please make it clear that spaces wiii only be a!located to those who have paid for
Winter Storage. To this end I work on a list provided by Liz Hill, so please do not contact me until you have paid. Any
trailers/boats in the Cruiser Park not having been paid for will be removed and the space re-allocated.

As always we will be having a monthly get-together during the winter months. with the exception of December. Unfortunately, I
am unable to book the MASC Conference Room on Wednesdays, and rather than settle for the more cramped room, I have
decided to move the Meetings to Thursdays commencing with the Cruiser AGM on Thursday 21st November. The other
Cruiser Winter Meeting dates will be Thursdays: 16th January, 20th February & 20th March.

OPERATING THE FLOODGATES

We were approached one evening recently at the Club by a Cruiser Member who had arrived to go onto the water and found himself, in the dark, faced unexpectedly with the Floodgates closed (as they now must be until Ist May next year). After Ray described the method of opening the gates, the member suggested in a discussion with me that (a) all Members ought to be shown how to use the Floodgates and (b) full information on them should be published in the club circular. Though it is obvious how the gates work by looking at them (in daylight), I agreed it might be
useful to put a few pointers in Navigans - a couple of which
genuinely might not be all that obvious.

1. For those of us without the strength of an ox, the Floodgates are much
easier to operate than the old Floodboards.
2. If you are faced with closed Floodgates in the dark and haven’t had
much practice using them, you will need a torch or your car headlights to see what you're doing. A practice run in daylight is even better and/or ask for a demo from a seasoned Cruiser member before the need arises.
The Floodgates are never locked by the Sailing Club and no key is required to open them.
+. Looking at the closed Floodgates from the landward side:

(a) The gate on the left is held in the closed position by a large square bolt
which drops into a square slot in the ground and the bolt is raised and lowered by the winding handle on top of the left hand gate. When closing, this gate must be closed first.
Clockwise turn of the handle raises the bolt to open the gate Anticlockwise turn of the handle lowers the bolt to secure the gate in the closed position.
There is a hinged metal plate which can be dropped across the slot in the ground when the gate is open to keep it
Clear of stones, litter etc.

(b) The gate on the right is held in the closed positon by a lever
which engages with the closed and bolted left-hand gate.
5. To take a tender through the gap, opening the right hand gate
only should be sufficient and will save time.
6. Always close the gates after use at the times of year when they
should be closed - this information is painted on the gates.
The Club has a duty to keep the Floodgates closed during the winter (1st September 96 to Ist May 97) in order to keep any exceptionally high tides out of the site and the surroundi ng countryside. The mention of Floodboards on Page 5 of
the
Yearbook refers to the Floodgates.
7. It requires a dit of physical strength when closing the gates, to
pull each gate
firmly to its closed position as you lower the left-hand gate bolt or the right-hand gate lever. Most could manage it single-handed but a helper makes it easier,
8. If there is a strong onshore breeze blowing, make sure you open
the gates right back against the wall. I was suprised to see
that they can be blown shut - on anything passing through the
gap.

I'm afraid it wasn't much use on that particular evening informing
an unprepared Navigans Editor that she should know - then
and there in dark - how to open the gates. She'd Jorgotten what she'd practised
at least a year earlier. She also claims to belong to the last generation we are likely to see of helpless females and she still looks to the men in her householdfor
most
technical matters. However, she’s since had another practice, for the purpose of these instructions, and could probably do it
now!

The last of our organised Cruises was due to be held on the weekend 28th-29th September with a sail to Brightlingsea on the
Saturday with an evening meal in the Colne Yacht Club. culminating in a pleasant sail back to the moorings on Sunday. That
was the plan! Unfortunately the weatherman had other ideas and whilst the weather for Saturday would have given us a pleasant
sail to Brightlingsea. the forecast for Sunday was not so good so. reluctantly. twenty of us took the long route and arrived by road.
However. two boats did make the trip. namely. AVOCET and JULIET WHISKY so full marks to them. The one
