remove as much equipment as possible from your boat. Personally. 1 gut the boat completely. leaving curtains open
showing all lockers open and empty. I know it is a bind but I feel it is worth it. Please. please. remember to LOCK UP

THE BLACKWATER PROJECT

After 3 years of consultation and preparation the Blackwater Estuary Management Plan was officially launched in July of this
year, A full copy of the Plan. for members to read. is available in the Clubhouse lounge at Stansgate. It is also available to view
in local libraries and in the Maldon and Colchester Planning Departments. It is well produced and covers a wide range of topics
and interests related to the sustainable use of the Estuary and its surroundings..

The interests of the Sailing fraternity have been channelled. in the main. through the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection
Association. BACSPA of which the Marconi Sailing Club is a longstanding member. BACSPA also has representatives on the
Eastern Region Committee of the RYA. The primary concern of BACSPA is the conservation and protection ofthe Rivers in the
interest of sailing and other watersports. As a result of the extensive consultation and involvement of local interest groups such
as BACSPA the Plan has achieved widespread support.

The Plan is expected to evolve with ume and be modified to meet new and changing requirements. It is recognised that the
project will be judged on the speed and effectiveness of the implementation process. An Implementation Forum is to be held
annually to formally assess progress and make new proposals. The main thrust. however. will be the continued use and
involvement of local interest/topic groups to actively implement and progress particular aspects.

The first Implementation Forum was held on 24th September 1996 where both BACSPA and Marconi SC were represented.

The Blackwater Project team also issues a free quarterly newsletter entitled “The Blackwater Matters’. The object of this
publication is to keep everyone up to date with what's happening on and around the Blackwater Estuary. Copies ofthis are also
available at Stansgate. Perhaps one of our members could contribute an article”?

If anyone would like to Know more about the Estuary Plan. or have any suggestions to make. please don’t hesitate in coming
forward,

Take two grown men who should know better, a handful of sleepy students and forty-odd enthusiastic kids and you've
got the basics of Cadet Week. Of course you need the support of parents and helpers ... and a few seaworthy dinghies.
too. And you pray for good weather.

is. we find. often quickly followed by the realisation that there are insufficient dinghies... but not this time.

awarded - no Cadet 1s allowed
to go away empty handed. Despite the usual wide spread of ages. everybody learned
something and many made significant improvements in their skills and abilities. A list of the main awards appears
below.

Thanks again to the many people who contributed to the success of the week. So far as we can tell. a good time was had
by all and once again we two managed to escape the Awards Ceremony intact. Can our luck hold? Should we risk
another vear? Well. maybe the one.......

Commodore’s Report

The last year has seen further consolidation of the Club’s position, with little material change since 1994. However, as the investment in 1994 was so great, this is perhaps no great surprise.

In continuing efforts to improve the facilities available at the club, and overcome the OOD problem, we decided to recruit a Steward to run the Bar and Clubhouse on Saturdays and Sundays. I think that the consensus is that the experiment was a great success, despite the short term duration due to the individual’s financial circumstances. With the term coming to a close in August, the Committee decided that it was not appropriate to recruit a replacement at that stage, but to hold off until the start of 1996.

Moving on to our relationship with MASC. This has been fairly much “on hold” for most of the year, due to Peter Woodhouse leaving the company and having to step down from his post as Chairman. In addition, recent changes with the departure of Gerry Wignall, new MASC trustees, and a review of the relationship with other sections bode well for us for the future.

As far as 1995 events go Regatta was undoubtedly a failure, with only some 60 competitors. The Committee has taken the view that this event will go “on Ice” until demand turns round and we can again run a viable event. On the other hand ECPR was again a major success. The club has been mentioned extremely favourably in correspondence in the Yachting press which has covered the ability of clubs to organise successful multihull events. Other clubs have been criticised (notably Stokes Bay and Rutland) whilst we have been held up (along with Texel) as an example. This is obviously excellent PR, and probably has greater value than any advertising that we could do.

Last year I made a plea for “successors” to come forward and outlined the reasons why we needed fresh volunteers to bolster all the committees. With very few exceptions this has been a complete failure. As a group the membership MUST realise that the future of your enjoyment of these facilities is dependent upon their successful management. It is no excuse to say that you only use the Club “a bit” and can’t contribute. That attitude will eventually lead to the gradual and then speedy decline of the organisation. I believe that every single one of us realises what a precious sailing site we have, and that none of us would wish to lose it. My warning may appear alarmist, but the average attitude of individuals will lead to this situation. Please search your conscience and if you can for goodness sake volunteer.

At the end of my term as Commodore, I must place on record my thanks to all the Executive and Committee members that I have had the pleasure to work with over the last few years. The standard of discussion and sometimes lively debate at meetings has resulted in several good ideas and decisions coming forward. The Committee is no longer a real talking shop, but very much an action oriented decision making body.

As last year I have no reservation in thanking a few individuals. Firstly, Jean Flook has decided to hang up her apron after a number of years of providing an excellent service from the Galley. I should like everyone to show their appreciation in the traditional way. Secondly, Colin Kidner, who is now passing into retirement as Rear Commodore; his organisational abilities have been of huge assistance. I hope he enjoys the “rest camp” of the Commodore’s role! Finally, again, Frank Bennett. Frank has again carried out a huge amount of work unseen by the vast majority; from tractor maintenance through the club radios and electrics to the sewage plant, as well as counting the beans, it has been a great privilege to work with someone so committed to the future of the Club, and someone whom we should all look to with gratitude.

As you see, I do not escape entirely scot free, some people think that after making this mess I should still be
involved as a Vice President - just as I thought I could put my feet up for a while. You never know, Alex

12.

and I might get some more sailing in! It has though been a great pleasure and privilege to hold the position,
and to see the way in which the various interest groups have become united over the last few years. I wish
Colin and his new team all the best, and thank all of you for your support over the last three years.

Larry Botheras

training sessions will be held. This will continue next session. hopefully reducing the burden further.

Finally. I would like to thank all the Race Officers. their assistants and the Support Boat crews for their efforts this
season.

COMMODORE’S REPORT 1996 Colin Kidner

1996 has not been a good year for me and sailing. I have not been able to spare the time to get down to the club at weekends.
Those of you who read my notes in Navigans will know that I have been a victim of the continuing change in the education field.
I sincerely hope that 1997 should see an end to the results of change. which will mean I have to work less and can play more at
weekends.

I should like to deal with the negative side of the Club first.

The access road to the Club is a cause for concern. The repairs to the damage which the NRA traffic caused are not satisfactory.
Privatization has its down side. The NRA is now called the Environmental Agency and seems to be playing “hard to get’ over
the road repairs. I suspect that the grip which is being put on public spending by the government has something to do with the
reluctance of the Environmental Agency to agree to do something about the poor reinstatement work done by the NRA. to the
access road. I have to thank Larry for taking on the task of dealing with the Environmental Agency and trying to get some
redress. So far he has no success. What we need is a high profile barrister to help fight our claim.

The second half of camping fortnight seems to be a cause for concern. Some Club Members are of the opinion that there is a
lack of control and order which results in club facilities being abused. Others are of the opinion that this is a time for relaxation
and enjoyment and do not do not feel that there is a problem. The arguments will be considered in the next few months. so any
ideas which members may have will be gratefully received by the main committee to allow full and frank discussions to take
place in order to resolve any difficulties.

Now the good news.

[ wish to put on the record my sincere thanks to all Club Members and particularly Executive and Committee members who
have worked to ensure that the Club ‘works’ for us all. I have no hesitation in mentioning the work done by Frank Bennett in
spite of a very serious accident earlier in the year. Fortunately Frank is now well on the way to a full recovery. Ironically this
accident led to Frank looking at our Club Insurance and to his horror he found that Club Members were not covered for
‘waterside activities’ I am pleased to say that this oversight has now been remedied.

Management of the MASC and its finances seem to be under much tighter control. I feel confident that the future of MASC
remains assured. Mr Brocklesby and Mr Marsh visited the Club during Camping fortnight and saw the results of the hard work
done by MSC members. They were impressed.

The membership has gone over the 400 mark this year. which means that the Club finances will remain healthy. It is intended
to run the series of advertisements in Yachts and Yachting again and to signpost the Club whilst this campaign is running.
This tactic resulted in members joining the club.

I hope you all agree that new Galley service provided by Mark Fletcher has been a great success. I am confident that this
service will continue next season together with an improved bar service. The latter will depend on agreeing mutually
acceptable terms and conditions with Mark.

I have to pay tribute to Charles Anderson and Chris Davis and their team of helpers for their efforts in running a very
successful Cadet Week. I believe some 40 young people took part. learnt a great deal and had a great time. Congratulations
Charles and Chris and many thanks. It is through these activities that the enjoyment of sailing is allowed to develop in the
minds of young people. Enthusiastic youngsters will be the life blood of the sport and this Club in the years to come.

I am sure that you will all join me in wishing Jo Jo Anderson and her helm. Dominica, every success in the Cadet World
Championships in Bombay during December. I look forward to seeing many club members at the Curry Evening on the 29
November at 7.30pm at MSC. I understand that both girls will be at the curry evening and I urge you to attend so that you can
meet them and wish them the very best of luck.

ECPR was again a successful event. and allows the Club to work as a team in running a high profile sailing race as well as
raising money for RYA Sailability. Thank you Mike and your team, who organised and ran the event. I would like to pay
special thanks to the Cruiser Fleet for their support in providing the mother boats between here and Walton on the Naze.
Without your support the event could not take place.

Next year will be the tenth anniversary of the ECPR and we are looking forward to a bumper entry from the continent if all
goes well. It is hoped that the Prindle and Nacra European Championship will occur just before or just after the Piers race so
that continental sailors can attend ECPR and Championships and only have to make one trip across the Channel.

Keith Starky works very hard every month sending out Navigans to us all. He has had to relinquish this task for reasons
connected with his work. Thank you Keith you have done a great job. This means we are looking for a Club Member to take on
this task. See me or put your name on a post card.

My hope for the future is that all members of the Club can work together so that the interests of all Club Members can be
advanced in 1997 and beyond.

Remember. sailing has been around for a long time. In 7000 BC., Greek seafarers sailed to the Aegean island of Miles, 75
miles from the mainland. to obtain obsidian. Let's hope that Marconi Sailing Club will be around long into the future.

RNLI SPONSORED ROWING RACE

This annual fun event is taking place on Boxing Day. Thursday 26th December 1996. Start time 12.30 hrs from MLSC
Clubhouse. Hythe Quay. Maldon. Race is over a distance of 5km.

Entry fee for boats taking part is £1, and the real funds are raised when those taking part get sponsorship from family. friends
and work colleagues. etc. Over £6.000 was raised by the event last year.

The Classes are: Men’s Singles or Men’s Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Men’s Multiple.
Ladies Singles or Ladies Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Ladies Multiple.
Mixed Pairs in either Yacht Tenders or Non-Yacht Tenders: Multiple Mixed.
Anyone mad enough to row a Rubber Dinghy.
Under Fifteen.

Prizes include: Fastest Men’s/Ladies Boat: Best Fancy Dress: Panther Award for Highest Sponsorship Money Raised:
Cadet Class Trophy for Under Fifteens

Sponsorship Forms and Entry Forms required by those taking part are available from Michael McCarthy. [redacted]

For the less active among us it is an enjoyable event for the many spectators who come along to watch - you just need to dress up

Refreshments available and 2 pubs very close by.

CRUISER COMMENTS

It is possible that by the time you read this the Christmas Festivities will be a pleasant memory and we are now either into or
approaching the New Year, so first of all a Very Happy New Year to you all.

The Cruiser Annual General Meeting was held at MASC on Thursday 21st November and was attended by 47 members
representing 33 craft, with apologies received from Mike Egerton. Pete Sayer. Mark Whitely, Roy Bellord and Mike Turner.

Cruises in 1996. The meeting commenced with a review of the 1996 Sailing Season starting with the Fleet Cruise to Burnham
(16 boats): Neptune Marina. Ipswich (18 boats with 11 boats staying on for a cruise up the River Deben to Woodbridge.) The
final event was to have been a Cruise to Brightlingsea, however, the weather intervened resulting in the crews of 10 boats
making the trip to the Colne Yacht Club by road whilst 2 boats “Juliet Whiskey’ and Avocet’ did make the passage. Twenty
Five Members that evening sat down to a fish and chip supper plus a jug or two.

Cruiser Racing. The introduction of Races or Chases on the back of Club Cruises is proving popular and credit to Mike Turner
& Derek Gardiner for bringing in this new dimension to our sailing events. Prizes were awarded for the following:

Freshers Chase: Ist Moonfleet 2nd Timari Two 3rd Gintrap
Mid Summer Chase: Ist Timari Two 2nd Petronella 3rd Gintrap
Fancy Dress Chase: Ist Moonfleet 2nd Ocean Slipper 3rd Reflections
Green Man Chase: Abandoned due to weather conditions but consolation prizes awarded to the four entrants.
Overall Winner: Barnacle Trophy awarded to Moonfleet.

ECPR. Once again the Cruiser Fleet gave their support to the East Coast Piers Race for which a special vote of thanks was given
by our Commodore at the Club AGM and was recorded on last month's Navigans.
Winter Storage. With the Winter Laying Up now complete, attention was drawn to the limited space available for what seems to
be a growing need. This will have to be addressed to the Main Committee. The need of Cruiser Members to observe
the security code was stressed as was the case of maintaining trailers, plus the need to fix towing eyes on both ends of
the trailer if not already fitted.
Paint. Chain & Shackles. Malcolm Shaft will be ordering Paint, and Don Holdsworth will be ordering Chain, Shackles, and
Anodes so please get your orders in early.
Fleet Captain & Vice Fleet Captain. Yours truly and Malcolm Yeoman respectively were re-elected to these posts, with Mike
Turner and Derek Gardiner again looking after the Cruiser Racing Events.
Cruises in 1997. Tentative arrangements are in hand for Mayday Weekend (4th-6th May) to Brightlingsea; Spring Bank
Holiday (24th-26th May) to Burnham: August Bank Holiday (23rd-25th August) to River Orwell, either
Shotley or Wolverstone Marina and for those who can take the rest of the week off another trip up to
Woodbridge. Watch out for details in Navigans nearer the time.

very little quality sailing time on the Blackwater. This year I managed to get my Silhouette launched. and sailed a little. but

I made all the long-distance arrangements to recover on the last weekend in October. and flew home especially. Murphy's Law
operated. as might be expected. and after a tiring and frustrating day. she had moved from F11 to C4 and had lost the outboard
prop!
Just before my outward flight. I phoned Peter Clayton to ask him to try to arrange for her to be towed back to my own mooring,
more in hope than in...whatever.

To cut the saga short. when I later got in touch with Peter. he. together with an unknown band of heroes. had actually recovered
the boat. Special thanks to Ian (?) who went into the water. I believe. To say that I was relieved and grateful would be an
understatement. as I had no idea how I was going to arrange matters at a distance and was getting pretty worried about the
situation. Please express my appreciation through the pages of the newsletter.

Bryan Simpson, Co. Tipperary, Republic of Ireland.

Over the weekend of 16th-17th November, eight members of the SOLO fleet spent the weekend on the Solent. This has become
an annual event. but this year was in “Ist Class Eights”, rather than the usual Sigma 36s. The Ist Class Eights are used for
match racing and the boats were ex. RYA.

We soon found that there was a little more to match racing than we realised. including differences in the rules. The wind on
Saturday was O to force 2 so it was relatively easy to become familiar with the boats. They handle like a large dinghy. Sunday
was a different story with wind up to force 5. We switched to racing round the cans (old habits die hard) but had to lengthen the

legs as we did not have time to hoist and lower the spinnakers. Much room for improvement here! Thanks to Roger Smith who
made all the arrangements for a very enjoyable weekend.

Geoff Josey, SOLO Fleet Captain

MSC Member embarking on another Worlds sailing Venture! They can certainly count on OUR support. We will keep you
posted about JoJo's sailing in Bombay and wish all members “A Very Happy 1997°

CRUISER COMMENTS

Firstly, may I wish you all a Very Happy New Year coupled with good sailing during 1997. I for one will be glad to see the back
of this snow and cold weather. roll on summer.

There was nothing better to focus the mind on either sailing or the weather than to be at Dave & Joan Thomas's presentation
held at MASC when they shared with us the experiences of buying a new Catamaran Cruiser in South Africa. commissioning it.
then sailing it from South Africa to the Mediterranean. Talk about the spirit of adventure! Wow! It was fascinating. many
thanks.

Ed's Note: The film covered briefly the completion of the new Catamaran ‘Dajo’; her delivery by road from boatvard to the
water and the trip from Cape Town, via St Helena, the Ascension Is, the celebration of crossing the Equator for the first time,
and the approach to Cape Verde Is. Here the film ended but ‘Dajo’s’ trip continued via the Azores to her destination of
(ribraltar. It was watched with great interest by a sizeable audience of Cruiser Fleet \fembers, some (a verv few - well, two) of
whom think that getting asfar as the Bench Head feels like a trip into dangerous, foreign waters!

Most of you will know we have for the past few years been trying to improve the quality of our Winter Storage Trailers.
especially since the increase in demand for Winter Storage made the mobility of trailers more essential. I must say the standard
of maintenance by Members has increased greatly and is much appreciated by all concerned. However. a census of trailers this
winter shows there are 34 (including the Club's Jack B. Workboat and Mooring Barge Trailers) which require towing eyes on
both ends and there are a further 6 Trailers requiring an eye at one end. We are currently engaged in obtaining a quotation for
having this work done as a one-off exercise. As soon as the information is to hand. Members affected will be contacted with a
view to having this work carried out. Naturally this does not apply to those craft using road trailers. Should anyone have any
queries regarding this or wish to take advantage of the situation to rectify steering problems etc. please contact me.

With regard to Flotilla sailing this year, the proposals outlined in the January Navigans are pretty well completed - full details
will be made known at the last of our Winter Meetings on 20th March. and of course through Navigans. Don’t forget if planning
your summer holiday. why not add four days onto the August Bank Holiday and join us up in the River Deben.

Our next Winter Meeting is due on Thursday 20th February when our speaker will be Frank Turner who has done a study and
written two books on the World War Two Maunsel Forts in the Thames Estuary. Most of us have sailed close to these and it is
impossible to do so without wondering about the How. When and Why. so come along. | am sure you will find it most
interesting.
Derek Kirby. Cruiser Fleet Captain.

RYA EASTERN REGION CLUB FORUM

This year’s forum was held at the Gosling Sports Park. Welwyn Garden City on Ist February. and Sailing Secretary
John Salmon
and myself attended the day's proceedings which lasted from 10.30 to 16.45, The event was well supported, largely due to the
interest in the content and implication to Clubs ofthe introduction of the new Racing Rules of Sailing (RRS) 1997-2000 issued
by the International Sailing Federation (ISAF) and which become effective on Ist April.

The morning session was taken up by a series of presentations on the role of the Sports Council. Legal Matters. and Club
Development. In the afternoon there were sessions on the Dinghy Handicap System. the New Racing Rules (1997-2000) and a
Joint Session by Eastern Region Co-Ordinators for Coaching. Race Training. Windsurfing and Race Management.

The Sports Council's Role: This talk was given by Rosie Mayglothling. Senior Development Officer of the ‘English’ Sports
Council, On Ist January “97 the Sports Council was divided into two parts - ‘UK’ and ‘English’. A more corporate
approach would be applied across the country in order to remove inconsistencies between the former Regions. She stressed that
very large sums of money were now being put into Sport for both Capital and Revenue projects. and that the driving force was
the achievement of success at the national and world levels. i.e. More Medals!

A number of sports had been awarded ‘priority’ status and sailing was amongst them. Regional and local coaches would be
funded to help identify and develop talent from an early age. Also Sports Services teams would be set up for Priority Sports.
Each Region and the Club needs to analyse and plan for the identification. training and development of the talent within its
ranks. The aim is to take the sport forward at Club level. The organisation is in place and money is available. The RYA Youth
Training Scheme has been achieving good results. e.g. Olympics and World Youth Championships, but further development is
possible.

Legal Matters: This talk was given by Edmund Wheelan. Manager of the RYA Legal and General Services Dept. He first
outlined the work of the Department in monitoring and searching for any legislation which could unfavourably affect sailing.
Legislators range from the UN. EU & UK Government. through to the local Council or Harbour Master.

He stressed the point previously made that more money than ever before was available to Sailing Clubs - “Every Honorary Club
Secretary should become a ‘Serial Begging Letter’ Writer.” He advertised publication G13/95 - ‘Round the Red Tape’ and
advised Clubs to fight for a reduction in Rating Valuation and to apply for Discretionary Rate Relief. Councils claim back from
the Government 75% of any relief given. He spoke also of concerns expressed by Race Officers and other Club Officers over
their liability in case of accidents during a race. Participants are still responsible for their own actions. They accept the risks,
However anyone found ‘negligent’ may be liable for claims for damages. Clubs should ensure that all members are insured
against such claims. He recommended the Policies offered by Fenchurch as being the best (but not the cheapest) available.

Club Development: Keith Ellison, RYA Development Officer. defined Club development as “getting new members and keeping
them’ and it required forward planning. He believed that the best way to attract new members was by means of Open Days (n.b.
we have one scheduled for Sunday 25th May). He then made the following suggestions

a) Promote event widely - invite local sports writers to the Club before the event to optimise publicity in local publications.
b) Go to Local Authority Sailing Centres and Schools to invite anyone who has attended a course. but as vet has no Club
application.
c) Smarten up Club and ensure everything works.
d) Meet at gate - take names and addresses. Welcome them.
c) Take for a sail in suitable boat. Reef if windy - must not frighten them. at all costs.
f) Talk to them and ask. *Would you like to join?”
g) Keep in touch - invite to a Social event.
h) Have clear policy on training. e.g. before or after joining.
i) Try to attract small groups from Schools and Youth or Company Organisations.
Jj) Talk to new members. keep up the welcome or they will drift away.
k) Invite the new members and those who did not join to a Social event.

On the last question of how to introduce new members and novices to Club Racing. he suggested No Racing Days when a
treasure hunt could be organised (around the racing marks?) He spoke scathingly concerning experienced racers who shout
abuse at novices. In his opinion they should be told to go and sail elsewhere. As volunteers were harder to find. he advocated
that Clubs should franchise out as many non-sailing based activities as possible or employ staff where this is practical.

Suitable Club boats should be available for beginners to use (or possibly hire). Some Clubs buy new ones and sell them off after a
few seasons hopefully to new members. “New” would mean brand new or one of the unused boats littering the dinghy park. He
concluded by stressing the need to plan ahead. and offered to visit Clubs in the area if there was sufficient interest to make the
journey from Lancashire worth while.

Lunch was taken with old friends Derek Baker and Stan Attans of Stone Sailing Club.

Dinghy Handicap System: John Anstey, Chairman of the Portsmouth Yardstick Advisory Panel. gave a very lively discourse on
the methodology and the limitations of the system. He strongly advocated that Clubs adopt local handicap which reflect the
conditions pertaining on their own stretch of water. and take account of the relative skills of the participants. Scepticism
abounded!

New Racing Rules (1997-2000): This was the talk everyone was waiting for. Trevor Lewis is a ‘Class Act’. He is Vice
Chairman of the RYA Racing Rules Committee. He bears an uncanny resemblance to our own ex-Commodore John Witter. has
an encyclopaedic knowledge of the old and new rules which he can deliver with considerable wit and at a breathtaking speed. He
began by showing the assembly a copy of the new mules book. which is now being distributed. one free copy per Club. Additional
ones are available £5.50 per copy.

You will be glad to hear that this new ‘simplified’ version of the rules contains more pages than the old one. Trevor has
published an article giving his interpretation of the rule changes and used it as the basis for his talk. He has given permission for
this to be published in this issue of Navigans PAGES 9-11. Everyone who participates in racing and race management should
read his article in association with a copy of the new nules.

In next month's issue of Navigans I will report on the remainder of the proceedings. and offer a few personal comments.

Please make a note in your diaries for Wednesday 9th April, 7.30pm at the MASC. when it is planned to hold a New Rules
and Race Management Appreciation evening. Make sure you bring this Navigans and your new ISAF Rule Book with you.

Ron Greygoose

ETIQUETTE FOR MEN - YACHTING

Contributed to Navigans by Club \fember Of Silvey, Varuna Il. First published in 1901, the article applies to a style of
Yachting not likely to be familiar to many MSC sailors, and belongs to a different age and from ours. It states rules of etiquette
that I'd love to see us trving to practise in our hectic modern sailing and racing, has much that is good sense, and much that
can only be amusing to the modern Club sailor... I can't resist publishing it all, as space permits, in a couple of Navigans
editions.

Dress As far as mere appearance is concerned the blue serge yachting suit is infinitely more becoming to a man than
any other he may wear on board, or for the matter of that, ashore either. The others are a blue or black flannel pin-strip or
xarey flannels. With these you may wear a yachting cap, which may be covered with white linen as a protection to the head: or
a cloth cap, but the latter does not go well with a serge suit.
Take an oilskin suit for rough weather.
Two of the greatest essentials in any man’s outfit when asked on board a yacht are a cordial desire to be amiable
under all conditions, and to be possessed of fit and proper foot covering.
Your boots and shoes should be of brown or white leather with indiarubber soles it possible, red rubber (not black,
which has a nasty habit of staining), or with leather soles, sewed.
If the sole has any nails in it they should be brass, on no account iron or steel, as these rust when decks are wet and
the rust comes off on the deck. Some owners are excessively faddy about their decks, so it possible have no nails at all.

Lite on Board The great guiding rule is that on a yacht every one - host and guests - has an interest in the spotless
appearance of everything. The cabin room 1s, at best, of course tar less than the room allowed to a guest in a house. The lite 1s
luxury qualitied by a campaigner’s care to fold everything away, do everything in the least possible space, and submit to
certain exigencies of the sea.

75 ENTERING A RACE
A boat no longer needs to owned by or chartered to the person or body that enters it in the race.

76.1 EXCLUSION OF BOATS OR COMPETITORS
When a entry is rejected or cancelled before the event starts, a reason must be given. This requirement cannot be changed by sailing instructions.

78 COMPLIANCE WITH CLASS RULES; CERTIFICATES
The duty to ensure that a boat complies with her class rules is extended from the owner to include any other person in charge (such as a charterer).

86 RULE CHANGES
The magic words 'unless otherwise prescribed in the sailing instructions' now hardly feature, and rule 86.2 states that Sailing Instructions may change a racing rule (where it one of the rules that may be changed) only by referring specifically to it and stating the change. Care must therefore be taken to identify clearly where it is intended that the provision of a sailing instruction is different from a racing rule. Situations which for the first time require a reference to the rule being changed include:
Rule 26, Starting Systems 1 and 2: when starting signals are made at intervals other than five minutes, the sailing instruction must state that rule 26 is changed.
Rule 29.2, Individual Recall: this rule must be referred to when using some system other than flag X to denote an individual recall - particularly important where the older 'at the dip' procedure is retained.
Rule 33, Changing the Course After the Start: the rule requires the new compass bearing to be displayed with the C flag, with a '+' or '-' sign if the leg length is either lengthened or shortened: if it is intended that, say, a red or green flag is used rather than a bearing, and/or if it is not proposed to advertise a change of leg-length, the sailing instructions must say so, and must refer to the rule.
Rule 35, Time Limit: this states that one boat finishing within a time limit means that all boats shall be scored. Where the intention of the race committee is otherwise, so that any boat finishing outside the time limit will NOT receive a finishing place, the sailing instruction must not only say so, but also state that rule 35 is altered.
Rule 47, Limitations on Equipment and Crew: must be referred to when permitting a person to leave the boat, except for specified reasons - note that the RYA prescription negating the rule is abolished, and 'leaving' is now rule-limited.
Rule 40, Personal Buoyancy: the rule must be referred to when using some signal other than flag Y and/or giving the signal a different meaning (such as to extend to apply at all times when afloat).
removing the option to exonerate by performing a 720° turn penalty, but not offering any other option except retirement or protesting.

When the meaning of a flag that is defined in the Race Signals section is to be changed, the change must be spelt out, and words to the effect of 'Alters the meaning of flag should be added. Examples include:
using a blue flag for some purpose other than designating a committee boat in position at the finishing line
changing the meaning of 'First Substitute', for instance, to add that the start of a recalled fleet will be postponed until after all other fleets have started
using flag X for some purpose other than for individual recall
using flag Y for some purpose other than requiring personal buoyancy to be worn when racing.
using flag S after the start to designate the operation of a system of shortening course that is set out in the Sailing Instructions, but is not in the rule book. In my experience, this is common, particularly at inland venues.
using flag Z for some purpose other than its new function, which is to designate a new 20% place penalty for what used to be called 'premature starters' (for which the new abbreviation is 'OCS'). The Sailing Instruction Guide, Appendix N, favours the use of orange flags to denote starting and finishing marks.

Some changes might affect both the meaning of a rule and the meaning of a flag - flag C is a prime example. It seems that both the change to the rule and to the meaning of the flag must be explicitly referred to. All this is obviously a strong incentive to adopt the standard procedures in the rules, since unnecessary local variations can only ever be a potential source of problems: it is suggested that there has never been a better moment to standardise.

89 PROTEST COMMITTEE
A protest committee can no longer be the race committee itself, but must be appointed by the race committee, although there is nothing to stop a race committee appointing all its members as a protest committee.

APPENDIX A, SCORING
The ISAF Low Points Scoring System is that first place now gets 1.0 point, rather than 0.75. The effect of the previous system is, however, retained by the standard first-line tie-break system being 'most firsts'. A 'last race sailed and counted by both' second-line tie-breaker is introduced.

The favoured abbreviations for categories of non-finishing pl include OCS (replacing PMS) and RDG (replacing YMP).

APPENDIX C - MATCH RACING RULES
The appendix offers the organisers the option of using in stan form the 'delayed penalty' system that has increasingly been ado in event Sailing Instructions in recent years.

APPENDIX D - TEAM RACING RULES
A standardised system of umpiring or observing events is n available to organisers.

RACE SIGNALS
Postponement for fixed numbers of hours are from the sched starting time: therefore, when a two-hour postponement sign replaced after that time by a four-hour postponement signal, earliest start time is four hours (and not six hours) from scheduled start time.

RYA PRESCRIPTIONS
Two of them will no longer appear - the one that negates 'leaving' rule (Sir Edward Heath no longer having to be allowe leave a boat in mid-race to attend to matters of state); and prohibition against wearing an ensign when racing, which sh now be a matter for sailing instructions or class rules if it is tho to be relevant.

The prescriptions will appear all together at one end of the RYA book, so that they can easily be copied to give to overseas entran domestic competitions, as required. Any rule affected b prescription will be asterisked. The only prescription that appea affect a competitor when racing is the one that negatives the I score for breaking the Fair Sailing or Propulsion rules.

RYA APPENDICES
These are abolished. There is no longer a separate RYA sco appendix, since it is judged that the improved ISAF Appendix A now serve. This does, however, take the 'best discard' tie-break of circulation, and, to retain it instead of the standard 'most fi etc.' (with the back-up of 'best score in the last race in which the boats raced and scored differently), this must be specified in sailing instructions, referring to the change to rule A2.3, Ties. other changes inherent in this are that the three-tier system for finishing scores is reduced to a simple single tier, and the 'decl entry' basis for non-finishing scores is replaced by a more lo method.

The RYA Time Penalty, which offers a useful alternative to tur places, is now to be found as an addendum to the Sailing Instruct Guide, Appendix N.

There is no longer thought to be a need for the book to pres RYA warning signals. These can be identified in class rules, clubs will know them, there is a trend towards logos in any (Lasers being an example), and the forced retention of n numerals is an unnecessary complication.

SAILING INSTRUCTIONS GUIDE
Previously, the RYA has published its own, but this was never i rule book: on the other hand, YR1 (the RYA version of the rule b did not reproduce the IYRU appendix that contained the sugge world-wide method. The price of what was thought to be a sli superior model being available via the RYA was that there wa guidance ready to hand for most writers of sailing instructions, the result, it is clear from appeals, is that wide variations occur i drafting of sailing instructions, many of which, while well-meant ambiguous or faulty.

The UK will now have the best of both worlds. There will b separate RYA model sailing instructions: instead, the I recommends - and prints in the rule book - the ISAF Sa Instruction Guide, Appendix N, with some added words for Starts, the RYA Time Penalty and the Liability (Attempted Exclu Of) Clause.

There are two themes to this article: first. to encourage the Handicap Fleet to race. and
second. to solicit help with race duties.
Before tackling these themes can I. on behalf of the Fleet. congratulate Malcolm Gandy and Graham
Richmond on winning the
1996 Kestrel Nationals.

Racing: Last year the turnout in the Fleet races was pretty dismal and | guess | now have to encourage
people to race. | did this
exercise in Navigans some years ago which resulted in Navigans being livened up by letters from
you explaining why some of
you chose not to race, and exhorting the alternative pleasures of sailing. Nevertheless. there might have been
other results since
in one race that year there were 10 boats competing against each other. | will put my argument to you again and hope for
new
miracles.

And why not race? OK. so some of you like pottering around exploring creeks and things. or perhaps vou don’t have the
competitive urge (Yes. I suppose I was being provocative!) But consider some of the advantages of racing. First you can go out
in all weathers and have the comfort of knowing that the race box is keeping an eye on you and there
are two safely boats out
there if you do get into trouble. It’s exciting sailing in conditions you might otherwise have avoided. It's fun trying to get the
best out of your boat. playing with spinnakers and experimenting with the trim of your boat. It’s fun trying to find the best
course. allowing for wind and tide. It’s fun being out on the water with other boats and you can learn a lot about sailing when
you discuss the race afterwards. So why not join in the racing and make friends with your fellow sailors”

ETIQUETTE FOR MEN - YACHTING - 1901 continued from last Navigans.

Dinner Dress On some big yachts (mostly steam yachts) the men dress for dinner when at anchor in harbour. But a
sounder rule is a dark blue suit for dinner at sea or at anchor. In small yachts - anything under a hundred tons - you would not
dream of putting on a dress suit. In fact is better not to under any circumstances. but you must of course be guided by the rules
of
your host. Of course it often happens at sea that no proper dinner can be served at all. and even if it be managed the state of the
weather will prevent any change of dress.

The Helm Do not interfere with the skipper. Do not. even if you fancy yourself. offer to take the helm unless the wind
be steady. and from the skipper’s manner you are pretty sure he will not mind. Bear a hand if vou see that you can be of service.
but ask first. But. unless the yacht is being worked by a “Corinthian” crew (/.c. an amateur crew), the supposition is that the paid
hands will be equal to their work.

Tact Life on board a yacht is by necessity - the whole menage being packed into so small a space - one that calls for
tact. Do not blunder all over the ship in the early hours when folks are dressing.
You will be awakened perhaps at 6.30 by the men scrubbing the decks overhead - early to bed and early to rise on board.
- if you wish a cold bath go up. not too late after they have done scrubbing. and take a tub cither by a swim overboard or by
Stripping and asking one of the crew to douche you with a bucket. There is no bath so delicious.
The crew may have begun already to polish the brasswork. so take your stand at a place where the splashing will not
interfere with them. and see also that vou are not near any open skylight through which the water can make its way into cabins
below. The bath over. remember to wrap up sufficiently before descending to your own cabin to dress. for there is only one
stairway in the ship. that is to say only one which you and your host and fellow guests can use. Therefore it is advisable to
tumble out for this little treat as early as possible. and before the ladies have left their cabins .

Ladies’ cabins usually have a bath sunk in the floor. so have some men’s cabins. and sometimes you may have access to
a real bathroom on board. In these cases of course the above does not apply.

The Crew Remember that the crew like their privacy. and respect it. Let your walk forward be bounded by the
mainmast in a cutter or yvawl. or a little beyond. and by the foremast in a schooner yacht. Don’t stare down the forecastle
hatchway. or thrust yourself into the bows of a ship where the crew are gathered and talking by themselves. Remember that they
have far less space than you.

A Common Dilemma If you feel sea-sick. and can remember such a detail. take up your position to leeward. The ship
of course heels that way. and (what is most important) the wind there blows off the ship. This advice is obvious enough. but in
nine cases out of ten the sea-sick tyro tries to climb up on the side of the ship facing the wind. as a shecp makes for the exposed
hedge. This is not a pleasant subject. but the advice is necessary and many an owner as Well as guest will be thankful for it if it is
followed.
Be careful at sea not to lean your elbows on the table when dining. Yacht tables are swung so that they keep Ievel no
matter how the yacht rolls. If vou lean on the table this adaptability is disturbed. and the glass and crockery may be upset.
Do not be fussy or nervous. even in difficulties. Nothing in the world is so little likely to come to grief as a well-found
yacht.

Ensigns and Burgees (in 1901) A yacht should fly the burgee of the club its owner belongs to at its main-top mast
head.
Yaw! yachts and steam yachts at sea fly the ensign when the owner is on board. Cutter vachts and schooner vachts do
not ordinarily fly the ensign at sea. but hoist it on an ensign-staff astern when in harbour and when the owner is on board.
When a yacht is in harbour and waiting for the owner to come on board she flies the burgee as usual. but the ensign is
hoisted as the owner steps on board.
Only yachts belonging to the Royal Yacht Squadron and above a certain tonnage are allowed to fly the White Ensign of
His Majesty's Navy.

2,

Members of certain royal yacht clubs (e.g. the Royal Thames Yacht Club. the Royal London
Yacht Club. and the Royal
Western Yacht Club) are allowed to fly the Blue Ensign.
Other clubs fly the Red Ensign. But even some royal clubs choose to fly this. with or without their
distinguishing badge
in the “fly” (e.g. the Royal Victoria Yacht Club. the Royal Yorkshire Yacht Club),
Flags must be hoisted at 8am and hauled down at sunset.
It is good form. if you belong to several clubs and enter the harbour of one you belong to. to hoist that
club’s flag. even
though it be not the flag of the club you are most proud to belong to. and to wear that flag during your stay in port.
Flag officers of a club do not carry a burgee but a swallow-tail flag. The commodore’s is plain. the vice-commodore’s
has one ball. the rear-commodore’s two balls.
If vou belong to a club and pass a yacht which. by its swallow-tail. tells you that it belongs to a flag-officer of that
club.
it is good form to dip your own burgee three times. whereupon he will acknowledge the salute by dipping in
return.
In steering a boat up alongside a yacht do not go straight for the steps or ladder. but take the boat up with
a sweeping
curve. much as a coachman drives up to a front door when he has plenty of room.

The Essence of Good Manners Apart from these fidgety little points. with which a guest on board will have
nothing to
do. the essence of good manners on shipboard is. first. good comradeship and a willingness to accommodate yourself to a
life
liable to be directed by the weather: and second. unselfish resolve to take up as little room as possible. make
as little fuss. and
give others as much privacy as you can manage.

Historical Titbit

Most of us are clued up enough to know the most common mainsail rig these days is known as ‘Bermudan’. Our high flyers
may even be aware that this same system is alternatively known as “Marconi Rig’ in some parts of the world. What is
probably not universally known is how or why.

The following explanation is not only logical but was lifted from an old encyclopaedia. so must be close to the facts!
Apparently the earliest Marconi radio aerials (very high) were held upright with a system of wires called (you've guessed it)
“shrouds” and the assembly was called Marconi Rigging! It was later applied to the support system of the higher aspect
triangular mainsails being developed for 20th century sailing craft (particularly racers) and hence the name.

Now for the homework question: (Editor will do the marking)

Given that a spritsail is held up with a sprit. a gaffsail is held up with a gaff. and a lugsail is not held up with a lug. how did
the more common name “bermudan’ which we all use replace the name ‘Marconi’ in the sailing boat context?

Ron Phillips.

LEARNING TO SAIL & ACQUIRING MORE ADVANCED SKILLS

When you belong to a sailing club such as ours you can learn all about sailing with time and practice and the support and advice
of fellow members. If you would like a course on sailing, either basic or more advanced, you can do so on our own river at
Bradwell Waterside.

Bradwell Environmental & Outdoor Education Centre (calling it ‘Bradwell Sailing Centre’ saves time) is run by Essex County
Council Community Education. One-day. weekend and mid-week courses are available. (I believe the minimum age for
residential courses is usually 13, but worth checking this with the centre.) Adults as well as young people are catered for, and
can take part in the courses either to gain certificates or just to participate in sailing - learning as they go without the feeling of
pressure - under the care of experts.

Some of the courses available in 1996 were:

RYA Shorebased: Dayskipper. Yachtmaster. RYA Practical: Competent Crew. Dayskipper. Coastal Skipper
RYA Dinghy Levels 1.2.3.5 Instructor RYA Inland Waterways Helmsmans Course
RYA VHF Course RYA ICC Certificate of Competence
RYA Powerboat Levels 1.2. Safety Boat - 2 day course. Advanced & Instructor Courses.
RYA Small Craft First Aid RYA Diesel Engine Course - useful for Cruiser owners.
Canoeing and Windsurfing also available.

The centre's Sigma 33 cruising yacht “Brigantes’ is used for RYA Practical Courses and also Taster Courses - weekend or day
sailing within the sheltered Blackwater Estuary for the beginner in sailing. or further afield for the more experienced. Boat
comes with a professional skipper and takes a maximum of 5 additional people.

Full details of courses and prices available from Bradwell Environmental & Outdoor Education Centre. Bradwell Waterside.
Southminster. Essex. CMO 7QY. Tel. 01621-776256 or Fax 01621-776378.

The centre can be found by following the road from the Club to Bradwell Waterside (passing the Bradwell Marina entrance) and
you ll find it on your left. behind Bradwell Quay Yacht Club. shortly before the road rises over the sea wall. Jenny and David
(Ball). and other Cadets of their generation. have learned many of their skills at Bradwell. and they have done some teaching
there. both experiences they have enjoyed. Just as important, Mum and Dad found the costs of courses quite reasonable.

Historical Titbit

I was most interested in Ron Phillips” historical titbit. My records seem to imply that since the turn of the century yachtsmen on
both sides of the Atlantic had been experimenting with a new rig that would eventually replace the traditional gaff rigged topsail
and mainsail, which had a heavy spar. clumsy mast rings and bulky mast attachments, with a single triangular sail that rose
straight to the top of the mast. The British called this new arrangement a Bermuda rig because a
similar one had been in use on
that island for two centuries. In America it was called the Marconi rig because of the many shrouds needed to stay the new mast
made it resemble a transmitting tower used by Marconi the Italian inventor of Wireless Telegraphy.

A large jib overlapping the mainsail was later added to the new rig, and since it was first used in a regatta off Genoa in 1927 it
became known as a genoa. It eventually got the nickname Jenny.

The new rig found its finest application in the J” class boats with a 75 - 87 foot water line, of which it seems only 10 boats were
ever constructed. and by 1940, economic conditions and I suppose the war made them obsolescent.

Derek Kirby.

Dart 15 News

Dart 15 Open Meeting - 19th & 20th April 1997 - at Marconi Sailing Club.

Extract from Yachts and Yachting. May 1997: Perfect Dart 15 weather hit Marconi SC on April 19th-20th with a steady
strong wind sorting out the good sailors from the brilliant ones. Twenty-seven boats turned up at this popular venue from
clubs from North, South, East and West. Young and older, ladies and gentlemen, all pitted their skills and wits to compete
on equal terms on a variety of testing courses. —

The competitors in the first race proved too keen and a general recall encouraged a concentration of the mind. However,
once off there was an exciting fetch to A mark - some competitors enjoyed it so much that they went sightseeing to Stone
andfound themselves rather off course. With a building wind there were a number of thrills and spills, with some
particularly exciting downwind legs with big waves - a shock for some of our reservoir enthusiasts. At the front were Bob
Carter, and local men Peter Tovey and Willie Pitcairn.

The wind and waves got even bigger and a number of retirements occurred but the afternoon race was close and exciting
with some very experienced sailors surprising themselves with capsizes and quick recoveries. Nick Dewhirst proved too
fast to catch, closely followed by Andy Jeffries and Barrie Hoggardfrom Beaver. The eagerly awaited long distance
course took competitors around Osea and Northey Islands. This proved a tactically testing course with shifting winds and
long reaches and beats. Stamina was high on the list of requirements and muscle man Paul Frost was closely followed by
Tim Dieu de Bellefontaine, with three seconds separating them on the line. Hoggard came third. All to play for in the
fourth race.

With tide pushing over a start line there was much excitement on another recall - a short race followed, with an arrow
shaped course and the first ten positions changing hands with surprising regularity on the last beat. Carter kept his head
and took line honours followed by Peter Tovey and Kevin Kirby (MSC). Overall Results:

Ist: Bob Carter (Grafham Water SC), 2nd: Peter Tovey (Marconi SC)
3rd: Nick Dewhirst (Whitstable YC), 4th: Willie Pitcairn (MSC), Sth: Paul Frost (Grafham Water SC).

Many Thanks to Hillary Dieu de Bellefontaine for the write-up.

Roger and Kathleen Smith did an excellent job as Race Officer and Assistant Race Officer, shortly followed by Bob Anderson as
a good marksman with the cannons. We were also very grateful to Harlow Sub Aqua Club for providing rescue cover for
Sunday racing, including the long distance race. Lastly thanks to my wife Heather, and my children Rebecca and James for
manning the race reception all weekend.

Peter Tovey, Dart 15 Fleet Captain

PS: Thanks to Colin Kidner (Commodore) for stepping in at the last minute to be OOD on Sunday and giving out the prizes.

Channel Mark No.1

No. 1 buoy has always been a feature of our courses as it marks the eastern end of Goldhanger Spit. In the past
the positions of
No.1 buoy has varied slightly on each occasion that it hasbeen removed and replaced. ‘i

Last year it was upriver from our start line and dried out at low water, making entry into Goldhanger Creeks a ‘hit and miss”
affair. This season, No.1 is positioned several hundred metres further down river. This location is so different from previous
experience that I queried the position with Nigel Harmer the River Bailiff. A somewhat exasperated Nigel assured me that
it had
been placed in the correct position as shown on Admiralty Chart 3741 (1995) and that he had recently checked the position.

In order to be more sure of our facts Peter Clayton and Tony Ferguson volunteered to measure the position of No.1 buoy using
both GPS and shore bearings.

Surprise. surprise! Guess what? No. 1 buoy is positioned exactly as shown on the chart. Full marks. Nigel (but you said that
last year).

No.1 buoy is located at 51° 43°.43N..0° 48°.12E.

Ron Greygoose

Oil Pressure Alarm

The Engine Display Panel for our boatis at our feet!! If the oil pressure warning light were to come on, thereis no way that we
would see it in the seconds, that I am told, it would take the engine to seize! The Volvo Alarm Panel costs the earth.

My solutionis to connect a Sounder directly across the oil warning light. A suitable one can be obtained from Tandy’s for about
£7. (Piezo Electric Siren 49-489.) Don’t use the cheaper buzzers, they're not man enough. When switching on the engine
electrics, the alarm sounds until the engine is started and the oil pressure is up. When shutting down the engine. as the oil
pressure drops, it reminds you to switch the electrics off! Therefore, as with all proper alarms, it is self checking.

Things That Stick Up....Antennae

If you are a high tech Marconi person, go and put the kettle on!! This is not for you. As a Radio Amateur I am well aware that
antennas are a mystic art, even more so to sailors who just want to sail. Fortunately, we are able to purchase ready made marine
antennas ready to “stick up”. But, there’s more to it than that!

Fitting.

1. Fit as high as possible. The range for a VHF antenna atop of, say, a 10 metre mast, in open sea should be about 27 miles. At
2 metres it’s about 9 miles! (Refer to Dipping Distances).
2. No tight bends or kinks in the cable. The piece of “wire” attached to the aerial when purchased is a co-axial transmission
line and as such depends on the relationship of the centre conductor to the concentric copper braid and must not be bent
on too tight a radius and must not be kinked. Depending on the quality of the cable, a 1” radius is getting too small.
Any distortion will look like a short circuit to the RF signals.
3. Always use good quality connectors at the base of the mast. A pair of “N” connectors is recommended....they are not cheap
but are the only “watertight” ones. fit a plastic boot and smear with silicone grease. Don’t cut the cable very
short....push some of it back into the mast....if you need to remake the cable later you will probably have to cut off at
least 4° due to corrosion. Don’t leave a large loopin free space....crews are notoriously clumsy! If you haven’t fitted
connectors before find someone who has (a Marconi fitter or Radio Amateur?)

Testing.

at the Club you should be able to hear clearly Port of London Control and Thames traffic on Ch.12. Most traffic
around high tide. This doesn’t prove the antenna and cable. The only proper way to test is by using a VSWR Bridge. This
samples the forward power and the reflected power and gives the result as a ratio. Ideally this should be close to 1.1:1 but
anything less than 2:1 is acceptable. Measuring DO resistance proves very little since a 10m piece of cable shorted at the far
end could measure a fraction of an ohm...not readable on an analogue meter.

Notes:

a) Sets are designed to give max power, 25 watts, with the alternator running at 13.8 volts. expect only 20 Watts from a fully
charged battery without the alternator.
b) Current on transmit could bein region of 5-6 amps so ensure 12volt supply leads are stout and all connections really good
preferably straight back to the battery terminals without joins, but with an in-line fuse. If connections are not good
there will be loss of power: sparking can ignite any Calor or battery gases!

Other Antennas.

GPS and Decca antennas use similar cable which should be treated as above. However they are usually “active” antennas....they
have an amplifier inside them. These are powered by “phantomingTM a DO voltage up the cable so great care must be taken to
avoid any short circuits.

Story.

Having the right test equipment I always check out my installation before launching each year. Testing a friend’s rig I found
that virtually no RF was getting beyond the deck connector. On removal of the plastic boot from the connector I was confronted
with a cable resembling a curly cord complete with a kink. I cut off the offending 4” of cable and refitted the plug. Measured
results were really good and were confirmed by a radio check with the coastguard. I rest my case!

Eric Lawley. “Pegasus”

CRUISER COMMENTS

Having missed the July edition of Navigans due to being on holiday (although I noticed the Ed. ghosted a couple of
comments
from my June ramblings) the Ed’s got me on the run again looking for copy to cover August, September
and early October! The
year’s gone and IJ have hardly got my feet wet, apart from rain that is. Where to start? Oh, well, here goes.

First may I say thank you to Malcolm and Margaret Yeoman for taking over the shakedown Cruise
to Burnham. I was most
impressed, listening to the VHF whilst on passage to St Katherine’s with the way Malcolm had got all the
berths organised. I am
sorry the function at the Royal Burnham was a bit noisy, no doubt the pros and cons of this venue for
next year will be discussed
at the end of year review at the Cruiser AGM. The fact that 19 boats attended says much for the choice of Burnham
Yacht
Harbour as a shakedown venue. .

On weekend 14/15 June we hosted boats from the Polynesian Catamaran Association together with 6 Cruisers
from Walton who
were taking part in a 24 hour endurance event in aid of the RNLI. Eight boats were in fact on passage, however
one had to
return with engine trouble, causing another to return with it as escort. Both groups, together with some of our
own members had
a great get-together and Bar B Q at the Dell Bar. My thanks to all the helpers and those members who made their moorings
available. Enough to say the Walton event was such a success a repeat next year is well on the cards. It may even become
an
annual event. Since we often enjoy the facilities of other Clubs it is nice to be able to reciprocate.

Whilst I realise you may be reading this rather later than invisaged, I would like to draw your attention to the following chart
amendments, just in case you have missed them. These were published in Macmillan 2nd Supplement to April 1997:
Swin Spitway: 51 40 44N 01 04 81E Woodbridge Haven Buoy: 51 58 15N 01 23 90E

Again just in case you are interested. BBC Essex transmit inshore broadcasts
Mon-Fri at 0740 & 0840: Sat
at 0657, 0757, 0857, 1205 & 1305. Sun 0657, 0757 & 0857.

Our next Flotilla Cruise will be to Shotley Marina on August Bank Holiday weekend 23-25 August. Arrangments have been
made with the Marina where it is anticipated most of us will arrive during the early afternoon. On Sunday evening a meal has
been arranged in the ‘Shipwreck’* in fact I believe we are taking over the upper lounge and bar which has excellent views of
the
river. The meal will be: Starter: Melon Port Balls or Smoked Peppered Mackerel. Main Course: Carvery with choice of meats,
potatoes fresh vegetables. Vegetarian meal available if required. Sweet: Choice of Blackcherry & Kirsch Gateaux with cream
or Home made Fruit Crumble with Custard. Coffee and Mints. Cost £12 per head. A list will be placed on the Club Nitice
Board nearer the date. Will those wishing to attend please indicate in spaces provided so Marina bookings and meals can be
notified. P.S. SHOTLEY VISITORS: Please see Lock Guidance Notes in this Navigans; also please fill in the
Shotley Marina Visitor form and send to Derek as soon as possible.

For those able to take the rest of that week off, another trip to the River Deben and Woodbridge has been arranged. I have
already made provision with the Tide Mill Yacht Harbour and, again, would those wishing to come along please signify on the
list when it is on the noticeboard. The proposal at present is that we lock out of Shotley on Monday, stopping over at Ramsholt
in the Deben on Monday night. Then up to Woodbridge on Tuesday, who knows, we may even get our Bar B Q in on the return
trip at Prettyman’s Point before leaving the River Deben.

Winter Laving Up. Since Ed’s asked for copy up to early October I suppose. reluctantly, I must turn my mind to this year’s
winter lay-up. I notice at the time of writing there are some pallets stacked by the sea wall. Those of you who need pallets for
your moorings had better lay claim to one before the campers use them for firewood. I will shortly be making up the Winter
Storage Layout Plan, so please be advised spaces will only be allocated to those who have paid 1997/8 Winter Storage Fees.
Space is at a premium and it is possible some reorganisation/reallocation of existing spaces may be necessary.

Lastly, please do not ignore your trailer until lay-up time. A little maintenance now could save a lot of trouble later.

MIDSUMMER BARBECUE - CRUISER FLEET

June 21st This day dawned, or rather the situation at 0900 was, as any other day in June, windy and showery. Only
extremely brave souls risked the violent gusts and put to sea, so there was Muna battling down the river under, it has to be said,
rather reduced rig. On shore, activity centred around the tractor shed where strange things were happening. As the afternoon
wore on the showers increased in intensity and one, witnessed from safety within the “Jolly Sailor” in Maldon almost washed the
moored barges away!

The reason for the activity at the Club was made clear that evening as, coming ashore in a lull from the weather, a delighful
smell wafted across the water towards us from the tractor shed. No, it was not tractor au win but the most mouth watering
display of barbequed chicken, succulent sausages and a delicious assortment of salads. The evening was rounded off with a
rowdy sing song led by Bob off Seachrain, ably assisted by birthday boy Dick Papworth (we won’t report his age).

On behalf of everybody present I would like to thank Murray and Anne Bates and their band of helpers for the splendid food;
Neil and Boo for managing to tend the bar; and Bob and Dick for the singing (not to mention Tambourine Lady Margaret
Yeoman). Sue Armold

LOCK TRAFFIC CONTROL

The lock is manned 24 hours a day enabling access to and from the marina at all states of the tide (although
those
vessels who draw over 2 metres should always check first. in case of extreme low tides).

TRALIGHT
FFI CONTROL
C

Lock movements are generally controlled by Traffic Lights and boats are requested not to enter the lock against a
Red
Traffic Light unless specifically advised to do so by the duty lockmaster.

BERTH ALLOCATION

Berth allocation is normally conducted in the lock and a map showing the allocated berth is issued with other relevant
Marina information.

V.H.F
COMMUNICATIONS

Shotley marina operates on Channel 80 for general Marina Traffic Control.
Channel 37 is also monitored for those vessels not fitted with Channel 80.

Vessels are advised to monitor those channels whilst approaching the marina. locking through and whilst underway within the marina basin. This allows for instant communication between the tower and yourselves if and when
required.

MARINA APPROACHES

The Lock is approached by passing through the Marker Posts positioned in the river Stour and proceeding along the dredged channel to the Lock entrance using the Inogon Leading light as guidance.

The marker posts are positioned 2.5 cables North West of the Ganges Buoy and are marked as follows:

Port Hand - Yellow and Black post with an East Cardinal Topmark
- Quick flash White every 5 seconds

Starboard Hand = - Green post with Starboard Hand Topmark
- Group flash (4) Green every 15 seconds.

The Marker Posts are approximately 50 fect apart.

INOGON LEADING LIGHT

The Inogon Leading Light is situated on the starboard side of the Lock Entrance. When a vessel is on the correct line of approach in the Entrance Channel a vertical Black line is scen in the centre of an orange screen. Any deviation from the correct bearing will cause the black vertical line to change to arrows. Follow the arrows to come back to the correct line of approach.

10.

LOCKING
IN

When approaching the Marker Posts it will be apparent whether or not the Lock is busy.

A). If there is little or no other traffic and a green traffic light is being displayed then proceed to the Lock. if a red
light is being displayed call the Lockmaster on the V.H.F.

B). If a number of boats are waiting at the posts, join them and stem the tide to await your turn.

Owners of particularly large or difficult boats to manoeuvre should call the Lockmaster on the V.H.F. on arrival.
Specific instructions will be given as to when to enter the channel. Other vessels should monitor the V.H.F.. however.
it is generally not necessary to call unless specific information is required.

On entering the lock be prepared to moor either side and move to the front of the lock. or as near to the next boat's
stern as safety allows. Boats should be secured fore and aft by lines to the cleats on the floating fenders.

LOCKING OUT

A). If there is little or no-other trafficand a green traffic light is being displayed. proceed to the lock. Ifa red light is
being displayed call the duty Lockmaster on the V.H.F.

B). If the lock is busy then proceed to the waiting pontoon to await your turn.

Owners of particularly large or difficult boats to manoeuvre, should call the Lockmaster on the V.HF. advising
him of the boats size before leaving the berth. Specific instructions will be given as to when to Icave the berth.

On entering the Lock be prepared to moor either side and move to the front of the Lock . or as near to the next boat's
stern as safety allows. Boats should be secured fore and aft by lines to the cleats on the floating fenders.

On proceeding from the Lock towards the Marker Posts at the end of the dredged channel. the
helms person should
look behind him/her at the Inogon Leading light to ensure that the boat is keeping to the channel.

FREEFLOW

Freeflow occurs at the time leading up to high water, and varies in length from a few minutes to one
hour or more. In

FLOODGATES - Reminder

We are required to keep the Floodgates closed between Ist September and Ist May over winter each year (these dates have been
permanently marked on the gates). This is to prevent the possibility of the higher tides more likely to occur at this time from
flooding through the sea wall gap which has been left for our convenience. It is the responsibility of each and every Member to
check at the end of the day before leaving the site that the Floodgates are properly closed.

The Floodgates are not locked so no key is necessary to open or close them. On windy days make sure you open them up right
back to the wall - they could be blown shut on your car as you drive through.

Viewing the gate from the landward side, the left hand gate is bolted into a slot in the ground and is closed first. Turning the top
handle anticlockwise lowers the bolt into the ground to close the gate. The right hand gate has a lever to secure it closed against
the left hand one - this is where a little bit of muscle is required. Reversing these actions allows you to open the gate.

Opening the right hand gate only gives enough room for a tender to pass through, but both gates need to be open to make enough
room for a car. : at a

APPEAL TO DOG OWNERS

This is a salutary tale of a nasty illness which has spoiled my summer, as I picked up the food poisoning bacteria
‘Campylobacter’ in the later part of June. I quote from the Information Booklet sent to me by the Local Health Authority when
my doctor had to advise them that I had this illness. “Campylobacter Enteritis is not only associated with raw meat and poultry
but infects pets. Around 50% of dogs excrete the bacteria in their faeces and as a result the animals’ coats become infected, and
the infection passes to humans who stroke their pets.”

I do not know howI became infected as I have known about this risk since a neighbour’s small son was blinded by the illness 30
years ago and I never handle animals without washing my hands afterwards. We have no pets at home. However, I do know that
I ate “al fresco’ at the Club at the time that I must have contracted the disease, so the Club grounds have to be a possible source.

I do, therefore, appeal to dog owners to follow the Club guidelines and keep their pets leashed so that they are aware of their
movements, and please poop-scoop after them. It is not good enough to let them defecate on the shingle and hope the tide will
wash it away.

So, come on. Dog Lovers. we all know that theyre cuddly with heart-melting eyes, and it’s not their fault that they push their
noses into some unsavoury places. Surely it’s worth a little extra care to make sure that your pet is not respnosible for someone
being sick for a couple of months or, even worse, a child being disabled for life.

Barbara Holdsworth

BURNHAM WEEK

People talk about “Burnham Week” but what really is it all about? If you have not “done the week” then really you don’t know
what it is. I can tell you it is a wonderful combination of many aspects of life. It combines qualities such as skill, judgement,
patience, nerve, brute strength, gentleness, co-ordination, co-operation, endless resources of energy, tact and diplomacy and, most
important of all, to be able to consume vast quantities of alcoholic beverages until the early hours of the morning and recover by
0700in the morning.

Burnham Week consists of eight days of racing, so this has to be repeated without the loss of concentration or energy reserves for
this period of time. If you reach the end of Burnham Week and you feel refreshed and fit, then I cesta that you ve not worked
at it hard enough and can’t possibly have enjoyed it!

Over two hundred boats of 30 differing classes with 5 minutes between start times took part this year.. All on the Crouch
between Whittaker No.6 and Cliff Reach. You certainly need to know your Port from Starboard particularly when in the
confined waters of the Roach on Low Water Springs. The Sailing is the No.1 for Burnham Week with many evening activities
being organised by all the Clubs in the evening, where analysis of the day’s performance, celebrations and commiserations can
result in an even poorer performance the following day.

“Timari Two’ and “Helm’s Angel’, both cruisers from MSC, took part this season, unfortunately in the same class. Start lines
were rather crowded as our Class 7 had up to 20 boats competing and on most days there were spinnaker runs out of the river to
the ‘battleground’; the ‘battleground being the chosen area of the river for the day where we chased each other round courses of
sausages and triangles with gay abandon until we ran for ‘home’, This occurred all week because West or South West winds
meant beating in conditions so varied - from 2 or 3 knots to 35 knots of wind. One day we estimated 200 plus tacks trying to
keep in the shallow water on the northerly bank. The biceps are now bulging well, but unfortunately after this day’s exercise the
skin on the fingers had been worn away revealing several red looking divots that are just starting to heal over.

You also have to be brave and bold anda little daft. On launching our ‘small’ kite in 30 knots of wind, the boat speed rose from
4 to 8.5 knots in about 0.5 seconds, but a weak fitting broke and let the pole pull upward, spinnaker now wildly out of control. A
glance sideways revealed one of our opponents struggling as his spinnaker caused a violent broach and he lay flat on the water,
motionless, for a few seconds. This was a 3'/> ton 28ft. cruiser, not some flimsy dinghy.

We survived the week's racing however, having had to watch the fleet on Monday sail past us as we sat motionless, stuck on the
mud by trying to tack in too shallow water! Alert offered assistance but we hid with embarrassment, declining a tow! *Timari
Two’ did not disgrace herself however. finishing third overall, having gained two ‘firsts’ and a trophy as well, Many thanks to
our crew and especially Mike and Graham from ‘Seabrume’ who so kindly helped us survive the week.

‘Helm’s Angel’, crewed by a group of wild Scotsmen did very well with two ‘firsts’ and two ‘seconds’ and were duly awarded
runner up cup.

As I said earlier, Burnham Week is not all plain sailing. Evening activities diverse as Quiz Evenings. Mad Cow Disco, Guinness
Night, Street Parties, Pimms Parties and, best of all, RBYC Fancy Dress “what you were wearing when the ship went down”
were fantastic. I’m glad I’m back at work now this week. I nodded off today and woke up with a jolt as I dreamed of Burnham
Week 1998. If you've never ‘done Burnham Week’ then make sure in 1998 that you “do it”!

Derek Gardner

As we near the end of another season (didn't it go quickly?) I make a rare foray into print to thank a few hard working members
and to ask for volunteers.

You may not know that the Rear Commodore's job involves three committee meetings every month plus some others for Open
Day Organisation and ECPR liaison. In addition to this commitment I had to take on the role of Safety Boat Co-ordinator and it
is for this job that I seek a volunteer so I can "See more of the Family" next year. So what does it entail?

The Safety Boat Co-ordinator's job is to schedule the crews for the Jack B and Rib. using the list of drivers and crews that I have.
The Schedules are then published in Navigans. The next part of the job is maintaining and updating the schedules as inevitably
people swap their duties with others on the list. You do not have to arrange the exchanges, only update the schedule. The Sailing
Secretary then informs the Race Officer for the Day of the names of the crews and it is the RO's job to check their availability.
The job does not necessarily involve attending Sailing Sub-Committee Meetings although it would be nice to see you if possible.
If you would like to help me and the Club please phone me on [redacted] and I will give you more information.

Now to the thanks.

Firstly, thanks to all the drivers and crews of the Rescue Boats who turned out and did their duties without causing me further
loss of hair. I appreciate your efforts.
Next my thanks to the unsung heroes who keep the Rescue boats serviced and fuelled. Graham Jones on the Rib, Ray Ball on the
Jack B and Dave Bladon who keeps the Rib fuel bunkers topped up.
Thirdly. thanks to all the members of the Sailing Sub Committee for their regular attendance and contributions. The meetings
were often long as we tried to make your sailing more enjoyable and better organised.
Lastly I must single out one Sail-sub member for special thanks. Your Sailing Secretary, John Salmon has worked tirelessly and
efficiently at his job. He has always sought to drive us onwards and upwards, never being afraid to criticise our current
practices to provoke ideas and enthusiasm for improvement, and then working hard to implement the solutions. Many
Thanks John.

On a purely personal note I did little sailing last year, but what I did do was most enjoyable. I thought the Piers Race was the
best one yet. and the welcome extended to the Tornados, Prindles and Nacras at Yaverland was memorable. Unfortunately,
apart from a glorious second on the first day my performance was better forgotten. My aim is to get more sailing done next
season. as | am still too young to take up golf. regardless of what my wife says.

Have a good winter. and I look forward to seeing you all next season. Clive Shenton, Rear Commodore

After a few days of gale force winds, Saturday 11th October dawned bright and sunny with light winds. It was not to last - by

two. Race 3 was abandoned when the wind died to nothing. and Tim Wallace won Race 4.
