Helm Of the Year 1997. Congratulations. Tim.

Our thanks to the rescue drivers and crews who carried out their duties in the cold and rain and to Clive Shenton for arranging.
collecting and returning the Toppers. and for helping in the Race Box.

Cruiser Comments Dates: Cruiser Fleet AGM, Thu 20th Nov1997, MASC, Beehive Lane, 8pm.
Cruiser Winter Meetings, Thu, 22nd January, 19th February, 19th March.

The highlight of this year’s cruising activities must have been the August Bank Holiday flotilla cruise to Shotley Marina and
River Deben. Over the whole week a total of 30 Club Cruisers took part. 24 visiting Shotley Marina - some of which had to
return home on the Monday - but these were replaced by others who joined us up to Woodbridge in the River Deben, resulting
in
22 Cruisers being present. Seven boats got off to a flyer on the Friday, stopping overnight at Brightlingsea. the remainder
Starting from various other points to ease the early morning start. However. with a following wind and a strong ebb tide the
passage to Shotley did not take long. It took us just 2'/, hours from Brightlingsea, in fact, we all arrived a little too early for the
Marina to have cleared the pontoon allocated to us. On arrival we found we were allocated the whole of F & G pontoons, thus
keeping us all together, which was great.

The rest of Sunday was spent settling in and on Sunday evening 60 members sat down to an excellent three-course meal in the
marinas ‘Shipwreck Bar’. Monday saw the departure of those who were returning home, with the rest of us locking out at
various times to make the short trip to the River Deben. Our single handed members decided to lock out early to take part in a
foul weather exercise, being caught in the mother and father of rain storms. but this soon cleared with the rest of the day turning
out to be bright and sunny. The majority of the fleet had an overnight stop at Ramsholt, making the 9 mile trip up to the
Woodbridge Tidemill Yacht Harbour the following day. Here again the Harbour Master did all he could to keep the fleet
together. his task not helped by some visiting yachtsmen not leaving when expected. Nevertheless he did an excellent job. It’s

S.

not easy to handle 22 boats in such a confined space, we did our best to help by staggering our arrivals, each boat arriving at five
minute intervals. On Tuesday night the crews of the single handed fleet, namely Rasputin, Icarus, Aldebaran, Sundowner,
Capricorn II, Winkler and Juno hosted the rest of the flotilla to a second evening ashore at the Yacht Harbour
producing,
amongst other things, some potent punch which did wonders for the vocal cords during the resultant singalong to the musical
accompaniment of Bob Baker and John Walker on their guitars.

As with last year, the weather prevented us holding the proposed Bar B Q down river at ‘Prettymans Point’, the strong winds
making it difficult to anchor in such numbers. From this point on the fleet started to do a sort of bomb burst. each choosing
their
time to exit the River Deben and their venue to wait until their return home. All in all it was a most successful and enjoyable get
together.

1997 Cadet Week Charles Anderson

For Chris and me it seems hard to believe that another Cadet Week slipped by with so many apparently enjoying it. We started
the week with 74 cadets and lost a couple on the way due, fortunately, to other commitments and not to an accident. This
number was split roughly into two fleets of senior and junior sailors. Lucy Boreham and Sam Ashley put the senior fleet through
their paces while the junior instructors were Olly Waller, Claire Davies, Peter Clayton. Jenny Ball, Mark Bulkeley, Grant Strong,
Ian Chaplin, Thomas and Rupert Anderson: each junior tutor had a small groups of about 4 or 5 pupils to instruct.

The week started with the traditional capsize drill in the teeth of a 5 gusting 6 from the east: a wind which was to stay with us for
four of the five days. For the juniors the week then continued with a variety of shore-side activities which included points of sail,
knots. parts of the boat and sailing theory all mixed with sailing and relay races afloat. Sadly the strong winds did not allow
much helming for the juniors and some of the smaller sailors found even the jib work tough going.

The seniors started the week with some assessment trials from which the fleet was subdivided to allow the more advanced sailors
to get on with racing while the others were reminded of some fundamentals. The races were keenly fought with only 34 points
between first and third places out of four qualifying races.

The fleets came together for the Long Distance Race which is normally to the Thirslet buoy and back. However the one day
when the wind vanished meant a change to an up-river race followed by a round Osea race. Sadly the former was abandoned and
an extremely enjoyable picnic lunch and swimming on the East End of the island saw the wind make with the tide. This allowed
the second half of the long distance event to take place and at both junior and senior levels it was greatly enjoyed.

We had the good fortune of the Bradwell Outdoor Centre issuing RYA level and stage certificates. I am pleased to confirm that
they signed 24 adult stage levels and 5 junior stages. well done to you all. They did mention that the address section in the back
of each book must be filled in so please make sure you have done this.

Although the club is not itself a recognised training centre, this exception to an RYA rule was made possible by the fact that we
boast two RYA instructors on the team in Lucy and Olly. Our thanks go to John Perrott and Malcolm Yarwood at the Centre for
their support and for the six Toppers they lent us. These were extensively used by the cadets and one or two adults.

I think it fair to say that everybody enjoyed the sailing helped largely by the weather and even more by all those who helped us
each day. Although individual thanks were announced at the end of the week Chris and I would like to once again express our
gratitude to everyone who helped, from the tutors to the rescue crews.

Thank you all once again and we look forward to seeing you all out on the water before next year’s cadet week.

COMMODORE’S REPORT 1996

1996 has not been a good year for me and sailing. I have not been able to spare the time to get down to the club at weekends. Those of you who read my notes in Navigans will know that I have been a victim of the continuing change in the education field. I sincerely hope that 1997 should see an end to the results of change which will mean I have to work less and can play more at weekends.

I should like to deal with the negative side of the club first. The access road to the club is a cause for concern. The repairs to the damage which the NRA traffic caused are not satisfactory. Privatization has its down side. The NRA is now called the Environmental Agency and seems to be playing ‘hard to get’ over the road repairs.

I suspect that the grip which is being put on public spending by the government has something to do with the reluctance of the Environmental Agency to agree to do something about the poor reinstatement work done by the NRA. to the access road.

I have to thank Larry for taking on the task of dealing with the Environmental Agency and trying to get some redress. So far he has no success. What we need is a high profile barrister to help fight our claim.

The second half of camping fortnight seems to be a cause for concern. Some club members are of the opinion that there is a lack of control and order which results in club facilities being abused. Others are of the opinion that this is a time for relaxation and enjoyment and do not do not feel that there is a problem. The arguments will be considered in the next few months, so any ideas which members may have will be gratefully received by the main committee to allow full and frank discussions to take place in order to resolve any difficulties.

Now the good news.

I wish to put on the record my sincere thanks to all club members and particularly Executive and Committee members who have worked to ensure that the club ‘works’ for us all. I have no hesitation in mentioning the work done by Frank Bennett in spite of a very serious accident earlier in the year. Fortunately Frank is now well on the way to a full recovery. Ironically this accident led to Frank looking at our Club Insurance and to his horror he found that club members were not covered for ‘waterside activities’ I am pleased to say that this oversight has now been remedied.

Management of the MASC and its finances seem to be under much tighter control. I feel confident that the future of MASC remains assured. Mr. Brocklesby and Mr. Marsh visited the club during Camping fortnight and saw the results of the hard work done by MSC members. They were impressed.

The membership has gone over the 400 mark this year, which means that the club finances will remain healthy. It is intended to run the series of advertisements in Yachts and Yachting again and to sign post the club whilst this campaign is running. This tactic resulted in members joining the club.

I hope you all agree that new galley service provided by Mark Fletcher has been a great success. I am confident that this service will continue next season together with an improved bar service. The latter will depend on agreeing mutually acceptable terms and conditions with Mark.

I have to pay tribute to Charles Anderson and Chris Davies and their team of helpers for their efforts in running a very successful cadet week. I believe some 40 young people took part, learnt a great deal and had a great time. Congratulations Charles and Chris and many thanks. It is through these activities that the enjoyment of sailing is allowed to develop in the minds of young people. Enthusiastic youngsters will be the life blood of the sport and this club in the years to come.

MOORING SHACKLES

Following on from Derek's comments re mooring shackles in Cruiser Comments. I would endorse Derek’s comments that
moorings should be thoroughly checked during the winter.

However the fitting of new shackles, whilst the responsible thing to do, should not induce a sense of complacency. I have found
over the past few seasons that shackles near the surface have suffered badly despite being renewed at the beginning of the season
and using an anode. Last year, when my mooring was recovered, | found that it was only the wiring that was stopping the pin
falling out. This year I changed the shackle under the buoy halfway through the season to make sure.

There is a school of thought that says monel seizing wire increases the erosion of the shackles. The scientists amongst us may
care to comment on this. On the other hand I have found that plastic cable ties tend to harden and break off, leaving the boat
totally at the mercy of the shackle pin thread. A bit of a Catch 22 all this!

Perhaps it would be worth sharing a few shackle pin horror stories in Navigans with a view to identifying a ‘best practice’ for
ensuring the safety of our boats. My method is to thoroughly grease shackles with petroleum jelly and secure them with two
independent wraps of seizing wire. Any other ideas/comments to Navigans. please.

Incidentally | understand that the ‘lost’ race marks were also fitted with new shackles at the beginning of the season which,
perhaps, underlines my points above.

Ray Ball

Notes from Triton of Osea, Ionian Islands, Greece

Ray and Hazel left England in March 1997, and travelled overland via Calais, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, and
Switzerland to Brindisi in Italy from where they took a ferry to Greece to join their boat:

It was great to be back on board and we set about tackling the jobs we had scheduled for the season. Cleaning, painting,
varnishing. gluing - all the usual chores plus a bit of plumbing, mechanics and electrics etc. As we had the car
this year we
managed to get out and about the surrounding area a bit and, as everywhere in Greece seems to be steeped in history, mythology
and ruins, there is plenty to see.

We had the boat relaunched on 13th May and sailed into the Gulf of Amvrakia, a local nature reserve which has dolphins, otters,
jackals, pelicans and other rare sea birds. We were in company with Jack and Jackie Manning who are on their fourth season
here, so are local experts on the area. That first balmy evening we sat in our cockpits in the setting sun having a leisurely drink
and watching the local fishermen setting their nets while standing up in their small boats, and Jack said “This is one of those
evenings you will always remember.” How right he was! By the middle of the night the wind had turned. we had swung onto a
lee shore and we had one fishing net around our anchor chain and another round our propeller and rudder. Not a comfortable
position to be in. However, it could have been worse and after some hours of diving and cutting, Ray and Jack finally freed us.
The high spot of the disaster was that in the nets they cut off were a dozen Tiger prawns, so at least we got a tasty lunch. Over
the next few weeks we had the Manning Cook’s Tour of their favourite anchorages.

Roy and Margaret Bellord were with us briefly at the start of the season but soon set off for the French canals as they were
making their way back to the UK. We had also been listening out on the HF radio for Joan and Dave in Dajo, following their
progress through the Balearics, Sardinia and Sicily, and they finally arrived on 17th June for another Marconi reunion. They
arrived about 1.30am into the bay at Sivota on the Island of Levkas. It was not easy in the dark so we talked them in on the VHF
and then Ray and Jack went out to meet them in the dinghy (they were in company with another yacht) and they each took on a
pilot for the last part of the journey and anchoring. Great celebrations and rather a late night for us all.

It was very good fun to sail together after all this time and we had great pleasure in accompanying them to the spots we had now
made our favourites. We had one evening at a taverna run with a rod of iron by a matriarchal figure nicknamed Olive Oil by the
Brits due to her likeness to Popeye's girlfriend. This lady, of a certain age, will treat the customers to the amazing sight of her
dancing with a table on her head - usually searing her apron! One of her sons leads the traditional Greek dancing in which
everyone is encouraged to join and, inevitably, ends up with at least one yottie falling over. Needless to say a good time was had
by all.

July and August tend to get more crowded here with both the Greeks and Italians having their annual holidays and we decided to
take the opportunity to visit a less popular area and explore the Gulfs of Patras and Corinth. By now we were all ‘doing our own
thing’ and not sailing in company, and we had a quiet leisurely cruise calling in at new harbours and finding peaceful little bays
on our trip south. The weather had been particularly kind to us this year and we have had some good sailing winds. Through the
gulf of Corinth the strength of the wind is always enhanced and we surfed into Trizonia in 35 knots of wind. gusting up to 43
knots (force 8. gusting 9). There were. luckily, plenty of willing hands to help and we were soon safely alongside a quay in the
abandoned marina (started about 5 years ago but the project shelved due to lack of money). Trizonia is a delightful little island,
no vehicles and everything delivered by the ferry which is about 25° long and carries people, animals and all goods. We had
arrived a week early in order to sail further east to visit the ancient site of Delfi before returning to Trizonia in time for Ray's
special birthday party get-together with other boats, but as the strong winds persisted we did our sightseeing by taxi and stayed
snugly in harbour.

In the area surrounding the Ionian Islands where we are usually based, which is known as the Inland Sea, the Greeks have got
used to the many foreign visitors, but in the gulf area they do not see so many and are not used to speaking English. Those who
can, really enjoy the opportunity to speak to you. In the town of Messolongi we were befriended by a couple of locals. Christos
showed us his pride and joy, a vintage Harley Davidson motorbike which he and his son are rebuilding and Spiros who owns a
local restaurant and became a great friend over the times we went there. He took us up into the mountains for the day and
showed us his local village. It seems a tough lifestyle, keeping goats or growing tobacco, and life is still very basic. We had a
typical Greek lunch including fried pumpkin which we had never tasted before. It was a wonderful day and quite an eye-opener
on how other people live.

6. fh

Since returning to the Inland Sea we have continued our gentle cruising style. The weather has not been as stormy or as windy
as this time last year and it has been possible to visit some of the areas which are very beautiful but only tenable in calm
conditions. The general holiday season is now drawing to an end and even the most popular anchorages are no longer crowded
with is wonderful. We have really enjoyed this year and it has been so different as we have done no passage making. The
novelty of returning to towns and anchorages that we have visited before has been very relaxing. We have made many new
friends and have met up with many people that we met before in previous seasons and are now even recognised by the local
shopkeepers and taverna owners.

The Greek Ionian Islands are an ideal cruising ground. Beautiful scenery, friendly locals, cheap tavernas (average two course
meal with wine, approx £6). and lots of free. safe, anchorages. You can be charged on the town quays, although it is a bit hit and
miss, and so far this year we have only paid out 480 drachmas (£1.10), which was for two nights tied to a quay.

Hazel and Ray Beckett, September 1997

Commodore’s Report 1997

In case any of you are wondering who the Commodore is, it’s me! My reasons for not being able to do a great deal of sailing are
the same as last year, so I won’t repeat them! However I really do see an end to the turmoil in my job and expect to be spending
most weekends at the Club next summer.

From the point of view of the Club, I am delighted to report that this year has been mucha better one than last year, in most
respects. However the galley service has not proved to be as reliable as we would have liked. When Mark and his team were
here
the service and food were to most people’s taste. It was a shame that the reliability was not of the same standard. The Club was
left without a service on a number of high profile occasions and I and other Club officials were left to apologise to guests for the
lack of food. I have to thank Pat Black for spending time liasing with Mark on many occasions after contractual agreements
were broken. The main committee agreed that he should be formally censured by letter. It simply is not acceptable to fail turn up
to provide a service after agreeing to do so. A lack of explanation or apology when there has been no galley service is also
unacceptable and unprofessional. Mark decided he no longer wished to complete his contract and left. The matter will be
pursued by the main committee.

What is being done about the situation I hear you say? A number of organisations have been contacted and are being invited to
tender for the service. The committee will try to ensure that a reliable organisation wins the contract. If there are any Club
members who feel that they would like to provide the Club with a galley service they are welcome to put in a bid.

Pat Black steps down at the end of the season after three years as Vice Commodore. His efforts have resulted in a great many
improvements to the Club. Patio area, barbecue area, relocation of the fuel shed, alteration of the dinghy park to accommodate
the Windsurfer rigging area, ditch filling, window replacement, repairs to the hard, galley service, to name but a few. I am sure
that you will join with me in thanking Pat for all his hard work over the past three years.

You will be pleased to hear that the environmental agency (nee NRA) have finally agreed to pay up for the necessary repairs to
the access road. Clive Shenton is the engineer who we have to thank for providing a professional report on the state of the road,
costing and specifying what needed to be done to put it right. Armed with this professional report, Larry Botheras was the ‘front
man’ who did the negotiations with the environmental agency and convinced the ‘men from the ministry’ to part with the cash to
put matters to rights. I am quite sure that without their input the Club would still be arguing with the Environmental Agency.
A big thank you to both of you. The work will start after tenders have been received and the contract awarded.

The mooring barge had to be replaced this year. Peter Clayton and the mooring team ‘supremos’ designed the improved version
and I understand that recovering moorings is now a much easier and safer task. The old barge was sold. Thank you, Peter for
your hard work in overseeing the job.

The ECPR was again a success and, whilst we didn’t get the expected entry from the continent, everything else seemed to go off
without a hitch. We were very lucky to have Libby Purves to present the prizes. I feel sure she will spread the good word about
Marconi Sailing Club and the Piers Race. I am delighted that the money which was raised will be going to the Cirdan trust to
provide bursaries for deserving young people. Watch for reports from the trust, in Navigans, giving details of how the money we
donated was spent. Thank You to Mike Duckmanton and to your team who organised the event and of course to the Cruiser
Fleet for providing the mother boats.

Once again Charles, Chris and their team of helpers have run a superb Cadet Week. Bigger and better than before. Well done
and thank you. | understand that activities for cadets will continue during the winter. Thank you to those Club Members who
are taking on the responsibility for running those meetings.

The sailing sub committee have worked tirelessly under the direction of Clive Shenton, organising and running a number of very
successful open events as well as our own sailing programme. I have mentioned the ‘open day’ in Navigans. I cannot let this
opportunity pass without mentioning it again and thanking all those Club Members who contributed to a very successful day
which resulted in a number of people joining the Club.

I have to thank Liz Hill for her unsung work as membership secretary. The job sounds fairly straight forward and indeed it
would be if we all managed to get the paper work right first time and on time! Alas this is not always the case.

PRESIDENT’S PATTER

No, I am not competing with the Commodore’s Column! - Just a few personal observations as another season ends.

In his Commodore's Report at the AGM Colin felt moved once again to refer to his absence from the Club at weekends. It was
extremely good news to hear that he will be able to enjoy his sailing once again next year. We all owe him a considerable debt
of
gratitude as, despite his extreme workload, his service and leadership to the Club has never faltered. Thank you, Colin, for your
dedication and I look forward to ‘dodging’ you on the water next season.*

On a personal note I would like to express my appreciation to those of you who attended the AGM and elected Neil. Steve, Peter
and Patrick as Vice Presidents and myself as President. Elections to office at the AGM are usually unopposed, but this does not
mean that the Officers and Committee members are in any way complacent. The opposite is the case, as more support is urgently
needed to share the workload and guide the Club’s development.

Another person who deserves special mention is Patrick Black who has completed his three year maximum term as Vice
Commodore. In my opinion he has done more than anyone else in recent times to engender a sense of pride in our Club facilities
and surroundings. It is up to the membership at large to sustain this effort by ensuring that it becomes the ‘norm’ to ‘tidy up’
before we leave.

One aspect of the AGM which disappointed me was the apparent lack of interest by prizewinners in attending to collect their
awards. A not inconsiderable amount of work is placed on the Sailing Secretary in organising the proceedings. Surely those who
come to the Club each week-to race could make the effort to attend on this important day, or if this is impossible, send their
apologies in advance.

Finally, Mary and I would like to express our sincere thanks to Ian Caruth, ably assisted by Roseanne, for his term as Social
Manager; and congratulate him for organising such a superb Laying Up Supper. The meal was excellent and the music great.
Members who don’t come because they think it too formal and stuffy are living in the past. Come on all you wives and
girlfriends, make sure he brings you next year.

Ron Greygoose

Happy Memories of Sailing Visitors to the Club on 19th/20th July 1997

Part of a thank-you letter from Tollesbury Mudclub: “The four or five boats which made the trip set out on the turn of the tide
from Tollesbury in somewhat light winds but a perfect summer’s day. Making headway against the tide made for slow progress
but, as time was not of the essence, still most enjoyable. However, the best was yet to come. Having moored to your visitors’
buoy we were received in a most friendly and hospitable way by one of your members and directed to the moorings available for
our overnight stay. Coming ashore we found the barbecue already set up and ready to cook our food - what service.

The evening progressed and we enjoyed the convivial company of your members and cheap beer. After playing some daft games,
a favourite activity of our club, the evening concluded with one of the most beautiful sunsets I have ever witnessed on the river.
As we all rowed back to our vessels for the night we could only reflect on what a great experience our trip had been. It seemed
somewhat ironic that a cruise which had only involved a voyage of a few miles had been so enjoyable.

On behalf of our Club I can only thank you and your members very much indeed for allowing us access to your club facilities, for
making us so welcome and for the friendly company. As you may know Tollesbury Mud Club members occupy the moorings
owned by Tollesbury Saltings Ltd off Woodrolfe Creek and therefore we do hot have any premises of our own. We do have a
rather primitive barbecue and if any of your members are coming our way we will do our best to reciprocate, but doubt if we can
come close to the standard of Marconi.
Kindest regards, Yours sincerely, Roger Lankester, Chairman, TMC.”

Dinghy Park Layout 1998

First of all, thank you to all Dinghy owners who have marked their trolleys with their name, etc. and who put their
names on the layout to show where they have put their boat. It does make my job easier.

You may have noticed that at the peak time of last year, around the end of August, there were only a few spaces left in
the Dinghy Park; indeed, some people had parked their boats outside the area. Also we will expect a few new members
in 1998, hopefully swelled by some members of Steeple Bay joining. That means we have had to look at how to get
more boats in. The layout on Page 17 shows how we can accommodate about 30 extra spaces. It means losing one of
the walkways through the dinghy park and the smaller boats having less space allocated to them.

It also means that we will have to largely revise the layout and markings before the start of the season. So, please be
sure to remove your boat from the Dinghy Park as soon as posssible and recover your anchors, etc.

When the new season starts, please do not concrete your anchors in as we need to continue to be flexible in the way the
dinghy park is laid out from year to year.

Please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any queries about the new layout. or any other questions come to that.

Also I am looking for someone who is willing to take over the dinghy park secretary job - so I will look forward to your
call.

Roger Smith, Solo 3872, [redacted]

Wednesday Evening Pursuit Races 1997

Over quite a number of years now Colin Phillips and Colin Leveridge have between them taken on the Jack B Driver
duty for the Evening Pursuit Races, each one taking alternate Wednesdays. This year, due to work commitments, Colin
Phillips was unable to continue after the first couple of races, but I would like to use this end-of-year issue of Navigans
to once again say thank you to the ‘two Colins’ for all they have done in the past to help with this event. I understand
our Clive (Shenton) stepped in on several occasions this year to fill the gap. thank you, Clive.

Our thanks also go to John and Mavis Weedon who again this year looked after the Race Officer duties for Wednesday
evenings. Without this small team turning up regularly the event, of course. would not happen. The Club is a lovely
place to be on a nice summer evening, it is a pity that the journey home from work is too late for many more of our
members to be able to take part. Ed.

Commodores Notes.

Time and Tide wait for no man. | have resolved to be more consistent with producing these notes this year. At the January Main
Committee Meeting the question of publishing the minutes was discussed and it was agreed that this practice could lead to
problems when matters relating to the conduct of members was discussed. The main committee has decided that a prédis of the
matters discussed should be published rather than the full minutes. I now have a ‘spur’ as this job falls to me!

1997 ECPR The Club has donated £3500, the proceeds from the 1997 East Coast Piers Race, to the Cirdan Trust. I received a
letter form Nick Back, who runs the Trust, thanking the Club for the donation together with details of the Bursaries this money
funded. Lee Harrison, chair of the ECPR committee, will publish the details after the next ECPR meeting.

Clubhouse and Site The regular users of the Club will have seen that the ditch between the Cruiser park and Cat field has been
filled. Danny Ainge was instrumental in organising the transportation and levelling of this clay. Once the clay has settled the
additional space will be used for cruiser storage. The storage of 14 Steeple Bay Cruisers in the Cat Field is a temporary
arrangement which had to be organised at very short notice and may have resulted in some ‘ruffled feathers’ in the dinghy fleet
whose trailers were moved without prior consultation. This was because Haven Leisure gave Steeple Bay SC members some two
weeks’ notice to quit. Sorry about that, but I hope you now appreciate why we needed to move so quickly.

The repair work to the access road has now been carried out. The windows on the north and west sides of the Clubhouse have
been replaced with double glazed, low maintenance units.

A specification for the galley service was agreed. The committee agreed that breakfast, snack lunch and after-racing tea and
cakes should be provided during the sailing season as outlined in the year book. The lunch menu should be similar the that
offered when Jean Flook was in charge. This specification will be sent to three interested parties who may decide to quote.
The interior of the Club will be decorated, a power point provided on the outside of the Race Control Cabin and the Diesel Fuel
Store BUND will be constructed.

Moorings A proposal to build a Travel Hoist for recovering cruisers has been made. Peter Claytonis gathering design and
construction details for the Committee to consider.

Social The Laying Up Dinner Dance was a success and we have to thank Ian Caruth for organising the event. Ian has
relinquished his position as Social Secretary and we need a replacement please. In the meanwhile Steve Glynn has stepped in to
organise the next Laying Up Dinner Dance on Saturday 14 November 1998. Neil Pembleton has agreed to organise an MSC
Cruising Association Barn Dance for 1999.

Sailing Sub Committee A draft programme for 1998-was presented and agreed. The following revisions are being considered:
e Starting sequence and times
e Safety boat rationalisation with regard to the Orkney
e Prize giving phased throughout the season
Maldon District Council are laying a new port hand bouy at the west end of the moorings off the hard. The Starting canons are
no longer ‘verboten’ and will be returned to the Club when Steve Hill can get the relevant police department to return his
telephone calls to fix the details.

Bar A new cold shelf and bottle cooler will be fitted to the Lounge and Dell Bars respectively. MASC has obtained a Club
Registration License for MSC after protracted negotiations.

Membership Mrs Lynda Chaplin’s offer to become Club Registrar was accepted. Thank you, Linda, for taking this job on.
Next Main Committee Meeting will be in March. (Extended Christmas festivities and the short month of February means a
couple of weeks between meetings)

That’s all folks. Colin Kidner

conveyed the boat to Maldon for the event and returned it to its home afterwards. Ed.

BACSPA News

The AGM of the Blackwater and Colne Sailing Protection Association was held on the 27th November at the Maldon Little Ship
Club. Mr Eric Rust of Brightlingsea SC was re-elected as Chairman and I continue as Honorary Secretary.

New arrivals to the Blackwater may not be aware of the existence of the Association. It was formed as long ago as 1962 by 14
Clubs with the objective of protecting sailing interests on both the Colne and Blackwater estuaries. At that time the major
concern was the possible adverse effect on sailing of the creation of marinas. Today the concerns are speeding by jetskis and
powerboats: control of access; the environment; sustainable development of leisure activities, etc. The local councils are duty
bound to produce so called ‘Estuary Management Plans’ to ensure harmony and sustainability. These plans are non-statutory for
the time being but legislation will soon be invoked statutory powers.

The plan for the Blackwater was published in 1996 and is gradually being implemented. A copy is available for inspection in the
Clubhouse at Stansgate. The consultation process has only just begun on the Colne Estuary and it is unlikely that their plan will
be completed until 1999. BACSPA has representation on the Eastern Regional Committee of the RY
A along with other
associations from the Norfolk Broads, Herts and Cambridge, Crouch and Southend. The Regional Committee is working hard to
try to persuade RYA Headquarters to decentralise some of its budget and responsibilities into the regions, in order to make the
RYA more accessible and relevant to the needs of the ‘grass roots” sailing fraternity atlarge.

Anyone having any queries concerning either the RYA or BACSPA should contact Derek Kirby or myself.

Ron Greygoose, Hon. Secretary, BACSPA.

A Piers eye view
by Charles Anderson

The settling days of autumn are now past and we can all look forward to the lengthening
daylight and warm spring days - hopefully.
However, this time of year also lends itself to fireside reminiscence and plans for the forthcoming season. At the moment I have only just reached the former and my reminiscence has recently been focusing on last year’s ECPR.
It has been prompted by Frank sending me a breakdown of the finances and I am pleased to see that the day raised about £4500 (includes some cheques sent direct to the Trust). Not bad I believe for a voluntary effort by all, both competitors and club helpers.

The latter encompasses a lot and as the one who tends to purloin the assistance and stretch the good will of most club members, I have the most to thank you all for. Slim justice could be done to try and isolate the individual contributions but as a section there is no doubt that the cruiser fleet continues to hold the lion’s share. The years of involvement by many have formed a tight, disciplined fleet under the admiral eyes of Derek Kirby.
It provides great comfort for those at base that as the fleet takes to the sea in the early hours of the day, the complexities of the coastline and weather are covered by such competent and experienced sailors. Although I have never done it myself I believe the same feeling of security must extend to the competitors as they run their keen eyes from orange flag to orange flag in the knowledge that they are at least heading in the right direction if not actually leading the pack.

I like to think that the involvement provides an added excuse to enjoy a days sailing as well as providing a purpose to the weekend.
Perhaps extending the activities in general of the cruiser fleet’s season which are extensive; indeed it is a privilege to be included in their busy calendar of racing, visits to marinas, other clubs, pubs and
breweries. What a life!

But seriously, the bottom line is thanks and sincere gratitude. I know I have said it at dinners and others have said it on various occasions and it is not because there is the standard response form at the back of this edition. For those well organised members to return and those less _diarised (terrible
Americanism sorry) to hang on to and return it later when the engine is fixed, the hull is painted and the sails
bent-on.

ANNUAL START OF SEASON SAFETY REMINDERS:

ADDERS: Members should be aware (and should remind any children they bring to the Club) that at this time of year they
might sometimes come across an adder lying in the sun, often concealed in long grass. Please be careful where you walk and try
not to disturb the animal which is harmless if left alone.

THE SCRUBBING POST is not a safe place for children to play on at any time. Members please ensure that any children you
bring to the Club keep off the Scrubbing Post.

THE RIVER IS COLD for many months into the Sailing Season, even on apparently warm sunny days. Though Support Boats
are out during all Club Races, it may happen that for some reason you can’t be picked up quickly after a capsize. It is important
that you take measures before you leave the shore that would delay the onset of hypothermia. The following advice is offered in
Navigans early in every season:

Wear adequate clothing, ic. Wet Suit/Dry Suit etc. and Buoyancy Aid.

Need ,
Make sure your boat and its gear are sound.
Ensure Personal Buoyancy and the Boat’s Buoyancy are both adequate.
if you are inexperienced, cither in sailing or in our sailing area, please ask advice from other
; experienced helms.
: 5. If you find yourself beginning to feel cold and tired while Sailing, return to shore straightaway, rather
than wait until you are too cold to think rationally.

IN ROUGH WEATHER: If Club Racing goes ahead in windy conditions this does not necessarily imply that it is safe to go
afloat. Some very experienced helms and crews may be well able to cope with that day’s conditions but less experienced sailors
could have a difficult and uncomfortable time. So please remember that even though Support Boats are there for Club Races,
you should aim to be entirely self-sufficient, sail within your limitations, and remember on all occasions that your decision to go
afloat, whether to race or to potter, is always made on your own responsibility.

“IT’S HAD A COAT OF PAINT”

The nautical equivalent of that pleasurable country pursuit of leaning on the farm gate is to look over the gunwale of a boat,
passing the time of day with the people (usually working) on board.

Those who did this on Jack earlier
B in the year will have noticed that the engine and gearbox are nowa rather pleasing shade of
light green. Indeed the heading of this piece came from someone who inadvertantly uttered the understatement of the year.

Over the winter Jack B’s engine was in fact changed for a factory rebuilt unit. At the same time the gearbox was overhauled by
the manufacturer's agent and the opportunity was taken to replace/refurbish many of the other items such as sea water pump and
engine mountings.

Many questions have been asked as to what was wrong with the old engine, why was the work necessary and (from a few cruiser
owners who have engines of about the same age) what did we know about 11 year old engines that they did not?

The answer to all this is that the old engine and gearbox had given reliable service over the previous 11 seasons and had clocked
up several thousand hours of running. It is possible that the units may have continued to give satisfactory service for years to
come. However, Jack B is essential to all the waterborne activities at the Club; from laying moorings to covering local and long
distance racing. Any failure during the season due to the ageing of the major units would take the boat out of service for a long
time and could happen when the people with the necessary skills were not available to do the work. It was felt that it would be
better to replace and overhaul these major units before any deterioration in reliability occurred. By carrying out the work out of
season it was possible to spread the effort and to take the time to get the best deals and do the work in the most economical
manner.

Hopefully the Club will get as good service out of the new engine as we got from the old. As usual. drivers are asked to follow
the User Guide and to report any problems

Thanks are due to Nick Beavins, Murray Bates, Peter Clayton and Mick Richardson for their contributions to the work.

The Club is particularly grateful to Geoff Josey who masterminded the whole project and did the lion’s share of the work. Geoff
drove many miles delivering the old engine and gearbox and collecting the new/overhauled units. Rebuilt engines do not come
ready to drop into a boat, but have to be completed and marinised. Geoff undertook most of this work in his garage, burning a lot

RYA EASTERN REGION DINGHY SEMINAR

This was held at Grafham Water Sailing Club on 14th February 1998. Sailing Secretary John Salmon and myself attended again
this year on behalf of the Club. The Programme was full and the event well supported. Key points noted were as follows:

1. Latest changes in the RYA proficiency scheme - John Laws. He recommended the new publication ‘Sailing Across the
Curriculum’ (ZS10, £9.95 from the RYA). This is a practical guide for those interested in promoting sailing for young people.
Courses for Senior Instructor training and assessment are now more management oriented. Courses can be run for 20 persons on
request (minimum age 18 years). The Powerboat Scheme is up and running and a similar scheme is being proposed for Personal
Water Craft (Jetskis to you and me).

2. New 1998 Race Training Programme - Richard Watson. As from January 1998 ‘Race Trainers’ become a ‘Club Racing
Coach’. The RYA ideally want one Club Racing Coach for every 50 members in a club. A new ‘Racing Coach’s Handbook’ is
to be published this month, ref: YR10/98. (23,000 proficiency certificates are issued in schools each year, but very few join clubs
and go on to race.) The two-day course can be organised on request for 8-15 people. There is a need to run a racing course to
move from learning to sail to racing.

3. Youth Development for Clubs - John Allen. John Allen is the RYA Youth Development Officer. He is very enthusiastic,
dynamic and knowledgeable, an ideal person for the job. The World Class Programme has £2.2 million backing from the Sports
Council. The aim is to target the kids and to create world beaters.

The Sports Council will only link with and fund ‘Top Clubs’, i.e. those judged to comply with certain essential requirements for
their facilities and coaching abilities, e.g. a minimum of 1 male and 1 female Club Racing Coach within 3 years. A key issue is
how to bring ‘non-family’ youngsters into sailing clubs. The social scene is the key - there must be a good youth social scene to
attract and keep them. The rules of some clubs (not ours) prohibit or discourage youth membership.

Clubs should ensure that all Race Training Establishments have full details of the facilities offered by clubs in their locality - a
video was recommended. N.B. Bradwell RTE claimed to have no information on local clubs.

4. Sailing for the Disabled - Bill Smith, East Anglian Sailing Trust. He requested that clubs complete and return the latest
single-page questionnaire from Sailability. There is currently no-one co-ordinating activities for disabled sailing in the Eastern
Region. Requirements to be considered include:
Access - parking, and water (pontoons); bar and changing rooms.
Boats - must have a reasonable degree of stability.

5. Adventure Activities Licensing Regulations 1996 --John Laws. The scheme is up for review in the near future, now looking
at a voluntary scheme for clubs to come into the main licensing scheme. Clubs at the moment have a privileged position. It is
recommended that clubs have a manual showing responsibilities and codes of practice. A Code of Practice must represent what
instructors actually do on the water. The RYA has an information pack ‘Risk Assessment Principles’ available on request.

6. Review of experience with the 1997 Racing Rules of Sailing This review was given by Jim Saltonstall MBE, the RYA Senior
Racing Coach, (where did you get that extraordinary accent from, Jim?) My guess, in Birmingham.

He was concerned that some competitors (even those at the highest level) do not observe any rules; and that the problem was
world wide. Who is to blame for this? There is no referee on the ‘race track’. Race Management teams see infringements and
do nothing about it! He referred to Racing Rule 69 ‘Allegations of Gross Misconduct’. If a protest committee believes that there
has been a gross breach of a rule, or of good manners, or sportsmanship, or the sport has been brought into disrepute, it may call
a hearing. Penalties include: warning, exclusion, suspension, reporting to National Authority. He then proceeded to give
examples of typical right of way situations under the new rules. He emphasised the need for all competitors to learn and
understand the 18 definitions in the new rules. (N.B. ‘Keep Clear’ and ‘Obstruction’ have been amended for 1998)

7. Final Question Session RYA was requested to produce a summary of the Adventure Activities Licensing requirements.

Ron Greygoose.

and our neighbours.

whether racing, cruising or just for fun.

Clive will be discussing, with the sailing sub committee, proposals for improving the sailing facilities at the club. Watch this
space for future developments.

Safety

Safety is exercising the executive and main committee following advice received from the RYA. I am reading an RYA
publication called Around the Red Tape, Law and Administration for Clubs and Schools. [Some of you may have read it!] I
quote from the introduction of this publication.

“The enormous increase in legislation in recent years and the ever rising tide of liability claims which threaten anyone
organising recreational activities, particularly those withan inherent element of risk, make it essential for the club administrator
to have access to comprehensible advice on the relevant law and practice. To ignore the potential dangers is not only foolhardy
but may also land the volunteer's fellow members in trouble if any injured litigant chooses to take action against the club as a
whole as well as the individual club officers.”

“It is hoped that as well as being a source of information to those involved in the administration of sailing clubs and schools, this
book will also be a source of comfort and reassurance.”

The author is a Barrister at Law.

The main committee is looking at the question of potential liability to third parties. We are concerned with the possible legal
liability of a yacht club as a result of things done [or not] in the course of its normal activities, especially organising yacht races,
and ancillary activities such as launching vessels and providing rescue services.

In most cases the plaintiff will allege that the cause of the injury or damage was the negligence of the club. Negligence can be
described as either the carrying out of any act which a reasonable man would not have carried out, or the failure to do something
which a reasonable man would have done. The reasonable man test is used by the law to determine what standards persons must
live up to when carrying out those activities which affect others.

What this means in practice is that eventually all the activities which happen at the club will come under consideration to ensure
that what we do at the club is as safe as we can reasonably make it. ( Will it pass the “Reasonable man” test?)

7.

I do not wish to spread alarm and despondency amongst any of you. I am confident that the way we run the activities at the club
are safe. I and the executive wish to consider what happens at the club so that it can be demonstrated that none of us are
Carrying out activities on behalf of club members which can be considered to the negligent. This review will be carried out in
Stages. In the mean time don’t panic!
Perhaps we might all “think safety” in future.

See you on the water. Colin Kidner.

The following SOLO tuning tips are as supplied by Speed Sails and you may find them useful.

SOLO TUNING GUIDE _

This guide was first included in Navigans in 1997 and is repeated for new members and those with poor memories !

Mast Position The distance from the front of the mast at the heel to the outside of the transom at the floor is 3055mm.
Forestay This should be just in tension when the mast (without sail) is pushed to the back of the gate.
Shrouds These should be just in tension when the mast (without sail) is 10mm from the front of the gate.
Chock Use one chock which just fits in front or behind the mast .

Light airs Up to just sitting on the side deck.
Upwind Chock behind the mast.
No cunningham.
Centreboard 25-50 mm of forward rake.
Outhaul 20mm from black band.
Kicker just slack
Traveller 0-50mm from centreline.
A small amount of leeward heel is acceptable.

Off wind Use only enough centreboard to keep the rudder neutral.
Leave outhaul on it’s upwind setting.
Use enough kicker to stop the boom rising in gusts.

Medium Airs __Up to fully hiked
Upwind Chock in front of mast.
No cunningham.
Centreboard vertical.
Outhaul 10mm from black band.
Kicker just slack
Traveller 0-100mm from centreline.
Increase mainsheet tension as the traveller moves away from the centreline.

Offwind As for light airs except :
Ease outhaul up to 100mm
Use enough kicker to keep the back of the top batten parallel to the boom.

Heavy Airs Fully hiked overpowered.
Upwind Remove chock
Use cunningham to progressively depower the sail (too much and pointing will suffer)
Lift centreboard progressively to reduce weather helm.
Outhaul to the black band.
Kicker just tight.
Ease traveller up to 380mm from the centreline to keep the boat footing - but pull it closer to the centreline in
flatter areas to maintain pointing.
Use more kicker if the mainsheet needs to be eased often in gusts

Offwind Same as medium airs except only ease outhaul and cunningham if more power is needed.

CADET CAMPAIGN COMMENCES CONVINCINGLY

Personally, I am still in shock that I’ve been out on the water already. Usually at this time I am searching the
garage wondering
where we put the boat. However, this year | thought that I’d better try and make it look as if I had made the effort
to get myself
organised in time for the first Cadet meeting - in order not to show Dad up.

We met on the Saturday of the Bank Holiday weekend at the front of the club house. Dad was worried at 11:55
when there were
still only five of us but by about 12:10 there were thirty-four of us! We started of with a quick treasure hunt to
wake us all up
and then had a capsize drill recap. The younger ones did some rigging then whilst the older ones revised the start
sequence.
Because the wind was very strong we didn’t get out onto the water until Monday and then, of course, the wind died
totally. Due
to our remarkable lack of progress the race was abandoned before anyone reached the second mark. The afternoon
race was
better as the wind had picked up and everybody finished - although it did take me about an hour longer than everyone
else to do
so.

The next weekend enough Cadets turned up to persuade the Race Officer to organise a couple of Cadet races. The first one
went
very well, with some close racing and everybody finishing. The afternoon race was a different story.
The wind became quite
strong and a lot of us, me especially, spent most of the time upside-down and had to find alternative transport
back to the Club.
All in all, it was an extremely good start to the season and according to Dad we all worked together well.
Thanks to all of those
people who made it happen because we all really enjoyed ourselves.

Sarah Davies, May 12th 1998

Is Your GPS Bugged?

As far as I can establish there will be two ‘bugs’ infesting our GPSs in 1999/2000. If you have a Garmin GPS you can stop
worrying right now because Garmin have assured me that none of their equipment will be affected. For the rest of you, you will
have to contact the manufacturer/supplier of your equipment.

These are the problems as I understand them:

1. “Week Rollover.” The signal sent down by the satellites to adjust the date in GPS receivers is a 10 bit data stream and deals
in weeks. The programme has a capacity of 1,024 weeks and started in 1982. Apparently 1,024 weeks takes it up to 31 August
1999 when, unless this has been taken care of in the receiver's internal software (as with Garmin) then the receiver will revert
back to August 1982 with associated time and distance errors. (I haven't checked the maths, this was how it was explained to
me!)

2. “Millennium Bug.” The second problem is the infamous computer problem. If the receiving equipment utilizes only the last
two digits of the year, when it sees the 00 of 2000 it will revert back to 1900 again with associated errors

Extra information gleaned along the way:

VALSAT: All modern sets including 8 channel parallel are compliant (OK) Source Mantsbrite [redacted]

PHILLIPS AP Mk6: All recently (within the last 2 years) purchased or upgraded equipments should be OK. Software version
016 is the latest and is recommended. It was not divulged to me which previous versions are OK, so check your version and
then give Comar a bell. To check your version: Enter “Setup’.... then .... “Security Reset’ .... then use keys until “Phillips...
Ser No. ....Software Version is displayed. Source:- Comar (1.0.W.) @ [redacted]

Eric Lawley, Pegasus

CADET CORNER- See also Cadet Week Form on P. 18 Thomas Anderson
It was brilliant to see so many of us on the water over the weekend of the 23" May, and I know that a great time was had by all.
On the Saturday we did lots of practise starts, in order to make sure that everyone could recognise their five minute flag and start
flag, although it was interesting to see who hadn’t been listening during the briefing, and therefore had to keep asking the
committee boat “Is that the four minute/two minute/start gun?” I won’t mention any names (Tim Dowley), but it was good to
witness a marked improvement in the starts of those who were there, although more practise is still needed, I suspect! The disco
in the evening was thoroughly enjoyed by all the age groups that boogied away until well past their bedtimes!

On the Sunday and Monday the bright-eyed cadets took to the water in their Toppers and Mirrors and there was some very
competitive racing, especially in the Topper class, and the overall results were as follows:

Sunday, 24" May:

Race | Race 2 Overall
Mitch Glynn 2 1 1*
Quintin Hardwick l 4 ’
Michaela Glynn 4 3 :i
JoJo Anderson 3 2 gmc

As you can see, the top positions were very closely contested, with only two points separating first and second places.
Unfortunately I do not have the results for the Monday races, (they should be on the results noticeboard in the clubhouse), but I
know they are excellent as well.

I would like to mention the Wednesday Night races. These take place every Wednesday evening at the club. They are Pursuit
races, the slowest boat goes off first and everyone else starts after it, depending on their handicap. You start off the hard, but
after that it’s a normal race. This week we had five cadet boats racing, out of about ten, two of them came in the top three, so
come down and try and improve your racing skills.

As well as this series, there will also be a Summer Term Series over the 14 & 28 June and the 12 & 26 July.

Finally, there will be a big race at some point after Cadet Week against cadets from the Blackwater and Royal Burnham sailing
clubs, and so we should be honing our skills so we can thrash the pants off them.

ECPR. Congratulations to Lee Harrison and the East Coast Piers Race Committee for organising a highly enjoyable
and successful event. Thanks must also go to all the many folk who supported the event in a variety of ways, the event
would not be nearly as successful were it not for your help. The money raised will again be used to provide Bursaries to
allow some seventy disadvantaged youngsters to experience the joys of sailing as part of a team. Watch this space for
details of who benefited.

‘Lost’ Property. Peter has had his sailing boots returned but his gloves and watch are still missing. Thank you to the
person who mistakenly took the boots and returned them when he realised his mistake. I am deeply ashamed of the lack
of respect for personal property which some other member/s of this Sailing Club have exhibited in this case. I hope the
person/s concerned are able to live with their conscience knowing that they have stolen property belonging to a fellow
Club Member.

Bricklayer Needed! The Club could do with the services of a club member who has Bricklaying skills. The
Environmental Agency state that if the Diesel in the Fuel store should ‘spill’ it must be contained. This means a ‘bund’
(wall of bricks to form a dam) has to be taid on the existing concrete base. If you can help please give Peter Bloomfield
(Vice Commodore) a ring on [redacted].

Laying Up Supper. Steve Glynn has taken on the job of organising this year’s Laying Up Supper and yet again has a
novel idea to move the event on from last year’s successful event. Please see your fleet captain or any member of the
Main Committee for tickets. The event is at the Three Rivers Golf and Country Club and the ticket price is £21.50.
Those of you who in the past have found the music too loud can be assured that effective steps will be taken to control
the music volume this year. There will also be seating which will be in a quieter part of the room.

Club’s Rubbish Skips. The Rubbish Skips provided for the use of Club Members should only be used for typical
domestic rubbish. When the skips are collected the driver will check that ‘unauthorised’ rubbish has not been placed in
the skip. This means that if he finds objects like car/ lorry tyres, caravan windows or aluminium masts in the skip he
retums to base without the skip. The Club receives a letter explaining why the skip has not been emptied and a bill for
the “wasted journey’. The offending item/s have to be removed from the skip by us before a further request to empty
the skip is made, and separate arrangements have to be made for the disposal of the unauthorised items. I am sure that
you agree that the extra work and cost to the Club is unacceptable. Please do not abuse the facilities offered by the
Club.

Money sent to Club Treasurer. If you send money to the Club Treasurer can you tell him what the money is for and
give him your full name so that the funds can be accounted for. (The Treasurer may assume that you are donating
funds to his holiday account!)

See you on the water. Colin Kidner

The Piers Race Day Charles Anderson

What canI say to you all but a big ‘thank you’.

A fresh force 4 started this year’s event with a steady build through the race to the top-end of a 5 before
returning to the
calmer tolerances of a 3 - 4 by the end.

Tony Bullimore finally arrived to get everyone off to an excellent start for both races. His plans originally
included
staying for the day but a late arrangement to go to Belgium on Monday meant he left us shortly after
the starts.

He did however satisfy the requests of three cadets JoJo & Charlotte Anderson and Quintin Hardwick. signing
the
bottom of their Toppers. His advice to them both was ‘if you ever see the signature don’t get stuck underneath’!

The 140 competitors were delighted to hear they were destined to do the full course. All the mother boats completed
their radio checks and proceeded to stations. The lead boats were very quickly among them reaching Walton Pier
in
about 1’ hours. With a lively sea running on the ebb one competitor and a TA operator were taken off boats feeling
seasick. Another crew member was taken on board the Jack B with severe back pain and Vince and Mark had to retire
after Mark sprained his hand badly. They successfully sailed home without requiring assistance.

One competitor was dismasted and three others had to be taken in tow. On their return they all came up to thank me
(YOU) for the amazing cover and speedy response of all those involved in providing assistance. I think what is
rarely
remembered and without becoming complacent, is that the ECPR is quite unique in the multihull calendar and
that
includes the rescue cover provided.

I would like to add my word
of thanks to all of you for your tremendous support and seamanship throughout three day.
I do hope those of you booked in to the Maldon Fantasia arrived bright, breezy and managed to stay awake for the
performance.

Good sailing for the rest of the season.

The day is split into land based and on-the-water instruction. The land based session starts with rigging a SOLO and then a detailed review of the settings for each point of sailing in various wind strengths. The sailing instruction usually comprises of a number a race starts with short windward legs - finish and then another start etc. Jim observes, coaches and comments from a support boat. It's all informal, with plenty of opportunities for questions and discussion with Jim whose results speak for themselves with National and World SOLO titles to his credit.

CRUISER COMMENTS

First, may I say how nice it is to be back with you all having spent the past month cruising Holland aboard ‘HAPPY
MEDIUM’ in company with Malcolm & Margaret aboard “SURUCA’. Whilst the weather could have been a lot better,
the company could not have been and a great time was had by all.

One of the first tasks we had to perform on our return was as Matriarch boat off Weymarks. Fortunately, the weather
was an improvement on that generally experienced during our holiday. At this point I would like to thank those Cruiser
Members who supported the East Coast Piers Race event. Unfortunately we seldom get to see the celebrities - in this
case Tony Bullimore - or the competitors, some of whom travel from foreign parts to take part in this charity event. |
was. however, ashore putting my dinghy away in time to hear the Commodore express his thanks to the Cruiser Fleet,
together with the warm appreciation from the competitors. Well done, and Thank You.

Maureen Ball tells me the next NAVIGANS may be a couple of months away due to the summer break* so I am
exercising my mind on what to include in this issue.

The most important, I feel, is the Flotilla Cruise to Shotley Marina during the late summer Bank Holiday weekend
29/30/31 August. The plan will be to leave MSC Saturday, locking into Shotley Marina during the afternoon. As with
last year. we have been allocated the whole of pontoons *F’ and *G’, the cost being the same as last year, i.e. £1 per
metre plus VAT. Those who have been to Shotley Marina before will already be on their computer; for those who have
not. it will save time if you complete Shotley’s registration form (copy of which is on P.13) and return it to me by
Sunday 23rd August. Sunday 30th August will be a layday for you to do your own thing, however, it is intended we all
meet up in the “Stour Suite’ of the Shipwreck Public House at the Marina for an evening meal. Details of the Menu are
listed below and the price of the meal is £15 per head with a concessionary price of £7.50 for children. Members who
are not sailing up to Shotley but wish to travel by road to join us for a meal will be most welcome. Please complete the
reply slip on P. 13 and return it to me, together with your cheque by Sunday 23rd August.

For those of you who are able to take the remainder of the week off, a visit to the River Deben is again scheduled for
Monday 31st August, stopping off at Ramsholt for the evening before proceeding up to the Tidemill Marina at

Camping Fortnight

Another excellent two weeks with good weather apart from some rain on a couple of occasions. Cadet Week started with 70
Cadets and the wind just a bit strong for the beginners’ comfort. The Cadets soon became confident in going out in any
reasonable breeze and were only kept ashore on those occasions when there was no wind at all. The usual disco and prize-giving
took place during the middle weekend, details later in this issue. Lack of wind on the middle Sunday prevented a planned race
against visiting cadets from Burnham, which was a pity. There are now an extra 6 Picoes added to the fleet of monohulls at the
Club - the 6 demonstration boats having been offered at a reduced price and being snapped up by Cadets who had tried them and
liked them. It was lovely to see several boats out regularly on the water during the second camping week, manned by
increasingly confident cadets.

On the last Friday evening there was a ‘hog roast’ cooking all afternoon over an open fire on a rotating spit. Several campers
brought their tables and chairs onto the Commodore’s lawn and it became an excellent social evening for those who took part.

Grateful thanks go to Charles Anderson and Chris Davies who led the way with organising Cadet Week, to all those former
cadets who volunteered as instructors (having a tiring but enjoyable week in the process), and to those adults who helped with
instructing and/or who went on the water with the various support boats. Cadet Week could not be the success it is without all of
you. As an onlooker J could see Steve Glynn and Mick Richardson amongst others doing various tasks to ensure the smooth
running of Camping and Cadet Weeks; thanks to them and to all others who contributed anything to the work involved.

The very necessary decision to restrict the number of camping units paid off, especially for those using the dinghy field which
was extremely cramped last year. The disadvantage was that some may not have been able to have their preferred spot and some
may have been disappointed in not being able to camp at all, especially in the first week. It is a pity, but we have no choice but to
tailor the Club’s most popular event to fit into the space available. One other improvement we need is the co-operation of non
camping members - that they do not leave their cars parked, at the time camping starts, where the pitches will be. This request
and a sketch of the pitches will be published in next year’s pre-camping Navigans, as it was in this year’s, and I do hope those
concerned will be willing to help us out.

Jack B was hauled out for her-annual summer maintenance during the middle camping weekend and, with the weather so good
again this year, the work did not take long. Thanks to Murray for spraying off the weed and barnacles, to Jenny and David (with
the help of Jo) for sanding the old varnish, followed by re-varnishing and painting: and to those who offered to help but weren’t
required because the work went so quickly. Jack B, at my request, was kept on the hard for all these tasks, it was the coolest
place to work on the boat when the forecast for a heatwave turned out to be an accurate one!

David found his lost waterproof jacket in the end - did anyone lose an unusual key fob of the noisy variety at the site during
camping? Contact a Ball family member and we'll get it back to you.

Ed.

Solos at Marconi

Despite dire weather forecasts‘as a result of hurricane Danny, 28 boats, comprising 15 visitors and 13 locals, turned out for
Marconi Sailing Club’s Solo Open Meeting on the River Blackwater in Essex on 6th September.

Hurricane Danny or not, the start of the first race had to be delayed waiting for the wind to fill in, and light winds were to be the
order of the day. After a curious start with the boats trying to avoid being swept over the line by the tide, Roger Smith led the
way round in a fading breeze, hotly pursued by Gordon Barclay. In fact Gordon, using his experience of tidal estuary sailing to
good effect, just pipped Smith on the line, with Steve Ede third.

The boats had to be towed back to the Club for an extended lunch break waiting for the wind to settle and fill in again. It
eventually filled in from the South and in the second race Barclay and Jerry Garner battled it out up front against the breeze and
the tide, Barclay ultimately coming out on top again, giving him two wins and the overall result. The end of his successful three
year term as the President of the Solo Class Association has obviously revitalised his sailing performance.

The third race had plenty of incidents, not least of which was the diversion of the rescue craft, at the request of the Coastguard,
to rescue the crew of an incendiary power boat on the river.** However, the Solo Fleet was largely unaware of this as they raced
to settle the other places. Ron Laurie set the pace, chased by Samantha Husk, Steve Ede, Mike Wilkie and Tony Cook. At the
end of the second beat Laurie and Ede had to do turns having touched the windward mark due to the tide, leaving Husk in the
lead followed by Cook and Smith. At the end Steve Ede came back to take the race, followed by Cook, Smith and Samantha
Husk fourth.

ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING - ELECTION OF COMMODORE

It is my intention to offer myself for election as Commodore of the Club at the Annual General Meeting in November.

I have been a member of the Marconi Sailing Club committee since 1980 and during that time served in a number of positions
including Treasurer, Commodore and Vice President. I am also a Vice President of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club. In
addition I am also a member of the committee for the Essex Section of the Cruising Association.

I have been sailing since my youth, initially on other people’s boats, then in Graduate and Mirror dinghies until I bought my
Snapdragon ‘Rasputin’ in 1987. For a number of years I was actively involved with the East Coast area of the Ocean Youth
Club.

I passionately believe that the greatest strength of the Club is the diversity of the boats and sailing that we have available to
us,
from sailboards through monohull and catamaran dinghies to cruisers; and from very competitive racing to “Mucking about in
boats’. Another great strength is the ‘Self Help’ aspect from the acquisition of items to improve and develop the Club, to the
volunteers who organise all the activities both on and off the water, resulting in our reasonable membership fees.

If I am elected as Commodore, it is my intention to build on these strengths to carry the Club successfully forward into the
next
Millennium. To this end, I will be arranging a discussion evening early in 1999. This will be similar to the one held during my
previous term as Commodore to seek the views of the membership on a number of subjects, including the maximum number of
members, improvements to the facilities within the club house, general improvements to the grounds of the Club, and any other
comments. This will be your opportunity to express your views to the Committee so that they can develop future short and long
term plans to the benefit of all members, fleets and interests of the Club.

Jenny Ball will be offering herself for election as Rear Commodore at the same time. As most of you will be aware, Jenny has
been a member of the Club for a considerable time, initially as a Cadet and then as a Full Member. During this time she has
always been active in her sailing and her support for the behind the scenes activities, such as her help during Cadet weeks and
involvement with a number of committees. | fully support her offering to stand and will be proposing her for the position.

Cruiser Comments

August Bank Holiday Cruise. The late summer bank holiday weekend marked the last of this year’s organised flotilla sailing
events with a visit to Shotley Marina followed by a meal in the “Stour Suite” of the “Shipwreck Public House” on Sunday 30th
August. As with last year the support was tremendous. The weekend started with 8 boats making an early start from the Club
for an overnight stopover at Brightlingsea and, whilst it was nice to meet up with Peter Clayton & Family aboard “PEACE”, it
was sad that this was the end-of their holiday up the East Coast and they were in fact on their way back to MSC. Saturday
turned out to be another glorious day, perhaps too good, since there was little or no wind to sail by. Those leaving Brightlingsea
were soon joined by other members off Colne Point sailing up the Wallet towards Walton.

Possibly learning the lessons of last year when we arrived almost en b/oc, arrivals this year were more random, with some
choosing to sail into the river Stour to visit the hostelry at Wrabness - no prizes for guessing who! - whilst 2 other intrepids
ventured into the River Deben since they were unable to join us there later. By Saturday evening 21 Club boats had arrived into
Shotley, the last being VARUNA II arriving about 22.30, Roger having to wait for Mike who had come directly from the airport
having just returned from Tenerife. The fleet so far comprised: HAPPY MEDIUM, ICARUS, FANTASEA, CAPRICORN,
WINKLER, ANGEL II, GAIETY OF LYMINGTON, ALDEBARAN, GREEN PANTHER, PEPPER, CLANEDA, SABRE,
RIMFIRE, JAED, RUBICON, TELEMON, WINDSONG, SERUPIN II, MILADY D, KAYMAR, VARUNA II.

Sunday saw the arrival of SEA GEM, OCEAN SLIPPER, JUNO, ANTIGUA KISS, HARTLEY, and REFLECTION who had
left Ramsgate at 0300 that morning to join us. What dedication! This made the total of boats attending 27, a truly excellent
turnout and credit must go to Shotley Marina who made available the two linear berths F & G for our sole use. Even so, the
family was not yet complete for Leonard Scholl, who was unable to sail his yacht COMOCEAN up to Shotley arrived by car to
join us for the evening meal. So there we were, 28 boats in all. The meal was excellent, the compan, treat and I am sure a good
time was had by one and all.

Monday saw the break up of the fleet, those needing to return to MSC took their leave whilst the rest ventured forth into the
River Deben and up to the Tidemill Yacht Harbour at Woodbridge, arriving by the late afternoon. Learning the lessons of the
two previous years, it was decided to hold the Bar B Q at the Tidemill on Tuesday evening. At first this also seemed doubtful as
the rain poured down all the previous night into the morning but, undaunted, the arrangements were made, food and drink
bought and by the middle of the afternoon the sun was out and a very pleasant evening was had by all, probably helped along by
Doreen’s Rum Punch.

After this it was everyone doing their own thing, some stayed on in the Deben for another day returning to Brightlingsea the
following day, others had already made it to Brightlingsea, others went back into the River Orwell. Was it something I said? By
this tme CORNISH GOLD and SURUCA had arrived in the Walton Backwaters being too late to join us in the Deben, so
yours truly together with REFLECTION, joined them and, thanks to Peter Arnold’s magnificent water taxi service, we were all
able to meet on board SURUCA for an exchange of banter and, of course, refreshments. Sadly the weather put paid to the
proposed gathering of the clans at Brightlingsea for a fish and chip supper, but at least everyone arrived back home safe and
sound.

RNSA Visit. During the weekend 25th/26th July we hosted members of the RNSA to a Bar B Q etc. in the Dell Bar. The
weather was fine and a grand time was had by all, resulting in a letter from Terry Ryser, Hon Sec of the RNSA-east coast unit,
thanking MSC members for a very warm welcome. (I’m sure no pun was intended.) We look forward to them visiting us again

JACK B DRIVERS

Propeller Shaft Greaser

The shaft greaser should be screwed down just until resistance is felt. It should not be screwed down tight as
this creates excessive pressure in the shaft seal which will force it apart, letting in the water.

Water Cooling

There is a large amount of very fine weed floating in the water. When drawn into the cooling water inlet this
is capable of creating a total blockage. The filter may be clean but the hull inlet may be totally blocked.
Drivers are asked to keep a constant check on water flow from the exhaust. If flow is inhibited, check the
filter and inlet. A piece Of cane is stored aboard for cleaning out the water inlet.

Please don’t rely on the engine overheat alarm as, by the time this is activated the raw water circuit will have
been running dry for 10 minutes or so, and damage to the raw water pump will occur.

Navigans is the means by which all Club Members and Committees can be in touch with each other and keep abreast of Club events throughout the year. Our new Navigans Editor/s are Belinda and Kevin Dowley, whose offer to take over from me at the end of this year was a welcome one which means the magazine can now continue without any break.

The new address for all future Navigans contributions is on the front page of this edition so please remember to send them there, though any finding their way to me will be passed on.

Any Members, and particularly Club Officers, who would like to communicate with the club at large through Navigans, please make sure you let the Editor’s team have the information in good time — please don’t leave them guessing! Rule of thumb is that an item for a particular month’s edition should reach the Editor at the start of the previous month.

A new Editor will mean the chance of a new look and a fresh approach to Navigans and I look forward to seeing the magazine flourish in new hands over future years. Ed.

This is my last production of Navigans. During my time with the magazine it has been an enormous help that the printing and distribution have been done by other volunteers. Leon White took care of this for several years (and still helps out occasionally), followed by Keith Starkey, who now shares the work with Tony Holbrook. Thanks are due to them all for giving their time and I always knew my work was finished once the typing was done and the pages were on their way to the next stage.

My thanks also go to Committee Members over the years who I know have taken care of many details in the background for me, to Larry Botheras and his Committee three years ago for providing the equipment to make the work so much easier, and lastly to my husband Ray for sensible advice, proof reading, and reminders of what should appear in an issue.

On Pages 12 & 13 there is a brief nostalgic trip through Navigans and Editors Past, including a copy of the first
issue ever produced, which includes a piece of history - a petrol shortage - due to Suez, I’m told. Ed.
