You may have noticed from elsewhere in this issue that the post of Commodore is being contested for the first time in ages. I
believe that it is a sign of a healthy club that people are clamouring to serve its interests. You will also note that I am one of the
nominees. I would like to tell you something about me and the direction in which I would seek to take the Club in the next three
years.

I have been a member for ten years and have been Fleet Captain and, for the last 3 years, Rear Commodore. I sail a Tornado
catamaran with my son and I intend to carry on as long as my body lasts.

I believe we have a Club to be proud of. My trips to various Clubs throughout the country while campaigning the Tornado have
reinforced this belief. Our site and sailing waters are excellent and our broad based approach to sailing adds greatly to the
strength of the Club. I see my first duty as Commodore would be to ensure the continued existence of the Club, not for one
section of the Club but for all, regardless of whether a member sails a cruiser, dinghy, catamaran or windsurfer either racing or
not.

The financial administration of the Club been somewhat "hand to mouth" over recent years with self interest groups within the
Club pushing for expenditure. I will seek to improve the predictability of our spending by the introduction of a Five Year Plan
which would programme all future expenditure. It is no secret that my own vision for the Club is to improve our on-shore
facilities so that they reflect my perception that our Club is in the "Top Ten" of national sailing clubs. We are all aware that
Lottery money is available for well thought out schemes and it would be my intention to seek funding from that source. Lottery
money is not all good news as organisations are expected to find half the money for capital projects themselves.

Almost every Club member has his or her own vision of their future requirements for the Club, just as I do. By consultation and
consensus the Five Year Plan would be developed to take "on board" as many of these visions as can be practically and
financially achieved. The decision to adopt the Plan would be made by the whole Membership, probably at an AGM.

I would now like to tell you what I am not. I am not retired, not an ex Marconi employee and I do not sail a cruiser. I truly
believe each of these attributes are admirable, and my admiration for Pat Black, Frank Bennett and Peter Bloomfield, who are
nominated unopposed for election to the Executive Committee, is unbounded. However, if my rival for the post of Commodore is
elected, 80% of the Executive Committee would then be composed of such members, and I do not think that would be
representative of the Club as a whole.

If elected I will deal fairly and evenly with each section of the Club. If Cat sailors think I will always take their point of view will
be disappointed, but they can be assured that their views as well as others will be heard and put on the balance.

I have proposed John Salmon as Rear Commodore. John, who sails a Solo, has been Sailing Secretary for two years, and I have
come to rely on his perceptive ideas and energy in their implementation. As Rear Commodore, John would Chair the Sailing Sub
Committee and be a member of both the Executive and the Main Committee. Together, and with the experience of our
colleagues, we will make an effective and representative management team for the Club.

Whatever your views and loyalties I urge you to attend the AGM on 15" November and cast your vote in the way that will
benefit the Club as a whole.

Above all let's remember that we are all members of this Club so we can enjoy our sport of sailing.

Clive Shenton, Rear Commodore

THE
MOLLIETTE

When taking the short cut across Mersea flats there is an east cardinal mark on the Cocum Hills that stands up like a signpost.
Whether you are cutting across in the Piers Race or trying to cheat the tide in your cruiser you can’t miss it. In the old days
(well up until sometime in the 1970s) this was a green wreck buoy. The locals called it the ‘Molliette’ buoy.

At low tide some of the wreckage that the cardinal mark is guarding is visible. What was the Molliette and how did the
wreckage come to be there?

The story starts with the U-boat successes of the Great War. Steel for shipbuilding was in short supply and a number of ferro-
concrete vessels were built on both sides of the Atlantic. (Incidentally this method of building was not new as the first ferro
boats were reputed to have been built in 1848.)

In 1919 two ferro-concrete vessels were built in the yard of James Pollock, Sons & Co Ltd at Faversham. The first to be
completed was the Molliette and the second the Viollette.

These vessels were auxiliary schooners with three masts, all gaff rigged but without topsails. As built Molliette had a bowsprit.
Each had a 120hp, two cylinder Bolinders oil engine running at 225-250 revolutions per minute. They were very boxy vessels
designed for ease of construction. Dimensions were 125 ft. long by 25 ft. beam. The concrete on the hulls was three inches
thick. Performance under sail was reputed to be ‘sluggish’. The crew of four or five men lived in the foc’s’le and three officers
lived in the deckhouse aft.

The story of Viollette is soon told. This unhappy vessel appears to have been unsatisfactory during trials and was not accepted
by her intended owners. However she presumably traded until 1921 when in January, in bad weather, she dragged into Southend

11.

pier. The pier was severed (marooning the Pierhead Keeper and his family, who in those days lived in a bungalow at the
pierhead) and the Viollette sank. She was raised and ended her days as a hulk on the Medway.

Molliette had a longer life, although she appears to have had more than her fair share of mishaps. She was damaged
in a
collision in 1919, was ashore a few times and is reputed to have collided with Tower Bridge although there does
not appear to be
any record of this. When her coasting days were over Molliette was sold to Essex owners and was fitted out as
a night-club.

The Molliette story finished (almost) on the Mersea flats during the last war when she was used for bombing target
practice.
However ferro-concrete vessels are well nigh indestructible thus the wreckage remains on Cocum Hills to this day.

(Most of the above information was obtained from the East Coast Digest of February 1976. If anyone has any further
information on the Molliette’s history please put pen to paper.)

Ray Ball

Commodores report 1997.

In case any of you are wondering who the Commodore is, it's me! My reasons for not being able to do a great
deal of sailing are the same as last year, so I won't repeat them! However I really do see an end to the
turmoil in my job and expect to be spending most weekends at the club next summer.

From the point of view of the club, I am delighted to report that this year has been mucha better one than last
year, in most respects. However the galley service has not proved to be as reliable as we would have liked.
When Mark and his team were here the service and food were to most people's taste. It was a shame that the
reliability was not of the same standard. The club was left without a service on a number of high profile
occasions and I and other club officials were left to apologise to guests for the lack of food. I have to thank pat
black for spending time liasing with mark on many occasions after contractual agreements were broken. The
main committee agreed that he should be formally censured by letter. It simply is not acceptable to fail
turn up to provide a service after agreeing to do so. A lack of explanation or apology when there has been no
galley service is also unacceptable and unprofessional. Mark decided he no longer wished to complete his
contract and left. The matter will be pursued by the main committee.

What is being done about the situation I hear you say? A number of organisations have been contacted and are
being invited to tender for the service. The committee will try to ensure that a reliable organisation wins
the contract. If there are any club members who feel that they would like to provide the club with a galley service
they are welcome to put in a bid.

Pat black steps down at the end of the season after three years as vice commodore. His efforts have resulted in a
great many improvements to the club. Patio area, barbecue area, relocation of the fuel shed, alteration of
the dinghy park to accommodate the wind surfer rigging area, ditch filling, window replacement, repairs to the
hard, galley service, to name but a few. I am sure that you will join with me in thanking pat for all his hard work
over the past three years.

You will be pleased to hear that the environmental agency (nee NRA) have finally agreed to pay up for the
necessary repairs to the access road. Clive Shenton is the engineer who we have to thank for providing a
professional report on the state of the road, costing and specifying what needed to be done to put it right. Armed
with this professional report, Larry Botheras was the ‘front man’ who did the negotiations with the environmental
agency and convinced the 'men from the ministry’ to part with the cash to put matters to rights. I am quite sure
that without their input the club would still be arguing with the environmental agency. A big thank you to both of
you. The work will start after tenders have been received and the contract awarded.

The mooring barge had to be replaced this year. Peter Clayton and the mooring team 'supremos' designed the
improved version and I understand that recovering moorings is now a much easier and safer task. The old barge
was sold. Thank you peter for your hard work in overseeing the job.

The ECPR was again a success and whilst we didn't get the expected entry from the continent everything else
seemed to go off without a hitch. We were very lucky to have Libby Purvis to present the prizes. I feel sure she
will spread the good word about Marconi sailing club and the piers race. I am delighted that the money which
was raised will be going to the Cirdan trust to provide bursaries for deserving young people. Watch for reports
from the trust, in Navigans, giving details of how the money we donated was spent. Thank you Mike
Duckmanton and to your team who organised the event and of course to the cruiser fleet for providing the
mother boats.

21.

Once again Charles, Chris and their team of helpers have run a superb cadet week. Bigger and better than before.
Well done and thank you. I understand that activities for cadets will continue during the winter. Thank you to
those club members who are taking on the responsibility for running those meetings.

The sailing sub committee have worked tirelessly under the direction of Clive Shenton, organising and running a
number of very successful open events as well as our own sailing programme. I have mentioned the ‘open day’ in
Navigans. I cannot let this opportunity pass without mentioning it again and thanking all those club members
who contributed to a very successful day which resulted in a number of people joining the club.

[ have to thank Liz Hill for her unsung work as membership secretary. The job sounds fairly straight forward and
indeed it would be if we all managed to get the paper work right first time and on time! Alas this is not always
the case.

There are of course a large number of other people who put in a great deal of time and effort to make the club
‘work’ for us all. I hope all members will think about these folk and thank them as and when they meet them
during the sailing season.

Last year I hoped that all club members would work together so that the interests of all club members could be
advanced in 1997, I am sure that you will all agree that this has happened in 1997, thank you all for your
efforts.

In conclusion you will be aware that Steeple Bay sailing club has had to close through no fault of their own. A
large number of members from SBSC will join Marconi Sailing Club. Some already have and I am sure that you
will all make them feel welcome. Derek Kirby has already started the process by 'sorting out’ winter storage for

I look forward to everyone's continued support in 1998.

Colin Kidner.

Sailing Secretary's Report 1997 Season

This season has again been less than ideal from the weather viewpoint, with 14 events being lost from the regular Points Series schedule of 44 races due to wind conditions. 67 boats participated in the 30 events sailed in these Series, down on last years 81. The largest fleets were the Dart 15 with 18 competitors, but all fleets had reduced numbers compared to last year except the Solos who repeated last year's 17.

The weather did bless our chosen Open Day with sunshine and a blissful force 3 which enabled us to provide enjoyable sailing experiences to a large number of visitors to our Club, some of whom are now members. Many thanks to the substantial number of members who made themselves and their boats available for that event.

An informal racing series for cruisers was organised successfully this year by Mike Turner, and it is hoped that this can be built on next year in order to promote competitive sailing in the cruiser fleet.

Successful Open Meetings for D15 and Solo Classes were hosted by the Club this year with entries for both in the 20s, and the East Coast Piers Race was blessed by good weather and an entry in the high 70s. This event continues to attract the best crews from Europe and the UK, and greatly adds to the Club's reputation. Although it is mainly Fast Cats from the Club who enter, the event could not be held without the enthusiastic backing of the Cruiser Fleet and the other dinghy fleets. Thanks to all who took part.

Members competing elsewhere have again put the name of Marconi S.C. on the map, starting back in Dec 96 with JoJo Anderson's outstanding 4th place in the Cadet World's in Bombay. Our 6 boat entry at the Hurricane Nationals won the Team Trophy for the Club, and Mick Jones and Andy Sharp are the Prindle European Champions. Nearer to home, Paul Metcalfe and Steve Glynn finished 2nd and 3rd respectively, in the BJRC Cock of the River Series.

I would like to take this opportunity to offer my personal thanks to the Race Officers and Assistants whose efforts this season have made my job both easy and enjoyable. I must mention particularly John Weedon's contribution in running the Wednesday Evening Series which remains a popular feature of our racing programme. Thanks also to all who helped crew the rescue boats.

Your Sailing Sub Committee, under Clive Shenton's able leadership, strives to provide you with the best sailing programme that we can, but it is not always easy to know what to aim for. Please tell us through your Fleet Captains, or directly to me, how you want your sailing to be in the future.

Finally, I would like to end on a very positive note, with the observation that this season has seen the emergence of growing numbers of new cadets into our sailing programme. Let us give them every help and encouragement, for the future health of our Club lies in their hands.

John Salmon

Cruiser Comments

As this is being written for the December issue of Navigans, I expect by the time you read this, many things will have happened,
namely both the Cruiser Fleet and Club AGM’s, the Club Laying Up Supper and Cruiser Working Party, all of which I hope were
well attended. In addition of course there are the Mooring Parties.

Hopefully the Cruisers will by now be safely ashore, I must say October went out more like a raging bull than a lion or lamb. Sadly
some boats did go astray, one receiving substantial damage, fortunately above the water line. Juno took herself over to Rolls Farm
on the north bank and even though she is a fin keeler I am delighted to report Peter Cullen was able to float her off without any
apparent damage. Clearly I am unable to comment on what caused these boats to slip their moorings but it does highlight the
necessity to ensure your moorings are adequate for all conditions. Better safe than sorry, don’t’ use the bare essential, go one stage
further.

The task of getting rid of old cruiser trailers continues, however may I draw your attention to the fact that in future it will be the
owners responsibility to remove unwanted trailers from the site. You will have noticed there is now an annual charge of £25 for
trailers not being used for winter storage of boats. So if you have a trailer on site and you choose to winter your boat elsewhere you
will have to pay to store your trailer.

I have received from Essex Police a notice which has been displayed in the Clubhouse stating “REMEMBER VESSELS LAID UP
ASHORE FOR THE WINTER ARE VUNERABLE TO THEFT REMOVE ALL EQUIPMENT AS SOON AS POSSIBLE” need I
say more? and please don’t forget to lock your ladders and shut the gate. On the question of ladders, it is a practice of mine when
walking around the Cruiser Park to remove any ladders that are not secure and place them in the Cruiser Garage, so if you’ve lost
one look in there but we will not store it for long.

May I close on a more nautical note. In case you have not seen it in the yachting press this was reported in the August edition of
“Sailing Today”

“The Holland Decca Chain ‘D’ Purple Slave Station at Thorpness in the UK (52 11°N 01 36’E) is to close at 2359 on July 31 this
year. This means you will no longer be able to get Decca fixes in the Southern part of the North Sea using the Purple and Green

First the good news, GPS Systems do not have a Year 2000 problem.
Now the bad news, some may have a 21st August 1999 problem!

The following information was received over the Internet. A US Air Force worker noticed that there was no mention of any field
in any GPS message to tell him which 1024 week cycle he was in.
Guess when week 1025 arrives? Yes 21st August 1999.

The Air Force worker contacted GPS Companies in the USA, some of whom were aware of the problem, some were not.
Apparently manufacturers who were aware of the problem kept quiet in the hope of putting some of their rivals out of business.

This will be of scant comfort to our cruisers returning from Holland on 22nd August next year. Perhaps a check with your GPS
manufacturer might be a good idea.

Navigans sent their roving reporter to Stansgate to cover the contest for this the premier sailing title in the club’s calendar, and
what a sensational contest it turned out to be, with the championship only settled in the last race of a closely contested 5 race
series.

Sailed in Toppers in an almost ideal force 4 breeze, the event was contested between the top helms from each of the regular sailing
fleets, determined from the summed results of spring and summer points series. Only Jenny Ball from the Dart 15 fleet was absent
from the first choice qualifiers, so the five contestants were Roger Smith (Solo), Steve Monks (Handicap), Jon Yorston Medium
Cat), Tim Wallace (Fast Cat), and Peter Tovey (Dart 15). To ensure a fair contest the boats were rotated between the competitors
such that all sailed one race in each boat. One result discard was allowed. The event was staged using committee boat starts on
short courses around M and D marks, so the clubhouse, sea wall and the hard provided excellent grandstands for the enthusiastic
followers.

Race 1.
Tim, the defending champion, got the jump on his competitors from the start and held them off determinedly to the finish line,
thus demonstrating that he was not about to give up his title easily. Steve, showing good boat speed, and benefiting from capsizes
of his competitors worked his way through to second.
Race 2.
Tim’s turn for swimming practice which allowed Steve to steal away for a win from Roger and an improving Peter.
Race 3.
Steve’s speed and steady boat handling recorded another win, this time chased to the line by Roger and Jon. Tim had the bad luck
to be forced into retirement, when well placed, by his outhaul letting go.
Race 4.
All competitors were getting the hang of the Toppers and competing really hard right from the gun. Tim once again charged his
way to the front from Peter with Roger forcing Steve down to fourth.
Race 5.
Steve and Tim started the last race with two wins each under their belts and everything to play for. Understandably they were
keeping a close eye on each other, but this allowed Roger, who had been improving his boat speed throughout the series, to break
away for a convincing win. Steve kept Tim at bay all the way to the finish line thus clinching the series.

All competitors deserve credit for a keenly contested series in a good spirit.

Final Results:-
Points Position
Steve Monks 5 1/2 Ist
Roger Smith 7 3/4 2nd
Tim Wallace 8 1/2 3rd
Peter Tovey 13 4th
Jon Yorston 16 Sth

The sailing sub committee asked that their thanks be recorded to all those members who kindly donated the use of their Toppers
for what was a highly successful event.

John Salmon.

Commodores Notes

It is less than three weeks since I was elected to serve as your Commodore and I appear to have been busy. In addition to the
normal Executive and Main Committee I have attended the Cruiser Fleet AGM, the BACSPA AGM and the Sailing Sub
Committee to hand over to Jenny, our new Rear Commodore.
Someone told me that Rear Commodore was the hard job and Commodore was a rest cure, I don't know who it was, but it could
have been Colin Kidner. Thanks Colin.

My overwhelming impression having attended the Cruiser Fleet AGM was one of awe. You are so well organised all the other
Fleets could learn a thing or two. The attendance was more than most Clubs can assemble at their Main AGM. The planning of
the Cruiser working party was so detailed it could have been for D-day. All presided over by Derek Kirby with an air of
determined authority.

I have been very pleased with the level of enthusiasm that is evident within the Club. Neil Pembleton immediately accepted my
offer to co-opt him back onto the Main Committee and John Salmon quickly agreed to serve in his old position as Hon. Sailing
Secretary. Mick Richardson, Lee Harrison and Rob Davies all volunteered to be co-opted onto the Main Committee and all these
appointments have been ratified by the Committee.

That's not the end of the volunteers. Laura Gill, Hillary Ashley and Clare Davies will form an Entertainment’s sub Committee to
develop that side of our activities, while Steve Glynn will continue to run the Laying Up Supper.

My thanks to you all.

Phil Longhurst, with the help of Tim dieu de Bellefontaine and Lee Harrison have organised a Winter Series this year. We have
had three races so far, each with near perfect conditions. Alex and myself have entered the series and we can both attest to the
warm properties of the new(and matching) dry suits that were necessary. Thanks lads - I think!

Now two key roles in running the Club remain unfilled, those of Rescue Boat Co-ordinator and Club House Secretary. Mick
Richardson has kindly offered to extend his five year tenure of the latter job until a volunteer comes forward. If you would like to
serve the Club in either role please phone me on [redacted] for more details.

At Main Committee we decided to hold the AGM and Prize Giving in the Conference Room at MASC in Chelmsford next year.
So bringing to an end the fun of the scrum at the back of the upper saloon. The Year Book will have the details.

It is the night time of year for New Year's Resolutions. Here is a suggestion for the whole Club - Resolve to enjoy your sailing next
season. I resolve to sail more both at the Club and elsewhere. We intend to do the ECPR of course, plus the More and Forts Races.
Also with a bit of encouragement we might be persuaded to try Texel. So how about it?

My best wishes for Fair winds and warm seas in 1999.

Clive Shenton

CRUISER COMMENTS

On Thursday 19 November we held our Fleet AGM. which was attended by 68 members representing 46 cruisers. We were
pleased to welcome Paul Harris from Maldon Little Ship Club and John Titchmarsh from Maritime & Leisure also our new
Commodore Clive Shenton and Rear Commodore Jenny Ball.

The meeting opened with a vote of thanks from Neil Pembleton for the support given to him by members present in his bid to
become Commodore, however with the election of Clive Shenton he pledged his support to the new Commodore and urged any
members who had voted for him to do the same. Clive Shenton responded by revealing he had asked Neil to be co-opted onto the
main committee which he agreed to. Both expressed their desire to achieve greater cohesion between the various fleets within the
club.

A review of the 1998 sailing season commenced with the visitors presenting Frank Burgess with the BLACKWATER MARINE
CHALLENGE CUP which he won sailing “Ocean Slipper”, after which Messrs Harris & Titchmarsh left the meeting. The season
got underway with our traditional “Fitting Out Supper” held at Stansgate using outside caterers. This was a great success and a
similar event is scheduled for Saturday 24 April 1998. Watch Navigans for further details.

Burnham has become a regular venue for our “shakedown cruise” 14 cruisers attended with 39 members sitting down to an
excellent meal at the Royal Corinthian Yacht Club. The late Summer Bank Holiday cruise at Shotley attracted 26 Cruisers with
60 members sitting down to eat in the “Stour Suite” of the Shipwreck public house. Whilst some members had to return home on
the Monday, 14 cruisers went onto the River Deben stopping off at the “The Tidemill” for an enjoyable Bar B Q.

The support given by the cruisers at the East Coast Piers Race had been greatly appreciated, it is understood that approximately
£5,000 had been donated to the Cirdan Trust. The club had been host to members of the R.N.S.A. who joined us for a Bar B Q
and drinks in the Dell Bar.

Two club trophies were presented, the first being the “BARNACLE TROPHY” won by Nick Bevins sailing “Gabelle” as overall
winner of the clubs series of cruiser races. The now infamous “BIG COCK TROPHY” or is it “cock up trophy” was contested by
seven members with the ultimate winner winning hands down. The winner was present to graciously receive this trophy but in
accordance with established protocol only those members present at the A.G.M. know the recipient, next year it could be you!!!

The winter lay up was discussed and it was acknowledged some craft were short of space. This is sometimes caused by members
changing boats, however, I am aware of the situation and it is hoped more space may be made available by this years working
party for next year. The introduction of £25.00 annual fee for trailers not being used for storing boats was explained, it was also
noted there was a shortage of pallets for moorings due to some being used for bonfires during camping week. Tony Holbrook said
he would try to obtain some more.

Proposals for the December working party were discussed and where possible team leaders were identified with associated helpers
so that when members arrived they knew what to do and what tools to bring. Maureen Ball was going to provide hot soup and
french bread and asked if any ladies present would help her in this and also cleaning up of the clubhouse.

The election of both Fleet Captain and Vice Captain took place and since there were no other contenders for the job both Derek
Kirby and Malcolm Yeoman were elected respectively.

Paint Orders - Malcolm and Helen Shaft have performed this onerous but much appreciated task for nine years but now felt they
could no longer carry on. Gordon Preston agreed to take it on having first been briefed by Malcolm on the system he had
successfully built over the years. At present Boatacs in Southend give a 33 percent discount which may be difficult to better.

Chain and Shackles - Don Holdsworth still has plenty of *4” chain at £2.00 per foot. There had been problems with boat anodes
which is still under investigation. Don stressed members should not leave their orders till the last minute, to do so may cause
disappointment. Rod Hillman said he could obtain mooring anchors at a cost of £65.00 each providing he could make up an order
of at least 12. A sample is in the garage and can be viewed by arrangement with Don.

Burnham 29/30/31 May Shakedown Cruise Evening meal on 30" at Royal Corinthian Yacht Club.
Shotley 28/29/30 August Evening meal on the 29" in the Stour Suite of Shipwreck Pub.

Apart from the fact that the above are popular venues, it was also stressed that there are few venues that can cater for the number
of cruiser/members attending these events, we are so to speak victims of our own success. Long may it be so and thanks for your
support.

London 31° July to 8” August. Single handed cruisers are planning a weeks cruise, stopping over at

The Jack B has a leaking exhaust pipe resulting in the cooling water being deposited inside the boat. This is not a problem
providing the user is aware of the fault. In order to bring faults to the attention of Jack B drivers a “fault status board” is to be
placed on the boat and another on shore in a location yet to be determined.

Gordon Preston is taking over from Ray Ball as Jack B Bosun.

Travel Hoist. The Design Consultants hired by Maldon Marine have reached a conclusion on the final design.
The next stage will be to approve the design (MSC. Maldon Marine and the Design Consultants). Once approved the new design
will carry a full engineering certificate. Due to delays in finalising the design the Travel Hoist will not be available for hauling out
boats this year. With this in mind C Shenton proposed that we pay for the approved design when it is available and delay the start
of construction to a future date. The date to put work in hand for construction will be considered at the February 99 meeting.
Seconded N Pembleton.

As a result of the non availability of the Travel Hoist the committee felt that the second phase of window replacements for the club
house should be put in hand. P Black was requested to obtain current estimates for the work.

Social Tickets are reported to be selling well for the Laying Up Supper and the Barn dance.

Bar R Godbold reported that apart from the donation of a microwave cooker for the Dell bar, these was nothing to report.

Sailing Mr C Shenton presented a summary of matters discussed at the October meeting.

1. Next year's events. 2. Fleets AGM 3. | Helmsman of the Year. 4. Winter Racing.

The Winter Racing programme will extend from the end of the current season through to the beginning of the next. Support boat
services are to be met by the RIB. Frank Bennett said there could be a problem with servicing the radios, this being a task usually
undertaken during the winter. It was agreed that a suitable time would be nominated for this activity.

New Members The committee approved the application of Mr Barry Unger, cruiser owner.

Correspondence 1. Publicity for the RNLI Winter Rowing Race passed to C Shenton.
2. Letter of thanks to the club from St Lawrence Bay Fairways Committee concerning recovery of a
small cruiser. - Copy to Roger Gibson.
3. Letter from Peter Melville, Maldon District Council Sports Development Officer introducing
himself and publicising the Essex Coach of the Year Awards.

AOB
Mr D Kirby asked why channel 67 is not available on the club base station. The reason given is that it is not permitted.
Mr D Kirby proposed the MSC AGM should in future be held at MASC. Seconded by M Smith.
Mr D Kirby noted that the AGM notice stated that 1997 should have been 1998.
Mr N Pembleton referring to the contest for the position of Commodore this year asked how votes were to be validated. Colin
Kidner said that voting would be by secret ballot and voters would be checked off against the current membership list.
The MSC was represented by C Kidner, C Shenton and C Rusbridge at the MASC open evening, they reported a number of
enquiries.

Committee approved the purchase of an award to be presented to Maureen Ball in thanks for her dedication as Navigans Editor.
A vote of thanks was proposed by N Pembleton and seconded by F Bennett to Colin Kidner on the completion of his term of office
as Commodore.
Mr C Shenton has the signed and framed photograph of Tony Bullimore. A suitable site for it is to be found in the lounge.
Mr R Greygoose reported that Mr George Baker had been elected to serve on the RYA Council.
The next BACSPA meeting is to be held at the Maldon Little Ships Club on the 3° December 1998,
A complaint had been received from a member about the lack of space allocated to him in the cruiser park.

COMMODORES NOTES

Some of you may have heard about the happenings of Sunday 3 January. The forecast was 6-7 from the SW and Tim
Bellefontaine phoned around early to cancel the Winter Series Race. However such wind is meet and drink to the board sailors and
several were out for a New Year adrenaline rush. But the forecast was wrong, the wind did a 90 degree swing to the north and
increased to storm force. Several board sailors got into difficulties and a club member, very properly, called the Coastguard. As
several other Clubs had not cancelled their racing, the Mersea RNLI were too busy to attend. This led to one of our members being
airlifted by RAF helicopter, back to the Club, after he had taken shelter on Osea. Several other boarders made it back to the Club
under their own power and another was picked up by a passing yacht. Fortunately no one was hurt, but the incident does underline
the uncertainty of the weather and what an alien environment the sea can be to we land based creatures. Also it shows that the
Emergency Services are worth every penny that we put in collecting tins or pay in taxes.

Speaking of collecting tins, the RNLI rowing race took place on New Year's Day at Maldon. The weather was excellent and there
appeared to be at least forty starters, including the "Yellow Brick Road Crew" from our Club. I thought the Cowardly Lion crew
member had a passing resemblance to a Flag Officer, but I could be wrong. The many spectators along the shore had an
entertaining morning and I saw many Club Members taking the air and working up a thirst. Will there be a Cat Entry next year?
Watch this space!

It now seems right to mention that we have three volunteers who will divide the duties of Rescue Boat co-ordinator. They are
Barry Hut, Tony Ferguson and Dennis Gilbey. Thank you Gentlemen. The Sailing sub Committee intend to give some thought to
methods of making the job easier to administer and implement. Having done the job for a year myself, I can say that every member
who is scheduled for a duty could be very helpful to the co-ordinators by turning out willingly, or failing that reliably. Most are
reliable and willing but the odd "rogue" makes life very stressful for the co-ordinator.

Colin Kidner has volunteered to undertake a newly created role on the Main Committee, that of Safety Co-ordinator. The RYA
tell us that some aspects of Health and Safety Legislation are increasingly being applied to Clubs such as our own. Colin will
ensure that we formalise our working practices throughout the Club so that we do not fall foul of the Law. He has already enlisted
the help of Malcolm Robertson and formed a Safety Committee. This is a complicated and detailed business and I hope to
persuade Colin to do a piece for Navigans to tell us more.

The Cruiser Fleet achieved great things at their Working Party in December. The Vice Commodore, Peter Bloomfield, now
intends to contact other Fleet Captains to encourage them to emulate the efforts of their fellow members. Please give your Fleet
Captain your full co-operation so that all the non-sailing tasks can be completed before the New Sailing Season starts in March.

See you all at the Barn Dance on the 30" January Clive Shenton

You may think it’s all a bit crazy sailing in the winter, but to date the organisers and sailors involved in Marconi’s latest sailing
venture have had nothing but almost ideal sailing conditions. We are now almost half way through the series, which consists of

with all those jobs which get put off due to the busy summer sailing calendar. So far in the sailing there is no clear leader, and to
date the sailing has all been very close, with results being just seconds apart after a whole hours sailing.

Commodores Notes

The big news this month was the demerger of Marconi from GEC and the subsequent acquisition by British Aerospace, although
those in the know tell me that it is not as simple as that. I assure you that the Main Committee will keep in close touch with
developments and be ready for any eventualities.

Ardent readers of this part of Navigans will remember that last month I said that our taxes were being well spent on Rescue
helicopters. Well, we must have a taxman reader, because three days later I got a bill for several thousand that it is alleged that I
owe in unpaid taxes. I will leave the reader to decide on the moral of the story.

With not too much happening on the sailing front, it was the Barn Dance that was centre stage this month. All tickets were sold,
the band was good and the place was jumping, literally in many dances. The band seemed to have added to the repertoire since we
last heard them two years ago. The Black Sabbath/Status Quo/Brian May riffs were unexpected in a square dance, but welcome all
the same. Well done Neil and the Entertainment's team, I understand that plans are underway for next year already.

Speaking of Entertainment's, Claire Davies told the Committee on Monday, of the delights she has planned for us during the year.
A Fitting Out Supper, Quiz night and several other events are in the pipeline.

On Monday our discussions once more turned to how we can improve the ambience of the Upper Saloon, especially for the non
sailing members. There is a need to avoid major expenditure and so conserve our reserves at present, however we cannot neglect
the service we give our members and there is a feeling that "Something must be done". My thoughts extend to a suspended ceiling
with concealed lighting, a resurfaced floor and some curtains. If any member has expertise in interior design I would welcome
some professional, but unfortunately unpaid, advice. Advice from gifted amateurs and indeed any member with an opinion would
also be welcome.

I would also like some feedback on the Main Committee Minutes that we publish in Navigans each month. Pat Black does a
comprehensive job which runs to several pages. The monthly printing costs for the extra sheets are considerable. Are the minutes
useful? Do you read them? Would a shorter edited version be as good? I would like your opinion please.

A good method to contact me is by email on [redacted] or just grab me when you see me at the Club.

The nights are shortening already and the Spring will be with us before you know it, so start your plans for 99 now. Good Sailing.

Clive Shenton

CRUISER COMMENTS

Our January meeting was very well attended, it was especially great to see members of our dinghy fleets, who, like the rest of us
enjoyed the talk given by Charles Stock on the subject of the rivers, Ore, Butley and the entrances to Southwold (hairy), Lowestoft
and Great Yarmouth, taking us into Breydon Water and the river Bure. Not only is he an interesting and witty speaker; his wife
Joy wields a nifty camera, sometimes under difficult circumstances.

Those who have their boats in the “Cat Field” will by now have realised my mistake in requesting them to enter the field at the
southern end. At the time of writing I did not realise a barrier had been placed there! However, with the excellent work done on
filling the ditch, access is now possible by using the road through the Cruiser Park and entering at the eastern entrance. You
don’t need me to tell you the grounds are a quagmire and it does not take much to cut up and rut, so please do take care.

At the last meeting it was mentioned that Geof Baker (Bosham Dreamer) is able to arrange a block booking with Sail Spar for
those members wishing to have their standing rigging tested. If you are interested please contact him direct - [redacted].

Followers of the deliberation regarding the future of VHF may have noted that the International Maritime Organisation have
agreed the ships should keep a radio-listening watch on VHF CH16 until February 2005. Ships were due to cease keeping watch
on this channel in February 1999 as developments in GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress & Safety System) took over. But,
recognising few yachts will be equipped with GMDSS the IMO has made listening mandatory for member nation vessels whilst at
sea. I would mention it is everyones responsibility to maintain a listening watch on VHF 16 which of course is the distress, as
well as the calling frequency.

BOAT JUMBLES are due to be held at Chatham on Sunday 14" February and Great Leighs on Sunday 7" March. There is also
the Tollesbury Easter Boat Show due to be held between Friday 2" and Monday 5" April from 10.00am to 5.00pm.

Vice Commodore Peter Bloomfield attended the last Sailing Sub Committee Meeting where he requested each of the fleets to take
on various tasks at their next working parties. Obviously we would like to get ours out of the way quickly so we can get on with
our boats and moorings, therefore, it was decided to hold our working party on Sunday 21“ February commencing at 10.00 hrs.
The jobs to be undertaken as as follows:-

DIESEL FUEL STORE: remove hard core to far end of cruiser park.
CRUISER PARK: check, test & service security lights.
TRACTOR SHED ROOF: inspect roofing felt & make good as required.
CLUB HOUSE PATIO: window shutters, rub down & re-coat with preservative.

Our next Cruiser Meeting is on Thursday 18 February when Lynn Guy will be talking about her experiences whilst sailing
aboard “Ocean Rover” during the Whitbread Round The World Race. This then leaves the last of our current series of winter
meetings which will be held on Thursday 18" March and I believe John Todd “CHIMO” is preparing a most interesting talk with
slides, it is also hoped to run through the events that have been organised for this years sailing season.

Lastly, may I on behalf of Doreen and myself thank those of you who clubbed together to present us with a treasured nautical gift.

Derek Kirby - Cruiser Fleet Captain.

Commodores Notes

Last month I was getting excited about the close competition for honours in the Winter Series, however the series did not end with
a bang but a whimper. The last race was cancelled due to lack of wind. After close attention to the results of previous races, Tim
Bellefontaine was presented with the prize for first place at the gathering held at the Green Man at Bradwell. Well done Tim, a
good consistent performance.

The difficulties with subscriptions to MASC have been largely overcome, but there is still a list of about 20 members who are
behind with their dues. Remember that, to be a member of the Sailing Club, you must first be a member of MASC, so pay the
invoice when it hits the door mat please. We have tried a policy this year of holding onto the Renewal Packs until we have
confirmation that your MASC subs are up to date, so if you have not received yours this year, check you are not holding onto an
MASC invoice. ;

Our Entertainment's Committee have devised a Fitting Out Supper to be held on Friday 7" May at Chelmsford. This is open to all
members and is a new event in the Club diary. I ask you to give our new committee every support and buy your tickets early, I
already have mine. Claire Davies, Hilary Ashley and Laura Gill are the people to see.

| have had some more reactions from members concerning the upper saloon and redevelopment of the Club. I was elected to the
position of Commodore on the manifesto that I would implement a redevelopment scheme at the Club. I also said that any scheme
would involve a hike in subscriptions to make it viable. Even if we could negotiate a Lottery grant we would have to match the
grant £ for £ with our own funds.
How would you feel about paying another £50 per year to pay for a really excellent shore based clubhouse? Your
comments/opinion on email:- [redacted] or on [redacted] would be welcome. Don't let the vocal minority
decide, let me have your opinion.
My current feeling is that we can only afford to carry on with our progressive improvement of the Upper Saloon in the current
year. Redevelopment would then be part of the Five Year Plan that is occupying the Main Committee at present.

Many members have been working hard to get the Club ready for the season and my thanks go out to all. However I would like to
mention Bob Goldbold who has sealed the cellar floor and to Bob and Elsie Anderson who have again brightened the
Commodore's Lawn with flowers. Also, Eric Cockerton has replace the taps in the Gent's Changing Room. Thanks to them and all
those I have not named.

I would like to leave you this month with a thought with which Graham Sawyer ends his emails,
"A bad day's sailing is better than a good day at work”

Good Sailing!
Clive Shenton

View From The Rear

By the time this Navigans reaches you. the season will be well underway and I hope that the Easter weather we are experiencing as
I write is a good omen for the weather to come this year!

The Support Boat Rota for 1999 has been included in this Navigans - may I encourage you all to check the dates that you have
been assigned on it and to book them in your diary accordingly. I hardly need say that the manning of our support boats is crucial
to our racing programme and a lot of other members are inconvenienced if someone fails to turn up or leaves it late to make other
arrangements. I would like to thank the Support Boat Co-ordinators, Tony, Barry, Dennis and, in particular, the Sailing
Secretary, John Salmon for their work in ensuring that all the arrangements are in place so that the rest of us can turn up and race
each Sunday.

[ would also like to thank Roger Smith for his hard work in organising the dinghy park spaces so that everyone can fit in. Whilst
it is a good sign to have so many boats to allocate, they would not all fit in without Roger’s planning! The dinghy park layout is
displayed on the Handicap notice board at the club - please write your name and boat on this plan once you have selected a space.

I would also like to emphasise the importance of identifying your boat with your name and contact number. It is important that we
can contact an owner of a boat quickly for a whole range of reasons eg, if the boat needs to be moved for any reason or, worst case
scenario, should it be damaged in any way. I was disappointed that someone chose to query this requirement by writing
anonymously on the club noticeboard - perhaps that person would like to call me on the number below to discuss the concerns they
have.

some interesting games of football! Thank you to the Cadets and parents who turned out, (there were around 20 cadets at each
session) - and a special thank you to David Ball for organising the meetings with his able assistants, Lucy Boreham, Claire Davies
and Sam Ashley.

For those of you who can remember, about 8 years ago, following g lots of damaged boats due to the high winds, a small team headed by John Nickalls tasked themselves with finding a boat tie down system. One, which was up for the job and

The result of this investigation was the introduction of Duckbills. These were small, easy to use and could withstand approx. 2 tonnes, and had an estimated life of about 5 years before needing replacement.

those of you who have these tie downs know, they are invaluable e and have possibly saved our boats several times.

Commodores Notes

May is here and the Sailing Season seems to be well underway. The excellent weather of the early May holiday was just a
backdrop to my sailing event of the year- the genneker halyard held the sail up for once, and exciting 3 sailed reach caused hearts
to pound harder.

In my last article I asked for feedback on an idea to increase subscriptions by £50 and spend the extra on really good on-shore
facilities. I have had twenty two replies so far, two of which thought it a good idea and the others against. I have replied to all the
emails but not the letters, so I will attempt to summarise the comments and my replies.
Firstly, I would like to thank everyone who took the time to contact me. All feedback is useful and will be taken into account as
policy is made.
Secondly, no increase in subs would be possible unless a majority vote sanctioned it at an AGM. My article last month was just
floating an idea to see what reaction I would get.
Several respondents have said they like the Club like it is, and no changes are necessary. All dinghy and cat people who have
ventured an opinion, say they would be against moving the wet bar downstairs, especially into existing facilities. Various reasons
have been cited, but that is the summary position.
If you have another view I would be pleased to hear from you. Email is best, but a stamp on a letter still gets through.

Now its time to talk about Protests, we had one at the weekend. The protest committee really had to think hard about the Rules
before reaching the view that, although the rules had been broken, insufficient notice was given at the time of the incident i.e. No
yell of "Protest" nor a flag flown, so the offender had no opportunity to do an alternative penalty. The Sailing Secretary and I both
think that a few more protests in the Club would be good for us - they certainly reacquaint you with the Rules. They must not be
accompanied by ill feeling however, usually protests arise due to different interpretations of the Rules, and it does no racing sailor
any harm to get these things cleared up.

The East Coast Piers Race is not too far away in July. This is our Club's blue-ribbon event which puts us on the map nationally
and internationally. The fact that we are able to donate up to £4,000 each year to Charity as a result, can make every member
justifiably proud. The Club as a whole make the event possible. Charles and Lee tell me that they could do with a few more mother
boats and | ask you to consider volunteering by using the form printed on pages 13 - 15 in this edition. We cannot run the Race
without them.
Clive Shenton

FIVE YEAR PLAN

The Main Committee recognised the need for a Five Year Plan at least a year ago. An embryo Plan was published last year, which
reasserted the aims of the Club and identified some areas in need of improvement. We now need to define the detail of the Plan
and the Main Committee needs your help to do this.

Almost every member has, in his or her mind, that some aspect of the Club's activity that is in need of improvement - I know
because individual members mention them to me. The snag is, that although we have some money for capital buys each year, it is
impossible to fund every one immediately. The object of the Five Year Plan will be to identify what needs doing and then set out a
timetable for its achievement during the period of the Plan. We can thereby introduce a greater measure of predictability into our
organisation.

The method for getting the Plan into place is seen as:-

1. Consultation to identify members requirements for improvement of the Club.(Or "wish list" for short)
2. Estimate costs of requirements
3: Decide which requirements will be met within the Five Year Period.
4. Decide on the priority for achievement of the requirements.
2: Main Committee draw up a Five Year Income and Expenditure Plan.
6. The contents of the Expenditure Plan explained to the Membership at a special meeting.

I expect that the stages will overlap to some extent, in what is fashionable to call an iterative process, but the above show the
intended method.

Item 1 is a most important phase of this process. If your requirements are not on the "wish list" then they will not see light of day.
So I ask you to think deeply about the direction you think the Club should take, then discuss your thoughts with fellow members so
as to refine and develop your ideas. If you like the Club just like it is, then it is equally important that you make this view known.
When you have formed definite ideas, then it is necessary to make sure they get on the list. The best way to accomplish this is by
writing it down and passing it either to your Fleet Captain, a Main Committee member or myself.
Members who have emailed me with suggestions already need not repeat the process unless their requirements have changed.

To reflect the importance of the consultation process we have allocated until mid August for you to give us your ideas, thoughts
and requirements. The list will then be discussed for the first time at the early September Meeting.
Clive Shenton

Saturday morning dawned sunny with shifting light airs making it a real challenge for the Race Officer, Roger Smith, to set a
course. With the wind filling slightly, competitors set off against the tide on a triangle course with Bob Carter quickly gaining
clear air and establishing an early lead. Meanwhile, Andy Jeffries entertained the rest of the fleet by letting his mast fall down and
Dave Bladon, having missed the mark on his first attempt. took no chances and hit it on the second rounding. Bob Carter went on
to win the race with Nick Dewhirst taking second after a close race with Jenny Ball.

Back by popular demand, the long distance race around Northey and Osea Islands was again scheduled for Saturday afternoon -
and with a freshening wind, competitors looked forward to a good race and a chance to do battle with the Blackwater tides. Bob
Carter again took the lead by the first mark, closely pursued by Peter Tovey. With a failing wind, Bob Carter rounded Northey
Island , chased by Kevin Kirby with Nick Dewhirst, Peter Tovey, Paul Frost and Jenny Ball battling it out behind. Following a
lengthy drift with the tide, the wind finally filled in to provide a romping reach back to Marconi and round the final triangle of the
course. Undoubtedly the best of the wind of the weekend, this last lap saw Bob Carter take another convincing win, followed by
Nick Dewhirst, Paul Frost and Peter Tovey reclaimed two places to take fourth place. The wind was not, however, welcome to
Andy Jeffries who, having restored his mast, had broken his tiller extension and he again entertained the fleet by promptly
capsizing. Having righted the boat, Andy rounded off the day by proceeding to miss out a mark of the course! Saturday ended in
perfect style with an excellent meal provided by Colin Kidner and a few drinks to keep out the cold!

Sunday dawned and can only be summed up as: no wind, no water, no race! Although the incoming tide solved the water
problem, competitors could only watch in frustration as the wind failed to materialise. The Sunday racing was eventually
abandoned - a disappointing end to what had been a great weekend. The event could not end, however, without the presentation
of the Coveted Dart 15 Green Jersey award for the most memorable competitor to Andy Jeffries - a well-earned trophy!

Final Results: lst: Bob Carter (Grafham Water SC.), 2nd: Nick Dewhirst (Whitstable SC.).
3rd: Paul Frost, (Grafham Water SC.), 4th: Jenny Ball (Marconi SC) 5th: Peter Tovey (Marconi SC).

Jenny Ball - Rear Commodore

LETTER RECEIVED FROM THE CIRDAN SAILING TRUST

On behalf of The Cirdan Sailing Trust I would like to extend our heartfelt thanks to the Marconi Sailing Club for their very
generous donation of £3,300 towards our work with disadvantaged young people. This donation was used for bursaries, providing
groups from the following organisations, the opportunity to sail with us in 1998.

l. Kingswood Youth Group - This group travelled from Corby, Northamptonshire to sail on Queen Galadriel for
5 days in November. All members of the group live in a low income area. The Kingswood estate has one of the
highest rates of unemployment in the 16-25 years age range in the country. A trip like this helps improve
confidence and low self esteem.
Bursary - £455

pa Surrey Youth Service - A group of young people from Surrey who all have personal and social disadvantages
stemming from family and other issues. They sailed on Xy/onite for 4 days in April.
Bursary - £250

3. 1st Harlington Scouts - A group of 16 from this scout group from Middlesex sailed on Galadriel for a week in
August. A number of scouts, who attend this group, are from low income/single parent families. The bursary
ensured that the less fortunate in the group also had the opportunity to benefit from sailing with us.
Bursary - £290

4. Project 66 - A group of 12 from Blackburn in Lancashire sailed on Queen Galadriel for 7 days in September.
The project aims to provide young single homeless people the necessary support, skills confidence, etc. to live
independently.
Bursary - £665

5. The Cedarwood Trust - A group of 17 from this charitable youth organisation based in North Shields, Tyne
and Wear sailed on Queen Galadriel in September for 7 days. Cedarwood Trust work on an estate of multiple
deprivation caused largely by long term high level unemployed families. Being caught in the poverty trap, they
find it almost impossible to afford the opportunity to take part in activities such as sailing.
Bursary - £300

6. Aycliffe Young People Centre - This group based in County Durham is made up of young people from deprived
backgrounds. They are currently undergoing a treatment programme with high levels of supervision. Most are
on Court Orders. They sailed on Xylonite for 4 days in September.
Bursary - £840

7 New Horizons Youth Centre - The New Horizons Centre offer support, information and advice to homeless
young people in central London. They had the opportunity to sail on Duet for a week in September.
Bursary - £500

All the above youth organisations have told me they were very grateful for the funding help provided by Marconi Sailing Club and

grateful for this generous donation (£3,300) which were the proceeds of the Three Piers Race. We are also very grateful to Charles
Anderson for his help in generating a further £1,900 from sponsors, which we used to help with our vessel refit costs.

We are delighted to confirm that we put aside our Thames Sailing Barge Xylonite, for this year's Three Piers Race. She will be

An open letter to Mr Clive Shenton received from Sue Arnold

Dear Mr Shenton,

I read with some interest your suggestion in the May edition of Navigans that the membership be invited to donate an extra £50 in
fees in order to update the existing club house facilities. I also noted your assertion that you were elected Commodore on a
mandate to do just this. My recollection is that the voting for commodore last year was extremely tight. This would seem to
indicate that there is by no means universal favour for the idea.

I am sure that most of us would see a five year plan for the club as being entirely sensible. particularly in the present
circumstances. If the press is anything to go by, Marconi would not seem to be the most stable company at the moment and one
wonders where this leaves us as a club. Perhaps therefore the membership would like to know the views of the committee on how
they see our future, indeed do we have a future? How is this reflected within the five year plan and where does updating shore
based facilities fit into the broader picture?

I would like to suggest that it is very difficult for the average member to agree to a hike in fees of £50 without any clear idea what
the money is to be used for. Perhaps the committee would like to publish the five year plan in order that the rest of us be in a
position to make an informed decision? We are, after all, proud of our position as a self help club and as such are not used to
overcoming problems by "throwing money" at them. Most of us were attracted to Marconi Sailing Club because of its small family
atmosphere and affordable fees.

I seem to remember that the manifesto of the other candidate for the position of commodore last year suggested that, should he be
elected, he would call an extraordinary general meeting in order that the membership have an opportunity to discuss the way
forward. This would seem to be the appropriate way of harnessing opinion and would leave the committee with a clear mandate
upon which to act. I would be interested to learn your views on this.

Yours faithfully
Sue Arnold Cruiser Fleet.

For those that are not familiar with the event, the club is unique in its annual ECPR. The race is the only one of its kind in Europe
and we believe the world. It is a water-borne version of the London Marathon attracting sailors from all over the UK as well as
mainland Europe. The event and the individuals get themselves sponsored and the money raised goes to the Maldon based
charity, The Cirdan Trust.

The Trust provides sailing breaks for the disabled, disadvantaged as well as their helpers (not necessarily together), The money we
raise goes towards bursaries which help those less able to pay make use of the charity’s services.
For those of us that have read the letters of gratitude that flood into the Trust’s offices it is easy to see how much our support is
appreciated and how much others benefit from the sailing experience. Something that most of us take for granted.

You may well be familiar with the Trust’s fleet which include Hartlepool Renascence, Duet, The Queen Galadriel and the sailing
barge, Xylonite (she still carries the ‘Friends of the Earth’ symbol on her topsail). All of which are often in the Blackwater.

It is now mid June. My last 6 weeks seem to have been totally dominated by Texel. The preparations, the event and the aftermath. I

Texel - A pilgrimage

Texel had been on the "must do" event list for some years for myself and Alex. This year we got there.

Texel is an island off the north coast of Holland, and for the last 20 odd years it has hosted what has become the largest cat race in the
world. For the last few years the entry has been limited to 700 for safety reasons, and competition to get ones entry accepted is fierce.
After discovering that entries were only being accepted via the Internet, we made our application which was quickly confirmed.
Preparations started.

First the trailer had a total overhaul, new hubs and suspension and a paint job. A Hotel was booked and the boat examined with a fine
toothcomb. Many minor jobs were completed to ensure the boat was on the top line.

We left Harwich by the Sea Cat on Thursday morning and by evening we had formalised our entry, had the boat towed onto the
beach by tractor and booked into, what turned out to be, a comfortable hotel. Day one missions accomplished.

Day 2 dawned cold, wet and windy. We assembled the boat and improvised some holding down methods to prevent it being blown
away. The shake down sail before the Race did not seem sensible in the force 7 that was blowing, so we retired to the hotel hoping
for better weather on the morrow.

Day 3 - Race Day dawned with no wind, slate grey skies and a thunderstorm, Oh yes and rain - lots of it. Undaunted we rigged the
boat after as good a breakfast as the excitement would permit, and attended the briefing. Result -race postponed for 90 minutes while
the storm moved away. Then the sun came out to the accompaniment of a gentle force 3 anda start time was confirmed.

Launching at Texel is over a flat sandy beach and the surf was curling in nicely while 700 cats attempted to launch. We were just
about to take our turn, I was sorting out the mainsheet and tiller extension prior to jumping aboard when the tiller connecting bar
parted company from one rudder - The 6mm stainless connecting pin had sheared!

But we are experienced campaigners, we have spare runners and tillers. The rudders were in the car about 1000m away across sand
dunes. Alex ran both ways, in his full dry suit in record time while I took off the failed rudders. New rudders quickly fixed in the surf
and we were off the beach before the 5 minute. Now for the Race. As we sailed out through the surf I must have got them down too
early, the waves dumped us onto the bottom severely damaging the gudgeon to the extent that I later needed an hour with a hacksaw
to get the rudder off the boat. Thoughts of starting immediately evaporated - we now had a new problem, how do we go about and get
back through the surf without causing major damage. Well somehow we did it in time to watch the smoke from the helicopter on the
start line turn to white and the race got underway accompanied by Alex's screams of frustration. I just felt numb.

An hour later we were half way through dismantling the boat when the thunder came back, it belted with rain and the wind rose to
force 7. It was not until next day, when we saw the broken masts and empty trailers, that we heard that less than half the entrants had
finished and that abandoned boats littered the 60 km perimeter of the island. It slowly dawned on us that perhaps, just perhaps, we
had had a lucky escape.

Within 10 minutes of coming ashore with broken rudders we had resolved to return next year and get the job done. This time its
personal!

Positive things that came out of the trip were the friendly welcome of the Dutch, the good hotel, quick passage by seacat and most of
all the excellent Race organisation. When we return next year we want to feel that we deserve to enjoy the much hyped social scene.
Only one thing will make that possible and that is to finish the biggest cat race in the world.

Clive Shenton

LETTER RECEIVED FROM MIKE BOREHAM

Dear Editor,

After 50 years - we know where we bin but which way do we be gain?

I would like to follow up on a couple of points which have been raised in recent issues of Navigans.

MSC 50th Anniversary:-

In November, 1998 issue of Navigans, our retiring Editor (Maureen Ball) reminded us that the MSC was not too far off its 50th Anniversary.

The Sailing Section of the Marconi Athletic and Social Club (i.e. Marconi Sailing Club) held its Inaugural Meeting on 18 April, 1952, thus we have
some way to go before celebrating our 50th. The MSC's first clubhouse was a former workshop on the sea wall at Heybridge and the club later
moved to the somewhat neglected barge-yacht M/amgu moored nearby.

So how come the ‘Honours Board’ shows the names of Commodores for 1950 and 1951? I believe the late Eric Payne was consulted about the list
of past Commodores in about 1975 and presumably End named L L Jackson and C Christensen as past Commodores because of the pre-1952
activities. During the time that | was writing the Navigans Past series of articles, I met quite a number of ‘old members’ but none could elaborate
upon, or even remember, the existence of a recognisable group prior to the Inaugural Meeting in 1952.

Following a proper course - part 1:-

In June, 1999, Navigans, I was relieved to be able to infer from Frank Burgess’ Cruiser Racing News that perhaps Maggie and I were not the only
ones to be unaware that there are now two channel markers designated No. 10. The Mona's Cup race was run on the same day as the cruiser race
and the fact of there being two No. 10 cans in existence was not notified in the course instructions. In the event, it should come as no surprise to the
Sailing Sub-Committee that some (perhaps even just one) competitor innocently sailed what was, in fact, a proper course as instructed even though
it later transpired it was not the intended course. At the time of writing, Maggie and I are quite happy to retire from the race whatever our position.

Following a proper course - part 2:-

Commodore Clive Shenton's notes in recent issues of Navigans and Sue Amold's letter make interesting reading.

Clive's original question was "How would you feel about paying another £50 per year to pay for a really excellent shore based clubhouse”. “Not a
lot" might have been my reaction, I had no detail or idea of why it might be necessary to charge me an extra £50 subscription each year to improve
upon that which I already consider to be generally adequate shore-based facilities. | will need to know "why, where, when and how" of the plan in
detail - in that order - before even considering saying "Yes".

As a not particularly active member, I am generally content to have a place to park my dinghy, a loo to use when nature demands (complete with loo
paper!), somewhere to change and hot water to shower. I regard these as the essential services, together with a reasonably safe and clean
environment, which ought ultimately (even if indirectly) be provided by Marconi Athletic and Social Club to members of its Sailing Section. I
would be more interested in upgraded changing rooms rather than an upgraded bar but I'm not sure if either are worth an extra charge of £50 on my
annual subscription - but I could be persuaded.

Five-year long term plans and ‘wish lists’ are nothing new in the club but it is good to see that the debate continues.

I look forward to the outcome of this particular exercise and hope | will be able to keep an open mind on whatever ‘new ideas’ are forthcoming.
Perhaps, when the real 50th anniversary comes around, we'll be able to look as eagerly to the future as we can look back with pride on our past.

Defining the proper course:-

With reference to ‘following proper course’ (be it literal or metaphorical) I hope it will not continue to be the assumption that “everybody knows". A
fair number of us ordinary members are not as aware of factors affecting club affairs and activities as we ought to be, despite the best efforts and
beliefs of those in charge. ‘Tis nobody's particular fault - merely one of those difficult facts of club life that those in charge must continually bear in
mind.

Mike Boreham

SOLO TUNING GUIDE

Mast Position The distance from the front of the mast at the heel to the outside of the transom at the floor is 3055mm.

Forestay This should be just in tension when the mast (without sail) is pushed to the back of the gate.

Shrouds These should be just in tension when the mast (without sail) is 10mm from the front of the gate.

Chock Use one chock which just fits in front or behind the mast .

Light airs Up to just sitting on the side deck.

Upwind
Chock behind the mast.
No cunningham.
Centreboard 25-50 mm of forward rake.
Outhaul 20mm from black band.
Kicker just slack
Traveller 0-50mm from centreline.
A small amount of leeward heel is acceptable.

Off wind
Use only enough centreboard to keep the rudder neutral.
Leave outhaul on it’s upwind setting.
Use enough kicker to stop the boom rising in gusts.

Medium Airs Up to fully hiked

Upwind
Chock in front of mast.
No cunningham.
Centreboard vertical.
Outhaul 10mm from black band.
Kicker just slack
Traveller 0-100mm from centreline.
Increase mainsheet tension as the traveller moves away from the centreline.

Offwind
As for light airs except :
Ease outhaul up to 100mm
Use enough kicker to keep the back of the top batten parallel to the boom.

Heavy Airs Fully hiked overpowered.

Upwind
Remove chock
Use cunningham to progressively depower the sail (too much and pointing will suffer) Lift centreboard progressively to reduce weather helm.
Outhaul to the black band.
Kicker just tight.
Ease traveller up to 380mm from the centreline to keep the boat footing - but pull it closer to the centreline in
flatter areas to maintain pointing.
Use more kicker if the mainsheet needs to be cased often in gusts

Offwind
Same as medium airs except only case outhaul and cunningham if more power is needed.

Cruiser Racing News

The Race during the Burnham Rally was changed to a cruise in company to the Ferry Boat Inn at Fambridge. Approximately 30
people sailed aboard Gabelle, West Marie, Killara 2 and Ocean Slipper, in strong winds, with the usual alcoholic refreshments at the
pub!

The Steeple Bay Trophy, was contested by 12 yachts on the traditional Steeple Bay SC course around Osea Island As expected it
proved attractive to the smaller yachts, and included our first catamaran entry, Mr Clark’s Hirondelle Claneda. The fleet rounded the
green buoy at the end of the Osea spit and then found they needed to beat upwind to keep clear of the spit itself. The catamaran
showed its reaching/running potential by moving ahead of the fleet by the top of the island, however on the beat back it was ‘reeled
in’ by the windward performance of Roger Brown’s Seal 26 ‘Out of Focus’ and Dave Payne’s Sonata ‘Live Wire’. The Seal just beat
the Sonata to the line with Robin Lovett’s Moonfleet and the cat arriving soon after, but it was the performance of the slower yachts
which provided the surprise. John Walker’s Snapdragon, John Easton’ Westerly Pageant, J.Burgoyne’s Jaguar 22. and the Vivacity
21, all achieved a good result. Eric Cockerton’s Griffon, Jess and Sophie’s Contessa 26, and Chris Davies’s Hunter Duette completed
the field....... and the winner?....Colin Leveridge in the Debutante ‘Bluster’.

The next races offer the prospect of longer distances.
July 11th Cruiser race 2 starts at 10.00am and we have the opportunity to set a course from the published list for perhaps 4-5 hours
duration.
August 28" is the passage race to Shotley for the club Rally starting at 13.00hrs (HW 14.32)
September 18" The Big One, ‘The Medusa Race’ to Medusa Buoy and back to Bradwell starting at 6.30am (HW Stansgate).
Colin Leveridge has sportingly promised, he will enter this long distance event, so come on, who can beat him?

Good Sailing................ Frank Burgess, Ocean Slipper.

Attention all GPS Users.

First the good news. GPS Systems do not have a Year 2000 problem.
Now the bad news, some may have a 21st August 1999 problem!

The following information was received over the Internet. A US Air Force worker noticed that there was no mention of any field in
any GPS message to tell him which 1024 week cycle he was in.
Guess when week 1025 arrives? Yes 21st August 1999,

The Air Force worker contacted GPS Companies in the USA, some of whom were aware of the problem, some were not. Apparently
manufacturers who were aware of the problem kept quiet in the hope of putting some of their rivals out of business.

This will be of scant comfort to our cruisers returning from Holland on 22nd August 1999. Perhaps a check with your GPS
manufacturer might be a good idea.

One last piece of advice from our helpful American friend - don’t travel on 22nd August 1999, unless you have a sextant with you.

Commodores Notes

Its July already and I expect it will be August and Camping Fortnight before you are reading this.

Alex and I have been on our travels again, this time it was the ARTI cat race around the Isle of Wight. Two other Marconi boats joined
us, helmed by Phil Longhurst with Marcus and Paul Harrison with Michele. We all finished safely in about mid order in times of
around 9 2 hours. The sailing was very varied, with many calms but a good 3-4 geneker reach from St. Catherine's to the Needles. An
unusual feature of the area was the several overfalls at headlands where the sea was very confused, flat one second and boiling, swirling
and breaking the next, accompanied by a calm. We expected a sea monster to rise up and eat us like a sixties sci-fi film. So, it was
better than Texel for us, but still room for improvement. Phil is already getting together the 'posse’ for next year.

I want to remind you about your ‘wish list’ for the Five Year Plan as set out in the June edition of Navigans. You have until mid August
to tell me, your Fleet Captain or a Main Committee member, the direction you would like to see the Club take over the next five years.
I have had several people tell me that they like the Club like it is, and they don’t want improvements. This is a legitimate opinion and
should be expressed. However most responses so far have wanted some improvements somewhere, and it is the purpose of the Plan to
first assemble all ideas(whichI refer to as the wish list for short) and then to structure, costs and prioritise the list. The Main Committee
will begin this task at the early September meeting, hence the deadline of mid August.
We anticipate that much discussion will take place during Camping Fortnight to enable members to clarify their views. If you don't let
us know your views they are unlikely to be actioned within the next five years, so make sure you tell someone. Views should be in
writing or email as verbal opinions are very difficult to correlate.

I make no apology for repeating my warning of last month about the Club bars. The Main Committee is determined to ensure that the
licensing laws are followed. The Bar Supervisors have the full backing of the Main Committee, when they say the bar will close, that is
what they mean. The rules will be posted in the bars and a copy is included in this edition.

Now to something a little bizarre - Mooring E7. Leonard Scholl, who is allocated this mooring, is convinced that the mooring has been
tampered with in some way, causing the anchors to break free and cause a hazard. Neither the Executive nor the Moorings sub
committee can find any logic or motivation for such an act. If you have any information please contact me.
I am very keen to get to the bottom of this one.

The Piers Race is less than two weeks away and its all systems go. My thanks, as always, go to Lee Harrison, Charles Anderson and
their hard working ECPR Committee. My equally heartfelt thanks go to the Cruiser fleet and to every other fleet, except the Cats, who
give up their weekend so the glory boys can race. Thank you all. All we need now is a good wind and reasonably fine weather and the
Cirdan Trust should be anticipating another sizeable donation.

See you on the water, have a good summer's sailing,

24 yachts gathered at the start line off Osea to race for the Blackwater Challenge Trophy. The fleet was equally split between
Maldon Little Ship Club, and Marconi plus a lone competitor from Colne Yacht Club, and comprised a variety of designs from Maxi,
Sadler, Hustler, and Carter, to Folksong, Contest, Westerly, Newbridge, Sabre, Hunter, with also a ferro ketch a Yachting World 5
Topper, and ‘our’ Debutante.
The race started in an Easterly F5-6 wind, which made a heavy beat to the Bench Head, and with wind against tide conditions, it was
pretty rough. The course then took the fleet out to the North Eagle where it got rougher! finishing at Batemans Tower in the Colne.
Line honours were taken by Derek and Hillary in Killara, with Ray Bailey's Hartley, and Mike and Graham’s Sea Brume close behind,
but it was a beautifully restored Y.W. 5 ton expertly sailed single handed, by Mike McCarthy of Maldon Little Ship Club that won on
handicap.
In the evening 60 members from the Colne, Maldon Little Ship, and Marconi clubs dined together at Colne Yacht Club to celebrate the
event with prizes being awarded by the sponsor Leisure Harbours Ltd to, Elfreda and Sea Brume.
Special thanks go to Ray and Maureen Ball with Rear Commodore Jenny for the Committee Boat start with their Centaur “Any Jack’.
The keynotes, were the enjoyment people derived from the race, the evening celebration (assisted by the free wine issue), and the high
completion rate by Marconi yachts.
I am certain the event will be bigger next year, I am also certain that Marconi is the fleet to beat!
