SOLOS AT MARCONI

Marconi Sailing Club held it's annual Solo Open Meeting as part of the Eastern Travellers Series on Sunday 27th June. 25 Solos,
comprising of 14 visitors and 11 club members, arrived at the club on the River Blackwater Estuary in cool, showery and overcast
conditions in stark contrast to the beautiful weather on Saturday.

Mike Turner, the Race Officer, ably assisted by Kate Williams, Richard Green and others, set long courses to cover the area of the river
normally sailed by Marconi to allow visitors to experience the full range of our great site. The first race was held in a gusty force 4 over
a choppy sea. A kerfuffle at the start resulted in the capsize of two prominent visitors and Steve Ede set the pace to round the first mark
in the lead. In the long broad reach against the tide to No. 1 mark, he decided to battle it out against the tide in the middle of the river,
whereas others tried to keep out of the tide by taking the longer route along the shore. Steve Ede still prevailed however and led the
race to the finish followed by Jerry Garner and Tony Cook. John Salmon, showing good speed in his new boat was 4th.

Following back to back, the second race was over the same course as the first, the difference being that the tide changed halfway
through the race. The lead changed several times but eventually Steve Ede came through again for another first place, this time
followed by Mike Wilkie and Tony Cook. The changing tides caused many reversals and changes of places throughout the fleet, as
people who had overstood the 3rd mark in the first race found that they could not lay it this time. John Salmon was again the best
placed Marconi helm at 5th, with Doug Eyles showing a creditable 8th place.

After the break the wind has eased slightly and the third race followed a similar course against the ebbing tide. This time Mike Wilkie
established an early lead and held it to the finish. Steve Ede came second, making him the overall winner. Jerry Garner was third giving
him second overall. John Salmon was 5th again with Doug Eyles and Steve Ash again showing well. Steve Monks had a good outing in
the Club Solo, now watertight following some homework by Fleet Captain Geoff Josey.

Results: 1st 4226, Steve Ede, Ardleigh S.C. 2nd 4189; Jerry Garner, Littleton S.C. 3rd 4150; Tony Cook, Littleton S.C. 4th 4005;
John Salmon, Marconi S.C. 5th 4190; Mike Wilkie, Littleton S.C. 6th 4210; Gordon Barclay, Chichester Y.C.

CADET WEEK 1999

As most people will now know, Cadet week 1999 was to be our swan song. After seven years of running the event, we were hoping
for a good turn-out of Cadets, an excellent offering of well-maintained boats and weather which graduated from flat calm for capsize
drill on Monday to something more demanding at the end of the week. It is truly astonishing to report that we got virtually everything
we wished for.

We were once again able to borrow a selection of boats from the Laser Centre to enhance what has become an extensive and well-
presented fleet of club-owned Cadet boats. During the week we had use of Mirrors, Picos, Toppers, 420s, Lasers, Laser 2, Byte,
Laser Fun and Wayfarers - all owned by club members. These were augmented by 5 Picos and a showroom-fresh Laser 3000, The
rhubarb and custard colours of some of the Picos added vibrancy to the overall scene.

The ability to source a number of high-performance dinghies this year provided Jenny Ball, Claire Davies, Lucy Boreham and Mark
Bulkley with an exciting opportunity to introduce some of the older Cadets to spinnakers and trapeze work. For this quite sizeable
group there was also great attention given to racing starts and race techniques.

The remaining 45 or so youngsters were divided into a Beginners section and a much larger Intermediate group. The Intermediates
were sub-divided in to nine tutor groups for work both ashore and afloat. They developed their sailing skills in Mirror dinghies,
usually sailing in pairs accompanied by their tutor, and the more confident Cadets were able to move on to helm Toppers at the end
of the week. The Beginners’ activities for the most part mirrored those of their more experienced friends and relations but were
carried out in larger groups aboard the Wayfarers and other large dinghies.

We are not always blessed with weather and tide conditions which allow an Osea Outing and a Thirslet Treat in one and the same
Cadet Week. In 1999 we enjoyed picnics at both locations, with excellent racing out and back on both occasions. Miraculously,
everyone concerned was re-united with their own lunch pack on arrival and, unusually, we got off Thirslet before Charles and I were
knee-deep on the highest point of the spit!

Having been blessed with an annually expanding Cadet section, we now find ourselves doubly blessed by the addition of a Cadet
Centre for the club. Full credit for this must go to Debbie and Steve Glynn; their work and negotiation skills with British Petroleum
enabled us to acquire this large cabin free, yes completely free. As with any negotiation, it takes two to tango and our unbounded
gratitude must go to Lindsay Walker of BP for his great support (not least of which included talking to Debbie a lot) in securing such
a favourable arrangement.

As usual, we held the awards ceremony on Saturday (see end of report) and we were delighted that Lindsay was able to join us to
present the trophies to the lucky Cadets. This presentation was then followed by a naming ceremony for the BP Cabin (see photo in
August Y&Y), which again was performed by Lindsay Walker. After popular acclaim, and as the scissors hovered over the ribbon,
the sealed envelope was ripped open to reveal that it was to be known as ‘Jabbah’.
( Please don’t ask either of us oldies why - all enquiries to [redacted] ).

Formalities over, a very successful under-18s Regatta was held in which 36 dinghies took part . There were visiting boats from
Blackwater SC, Harlow SC, and Brandyhole SC to join us in good racing in variable conditions. We even signed-up the Brandyhole
Cadets Joshua, Jerram and Joseph; we are pleased to welcome them as members of the Cadet section and secretly we think dad (John
Bird) will join as as well.

Cadet Week 1999 for us will be especially memorable for having produced the best possible combination of support, circumstances
and conditions that we could have wished for. The support of our ever-willing and oh-so-patient tutors is a crucial factor to Cadet
Weeks as we know them. Our gratitude is immense and so our alphabetical thanks go to Rupert Anderson, Thomas Anderson, Ben

The Dismasting Of "TAHITI"

It was to be for us a cruise to Brightlingsea following a chase with several yachts taking part and then once there we were
to split from the rest of the fleet as we had been invited to a wedding reception in Wivenhoe, just 15 minutes by bus.

The breeze being an easterly 3-4 with a bit of north in it was adequate for a good beat down river. The event was due to
start at 13.30 hours, we were soon ship shape and heading out towards the start, luffing up in a stiff breeze opposite Osea
Island. Suddenly "BANG", in a split second mast, sails and rigging were over to port side , Pauline and I were
momentarily stunned but fortunately unhurt. Then I saw the base of the starboard lower stay toggle with nothing
attached to it, the toggle had parted putting all the pressure at the top of the mast making it banana shaped and breaking
just below the cross trees. Checking to see that no rigging was near the prop, I started the engine and slowly edged our
way over towards Osea Island where I could safely drop anchor and take stock of the situation. Our first task was to get
the sails from the mast, boom and forestay. "Want some help there" a voice from a yacht circling us. I think we can
manage thank you, "are you sure". Yes, but he continued slowly circling. Then Jenny and Ray came over in their avon
to assist. As they were near to the water they started to sort out the masses of rigging over the side. The circling yacht
now came along side. I'm John from the Little Ship Sailing Club, this happened to me some time ago, I think I may be of
some use.

Welcome aboard we said, within two hours everything was sorted out and the mast lashed down. Poor Tahiti looking a
sorry sight headed back to our mooring reflecting our luck of not being out in the open sea and nobody had been hurt.
We did eventually get to the wedding, only 2 hours late!!

Next day I contacted St Margarets Insurance and after weeks of haggling got a fair settlement from them. The problem
was the grey area of the age of the rigging and when it should be replaced, it depends on the type of yacht and how it is
used. There are no hard and fast rules governing the situation. The surveyors recommend every 10 years for
replacement and my rigging was 15 years old.

Finally we would like to thank everybody who helped to get Tahiti back sailing again, especially

Medusa Race September 18TM Start 6.30am.
A doom laden forecast discouraged many entrants, but 6 yachts came to the line at high-water, to start for the Medusa Race. With a F5-6 South Easterly Sea Gem and Live Wire were sent on a less exposed course to Colne No 16 upriver from Pyfleet via the Bench Head, returning to Bradwell the same way. Both boats had a heavy return beat out of the Colne, Dave Payne and his crew in Live Wire reaching Bradwell first, but beaten on handicap by John Easton single handing Sea Gem.
On the Medusa course Derek and Hilary with Dave Stewart in Killara led the fleet down river pursued by Ray Bailey in Hartley, and Mike Turner’s Sea Brume. Frank Burgess with son Mark and Kevin Dowley in Ocean Slipper eventually passed Sea Brume as the fleet ploughed on through the heavy conditions of the Wallet, the fleet reaching the Medusa in 3 hours! The return against a foul tide was very heavy going but the wind remained in the South East providing a close reach, and a final beat to the line at Bradwell. Killara crossed the line first and won the race saving her time on handicap.
An evening in the ‘Bradwell Green Man’ for all the crews rounded off a great race. Congratulations to the winners and well done to all crews for a tough race well sailed.

Commodore’s Report 1998

The main committee has a agreed a five year plan which you will have read about in Navigans. Members

will be aware of the reduction in the size of GEC Marconi and the knock on effect this has on the

membership of the MASC. I have to report that the Rochester Sailing Club lease has not been renewed by

the Company and there are a number of sailors who have had the same experience as Steeple Bay Sailing

Club. I hope all members will think carefully about the future and where Marconi Sailing Club might find

itself in the next few years. If we need to purchase the Sailing Club, we will need to be able to show banks

that we have managed our finances carefully and that the Club is a worthwhile investment.

The club will be presenting about £5000 to the CIRDAN TRUST this year, the PROFITS from the 1998

East Coast Piers Race. This money provides BURSARIES to enable disadvantaged youngsters to experience

life under sail. Thank you Lee Harrison and your committee for organising an excellent event and the

CRUISER fleet members who took their boats out and stayed at the end of an anchor chain acting as Mother

Boats between here and Clacton. Not a pleasant experience so the TA Signal Soldiers found out!

The event can not run safely without the support of many other organisations, so I am sure you would like

me to thank them on your behalf.

I wish to thank the executive team of STEVE HILL, CLIVE SHENTON, FRANK BENNETT and PETER

BLOOMFIELD for their hard work and support during my tenure as Commodore. I know how much work

you all do to keep the club running smoothly for the members, much of it behind the scenes and unnoticed.

This year Maureen Ball is stepping down as NAVIGANS EDITOR, camping fortnight freezer supervisor
/

cleaner! Maureen has been editor since JULY 1986 a record tenure. I suspect she probably used the

equivalent of quill and parchment to produce the MASTER COPY of Navigans for the printers in those

early days. I know her life became much easier in terms of producing Navigans when the club updated her

P.C. a few years ago. Thank you Maureen for many years typing and NAVIGANS PRODUCTION and

putting up with my late notes!

Another Club stalwart steps down this year. Club House secretary MICK RICHARDSON. Mick has

‘mended’, installed and provided so many things for the club it would take me an age to mention them all.

What I appreciate about Mick is he never says no and I always felt he was glad to do what ever the job was.

Mick was also kind enough to introduce me to club members and show me round on the few occasions

when I managed to get down to the club as the new member who was also the Commodore. Thank you

Mick.

Finally I would like to thank Steve and Debbie Glynn for organising this years laying up supper. I know that

Debbie spent a lot of time chasing tickets at the last moment as well as producing the seating plans, place

names, menus not to mention organising all these things on the night. It all paid off with a delightful meal,

excellent entertainment from Ian Irving and the disco. 179 people enjoyed a superb evening. Many thanks

Steve and Debbie.

There are many of people who are too numerous to mention by name who work tirelessly for the benefit of

the club and the members so that we can come down here and sail. I hope all of us when we are out sailing

will think of those “behind the scenes folk’ who give up their spare time do make the club work.

My best wishes to you all for the future.

Colin Kidner.

Sailing Secretary's Report 1998 Season

This season started well with all /4 scheduled races in the Spring Points Series being sailed. The weather was not so kind, however, during summer and autumn, causing abandonment of 7 events from the points series. In total 34 of the scheduled 4/ events were sailed, but not always supported by all the classes. The number of boats competing in the Fast and Medium Catamaran, and Handicap fleets, were similar to last year, but the two largest fleets from 1997, Dart 15 and Solo, both suffered major reductions.
Open Meetings for DIS and Solo Classes were again staged successfully by the Club this year. The DIS entry at 16 boats was down on last year, but Peter Tovey and Jenny Ball performed creditably with Peter achieving 2nd Overall. The Solo Open which attracted 15 visitors and 13 club boats was an outstanding event. Roger Smith claimed some notable scalps in finishing 3rd overall in a very competitive fleet. An entry of 80 boats and excellent reaching breezes ensured that the East Coast Piers Race was once again very successful. Guest celebrity Tony Bullimore was starter for the event which was able to sail the full course to Walton pier. The event generated approx. £5000 for charity, and the gratitude of the Club is again due to the many Cruiser Fleet and other members who helped with it's organisation and execution. A notable achievement outside the club was provided by Steve Glynn claiming line honours in the More Race this year.
We now have a skilled and experienced team of race officers and assistants who are a great asset to the Club. They have once again showed this year that their judgement can be relied upon to provide safe and interesting racing for our domestic program and, when required, open meetings as well. All this would of course be impossible without the many members who have supported the racing program by manning or maintaining the rescue boats. My sincere thanks to you all.
Yet again, this year the Wednesday Evening Series has proved to be one of the most popular features of our sailing program, and once more I am indebted to John Weedon for managing that Series and acting as for most of the races.
The structured part of cruiser sailing from the Club has seen three well supported cruises-in-company to Burnham, Shotley, and Woodbridge this year, with up to 26 boats taking part. Cruiser racing within the Club was again centred on the series of events for the Barnacle Trophy, won this year by Nick Beavins of Gaballe. 6 boats took part in the series and it is hoped to expand this number next year. The highlight of the cruiser racing season was the Blackwater Marina Challenge Cup, won by the Marconi boat Ocean Slipper skippered by Frank Burgess.
Both Cruising and Dinghy activities have been enhanced this year by the new membership transferred from the Steeple Bay Club, which has added some spice to the completions, and indeed it was one of these, Steve Monks, who carried off our "Helm of the Year" trophy.
The year has seen a further growth of Cadet activities in the sailing programme with a Summer Points Series sailed along with the regular club races, as well as the Camping Week Series and a total of 29 Cadets took part in these events. This has been a promising step forward under the guidance of a Cadet Management Team appointed a year ago comprising Charles Anderson, Chris Davies, Tim Sweet, Debbie Glynn, Jenny Ball, and Peter Tovey. This team, who deserve our congratulations, have perhaps become an example of what can be achieved by sharing tasks and responsibilities to achieve a specified objective.

John Salmon

At the Main Committee Meeting yesterday the Hon. Treasurer Frank Bennett was able to present the Account for ECPR 99, The
good news is that after making a prudent reserve, we have been able to donate a record total of £5,300 to the Cirdan Trust. This is a
fantastic achievement, Lee Harrison and Charles Anderson and their Team are due hearty congratulations, The Event involves the
whole Club in a concerted effort and we can all take pride in our achievement.

I wish to take an unusual step of singling out one ECPR helper for special mention, he is Graham Sawyer. I did not know until a
week ago that Graham gathers information, collates and prints about 500 copies of the ECPR Programme all at no cost to the Event.

Yachts and Yachting article on the Race, but due to a journalistic error did not get the by-line. Graham has many photographs of Club
events and boats and we are looking at ways of posting them on the web site.

Helm of the Year Final - 9th Oct 99

Once again Navigans sent their roving reporter to Stansgate to cover the contest for this the premier sailing title in the Club’s
calendar. It is contested between the champions of each racing class determined from combined results of spring and summer points
series, and this year the event was further enhanced by inclusion of the champions from Cadet series and Cruiser racing. Hence, the 5
race series had 7 competitors, and was sailed this year in Picos. The wind was somewhat variable but generally about force 3. The
choice of boat was well received by the competitors as their performance seemed very closely matched and they are a little more
comfortable and buoyant for the larger competitors than the Toppers used in the recent past. To ensure fairness the boats were rotated
between competitors after each race. One race result discard was allowed.

Only Phil Longhurst from the fleet qualifiers was unavailable, and his place was taken by Tim Wallace, so the contestants were:-
Sarah Davies (Cadet); Frank Burgess (Cruiser); Roger Smith (Solo); Steve Monks (H’cap), Jenny Ball (D15), Paul Ellis (Med
Cat); Tim Wallace (Fast Cat),

The event was staged using committee boat starts, and , in the morning, for the first 3 races, short courses around No.1 and M mark
were used with a wing mark just off the hard providing the enthusiastic band of followers excellent viewing.
Race 1 Defending champion Steve made the best start but was passed on the first beat by Roger who extended his lead through to the
finish. Tim who started well behind having been caught in stays at the start, made an excellent recovery to sail through to a close
third.
Race 2 brought a perfectly timed fast start from Jenny at the committee boat end, and she Red the fleet away, but Frank sailed fast up
the middle of the course to round the windward mark first. Jenny then provided the first capsize of the day on the broad reach,
dropping to the back of the fleet. Steve, Roger, and Sarah, all showed good reaching speed and finished the first lap in that order.
Roger passed Steve on the final run but Steve fought back with a tighter gybe round the leeward mark and held hi« slight advantage
to the finish. Paul, after a poor start, showed good boat speed to work his way through the fleet to finish a close third.
Race 3 Roger and Steve again led the fleet up the beat, with Steve establishing an advantage at the windward mark. On a revised
course the positions at the end of the first lap were Steve from Tim, Sarah, Paul, Roger, Frank, and Jenny, and this was still the order
at the finish except for a late surge by Jenny to take her past Frank.
After lunch a strong ebbing tide had developed, which together with temporarily depleted wind caused the next start to be aborted.
The R.O. decided to reset the course around the headland in Stansgate bay where there was less tide, and here the final 2 races were
successfully completed.
Race 4 saw Steve demonstrate another blistering start and at the windward mark it was Steve from Tim and Frank. On the second
beat Tim passed Steve into the lead while Jenny moved into third. Tim and Steve held position to the finish but Frank fought back to
recapture third.
Race was a Steve Monks demonstration run, leading off the line and building a huge lead round the course to finish entirely
unchallenged and claim the Helm of the Year title for the second year running. Behind him various penalties were executed around
the course but Jenny fought through for a good second place, while Frank chalked up his second successive third to demonstrate that
he was beginning to feel more at home in the Pico. Thus ended the event, in which all the competitors deserve credit for keenly
contesting the series in a good spirit.

much as is possible from your boat and always remember to lock your ladder up, not only to protect your boat but also others. Any
ladders found unlocked will be removed and locked up in the cruiser garage.

Winter is a time when many of us review the equipment we have with a view to updating it in time for next years sailing, so if you
are worried about your VHF set being suitable for emergencies in the move towards GMDSS (global maritime distress and safety
system). The International Maritime Organisation have agreed that ships keep a mandatory radio-listening watch on VHF Channel
16 until February 2005, Ships were due to cease keeping watch on VHF 16 last February.

CLANEDA LOG - THE LOG WITH A DIFFERENCE !

SHOTLEY/WOODBRIDGE CRUISE 1999

Friday 27th August 1999 At 5.15 is when we got here.
There's a huge queue at Shotley, awaiting the lock,
We arrived at the Clubhouse at half past one, An hour or so later, we looked at the clock, Only to find that many had gone. Helped by the 'Kirbys’, securely we tied, "Is there racing tomorrow?". we asked. So Eric and Pauline could raft alongside. "We are", said Eric*, "we've got a new mast!" Twenty-two boats are expected here soon, Claneda is laden, the beer stowed below, All from Marconi, along this pontoon. "But how can we race, when we're floating so low? After our supper, we went for a drink Let's drink some tonight with Pauline and Eric*, With Eric and Pauline and John, I think. (But leave some for Shotley for Doreen and Derek!"**) Before we return, it's twenty to one, The flag of the Dell Bar we noticed at ten, The company here is second to none.
So over we went to start drinking again!
(*Claneda) (**Sea Gem)
(*Tahiti) (**Happy Medium))
Sunday 29th August 1999
Saturday 28th August 1999
The sun's shining brightly, the sky is all blue,
Today's Eric's birthday, not a cloud in the sky, "Must I really have bacon and eggs like you?"
The sea's like a mill pond - "Let's motor!", said I. A walk of five miles, our legs feeling heavy,
We're still on our moorings, but Allan's* ashore, We found a good pub and stopped for a ‘bevvy'. Reflection's behind us, Tahiti before. We got back to Shotley in time for our Lunch, I've tidied the boat, I'm now in the sun, And there at the ‘Bristol’ was the rest of the bunch, "You can come back, Allan, the washing up's done!" We rested ourselves in the afternoon heat, We've spoken to Sea Gem, Reflection agrees, If we don't laze about, we'll feel dead on our feet. There's no point in waiting, there's no sign of breeze. We're pacing ourselves for the 'Shipwreck' meal.
John** radioed Live Wire before we departed, We've eaten too much - "How fat I feel!"
There's no race today - we're all broken hearted! A jolly good time was had by all,
They do us proud, this port of call.
We set off in convoy close to midday
And soon on the radio, we heard Christine May. Monday 30th August 1999 Shamaal's on her mooring, as we motor near,
She's coming to join us; she'll bring up the rear. It's sunny again, how long can it last? We caught Out of Focus by Bradwell Marina, The Bradwell boats have all sneaked past.
That's seven at least, now that we've seen her. Tahiti went too, just after eight, With others, like us, slightly more late,
When just past West Mersea, a slight breeze arose, No waiting around, we're straight in the lock, We hoisted the sails, but it's right on the nose. An hour to catch up, it's gone nine o'clock. The breeze then picked up, we started to beat, There's just a slight breeze, though merely a smidge,
We could have raced now - “Where's the rest of the fleet?" Our engine's still on - but, it's charging the fridge!
John did his best to rally us all, We hoisted the sails and started to reach, But some of them didn't respond to his call. At just about ten, we passed Languard beach. We passed the Bench Head and wrote down our time, By half past eleven, we arrived at the mouth But so far away, you can't see the line. Of the Deben River, most boats heading South.
Tahiti woke up, put his radio on, We took a decision to SAIL over the bar,
"It's not Bench Head, it's Colne Bar!" said John. A beat it was now - "Are we over too far?"
There is some confusion, the times are still real, The bank loomed ere closer, it soon became hairy, We've reached Walton Pier, just ahead is the ‘Seal’. "Quick, start the engine! Phew, that was scary." We finished the race at Dovercourt Pier,

10

At Ramsholt we tied alongside of Eric, There's a crisis at home and our family has ‘phoned. Whilst eating our lunch we must have missed Derek. We're all very tired, so off to our beds, We motored to Woodbridge and who should appear, But not before trying our non-squeaking ‘heads'!
But Derek and Doreen - "How'd you get here?"
We were given a berth at the end of the trot, Thursday 2nd September 1999 But soon we decided it wasn't our slot.
We moved to another as fast as could be, We must set off quite early, the weather's so hazy,
Yet, then moved again - in all that makes three. We must plot our course and not be so lazy.
Some beers were offered aboard Cornish Gold, We can just see the marks, as they start to loom near,
But Gordon was missing - he hadn't been told! The sun's breaking through, let's hope it will clear.
We went for a walk to make a ‘phone call, We reached the Pye End, visibility poor, And picked up the times we can swim at the pool. The telephone rang and we can't see the shore. The evening is quiet, we've heard not a peep, With me on the ‘phone and Allan below, So not it's Goodnight’ and then off to sleep. That wasn't the time to let the helm go! With water all round us and no sign of land,
Tuesday 3ist August 1999 Our sense of direction got out of hand.
The water's so shallow, this cannot be right,
The morning is lovely, the forecast is great, "Oh, why isn't Harwich somewhere in sight?!"
It' bacon and eggs - please, think of my weight! We sorted ourselves and returned to the ~ourse
We went to the pool and had a good swim, With faith in the chart - perhaps we'll learn morse!
Then walked to relations to keep us in trim. Al a quarter past nine, we passed Stone Banks, We shopped for the 'Barbie’ whilst still in the town, The fog is now lifting, for that we give thanks. And then bought more beer to wash it all down! We're sailing with engine, the wind from ahead There were big chips from Bob* and bananas, too, (But why can't it come from behind instead?) And a short burst of singing from Peter and Sue.** At least, for a change, we have a fair tide We said our goodnights and expressed our joy, (But why can't the wind come from the side’”) Then returned to our boats with Margaret and Roy.***
We've got some more news, our Mum's very poorly, (*Icarus) (**Fantasea) (***Serupin II) We're trying our best, we will get back, surely? It's baking hot sunshine, as we motor along,
Wednesday ist September 1999 We cannot see Bradwell - have we gone wrong?
We picked up our mooring with not too much water,
A glorious morning to greet us once more, A trip of six hours, certainly no shorter. It can't last forever, of that I am sure.
We ate up our breakfast and went for a shower, The dinghy is ready, we've no time to lose, "What have we been doing for this last hour?" It's straight to the hospital, the end of our cruise.
We walked to the shops. both Pauline and |,
Whilst Allan and Eric let time pass by.
We ate up our lunch, then got the boat ready
To leave by two twenty and take it quite steady.
We motored down river, the wind dead ahead, CAROL CLARK, "It's only Force 2, though", the harbourman said.
At just sixteen thirty, Reflection arrived,
We crossed over the bar against the foul tide.
Too small is the work jib, the jenny we need, "CLANEDA"
We sailed with the engine to gain extra speed
As we passed Pye End, Green Panther did call,
They're with 4nge/ Two and Derek and all.
We picked up a mooring quite close to the Naze,
Then along came 7ahiti, out of the haze.
They tied alongside us, our meal was a treat,
They cooked the veg, and we cooked the meat!
They gave us some oil to stop our loo squeaking, (Now Allan wants more to stop me from speaking!)
We've got to leave early, our holiday's postponed,
